Researchers on Earth have developed an atmospheric scanning electron microscope (ASEM) platform that delivers ultra-fine precision scans to probe materials with extremely thin interfaces by scanning light over thin layers of nanocrystalline metal or graphite. The system has demonstrated remarkable spatial resolution, enabling probes about 1 micrometer thick to reach features as small as about a thousandth of a hair across an individual hair. A more detailed analysis shows that the scanning technology may be well suited for applications from environmental science to drug discovery, particularly when combined with new generations of microfluidic sensors with superior optical properties.

In this paper, we present a novel framework for certified self-stabilization of distributed systems. Our approach leverages recent advances in formal verification and control theory to provide a rigorous guarantee of stability and convergence for distributed algorithms, even in the presence of faults and malicious behavior.

We introduce a new notion of "certified self-stabilization," which ensures that a system not only converges to a stable state, but also remains stable under arbitrary perturbations and faults. We then develop a framework for achieving certified self-stabilization in distributed systems, which consists of three main components: (1) a formal specification of the desired stability properties, (2) a controller that enforces the specification, and (3) a verification mechanism that guarantees the correctness of the controller.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework through a series of case studies on various distributed algorithms, including consensus protocols and distributed file systems. Our results show that certified self-stabilization can be achieved in a wide range of scenarios, including those with high levels of fault tolerance and security requirements.

Our work makes a significant contribution to the field of distributed systems by providing a formal framework for ensuring stability and convergence in the presence of faults and malicious behavior. The framework proposed in this paper can be applied to a wide range of distributed systems, including those used in critical infrastructure, such as power grids and transportation systems, and can help ensure their reliability and security.

In this study, we report on the electrochemical reactions in single-layer molybdenum disulfide (MoS2) nanosheets, where nanopores were openened atom by atom. Using a combination of experimental and computational methods, we investigated the electrochemical activity of MoS2 nanosheets in various electrolytes and demonstrated the formation of nanopores through the atomic layer. The results show that the electrochemical reactivity of MoS2 is highly dependent on the type of electrolyte used, with some electrolytes promoting the formation of larger nanopores than others. Atomic simulations revealed that the opening of nanopores occurs through a concerted mechanism involving the coordination of sulfur atoms with the electrolyte ions. Our findings provide new insights into the electrochemical properties of two-dimensional materials and pave the way for further exploration of their potential applications in energy storage and conversion devices.

Abstract


This paper investigates two fundamental questions, namely (i) how accurately one can make reliable, exact reconstructions of graphs (in graph theory) given their degree-4 sum-of-squares hierarchy (which is a particular representation scheme but may be well approximated by some other such schemes not discussed here), and


(ii) how it generally works at different types of computational problems - in contrast to, e.g., ordinary linear programming, which has no such question at all. The answers provide insights into the general limitations we encounter compared with classical machine learning techniques when dealing with these representations. We also discuss, among other things, the limits on accuracy that this approach imposes. At some cases we show examples where certain sub-optimal solutions are obtained because our reconstruction algorithm cannot converge rapidly enough or reliably close the precision-vs.-accuracy trade-off between accuracy and computation time. Finally, we present new experimental results showing that even after several iterations the result remains rather stable under different statistical/statistical inference rules for our representations.

We introduce a deep learning image segmentation framework that is extremely
robust to missing imaging modalities. Instead of attempting to impute or
synthesize missing data, the proposed approach learns, for each modality, an
embedding of the input image into a single latent vector space for which
arithmetic operations (such as taking the mean) are well defined. Points in
that space, which are averaged over modalities available at inference time, can
then be further processed to yield the desired segmentation. As such, any
combinatorial subset of available modalities can be provided as input, without
having to learn a combinatorial number of imputation models. Evaluated on two
neurological MRI datasets (brain tumors and MS lesions), the approach yields
state-of-the-art segmentation results when provided with all modalities;
moreover, its performance degrades remarkably gracefully when modalities are
removed, significantly more so than alternative mean-filling or other synthesis
approaches.

Recently, Fully Convolutional Network (FCN) seems to be the go-to
architecture for image segmentation, including semantic scene parsing. However,
it is difficult for a generic FCN to discriminate pixels around the object
boundaries, thus FCN based methods may output parsing results with inaccurate
boundaries. Meanwhile, level set based active contours are superior to the
boundary estimation due to the sub-pixel accuracy that they achieve. However,
they are quite sensitive to initial settings. To address these limitations, in
this paper we propose a novel Deep Multiphase Level Set (DMLS) method for
semantic scene parsing, which efficiently incorporates multiphase level sets
into deep neural networks. The proposed method consists of three modules, i.e.,
recurrent FCNs, adaptive multiphase level set, and deeply supervised learning.
More specifically, recurrent FCNs learn multi-level representations of input
images with different contexts. Adaptive multiphase level set drives the
discriminative contour for each semantic class, which makes use of the
advantages of both global and local information. In each time-step of the
recurrent FCNs, deeply supervised learning is incorporated for model training.
Extensive experiments on three public benchmarks have shown that our proposed
method achieves new state-of-the-art performances.

Generative adversarial networks (GANs) have shown great success in
applications such as image generation and inpainting. However, they typically
require large datasets, which are often not available, especially in the
context of prediction tasks such as image segmentation that require labels.
Therefore, methods such as the CycleGAN use more easily available unlabelled
data, but do not offer a way to leverage additional labelled data for improved
performance. To address this shortcoming, we show how to factorise the joint
data distribution into a set of lower-dimensional distributions along with
their dependencies. This allows splitting the discriminator in a GAN into
multiple "sub-discriminators" that can be independently trained from incomplete
observations. Their outputs can be combined to estimate the density ratio
between the joint real and the generator distribution, which enables training
generators as in the original GAN framework. We apply our method to image
generation, image segmentation and audio source separation, and obtain improved
performance over a standard GAN when additional incomplete training examples
are available. For the Cityscapes segmentation task in particular, our method
also improves accuracy by an absolute 14.9% over CycleGAN while using only 25
additional paired examples.

Open-set person re-identification is a challenging problem in computer vision that involves identifying individuals across multiple camera views, even when some individuals may not be present in all views. This is in contrast to traditional closed-set person re-identification, where all individuals are present in all views. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to open-set person re-identification, which leverages a combination of deep learning and domain adaptation techniques.

Our approach consists of two main components: a domain adaptation module and a person re-identification module. The domain adaptation module is used to adapt the feature representations of individuals across different camera views, while the person re-identification module is used to match individuals across views. We train our model on a large-scale dataset of synthetic images, and evaluate its performance on several real-world datasets.

The main contribution of this paper is the introduction of a new loss function that is specifically designed for open-set person re-identification. This loss function takes into account the fact that some individuals may not be present in all views, and encourages the model to produce high-quality embeddings for both seen and unseen individuals. We also propose a novel evaluation metric that is better suited for open-set person re-identification, which takes into account the fact that some individuals may not be present in all views.

Our experiments show that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods on several benchmark datasets, and is able to handle a large number of camera views and individuals. We also perform a series of ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of different components of our approach, and demonstrate that our domain adaptation module and loss function are crucial for achieving good performance.

Overall, this paper makes an important contribution to the field of open-set person re-identification, and demonstrates the effectiveness of using domain adaptation and deep learning techniques for this task. Our approach has important applications in real-world scenarios, such as surveillance and human-computer interaction.

This paper proposes a novel approach to image segmentation based on overlapping group sparsity. The proposed method leverages the idea that images can be represented as a collection of groups, where each group consists of pixels that are similar in intensity or color. By imposing sparsity constraints on these groups, we can encourage the algorithm to identify meaningful regions in the image.

The key innovation of our approach is the use of overlapping groups, which allows us to capture complex structures and patterns in the image. Unlike traditional non-overlapping methods, our approach does not require artificial boundary enforcement between groups, leading to more accurate and efficient segmentation results.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through extensive experiments on various benchmark datasets. Our results show significant improvements over state-of-the-art algorithms, including both non-overlapping and overlapping methods. We also provide a thorough analysis of the computational complexity of our approach and show that it scales linearly with the number of pixels in the image.

Our work has important implications for applications such as object recognition, tracking, and scene understanding, where accurate image segmentation is a critical component. Additionally, the proposed method provides a new perspective on sparse representation, which could lead to further advances in signal processing and machine learning.

This paper proposes a novel approach for improving the efficiency of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for pixelwise classification tasks. The proposed method leverages the concept of forward and backward propagation to enhance the accuracy and speed of CNNs.

The authors introduce a new technique called "dual-path propagation" that allows the network to perform both forward and backward propagation simultaneously. This approach enables the network to learn both the forward and backward pass information in a single pass, reducing the computational complexity and memory usage.

The proposed method is evaluated on several benchmark datasets, including CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. The results show that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of accuracy and speed. Specifically, the authors achieve a 10% improvement in accuracy compared to the baseline model on CIFAR-10, while reducing the number of parameters by 50%.

The authors also perform a series of ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results show that the dual-path propagation mechanism is essential for achieving the improved performance. Furthermore, the authors demonstrate that the proposed method can be easily integrated into existing CNN architectures, making it a versatile and practical solution for pixelwise classification tasks.

The main contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows:

* The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of accuracy and speed on several benchmark datasets.
* The authors introduce a novel technique called dual-path propagation that enables the network to perform both forward and backward propagation simultaneously.
* The proposed method reduces the computational complexity and memory usage, making it a practical solution for large-scale pixelwise classification tasks.
* The authors demonstrate the versatility of the proposed method by integrating it into existing CNN architectures.

Overall, this paper provides a significant contribution to the field of computer vision and deep learning, and the proposed method has important implications for a wide range of applications, including image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation.

Current image segmentation techniques usually require that the user tune
several parameters in order to obtain maximum segmentation accuracy, a
computationally inefficient approach, especially when a large number of images
must be processed sequentially in daily practice. The use of evolving fuzzy
systems for designing a method that automatically adjusts parameters to segment
medical images according to the quality expectation of expert users has been
proposed recently (Evolving fuzzy image segmentation EFIS). However, EFIS
suffers from a few limitations when used in practice mainly due to some fixed
parameters. For instance, EFIS depends on auto-detection of the object of
interest for feature calculation, a task that is highly application-dependent.
This shortcoming limits the applicability of EFIS, which was proposed with the
ultimate goal of offering a generic but adjustable segmentation scheme. In this
paper, a new version of EFIS is proposed to overcome these limitations. The new
EFIS, called self-configuring EFIS (SC-EFIS), uses available training data to
self-estimate the parameters that are fixed in EFIS. As well, the proposed
SC-EFIS relies on a feature selection process that does not require
auto-detection of an ROI. The proposed SC-EFIS was evaluated using the same
segmentation algorithms and the same dataset as for EFIS. The results show that
SC-EFIS can provide the same results as EFIS but with a higher level of
automation.

We define a weakly threshold sequence to be a degree sequence
$d=(d_1,\dots,d_n)$ of a graph having the property that $\sum_{i \leq k} d_i
\geq k(k-1)+\sum_{i > k} \min\{k,d_i\} - 1$ for all positive $k \leq
\max\{i:d_i \geq i-1\}$. The weakly threshold graphs are the realizations of
the weakly threshold sequences. The weakly threshold graphs properly include
the threshold graphs and satisfy pleasing extensions of many properties of
threshold graphs. We demonstrate a majorization property of weakly threshold
sequences and an iterative construction algorithm for weakly threshold graphs,
as well as a forbidden induced subgraph characterization. We conclude by
exactly enumerating weakly threshold sequences and graphs.

This Research Paper introduces the use of semi-supervised learning to derive semantic segmentation models, which we compare both on tasks such as human translation (or machine interpretation) and natural language processing applications where there are both high levels of generalisation (i.e., in many cases the same output may appear more than once ) and low level prediction difficulties (a limited number or context free phrase matches in a corpus). We report results comparing four different semi-supervised learning approaches: unsupervised regularising, deep reinforcement learning, neural network based recurrent networks and an extended generative model that includes word embeddings. Our approach does only simple feature extraction with no feature selection and is based on a small family of convolutional layers used by traditional image classification systems. The main findings obtained show that semantically motivated classifiers have significantly lower error rates than previous state-of-the-Art solutions as well as faster convergence when solving larger and more complex problems (in various domains) while having higher performance on some tasks. This shows that an accurate and efficient semantic segmenting algorithm can be built without training labeled data – that is, it avoids having to compute features, preprocessed data through regularisations etc.

The MSiCOR algorithm combines clustering and ensemble techniques to solve sequence correlation problems, in particular with non-convex problems on sequences of random variables (such as sequence alignment), where the total number of positions per sample is not known. In our implementation one must provide a sequence that corresponds exactly to the desired solution in order to cluster it [1]. We describe two implementations based on fast approximation schemes with sparse matrices obtained via an approximate Bayesian linearization method and several other standard optimizations employed by RMS-based solutions of such problems and show how these schemes make generalizations possible when the problem space involves more than 2 or 3 data vectors and to clusters up to a few hundred data points. As clustering does not depend upon any prior knowledge, it will be applicable also to situations beyond this domain – for example the distribution of sequences over N data points.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) are a class of machine learning algorithms that are based on the idea of learning to represent the world in terms of a large number of simple, interconnected, and sparsely connected components. In this paper, we propose a new approach to training DNNs that is based on the idea of learning to segment fluorescent microscopy images. We propose a novel, deep, and efficient method for training DNNs that is based on the idea of learning to segment fluorescent microscopy images. We train a DNN to segment fluorescent microscopy images by first training a DNN to predict the location of a fluorescent microscopy image in a set of images. We then train a DNN to predict the location of a fluorescent microscopy image in a set of images. We show that the proposed method is able to learn to segment fluorescent microscopy images with high accuracy.

Activity of modern scholarship creates online footprints galore. Along with
traditional metrics of research quality, such as citation counts, online images
of researchers and institutions increasingly matter in evaluating academic
impact, decisions about grant allocation, and promotion. We examined 400
biographical Wikipedia articles on academics from four scientific fields to
test if being featured in the world's largest online encyclopedia is correlated
with higher academic notability (assessed through citation counts). We found no
statistically significant correlation between Wikipedia articles metrics
(length, number of edits, number of incoming links from other articles, etc.)
and academic notability of the mentioned researchers. We also did not find any
evidence that the scientists with better WP representation are necessarily more
prominent in their fields. In addition, we inspected the Wikipedia coverage of
notable scientists sampled from Thomson Reuters list of "highly cited
researchers". In each of the examined fields, Wikipedia failed in covering
notable scholars properly. Both findings imply that Wikipedia might be
producing an inaccurate image of academics on the front end of science. By
shedding light on how public perception of academic progress is formed, this
study alerts that a subjective element might have been introduced into the
hitherto structured system of academic evaluation.

Active contouring techniques are well known to reduce spectral artifacts caused by pixel density heterogeneity in a noisy (low‐resolution) imaging volume or by low contrast differences between high and low resolution data, but their scalability with respect to noise does not depend on how many elements they contain and thus the spatial patterning can be difficult to compute. Here we report an effective multi-object-contribution–guided contour interpolation scheme that uses an interleaved active contruction method to compute multiple subsets of sub‐pixel features while preserving fine structure. By taking advantage of simple nonlinearities such as gaussian filter functions based on cross‐coupled phase function mapping it can rapidly compute both accurate spatial patterns at low bandwidths and robust spatiotemporal regularization across higher bandwidth images. The improved results over comparable single component solutions suggest new avenues for multimodal reconstruction of images, provided that the required signal processing power remains affordable. We also show how this approach compares to classical methods without significantly improving visual quality at any frequency band other than the highest one.

We address the problem of segmenting 3D multi-modal medical images in
scenarios where very few labeled examples are available for training.
Leveraging the recent success of adversarial learning for semi-supervised
segmentation, we propose a novel method based on Generative Adversarial
Networks (GANs) to train a segmentation model with both labeled and unlabeled
images. The proposed method prevents over-fitting by learning to discriminate
between true and fake patches obtained by a generator network. Our work extends
current adversarial learning approaches, which focus on 2D single-modality
images, to the more challenging context of 3D volumes of multiple modalities.
The proposed method is evaluated on the problem of segmenting brain MRI from
the iSEG-2017 and MRBrainS 2013 datasets. Significant performance improvement
is reported, compared to state-of-art segmentation networks trained in a
fully-supervised manner. In addition, our work presents a comprehensive
analysis of different GAN architectures for semi-supervised segmentation,
showing recent techniques like feature matching to yield a higher performance
than conventional adversarial training approaches. Our code is publicly
available at https://github.com/arnab39/FewShot_GAN-Unet3D

This study investigates the sources and mechanisms of radioactivity-induced background events in the EXO-200 detector. Through careful analysis, we identify key contributors to this background signal and propose strategies for mitigating their effects on experimental results. Our findings have important implications for future dark matter detection experiments seeking to minimize radioactive contamination and improve sensitivity.

The development of high quality medical image segmentation algorithms depends
on the availability of large datasets with pixel-level labels. The challenges
of collecting such datasets, especially in case of 3D volumes, motivate to
develop approaches that can learn from other types of labels that are cheap to
obtain, e.g. bounding boxes. We focus on 3D medical images with their
corresponding 3D bounding boxes which are considered as series of per-slice
non-tight 2D bounding boxes. While current weakly-supervised approaches that
use 2D bounding boxes as weak labels can be applied to medical image
segmentation, we show that their success is limited in cases when the
assumption about the tightness of the bounding boxes breaks. We propose a new
bounding box correction framework which is trained on a small set of
pixel-level annotations to improve the tightness of a larger set of non-tight
bounding box annotations. The effectiveness of our solution is demonstrated by
evaluating a known weakly-supervised segmentation approach with and without the
proposed bounding box correction algorithm. When the tightness is improved by
our solution, the results of the weakly-supervised segmentation become much
closer to those of the fully-supervised one.

This paper presents a generalized asymmetric dual-front model for active contours and image segmentation. The model extends the traditional symmetric dual-front model by incorporating an asymmetric term that allows for more efficient and accurate segmentation of images with complex boundaries. The proposed model is validated through extensive experiments on a variety of images, demonstrating its effectiveness in accurately segmenting images with different levels of complexity. Overall, the generalized asymmetric dual-front model provides a powerful tool for image segmentation and active contours applications.

We present a proof of Rider's unpublished result that the union of two Sidon
sets in the dual of a non-commutative compact group is Sidon, and that randomly
Sidon sets are Sidon. Most likely this proof is essentially the one announced
by Rider and communicated in a letter to the author around 1979 (lost by him
since then). The key fact is a spectral gap property with respect to certain
representations of the unitary groups $U(n)$ that holds uniformly over $n$. The
proof crucially uses Weyl's character formulae. We survey the results that we
obtained 30 years ago using Rider's unpublished results. Using a recent
different approach valid for certain orthonormal systems of matrix valued
functions, we give a new proof of the spectral gap property that is required to
show that the union of two Sidon sets is Sidon. The latter proof yields a
rather good quantitative estimate. Several related results are discussed with
possible applications to random matrix theory.

This paper presents a numerical study of a model for a quantum particle interacting with a quantum environment. The model is formulated using the framework of quantum mechanics and is solved using numerical methods. The results provide insights into the behavior of a quantum particle in a quantum environment and have implications for understanding quantum systems and their interactions.

Additive deformations of bialgebras in the sense of Wirth are deformations of
the multiplication map of the bialgebra fulfilling a compatibility condition
with the coalgebra structure and a continuity condition. Two problems
concerning additive deformations are considered. With a deformation theory a
cohomology theory should be developed. Here a variant of the Hochschild
cohomology is used. The main result in the first partad of this paper is the
characterization of the trivial deformations, i.e. deformations generated by a
coboundary. Starting with a Hopf algebra, one would expect the deformed
multiplications to have some analogue of the antipode, which we call deformed
antipodes. We prove, that deformed antipodes always exist, explore their
properties, give a formula to calculate them given the deformation and the
antipode of the original Hopf algebra and show in the cocommutative case, that
each deformation splits into a trivial part and into a part with constant
antipodes.

Abstract: This research experiment examined the effect of users on the volume of tweets about people using several social media networks over time. To this end we observed two types of Twitter accounts in our study (e.g. @tweetmyfriends_1 and @twitmysfriend_1). Using both these user profiles and an indicator that measured their popularity, it was possible to determine changes in Twitter conversation over time due to change of the Twitter user profile. As expected, following both account caused users of each network to be exposed to more conversations than less popular or less-following accounts who also did not follow account. Additionally, since only 10% of all total tweets received during the month were related to two users that had no interaction with other accounts in any way. After being shown how popular @tweetmyfriends_1 was at any given moment between January 2011 to May 2012, we expected increased number of new Tweets received by users following this account over time. In fact, users following @lizbooshuys_5 generated 1.21 times as much new tweets compared to those below them [7], suggesting they gained significant visibility for posting about Liz. Therefore, users of a particular user's accounts are likely to influence the overall behaviour of a target network. Given that one of the key drivers behind the growth of social media sites is the desire among many to show off their celebrity, such information might prove useful in establishing new celebrities online as well.

A collection of $k$ sets is said to form a $k$-sunflower, or $\Delta$-system,
if the intersection of any two sets from the collection is the same, and we
call a family of sets $\mathcal{F}$ sunflower-free if it contains no
sunflowers. Following the recent breakthrough of Ellenberg and Gijswijt and
Croot, Lev and Pach we apply the polynomial method directly to
Erd\H{o}s-Szemer\'{e}di sunflower problem and prove that any sunflower-free
family $\mathcal{F}$ of subsets of $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ has size at most \[
|\mathcal{F}|\leq3n\sum_{k\leq
n/3}\binom{n}{k}\leq\left(\frac{3}{2^{2/3}}\right)^{n(1+o(1))}. \] We say that
a set $A\subset(\mathbb Z/D \mathbb Z)^{n}=\{1,2,\dots,D\}^{n}$ for $D>2$ is
sunflower-free if every distinct triple $x,y,z\in A$ there exists a coordinate
$i$ where exactly two of $x_{i},y_{i},z_{i}$ are equal. Using a version of the

The social force model has been widely used to simulate pedestrian dynamics and evacuation scenarios. However, existing studies have largely assume that these social forces remain constant over time, leading to stationary crowd behavior.

In this study, we investigate the effect of non-stationary social forces on evacuation dynamics using agent-based simulations. Specifically, we consider how changes in the strengths of the repulsive and attractive forces over time affect the evacuation time and the formation of bottlenecks. Our results show that evacuation times can be significantly affected by time-variant social forces, leading to either faster or slower evacuations depending on the nature of the change. We also find that the formation of bottlenecks is strongly influenced by the time evolution of the social forces, with dynamically changing forces leading to more frequent and severe bottlenecks.

Our findings suggest that assuming stationarity in the social force model may lead to inaccurate predictions of evacuation behavior in dynamic environments. Instead, incorporating time-dependent social forces into the model yields more realistic outcomes that account for the adaptable nature of human behavior during emergency situations. This work has practical implications for improving evacuation safety and efficiency through better design of building layouts and evacuation protocols.

Accurate segmentation of medical images into anatomically meaningful regions
is critical for the extraction of quantitative indices or biomarkers. The
common pipeline for segmentation comprises regions of interest detection stage
and segmentation stage, which are independent of each other and typically
performed using separate deep learning networks. The performance of the
segmentation stage highly relies on the extracted set of spatial features and
the receptive fields. In this work, we propose an end-to-end network, called
Trilateral Attention Network (TaNet), for real-time detection and segmentation
in medical images. TaNet has a module for region localization, and three
segmentation pathways: 1) handcrafted pathway with hand-designed convolutional
kernels, 2) detail pathway with regular convolutional kernels, and 3) a global
pathway to enlarge the receptive field. The first two pathways encode rich
handcrafted and low-level features extracted by hand-designed and regular
kernels while the global pathway encodes high-level context information. By
jointly training the network for localization and segmentation using different
sets of features, TaNet achieved superior performance, in terms of accuracy and
speed, when evaluated on an echocardiography dataset for cardiac segmentation.
The code and models will be made publicly available in TaNet Github page.

In this paper, we present a novel approach for increasing the analytical accessibility of multishell and diffusion spectrum imaging (DSI) data using generalized Q-sampling conversion. DSI is a widely used MRI technique that provides valuable information about tissue microstructure, but its analysis remains challenging due to the complexity of the data. Traditional methods for analyzing DSI data often rely on simplifying assumptions, such as Gaussian diffusion or spherical harmonic representations, which limit the accuracy and robustness of the results.

Here, we propose a new method called generalized Q-sampling conversion, which enables the efficient and flexible representation of DSI data in a more analytically tractable form. By leveraging recent advances in compressive sensing and machine learning, our method can accurately reconstruct high-quality Q-ball images from undersampled DSI data, thereby reducing the acquisition time and improving the computational efficiency of DSI analyses.

We validate our approach using simulations and experimental data, demonstrating improved performance compared to traditional methods in terms of reconstruction error, computation time, and resistance to noise. Moreover, we show that our method can be easily extended to other types of diffusion-weighted imagingdata, including multi-shell DSI and High Angular Resolution Diffusion Imaging (HARDI).

Our work has important implications for various fields, including neuroscience, cancer research, and materials science, where DSI plays a critical role in studying brain connectivity, tumor progression, and material properties. The proposed method has the potential to facilitate new studies and insights by making DSI data analysis more accessible, efficient, and accurate.

Abstract:

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to image registration called NeurReg, which leverages deep neural networks to learn a mapping between images. Unlike traditional methods that rely on hand-crafted features and optimization techniques, our approach learns a direct mapping from input images to their corresponding registered versions. This allows us to achieve state-of-the-art performance on various registration tasks while also providing interpretability into the learned transformations.

We evaluate NeurReg on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate its superiority over existing methods in terms of both registration accuracy and computational efficiency. Furthermore, we explore the application of NeurReg to image segmentation tasks, where it achieves promising results by exploiting the preserved spatial information in the registered images. Our experiments show that NeurReg can accurately segment objects even when the training data is limited or contains variations in pose, illumination, or occlusion.

The key contribution of this work lies in the introduction of a deep learning framework for image registration, which not only improves registration precision but also enables a more robust feature extraction process. The presented experiments highlight the potential of NeurReg as a fundamental tool for image processing and computer vision applications.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

1. Introduction of NeurReg, a deep learning-based method for image registration that outperforms conventional approaches in term of accuracy and efficiency.
2. Demonstration of NeurReg's versatility through its application to diverse registration tasks (rigid, affine, and deformable) and dataset scenarios.
3. Exploration of NeurReg's ability to improve image segmentation performances by utilizing the preserved spatial information in registered images.
4. Presentation of comprehensive evaluations and comparisons with state-of-the-art registration methods, exhibiting NeurReg's superiority in various aspects.

We extend first-order model agnostic meta-learning algorithms (including
FOMAML and Reptile) to image segmentation, present a novel neural network
architecture built for fast learning which we call EfficientLab, and leverage a
formal definition of the test error of meta-learning algorithms to decrease
error on out of distribution tasks. We show state of the art results on the
FSS-1000 dataset by meta-training EfficientLab with FOMAML and using Bayesian
optimization to infer the optimal test-time adaptation routine hyperparameters.
We also construct a small benchmark dataset, FP-k, for the empirical study of
how meta-learning systems perform in both few- and many-shot settings. On the
FP-k dataset, we show that meta-learned initializations provide value for
canonical few-shot image segmentation but their performance is quickly matched
by conventional transfer learning with performance being equal beyond 10
labeled examples. Our code, meta-learned model, and the FP-k dataset are
available at https://github.com/ml4ai/mliis .

This report provides an overview of the current state of the art deep
learning architectures and optimisation techniques, and uses the ADNI
hippocampus MRI dataset as an example to compare the effectiveness and
efficiency of different convolutional architectures on the task of patch-based
3-dimensional hippocampal segmentation, which is important in the diagnosis of
Alzheimer's Disease. We found that a slightly unconventional "stacked 2D"
approach provides much better classification performance than simple 2D patches
without requiring significantly more computational power. We also examined the
popular "tri-planar" approach used in some recently published studies, and
found that it provides much better results than the 2D approaches, but also
with a moderate increase in computational power requirement. Finally, we
evaluated a full 3D convolutional architecture, and found that it provides
marginally better results than the tri-planar approach, but at the cost of a
very significant increase in computational power requirement.

A single-elimination (SE) tournament is a popular way to select a winner in
both sports competitions and in elections. A natural and well-studied question
is the tournament fixing problem (TFP): given the set of all pairwise match
outcomes, can a tournament organizer rig an SE tournament by adjusting the
initial seeding so that their favorite player wins? We prove new sufficient
conditions on the pairwise match outcome information and the favorite player,
under which there is guaranteed to be a seeding where the player wins the
tournament. Our results greatly generalize previous results. We also
investigate the relationship between the set of players that can win an SE
tournament under some seeding (so called SE winners) and other traditional
tournament solutions. In addition, we generalize and strengthen prior work on
probabilistic models for generating tournaments. For instance, we show that
\emph{every} player in an $n$ player tournament generated by the Condorcet
Random Model will be an SE winner even when the noise is as small as possible,
$p=\Theta(\ln n/n)$; prior work only had such results for $p\geq
\Omega(\sqrt{\ln n/n})$. We also establish new results for significantly more
general generative models.

[Abstract] At present, future medical imaging is increasingly being used to diagnose patients with cancer or other life-threatening problems without a physician's input (1⇓⇓–4). In fact, this level of patient monitoring has emerged as an urgent need and a cost effective alternative to a conventional surgical strategy of operationally treating disease when clinical findings warrant it (5, 6). However, current techniques are relatively costly compared to human surgeons who still perform a significant portion of total imaging-related revenue (7). Consequently, healthcare systems must now prioritize not just what images should be captured but how they ought to be collected and organized (8). To date, many experts have agreed that large volumes do require to be recorded (9) for certain types of health issues such as cardiac infarction detection in which information is relevant beyond simply allowing doctors to detect atrial fibrillation [6]. These guidelines also dictate use of standardized storage methods for storing medically useful clinical information on large-scale data centers (10), although others would like to see greater transparency about which institutions hold the most medical data, thereby enabling citizens to decide whether privacy is important when making healthcare decisions using mass data (11). Despite these differences, no consensus approach exists regarding the best way forward with respect to both capturing mass imaging images and maintaining appropriate access, quality and security while recording them on centralized data sources. This raises the question: Should we seek solutions which maximize efficiency while minimizing the amount stored or rely only on technologies for storing information?

This paper presents a novel approach to image segmentation using Cellular Automata (CA). Image segmentation is a fundamental task in computer vision that involves dividing an image into its constituent parts or objects. CA are a powerful tool for image processing, and have been used in various applications such as image compression and feature extraction. In this paper, we propose a new method that leverages the properties of CA to perform image segmentation.

Our approach is based on the idea of evolving a CA state from a random initial state to a stable state that corresponds to the desired segmentation of the image. We use a fitness function that rewards the CA state for producing a segmentation that is consistent with the image data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several benchmark images, and show that it produces accurate segmentations with minimal computational overhead.

The main contribution of this paper is the introduction of a new image segmentation algorithm based on CA, which offers several advantages over traditional methods. First, our approach is very fast and efficient, making it suitable for real-time applications. Second, it is very simple to implement, and does not require a large number of parameters to be set. Third, it is robust to noise and other artifacts in the image data. Finally, it produces high-quality segmentations that are comparable to those produced by more complex methods.

We evaluate the performance of our algorithm using several metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. Our results show that our algorithm outperforms several state-of-the-art segmentation methods, including thresholding, edge detection, and clustering. We also perform a series of ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of different components of our algorithm, and demonstrate that the CA-based approach is the key to its success.

In conclusion, this paper presents a novel and effective approach to image segmentation using Cellular Automata. Our method is fast, simple, robust, and produces high-quality segmentations. It has important applications in various fields such as robotics, autonomous driving, medical imaging, and video surveillance.

focus on analysing images captured in visible spectrum. In this manuscript we
elaborate on the problem of segmenting cross-country scenes captured in IR
spectrum. For this purpose we proposed employing salient features. Salient
features are robust to variations in scale, brightness and view angle. We
suggest the Speeded-Up Robust Features as a basis for our salient features for
a number of reasons discussed in the paper. We also provide a comparison of two
SURF implementations. The SURF features are extracted from images of different
terrain types. For every feature we estimate a terrain class membership
function. The membership values are obtained by means of either the multi-layer
perceptron or nearest neighbours. The features' class membership values and
their spatial positions are then applied to estimate class membership values
for all pixels in the image. To decrease the effect of segmentation blinking
that is caused by rapid switching between different terrain types and to speed
up segmentation, we are tracking camera position and predict features'
positions. The comparison of the multi-layer perception and the nearest
neighbour classifiers is presented in the paper. The error rate of the terrain
segmentation using the nearest neighbours obtained on the testing set is
16.6+-9.17%.

The paper "On Lexicographic Approximations of Integer Programs" presents a novel approach to solving integer programming problems using lexicographic approximations. Integer programming problems are widely used in operations research and management science to optimize decision-making processes, but they are known to be NP-hard, meaning that their computational complexity grows exponentially with the size of the problem. This makes it difficult to solve large-scale instances exactly, leading to a need for approximation techniques.

The proposed method utilizes lexicography, which is a way of ranking objects according to their perceived quality or preference. In this context, we use lexicography to approximate the optimal solution of an integer program by iteratively improving a feasible solution based on a set of priority rules. These rules are derived from the structure of the problem and provide a way to navigate the vast search space of possible solutions.

Our method is tested on a variety of benchmark problems and compared to existing state-of-the-art approximation algorithms. The results show that our approach outperforms previous methods in terms of accuracy while maintaining a competitive computational efficiency. We also demonstrate its applicability to real-world examples including scheduling, resource allocation, and network optimization tasks.

Furthermore, we extend our analysis to address dynamic environments where the instance changes over time. By incorporating ideas from online algorithm design, we develop a adaptive lexicographic approximation scheme that can respond to changing circumstances while maintaining the same level of optimality guarantees as in static cases.

Overall, this paper introduces a new perspective on solving integer programming problems using lexicographic approximations. It provides an effective and efficient methodology that enables better decision-making in complex applications while remaining computationally tractable. Additionally, it contributes to the understanding of approximation algorithms for integer programs, opening up opportunities for further research and advancements in this area.

Complex arithmetic random waves are stationary Gaussian complex-valued
solutions of the Helmholtz equation on the two-dimensional flat torus. We use
Wiener-It\^o chaotic expansions in order to derive a complete characterization
of the second order high-energy behaviour of the total number of phase
singularities of these functions. Our main result is that, while such random
quantities verify a universal law of large numbers, they also exhibit
non-universal and non-central second order fluctuations that are dictated by
the arithmetic nature of the underlying spectral measures. Such fluctuations
are qualitatively consistent with the cancellation phenomena predicted by Berry
(2002) in the case of complex random waves on compact planar domains. Our
results extend to the complex setting recent pathbreaking findings by Rudnick
and Wigman (2008), Krishnapur, Kurlberg and Wigman (2013) and Marinucci,
Peccati, Rossi and Wigman (2016). The exact asymptotic characterization of the
variance is based on a fine analysis of the Kac-Rice kernel around the origin,
as well as on a novel use of combinatorial moment formulae for controlling
long-range weak correlations.

We propose a novel method for learning convolutional neural image
representations without manual supervision. We use motion cues in the form of
optical flow, to supervise representations of static images. The obvious
approach of training a network to predict flow from a single image can be
needlessly difficult due to intrinsic ambiguities in this prediction task. We
instead propose a much simpler learning goal: embed pixels such that the
similarity between their embeddings matches that between their optical flow
vectors. At test time, the learned deep network can be used without access to
video or flow information and transferred to tasks such as image
classification, detection, and segmentation. Our method, which significantly
simplifies previous attempts at using motion for self-supervision, achieves
state-of-the-art results in self-supervision using motion cues, competitive
results for self-supervision in general, and is overall state of the art in
self-supervised pretraining for semantic image segmentation, as demonstrated on
standard benchmarks.

Notions of simulation, among other uses, provide a computationally tractable
and sound (but not necessarily complete) proof method for language inclusion.
They have been comprehensively studied by Lynch and Vaandrager for
nondeterministic and timed systems; for B\"{u}chi automata the notion of fair
simulation has been introduced by Henzinger, Kupferman and Rajamani. We
contribute to a generalization of fair simulation in two different directions:
one for nondeterministic tree automata previously studied by Bomhard; and the
other for probabilistic word automata with finite state spaces, both under the
B\"{u}chi acceptance condition. The former nondeterministic definition is
formulated in terms of systems of fixed-point equations, hence is readily
translated to parity games and is then amenable to Jurdzi\'{n}ski's algorithm;
the latter probabilistic definition bears a strong ranking-function flavor.
These two different-looking definitions are derived from one source, namely our
coalgebraic modeling of B\"{u}chi automata. Based on these coalgebraic
observations, we also prove their soundness: a simulation indeed witnesses
language inclusion.

Learning long-term spatial-temporal features are critical for many video
analysis tasks. However, existing video segmentation methods predominantly rely
on static image segmentation techniques, and methods capturing temporal
dependency for segmentation have to depend on pretrained optical flow models,
leading to suboptimal solutions for the problem. End-to-end sequential learning
to explore spatialtemporal features for video segmentation is largely limited
by the scale of available video segmentation datasets, i.e., even the largest
video segmentation dataset only contains 90 short video clips. To solve this
problem, we build a new large-scale video object segmentation dataset called
YouTube Video Object Segmentation dataset (YouTube-VOS). Our dataset contains
4,453 YouTube video clips and 94 object categories. This is by far the largest
video object segmentation dataset to our knowledge and has been released at
http://youtube-vos.org. We further evaluate several existing state-of-the-art
video object segmentation algorithms on this dataset which aims to establish
baselines for the development of new algorithms in the future.

This work describes an approach that uses deep 3D fully convolution neural networks (CNN) which, like traditional CNNs, are trained by taking weighted averages/concentrated inputs and convolving them with each other, but where training outputs are used instead of weights. A feature extractor for training these CNN models called Neural-Seq is proposed which performs inference independent on the original shape of the input and output for each individual CNN class, thus greatly reducing loss on complex images. Through numerical evaluation and experimental validation the authors compare this new classifier with 2 existing state of art classification methods based on precomputed features, i.e., regularization and feature vector computation algorithms. In addition, they show how it can be applied to image segmentation tasks such as segmenting children's faces into non-face categories. We find that our method achieves a significant improvement over these two approaches in terms of accuracy for both image features and brain region detection, at negligible cost in network complexity and computational time.

Machine learning has been utilized to perform tasks in many different domains

language analysis. Data labeling has always been one of the most important

focus on reducing data annotation and labeling costs. Transfer learning was
designed and widely used as an efficient approach that can reasonably reduce

prediction accuracy of the model. Therefore, researchers started to pay more
attention on auto annotation and labeling. In this survey paper, we provide a
review of previous techniques that focuses on optimized data annotation and
labeling for video, audio, and text data.

This paper presents a mesoscale modeling approach for simulating the behavior of colloidal suspensions with adsorbing solutes. In this paper, we investigate the longest gapped repeats and palindromes in a given string. We present a novel algorithm that efficiently finds the longest gapped repeat and palindrome in a string, improving upon previous algorithms in terms of time and space complexity. Our approach leverages the concept of suffix trees and suffix links to efficiently identify and report the longest gapped repeats and palindromes.

We perform an extensive analysis of the time and space complexity of our algorithm and show that it outperforms previous algorithms in terms of computational efficiency. We also conduct experiments on a variety of datasets to demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithm and compare its performance to existing methods.

Our results show that our algorithm is able to find the longest gapped repeat and palindrome in a string with a time complexity of O(n log n) and a space complexity of O(n), where n is the length of the input string. This represents a significant improvement over previous algorithms, which have a time complexity of O(n^2) or higher.

We also explore the applications of our algorithm in various fields, including text compression, data compression, and genomics. We demonstrate how our algorithm can be used to identify long-range haplotypes in genomic data, which is an important problem in genetics and personalized medicine.

Overall, our paper presents a significant contribution to the field of string matching and provides a novel algorithm for finding the longest gapped repeats and palindromes in a string. Our algorithm is efficient, scalable, and has practical applications in various fields.

In this article, we examine the behavior of the Riemannian and Hermitian
curvature tensors of a Hermitian metric, when one of the curvature tensors
obeys all the symmetry conditions of the curvature tensor of a K\"ahler metric.
We will call such metrics G-K\"ahler-like or K\"ahler-like, for lack of better
terminologies. Such metrics are always balanced when the manifold is compact,
so in a way they are more special than balanced metrics, which drew a lot of
attention in the study of non-K\"ahler Calabi-Yau manifolds. In particular we
derive various formulas on the difference between the Riemannian and Hermitian
curvature tensors in terms of the torsion of the Hermitian connection. We
believe that these formulas could lead to further applications in the study of
Hermitian geometry with curvature assumptions.

Deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) have contributed many
breakthroughs in segmentation tasks, especially in the field of medical
imaging. However, \textit{domain shift} and \textit{corrupted annotations},
which are two common problems in medical imaging, dramatically degrade the
performance of DCNNs in practice. In this paper, we propose a novel robust
cross-denoising framework using two peer networks to address domain shift and
corrupted label problems with a peer-review strategy. Specifically, each
network performs as a mentor, mutually supervised to learn from reliable
samples selected by the peer network to combat with corrupted labels. In
addition, a noise-tolerant loss is proposed to encourage the network to capture
the key location and filter the discrepancy under various noise-contaminant
labels. To further reduce the accumulated error, we introduce a
class-imbalanced cross learning using most confident predictions at the
class-level. Experimental results on REFUGE and Drishti-GS datasets for optic
disc (OD) and optic cup (OC) segmentation demonstrate the superior performance
of our proposed approach to the state-of-the-art methods.

In this paper, we present a novel approach for interactive image segmentation that leverages content-based propagation of user markings to accurately separate objects from their backgrounds. Our method is designed to handle patterned images with complex shapes and structures, where traditional segmentation techniques often struggle.

We propose a two-stage framework that first involves generating an initial segmentation mask using user annotations, and then propagating these annotations content-wise throughout the image to refine the segmentation mask. The proposed propagation technique takes into account both local and global contextual information, ensuring accurate boundary detection and minimization of fragmentation. We also introduce a novel optimization model that incorporates user feedback to improve the accuracy of the segmentationmask over time.

Extensive experiments on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of our method compared to state-of-the art interactive segmentation algorithms. Specifically, we show significant improvements in segmentation accuracy, efficiency, and robustness, especially when dealing with large and/or occluded objects. Moreover, we evaluate the usability of our method throughuser studies, which confirm its effectiveness in terms of annotation effort and user satisfaction.

Our main contribution lies in introducing a powerful content-based propagation mechanism that adaptively absorbs user markings and produces high-quality segmentation masks, even when the object boundaries are intricate or unclear. By combining this mechanism with optimized user interaction,we provide a more efficient, robust, and reliable interactive segmentation method that can be applied to various applications such as medical imaging, industrial inspection, and multimedia processing.

This study proposes a novel top-down salient object detection approach that combines classifier guidance with feature embedding. The proposed method utilizes an off-the-shelf classifier to predict saliency maps, which are then refined by incorporating low-level features extracted from images using convolutional neural networks (CNN). Experimental results demonstrate superior performance of the proposed method compared to state-of-the-art approaches on benchmark datasets, attesting to its efficacy and robustness in detecting salient objects. Overall, this work presents an effective and efficient solution for top-down salient object detection guided by classifiers and embedded features.

Given two labelled Markov decision processes (MDPs), the trace-refinement
problem asks whether for all strategies of the first MDP there exists a
strategy of the second MDP such that the induced labelled Markov chains are
trace-equivalent. We show that this problem is decidable in polynomial time if
the second MDP is a Markov chain. The algorithm is based on new results on a
particular notion of bisimulation between distributions over the states.
However, we show that the general trace-refinement problem is undecidable, even
if the first MDP is a Markov chain. Decidability of those problems was stated
as open in 2008. We further study the decidability and complexity of the
trace-refinement problem provided that the strategies are restricted to be
memoryless.

Min-cut clustering, based on minimizing one of two heuristic cost-functions
proposed by Shi and Malik, has spawned tremendous research, both analytic and
algorithmic, in the graph partitioning and image segmentation communities over
the last decade. It is however unclear if these heuristics can be derived from
a more general principle facilitating generalization to new problem settings.
Motivated by an existing graph partitioning framework, we derive relationships
between optimizing relevance information, as defined in the Information
Bottleneck method, and the regularized cut in a K-partitioned graph. For fast
mixing graphs, we show that the cost functions introduced by Shi and Malik can
be well approximated as the rate of loss of predictive information about the
location of random walkers on the graph. For graphs generated from a stochastic
algorithm designed to model community structure, the optimal information
theoretic partition and the optimal min-cut partition are shown to be the same
with high probability.

replaced by a self-adjoint operator $L$. In the case of Lipschitz

$E\subset \mathbb{R}^d$ and $L\!\!=$Laplacian to fractional Laplacians. We also

In this paper, we present a femtosecond resolution timing jitter correction method for a TW scale Ti:sapphire laser system used in pump-probe experiments for Free Electron Lasers (FELs). correct boundary conditions to impose at the moving contact line. The classical
no-slip condition is generally acknowledged to lead to a non-integrable
singularity at the moving contact line, for which a slip condition, associated
with a small slip parameter, $\lambda$, serves to alleviate. In this paper, we
discuss what occurs as the slip parameter, $\lambda$, tends to zero. In
particular, we explain how the zero-slip limit should be discussed in
consideration of two distinguished:: one where time is held constant $t =
O(1)$, and one where time tends to infinity at the rate $t = O(|\log
\lambda|)$. The crucial result is that in the case where time is held constant,
the $\lambda \to 0$ limit converges to the slip-free equation, and contact line

Our proposed method consists of three main stages: (1) coarse-scale feature extraction, (2) fine-scale feature extraction, and (3) fusion and refinement.

In the first stage, we extract coarse-scale features from the input volume using a 3D convolutional neural network (CNN) with a large filter size, which provides a high-level overview of the input data and helps to reduce the computational cost. In the second stage, we extract fine-scale features using a 3D CNN with a small filter size, which captures detailed information and improves the accuracy of the segmentation.

The two sets of features are then fused using a novel multi-scale feature fusion strategy, which combines the complementary information from both scales to produce more accurate and robust segmentation results. Finally, we refine the segmentation results using a conditional random field (CRF) model, which incorporates spatial priors and contextual information to further improvide the accuracy and smoothness of the segmentation masks.

The main contributions of this work include: (1) the introduction of a 3D coarse-to-fine framework for volumetric medical image segmentation, (2) the development of a novel multi-scale feature fusion strategy, and (3) the application of CRF models to refine the segmentation results. This study has important implications for various medical applications, such as surgical planning, radiation therapy, and disease research, where accurate segmentation of complex structures is crucial.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to multimodal and semi-supervised image segmentation, which leverages the strengths of both modalities and annotations to improve segmentation accuracy. Our method, called Disentangle, Align, and Fuse (DAF), consists of three main stages: 1) disentanglement, where we separate the input images into their independent factors of variation; 2) alignment, where we register the modalities and annotated labels across different domains; and 3) fusion, where we combine the aligned modalities and labels to produce accurate segmentations.

We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate its superiority over state-of-the-art methods in terms of segmentation performance and robustness to variations in modality and annotation quality. Additionally, we provide an extensive ablation study to analyze the effectiveness of each component of DAF and show that it can adapt to various scenarios with different levels of annotation scarcity and modality disparity.

Our key contributions include the introduction of a new probabilistic framework for jointly modeling multimodal images and semi-supervised learning, and the development of an efficient optimization algorithm that enables iterative refinement of the proposed model. The DAF method has broad applications in medical imaging, object detection, and scene understanding, where multiple modalities are often available butannotated data is scarce or difficult to obtain.

In this paper, we propose an unsupervised domain adaptation network with a category-centric prototype aligner for biomedical image segmentation. The proposed method aims to address the challenge of segmenting images from unseen domains, which is a critical problem in many biomedical applications.

Existing domain adaptation methods for image segmentation typically require annotated data from the target domain, which can be difficult and expensive to obtain. In contrast, our proposed method uses an unsupervised domain adaptation approach that does not require any annotated data from the target domain.

The key innovation of our method is the use of a category-centric prototype aligner, which aligns the prototypes of the source domain categories with the prototypes of the target domain categories. This alignment is achieved by minimizing the distance between the prototypes of the corresponding categories across domains. The aligned prototypes are then used to adapt the feature extractor and classifier of the segmentation model to the target domain.

We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets, including a dataset of brain tumor images and a dataset of retinal fundus images. The results show that our method outperforms several state-of-the-art domain adaptation methods for image segmentation, including methods that require annotated data from the target domain.

Our main contributions can be summarized as follows:

* We propose an unsupervised domain adaptation network with a category-centric prototype aligner for biomedical image segmentation.
* We demonstrate that our method does not require annotated data from the target domain and still achieves better performance than state-of-the-art methods that require annotated data.
* We show that our method is effective in adapting the segmentation model to new domains with different distributions, which is critical in many biomedical applications.

Overall, our proposed method has the potential to significantly improve the accuracy of biomedical image segmentation in situations where annotated data from the target domain is not available.

Energy minimization algorithms, such as graph cuts, enable the computation of
the MAP solution under certain probabilistic models such as Markov random
fields. However, for many computer vision problems, the MAP solution under the
model is not the ground truth solution. In many problem scenarios, the system
has access to certain statistics of the ground truth. For instance, in image
segmentation, the area and boundary length of the object may be known. In these
cases, we want to estimate the most probable solution that is consistent with
such statistics, i.e., satisfies certain equality or inequality constraints.
  The above constrained energy minimization problem is NP-hard in general, and
is usually solved using Linear Programming formulations, which relax the
integrality constraints. This paper proposes a novel method that finds the
discrete optimal solution of such problems by maximizing the corresponding
Lagrangian dual. This method can be applied to any constrained energy
minimization problem whose unconstrained version is polynomial time solvable,
and can handle multiple, equality or inequality, and linear or non-linear
constraints. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method on the
foreground/background image segmentation problem, and show that it produces
impressive segmentation results with less error, and runs more than 20 times
faster than the state-of-the-art LP relaxation based approaches.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to training multi-organ segmentation networks using sample selection based on relaxed upper confident bound (RUCB). Our method addresses the challenge of annotating large datasets for medical image segmentation tasks, where obtaining high-quality annotations can be time-consuming and expensive.

We introduce an algorithm that selectively samples the most informative images from a large dataset, leveraging the RUCB principle to ensure a robust selection process. The selected images are then annotated expertly, resulting in a smaller but highly accurate annotation set. We evaluate our method using several experiments on publicly available datasets for liver, kidney, and lung segmentation.

Our experimental results show that the proposed method achieves superior performance compared to random sampling and other existing methods. Specifically, we observe a significant reduction in segmentation error when employing our method in conjunction with popular deep learning architectures like U-Net and CNN-CRFs. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our technique is effective across different organ segmentation tasks and imaging modalities.

The key contribution of this work lies in introducing RUCB-based sample selection as a strategy for reducing annotation effort while maintaining segmentation accuracy. By judiciously selecting a subset of images for expert annotation, our method offers a cost-effective solution to the challenges associated with collecting and labeling large-scale datasets. This novel approach can potentially benefit various applications within medical image analysis and related fields.

This academic paper presents the design and development of a double-helix neutron detector using micron-size boron-10 powder. The detector utilizes the nuclear reactions induced by neutrons in the boron-10 powder, which emit alpha particles and lithium ions. Purpose: To improve kidney segmentation in clinical ultrasound (US) images,
we develop a new graph cuts based method to segment kidney US images by
integrating original image intensity information and texture feature maps
extracted using Gabor filters. Methods: To handle large appearance variation
within kidney images and improve computational efficiency, we build a graph of
image pixels close to kidney boundary instead of building a graph of the whole
image. To make the kidney segmentation robust to weak boundaries, we adopt
localized regional information to measure similarity between image pixels for
computing edge weights to build the graph of image pixels. The localized graph
is dynamically updated and the GC based segmentation iteratively progresses
until convergence. The proposed method has been evaluated and compared with
state of the art image segmentation methods based on clinical kidney US images
of 85 subjects. We randomly selected US images of 20 subjects as training data
for tuning the parameters, and validated the methods based on US images of the
remaining 65 subjects. The segmentation results have been quantitatively
analyzed using 3 metrics, including Dice Index, Jaccard Index, and Mean
Distance. Results: Experiment results demonstrated that the proposed method
obtained segmentation results for bilateral kidneys of 65 subjects with average
Dice index of 0.9581, Jaccard index of 0.9204, and Mean Distance of 1.7166,
better than other methods under comparison (p<10-19, paired Wilcoxon rank sum
tests). Conclusions: The proposed method achieved promising performance for
segmenting kidneys in US images, better than segmentation methods that built on
any single channel of image information. This method will facilitate extraction
of kidney characteristics that may predict important clinical outcomes such
progression chronic kidney disease.

In this paper, we present a novel approach for neuron segmentation in electron microscopy images using learning metric graphs. Electron microscopy imaging is a powerful tool for visualizing the morphology of neurons, but segmenting neurons from the background and identifying their boundaries can be a challenging task. Existing methods for neuron segmentation often rely on hand-crafted features and manual annotation, which can be time-consuming and limited in accuracy.

In contrast, our approach uses a learning metric graph to model the similarity between pixels in the image and learn a representation that captures the structural information of the neurons. The learning metric graph is a flexible and efficient way to incorporate prior knowledge about the structure of neurons and the image acquisition process. We show that our method outperforms traditional segmentation methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency, and provides a more robust and reliable way to segment neurons in electron microscopy images.

Our approach consists of two main components: a graph construction step, where we build a graph that encodes the similarity between pixels in the image, and a graph-based segmentation step, where we use the graph to segment the neurons. We evaluate our method on a dataset of electron microscopy images and show that it produces high-quality segmentations that are consistent with manual annotation. We also demonstrate the versatility of our approach by applying it to a variety of different imaging conditions and neuron types.

The main contribution of this paper is the introduction of a learning metric graph for neuron segmentation in electron microscopy images. Our approach provides a powerful tool for analyzing the structure of neurons in large-scale electron microscopy datasets, and has the potential to enable new applications in neuroscience research.

This paper proposes a novel approach to image segmentation using deep learning, specifically the Mumford-Shah loss functional. The Mumford-Shah loss functional is a regularization term that encourages the segmentation mask to have a piecewise constant structure, which is well-suited for images with complex structures. In this paper, we incorporate the Mumford-Shah loss functional into a deep learning framework for image segmentation, and demonstrate its effectiveness in segmenting images with varying levels of complexity.

Experiments conducted on several benchmark datasets show that the proposed method outperforms traditional deep learning-based segmentation methods, such as fully convolutional networks (FCNs) and U-Net, in terms of segmentation accuracy and computational efficiency. We also show that the Mumford-Shah loss functional is able to capture the underlying structure of the images, leading to more accurate and interpretable segmentation results.

The main contributions of this paper are:

* The introduction of the Mumford-Shah loss functional for image segmentation with deep learning
* The development of an efficient optimization algorithm for minimizing the Mumford-Shah loss functional in a deep learning framework
* An extensive evaluation of the proposed method on several benchmark datasets, demonstrating its superior performance compared to traditional methods

Overall, this paper presents a novel approach to image segmentation using the Mumford-Shah loss functional, which can be useful for applications where accurate and interpretable segmentation results are crucial, such as medical imaging and object detection.

The NA62 experiment at CERN requires a highly precise and efficient trigger and data acquisition system to capture rare particle decay events. In this paper, we present the development of a high-resolution Time-to-Digital Converter (TDC) based board for a fully digital trigger and data acquisition system. The designed board is capable of processing timing information with resolutions as low as 100 picoseconds, allowing for accurate identification of particles and their arrival times.

The board is built using FPGA technology and features four Input/Output (I/O) interfaces, each able to handle up to 400 MHz of clock frequency. The design also incorporates multiple Trigger Logic Units (TLUs), enabling complex trigger conditions to be implemented in real-time. Additionally, the board includes dedicated hardware for zero-suppression and time-stamping, further optimizing the signal processing performance.

The paper presents the detailed design and simulation of the high-resolution TDC-based board, including the FPGA hardware and software implementation. Performance tests demonstrate that the board achieves the desired timing resolution and throughput requirements for the NA62 experiment. Moreover, the study discusses potential applications in other experiments and future upgrades aimed at improving the performance of the trigger and data acquisition system.

This contribution highlights the significant advancements made in developing powerful and flexible digital electronics for high-energy physics experiments. With its capabilities of handling vast amounts of data and complex trigger logic in real-time, the presented board offers critical advantages for experiments relying on fast and accurate data acquisition systems.
