This paper proposes a novel compression algorithm, called Universal Parallel Two-Pass MDL Context Tree Compression (UPTC), which achieves high compression ratios for various types of data. The proposed algorithm combines the advantages of both context tree-based compression and parallel processing, resulting in a fast and efficient compression method.

The UPTC algorithm consists of two passes: the first pass builds a context tree using a modified Definition of Maximimum Length (MDL) encoding technique, while the second pass performs compression using dynamic programming. The algorithm takes advantage of parallel processing techniques to accelerate the compression process.

Experiments conducted on several benchmark datasets demonstrate that UPTC outperforms existing state-of-the-art compression algorithms, including those that use context trees, in terms of both compression ratio and computational efficiency. Specifically, UPTC achieves an average compression ratio that is 12% higher than that of the closest competing algorithm, along with a significant reduction in computation time.

The universality of UPTC makes it suitable for compressing a wide range of data types, including text, images, audio, and video. Its ability to efficiently exploit the redundancy inherent in data ensures that UPTC can effectively handle large datasets, making it particularly useful for applications where storage space and transmission bandwidth are limited.

Overall, this paper presents a significant advancement in the field of data compression, offering a fast and efficient algorithm capable of delivering high compression ratios across diverse data types.

A new study addresses questions relating to graph data structures (active contour trees) through two empirical studies and a formal analysis. In this work, we present and analyze theoretical analyses that shed light on their properties, as well as construct a novel tree with eight active contour graphs at the single-objective limit. We derive in details how our tree corresponds specifically to graph structure. Furthermore, one of the most important observations made is how simple to construct these tree are compared to graph theoretical representations of such trees. However, it could be argued that not all existing computational descriptions for graph theoretic tree construction is fully accurate concerning aspects related to efficient algorithms and correctness requirements. Therefore, our second investigation aims at improving all known theoretical or numerical implementations for the common cases. Our approach involves three steps. First, a general algorithm that allows us to construct a graph efficiently across different object types - all that needed have been provided by existing graph theory representations. Second step is a detailed characterization on how to evaluate graph designs on various problem domains. Third step is an implementation on modern GPU hardware. Results show that our results are comparable to published implementation schemes based on traditional finite state automata. Moreover, our proposed method can achieve order of magnitude speed-ups over previous methods for tree construction when certain design restrictions are also satisfied. By exploiting the fundamental structural similarities between trees based on topologically structured nodes and graph structure, we come closer to finding a new paradigm of computation on graph data models.

In this work, we address the challenging task of few-shot segmentation.
Previous few-shot segmentation methods mainly employ the information of support
images as guidance for query image segmentation. Although some works propose to
build cross-reference between support and query images, their extraction of
query information still depends on the support images. We here propose to
extract the information from the query itself independently to benefit the
few-shot segmentation task. To this end, we first propose a prior extractor to
learn the query information from the unlabeled images with our proposed
global-local contrastive learning. Then, we extract a set of predetermined
priors via this prior extractor. With the obtained priors, we generate the
prior region maps for query images, which locate the objects, as guidance to
perform cross interaction with support features. In such a way, the extraction
of query information is detached from the support branch, overcoming the
limitation by support, and could obtain more informative query clues to achieve
better interaction. Without bells and whistles, the proposed approach achieves
new state-of-the-art performance for the few-shot segmentation task on
PASCAL-5$^{i}$ and COCO datasets.

Self-organizing systems, which are characterized by their ability to organize themselves without external direction, are ubiquitous in nature and have been studied extensively in various fields, including physics, biology, and social sciences. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework using several case studies from diverse domains, including biological systems, traffic flow, and social networks. We also show how our framework can be used to optimize system performance and achieve desired outcomes in various contexts.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have achieved state-of-the-art
performance in many different 2D medical image analysis tasks. In clinical
practice, however, a large part of the medical imaging data available is in 3D.
This has motivated the development of 3D CNNs for volumetric image segmentation
in order to benefit from more spatial context. Due to GPU memory restrictions
caused by moving to fully 3D, state-of-the-art methods depend on
subvolume/patch processing and the size of the input patch is usually small,
limiting the incorporation of larger context information for a better
performance. In this paper, we propose a novel Holistic Decomposition
Convolution (HDC), for an effective and efficient semantic segmentation of
volumetric images. HDC consists of a periodic down-shuffling operation followed
by a conventional 3D convolution. HDC has the advantage of significantly
reducing the size of the data for sub-sequential processing while using all the
information available in the input irrespective of the down-shuffling factors.
Results obtained from comprehensive experiments conducted on hip T1 MR images
and intervertebral disc T2 MR images demonstrate the efficacy of the present
approach.

Objective: Deformable image registration is a fundamental problem in medical
image analysis, with applications such as longitudinal studies, population
modeling, and atlas based image segmentation. Registration is often phrased as
an optimization problem, i.e., finding a deformation field that is optimal
according to a given objective function. Discrete, combinatorial, optimization
techniques have successfully been employed to solve the resulting optimization
problem. Specifically, optimization based on $\alpha$-expansion with minimal
graph cuts has been proposed as a powerful tool for image registration. The
high computational cost of the graph-cut based optimization approach, however,
limits the utility of this approach for registration of large volume images.
Methods: Here, we propose to accelerate graph-cut based deformable registration
by dividing the image into overlapping sub-regions and restricting the
$\alpha$-expansion moves to a single sub-region at a time. Results: We
demonstrate empirically that this approach can achieve a large reduction in
computation time -- from days to minutes -- with only a small penalty in terms
of solution quality. Conclusion: The reduction in computation time provided by
the proposed method makes graph cut based deformable registration viable for
large volume images. Significance: Graph cut based image registration has
previously been shown to produce excellent results, but the high computational
cost has hindered the adoption of the method for registration of large medical
volume images. Our proposed method lifts this restriction, requiring only a
small fraction of the computational cost to produce results of comparable

ensemble system which combines various deep learning architectures. We propose
a two-layer ensemble of deep learning models for the segmentation of medical

first layer is used as the augmented data of the training image for the second
layer of the ensemble. The prediction of the second layer is then combined by
using a weights-based scheme in which each model contributes differently to the
combined result. The weights are found by solving linear regression problems.

In this paper, we propose spatial propagation networks for learning the
affinity matrix for vision tasks. We show that by constructing a row/column
linear propagation model, the spatially varying transformation matrix exactly
constitutes an affinity matrix that models dense, global pairwise relationships
of an image. Specifically, we develop a three-way connection for the linear
propagation model, which (a) formulates a sparse transformation matrix, where
all elements can be the output from a deep CNN, but (b) results in a dense
affinity matrix that effectively models any task-specific pairwise similarity
matrix. Instead of designing the similarity kernels according to image features
of two points, we can directly output all the similarities in a purely
data-driven manner. The spatial propagation network is a generic framework that
can be applied to many affinity-related tasks, including but not limited to
image matting, segmentation and colorization, to name a few. Essentially, the
model can learn semantically-aware affinity values for high-level vision tasks
due to the powerful learning capability of the deep neural network classifier.
We validate the framework on the task of refinement for image segmentation
boundaries. Experiments on the HELEN face parsing and PASCAL VOC-2012 semantic
segmentation tasks show that the spatial propagation network provides a
general, effective and efficient solution for generating high-quality
segmentation results.

In this paper, we propose a novel interactive segmentation framework for correcting mispredictions during the clinical evaluation of medical images. This article provides an overview of multi-fidelity modeling trends. Fidelity
in modeling refers to the level of detail and accuracy provided by a predictive
model or simulation. Generally, models with higher fidelity deliver more
precise results but demand greater computational resources. Multi-fidelity
models integrate high-fidelity and low-fidelity models to obtain fast yet
accurate predictions. Their growing popularity is due to their ability to
approximate high-fidelity models with high accuracy and low computational cost.
This work classifies publications in multi-fidelity modeling based on various
factors, including application, surrogate selection, fidelity difference,
fidelity combination method, field of application, and year of publication. The
study also examines the techniques used to combine fidelities, focusing on
multi-fidelity surrogate models. To accurately evaluate the advantages of
utilizing multi-fidelity models, it is necessary to report the achieved time
savings. This paper includes guidelines for authors to present their
multi-fidelity-related savings in a standard, succinct, yet thorough way to
guide future users. According to a select group of publications that provided
sufficient information, multi-fidelity models achieved savings of up to 90%
while maintaining the desired level of accuracy. However, the savings achieved
through multi-fidelity models depend highly on the problem.

In this study, we investigate the dielectric properties of molybdenum disulfide (MoS2) crystals in both terahertz and visible regions. Utilizing a combination of experimental techniques such as spectroscopic ellipsometry and computational methods including density functional theory calculations, we observe that MoS2 exhibits unique dielectric characteristics in these frequency ranges. Our findings reveal that MoS2 displays high dielectric constant values in the terahertz region, indicative of strong absorption and conduction mechanisms. In contrast, a significant decrease in dielectric response is observed within the visible spectrum, suggesting weak intervalence charge transfer. We attribute these differences to the structural anisotropy of MoS2 and propose potential applications in optoelectronic devices where tailored dielectric responses are advantageous. This comprehensive analysis improves our understanding of MoS2's interfacial interactions and their role in emerging technologies, enabling further advancements in device engineering.

The EXO-200 experiment is a search for neutrino-less double beta decay ($0\nu\beta\beta$) using a high-purity germanium detector. To achieve a competitive sensitivity, it is crucial to understand and mitigate the impact of radioactive backgrounds on the measurement. This work presents an investigation of radioactivity-induced backgrounds in the EXO-200 detector.

A comprehensive analysis of the data collected during the first three years of operation was performed to identify and characterize the background sources. The study includes a detailed examination of the energy spectrum, spatial distribution, and temporal behavior of the events.

The results show that the dominant background contribution comes from radon-related events, which are found to be consistent with previous studies. Additionally, we observe a distinct component of background events that correlate with solar activity and are likely attributable to cosmic ray-induced muons. We also find evidence for a small number of event clusters, potentially originating from short-lived radioactive species produced in the detector material or surrounding rock.

To mitigate these backgrounds, we implemented a series of novel event selection criteria and developed sophisticated reconstruction algorithms. By combining these techniques, we demonstrate a significant reduction in background events while maintaining a high efficiency for $0\nu\beta\beta$ decays. Our approach paves the way for future experiments aimed at observing this rare process and shedding light on the nature of the neutrino mass hierarchy.

This study's findings have important implications for the design and operation of ultra-sensitive detectors for various applications, including neutrino physics, dark matter searches, and nuclear non-proliferation monitoring. As the quest for answering fundamental questions in these fields continues, understanding and suppressing backgrounds becomes increasingly crucial, and our research provides valuable insights into tackling these challenges.

network for interactive segmentation of 3D medical images. Provided by user

partitioning problems. In the basic formulation of the dual-front models, the
evolving contours can be considered as the interfaces of adjacent Voronoi
regions. Among these dual-front models, a crucial ingredient is regarded as the
geodesic metrics by which the geodesic distances and the corresponding Voronoi
diagram can be estimated. In this paper, we introduce a type of asymmetric
quadratic metrics dual-front model. The metrics considered are built by the
integration of the image features and a vector field derived from the evolving
contours. The use of the asymmetry enhancement can reduce the risk of contour
shortcut or leakage problems especially when the initial contours are far away
from the target boundaries or the images have complicated intensity
distributions. Moreover, the proposed dual-front model can be applied for image
segmentation in conjunction with various region-based homogeneity terms. The
numerical experiments on both synthetic and real images show that the proposed
dual-front model indeed achieves encouraging results.

"Background subtraction" is an old technique for finding moving objects in a
video sequence for example, cars driving on a freeway. The idea is that
subtracting the current image from a timeaveraged background image will leave
only nonstationary objects. It is, however, a crude approximation to the task
of classifying each pixel of the current image; it fails with slow-moving
objects and does not distinguish shadows from moving objects. The basic idea of
this paper is that we can classify each pixel using a model of how that pixel
looks when it is part of different classes. We learn a mixture-of-Gaussians
classification model for each pixel using an unsupervised technique- an
efficient, incremental version of EM. Unlike the standard image-averaging
approach, this automatically updates the mixture component for each class
according to likelihood of membership; hence slow-moving objects are handled
perfectly. Our approach also identifies and eliminates shadows much more
effectively than other techniques such as thresholding. Application of this
method as part of the Roadwatch traffic surveillance project is expected to
result in significant improvements in vehicle identification and tracking.

In this paper, we present a rigorous verification of the Nernst theorem for the Casimir-Lifshitz free energy, which states that the entropy of a system in thermodynamic equilibrium is minimized when the temperature is uniform throughout the system. Our proof relies on a careful analysis of the curvature of the free energy landscape and employs techniques from differential geometry and mathematical physics. We demonstrate the validity of the Nernst theorem for a wide range of systems, including those with non-trivial topology and boundary conditions. Our results have important implications for the understanding of phase transitions and the behavior of complex systems, and provide a new perspective on the relationship between entropy, temperature, and energy.

In this paper, we present a novel approach for directly imaging the nanoscale conductance evolution in ion-gel-gated oxide transistors using a combination of advanced techniques. By utilizing a transmission electron microscope (TEM) and scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM), we are able to visualize the morphology and conductivity of the ion gel layer at the nanoscale, providing new insights into the mechanisms governing the device's operation. Our results demonstrate the ability to map the conductance variations across individual grain boundaries and nanoparticles, allowing us to identify the specific locations where charge transport is facilitated or hindered. The findings of this study have significant implications for the optimization and scaling down of ion-gel-gated oxide transistors, paving the way for their widespread adoption in emerging technologies such as neuromorphic computing and the Internet of Things.

This paper presents a new Bayesian collaborative sparse regression method for
linear unmixing of hyperspectral images. Our contribution is twofold; first, we
propose a new Bayesian model for structured sparse regression in which the
supports of the sparse abundance vectors are a priori spatially correlated
across pixels (i.e., materials are spatially organised rather than randomly
distributed at a pixel level). This prior information is encoded in the model
through a truncated multivariate Ising Markov random field, which also takes
into consideration the facts that pixels cannot be empty (i.e, there is at
least one material present in each pixel), and that different materials may
exhibit different degrees of spatial regularity. Secondly, we propose an
advanced Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm to estimate the posterior
probabilities that materials are present or absent in each pixel, and,
conditionally to the maximum marginal a posteriori configuration of the
support, compute the MMSE estimates of the abundance vectors. A remarkable
property of this algorithm is that it self-adjusts the values of the parameters
of the Markov random field, thus relieving practitioners from setting
regularisation parameters by cross-validation. The performance of the proposed
methodology is finally demonstrated through a series of experiments with
synthetic and real data and comparisons with other algorithms from the
literature.

This paper introduces a novel approach to image segmentation called CFCM (Coarse to Fine Context Memory). The proposed method leverages the concept of context memory, which captures the relationships between pixels in an image, to achieve accurate and efficient segmentation. Unlike traditional methods that rely on hand-crafted features or deep learning models, CFCM uses a coarse-to-fine strategy to progressively refine the segmentation results.

The CFCM model consists of three main components: a coarse segmentor, a fine segmentor, and a context memory module. The coarse segmentor generates an initial segmentation mask, which is then used to compute the context memory. The fine segmentor refines the segmentation mask by iteratively adding or removing pixels based on the information stored in the context memory.

Experiments conducted on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of CFCM over state-of-the-art segmentation methods. Compared to traditional methods, CFCM achieves better accuracy while requiring significantly fewer parameters and computations. Additionally, the proposed method exhibits improved robustness to noise and occlusions, making it well suited for real-world applications.

The key contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows:

* Introduction of CFCM, a novel image segmentation method that leverages context memory to improve accuracy and efficiency.
* Development of a coarse-to-fine strategy that progressively refines the segmentation results using a coarse segmentor and a fine segmentor.
* Design of a context memory module that captures the relationships between pixels in an image and facilitates the sharing of information across different scales.
* Demonstration of the effectiveness of CFCM through experiments on various benchmark datasets, outperforming state-of-the-art segmentation methods in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency.

Multi-atlas segmentation approach is one of the most widely-used image
segmentation techniques in biomedical applications. There are two major
challenges in this category of methods, i.e., atlas selection and label fusion.
In this paper, we propose a novel multi-atlas segmentation method that
formulates multi-atlas segmentation in a deep learning framework for better
solving these challenges. The proposed method, dubbed deep fusion net (DFN), is
a deep architecture that integrates a feature extraction subnet and a non-local
patch-based label fusion (NL-PLF) subnet in a single network. The network
parameters are learned by end-to-end training for automatically learning deep
features that enable optimal performance in a NL-PLF framework. The learned
deep features are further utilized in defining a similarity measure for atlas
selection. By evaluating on two public cardiac MR datasets of SATA-13 and LV-09
for left ventricle segmentation, our approach achieved 0.833 in averaged Dice
metric (ADM) on SATA-13 dataset and 0.95 in ADM for epicardium segmentation on
LV-09 dataset, comparing favorably with the other automatic left ventricle
segmentation methods. We also tested our approach on Cardiac Atlas Project
(CAP) testing set of MICCAI 2013 SATA Segmentation Challenge, and our method
achieved 0.815 in ADM, ranking highest at the time of writing.

This paper presents a novel selective constraint propagation method for
constrained image segmentation. In the literature, many pairwise constraint
propagation methods have been developed to exploit pairwise constraints for
cluster analysis. However, since most of these methods have a polynomial time
complexity, they are not much suitable for segmentation of images even with a
moderate size, which is actually equivalent to cluster analysis with a large
data size. Considering the local homogeneousness of a natural image, we choose
to perform pairwise constraint propagation only over a selected subset of
pixels, but not over the whole image. Such a selective constraint propagation
problem is then solved by an efficient graph-based learning algorithm. To
further speed up our selective constraint propagation, we also discard those
less important propagated constraints during graph-based learning. Finally, the
selectively propagated constraints are exploited based on $L_1$-minimization
for normalized cuts over the whole image. The experimental results demonstrate
the promising performance of the proposed method for segmentation with
selectively propagated constraints.

Our method is based on the observation that FCNs tend to focus on the most discriminative regions of an image, but often ignore other important regions. Most current semantic segmentation methods rely on fully convolutional
networks (FCNs). However, their use of large receptive fields and many pooling
layers cause low spatial resolution inside the deep layers. This leads to
predictions with poor localization around the boundaries. Prior work has
attempted to address this issue by post-processing predictions with CRFs or
MRFs. But such models often fail to capture semantic relationships between
objects, which causes spatially disjoint predictions. To overcome these
problems, recent methods integrated CRFs or MRFs into an FCN framework. The
downside of these new models is that they have much higher complexity than
traditional FCNs, which renders training and testing more challenging.
  In this work we introduce a simple, yet effective Convolutional Random Walk
Network (RWN) that addresses the issues of poor boundary localization and
spatially fragmented predictions with very little increase in model complexity.
Our proposed RWN jointly optimizes the objectives of pixelwise affinity and
semantic segmentation. It combines these two objectives via a novel random walk
layer that enforces consistent spatial grouping in the deep layers of the
network. Our RWN is implemented using standard convolution and matrix
multiplication. This allows an easy integration into existing FCN frameworks
and it enables end-to-end training of the whole network via standard
back-propagation. Our implementation of RWN requires just $131$ additional
parameters compared to the traditional FCNs, and yet it consistently produces
an improvement over the FCNs on semantic segmentation and scene labeling.

In this paper, we present a novel macroscopic acousto-mechanical analogy of a microbubble, which enables the study of the behavior of microbubbles at a larger scale. Microbubbles are small bubbles that are typically on the order of micrometers in size and are commonly used in various applications such as drug delivery, sonochemistry, and biomedical imaging. However, studying the behavior of microbubbles at the microscale can be challenging due to the limitations of current imaging techniques and the difficulty in manipulating and measuring the properties of individual microbubbles.

To overcome these challenges, we have developed a macroscopic acousto-mechanical analogy of a microbubble, which consists of a millimeter-sized air-filled sphere that is embedded in a soft, elastic matrix. The sphere is excited by an external acoustic field, which causes it to oscillate and deform in a manner that is similar to the behavior of a microbubble. By measuring the motion of the sphere using high-speed imaging and analyzing the resulting dynamics, we are able to study the behavior of microbubbles at a larger scale and gain insights into their mechanical properties and interactions with their surrounding environment.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our analogy by comparing the experimental results with numerical simulations of microbubble dynamics and showing good agreement between the two. Our results show that the macroscopic acousto-mechanical analogy of a microbubble provides a useful tool for studying the behavior of microbubbles in various applications, including drug delivery and sonochemistry, and can help to improve our understanding of the underlying mechanisms involved in these processes.

The authors present a path integral representation of a Lorentzian spinfoam model and analyze its asymptotics. The formulation is based on an embedding of simplicial geometries into spacetime using spin network states that represent geometric structures at each simplex. The asymptotic behavior of the model is shown to be related to the Regge action, which provides insight into the continuum limit of the theory. This work contributes to the ongoing effort to develop a viable quantum gravity Theory from a combinatorial perspective. The results may have implications for understanding quantized geometry in cosmological contexts and providing insights about emergence of spatial topology changes during evolution.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to unified perceptual parsing, which is a fundamental problem in computer vision that involves assigning a single label to each pixel in an image, indicating its belonging to a specific object or material category. Our approach, called the Deep Grouping Model (DGM), leverages the strengths of both deep learning and grouping-based methods to achieve state-of-the-art performance on this task.

Existing methods for unified perceptual parsing often rely on hand-crafted features and heuristics, which are limited in their ability to capture the complexity and variability of real-world scenes. In contrast, DGM uses a deep neural network to learn a rich representation of the input image, which is then grouped into a small set of clusters using a novel grouping algorithm. This allows DGM to capture subtle patterns and relationships between pixels that would be difficult or impossible to model using traditional methods.

The key innovation of DGM is the use of a deep neural network to learn a hierarchical representation of the input image, which is then used to guide the grouping process. This allows DGM to capture both local and global contextual information, leading to more accurate and robust parsing results. In addition, DGM includes a novel grouping algorithm that is designed to work effectively with the hierarchical representation, ensuring that the resulting parse tree is both accurate and efficient.

We evaluate DGM on several challenging benchmark datasets, including the PASCAL VOC dataset, the Cityscapes dataset, and the BSDS500 dataset. We also perform a series of ablation studies to analyze the contributions of different components of DGM, providing insights into the effectiveness of the various design choices.

This work presents a LiveWire 3D medical image classification pipeline, which enables live detection of heart arrhythmias in single subjects and automated visualization via computer vision applications. These are useful for patient management since cardiac events can frequently have unpredictable phenotypes with potentially tragic consequences, with some event types causing more morbidity than death. In this paper, we propose a novel deep neural network architecture called HyperDense-Net, designed specifically for multi-modal image segmentation tasks. The proposed model leverages the strengths of both densely connected convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and multi-scale feature fusion to improve segmentation accuracy.

In traditional CNNs, spatial hierarchy is often achieved through max pooling or atrous spatial pyramid Pooling (ASPP), which can lead to loss of valuable information. Densely connected CNNs, on the other hand, preserve spatial information by concatenating features from different layers, but may suffer from computational complexity. Our proposed HyperDense-Net strikes a balance between these two approaches by employing a hierarchical density connectivity pattern that progressively increases the number of connections between layers while maintaining a reasonable computational cost.

Furthermore, we integrate Multi-Scale Feature Fusion (MSFF) modules into the network to effectively fuse low-level, middle-level, and high-level semantic features across different modalities. This allows the model to capture rich contextual information and enhance feature representation across different scales.

Extensive experiments conducted on three publicly available datasets demonstrate the superiority of our HyperDense-Net over state-of-the-art methods in terms of segmentation accuracy, efficiency, and robustness. * Development of a hierarchical density connectivity pattern that enables the efficient integration of high-resolution contextual information without significant computational overhead.
* Integration of MSFF modules to facilitate effective feature fusion across various scale levels and modalities, leading to enhanced representation capabilities.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to few-shot segmentation, which is a challenging task in computer vision that involves segmenting objects from a small number of labeled examples. Our approach, called Few-Shot Segmentation with Global and Local Contrastive Learning (FSS-GCL), combines the strengths of global and local contrastive learning to improve segmentation accuracy.

Global contrastive learning has been shown to be effective in learning high-level representations that are useful for few-shot learning. However, it may not capture local information that is crucial for segmentation tasks. Local contrastive learning, on the other hand, can capture local information but may not generalize well to new examples.

In FSS-GCL, we propose a two-stage training strategy that first uses global contrastive learning to learn high-level representations and then uses local contrastive learning to refine the segmentation masks. We also introduce a novel mask-based contrastive loss function that encourages the model to produce accurate segmentation masks.

Experiments on several benchmark datasets show that FSS-GCL outperforms state-of-the-art few-shot segmentation methods, including those that use global or local contrastive learning alone. We also perform ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of the different components of our approach.

Our main contributions are:

* A novel few-shot segmentation approach called FSS-GCL that combines global and local contrastive learning
* A two-stage training strategy that leverages the strengths of global and local contrastive learning
* A mask-based contrastive loss function that encourages accurate segmentation masks
* State-of-the-art performance on several benchmark datasets

Overall, FSS-GCL demonstrates the effectiveness of combining global and local contrastive learning for few-shot segmentation, and provides a promising direction for future research in this area.

In the world of modern financial theory, portfolio construction has
traditionally operated under at least one of two central assumptions: the
constraints are derived from a utility function and/or the multivariate
probability distribution of the underlying asset returns is fully known. In
practice, both the performance criteria and the informational structure are
markedly different: risk-taking agents are mandated to build portfolios by
primarily constraining the tails of the portfolio return to satisfy VaR, stress
testing, or expected shortfall (CVaR) conditions, and are largely ignorant
about the remaining properties of the probability distributions. As an
alternative, we derive the shape of portfolio distributions which have maximum
entropy subject to real-world left-tail constraints and other expectations. Two
consequences are (i) the left-tail constraints are sufficiently powerful to
overide other considerations in the conventional theory, rendering individual
portfolio components of limited relevance; and (ii) the "barbell" payoff
(maximal certainty/low risk on one side, maximum uncertainty on the other)
emerges naturally from this construction.

Our work opens up new directions for future research in semi-supervised video segmentation, highlighting the importance of exploring temporal information to enhance segmentation performance.

In this paper, we present a novel approach for efficient energy minimization in statistical enforcement. Our proposed method leverages the concept of proxy functions to effectively enforce statistical constraints in machine learning models, while minimizing the energy function. We demonstrate that our approach significantly reduces the computational complexity of the optimization process, making it feasible to enforce statistics in large-scale machine learning applications.

Existing methods for enforcing statistics in machine learning models often rely on constraint optimization techniques, which can be computationally expensive and scalability-limiting. In contrast, our approach uses a proxy function to approximate the statistical constraint, allowing for efficient optimization using gradient-based methods. We show that our method achieves comparable or better performance compared to state-of-the-art methods, while providing significant speedups in computation time.

We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate its applicability to various statistical constraints, including moment matching and diversity promotion. Our results show that our method can efficiently enforce statistics in a variety of scenarios, including those where existing methods struggle to scale.

Our work has important implications for a wide range of applications, including fairness-aware machine learning, dataset augmentation, and generative models. By enabling efficient enforcement of statistics, we can promote more robust and diverse models that better capture the underlying data distribution.

In summary, our paper presents a novel approach for efficient energy minimization in statistical enforcement, which enables the scalable enforcement of statistics in machine learning models. We present a study on the large scale pattern of optical quasar polarization vectors using a sample of over 10,000 quasars from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) DR7 catalog. The polarization vectors are derived from the observed polarization degrees and position angles of the quasars. We apply a statistical method to identify the large scale pattern in the polarization vector field, which is represented by a Gaussian distribution with a coherence length of approximately 100 Mpc.

Our results show that the polarization vectors exhibit a strong correlation over large scales, with a correlation length of approximately 200 Mpc. We also find that the polarization vectors are aligned with the large scale structure of the universe, as traced by galaxy distributions and cosmic microwave background (CMB) temperature fluctuations.

We interpret the observed large scale pattern of polarization vectors as evidence for the existence of a large scale magnetic field in the universe, which is likely generated by the dynamo action of galactic winds and supernovae. The observed correlation length of the polarization vectors is consistent with the expected scale of the magnetic field generated by these processes.

Our findings have important implications for our understanding of the origin and evolution of cosmic magnetism, and provide a new probe of the physics of structure formation and galaxy evolution. The observed large scale pattern of polarization vectors can be used to constrain models of magnetogenesis and the properties of the primordial universe.

In this paper, we explore ways to avoid using fractional powers over the natural numbers in mathematical expressions. Fractional powers can lead to difficulties in numerical computations and ambiguities in interpretation, particularly when dealing with non-integer values. We present several techniques that can be used to rewrite mathematical formulas in order to avoid the need for fractional powers. These techniques include using integer powers, rational functions, and alternative forms of exponential functions. We also discuss the advantages and disadvantages of each method and provide examples of how they can be applied in practice. Our results are useful for mathematicians, scientists, and engineers who work with natural numbers and seek to simplify their calculations while maintaining accuracy. By avoiding fractional powers, we can improve the clarity and reliability of our models and promote more efficient computational methods.

This paper presents a novel framework in which video/image segmentation and
localization are cast into a single optimization problem that integrates
information from low level appearance cues with that of high level localization
cues in a very weakly supervised manner. The proposed framework leverages two
representations at different levels, exploits the spatial relationship between
bounding boxes and superpixels as linear constraints and simultaneously
discriminates between foreground and background at bounding box and superpixel
level. Different from previous approaches that mainly rely on discriminative
clustering, we incorporate a foreground model that minimizes the histogram
difference of an object across all image frames. Exploiting the geometric
relation between the superpixels and bounding boxes enables the transfer of
segmentation cues to improve localization output and vice-versa. Inclusion of
the foreground model generalizes our discriminative framework to video data
where the background tends to be similar and thus, not discriminative. We
demonstrate the effectiveness of our unified framework on the YouTube Object
video dataset, Internet Object Discovery dataset and Pascal VOC 2007.

In this sequel to our previous work, we continue to explore the relationship between crepant resolutions and open strings in string theory. We present new evidence for a conjectural correspondence between these two seemingly unrelated concepts, building on recent advances in algebraic geometry and topological string theory.

We begin by reviewing the concept of crepant resolutions, which are certain types of blow-ups of Calabi-Yau manifolds that can be used to resolve singularities in string compactifications. We then introduce the notion of open strings, which are fundamental objects in string theory that describe the dynamics of strings propagating through spacetime.

Our main result is the establishment of a one-to-one correspondence between crepant resolutions and open strings. Specifically, we show that each crepant resolution can be associated with a unique open string, and vice versa. This correspondence is based on a careful analysis of the geometric and topological properties of both crepant resolutions and open strings, and it has far-reaching implications for our understanding of string theory and its mathematical foundations.

One of the key insights of our work is that the correspondence between crepant resolutions and open strings is not just a matter of mathematical convenience, but rather reflects a deeper physical structure of the string landscape. We argue that the correspondence can be interpreted as a manifestation of the "strings = branes" duality, which is a fundamental principle of string theory that relates strings and branes (higher-dimensional objects) in a subtle way.

Our results have important consequences for the study of string dualities and the string landscape, which refers to the vast space of possible string vacua that arise from different choices of compactification manifolds and other parameters. By establishing a concrete connection between crepant resolutions and open strings, we provide a new tool for exploring the string landscape and for understanding the relationships between different regions of this space.

Overall, our work represents a significant advance in our understanding of the interplay between geometry, topology, and physics in string theory, and it opens up new directions for research at the interface of mathematics and physics.

The challenge focuses on two parameters which are commonly used in determining the correct position of an event: its epoch and distance to an event centre, often referred to as the time-distance relationship. Abstract: Images are one kind of data, but they are highly non-deterministic in their evolution. They exhibit strong similarity to each other across spatial locations, which has been termed hyper-similarity. While some aspects of it (such as its smoothness) may be hard or impossible to accurately characterize, others such as their similarity from image boundaries can readily be described by means of a number/space linear combination of feature maps—e.g., using sparsity models with multiple sub spaces/dimensions. These methods have played an active role into high level perception issues including object recognition, scene understanding, face detection and language translation; and while currently they comprise only 10 percent of all deep learning systems (in terms of overall training activity), it holds the key to a revolutionizing our ability to process visual information both rapidly (via memoryless deep learning) and robustly. Here we review four related theoretical approaches that together offer significant advantages over traditional spectral methods for image fusion: convolutional neural networks (CNNs), dense representations, sparse coding and hypersphere computing. We first introduce their empirical and conceptual limitations which require large input images/datasets in order to adequately capture their underlying structure. Finally we compare them against existing techniques and explore their potential applications under various conditions.

Keywords: CNNs, convolutional neural nets, sparse representations, hyper-representations, hyperspheres, vector space machine learning

A key requirement for the success of supervised deep learning is a large
labeled dataset - a condition that is difficult to meet in medical image
analysis. Self-supervised learning (SSL) can help in this regard by providing a
strategy to pre-train a neural network with unlabeled data, followed by
fine-tuning for a downstream task with limited annotations. Contrastive
learning, a particular variant of SSL, is a powerful technique for learning
image-level representations. In this work, we propose strategies for extending
the contrastive learning framework for segmentation of volumetric medical
images in the semi-supervised setting with limited annotations, by leveraging
domain-specific and problem-specific cues. Specifically, we propose (1) novel
contrasting strategies that leverage structural similarity across volumetric
medical images (domain-specific cue) and (2) a local version of the contrastive
loss to learn distinctive representations of local regions that are useful for
per-pixel segmentation (problem-specific cue). We carry out an extensive
evaluation on three Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) datasets. In the limited
annotation setting, the proposed method yields substantial improvements
compared to other self-supervision and semi-supervised learning techniques.
When combined with a simple data augmentation technique, the proposed method
reaches within 8% of benchmark performance using only two labeled MRI volumes
for training, corresponding to only 4% (for ACDC) of the training data used to

Over time, we find that the Twitter graph becomes more densely connected, with an increase in the number of edges between users. However, we also observe a decrease in the clustering coefficient, indicating a shift towards a more random graph structure. Additionally, we find that the community structure of the graph changes over time, with users becoming more segregated into distinct communities based on their interests and behaviors.

Our findings have important implications for understanding the dynamics of online social networks and their role in shaping social interactions and information diffusion. Computing problems that handle large amounts of data necessitate the use of
lossless data compression for efficient storage and transmission. We present a
novel lossless universal data compression algorithm that uses parallel
computational units to increase the throughput. The length-$N$ input sequence
is partitioned into $B$ blocks. Processing each block independently of the
other blocks can accelerate the computation by a factor of $B$, but degrades
the compression quality. Instead, our approach is to first estimate the minimum
description length (MDL) context tree source underlying the entire input, and
then encode each of the $B$ blocks in parallel based on the MDL source. With
this two-pass approach, the compression loss incurred by using more parallel
units is insignificant. Our algorithm is work-efficient, i.e., its
computational complexity is $O(N/B)$. Its redundancy is approximately
$B\log(N/B)$ bits above Rissanen's lower bound on universal compression
performance, with respect to any context tree source whose maximal depth is at
most $\log(N/B)$. We improve the compression by using different quantizers for
states of the context tree based on the number of symbols corresponding to
those states. Numerical results from a prototype implementation suggest that
our algorithm offers a better trade-off between compression and throughput than
competing universal data compression algorithms.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to image segmentation using nonparametric clustering. Traditional methods of image segmentation rely on parametric models, such as Gaussian mixture models or Bayesian inference, which can be limited by their assumptions about the underlying distribution of the data. Nonparametric clustering methods, on the other hand, do not make any prior assumptions about the number of clusters or the shape of the clusters, and have been shown to be effective in a variety of applications.

We apply nonparametric clustering algorithms, specifically the K-means algorithm and the Gustafson-Kessel algorithm, to the task of image segmentation. We evaluate the performance of these algorithms on several benchmark datasets, including synthetic images with known clustering structures and real-world images from various domains. Our results show that nonparametric clustering methods outperform traditional parametric methods in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency.

In addition, we explore the effect of different distance metrics on the performance of nonparametric clustering algorithms. We demonstrate that choosing an appropriate distance metric can significantly improve the quality of the obtained clusters. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of varying the number of iterations and the initial placement of the cluster centers on the final segmentation result.

Our findings suggest that nonparametric clustering is a promising approach to image segmentation, offering advantages in terms of flexibility, scalability, and robustness to noise. The proposed method has important implications for a wide range of applications, including object recognition, tracking, and scene understanding in computer vision.

able to sequentially adapt the mixture components as well as the mixture

We have extended classical pattern avoidance to a new structure: multiple
task-precedence posets whose Hasse diagrams have three levels, which we will
call diamonds. The vertices of each diamond are assigned labels which are
compatible with the poset. A corresponding permutation is formed by reading
these labels by increasing levels, and then from left to right. We used Sage to
form enumerative conjectures for the associated permutations avoiding
collections of patterns of length three, which we then proved. We have
discovered a bijection between diamonds avoiding 132 and certain generalized
Dyck paths. We have also found the generating function for descents, and
therefore the number of avoiders, in these permutations for the majority of
collections of patterns of length three. An interesting application of this
work (and the motivating example) can be found when task-precedence posets
represent warehouse package fulfillment by robots, in which case avoidance of
both 231 and 321 ensures we never stack two heavier packages on top of a
lighter package.

This paper presents a novel approach to image segmentation that combines Monte Carlo Markov chain (MCMC) shape sampling with nonparametric shape priors. The proposed method, called MCMC Shape Sampling for Image Segmentation (MSSIS), leverages the strengths of both techniques to achieve accurate and robust segmentation results.

MCMC is a powerful tool for exploring complex probability distributions, while nonparametric shape priors offer flexibility in modeling the diversity of shapes present in images. By integrating these two approaches, MSSIS can effectively capture the variability and uncertainty of shapes in real-world images.

The proposed method consists of three key components: 1) a probabilistic framework that models the likelihood of each pixel belonging to a particular class given its neighbors; 2) a nonparametric shape prior that captures the distribution of shapes in the image; and 3) an MCMC algorithm that iteratively samples from the posterior distribution over the class labels, incorporating information from both the image data and the shape prior.

Experiments on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of MSSIS compared to state-of-the-art methods. Our approach achieves high accuracy in various scenarios, including objects with irregular boundaries, multi-modal structures, and low contrast regions. Furthermore, we show that MSSIS outperforms traditional segmentation methods by adapting to unknown object shapes and handling boundary ambiguities more effectively.

We also provide theoretical analysis of the convergence properties of MSSIS and investigate the impact of different parameters on its performance. The insights gained from this study contribute to a better understanding of how to optimize the use of nonparametric shape priors in image segmentation tasks.

In summary, MCMC Shape Sampling for Image Segmentation offers a promising paradigm shift in image segmentation, addressing fundamental limitations inherent in existing approaches. By synergizing MCMC and nonparametric shape priors, our method provides a more complete representation of the structure present in images, leading to improved segmentation outcomes and enhanced robustness to varying imaging conditions.

Accurate image segmentation plays a crucial role in medical image analysis,
yet it faces great challenges of various shapes, diverse sizes, and blurry
boundaries. To address these difficulties, square kernel-based encoder-decoder
architecture has been proposed and widely used, but its performance remains
still unsatisfactory. To further cope with these challenges, we present a novel
double-branch encoder architecture. Our architecture is inspired by two
observations: 1) Since the discrimination of features learned via square
convolutional kernels needs to be further improved, we propose to utilize
non-square vertical and horizontal convolutional kernels in the double-branch
encoder, so features learned by the two branches can be expected to complement
each other. 2) Considering that spatial attention can help models to better
focus on the target region in a large-sized image, we develop an attention loss
to further emphasize the segmentation on small-sized targets. Together, the
above two schemes give rise to a novel double-branch encoder segmentation
framework for medical image segmentation, namely Crosslink-Net. The experiments
validate the effectiveness of our model on four datasets. The code is released
at https://github.com/Qianyu1226/Crosslink-Net.

We present a new method for isolating relativistic effects in large-scale structure. The method is based on the fact that the peculiar velocity of a galaxy is a function of its position and redshift. We use the redshift-space power spectrum to measure the velocity field, and then use the velocity field to predict the real-space power spectrum. We find that the real-space power spectrum is a good tracer of the underlying matter density field, and that the redshift-space power spectrum is a good tracer of the velocity field. We use these results to isolate the relativistic effects in the redshift-space power spectrum. We find that the relativistic effects are small, but not negligible. In particular, we find that the relativistic effects can account for up to 10% of the total power in the redshift-space power spectrum. This is a significant improvement over previous methods, which have been unable to isolate the relativistic effects in the redshift-space power spectrum.

It has been shown that many aspects of the noise in speech are separable, allowing them to be treated by simple regularization procedures and/or machine learning. For example, speech recognizers can separate out background noise such as wind, ambient noise at traffic lights, air flow, speakers voice pitch, etc., and classify those signals into different classes – speech-like or non-speech-like (Culpepper et al. 2009). This separation allows researchers to create more precise measures regarding how well a model is performing when applied to noisy data (e.g., Speech Recognition in Noise 2012) with far less computational effort than using traditional ways of extracting noise features like spectral analysis alone; such techniques lead to a 20 to 50 times reduction in the time required per training iteration (Razza et al. 2013), thus making it possible for models to run faster on noisy inputs. Another application involves classifying multiple recordings simultaneously into subsets based upon similarities in their spectrograms and then performing regression on each subset individually; this allows one to obtain additional predictions for each type of label (similarity, frequency, location, shape, duration, etc.) even considering an unknown number of labels, e.g. a noisy dataset consisting of recordings of 2 categories A and B. On top of these benefits, regularisation procedures facilitate the detection of outliers among classification accuracies derived solely from the standard deviation of counts (Davies & Dyer 1975). Such approaches have also been used to derive information about high level attributes of stimuli and infer their relationships to corresponding auditory components, such as noise characteristics or feature representations such as features that determine the strength of the acoustic signal (Furr et al. 2005), which should greatly assist future research. However, most types of learning algorithms have not yet succeeded in separating out these various effects from any reasonable margin (i.e., only using discrete labels, with some variation between and within subclasses). In previous work we showed that certain classes of speech recognizers could learn to distinguish noise features as effectively as, but worse than (Mottier et al. 2008; O'Donnell et al. 2010a), an average human discriminator and therefore have no difficulty distinguishing these noisy speech signals. The current study investigates whether some form of recurrent neural network (Recurrent Net) can accomplish this task.

In a k-linear triangulated category (where k is a field) we show that the
existence of Auslander-Reiten triangles implies that objects are determined, up
to shift, by knowing dimensions of homomorphisms between them. In most cases
the objects themselves are distinguished by this information, a conclusion
which was also reached under slightly different hypotheses in a theorem of
Jensen, Su and Zimmermann. The approach is to consider bilinear forms on
Grothendieck groups which are analogous to the Green ring of a finite group.
  We specialize to the category of perfect complexes for a self-injective
algebra, for which the Auslander-Reiten quiver has a known shape. We
characterize the position in the quiver of many kinds of perfect complexes,
including those of lengths 1, 2 and 3, rigid complexes and truncated projective
resolutions. We describe completely the quiver components which contain
projective modules. We obtain relationships between the homology of complexes
at different places in the quiver, deducing that every self-injective algebra
of radical length at least 3 has indecomposable perfect complexes with
arbitrarily large homology in any given degree. We find also that homology
stabilizes away from the rim of the quiver. We show that when the algebra is
symmetric, one of the forms considered earlier is Hermitian, and this allows us
to compute its values knowing them only on objects on the rim of the quiver.

Based on elastic collisions, the linear momentum of a fast neutron can be
measured from as few as two consecutive recoil ion tracks plus the vertex
position of the third collision, or `two and half' ion tracks. If the time
delay between the first two consecutive ion tracks is also measured, the number
of ion tracks can be reduced to one and a half. The angular and magnitude
resolutions are limited by ion range straggling to about ten percent.
Multi-wire proportional chambers and light-field imaging are discussed for fast
neutron tracking. Single-charge or single-photon detection sensitivity is
required in either approach. Light-field imaging is free of
charge-diffusion-induced image blur, but the limited number of photons
available can be a challenge. $^1$H,$^2$H and $^3$He could be used for the
initial development of fast neutron trackers based on light-field imaging.

An $N$-level quantum system is coupled to a bosonic heat reservoir at
positive temperature. We analyze the system-reservoir dynamics in the following
regime: The strength $\lambda$ of the system-reservoir coupling is fixed and
small, but larger than the spacing $\sigma$ of system energy levels. For
vanishing $\sigma$ there is a manifold of invariant system-reservoir states and
for $\sigma>0$ the only invariant state is the joint equilibrium. The manifold
is invariant for $\sigma=0$ but becomes quasi-invariant for $\sigma>0$. Namely,
on a first time-scale of the order $1/\lambda^2$, initial states approach the
manifold. Then they converge to the joint equilibrium state on a much larger
time-scale of the order $\lambda^2/\sigma^2$. We give a detailed expansion of
the system-reservoir evolution showing the above scenario.

Road network and building footprint extraction is essential for many
applications such as updating maps, traffic regulations, city planning,
ride-hailing, disaster response \textit{etc}. Mapping road networks is
currently both expensive and labor-intensive. Recently, improvements in image
segmentation through the application of deep neural networks has shown
promising results in extracting road segments from large scale, high resolution
satellite imagery. However, significant challenges remain due to lack of enough
labeled training data needed to build models for industry grade applications.
In this paper, we propose a two-stage transfer learning technique to improve
robustness of semantic segmentation for satellite images that leverages noisy
pseudo ground truth masks obtained automatically (without human labor) from
crowd-sourced OpenStreetMap (OSM) data. We further propose Pyramid
Pooling-LinkNet (PP-LinkNet), an improved deep neural network for segmentation
that uses focal loss, poly learning rate, and context module. We demonstrate
the strengths of our approach through evaluations done on three popular
datasets over two tasks, namely, road extraction and building foot-print
detection. Specifically, we obtain 78.19\% meanIoU on SpaceNet building
footprint dataset, 67.03\% and 77.11\% on the road topology metric on SpaceNet
and DeepGlobe road extraction dataset, respectively.

Autopilot methods have become critical platforms in various fields, including search, machine vision, self-driving cars and speech recognition. Recently it was shown that large datasets could be captured more quickly with conventional systems by running them on GPUs [41]. This has led to recent discussion concerning both the usefulness of GPU systems in such applications versus their limits when training complex systems that exhibit stochastic fluctuations [42]. Here we propose an alternative methodology of using AI algorithms in this context which is based on deep learning techniques introduced to a class of neural networks. We start with general classifiers applied to raw images or to single features only. We further study the performance characteristics of different classesifiers with respect to self-learning capabilities. These include three novel deep architectures (1st-order perceptrons, logistic regression, recurrent neural network) as well as two standard classes and the recently introduced nonlinear regression. Our results broadly support the idea that self-learning models can learn complex representations that result in better performances over traditional methods. Deep learning approaches are also able to solve tasks such as image segmentation, where classical multilayer representations are too fragile.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to image segmentation using deep learning and the Mumford-Shah loss functional. The Mumford-Shah functional is a popular tool in image processing and computer vision that measures the similarity between two images based on their gradient information. However, its use in deep learning frameworks has been limited due to its non-differentiable nature.

To overcome this limitation, we introduce a differentiable variant of the Mumford-Shah functional that can be seamlessly integrated into deep neural networks. Our proposed method, called Mumford-Shah loss functional for image segmentation (MSLF), combines the strengths of traditional image segmentation techniques with the power of deep learning algorithms.

The MSLF objective function consists of two main components: a data fidelity term that ensures accurate prediction of the output label maps, and a regularization term that encourages smoothness and consistency in the predicted labels. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several benchmark datasets, including Cityscapes, PASCAL VOC, and CamVid.

Experiments show that MSLF outperforms state-of-the-art image segmentation methods, including fully convolutional network (FCN) and U-Net, in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency. Additionally, we perform an ablation study to analyze the contribution of different components of the MSLF functional, providing insights into the role of each component in improving segmentation performance.

Our work marks the first successful integration of the Mumford-Shah functional into deep learning frameworks for image segmentation tasks. We believe that MSLF has great potential for applications in various fields such as autonomous driving, robotics, and medical imaging, where accurate image segmentation is critical.

This paper proposes a novel approach to semi-supervised medical image segmentation, which is a challenging problem due to the limited availability of labeled data. Our method leverages the concept of dual-task consistency to improve segmentation accuracy. Specifically, we train two separate neural networks for image segmentation and boundary detection, respectively, using both labeled and unlabeled data. We then enforce consistency between the predictions of these two networks, encouraging them to produce identical outputs for the same input images. This consistency regularization term helps to propagate knowledge from the well-performing boundary detection task to the segmentation task, leading to improved performance.

We evaluate our proposed method on several benchmark datasets, including CelebFaces, LUNA16, and MM2M, and demonstrate superior performance compared to state-of-the art semi-supervised segmentation methods. Additionally, we perform ablation studies to analyze the impact of different components of our framework, providing insights into the effectiveness of the dual-task consistency approach.

Our main contributions can be summarized as follows: (1) we introduce a novel semi-supervised learning framework for medical image segmentation that combines dual-task consistency with adversarial training; (2) we demonstrate the efficacy of our method on various benchmark datasets, outperforming existing semi-supervised segmentation approaches; (3) we provide thorough ablation studies to investigate the role of each component in our framework, shedding light on the mechanism behind its success.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section II reviews relevant works on semi-supervised medical image segmentation and dual-task learning. Section III describes our proposed method in detail, including network architectures, loss functions, and training strategies. Section IV presents experimental results and analysis, whileSection V concludes the paper and highlights future research directions.

Our proposed method enables the flexible and efficient transfer of styles between portraits, allowing for the generation of new and visually appealing images that combine the content of one image with the style of another.

Existing methods for style transfer are limited in their ability to handle complex and diverse portrait images, as they often rely on predefined templates or require manual segmentation masks. In contrast, our approach utilizes the attention mechanism to learn a mapping between the content and style domains, enabling the preservation of fine-grained details and subtle nuances in the output image.

We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate its effectiveness in generating high-quality style transfers. Additionally, we showcase its versatility by applying it to various artistic styles, including paintings, sketches, and watercolors. The results demonstrate the potential of our method for creating realistic and visually plausible style transfers, opening up exciting possibilities for applications such as digital art creation, image editing, and fashion design.

Our key contributions include:

* A novel approach for neural arbitrary style transfer of portrait images using the attention mechanism
* Preservation of fine-grained details and subtle nuances in the transferred image
* No requirement for predefined templates or manual segmentation masks
* Efficient and flexible processing of complex and diverse portrait images
* Demonstrated effectiveness on several benchmark datasets and various artistic styles.

transversals we give a normal form for a neighborhood of the submanifold, and
use that to define a generalized complex blow-up, which is up to deformation
independent of choices.

A severe application of stress on articular cartilage can initiate a cascade
of biochemical reactions that can lead to the development of osteoarthritis. We
constructed a multiscale mathematical model of the process with three
components: cellular, chemical, and mechanical. The cellular component
describes the different chondrocyte states according to the chemicals these
cells release. The chemical component models the change in concentrations of
those chemicals. The mechanical component contains a simulation of pressure
application onto a cartilage explant and the resulting strains that initiate
the biochemical processes. The model creates a framework for incorporating
explicit mechanics, simulated by finite element analysis, into a theoretical
biology framework.

Here we show how to efficiently apply neural networks' ability to extract visual features under constrained conditions even on high-dimensional images such as portraits, where the relevant features can vary systematically between people or objects. We evaluate our solution by training a convolutional neural network with 5 classes (male, female), which are composed of two binary dimensions (height/weight). Each class has five percepts for each dimension but these are all processed with the same hidden units. This means that there are only 16,000 possible values represented in hidden layer cells across all 5 classes. To make use of this limited feature space within the 10 core classes, we extract six subsets from classes with lower weight and 6 more through the second dimension, leading to 80 different categories per 5 classes. For each category we train one random network to convert the latent features as presented below into a RGB value while a random network performs the opposite (i.e., extracting unary features). We find three examples with over 95% accuracy on the validation data with one such example having less than 50% on real subjects! Importantly, the results depend heavily on the model type and it isn't sufficient to simply embed the output layer in another model either, although this would increase computational efficiency considerably! Two-dimensional (2D) topological insulators (TIs), also known as quantum spin
Hall (QSH) insulators, are excellent candidates for coherent spin transport
related applications because the edge states of 2D TIs are robust against
nonmagnetic impurities since the only available backscattering channel is
forbidden. Currently, most known 2D TIs are based on a hexagonal (specifically,
honeycomb) lattice. Here, we propose that there exists the quantum spin Hall
effect (QSHE) in a buckled square lattice. Through performing global structure
optimization, we predict a new three-layer quasi-2D (Q2D) structure which has
the lowest energy among all structures with the thickness less than 6.0 {\AA}
for the BiF system. It is identified to be a Q2D TI with a large band gap (0.69
eV). The electronic states of the Q2D BiF system near the Fermi level are
mainly contributed by the middle Bi square lattice, which are sandwiched by two
inert BiF2 layers. This is beneficial since the interaction between a substrate
and the Q2D material may not change the topological properties of the system,
as we demonstrate in the case of the NaF substrate. Finally, we come up with a
new tight-binding model for a two-orbital system with the buckled square
lattice to explain the low-energy physics of the Q2D BiF material. Our study
not only predicts a QSH insulator for realistic room temperature applications,
but also provides a new lattice system for engineering topological states such
as quantum anomalous Hall effect.

One usage of medical ultrasound imaging is to visualize and characterize
human tongue shape and motion during a real-time speech to study healthy or
impaired speech production. Due to the low-contrast characteristic and noisy
nature of ultrasound images, it might require expertise for non-expert users to
recognize tongue gestures in applications such as visual training of a second
language. Moreover, quantitative analysis of tongue motion needs the tongue
dorsum contour to be extracted, tracked, and visualized. Manual tongue contour
extraction is a cumbersome, subjective, and error-prone task. Furthermore, it
is not a feasible solution for real-time applications. The growth of deep
learning has been vigorously exploited in various computer vision tasks,
including ultrasound tongue contour tracking. In the current methods, the
process of tongue contour extraction comprises two steps of image segmentation
and post-processing. This paper presents a new novel approach of automatic and
real-time tongue contour tracking using deep neural networks. In the proposed
method, instead of the two-step procedure, landmarks of the tongue surface are
tracked. This novel idea enables researchers in this filed to benefits from
available previously annotated databases to achieve high accuracy results. Our
experiment disclosed the outstanding performances of the proposed technique in
terms of generalization, performance, and accuracy.

segmentation, image super-resolution, coloration and image inpainting. In this
work we propose the use of convolutional neural networks (CNN) for image
inpainting of large regions in high-resolution textures. Due to limited
computational resources processing high-resolution images with neural networks
is still an open problem. Existing methods separate inpainting of global
structure and the transfer of details, which leads to blurry results and loss
of global coherence in the detail transfer step. Based on advances in texture
synthesis using CNNs we propose patch-based image inpainting by a CNN that is
able to optimize for global as well as detail texture statistics. Our method is
capable of filling large inpainting regions, oftentimes exceeding the quality
of comparable methods for high-resolution images. For reference patch look-up
we propose to use the same summary statistics that are used in the inpainting
process.

In applied image segmentation tasks, the ability to provide numerous and
precise labels for training is paramount to the accuracy of the model at
inference time. However, this overhead is often neglected, and recently
proposed segmentation architectures rely heavily on the availability and
fidelity of ground truth labels to achieve state-of-the-art accuracies. Failure
to acknowledge the difficulty in creating adequate ground truths can lead to an
over-reliance on pre-trained models or a lack of adoption in real-world
