In this paper, we propose a novel approach to general medical image segmentation that leverages recent advances in deep learning and uncertainty quantification to achieve robust performance across various modalities and pathologies. Our method is based on a hybrid framework that combines the strengths of fully convolutional networks (FCNs) with the versatility of probabilistic graphical models (PGMs).

First, we train an FCN to learn high-level features from a large dataset of labeled medical images. Then, we use these features as input to a PGM, which models the spatial relationships between pixels and enforces label consistency across neighboring regions. The PGM is trained using a variety of datasets with different modalities and diseases, allowing us to learn a robust representation of the underlying anatomy.

To improve our model's ability to handle variations in image quality and artifacts, we incorporate uncertainty estimates into the segmentation process. Specifically, we use dropout regularization to induce aleatoric uncertainty during training, and combine it with epistemic uncertainty from the PGM's predictions. This allows us to generate high-quality segmentations even when dealing with noisy or low-resolution inputs.

We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets encompassing diverse medical imaging modalities, including CT, MRI, and US. The results demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of both accuracy and robustness. Furthermore, we perform a series of ablation studies to analyze the contributions of individual components and provide insights into the working mechanism of our proposed method.

The main contribution of this work lies in its ability to effectively integrate prior knowledge and uncertainty information to achieve robust medical image segmentation. Our approach has important implications for clinical applications where accurate and reliable segmentations are essential, such as tumor detection and monitoring, organ segregation, and treatment planning.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach for automatic quality evaluation of noisy-labeled image segmentation, called Pick-and-Learn. Noisy-labeled data, which contains incorrect or inconsistent labels, is a common problem in image segmentation tasks and can significantly degrade the performance of deep learning models. Existing methods for quality evaluation rely on manual annotation of a small subset of the data, which is time-consuming and expensive.

Our proposed method, Pick-and-Learn, leverages a small set of manually annotated images to learn a quality evaluation metric that can be used to evaluate the quality of the entire dataset. The key idea is to iteratively select a subset of images from the dataset, annotate them manually, and use these annotations to learn a quality evaluation metric. The metric is then used to evaluate the quality of the remaining images in the dataset.

We evaluate the effectiveness of Pick-and-Learn on several benchmark datasets and compare it to existing methods. Our results show that Pick-and-Learn achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of accuracy and efficiency. We also demonstrate the versatility of our approach by applying it to different segmentation tasks, including object detection and instance segmentation.

Our main contributions are:

* A novel approach for automatic quality evaluation of noisy-labeled image segmentation, called Pick-and-Learn.
* An efficient and effective method for learning a quality evaluation metric using a small set of manually annotated images.
* State-of-the-art performance on several benchmark datasets, outperforming existing methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

The paper is organized as follows: In section 2, we review related work on quality evaluation for image segmentation. In section 3, we describe the proposed Pick-and-Learn method in detail. In section 4, we present the experimental results and comparison to existing methods. Finally, we conclude the paper in section 5 with a discussion of the results and future work.

The ability to detect and characterize these structures has the potential to revolutionize fields such as materials science, physics, biology, and computer science, among others. Ultimately, this research paves the way towards the development of new materials, technologies, and strategies that exploit the unique properties of complex systems to solve pressing challenges facing society today.

The graph Laplacian is a fundamental matrix in graph theory and plays a central role in various applications, including graph partitioning, clustering, and solving linear systems. However, computing matrix-vector products with the graph Laplacian can be computationally expensive, especially for large graphs.

Our proposed method leverages the NFFT to efficiently compute the matrix-vector products by exploiting the spectral properties of the graph Laplacian. Specifically, we use the NFFT to approximate the inverse of the graph Laplacian, which enables us to compute matrix-vector products using a series of fast Fourier transforms. We also employ Krylov subspace methods to further accelerate the computation by exploiting the structure of the graph Laplacian.

Our experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of computational efficiency and scalability. We show that our method can handle large-scale graphs with millions of nodes and edges in a matter of seconds, while maintaining high accuracy. We also demonstrate the versatility of our method by applying it to various graph-related tasks, such as graph partitioning, clustering, and solving linear systems.

Our work has important implications for a wide range of applications that involve computing matrix-vector products with the graph Laplacian. Our method enables faster and more efficient processing of large-scale graph data, which can lead to breakthroughs in various fields, including social network analysis, recommendation systems, and machine learning.

In this paper, we explore the use of deep learning techniques to improve the performance of message passing inference in graphical models. Message passing inference is a widely used method for approximating complex probability distributions, but it can suffer from the problem of message passing divergence, where the messages become stuck in an infinite loop of iteration. We propose a novel approach that combines message passing inference with deep learning to learn a representation of the messages that allows for more effective inference.

Our approach, called Deep Message Passing Inference (DMP), uses a deep neural network to learn a mapping from the input variables to a lower-dimensional representation of the messages. We show that this representation can be used to improve the convergence of message passing inference, allowing for more accurate and efficient approximation of complex probability distributions.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of DMP on several benchmark datasets and compare it to state-of-the-art methods for approximate inference. Our results show that DMP achieves significantly better performance than existing methods, both in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. We also analyze the effect of different architectures and training techniques on the performance of DMP, providing insights into the design of effective deep learning models for message passing inference.

Overall, our work represents a significant advance in the field of approximate inference, and demonstrates the potential of deep learning techniques for improving the performance of message passing inference. We believe that DMP has the potential to enable new applications of graphical models in machine learning and related fields, and we plan to explore its use in a variety of domains in future work.

In this paper, we propose a new approach for building cellular automata to
solve real-world segmentation problems. We design and train a cellular
automaton that can successfully segment high-resolution images. We consider a
colony that densely inhabits the pixel grid, and all cells are governed by a
randomized update that uses the current state, the color, and the state of the
$3\times 3$ neighborhood. The space of possible rules is defined by a small
neural network. The update rule is applied repeatedly in parallel to a large
random subset of cells and after convergence is used to produce segmentation
masks that are then back-propagated to learn the optimal update rules using
standard gradient descent methods. We demonstrate that such models can be
learned efficiently with only limited trajectory length and that they show
remarkable ability to organize the information to produce a globally consistent
segmentation result, using only local information exchange. From a practical
perspective, our approach allows us to build very efficient models -- our
smallest automaton uses less than 10,000 parameters to solve complex
segmentation tasks.

In Elementary Cycles theory elementary quantum particles are consistently
described as the manifestation of ultra-fast relativistic spacetime cyclic
dynamics, classical in the essence. The peculiar relativistic geometrodynamics
of Elementary Cycles theory yields de facto a unification of ordinary
relativistic and quantum physics. In particular its classical-relativistic
cyclic dynamics reproduce exactly from classical physics first principles all
the fundamental aspects of Quantum Mechanics, such as all its axioms, the
Feynman path integral, the Dirac quantisation prescription (second
quantisation), quantum dynamics of statistical systems, non-relativistic
quantum mechanics, atomic physics, superconductivity, graphene physics and so

interactions, without postulating gauge invariance, directly from relativistic
geometrodynamical transformations, in close analogy with the description of
gravitational interaction in general relativity. In this paper we summarise
some of the major achievements, rigorously proven also in several recent
peer-reviewed papers, of this innovative formulation of quantum particle
physics.

In this paper, we investigate the domain dynamics of nonequilibrium random-field Ising models, which are widely used to describe the behavior of magnetic materials in the presence of external fields. Using a combination of analytical and numerical techniques, we study the evolution of domain patterns in these systems as they relax towards thermal equilibrium.

We first introduce a simple model for a random-field Ising system and discuss its thermodynamic properties. We then derive a set of mean-field equations that describe the dynamics of the domain walls in this model, taking into account the effects of the random field and the interface energy between domains.

Using these equations, we conduct a linear stability analysis to determine the perturbations that can lead to the formation of new domain patterns. Our results show that the instability boundaries separating different domain configurations exhibit a rich structure, with multiple transitions occurring as the temperature and other parameters vary.

Next, we perform simulations of the full stochastic dynamics using a Monte Carlo algorithm, focusing on a two-dimensional system as an example. We observe a variety of interesting behaviors, including the formation of stable spiral and vortex states, as well as transient dynamics such as domain coarsening and collapse. Our findings provide insights into the mechanisms behind the emergence of complex domain structures in nonequilibrium magnetic materials.

Finally, we discuss the implications of our results for the design and control of magnetic devices that rely on domain engineering. By understanding the principles governing domain dynamics in nonequilibrum conditions, researchers may develop novel strategies for manipulating magnetic properties such as magnetization strength and switching times. These advances could have significant impacts in areas like data storage technology and spintronics.

Data compression algorithms have become increasingly important in modern data analysis, with their potential to reduce disk storage requirements while retaining data availability and quality properties. In addition to being used by many major systems (e.g., Google), such algorithms are also frequently required during image processing computations in order to improve both accuracy, sensitivity, and speed at lower bit depth. While there exists some information about how many operations can be accomplished per second on common data compression libraries or techniques, there are few such benchmarks that measure performance using actual images rather than symbolic transformations at intermediate scale steps. The purpose of this article is therefore to perform such a test to determine, by means of Fourier transforms and high performance linear algebra calculations, the theoretical limit to which an image could compress before loss of visual fidelity due to data compression artifacts. We apply generalized Q-sampling conversion to images from two general purpose software applications, iQ3 and ImageJ 1.10, capturing over half trillion points of input pixel values per second for 30 minute runs in one cluster, and then observe significant performance differences across these data types including significantly better reduction ratios and significantly faster run times within ImageJ (1ms versus 21 minutes), but no significant difference between image formats either when run under GNU/Linux (4m vs 6 hours) or Android 4.0 operating system as described below. Overall, we find that for most popular datasets ImageJ gives superior results compared to other alternatives in terms of reduced compressed data access time and higher computational throughput. However, our tests do show notable differences between distributions resulting from different application optimizations. We further highlight several potential next steps towards improving our understanding of data compressing algorithms like Generalized Q-Sampling for use in image processing or for other situations commonly encountered in image processing environments where high data volume access (or memory consumption) should benefit greatly from this type of decompression scheme.

Few layer graphene systems such as Bernal stacked bilayer and rhombohedral
(ABC-) stacked trilayer offer the unique possibility to open an electric field
tunable energy gap. To date, this energy gap has been experimentally confirmed
in optical spectroscopy. Here we report the first direct observation of the
electric field tunable energy gap in electronic transport experiments on doubly
gated suspended ABC-trilayer graphene. From a systematic study of the
non-linearities in current \textit{versus} voltage characteristics and the
temperature dependence of the conductivity we demonstrate that thermally
activated transport over the energy-gap dominates the electrical response of
these transistors. The estimated values for energy gap from the temperature
dependence and from the current voltage characteristics follow the
theoretically expected electric field dependence with critical exponent $3/2$.
These experiments indicate that high quality few-layer graphene are suitable
candidates for exploring novel tunable THz light sources and detectors.

Flux braiding is a novel phenomenon that has been observed in various physical systems, including superconductors, superfluids, and optical lattices. It refers to the formation of topological defects in the form of braids or knots in the fluid flow or magnetic field lines, which can have significant impacts on the properties of the system. In this review article, we provide an overview of experimental studies on flux braiding, highlighting the different approaches used to observe and manipulate this phenomenon. We discuss the various techniques employed to create braided states, such as the injection of angular momentum, the application of external fields, and the use of dissipative dynamics. We also examine the characterization methods used to detect and quantify flux braiding, including measurements of the circulating current, the phase gradient, and the Knight shift. Furthermore, we explore the potential applications of flux braiding in both fundamental research and practical technologies, such as quantum computing, spintronics, and maglev systems. Finally, we discuss the challenges and opportunities that exist in the study of flux braiding, including the need for advanced theoretical models and the potential for new experimental techniques. This review provides a comprehensive summary of the current state of knowledge in the field and serves as a starting point for further exploration of the fascinating world of flux braiding.

A stable generalized complex structure is one that is generically symplectic
but degenerates along a real codimension two submanifold, where it defines a
generalized Calabi-Yau structure. We introduce a Lie algebroid which allows us
to view such structures as symplectic forms. This allows us to construct new
examples of stable structures, and also to define period maps for their
deformations in which the background three-form flux is either fixed or not,
proving the unobstructedness of both deformation problems. We then use the same
tools to establish local normal forms for the degeneracy locus and for
Lagrangian branes. Applying our normal forms to the four-dimensional case, we
prove that any compact stable generalized complex 4-manifold has a symplectic
completion, in the sense that it can be modified near its degeneracy locus to
produce a compact symplectic 4-manifold.

In this paper, we propose opportunistic jammer selection in a wireless
security system for increasing the secure degrees of freedom (DoF) between a
transmitter and a legitimate receiver (say, Alice and Bob). There is a jammer
group consisting of $S$ jammers among which Bob selects $K$ jammers. The
selected jammers transmit independent and identically distributed Gaussian
signals to hinder the eavesdropper (Eve). Since the channels of Bob and Eve are
independent, we can select the jammers whose jamming channels are aligned at
Bob, but not at Eve. As a result, Eve cannot obtain any DoF unless it has more
than $KN_j$ receive antennas, where $N_j$ is the number of jammer's transmit
antenna each, and hence $KN_j$ can be regarded as defensible dimensions against
Eve. For the jamming signal alignment at Bob, we propose two opportunistic
jammer selection schemes and find the scaling law of the required number of
jammers for target secure DoF by a geometrical interpretation of the received
signals.

The Riemann Hypothesis, a conjecture regarding the distribution of prime numbers, has been a longstanding problem in number theory. Over the years, various equivalent formulations and criteria have been proposed, each offering a different perspective on the problem. This paper explores the relationships between some of these formulations, specifically the Riemann Hypothesis Equivalences, Robin's Inequality, and Lagarias' Criterion.

We begin by examining the Riemann Hypothesis Equivalences, which provide a set of necessary and sufficient conditions for the Riemann Hypothesis to hold. We then discuss Robin's Inequality, a bound on the growth of the Riemann zeta function, and show how it is related to the Riemann Hypothesis. Lagarias' Criterion, which provides a sufficient condition for the Riemann Hypothesis, is also explored.

Our main result establishes a new connection between these formulations, showing that Lagarias' Criterion is in fact equivalent to a strengthened version of Robin's Inequality. This result not only deepens our understanding of the relationships between these formulations but also provides a new perspective on the Riemann Hypothesis.

Our work has important implications for the ongoing effort to prove the Riemann Hypothesis. By providing a new equivalence between well-known formulations, we offer a fresh avenue for attacking this problem. Furthermore, our result highlights the power of using multiple formulations to approach a problem, as each one can provide unique insights and opportunities for progress.

In conclusion, this paper contributes to the rich history of the Riemann Hypothesis by establishing new connections between its various formulations. Our work demonstrates the continued importance of exploring the relationships between different approaches to this problem, and we hope that it will inspire further advances in our understanding of the Riemann Hypothesis.

In this paper, we investigate the dynamics of spin squeezing, entanglement, and coherence in a system of two dissipative, nonlinear optical cavities that are coupled via photon exchange processes. The system is driven by both single-photon and two-photon inputs, leading to a rich variety of dynamical behaviors including the generation of non-classical states of light. By studying the behavior of various observables such as the number of photons, the spin variables, and the entanglement entropy, we uncover novel features of the system's behavior, including the suppression of decoherence through the formation of entangled pairs of photons. Our results demonstrate the potential for using these systems in quantum information processing applications, as well as providing new insights into the interplay between nonlinearity, dissipation, and quantum fluctuations in many-body systems.

A central problem in computer vision involves identifying different objects within an image; this can be considered as classifying the objects and not all the characteristics of the whole scene (e.g., distinguishing between humans, cats or animals). Training classifiers, while generally effective, are computationally intensive, time consuming activities on the scale of thousands to millions of trials at each level of abstraction, which prevents many classes of problems from being solved in practice. A recent challenge is thus how to build more efficient machine learning (ML) tools with very low computational costs so that they could be used in real systems where deep ML is applied to large volumes of images. We address this challenge by taking a cue from natural language processing, and propose that the classification task should not only involve samples of an input semantic space but also samples of multiple spaces (a sample set) representing distinct representations of the same space (e.g., training neural network models on both input semantic space with discriminative features that distinguish the object from non-object and sample sets with discriminant features allowing for sampling in the model that allow it to discriminate between two specific parts of the object). We apply this concept during data preprocessing and dataset acquisition using multi-level models, thereby permitting training the algorithm directly on multiple inputs representation without having to perform inference over other models. Our approach enables data sets from several sizes to fit into one big image with no memory footprint. Furthermore, after training over such samples we find that our trained models have good generalization accuracy of 0~1% when compared against another classifier trained on a different set of instances. This work highlights our ability to use supervised inference to solve problems involving large datasets while avoiding expensive deep ML operations.

Wood and Spekkens (2015) argue that any causal model explaining the EPRB
correlations and satisfying no-signalling must also violate the assumption that
the model faithfully reproduces the statistical dependences and
independences---a so-called "fine-tuning" of the causal parameters; this
includes, in particular, retrocausal explanations of the EPRB correlations. I
consider this analysis with a view to enumerating the possible responses an
advocate of retrocausal explanations might propose. I focus on the response of
N\"{a}ger (2015), who argues that the central ideas of causal explanations can
be saved if one accepts the possibility of a stable fine-tuning of the causal
parameters. I argue that, in light of this view, a violation of faithfulness
does not necessarily rule out retrocausal explanations of the EPRB
correlations, although it certainly constrains such explanations. I conclude by
considering some possible consequences of this type of response for retrocausal
explanations.

Medical image segmentation is a critical task in computer-aided diagnosis, but it is often challenging due to the domain shift between training and testing data. To address this issue, we propose Box-Adapt, a novel approach that utilizes bounding box supervision to adaptively segment medical images across different domains. Box-Adapt leverages the bounding box annotations available in medical images to guide the segmentation network and adapt it to new domains. Our extensive experiments on three medical image datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of Box-Adapt in improving segmentation performance across domains, achieving state-of-the-art results. The in vitro clonogenic assay is a technique to study the ability of a cell
to form a colony in a culture dish. By optical imaging, dishes with stained
colonies can be scanned and assessed digitally. Identification, segmentation
and counting of stained colonies play a vital part in high-throughput screening
and quantitative assessment of biological assays. Image processing of such
pictured/scanned assays can be affected by image/scan acquisition artifacts
like background noise and spatially varying illumination, and contaminants in
the suspension medium. Although existing approaches tackle these issues, the
segmentation quality requires further improvement, particularly on noisy and
low contrast images. In this work, we present an objective and versatile
machine learning procedure to amend these issues by characterizing, extracting
and segmenting inquired colonies using principal component analysis, k-means
clustering and a modified watershed segmentation algorithm. The intention is to
automatically identify visible colonies through spatial texture assessment and
accordingly discriminate them from background in preparation for successive
segmentation. The proposed segmentation algorithm yielded a similar quality as
manual counting by human observers. High F1 scores (>0.9) and low
root-mean-square errors (around 14%) underlined good agreement with ground
truth data. Moreover, it outperformed a recent state-of-the-art method. The
methodology will be an important tool in future cancer research applications.

This paper aims at developing an integrated system of clothing co-parsing, in
order to jointly parse a set of clothing images (unsegmented but annotated with
tags) into semantic configurations. We propose a data-driven framework
consisting of two phases of inference. The first phase, referred as "image
co-segmentation", iterates to extract consistent regions on images and jointly
refines the regions over all images by employing the exemplar-SVM (E-SVM)
technique [23]. In the second phase (i.e. "region co-labeling"), we construct a
multi-image graphical model by taking the segmented regions as vertices, and
incorporate several contexts of clothing configuration (e.g., item location and
mutual interactions). The joint label assignment can be solved using the
efficient Graph Cuts algorithm. In addition to evaluate our framework on the
Fashionista dataset [30], we construct a dataset called CCP consisting of 2098
high-resolution street fashion photos to demonstrate the performance of our
system. We achieve 90.29% / 88.23% segmentation accuracy and 65.52% / 63.89%
recognition rate on the Fashionista and the CCP datasets, respectively, which
are superior compared with state-of-the-art methods.

By employing first-principles density functional theory calculations and tight-binding models, we demonstrate that such structures can exhibit non-trivial band structure and spin texture, giving rise to the quantum spin Hall effect. We show that the buckling of the square lattice leads to a significant enhancement of the spin-orbit coupling, which is essential for therealization of the quantum spin Hall effect at room temperature. Furthermore, we find that the buckled square lattice geometry allows for an tunable spin gap, providing a means to control the thermal stability of the quantum spin Hall state. Our results pave the way for the experimental realization of room temperature quantum spin Hall insulators with potential applications in spintronics and topologically protected electronic devices.

Traditional image segmentation methods rely on hand-crafted features and heuristics, which often lead to suboptimal performance when dealing with complex scenes or low-quality data. The key insight behind Points2Polygons is to use adversarial training to learn a polygon-based representation of the image, where each polygon corresponds to a coherent region of the scene. This allows us to effectively capture object boundaries and handle irregularly shaped objects, while also propagating information across neighboring regions to produce more accurate segmentations.

We evaluate Points2Polygons on several benchmark datasets, including PASCAL VOC and Cityscapes, comparing it against state-of-the-art segmentation algorithms. Overall, this work represents an important step towards developing robust and efficient image segmentation techniques that can operate effectively in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we explore the concept of explicit evidence systems with common knowledge (EES-CK) and its applications in various domains. EES-CK is a novel approach to representing and reasoning about evidence that combines the advantages of both explicit evidence systems and common knowledge approaches.

Explicit evidence systems are formal frameworks for representing and reasoning about evidence, which have been shown to be effective in a variety of applications, including legal proceedings, scientific inquiry, and decision-making under uncertainty. However, these systems rely on the availability of high-quality evidence, which may not always be available or feasible to obtain.

Common knowledge, on the other hand, refers to shared beliefs or assumptions held by a group of individuals or a community. It has been recognized as an important factor in shaping social norms, cooperation, and collective action. However, common knowledge can also be ambiguous, and its use in evidence-based reasoning can lead to issues such as confirmation bias and circularity.

EES-CK addresses these limitations by combining the strengths of both approaches. By integrating common knowledge into explicit evidence systems, it allows for more robust and flexible representations of evidence, while still maintaining the ability to reason formally about the underlying uncertainties. We demonstrate the effectiveness of EES-CK through several case studies, highlighting its potential applicability in fields such as artificial intelligence, law, and public policy.

The main contributions of this paper include: (1) the development of a new framework for understanding and analyzing EES-CK; (2) the presentation of algorithms and techniques for constructing and querying EES-CK models; and (3) an evaluation of the performance of EES-CK in comparison to existing methods using real-world scenarios. Our results show that EES-CK outperforms traditional evidential reasoning approaches in terms of accuracy and efficiency, especially when dealing with complex, uncertain, or incomplete information.

Overall, our work advances the state of the art in evidence reasoning and provides a solid foundation for further research in this area. The integration of common knowledge into explicit evidence systems offers a promising path forward for better decision-making and problem-solving in a wide range of contexts.

ConvLSTMs are a type of deep neural network that combine the strengths of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. They are well-suited for processing sequential data, such as video, by learning both short-term and long-term dependencies between frames.

We evaluate our approach on several challenging datasets, including the Cityscapes and CamVid datasets, and demonstrate its superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. Our experiments show that ConvLSTMs outperform traditional CNNs and LSTMs in terms of segmentation accuracy, while also being more efficient in terms of computational resources.

We also perform a series of ablation studies to analyze the contributions of different components of our approach, providing insights into the effectiveness of ConvLSTMs for semantic segmentation of video sequences.

Our work has important implications for a wide range of applications, including autonomous driving, robotics, and video surveillance, where the ability to accurately segment objects in real-time is crucial. We focus on an important yet challenging problem: using a 2D deep network to
deal with 3D segmentation for medical image analysis. Existing approaches
either applied multi-view planar (2D) networks or directly used volumetric (3D)
networks for this purpose, but both of them are not ideal: 2D networks cannot
capture 3D contexts effectively, and 3D networks are both memory-consuming and
less stable arguably due to the lack of pre-trained models.
  In this paper, we bridge the gap between 2D and 3D using a novel approach
named Elastic Boundary Projection (EBP). The key observation is that, although
the object is a 3D volume, what we really need in segmentation is to find its
boundary which is a 2D surface. Therefore, we place a number of pivot points in
the 3D space, and for each pivot, we determine its distance to the object
boundary along a dense set of directions. This creates an elastic shell around
each pivot which is initialized as a perfect sphere. We train a 2D deep network
to determine whether each ending point falls within the object, and gradually
adjust the shell so that it gradually converges to the actual shape of the
boundary and thus achieves the goal of segmentation. EBP allows boundary-based
segmentation without cutting a 3D volume into slices or patches, which stands
out from conventional 2D and 3D approaches. EBP achieves promising accuracy in
abdominal organ segmentation. Our code has been open-sourced
https://github.com/twni2016/Elastic-Boundary-Projection.

In this paper, we present a minimalist design for a robust real-time quantum random number generator (QRNG) based on a single photon's quantum fluctuations. Our proposed QRNG utilizes a simple and efficient architecture that combines the advantages of both optical and electrical noise sources, ensuring high randomness and fast generation rates.

The proposed system consists of a laser source, a beam splitter, two phase-randomized Mach-Zehnder interferometers, and a pair of photodetectors. By carefully controlling the interference patterns and photoelectron arrival times, our scheme generates binary numbers with high probability and low bias. We also implement an online randomness test to ensure the generated bits are truly random and conform to empirical distributions.

Our simulation results show that the proposed QRNG can generate random bits at a rate of up to 50 Mbps, outperforming existing similar systems in terms of speed and compact size. Moreover, we analyze various potential sources of errors and develop feasible methods to mitigate them, resulting in a robust device suitable for practical applications.

This work has significant implications for both theoretical research and practical implementation of quantum cryptography. The introduced design provides a secure solution for generating random keys in encryption protocols, as well as shedding light on fundamental aspects of quantum mechanics through studies of photonic quantum entanglement and nonlocality.

WavePacket is an open-source program package for the numerical simulation of
quantum-mechanical dynamics. It can be used to solve time-independent or
time-dependent linear Schr\"odinger and Liouville-von Neumann-equations in one
or more dimensions. Also coupled equations can be treated, which allows to
simulate molecular quantum dynamics beyond the Born-Oppenheimer approximation.
Optionally accounting for the interaction with external electric fields within
the semiclassical dipole approximation, WavePacket can be used to simulate
experiments involving tailored light pulses in photo-induced physics or
chemistry.The graphical capabilities allow visualization of quantum dynamics
'on the fly', including Wigner phase space representations. Being easy to use
and highly versatile, WavePacket is well suited for the teaching of quantum
mechanics as well as for research projects in atomic, molecular and optical
physics or in physical or theoretical chemistry.The present Part I deals with
the description of closed quantum systems in terms of Schr\"odinger equations.
The emphasis is on discrete variable representations for spatial discretization
as well as various techniques for temporal discretization.The upcoming Part II
will focus on open quantum systems and dimension reduction; it also describes
the codes for optimal control of quantum dynamics.The present work introduces
the MATLAB version of WavePacket 5.2.1 which is hosted at the Sourceforge
platform, where extensive Wiki-documentation as well as worked-out
demonstration examples can be found.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach for anomaly detection in time series of graphs, leveraging the concept of locality statistics. Our method captures the spatial and temporal correlations in the graph data, and uses a statistical framework to model the normal behavior of the graph. We then detect anomalies as instances that deviate significantly from the expected behavior, based on a set of statistical measures.

We evaluate our approach on several real-world graph datasets and compare it to state-of-the-art methods. Our results show that our method outperforms existing approaches in terms of detection accuracy, while also providing interpretable results. We also perform a series of ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of different components of our method, and demonstrate its robustness to various types of attacks.

Our main contributions can be summarized as follows:

* We introduce a novel approach for anomaly detection in time series of graphs, based on locality statistics.
* We propose a statistical framework for modeling the normal behavior of graphs, and use it to detect anomalies.
* We evaluate our method on several real-world datasets and show that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods.
* We perform ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of different components of our method, and demonstrate its robustness to various types of attacks.

In this paper, we present a novel bound on genuine multipartite correlations, which are correlations that cannot be explained by any local hidden variable model, based on the principle of information causality. This principle, which states that the information contained in a system cannot be increased by performing a measurement on a distant system, has been previously used to derive bounds on the strength of correlations in bipartite systems.

Here, we extend this idea to the multipartite setting and show that the principle of information causality implies a bound on the strength of genuine multipartite correlations. Specifically, we prove that the correlation between three or more systems cannot exceed a certain value, which depends on the amount of information that can be shared between the systems.

Our result has important implications for the study of quantum non-locality and the foundations of quantum mechanics. It provides a new tool for testing the predictions of quantum mechanics and other theories of physics in multipartite systems, and sheds light on the nature of entanglement and the limits of classical explanations for quantum correlations.

Furthermore, our result has potential applications in the field of quantum information theory, where it can be used to quantify the amount of information that can be shared between different parts of a quantum system. This can be useful for the development of quantum communication and cryptography protocols, which rely on the ability to encode and decode information in quantum systems.

Overall, our paper demonstrates the power of the principle of information causality in constraining the strength of correlations in multipartite systems, and highlights the importance of considering the information-theoretic constraints on quantum mechanics in the study of quantum non-locality.

Real-time semantic video segmentation is a challenging task due to the strict
requirements of inference speed. Recent approaches mainly devote great efforts
to reducing the model size for high efficiency. In this paper, we rethink this
problem from a different viewpoint: using knowledge contained in compressed
videos. We propose a simple and effective framework, dubbed TapLab, to tap into
resources from the compressed domain. Specifically, we design a fast feature
warping module using motion vectors for acceleration. To reduce the noise
introduced by motion vectors, we design a residual-guided correction module and
a residual-guided frame selection module using residuals. TapLab significantly
reduces redundant computations of the state-of-the-art fast semantic image
segmentation models, running 3 to 10 times faster with controllable accuracy
degradation. The experimental results show that TapLab achieves 70.6% mIoU on
the Cityscapes dataset at 99.8 FPS with a single GPU card for the 1024x2048
videos. A high-speed version even reaches the speed of 160+ FPS. Codes will be
available soon at https://github.com/Sixkplus/TapLab.

In this paper, we present novel algorithms for scheduling moldable tasks, which are tasks that can be adapted to fit the available resources and time constraints of a system. Our approach leverages the moldability of tasks to optimize their scheduling, resulting in significant improvements in efficiency and productivity.

We first introduce a new mathematical model for scheduling moldable tasks, which captures the flexibility and variability of these tasks. We then propose two efficient algorithms for solving this model: a linear programming-based algorithm and a heuristic algorithm.

The linear programming-based algorithm optimizes the schedule by iteratively relaxing the constraints of the tasks, allowing them to be adapted to fit the available resources. The heuristic algorithm, on the other hand, uses a greedy approach to construct a feasible schedule that minimizes the total processing time.

We evaluate the performance of our algorithms using a set of benchmark instances and compare them to existing scheduling algorithms. Our results show that our algorithms significantly outperform the existing algorithms in terms of efficiency and productivity. In particular, our linear programming-based algorithm achieves a 20% to 40% reduction in processing time compared to the best existing algorithm, while our heuristic algorithm achieves a 10% to 30% reduction.

Our paper also includes a sensitivity analysis to evaluate the impact of various parameters on the performance of our algorithms. We vary the number of tasks, the variability of the tasks, and the availability of resources to investigate their effects on the scheduling performance.

Overall, our paper provides a significant contribution to the field of scheduling algorithms by introducing efficient algorithms for scheduling moldable tasks. Our approach leverages the flexibility and variability of these tasks to optimize their scheduling, resulting in improved efficiency and productivity. Our algorithms are applicable to a wide range of domains, including manufacturing, logistics, and service industries, and have the potential to significantly improve the performance of complex systems.

In this paper, we present a calculation of higher-order relativistic corrections to the fragmentation of gluons into spin-triplet S-wave quarkonium, which is a type of quark-antiquark bound state. We use a perturbative approach, in which the gluon is treated as a perturbation on the leading-order quark-antiquark pair, and calculate the corrections to the fragmentation function at next-to-leading order in the strong coupling constant.

We find that the relativistic corrections have a significant impact on the fragmentation function, particularly in the region of high transverse momentum. We also find that the corrections are sensitive to the choice of factorization scale, and that the scale dependence of the fragmentation function is reduced when the corrections are included.

Our results provide a more accurate prediction for the production of spin-triplet S-wave quarkonium in high-energy collisions, and demonstrate the importance of including higher-order relativistic corrections in the study of quarkonium production. The methods developed in this paper can be applied to the study of other quarkonium states and other hard scattering processes, and will be useful for improving the precision of theoretical predictions in high-energy physics.

Active transport is a ubiquitous process in biological systems, where molecular motors use energy to move molecules and organelles along the cell membrane. In this paper, we explore the potential of active transport to focus signals in cellular systems. We show that active transport can be used to concentrate signaling molecules in specific regions of the cell, allowing for more efficient signal transduction and amplification. We demonstrate this concept using a simple model of active transport, where molecular motors move along a one-dimensional track and interact with signaling molecules. Our results show that active transport can significantly enhance the strength and speed of signal transduction, and that the optimal transport rate and motor density can be tuned to maximize signaling efficiency. Structural support vector machines (SSVMs) are amongst the best performing
models for structured computer vision tasks, such as semantic image
segmentation or human pose estimation. Training SSVMs, however, is
computationally costly, because it requires repeated calls to a structured
prediction subroutine (called \emph{max-oracle}), which has to solve an
optimization problem itself, e.g. a graph cut.
  In this work, we introduce a new algorithm for SSVM training that is more
efficient than earlier techniques when the max-oracle is computationally
expensive, as it is frequently the case in computer vision tasks. The main idea
is to (i) combine the recent stochastic Block-Coordinate Frank-Wolfe algorithm
with efficient hyperplane caching, and (ii) use an automatic selection rule for
deciding whether to call the exact max-oracle or to rely on an approximate one
based on the cached hyperplanes.
  We show experimentally that this strategy leads to faster convergence to the
optimum with respect to the number of requires oracle calls, and that this
translates into faster convergence with respect to the total runtime when the
max-oracle is slow compared to the other steps of the algorithm.
  A publicly available C++ implementation is provided at
http://pub.ist.ac.at/~vnk/papers/SVM.html .

We propose a framework for top-down salient object detection that
incorporates a tightly coupled image classification module. The classifier is
trained on novel category-aware sparse codes computed on object dictionaries
used for saliency modeling. A misclassification indicates that the
corresponding saliency model is inaccurate. Hence, the classifier selects
images for which the saliency models need to be updated. The category-aware
sparse coding produces better image classification accuracy as compared to
conventional sparse coding with a reduced computational complexity. A
saliency-weighted max-pooling is proposed to improve image classification,
which is further used to refine the saliency maps. Experimental results on
Graz-02 and PASCAL VOC-07 datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of salient
object detection. Although the role of the classifier is to support salient
object detection, we evaluate its performance in image classification and also
illustrate the utility of thresholded saliency maps for image segmentation.

Medical image segmentation is a relevant task as it serves as the first step
for several diagnosis processes, thus it is indispensable in clinical usage.
Whilst major success has been reported using supervised techniques, they assume
a large and well-representative labelled set. This is a strong assumption in
the medical domain where annotations are expensive, time-consuming, and
inherent to human bias. To address this problem, unsupervised techniques have
been proposed in the literature yet it is still an open problem due to the
difficulty of learning any transformation pattern. In this work, we present a
novel optimisation model framed into a new CNN-based contrastive registration
architecture for unsupervised medical image segmentation. The core of our
approach is to exploit image-level registration and feature-level from a
contrastive learning mechanism, to perform registration-based segmentation.
Firstly, we propose an architecture to capture the image-to-image
transformation pattern via registration for unsupervised medical image
segmentation. Secondly, we embed a contrastive learning mechanism into the
registration architecture to enhance the discriminating capacity of the network
in the feature-level. We show that our proposed technique mitigates the major
drawbacks of existing unsupervised techniques. We demonstrate, through
numerical and visual experiments, that our technique substantially outperforms
the current state-of-the-art unsupervised segmentation methods on two major
medical image datasets.

We introduce a new machine learning approach for image segmentation that uses
a neural network to model the conditional energy of a segmentation given an
image. Our approach, combinatorial energy learning for image segmentation
(CELIS) places a particular emphasis on modeling the inherent combinatorial
nature of dense image segmentation problems. We propose efficient algorithms
for learning deep neural networks to model the energy function, and for local
optimization of this energy in the space of supervoxel agglomerations. We
extensively evaluate our method on a publicly available 3-D microscopy dataset
with 25 billion voxels of ground truth data. On an 11 billion voxel test set,
we find that our method improves volumetric reconstruction accuracy by more
than 20% as compared to two state-of-the-art baseline methods: graph-based
segmentation of the output of a 3-D convolutional neural network trained to
predict boundaries, as well as a random forest classifier trained to
agglomerate supervoxels that were generated by a 3-D convolutional neural
network.

Convolutional neural networks have shown great success on feature extraction
from raw input data such as images. Although convolutional neural networks are
invariant to translations on the inputs, they are not invariant to other
transformations, including rotation and flip. Recent attempts have been made to
incorporate more invariance in image recognition applications, but they are not
applicable to dense prediction tasks, such as image segmentation. In this
paper, we propose a set of methods based on kernel rotation and flip to enable
rotation and flip invariance in convolutional neural networks. The kernel
rotation can be achieved on kernels of 3 $\times$ 3, while kernel flip can be
applied on kernels of any size. By rotating in eight or four angles, the
convolutional layers could produce the corresponding number of feature maps
based on eight or four different kernels. By using flip, the convolution layer
can produce three feature maps. By combining produced feature maps using
maxout, the resource requirement could be significantly reduced while still
retain the invariance properties. Experimental results demonstrate that the
proposed methods can achieve various invariance at reasonable resource
requirements in terms of both memory and time.

for inductive types, including types of well-founded trees, or W-types, are
presented, and the basic homotopical semantics of such types are determined.

Using a variational method, we propose to use only three parameters in order to construct new neural representations by applying recurrent hidden units (RHDUs) with non-linear embeddings that are trained using a greedy algorithm. Our scheme can exploit existing computational resources of low dimensional networks and generate large number discriminative templates easily on small amount of datapoints, while allowing very strong generative model capabilities, enabling classification accuracies higher than currently available techniques like random forest. We demonstrate several applications for deep learning on real-world dataset, using various datasets such as image features, speech recognition etc., all of which uses different feature maps. By using one single RHDU input, we could generate an ensemble of four pre-trained models trained using a set of tensor products that is comparable with some state of the art results obtained without performing the full ensemble training. We further show how our proposed architecture provides better performances against many other popular datasets, including those presented at ICCV 2016 by researchers with leading roles in the field. The results highlight important aspects of deep learning and identify possible improvement directions through more refined approaches.

Information flow is the branch of security that studies the leakage of
information due to correlation between secrets and observables. Since in
general such correlation cannot be avoided completely, it is important to
quantify the leakage. The most followed approaches to defining appropriate
measures are those based on information theory. In particular, one of the most
successful approaches is the recently proposed $g$-leakage framework, which
encompasses most of the information-theoretic ones. A problem with $g$-leakage,
however, is that it is defined in terms of a minimization problem, which, in
the case of large systems, can be computationally rather heavy. In this paper
we study the case in which the channel associated to the system can be
decomposed into simpler channels, which typically happens when the observables
consist of multiple components. Our main contribution is the derivation of
bounds on the (multiplicative version of) $g$-leakage of the whole system in
terms of the $g$-leakages of its components. We also consider the particular
cases of min-entropy leakage and of parallel channels, generalizing and
systematizing results from the literature. We demonstrate the effectiveness of
our method and evaluate the precision of our bounds using examples.

In this study, we investigate the neutral hydrogen (HI) content of a sample of extremely metal-deficient blue compact dwarf (BCD) galaxies. BCDs are small, gas-rich galaxies that are characterized by their high abundance of ionized gas and low metallicity. Previous studies have suggested that these galaxies may also be deficient in neutral hydrogen, but the nature of their HI content has remained largely unexplored. Using the Green Bank Telescope, we conducted a survey of 24 BCDs with oxygen abundances less than 1/10th solar to determine their HI properties. Our results show that only two of the galaxies in our sample have detectable HI emission, both of which are detected at relatively low levels. Semi-supervised learning has recently been attracting attention as an
alternative to fully supervised models that require large pools of labeled
data. Moreover, optimizing a model for multiple tasks can provide better
generalizability than single-task learning. Leveraging self-supervision and
adversarial training, we propose a novel general purpose semi-supervised,
multiple-task model---namely, self-supervised, semi-supervised, multitask
learning (S$^4$MTL)---for accomplishing two important tasks in medical imaging,
segmentation and diagnostic classification. Experimental results on chest and
spine X-ray datasets suggest that our S$^4$MTL model significantly outperforms
semi-supervised single task, semi/fully-supervised multitask, and
fully-supervised single task models, even with a 50\% reduction of class and
segmentation labels. We hypothesize that our proposed model can be effective in
tackling limited annotation problems for joint training, not only in medical
imaging domains, but also for general-purpose vision tasks.

We apply generative adversarial convolutional neural networks to the problem
of style transfer to underdrawings and ghost-images in x-rays of fine art
paintings with a special focus on enhancing their spatial resolution. We build
upon a neural architecture developed for the related problem of synthesizing
high-resolution photo-realistic image from semantic label maps. Our neural
architecture achieves high resolution through a hierarchy of generators and
discriminator sub-networks, working throughout a range of spatial resolutions.
This coarse-to-fine generator architecture can increase the effective
resolution by a factor of eight in each spatial direction, or an overall
increase in number of pixels by a factor of 64. We also show that even just a
few examples of human-generated image segmentations can greatly improve --
qualitatively and quantitatively -- the generated images. We demonstrate our
method on works such as Leonardo's Madonna of the carnation and the
underdrawing in his Virgin of the rocks, which pose several special problems in
style transfer, including the paucity of representative works from which to
learn and transfer style information.

We propose a method to account for model error due to unresolved scales in
the context of the ensemble transform Kalman filter (ETKF). The approach
extends to this class of algorithms the deterministic model error formulation
recently explored for variational schemes and extended Kalman filter. The model
error statistic required in the analysis update is estimated using historical
reanalysis increments and a suitable model error evolution law. Two different
versions of the method are described; a time-constant model error treatment
where the same model error statistical description is time-invariant, and a
time-varying treatment where the assumed model error statistics is randomly
sampled at each analysis step. We compare both methods with the standard method
of dealing with model error through inflation and localization, and illustrate
our results with numerical simulations on a low order nonlinear system
exhibiting chaotic dynamics. The results show that the filter skill is
significantly improved through the proposed model error treatments, and that
both methods require far less parameter tuning than the standard approach.
Furthermore, the proposed approach is simple to implement within a pre-existing
ensemble based scheme. The general implications for the use of the proposed
approach in the framework of square-root filters such as the ETKF are also
discussed.

A fully automated knee MRI segmentation method to study osteoarthritis (OA)
was developed using a novel hierarchical set of random forests (RF) classifiers
to learn the appearance of cartilage regions and their boundaries. A
neighborhood approximation forest is used first to provide contextual feature
to the second-level RF classifier that also considers local features and
produces location-specific costs for the layered optimal graph image
segmentation of multiple objects and surfaces (LOGISMOS) framework. Double echo
steady state (DESS) MRIs used in this work originated from the Osteoarthritis
Initiative (OAI) study. Trained on 34 MRIs with varying degrees of OA, the
performance of the learning-based method tested on 108 MRIs showed a
significant reduction in segmentation errors (\emph{p}$<$0.05) compared with
the conventional gradient-based and single-stage RF-learned costs. The 3D
LOGISMOS was extended to longitudinal-3D (4D) to simultaneously segment
multiple follow-up visits of the same patient. As such, data from all
time-points of the temporal sequence contribute information to a single optimal
solution that utilizes both spatial 3D and temporal contexts. 4D LOGISMOS
validation on 108 MRIs from baseline and 12 month follow-up scans of 54
patients showed a significant reduction in segmentation errors
(\emph{p}$<$0.01) compared to 3D. Finally, the potential of 4D LOGISMOS was
further explored on the same 54 patients using 5 annual follow-up scans
demonstrating a significant improvement of measuring cartilage thickness
(\emph{p}$<$0.01) compared to the sequential 3D approach.

This paper presents an efficient energy minimization method for enforcing statistics in machine learning models. The proposed approach aims to optimize the trade-off between model accuracy and computational complexity by incorporating statistical measures into the training process. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in improving the performance of machine learning models while reducing the computational overhead. Overall, this study provides a promising solution for addressing the challenges of enforcing statistics in machine learning and has potential applications in various domains.

This paper presents a novel convolutional neural network architecture, in which deep nets are trained to form an image model that can segment pictures (similarity-based features and context or identity), and also produce results useful in scene analysis tasks such as image classification and object detection. On the one hand, they exploit topological information about objects based on similarity measures between different images; and on the other hand, they train them based on the context and object representation generated by their training input layer and learned hidden layers. A new convolutionary LSTM framework based on stateful layers is introduced as well, followed by two experiments showing speedups in performance compared with traditional algorithms like ResNets, SVM(2), MDS, VGG and similar networks. Our experiments show that these models provide superior results in both cases. The paper includes several demonstrations performed using various popular computer vision applications. Additionally, we describe our evaluation procedures based on the speedup in many common tasks. Finally, we show that our architectures provide even faster performance than those obtained with classical supervised classifiers. We present practical examples for a number of applications including online face recognition and semantic image segmentation. Our models and implementation could improve general perception in visual analytics and assist real world visual searches over time.

With the widespread success of deep learning in biomedical image
segmentation, domain shift becomes a critical and challenging problem, as the
gap between two domains can severely affect model performance when deployed to
unseen data with heterogeneous features. To alleviate this problem, we present
a novel unsupervised domain adaptation network, for generalizing models learned
from the labeled source domain to the unlabeled target domain for
cross-modality biomedical image segmentation. Specifically, our approach
consists of two key modules, a conditional domain discriminator~(CDD) and a
category-centric prototype aligner~(CCPA). The CDD, extended from conditional
domain adversarial networks in classifier tasks, is effective and robust in
handling complex cross-modality biomedical images. The CCPA, improved from the
graph-induced prototype alignment mechanism in cross-domain object detection,
can exploit precise instance-level features through an elaborate prototype
representation. In addition, it can address the negative effect of class
imbalance via entropy-based loss. Extensive experiments on a public benchmark
for the cardiac substructure segmentation task demonstrate that our method
significantly improves performance on the target domain.

The Belle 2 pixel detector is a critical component of the Belle 2 experiment, which aims to study the properties of particles produced in high-energy particle collisions. The read-out system of the pixel detector plays a crucial role in capturing and processing the data generated by the detector. In this paper, we present an FPGA (Field-Programmable Gate Array) based data read-out system designed for the Belle 2 pixel detector.

The proposed system utilizes FPGAs to perform real-time processing and compression of the data from the detector. This approach allows for faster data acquisition rates and reduced latency compared to traditional CPU-based systems. Moreover, the parallel processing capabilities of FPGAs enable efficient handling of large datasets generated by the detector.

We describe the architecture and implementation of the FPGA based read-out system, including the firmware design and testing procedures. Our results show that the system achieves high performance in terms of throughput, latency, and data quality. We also discuss the advantages and limitations of using FPGAs for data read-out in particle physics experiments and highlight potential applications of our system in future upgrades or new experiments.

Overall, this work demonstrates the feasibility and benefits of employing FPGAs for data read-out in high-speed particle detectors like the Belle 2 pixel detector. The developed system provides valuable insights into the use of FPGAs for similar applications and paves the way for further improvements in read-out technology for particle physics research.

A novel technique to reconstruct surface structure and morphology using high-dimensional molecular structures provides insights into early development, development patterns and mechanisms of diseases through understanding the morphogenesis of genes within protein aggregates. These new findings are crucial in understanding the evolutionary processes that led to the evolution of functional genomes and for establishing the underlying genetic principles governing protein aggregation. Their applications include the characterization and testing of computational models or experimental designs related to polymeric biomolecular networks with important implications on the study of protein interactions and aggregation as well as on development, health, disease and aging. More specifically, this study describes how hierarchical structure (i.e., local symmetry) provides an efficient way to construct an algal micro-structure in which the geometry provides stable intermolecular interaction, and explains how the nature of the local space constraints enable a nonlinear approach to the synthesis in large, 3D shapes.

By combining various methods used on other kinds of computer generated models with our own novel method, we have finally developed a method that leads naturally and quickly to the production of highly structured surfaces under conditions considered favorable by biologists; i.e., we can synthesize a surface whose architecture is robust at different scales. The ability to build up multiple surfaces quickly by manipulating protein components enables us not only to discover useful characteristics of a polymer but also to design the spatial arrangement of several surface proteins through precise mathematical manipulations. This brings our knowledge in these areas to unprecedented levels, providing a potential solution for biomedical applications on cellular levels.

In recent years, computer-aided diagnosis has become an increasingly popular
topic. Methods based on convolutional neural networks have achieved good
performance in medical image segmentation and classification. Due to the
limitations of the convolution operation, the long-term spatial features are
often not accurately obtained. Hence, we propose a TransClaw U-Net network
structure, which combines the convolution operation with the transformer
operation in the encoding part. The convolution part is applied for extracting
the shallow spatial features to facilitate the recovery of the image resolution
after upsampling. The transformer part is used to encode the patches, and the
self-attention mechanism is used to obtain global information between
sequences. The decoding part retains the bottom upsampling structure for better
detail segmentation performance. The experimental results on Synapse
Multi-organ Segmentation Datasets show that the performance of TransClaw U-Net
is better than other network structures. The ablation experiments also prove
the generalization performance of TransClaw U-Net.

Magnetic resonance (MR) protocols rely on several sequences to assess
pathology and organ status properly. Despite advances in image analysis, we
tend to treat each sequence, here termed modality, in isolation. Taking
advantage of the common information shared between modalities (an organ's
anatomy) is beneficial for multi-modality processing and learning. However, we
must overcome inherent anatomical misregistrations and disparities in signal
intensity across the modalities to obtain this benefit. We present a method
that offers improved segmentation accuracy of the modality of interest (over a
single input model), by learning to leverage information present in other
modalities, even if few (semi-supervised) or no (unsupervised) annotations are
available for this specific modality. Core to our method is learning a
disentangled decomposition into anatomical and imaging factors. Shared
anatomical factors from the different inputs are jointly processed and fused to
extract more accurate segmentation masks. Image misregistrations are corrected
with a Spatial Transformer Network, which non-linearly aligns the anatomical
factors. The imaging factor captures signal intensity characteristics across
different modality data and is used for image reconstruction, enabling
semi-supervised learning. Temporal and slice pairing between inputs are learned
dynamically. We demonstrate applications in Late Gadolinium Enhanced (LGE) and
Blood Oxygenation Level Dependent (BOLD) cardiac segmentation, as well as in T2
abdominal segmentation. Code is available at

Title: Deep Learning for Multi-Task Medical Image Segmentation in Multiple Modalities

Abstract:

Medical image segmentation is a crucial step in various medical applications, such as disease diagnosis, treatment planning, and monitoring. With the advent of deep learning techniques, there has been significant progress in automating this process, especially with the use of convolutional neural networks (CNNs). However, most existing works focus on single-modal image segmentation, where the model is trained on images from only one modality. In reality, many medical imaging modalities are available, each providing complementary information about the body. This paper proposes a novel deep learning framework for multi-task medical image segmentation that combines multiple modalities to improve segmentation accuracy and robustness.

Our proposed method leverages a shared encoder-decoder architecture to jointly learn features across different modalities, which are then used to perform task-specific segmentations. We explore different fusion strategies to combine the modalities, including early, late, and hybrid fusion methods. Additionally, we introduce a novel loss function designed specifically for multi-task segmentation tasks, which considers both inter-modality consistency and intra-modality quality. A thorough evaluation on several public datasets demonstrates the superiority of our approach compared to state-of-the-art methods. The results show an improvement in segmentation performance when using multiple modalities, and highlight the benefits of sharing knowledge across tasks and modalities.

This work has important implications for clinical applications where accurate segmentation is critical, such as tumor detection, organ segmentation, and non-invasive diagnostics. We envision our framework to be adapted and further refined for various medical image segmentation tasks, ultimately contributing to better patient outcomes and improved usage of medical imaging data.

We use Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs) for image segmentation
problems. DCNNs can well extract the features from natural images. However, the
classification functions in the existing network architecture of CNNs are
simple and lack capabilities to handle important spatial information in a way
that have been done for many well-known traditional variational models. Prior
such as spatial regularity, volume prior and object shapes cannot be well
handled by existing DCNNs. We propose a novel Soft Threshold Dynamics (STD)
framework which can easily integrate many spatial priors of the classical
variational models into the DCNNs for image segmentation. The novelty of our
method is to interpret the softmax activation function as a dual variable in a
variational problem, and thus many spatial priors can be imposed in the dual
space. From this viewpoint, we can build a STD based framework which can enable
the outputs of DCNNs to have many special priors such as spatial regularity,
volume constraints and star-shape priori. The proposed method is a general
mathematical framework and it can be applied to any semantic segmentation
DCNNs. To show the efficiency and accuracy of our method, we applied it to the
popular DeepLabV3+ image segmentation network, and the experiments results show
that our method can work efficiently on data-driven image segmentation DCNNs.

We build on recent works on Stein's method for functions of multivariate
normal random variables to derive bounds for the rate of convergence of some
asymptotically chi-square distributed statistics. We obtain some general bounds
and establish some simple sufficient conditions for convergence rates of order
$n^{-1}$ for smooth test functions. These general bounds are applied to
Friedman's statistic for comparing $r$ treatments across $n$ trials and the
family of power divergence statistics for goodness-of-fit across $n$ trials and
$r$ classifications, with index parameter $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$ (Pearson's
statistic corresponds to $\lambda=1$). We obtain a $O(n^{-1})$ bound for the
rate of convergence of Friedman's statistic for any number of treatments
$r\geq2$. We also obtain a $O(n^{-1})$ bound on the rate of convergence of the
power divergence statistics for any $r\geq2$ when $\lambda$ is a positive
integer or any real number greater than 5. We conjecture that the $O(n^{-1})$
rate holds for any $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$.

The effects of residual amplitude modulation (RAM) in laser interferometers
using heterodyne sensing can be substantial and difficult to mitigate. In this
work, we analyze the effects of RAM on a complex laser interferometer used for
gravitational wave detection. The RAM introduces unwanted offsets in the cavity
length signals and thereby shifts the operating point of the optical cavities
from the nominal point via feedback control. This shift causes variations in
the sensing matrix, and leads to degradation in the performance of the
precision noise subtraction scheme of the multiple-degree-of-freedom control
system. In addition, such detuned optical cavities produce an opto-mechanical
spring, which also varies the sensing matrix. We use our simulations to derive
requirements on RAM for the Advanced LIGO detectors, and show that the RAM
expected in Advanced LIGO will not limit its sensitivity.

Recently, neural architecture search (NAS) has been applied to automatically
search high-performance networks for medical image segmentation. The NAS search
space usually contains a network topology level (controlling connections among
cells with different spatial scales) and a cell level (operations within each
cell). Existing methods either require long searching time for large-scale 3D
image datasets, or are limited to pre-defined topologies (such as U-shaped or
single-path). In this work, we focus on three important aspects of NAS in 3D
medical image segmentation: flexible multi-path network topology, high search
efficiency, and budgeted GPU memory usage. A novel differentiable search
framework is proposed to support fast gradient-based search within a highly
flexible network topology search space. The discretization of the searched
optimal continuous model in differentiable scheme may produce a sub-optimal
final discrete model (discretization gap). Therefore, we propose a topology
loss to alleviate this problem. In addition, the GPU memory usage for the
searched 3D model is limited with budget constraints during search. Our
Differentiable Network Topology Search scheme (DiNTS) is evaluated on the
Medical Segmentation Decathlon (MSD) challenge, which contains ten challenging
segmentation tasks. Our method achieves the state-of-the-art performance and
the top ranking on the MSD challenge leaderboard.

Complex classification performance metrics such as the F${}_\beta$-measure
and Jaccard index are often used, in order to handle class-imbalanced cases
such as information retrieval and image segmentation. These performance metrics
are not decomposable, that is, they cannot be expressed in a per-example
manner, which hinders a straightforward application of M-estimation widely used
in supervised learning. In this paper, we consider linear-fractional metrics,
which are a family of classification performance metrics that encompasses many
standard ones such as the F${}_\beta$-measure and Jaccard index, and propose
methods to directly maximize performances under those metrics. A clue to tackle
their direct optimization is a calibrated surrogate utility, which is a
tractable lower bound of the true utility function representing a given metric.
We characterize sufficient conditions which make the surrogate maximization
coincide with the maximization of the true utility. Simulation results on
benchmark datasets validate the effectiveness of our calibrated surrogate
maximization especially if the sample sizes are extremely small.
