In this paper, we present a novel approach for joint segmentation and localization in videos and images, which we term "foreground clustering." Our method leverages the strengths of both clustering and contour-based segmentation techniques to simultaneously segment and localize objects in the foreground of an image or video sequence.

Existing approaches for joint segmentation and localization often rely on complex models that require careful parameter tuning and may not perform well in the presence of occlusions, clutter, or varying illumination conditions. In contrast, our foreground clustering method is robust, efficient, and easy to implement.

We begin by applying a background subtraction algorithm to the video or image sequence to obtain a sequence of foreground masks. We then apply a clustering algorithm to the foreground masks to group pixels into distinct clusters, which correspond to individual objects in the scene. Next, we use a contour-based segmentation algorithm to extract the boundaries of each object, which provides a precise segmentation mask for each object.

To localize the objects in the scene, we propose a novel feature called the "spatial layout map," which encodes the spatial relationships between objects in the scene. We use this feature to train a machine learning model to predict the location of each object in the scene.

We evaluate our method on several challenging datasets, including videos and images with complex scenes, occlusions, and varying illumination conditions. Our experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art methods for joint segmentation and localization in terms of both accuracy and efficiency.

* We propose a novel approach for joint segmentation and localization in videos and images based on foreground clustering.
* We introduce a new feature called the spatial layout map, which encodes the spatial relationships between objects in the scene.
* We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on several challenging datasets, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in terms of both accuracy and efficiency.

Overall, our work has important implications for a wide range of applications, including object tracking, human-computer interaction, and video surveillance.

To exploit the rich information contained in the 4D light-field representation, we propose two CNN architectures designed to learn spatial and angular features jointly: (i) a baseline architecture that extends traditional 2D CNNs to 4D by duplicating filters across views, and (ii) a novel View-adaptive Spatial-Angular Network (VUSAN) that dynamically adapts filter responses based on the viewer's perspective. VUSAN achieves state-of-the-art performance on our benchmark, outperforming the baseline model by 7% in terms of accuracy.

We evaluate both architectures on several challenging material classes, including fabrics, vegetables, and metals, and perform ablation studies to analyze their strengths and limitations. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of incorporating angle-varying cues in material recognition tasks and highlight opportunities for future research exploring multi-modal fusion and dynamic view synthesis techniques. The introduced dataset and CNN architectures pave the way towards robust and versatile material recognition systems suitable for applications such as robotics, computer graphics, and virtual reality.

The shape prior is incorporated into the model by defining a prior distribution over the space of possible object boundaries, which is represented using a nonparametric function.

The MCMC shape sampling algorithm is designed to sample from the posterior distribution of the random field, given the observed image data and the prior distribution. The algorithm iteratively updates the segmentation mask by proposing new configurations of object boundaries that are consistent with the observed data and the prior distribution. The proposed algorithm is efficient and scalable, allowing for real-time segmentation of large images.

The effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated through experiments on several benchmark datasets, including the Berkeley Segmentation Dataset, the Stanford Background Dataset, and the MSRA10K Dataset. The results show that MCMC shape sampling outperforms several state-of-the-art segmentation methods, including traditional parametric and nonparametric approaches.

The main contribution of this paper is the introduction of a novel approach to image segmentation that combines the strengths of MCMC sampling and nonparametric shape priors. spatially during segmentation. By simultaneously utilizing 3D-DWT features and
MRF priors for the first time, contextual information is fully integrated
during the segmentation to ensure accurate and smooth segmentation. To
demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, we conduct extensive
experiments on three real benchmark PolSAR image data sets. Experimental
results indicate that the proposed method achieves promising segmentation
accuracy and preferable spatial consistency using a minimal number of labeled
pixels.

This work studies our approach to image segmentation under unsupervised learning and how that can be applied within a supervised framework. A simple model for automatic segmentation has been proposed [5], [10]. The objective function, which we call AUC (Area Under Curve), estimates the region where feature maps overlap; the size of this area is the distance between features along a projection unit. Our method aims at automatically determining the optimal projection units for each set feature map, in order to create classification classifiers based on different projected unit images. In particular, we have focused on designing a prototype alignment algorithm that can take an arbitrary biopsies into account while detecting tumor types. Such aligners are usually used for cancer detection models to extract the distribution of cells and their tissues during imaging such as using light or electron microscopy. The goal here is just making these machines more convenient—for example it does not matter what kind of tissue was taken from patient or even the actual location of tumor, because all it is doing if its mapping process, and thus determining the optimal projection unit. By developing a generic tool of using two dimensional projections with no special care about any point selection mechanism, we demonstrate fully unsupervised segmentation of biomicroscopic sections such as T4E8 (3D tumor outline) microcircles without prior knowledge of the morphology or other relevant information of the biopsy specimen [11], [12]. Using this machine learning technique, we were able to generate thousands of unique categories that corresponded well to known tumor histology terms. Our model considers image segmentation tasks where each object has unique properties or features, such as rotation angles and pixel density. Many prior work on supervised hierarchical labeling have focused only upon the classification of the images using classifiers that can directly infer these properties from their label labels (e.g., discriminative models). In this paper, we propose to augment existing approaches by incorporating a new neural algorithm designed to perform image segmentation while detecting common objects based on data obtained from a sublinear classifier. The proposed architecture is inspired by recent methods that find significant structure in large multidimensional datasets, e.g., via maximum entropy representations and stochastic similarity measures [1]. In such cases the classification task assumes a latent space characterized by a discrete set of vectors describing distinct classes, with an associated nonlinear probability distribution for each class. A typical case would be the identification and classification of all trees with only 1 leaf node between any two nodes in the training dataset; with our algorithm, this inference process can also yield information about the hidden structures beyond a single layer or even one tree within the same network. The proposed method includes both supervised learning components including the combination of deep neural networks to estimate the probability distributions corresponding to multiple classes, and semi-supervised features, e.g., common elements, clustering coefficients and kurtosis functions. It was shown that our approach outperforms previous state-of-the art supervised methods compared against hand-coded algorithms which had an extensive set of parameters optimized by different researchers across several generations of image segmentations work. This finding suggests that we can use a structured, shared feature representation between supervised and semi-supervised learning, leading to additional insights in many traditional image segmenting problem domains. Given our framework, it should become possible to develop highly competitive unsupervised techniques at scales far beyond those achievable currently.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach for unsupervised domain adaptation on hip joint bone segmentation tasks, called Intra- and Cross-modality Semantic Consistency (ICMSC). Our approach aims to address the challenge of adapting a model trained on a source domain with a limited number of labeled images to a target domain with a different distribution, by leveraging the semantic consistency between the source and target domains.

We first introduce a novel domain adaptation method that aligns the feature distributions of the source and target domains using a domain confusion technique. We then propose a novel consistency loss function that enforces the semantic consistency between the source and target domains, both within and across modalities. The loss function encourages the model to produce similar predictions for the same subject across different modalities, and to produce different predictions for different subjects.

We evaluate our approach on a dataset of hip joint bone segmentation images, where the source domain consists of 300 images with manual annotations, and the target domain consists of 1000 images without annotations. Our results show that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art domain adaptation methods, with a mean Dice similarity coefficient of 0.83 compared to 0.76 for the best performing baseline.

We also perform a series of ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of the different components of our approach. Our results show that the domain confusion technique and the consistency loss function both contribute significantly to the performance improvement, and that the combination of the two components leads to the best results.

Our work demonstrates the potential of ICMSC for improving the performance of unsupervised domain adaptation on hip joint bone segmentation tasks, and has important implications for the development of domain adaptation methods for medical image segmentation tasks in general.

The design and performance of computer vision algorithms are greatly
influenced by the hardware on which they are implemented. CPUs, multi-core
CPUs, FPGAs and GPUs have inspired new algorithms and enabled existing ideas to
be realized. This is notably the case with GPUs, which has significantly
changed the landscape of computer vision research through deep learning. As the
end of Moores law approaches, researchers and hardware manufacturers are
exploring alternative hardware computing paradigms. Quantum computers are a
very promising alternative and offer polynomial or even exponential speed-ups
over conventional computing for some problems. This paper presents a novel
approach to image segmentation that uses new quantum computing hardware.
Segmentation is formulated as a graph cut problem that can be mapped to the
quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA). This algorithm can be
implemented on current and near-term quantum computers. Encouraging results are
presented on artificial and medical imaging data. This represents an important,
practical step towards leveraging quantum computers for computer vision.

In this paper, we introduce a novel approach to signal processing called coherent averaging, which enables the efficient and accurate estimation of a signal's properties in the presence of noise and interference. Unlike traditional methods that rely on incoherent averaging, coherent averaging exploits the inherent structure of the signal to improve the signal-to-noise ratio and reduce the impact of interference.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of coherent averaging through theoretical analysis and simulations, showing that it can significantly outperform traditional methods in a variety of applications, including image and audio processing, biomedical signal processing, and machine learning. We also discuss the limitations and challenges of coherent averaging and outline potential avenues for future research.

Our results have important implications for a wide range of fields, as they demonstrate a new way to extract valuable information from noisy signals that was previously thought to be inaccessible. By enabling the accurate estimation of signal properties in the presence of noise and interference, coherent averaging has the potential to revolutionize the way we process and analyze signals in a variety of applications.

Edge detection is a critical component of many vision systems, including
object detectors and image segmentation algorithms. Patches of edges exhibit
well-known forms of local structure, such as straight lines or T-junctions. In
this paper we take advantage of the structure present in local image patches to
learn both an accurate and computationally efficient edge detector. We
formulate the problem of predicting local edge masks in a structured learning
framework applied to random decision forests. Our novel approach to learning
decision trees robustly maps the structured labels to a discrete space on which
standard information gain measures may be evaluated. The result is an approach
that obtains realtime performance that is orders of magnitude faster than many
competing state-of-the-art approaches, while also achieving state-of-the-art
edge detection results on the BSDS500 Segmentation dataset and NYU Depth
dataset. Finally, we show the potential of our approach as a general purpose
edge detector by showing our learned edge models generalize well across
datasets.

This paper presents a study on quantitative automata, a model of computation that extends finite automata with real-valued weights. Our contributions include a formal definition of quantitative automata under probabilistic semantics, as well as a thorough analysis of their properties and computational complexity. We also provide experimental evidence demonstrating the effectiveness of this model in various application domains, such as natural language processing and bioinformatics. Overall, this paper provides a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners working on modeling and analysis of probabilistic systems.

We also show how easy it is to run computations over more than one function at a time. In this example we evaluate the performance of our method on large, multi-layer multiscale Bayesian models trained by Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), applying an admissible model size of 10-20 parameterized by five independent experiments each requiring up to 1GB of training data. We find both in theory and through empirical tests that our algorithm achieves average sensitivity and specificity comparable to existing approaches that rely on sampling data uniformly across all columns in feature space or simply perform forward pass priors on features without taking into account the spatial structure of features. The results are obtained regardless of whether the analysis is done using the standard R programming language, OpenCV3, or an alternative approach that combines these three types of models together. Also, despite significant improvements over prior attempts in terms of stability and speed; we note that future implementations of this type of methods may require modification. Overall, our result demonstrates how important sequential reasoning is when considering data that spans multiple functions—for instance data with dense multivariate features such as those generated by a neural network. We believe this technology opens a novel way to consider the nature of many complex problems, including those that involve spatially structured models and the ability to compute their effects simultaneously. This paper is intended to introduce the concept of simultaneous inference for complex systems to researchers who have not yet encountered it.

A datatype defining rewrite system (DDRS) is an algebraic (equational)
specification intended to specify a datatype. When interpreting the equations
from left-to-right, a DDRS defines a term rewriting system that must be
ground-complete. First we define two DDRSs for the ring of integers, each
comprising twelve rewrite rules, and prove their ground-completeness. Then we
introduce natural number and integer arithmetic specified according to unary
view, that is, arithmetic based on a postfix unary append constructor (a form
of tallying). Next we specify arithmetic based on two other views: binary and
decimal notation. The binary and decimal view have as their characteristic that
each normal form resembles common number notation, that is, either a digit, or
a string of digits without leading zero, or the negated versions of the latter.
Integer arithmetic in binary and decimal notation is based on (postfix) digit
append functions. For each view we define a DDRS, and in each case the
resulting datatype is a canonical term algebra that extends a corresponding
canonical term algebra for natural numbers. Then, for each view, we consider an
alternative DDRS based on tree constructors that yields comparable normal
forms, which for that view admits expressions that are algorithmically more
involved. For all DDRSs considered, ground-completeness is proven.

architecture search-based methods and tracking objectives. Extensive
experimental evaluations demonstrate the superior performance of our approach
over five commonly-used benchmarks. Meanwhile, our automated searching process
takes 41 (18) hours for the second (first) order DARTS method on the
TrackingNet dataset.

Deep neural networks enable highly accurate image segmentation, but require
large amounts of manually annotated data for supervised training. Few-shot
learning aims to address this shortcoming by learning a new class from a few
annotated support examples. We introduce, a novel few-shot framework, for the
segmentation of volumetric medical images with only a few annotated slices.
Compared to other related works in computer vision, the major challenges are
the absence of pre-trained networks and the volumetric nature of medical scans.
We address these challenges by proposing a new architecture for few-shot
segmentation that incorporates 'squeeze & excite' blocks. Our two-armed
architecture consists of a conditioner arm, which processes the annotated
support input and generates a task-specific representation. This representation
is passed on to the segmenter arm that uses this information to segment the new
query image. To facilitate efficient interaction between the conditioner and
the segmenter arm, we propose to use 'channel squeeze & spatial excitation'
blocks - a light-weight computational module - that enables heavy interaction
between both the arms with negligible increase in model complexity. This
contribution allows us to perform image segmentation without relying on a
pre-trained model, which generally is unavailable for medical scans.
Furthermore, we propose an efficient strategy for volumetric segmentation by
optimally pairing a few slices of the support volume to all the slices of the
query volume. We perform experiments for organ segmentation on whole-body
contrast-enhanced CT scans from the Visceral Dataset. Our proposed model
outperforms multiple baselines and existing approaches with respect to the
segmentation accuracy by a significant margin. The source code is available at
https://github.com/abhi4ssj/few-shot-segmentation.

A large number of problems in computer vision can be modelled as energy
minimization problems in a Markov Random Field (MRF) or Conditional Random
Field (CRF) framework. Graph-cuts based $\alpha$-expansion is a standard
move-making method to minimize the energy functions with sub-modular pairwise
terms. However, certain problems require more complex pairwise terms where the
$\alpha$-expansion method is generally not applicable.
  In this paper, we propose an iterative {\em tiered move making algorithm}
which is able to handle general pairwise terms. Each move to the next
configuration is based on the current labeling and an optimal tiered move,
where each tiered move requires one application of the dynamic programming
based tiered labeling method introduced in Felzenszwalb et. al.
\cite{tiered_cvpr_felzenszwalbV10}. The algorithm converges to a local minimum
for any general pairwise potential, and we give a theoretical analysis of the
properties of the algorithm, characterizing the situations in which we can
expect good performance. We first evaluate our method on an object-class
segmentation problem using the Pascal VOC-11 segmentation dataset where we
learn general pairwise terms. Further we evaluate the algorithm on many other
benchmark labeling problems such as stereo, image segmentation, image stitching
and image denoising. Our method consistently gets better accuracy and energy
values than alpha-expansion, loopy belief propagation (LBP), quadratic
pseudo-boolean optimization (QPBO), and is competitive with TRWS.

Building on previous work in the field, the GADM extends the classic active contour model by introducing an additional front that moves iteratively towards the object boundary, while simultaneously updating the shape prior. By incorporating anisotropic diffusion and a modified gradient flow, the model can effectively capture object boundaries that would be difficult or impossible to detect using traditional methods. The GADM also includes a new stopping criterion, based on the concept of "quasi-convexity," which ensures that the evolution of the contour stops when it has converged to a stable solution.

Additionally, the paper presents theoretical analysis guaranteeing the existence and uniqueness of the solution, as well as convergence properties of the proposed algorithm. We study a planar four-Fermi Gross-Neveu model in the presence of a tilted
magnetic field, with components parallel and perpendicular to the system's
plane. We determine how this combination of magnetic field components, when
applied simultaneously, affects the phase diagram of the model. It is shown
that each component of the magnetic field causes a competing effect on the
chiral symmetry in these fermionic systems. While the perpendicular component
of the magnetic field tends to make the chiral symmetry breaking stronger, the
effect of the parallel component of the field in these planar systems is to
weaken the chiral symmetry through the enhancement of the Zeeman energy term.
We show that this competing effect, when combined also with temperature and
chemical potential, can lead to a rich phase diagram, with the emergence of
multiple critical points and reentrant phase transitions. We also study how the
presence of these multiple critical points and reentrant phases can manifest in
the quantum Hall effect. Our results provide a possible way to probe
experimentally chiral symmetry breaking and the corresponding emergence of a
gap (i.e., the presence of a nonvanishing chiral vacuum expectation value) in
planar condensed matter systems of current interest.

The Voronoi diagram is a certain geometric data structure which has numerous
applications in various scientific and technological fields. The theory of
algorithms for computing 2D Euclidean Voronoi diagrams of point sites is rich
and useful, with several different and important algorithms. However, this
theory has been quite steady during the last few decades in the sense that no
essentially new algorithms have entered the game. In addition, most of the
known algorithms are serial in nature and hence cast inherent difficulties on
the possibility to compute the diagram in parallel. In this paper we present
the projector algorithm: a new and simple algorithm which enables the
(combinatorial) computation of 2D Voronoi diagrams. The algorithm is
significantly different from previous ones and some of the involved concepts in
it are in the spirit of linear programming and optics. Parallel implementation
is naturally supported since each Voronoi cell can be computed independently of
the other cells. A new combinatorial structure for representing the cells (and
any convex polytope) is described along the way and the computation of the
induced Delaunay graph is obtained almost automatically.

In this paper, we explore the concept of implication relation in classical logic and provide a formal definition that captures its essential properties. The implication relation is a fundamental component of logical reasoning, allowing us to infer conclusions from premises and build complex arguments. However, its meaning and behavior have been largely informal and intuitive, leaving room for ambiguity and misunderstandings.

We propose a rigorous approach to defining implication relations, drawing on the principles of category theory and model theory. Our definition emphasizes the dual aspects of implications: the antecedent-to-consequent direction, which reflects the notion of entailment or follows-from, and the consequent-to-antecedent direction, which represents the idea of implies-that or enabled-by.

OurDefinition of Implication Relation (DIR) consists of four axioms that ensure soundness and completeness of the logical system. Firstly, DIR1 (Antecedent Monotonicity) states that if A implies B, then any instance of A implies B. Secondly, DIR2 (Consequent Monotonicity) asserts that if A implies B, then A implies every consequence of B. Thirdly, DIR3 (Transitivity) ensures that if A implies B and B implies C, then A implies C. Lastly, DIR4 (Self-duality) requires that for any proposition P, there exists a dual proposition ¬P such that P implies ¬Q iff ¬Q implies ¬P.

The proposed definition subsumes various existing notions of logics, including propositional, predicate, and modal logic, making it widely applicable across different domains of research. Moreover, our formalism allows for concise representations of complex implicational structures, enabling effective reasoning about the relationships between statements.

Furthermore, we demonstrate how DIR can be used to formalize and clarify the semantics of natural language expressions, such as 'if', 'then', and 'therefore'. These linguistic constructs are often employed loosely in natural discourse, leading to potential misinterpretations and ambiguities. By embedding them within our formal framework, we enhance clarity and precision in communication.

We propose and study a task we name panoptic segmentation (PS). Panoptic
segmentation unifies the typically distinct tasks of semantic segmentation
(assign a class label to each pixel) and instance segmentation (detect and
segment each object instance). The proposed task requires generating a coherent
scene segmentation that is rich and complete, an important step toward
real-world vision systems. While early work in computer vision addressed
related image/scene parsing tasks, these are not currently popular, possibly
due to lack of appropriate metrics or associated recognition challenges. To
address this, we propose a novel panoptic quality (PQ) metric that captures
performance for all classes (stuff and things) in an interpretable and unified
manner. Using the proposed metric, we perform a rigorous study of both human
and machine performance for PS on three existing datasets, revealing
interesting insights about the task. The aim of our work is to revive the
interest of the community in a more unified view of image segmentation.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach for brain tumor segmentation using an ensemble of 3D U-Nets and overall survival prediction using radiomic features. Brain tumor segmentation is a crucial step in diagnosis and treatment planning, but it remains a challenging task due to the complexity and variability of brain tumors. To address this challenge, we utilize an ensemble of 3D U-Nets, which are deep learning models that have shown promising results in image segmentation tasks.

Our proposed method consists of two main components: (1) brain tumor segmentation using an ensemble of 3D U-Nets, and (2) overall survival prediction using radiomic features extracted from the segmented tumor regions. The ensemble of 3D U-Nets is trained on a large dataset of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans to accurately segment brain tumors. The segments generated by each model are combined using a novel fusion strategy to produce the final segmentation mask.

To predict overall survival, we extract a set of radiomic features from the segmented tumor regions, including intensity, texture, and shape features. These features are then used to train a machine learning model that can predict patient survival outcomes. We evaluate our method on a dataset of MRI scans collected from patients with glioblastoma, the most common and aggressive type of primary brain cancer.

The results show that our proposed method outperforms traditional tumor segmentation methods and achieves high accuracy in terms of Dice similarity coefficient and Hausdorff distance. Furthermore, the survival prediction model based on radiomic features shows strong predictive power, with a concordance index of 0.75. Our findings demonstrate the potential of using an ensemble of 3D U-Nets and radiomic features for accurate brain tumor segmentation and overall survival prediction. This approach could help improve clinical decision-making and personalized treatment strategies for brain cancer patients.

their peak in terms of segmentation quality and efficiency per number of

decoder which uses a set of shallow networks for capturing more information
content. The new decoder has a new topology of skip connections, namely

impact of our decoder to state-of-the-art segmentation techniques.
Additionally, we present a set of experiments augmenting semantic segmentation
with optical flow information, showing that motion clues can boost pure image
based semantic segmentation approaches.

We present a model, based on neural networks with latent Dirichlet allocation (LD) architecture, that enables one to generate a deep convolutional network (CNN) for processing an extensive visual input and extracting features from it in real time, by exploiting latent information hidden within image structures such as edges between neighboring regions. The CNN consists of four layer with three hidden units per node along with two output activations shared among all four layers. We demonstrate significant superiority over state-of-the-art classification methods using 2D thresholding and linear regression to achieve good results across image classes ranging from faces, cat faces, medical images or road signs to street scenes, car driving lines or city landscape architecture. Further, our evaluation leads us to conclude that our approach has superior performance even over classical convolutional nets when trained on large scale data sets without prior supervised learning. Our results emphasize the importance of capturing more deeply hidden feature vectors which was not done until now during conventional segmentation algorithms, and show how segmentation problems can also be easily solved on real-time streaming signals generated using distributed computation. Our algorithm is shown to produce substantial improvement compared to state-of-the-art LDA models that only learn features using traditional LDA techniques, but remain slower than those implemented in current architectures and have smaller feature representations. We thus show that the implementation of recurrent neural networks can provide significant gains in real-time multi-label classification over standard preprocessing pipelines including convolution and regularization filters used today [6]–[8], and may provide useful insights and practical application for processing real-time streams from other sources such as sensor capture and event data acquisition systems.

Supervised deep learning performance is heavily tied to the availability of
high-quality labels for training. Neural networks can gradually overfit
corrupted labels if directly trained on noisy datasets, leading to severe
performance degradation at test time. In this paper, we propose a novel deep
learning framework, namely Co-Seg, to collaboratively train segmentation
networks on datasets which include low-quality noisy labels. Our approach first
trains two networks simultaneously to sift through all samples and obtain a
subset with reliable labels. Then, an efficient yet easily-implemented label
correction strategy is applied to enrich the reliable subset. Finally, using
the updated dataset, we retrain the segmentation network to finalize its
parameters. Experiments in two noisy labels scenarios demonstrate that our
proposed model can achieve results comparable to those obtained from supervised
learning trained on the noise-free labels. In addition, our framework can be
easily implemented in any segmentation algorithm to increase its robustness to
noisy labels.

In this study, we propose a novel deep learning approach for automatic tracking of tongue surfaces in real-time ultrasound videos. Instead of relying on contour detection methods, which can be limited by image quality and require careful parameter tuning, our approach uses landmark detection to accurately locate the position and shape of the tongue surface. We employ a convolutional neural network (CNN) to learn patterns in the ultrasound images and detect key points along the tongue surface, enabling accurate tracking even in the presence of noise, artifacts, or variations in image intensity.

Our proposed method was evaluated using a dataset of real-time ultrasound videos captured during speech production tasks, and showed superior performance compared to traditional contour-based tracking methods. The CNN-based landmark detector demonstrated high accuracy and robustness across different speaking conditions, including varied speaking rates, voice qualities, and articulation modes. Additionally, our approach offers several advantages over existing methods, including reduced computational complexity, improved temporal resolution, and better interpretability of the tracking results.

The findings from this study have important implications for applications such as speech therapy, where accurate monitoring of tongue movements is crucial for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes. Moreover, the proposed technique has potential applications in other fields, such as biomechanical research, prosthetics, and robotics, where precise tracking of anatomical structures in real-time is required. Overall, this work highlights the potential of deep learning techniques for solving challenges in medical imaging analysis and paves the way for further advancements in this area.

In this paper, we present a rigorous verification of the Nernst theorem for the Casimir-Lifshitz free energy, which states that the free energy of a system at thermal equilibrium is a state function that is independent of the path by which the system reached that state. We demonstrate that this theorem holds for the Casimir-Lifshitz free energy, which is a fundamental concept in the study of non-equilibrium thermodynamics and is widely used to describe the behavior of systems in various fields, including materials science, chemistry, and physics.

Our verification is based on a careful analysis of the Casimir-Lifshitz free energy and its properties, using a combination of theoretical and numerical methods. We first derive the equations of state for the Casimir-Lifshitz free energy and its derivatives, and then use these equations to demonstrate that the free energy is indeed a state function. We also provide numerical examples to illustrate the validity of the Nernst theorem for the Casimir-Lifshitz free energy, and discuss the implications of our results for the broader field of non-equilibrium thermodynamics.

Our work provides a significant contribution to the understanding of the Casimir-Lifshitz free energy and its properties, and demonstrates the importance of the Nernst theorem in ensuring the consistency and reliability of thermodynamic calculations. The results of this study have important implications for the study of non-equilibrium thermodynamics and its applications in a wide range of fields, and will be of interest to researchers and practitioners in these areas.

Conventional deformable registration methods aim at solving an optimization
model carefully designed on image pairs and their computational costs are
exceptionally high. In contrast, recent deep learning based approaches can
provide fast deformation estimation. These heuristic network architectures are
fully data-driven and thus lack explicit geometric constraints, e.g.,
topology-preserving, which are indispensable to generate plausible
deformations. We design a new deep learning based framework to optimize a
diffeomorphic model via multi-scale propagation in order to integrate
advantages and avoid limitations of these two categories of approaches.
Specifically, we introduce a generic optimization model to formulate
diffeomorphic registration and develop a series of learnable architectures to
obtain propagative updating in the coarse-to-fine feature space. Moreover, we
propose a novel bilevel self-tuned training strategy, allowing efficient search
of task-specific hyper-parameters. This training strategy increases the
flexibility to various types of data while reduces computational and human
burdens. We conduct two groups of image registration experiments on 3D volume
datasets including image-to-atlas registration on brain MRI data and
image-to-image registration on liver CT data. Extensive results demonstrate the
state-of-the-art performance of the proposed method with diffeomorphic
guarantee and extreme efficiency. We also apply our framework to challenging
multi-modal image registration, and investigate how our registration to support
the down-streaming tasks for medical image analysis including multi-modal
fusion and image segmentation.

The spatial regularization term is introduced to improve the segmentation accuracy by incorporating the spatial information of the image. The proposed model is solved by the alternating direction method of multipliers. The experimental results on several benchmark datasets show that the proposed model can achieve better segmentation accuracy than the state-of-the-art methods.

Rapid growth in the field of quantitative digital image analysis is paving
the way for researchers to make precise measurements about objects in an image.
To compute quantities from the image such as the density of compressed
materials or the velocity of a shockwave, we must determine object boundaries.
Images containing regions that each have a spatial trend in intensity are of
particular interest. We present a supervised image segmentation method that
incorporates spatial information to locate boundaries between regions with
overlapping intensity histograms. The segmentation of a pixel is determined by
comparing its intensity to distributions from local, nearby pixel intensities.
Because of the statistical nature of the algorithm, we use maximum likelihood
estimation theory to quantify uncertainty about each boundary. We demonstrate
the success of this algorithm on a radiograph of a multicomponent cylinder and

This paper proposes a novel approach to unsupervised image segmentation, utilizing a combination of global and local criteria optimization based on Bayesian networks. The proposed method aims to overcome the limitations of traditional segmentation techniques that rely solely on hand-crafted features or shallow neural networks.

The proposed method first adopts a bottom-up approach to generate an initial set of regions of interest (RoIs) in the image, followed by a top-down refinement step that iteratively updates the RoIs using a Bayesian network. In this paper, we present a novel approach for dense 3D visual mapping, which we term "semantic simplification." This method leverages the power of semantic segmentation to reduce the complexity of 3D point clouds, while preserving the essential information required for accurate mapping.

Existing methods for dense 3D visual mapping often suffer from the "curse of dimensionality," where the complexity of the data grows exponentially with the number of dimensions. This makes it difficult to efficiently process and analyze large 3D datasets. Semantic simplification addresses this challenge by separating the point cloud into semantically meaningful regions, allowing for a significant reduction in the number of points while preserving the essential features of the environment.

Our approach is based on a deep neural network that learns to segment 3D point clouds into meaningful regions, such as walls, floors, and objects. This segmentation enables the creation of a compact representation of the environment, which can be used for efficient mapping, object recognition, and scene understanding.

We evaluate our method on several large-scale 3D datasets and demonstrate its effectiveness in reducing the complexity of the data while preserving the accuracy of the map. Our experiments show that semantic simplification can reduce the number of points in a point cloud by up to 90% while maintaining the same level of accuracy as the original data.

The main contribution of this paper is the introduction of a novel approach to dense 3D visual mapping that leverages semantic segmentation to reduce the complexity of 3D point clouds. Our method has numerous applications in various fields, including robotics, autonomous vehicles, and virtual reality.

In summary, semantic simplification is a powerful tool for dense 3D visual mapping that enables the efficient processing and analysis of large 3D datasets. Our approach has the potential to significantly improve the performance of various applications that rely on 3D data, and we believe it will play a crucial role in the development of future 3D data processing technologies.

Tensor networks provide an efficient approximation of operations involving
high dimensional tensors and have been extensively used in modelling quantum
many-body systems. More recently, supervised learning has been attempted with
tensor networks, primarily focused on tasks such as image classification. In
this work, we propose a novel formulation of tensor networks for supervised
image segmentation which allows them to operate on high resolution medical
images. We use the matrix product state (MPS) tensor network on non-overlapping
patches of a given input image to predict the segmentation mask by learning a
pixel-wise linear classification rule in a high dimensional space. The proposed
model is end-to-end trainable using backpropagation. It is implemented as a
Strided Tensor Network to reduce the parameter complexity. The performance of
the proposed method is evaluated on two public medical imaging datasets and
compared to relevant baselines. The evaluation shows that the strided tensor
network yields competitive performance compared to CNN-based models while using
fewer resources. Additionally, based on the experiments we discuss the
feasibility of using fully linear models for segmentation tasks.

This paper proposes a novel approach to infrared image segmentation using an Active Contour Model (ACM) that incorporates multiple features to handle intensity inhomogeneity. The proposed method, called Multi-Feature Driven Active Contour Segmentation (MF-ACS), combines the traditional ACM with a set of intensification functions that capture different aspects of the image information. The intensification functions are used to drive the evolution of the contour, allowing it to better adapt to the varying intensity characteristics of the image. Experimental results on several challenging infrared images demonstrate the superior performance of MF-ACS compared to traditional ACM and other state-of-the-art methods. The improved accuracy is achieved while maintaining the simplicity and efficiency of the ACM framework. Furthermore, the inclusion of multiple features provides greater robustness to noise and artifacts, ensuring more reliable segmentation. The presented approach has significant applications in various fields such as military surveillance, environmental monitoring, and medical imaging.

In this work, the case of semantic segmentation on a small image dataset
(simulated by 1000 randomly selected images from PASCAL VOC 2012), where only
weak supervision signals (scribbles from user interaction) are available is
studied. Especially, to tackle the problem of limited data annotations in image
segmentation, transferring different pre-trained models and CRF based methods
are applied to enhance the segmentation performance. To this end, RotNet,
DeeperCluster, and Semi&Weakly Supervised Learning (SWSL) pre-trained models
are transferred and finetuned in a DeepLab-v2 baseline, and dense CRF is
applied both as a post-processing and loss regularization technique. The
results of my study show that, on this small dataset, using a pre-trained
ResNet50 SWSL model gives results that are 7.4% better than applying an
ImageNet pre-trained model; moreover, for the case of training on the full
PASCAL VOC 2012 training data, this pre-training approach increases the mIoU
results by almost 4%. On the other hand, dense CRF is shown to be very
effective as well, enhancing the results both as a loss regularization
technique in weakly supervised training and as a post-processing tool.

In this paper, we explore the holographic Schwinger effect in the presence of a rotating probe D3-brane, which provides a novel and interesting scenario for studying the interplay between gravitational and electromagnetic fields.

Using the AdS/CFT correspondence, we map the problem to a thermal state in a gravitational background with a rotating boundary, and employ a combination of analytical and numerical methods to study the resulting gravitational and electromagnetic fields. We find that the presence of the rotating probe D3-brane leads to a rich and complex structure of the created particles, which depends on both the rotation rate and the strength of the electric field.

Our results provide new insights into the holographic Schwinger effect and its dependence on the rotational velocity of the probe brane. We also find that the rotation of the probe brane introduces a new scale into the problem, which affects the creation rate of particles and leads to a non-trivial competition between the gravitational and electromagnetic forces.

Our work sheds light on the interplay between gravity, electromagnetism, and rotation in the context of the AdS/CFT correspondence, and provides a new platform for exploring the holographic Schwinger effect in novel regimes. The results obtained in this paper may have implications for a wide range of physical phenomena, from heavy ion collisions to black hole physics and cosmology.

This article explores thin games, a mathematical concept used to analyze strategic situations. The focus is on examining how symmetry affects these games and how they relate to concurrent Hyland-Ong games. Through theoretical analysis and simulations, this research aims to provide new insights into the structure of symmetric thin games and their relation to other well-known game formats.

Although less studied than purely action or state based logics, state/event
based logics are becoming increasingly important. Some systems are best studied
using structures with information on both states and transitions, and it is
these structures over which state/event based logics are defined. The logic
UCTL and its variants are perhaps the most widely studied and implemented of
these logics to date. As yet, however, no-one seems to have defined UCTL*, a
trivial step but a worthwhile one. Here we do just that, but prove in the cases
of both UCTL and UCTL* that these logics are no more expressive than their more
commonplace fragments. Also, acknowledging the importance of modal transition
systems, we define a state/event based logic over a modified modal transition
system as a precursor to further work.

We consider the problem of approximate Bayesian inference in log-supermodular
models. These models encompass regular pairwise MRFs with binary variables, but
allow to capture high-order interactions, which are intractable for existing
approximate inference techniques such as belief propagation, mean field, and
variants. We show that a recently proposed variational approach to inference in
log-supermodular models -L-FIELD- reduces to the widely-studied minimum norm
problem for submodular minimization. This insight allows to leverage powerful
existing tools, and hence to solve the variational problem orders of magnitude
more efficiently than previously possible. We then provide another natural
interpretation of L-FIELD, demonstrating that it exactly minimizes a specific
type of R\'enyi divergence measure. This insight sheds light on the nature of
the variational approximations produced by L-FIELD. Furthermore, we show how to
perform parallel inference as message passing in a suitable factor graph at a
linear convergence rate, without having to sum up over all the configurations
of the factor. Finally, we apply our approach to a challenging image
segmentation task. Our experiments confirm scalability of our approach, high
quality of the marginals, and the benefit of incorporating higher-order
potentials.

This paper presents novel control strategies for intermittent contact mode atomic force microscopes (AFMs) that significantly improve the performance and efficiency of the instrument. Intermittent contact mode AFMs are widely used for imaging and manipulating materials at the nanoscale, but their performance is limited by the challenges of maintaining a stable and controlled contact between the probe and the sample surface. The control strategies presented in this paper address these challenges by incorporating advanced algorithms, machine learning, and real-time feedback control to optimize the contact force and scanning parameters.

The proposed control strategies are tested using a variety of samples and imaging conditions, and the results demonstrate a significant improvement in image quality, speed, and accuracy compared to traditional control methods. In particular, the new control strategies enable the AFM to achieve higher scanning speeds, improved resolution, and reduced artifacts, making it possible to image and manipulate materials at the nanoscale with unprecedented precision and efficiency.

The paper also provides a detailed analysis of the underlying mechanisms and trade-offs involved in intermittent contact mode AFM, which shed light on the fundamental limitations of the technique and provide a framework for further optimization and development. The results and insights presented in this paper have important implications for a wide range of applications, including materials science, biology, and nanotechnology, and are expected to contribute significantly to the advancement of the field.

In this paper, we investigate the concept of local quantum uncertainty in two-qubit separable states. We focus on a specific case study, where we consider two qubits that are coupled through a controlled-NOT (CNOT) gate and are measured in the Bell basis. We analytically derive expressions for the local uncertainty and the quantum uncertainty in the system, and compare them to the classical uncertainty bound.

Our results show that the local quantum uncertainty in the two-qubit system can be significantly higher than the classical uncertainty bound, indicating the presence of non-classical correlations between the qubits. We also find that the local uncertainty is strongly dependent on the measurement settings and the entanglement level of the system.

Our study demonstrates the importance of considering local quantum uncertainty in the analysis of quantum systems, and highlights the potential of using this concept to better understand the nature of quantum correlations. The results of this study have implications for the development of quantum information processing protocols, such as quantum cryptography and quantum teleportation, which rely on the manipulation of quantum entanglement.

Furthermore, our work provides a deeper understanding of the relationship between quantum uncertainty and non-locality, which is a fundamental aspect of quantum mechanics. The results of this study contribute to the ongoing effort to develop a comprehensive theory of quantum information and its role in the behavior of quantum systems.

The aim of this research is to establish upper bounds on quantifier depth for graph differentiation, a problem that arises in first-order logic. By analyzing various cases and scenarios, we demonstrate that these boundaries are achievable through careful application of established techniques from mathematical logic. Our results contribute significantly to the understanding of graph differentiation and its applications in computer science and related fields.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for biomedical image analysis are often
of very large size, resulting in high memory requirement and high latency of
operations. Searching for an acceptable compressed representation of the base
CNN for a specific imaging application typically involves a series of
time-consuming training/validation experiments to achieve a good compromise
between network size and accuracy. To address this challenge, we propose
CC-Net, a new image complexity-guided CNN compression scheme for biomedical
image segmentation. Given a CNN model, CC-Net predicts the final accuracy of
networks of different sizes based on the average image complexity computed from
the training data. It then selects a multiplicative factor for producing a
desired network with acceptable network accuracy and size. Experiments show
that CC-Net is effective for generating compressed segmentation networks,
retaining up to 95% of the base network segmentation accuracy and utilizing
only 0.1% of trainable parameters of the full-sized networks in the best case.

Learning of Image Dehazing Models for Segmentation Tasks

We present a novel approach to learning image dehazing models for segmentation tasks. We propose a novel learning algorithm that combines the learning of a dehazing model with the learning of a segmentation model. The proposed algorithm is based on the idea that the dehazing model is a good candidate for segmentation because it is able to extract features from the image that are not present in the segmentation model. We show that the proposed algorithm is able to learn dehazing models for a wide range of image segmentation tasks.

In this study, we investigate room temperature quantum spin Hall insulators based on buckled square lattice structures. We show that breaking time-reversal symmetry in these materials can lead to robust helical edge states and quantized surface transport properties indicative of topological protection. Our findings suggest that such systems could be promising candidates for spintronics applications due to their potential for low power dissipation and high efficiency. Overall, our work provides new insights into designing novel materials with unique electronic properties suitable for cutting-edge technologies.

This article explores the Structure Theory of Almost Abelian Lie Algebras. We show that any such algebra can be decomposed into a direct sum of simpler subalgebras, and classify these subalgebras using algebraic geometry techniques. Our results provide new insights on this class of objects which appear naturally in various areas of mathematics and physics, including Riemannian Geometry & Control theory. The main tools used are derived from Representation Theorem along with Homological Algebra principles like Ext functor properties. Overall our investigation sheds light onto rich combinatorial nature embedded within seemingly simple-looking mathematical structures thereby providing valuable guidelines towards solving open problems relevant not only academically but also industrially.

B\"acklund transformations (BTs) are traditionally regarded as a tool for
integrating nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs). Their use has been
recently extended, however, to problems such as the construction of recursion
operators for symmetries of PDEs, as well as the solution of linear systems of
PDEs. In this article, the concept and some applications of BTs are reviewed.
As an example of an integrable linear system of PDEs, the Maxwell equations of
electromagnetism are shown to constitute a BT connecting the wave equations for
the electric and the magnetic field; plane-wave solutions of the Maxwell system
are constructed in detail. The connection between BTs and recursion operators
is also discussed.

Caffrey, Egge, Michel, Rubin and Ver Steegh recently introduced snow leopard
permutations, which are the anti-Baxter permutations that are compatible with
the doubly alternating Baxter permutations. Among other things, they showed
that these permutations preserve parity, and that the number of snow leopard
permutations of length $2n-1$ is the Catalan number $C_n$. In this paper we
investigate the permutations that the snow leopard permutations induce on their
even and odd entries; we call these the even threads and the odd threads,
respectively. We give recursive bijections between these permutations and
certain families of Catalan paths. We characterize the odd (resp. even) threads
which form the other half of a snow leopard permutation whose even (resp. odd)
thread is layered in terms of pattern avoidance, and we give a constructive
bijection between the set of permutations of length $n$ which are both even
threads and odd threads and the set of peakless Motzkin paths of length $n+1$.

In this paper, we investigate the strong monogamy conjecture in a four-qubit system, which states that the entanglement of a group of qubits cannot be shared among multiple pairs of qubits. We present a thorough analysis of the conjecture and provide experimental evidence to support it.

Using a combination of analytical and numerical methods, we demonstrate that the strong monogamy conjecture holds for a large class of four-qubit states, including states with a high degree of entanglement. We also examine the robustness of the conjecture against various types of noise and perturbations, and find that it remains valid even in the presence of certain types of noise.

Our results provide new insights into the nature of entanglement in multi-qubit systems and have important implications for the study of quantum information processing and quantum communication. In particular, they demonstrate that the strong monogamy conjecture can be used as a useful tool for characterizing the entanglement properties of complex quantum systems, and for developing new protocols for quantum communication and cryptography.

Overall, our work represents a significant contribution to the field of quantum information science, and highlights the power of the strong monogamy conjecture as a tool for understanding the behavior of entangled quantum systems.

In recent years, the idea of using morphological operations as networks has
received much attention. Mathematical morphology provides very efficient and
useful image processing and image analysis tools based on basic operators like
dilation and erosion, defined in terms of kernels. Many other morphological
operations are built up using the dilation and erosion operations. Although the
learning of structuring elements such as dilation or erosion using the
backpropagation algorithm is not new, the order and the way these morphological
operations are used is not standard. In this paper, we have theoretically
analyzed the use of morphological operations for processing 1D feature vectors
and shown that this gets extended to the 2D case in a simple manner. Our
theoretical results show that a morphological block represents a sum of hinge
functions. Hinge functions are used in many places for classification and
regression tasks (Breiman (1993)). We have also proved a universal
approximation theorem -- a stack of two morphological blocks can approximate
any continuous function over arbitrary compact sets. To experimentally validate
the efficacy of this network in real-life applications, we have evaluated its
performance on satellite image classification datasets since morphological
operations are very sensitive to geometrical shapes and structures. We have
also shown results on a few tasks like segmentation of blood vessels from
fundus images, segmentation of lungs from chest x-ray and image dehazing. The
results are encouraging and further establishes the potential of morphological
networks.

The paper presents a novel approach to image segmentation using adversarial networks. The proposed method, called Points2Polygon, utilizes weak labels and contextual information to produce more accurate segmentations than traditional pixel classification methods. The model is trained in an end-to-end fashion with an adversary network that encourages the generation of coherent and realistic polygonal segments. Experimental results on several benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches while requiring less annotated data. Overall, this study provides a promising technique for efficient and effective semantic segmentation utilizing limited supervision.

This paper proposes a novel approach to hyperspectral and multispectral image fusion based on a sparse representation. The proposed method leverages the advantages of both hyperspectral and multispectral imaging, which provide rich spectral information and high spatial resolution, respectively. The proposed method uses a sparse representation to fuse the images, which allows for the preservation of the spectral and spatial information of the original images.

The proposed method consists of three main steps: 1) sparse representation of the hyperspectral and multispectral images, 2) fusion of the sparse representations, and 3) reconstruction of the fused image. The sparse representation is achieved using a compressive sensing approach, which enables the representation of the images using a small number of coefficients. The fusion of the sparse representations is performed using a weighted averaging technique, where the weights are determined based on the spectral and spatial similarity between the images. Finally, the fused image is reconstructed using an optimization-based approach that minimizes the difference between the fused image and the original images.

The proposed method is evaluated using several experiments on real-world hyperspectral and multispectral images. The results show that the proposed method outperforms traditional fusion methods in terms of both spectral and spatial information preservation. Additionally, the proposed method is computationally efficient and can be applied to a wide range of applications, including environmental monitoring, agricultural management, and military surveillance.

The main contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows:

* A novel approach to hyperspectral and multispectral image fusion based on a sparse representation is proposed.
* The proposed method preserves the spectral and spatial information of the original images.
* The method is computationally efficient and can be applied to a wide range of applications.
* The proposed method outperforms traditional fusion methods in terms of both spectral and spatial information preservation.

Overall, this paper provides a significant contribution to the field of image fusion and remote sensing, and demonstrates the potential of using a sparse representation for hyperspectral and multispectral image fusion.

Accurate segmentation of the prostate from magnetic resonance (MR) images
provides useful information for prostate cancer diagnosis and treatment.
However, automated prostate segmentation from 3D MR images still faces several
challenges. For instance, a lack of clear edge between the prostate and other
anatomical structures makes it challenging to accurately extract the
boundaries. The complex background texture and large variation in size, shape
and intensity distribution of the prostate itself make segmentation even
further complicated. With deep learning, especially convolutional neural
networks (CNNs), emerging as commonly used methods for medical image
segmentation, the difficulty in obtaining large number of annotated medical
images for training CNNs has become much more pronounced that ever before.
Since large-scale dataset is one of the critical components for the success of
deep learning, lack of sufficient training data makes it difficult to fully
train complex CNNs. To tackle the above challenges, in this paper, we propose a
boundary-weighted domain adaptive neural network (BOWDA-Net). To make the
network more sensitive to the boundaries during segmentation, a
boundary-weighted segmentation loss (BWL) is proposed. Furthermore, an advanced
boundary-weighted transfer leaning approach is introduced to address the
problem of small medical imaging datasets. We evaluate our proposed model on
the publicly available MICCAI 2012 Prostate MR Image Segmentation (PROMISE12)
challenge dataset. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model
is more sensitive to boundary information and outperformed other
state-of-the-art methods.

Apart from presenting some new insights and results, one of our main purposes
is to put some records in the development of von Neumann modules straight.
  The von Neumann or $W^*$-objects among the Hilbert ($C^*$-)modules are around
since the first papers by Paschke (1973) and Rieffel (1974) that lift
Kaplansky's setting (1953) to modules over noncommutative $C^*$-algebras. While
the formal definition of $W^*$-modules} is due to Baillet, Denizeau, and Havet
(1988), the one of von Neumann modules as strongly closed operator spaces
started with Skeide (2000). It has been paired with the definition of concrete
von Neumann modules in Skeide (2006). It is well-known that (pre-)Hilbert
modules can be viewed as ternary rings of operators and in their definition of
Hilbert-von Neumann modules, Bikram, Mukherjee, Srinivasan, and Sunder (2012)
take that point of view.
  We illustrate that a (suitably nondegenerate) Hilbert-von Neumann module is
the same thing as a strongly full concrete von Neumann module. We also use this
occasion to put some things in earlier papers right. We show that the tensor
product of (concrete, or not) von Neumann correspondences is, indeed, (a
generalization of) the tensor product of Connes correspondences (claimed in
Skeide (2008)), viewed in a way quite different from Bikram et al.. We also
present some new arguments that are useful even for (pre-)Hilbert modules.

Medical images are often accompanied by metadata describing the image
(vendor, acquisition parameters) and the patient (disease type or severity,
demographics, genomics). This metadata is usually disregarded by image
segmentation methods. In this work, we adapt a linear conditioning method
called FiLM (Feature-wise Linear Modulation) for image segmentation tasks. This
FiLM adaptation enables integrating metadata into segmentation models for
better performance. We observed an average Dice score increase of 5.1% on
spinal cord tumor segmentation when incorporating the tumor type with FiLM. The
metadata modulates the segmentation process through low-cost affine
transformations applied on feature maps which can be included in any neural
network's architecture. Additionally, we assess the relevance of segmentation
FiLM layers for tackling common challenges in medical imaging: multi-class
training with missing segmentations, model adaptation to multiple tasks, and
training with a limited or unbalanced number of annotated data. Our results
demonstrated the following benefits of FiLM for segmentation: FiLMed U-Net was
robust to missing labels and reached higher Dice scores with few labels (up to
16.7%) compared to single-task U-Net. The code is open-source and available at
www.ivadomed.org.

This paper presents a Matlab implementation of a machine vision algorithm for evaluating ballast degradation in railway tracks. The algorithm is designed to automatically assess the condition of ballast, which is a critical component of railroad infrastructure, by analyzing images captured by a camera mounted on a train. The image processing techniques used in the algorithm include histogram equalization, thresholding, and feature extraction. The extracted features are then used to classify the ballast conditions into three categories: good, fair, and poor. The classification model is trained using a support vector machine (SVM) classifier.

The proposed method offers several advantages over traditional manual inspection methods, including increased accuracy, efficiency, and cost-effectiveness. The automated system can operated at high speeds, allowing for rapid evaluation of large sections of track, and can also provide detailed information about the location and extent of ballast degradation. Additionally, the use of machine vision technology enables real-time monitoring of ballast condition, enabling early detection of potential problems before they become critical.

The performance of the algorithm was tested using a dataset of images collected from various locations and under different lighting conditions. Results show that the SVM classifier achieved an accuracy rate of 90%, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed approach. Future work includes refining the algorithm to improve its robustness against varying lighting conditions and integrating it with other sensors to create a comprehensive monitoring system for railroad infrastructure. The proposed method has the potential to significantly improve the maintenance and management of railway systems, reducing costs and increasing safety.

Proper inclusion of van der Waals (vdW) interactions in theoretical
simulations based on standard density functional theory (DFT) is crucial to
describe the physics and chemistry of systems such as organic and layered
materials. Many encouraging approaches have been proposed to combine vdW
interactions with standard approximate DFT calculations. Despite many vdW
studies, there is no consensus on the reliability of vdW methods. To help
further development of vdW methods, we have assessed various vdW functionals
through the calculation of structural prop- erties at equilibrium, such as
lattice constants, bulk moduli, and cohesive energies, for bulk solids,
including alkali, alkali-earth, and transition metals, with BCC, FCC, and
diamond structures as the ground state structure. These results provide
important information for the vdW-related materials research, which is
essential for designing and optimizing materials systems for desired physical
and chemical properties.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to few-shot learning for 3D medical image segmentation using bidirectional Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs). network on a dataset containing 120 abdominal CT scans and show that it boosts
segmentation performance significantly.

Federated learning allows distributed medical institutions to collaboratively
learn a shared prediction model with privacy protection. While at clinical
deployment, the models trained in federated learning can still suffer from
performance drop when applied to completely unseen hospitals outside the
federation. In this paper, we point out and solve a novel problem setting of
federated domain generalization (FedDG), which aims to learn a federated model
from multiple distributed source domains such that it can directly generalize
to unseen target domains. We present a novel approach, named as Episodic
Learning in Continuous Frequency Space (ELCFS), for this problem by enabling
each client to exploit multi-source data distributions under the challenging
constraint of data decentralization. Our approach transmits the distribution
information across clients in a privacy-protecting way through an effective
continuous frequency space interpolation mechanism. With the transferred
multi-source distributions, we further carefully design a boundary-oriented
episodic learning paradigm to expose the local learning to domain distribution
shifts and particularly meet the challenges of model generalization in medical
image segmentation scenario. The effectiveness of our method is demonstrated
with superior performance over state-of-the-arts and in-depth ablation
experiments on two medical image segmentation tasks. The code is available at

A relatively new type of contest in which contestants must play to win is known as a single elimination tournament. In this context, this type of tournament is distinguished by: a small number of rounds; an indefinite number of possible moves; and a winner declared after each round and final scores are tallied to determine who wins the game. Previous analyses have explored various facets of human decision making via tournaments; however, they have typically been based on highly simplified games involving just three distinct states where participants know nothing about how their choices affect a larger state space. While these games can provide interesting insights into the way that humans assess and make decisions under uncertainty, it has become clear from experimental studies of other types of uncertainty (e.g., gambling) that this approach leads towards misleading conclusions concerning the nature of competition and decision making [1]. Here we use a unique artificial intelligence system developed at Carnegie Mellon University to study what happens when contestants from two different games simultaneously try to maximize a utility function over a wider range of decisions. The goal was to develop techniques for extracting strategic information, such as strategies in each game situation, without requiring that players actually perform any actual strategy learning. This resulted in a method for developing and evaluating algorithms specifically designed to evaluate all kinds of decision problems. Our results show that multiple-game tournaments indeed do yield insights into the way that human competitors think. However, even simple multi-agent models may contain large amounts of non-strategic information and suggest the need to consider further techniques or approaches while the question of who can learn optimal strategies remains.

In this paper, we present a numerical study of a quantum particle interacting with a quantum environment. We consider a simple model of a two-level system (qubit) coupled to a bosonic bath, which is a common scenario in many quantum systems. Our aim is to understandingthe dynamical behavior of the qubit and its entanglement with the environment.

Using a numerically exact method, we solve the time-dependent Schrödinger equation for the total system and study how the qubit's population transfer and dephasing are affected by various parameters such as the coupling strength, temperature, and initial conditions.

Our results show that, depending on these parameters, the qubit can exhibit different types of dynamics such as Rabi oscillations, collapses, and revivals. We also observe non-exponential decay of the qubit populations and discuss its implications on qubits relaxation and decoherence. Furthermore, we find regime where the qubit and environment become strongly entangled and investigate the properties of this entanglement using measures such as negativity and entropy.

Our work provides new insights into the complex dynamics of open quantum systems and highlights the importance of numerical simulations in studying their behavior. The results have potential applications in fields such as quantum computing, precision measurement, and radiation chemistry.

In this paper, we present a novel approach to improving the sensitivity and resolution of spontaneous noise spectroscopy (SNS) measurements on atomic vapors. SNS is a technique that uses the random fluctuations in the absorption or emission spectrum of atoms or molecules to probe their interactions with an external driving field. However, these measurements are often limited by the presence of background noise, which can overwhelm the weak signals from the atom-field interactions.

Here, we demonstrate a method for reducing the impact of background noise on SNS measurements using a combination of spectral filtering and modulation techniques. We show that by applying a tailored frequency modulation to the probing laser beam, we can selectively suppress the background noise while preserving the signal from the atom-field interactions. This allows us to achieve a significant increase in the signal-to-noise ratio and Hyperfine Level Coherence (HLC), which enables detailed resolved studies of the interacting systems.

We apply our technique to a rubidium vapor cell and observe improved HLC and reduced noise levels compared to conventional SNS measurements. The results pave the way for extending SNS to investigationg previously inaccessible quantum systems, such as single atoms and molecules, and offer new possibilities for precision measurement applications.

We propose a new approach to image segmentation, which exploits the
advantages of both conditional random fields (CRFs) and decision trees. In the
literature, the potential functions of CRFs are mostly defined as a linear
combination of some pre-defined parametric models, and then methods like
structured support vector machines (SSVMs) are applied to learn those linear
coefficients. We instead formulate the unary and pairwise potentials as
nonparametric forests---ensembles of decision trees, and learn the ensemble
parameters and the trees in a unified optimization problem within the
large-margin framework. In this fashion, we easily achieve nonlinear learning
of potential functions on both unary and pairwise terms in CRFs. Moreover, we
learn class-wise decision trees for each object that appears in the image. Due
to the rich structure and flexibility of decision trees, our approach is
powerful in modelling complex data likelihoods and label relationships. The
resulting optimization problem is very challenging because it can have
exponentially many variables and constraints. We show that this challenging
optimization can be efficiently solved by combining a modified column
generation and cutting-planes techniques. Experimental results on both binary
(Graz-02, Weizmann horse, Oxford flower) and multi-class (MSRC-21, PASCAL VOC
2012) segmentation datasets demonstrate the power of the learned nonlinear
nonparametric potentials.
