In this paper, we investigate the interplay between sparsity and parallel acquisition in compressive sensing, and provide optimal uniform and nonuniform recovery guarantees for various sampling schemes. We consider both random and deterministic sampling methods, and examine their performance under different sparsity models, including the popular L1-norm and Lp-norm models.

Our main contributions include the derivation of precise recovery guarantees for uniform and nonuniform sampling schemes, which reveal the intricate relationship between sparsity, sampling rate, and recovery performance. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the choice of sparsity model can have a significant impact on the recovery guarantees, and that the Lp-norm model can provide better guarantees than the L1-norm model in certain regimes. Our results also reveal that the optimal sampling rate for uniform sampling schemes is not always the same as the optimal sampling rate for nonuniform sampling schemes, and that the latter can be significantly lower in some cases.

Our findings have important implications for the design and implementation of compressive sensing systems, and highlight the importance of carefully choosing the sampling scheme and sparsity model to achieve optimal recovery performance. The results of this paper provide a theoretical foundation for the development of efficient and robust compressive sensing systems, and will be of interest to researchers and practitioners in signal processing, machine learning, and related fields.

This study deals with semantic segmentation of high-resolution (aerial)

We study the Brown measure of certain non-hermitian operators arising from
Voiculescu's free probability theory. Usually those operators appear as the
limit in *-moments of certain ensembles of non-hermitian random matrices, and
the Brown measure gives then a canonical candidate for the limit eigenvalue
distribution of the random matrices. A prominent class for our operators is
given by polynomials in *-free variables. Other explicit examples include
R-diagonal elements and elliptic elements, for which the Brown measure was
already known, and a new class of triangular-elliptic elements. Our method for
the calculation of the Brown measure is based on a rigorous mathematical
treatment of the hermitian reduction method, as considered in the physical
literature, combined with subordination ideas and the linearization trick.

This work applies an innovative method to identify individual neurons in neuronal networks identified by nonlinear regression models, in contrast to neural network identification via pattern matching (e.g., Hinton & Tversky). We use this technique to automatically learn features to segment individual images by extracting points from interactive medical image segments based on their local spatial relationships and local motion information that we then use to create low-dimensional images using sequential patching with deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs). To characterize the results successfully we train our ensemble of CNN models using visual inspection data of patient-side CT scans of patients who have been diagnosed with various conditions via machine learning methods [19], [20]. Specifically, we classify images as normal or abnormal based on both spatial information, such as landmarks, size, color and orientation of anatomical structures, and local motion patterns, particularly when viewing the same objects at a different position in time. While human diagnostic professionals typically undergo training procedures involving extensive interaction and interaction learning across subjects, our approach leverages machine learning techniques learned directly from user interactions by exploiting recurrent neural connections among tasks of interaction between users and machines to infer features of object features [8], [9]–[13]. Through these continuous interactions across users during clinical visits, we can train CNN models fast enough to predict which abnormalities may benefit from interinteractions, allowing our automated approach to quickly evaluate whether user engagement will be effective at identifying abnormalities prior to diagnosis. In particular, our research has demonstrated that CNNs can readily distinguish healthy individuals from malignant states within a subgroup of cancer-related lesions without requiring a human interface, suggesting broad potential applications beyond pathology diagnosis. We also illustrate how we can augment these methods by incorporating hierarchical CNNs capable of recognizing high dimensional feature vectors representing spatial relationships over the entire dataset in the future.

coefficient and Hausdorff distance.The proposed joint learning framework of our
PC-U net is beneficial for automatic cardiac image analysis tasks because it
can obtain simultaneously the 3D shape and segmentation of the LV MYO walls.

Surgical tool segmentation in endoscopic images is an important problem: it
is a crucial step towards full instrument pose estimation and it is used for
integration of pre- and intra-operative images into the endoscopic view. While
many recent approaches based on convolutional neural networks have shown great
results, a key barrier to progress lies in the acquisition of a large number of
manually-annotated images which is necessary for an algorithm to generalize and
work well in diverse surgical scenarios. Unlike the surgical image data itself,
annotations are difficult to acquire and may be of variable quality. On the
other hand, synthetic annotations can be automatically generated by using
forward kinematic model of the robot and CAD models of tools by projecting them
onto an image plane. Unfortunately, this model is very inaccurate and cannot be
used for supervised learning of image segmentation models. Since generated
annotations will not directly correspond to endoscopic images due to errors, we
formulate the problem as an unpaired image-to-image translation where the goal
is to learn the mapping between an input endoscopic image and a corresponding
annotation using an adversarial model. Our approach allows to train image
segmentation models without the need to acquire expensive annotations and can
potentially exploit large unlabeled endoscopic image collection outside the
annotated distributions of image/annotation data. We test our proposed method
on Endovis 2017 challenge dataset and show that it is competitive with
supervised segmentation methods.

This paper proposes a novel approach to eye fundus images segmentation using deep neural convolution networks with a convex shape prior. The proposed method integrates a geometric prior into the network architecture, enforcing the output of the network to have convex shapes, which are consistent with the geometry of retinal vessels and optic disc in the eye fundus images. Experimental results on publicly available datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of segmentation accuracy and robustness to variations in image quality. Our approach has important implications for clinical applications where accurate segmentation is critical, such as diabetic retinopathy diagnosis and monitoring.

We consider referring image segmentation. It is a problem at the intersection
of computer vision and natural language understanding. Given an input image and
a referring expression in the form of a natural language sentence, the goal is
to segment the object of interest in the image referred by the linguistic
query. To this end, we propose a dual convolutional LSTM (ConvLSTM) network to
tackle this problem. Our model consists of an encoder network and a decoder
network, where ConvLSTM is used in both encoder and decoder networks to capture
spatial and sequential information. The encoder network extracts visual and
linguistic features for each word in the expression sentence, and adopts an
attention mechanism to focus on words that are more informative in the
multimodal interaction. The decoder network integrates the features generated
by the encoder network at multiple levels as its input and produces the final
precise segmentation mask. Experimental results on four challenging datasets
demonstrate that the proposed network achieves superior segmentation
performance compared with other state-of-the-art methods.

A total of 35 R packages were evaluated. Using uni-variate regression analysis of RStudio (version 6.5) and SPSS 21 (18 months ago), a set of 100 observations was extracted from an experimental data set comprising 24 variables representing various quantities or groups and 40 combinations of each. Linear regression techniques (both multiple regression models and Poisson regression) were tested on random samples of 1000 for which one could control the degree of aggregation, using fixed effects or independent variable specifications. Data sets used included both real world datasets using random permutations (uniform distribution, gaussian distribution) and mathematical modeling datasets (continuous Gaussians). Results revealed that all significant findings can be explained by nonlinearities. For example, all but three observations showed evidence of either 1(1) or 2 (2,0) transformations of values prior to transformation into continuous. Among the two dimensional Gaussian models where the error variance was not specified, both the mean squared correlation coefficient and the standard deviations of two different indicators significantly outperformed the corresponding means of the other variables in predicting errors. Overall performance also improved when the measurement error variable was introduced as a dependent variable. Additionally, within 2d-2d interactions between the dependent (error) and independent predictors significantly outperformed the mean differences between dependent and independent predictors in both single regression models and multi-way models (Friedman's t test). We perform this analysis by choosing a measure C and by performing multiplication. For example, we begin by finding the first few (first echelon) Mersenne primes where both Euler-Mascheroni and Schnorr numbers follow immediately after it! We see the impact of these primality tests as a way to discover new and unexpected cases such as prime numbers when they are involved in systems which are not known yet to be robust against the use of primality testing, in particular via cryptographic attack schemes. In this paper, we present a novel approach to active contour models using locally controlled distance vector flow. Traditional active contour models rely on global optimization techniques that can be computationally expensive and may not effectively capture complex image structures. Our proposed method utilizes a locally controlled distance vector flow to drive the evolution of the contour, allowing for efficient and flexible segmentation of images with varying levels of complexity.

We propose a new energy functional that incorporates both image information and user interaction, enabling real-time feedback and control over the segmentation process. The energy functional combines traditional image intensity terms with a novel distancevectorflow term that encourages the contour to move towards regions of high gradient magnitude. This allows the model to adaptively adjust its behavior based on local image features, leading to improved accuracy and efficiency in segmenting complex objects.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method through experiments on several benchmark datasets, including medical imaging and natural scenes. Our results show that our method outperforms traditional active contour models in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency, while also providing more intuitive and user-friendly interactions. We further validate our approach by applying it to real-world scenarios such as tumor segmentation in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans.

Overall, our work presents a significant advancement in the field of active contour models, providing a powerful tool for image segmentation tasks that can be used in a variety of applications. Keywords: active contours, image segmentation, distance vector flow, locally controlled,real-time feedback.

A linear function submission-based double-auction (LFS-DA) mechanism for a
regional electricity network is proposed in this paper. Each agent in the
network is equipped with a battery and a generator. Each agent simultaneously
becomes a producer and consumer of electricity, i.e., a prosumer and trades
electricity in the regional market at a variable price. In the LFS-DA, each
agent uses linear demand and supply functions when they submit bids and asks to
an auctioneer in the regional market.The LFS-DA can achieve an exact balance
between electricity demand and supply for each time slot throughout the
learning phase and was shown capable of solving the primal problem of
maximizing the social welfare of the network without any central price setter,
e.g., a utility or a large electricity company, in contrast with conventional
real-time pricing (RTP). This paper presents a clarification of the
relationship between the RTP algorithm derived on the basis of a dual
decomposition framework and LFS-DA. Specifically, we proved that the changes in
the price profile of the LFS-DA mechanism are equal to those achieved by the
RTP mechanism derived from the dual decomposition framework except for a
constant factor.

In this paper, we explore the role of function norms and regularization in deep neural networks. We begin by analyzing the concept of function norms and their relationship to the generalization ability of deep networks. We then examine the various regularization techniques that are commonly used in deep learning, including weight decay, dropout, and early stopping, and their impact on function norms.

Through a series of theoretical and empirical studies, we demonstrate that function norms play a crucial role in determining the generalization ability of deep networks. We show that regularization techniques can be effective in reducing overfitting and improving generalization by modifying the function norms of the network. Specifically, we show that weight decay and dropout regularization can reduce the Lipschitz constant of the network, while early stopping can reduce the supremum norm of the network.

Our results provide new insights into the role of function norms in deep learning and have important implications for the design and training of deep neural networks. We demonstrate that by carefully choosing regularization techniques and tuning their hyperparameters, it is possible to improve the generalization ability of deep networks and avoid overfitting.

Our work contributes to the growing body of research on the theoretical foundations of deep learning and has important implications for a wide range of applications, including computer vision, natural language processing, and speech recognition.

The paper presents a case study that demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed method in improving the accuracy of precipitation forecasts. Overall, the paper contributes to the understanding of how to better account for model error in ensemble Kalman filtering, which is crucial for improving the reliability of weather and climate predictions.

The medical image is characterized by the inter-class indistinction, high
variability, and noise, where the recognition of pixels is challenging. Unlike
previous self-attention based methods that capture context information from one
level, we reformulate the self-attention mechanism from the view of the
high-order graph and propose a novel method, namely Hierarchical Attention
Network (HANet), to address the problem of medical image segmentation.
Concretely, an HA module embedded in the HANet captures context information
from neighbors of multiple levels, where these neighbors are extracted from the
high-order graph. In the high-order graph, there will be an edge between two
nodes only if the correlation between them is high enough, which naturally
reduces the noisy attention information caused by the inter-class
indistinction. The proposed HA module is robust to the variance of input and
can be flexibly inserted into the existing convolution neural networks. We
conduct experiments on three medical image segmentation tasks including optic
disc/cup segmentation, blood vessel segmentation, and lung segmentation.
Extensive results show our method is more effective and robust than the
existing state-of-the-art methods.

Over the past few years, deep learning techniques have achieved tremendous
success in many visual understanding tasks such as object detection, image
segmentation, and caption generation. Despite this thriving in computer vision
and natural language processing, deep learning has not yet shown significant
impact in robotics. Due to the gap between theory and application, there are
many challenges when applying the results of deep learning to the real robotic
systems. In this study, our long-term goal is to bridge the gap between
computer vision and robotics by developing visual methods that can be used in
real robots. In particular, this work tackles two fundamental visual problems
for autonomous robotic manipulation: affordance detection and fine-grained
action understanding. Theoretically, we propose different deep architectures to
further improves the state of the art in each problem. Empirically, we show
that the outcomes of our proposed methods can be applied in real robots and
allow them to perform useful manipulation tasks.

In this paper we come back to a problem proposed by F. Hirzebruch in the
1980's, namely whether there exists a configuration of smooth conics in the
complex projective plane such that the associated desingularization of the
Kummer extension is a ball quotient. We extend our considerations to the
so-called $d$-configurations of curves on the projective plane and we show that
in most cases for a given configuration the associated desingularization of the
Kummer extension is not a ball quotient. Moreover, we provide improved versions
of Hirzebruch-type inequality for $d$-configurations. Finally, we show that the
so-called characteristic numbers (or $\gamma$ numbers) for $d$-configurations
are bounded from above by $8/3$. At the end of the paper we give some examples
of surfaces constructed via Kummer extensions branched along conic
configurations.

The self-configuration capability of SCFIS makes it a robust and versatile tool for image segmentation tasks, reducing the need for manual parameter tuning and increasing its applicability in real-world applications.

This paper aims to analyze the logical strength of Büchi's decidability theorem by examining its proof and its implications on the expressive power of finite automata. We show that the theorem can be seen as a combination of several weaker results, each with its own limitations, and that the combination of these results is necessary to obtain the full strength of the theorem. We also discuss how the theorem can be applied to other formalisms, such as pushdown automata and alternating automata, and how it can be used to prove the decidability of other problems in computational complexity. Overall, our analysis provides a deeper understanding of the logical strength of Büchi's decidability theorem and its role in the study of formal languages and automata theory.

The separation of intensity and warping effects enables the extraction of meaningful information from the images, such as the detection of subtle changes in the image intensity, and the quantification of the warping effects. This work has important applications in various fields such as computer vision, image processing, and medical imaging.

The Strong Monogamy Conjecture states that the total quantum correlation between three qubits cannot exceed a certain bound. In this paper, we investigate the Strong Monogamy Conjecture in a four-qubit system and provide evidence that the conjecture holds true in this case. We use a combination of analytical and numerical methods to calculate the quantum correlations between the qubits and show that the total quantum correlation remains below the bound predicted by the conjecture. Our findings provide insight into the nature of quantum correlations in multi-qubit systems and have implications for quantum information processing and quantum cryptography.

Automatic extraction of liver and tumor from CT volumes is a challenging task
due to their heterogeneous and diffusive shapes. Recently, 2D and 3D deep
convolutional neural networks have become popular in medical image segmentation
tasks because of the utilization of large labeled datasets to learn
hierarchical features. However, 3D networks have some drawbacks due to their
high cost on computational resources. In this paper, we propose a 3D hybrid
residual attention-aware segmentation method, named RA-UNet, to precisely
extract the liver volume of interests (VOI) and segment tumors from the liver
VOI. The proposed network has a basic architecture as a 3D U-Net which extracts
contextual information combining low-level feature maps with high-level ones.
Attention modules are stacked so that the attention-aware features change
adaptively as the network goes "very deep" and this is made possible by
residual learning. This is the first work that an attention residual mechanism
is used to process medical volumetric images. We evaluated our framework on the
public MICCAI 2017 Liver Tumor Segmentation dataset and the 3DIRCADb dataset.
The results show that our architecture outperforms other state-of-the-art
methods. We also extend our RA-UNet to brain tumor segmentation on the
BraTS2018 and BraTS2017 datasets, and the results indicate that RA-UNet
achieves good performance on a brain tumor segmentation task as well.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to semantic segmentation using the transformer architecture. Traditional methods rely on fully convolutional networks (FCNs) that suffer from limited receptive field and inability to model long-range dependencies. Our proposed method, called Segmenter, leverages the self-attention mechanism of transformers to overcome these limitations and achieve state-of-the-art performance on several benchmark datasets.

We begin by introducing our dataset preparation process, which includes data augmentation techniques and a new semi-supervised learning framework that enables us to train on large amounts of unlabelled data. Next, we outline the architecture of Segmenter, consisting of a multi-layer encoder and decoder with attention mechanisms. We also introduce a novel technique called Spatial Attention Masking (SAM), which allows the model to focus on relevant regions and reduce computational complexity.

Our experimental results show that Segmenter outperforms FCNs on multiple datasets including Cityscapes, PASCAL VOC, and CamVid. Specifically, we achieve an increase of +4.3% mIoU on Cityscapes and +5.1% mIoU on CamVid compared to the baseline FCN model. Additionally, we provide extensive ablation studies to demonstrate the effectiveness of SAM and other key components of Segmenter.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

* We introduce Segmenter, a transformer-based architecture for semantic segmentation that models long-range dependencies and outperforms traditional FCNs.
* We develop a novel technique called Spatial Attention Masking (SAM) to improve efficiency and accuracy.
* We establish new state-of-the-art performances on several benchmark datasets, including Cityscapes, PASCAL VOC, and CamVid.

Overall, this work demonstrates the potential of transformers in computer vision tasks, particularly in semantic segmentation where long-range dependencies are crucial.

We begin by introducing the basic concepts and definitions of quantum circuits and Spin(3n) groups, and discussing their relevance to quantum mechanics and quantum information. Our main result is the construction of a faithful representation of Spin(3n) groups on the space of quantum states, which allows us to study the properties of these groups in the context of quantum mechanics. We show that this representation is equivalent to the usual representation of Spin(3n) groups on the space of spinors, but provides a new and useful perspective on the behavior of quantum systems.

We also discuss the implications of our results for the study of quantum information and quantum computing, and suggest directions for future research. We studied the upper bounds on global warming due to CO2 and its effect at each wavelength of UV radiation with respect to water vapor. The global surface temperature over land was modelled by climate simulations based upon historical land surface observations until about 1980, when satellite measurements were introduced. Temperature variations were then correlated with altitude in space as well as surface gravity gradient (or topography). By correlating time series models and satellites to an altitude data set we can obtain the height that one might expect if there had indeed been no evaporation or transfer of heat to the air above the earth (which is not the case because surface energy transfer occurs), i.e., our measure of vertical greenhouse gas absorption on Earth by greenhouse gases (also called greenhouse effect) is similar to the standard measure based only on atmospheric radiation, including radiative forcing from the Sun. Moreover, even accounting for this natural increase over centuries through raindrop activity this measure still agrees extremely well with recent estimates of atmospheric radiative impact of sunlight. We consider the Longest Queue Drop memory management policy in shared-memory
switches consisting of $N$ output ports. The shared memory of size $M\geq N$
may have an arbitrary number of input ports. Each packet may be admitted by any
incoming port, but must be destined to a specific output port and each output
port may be used by only one queue. The Longest Queue Drop policy is a natural
online strategy used in directing the packet flow in buffering problems.
According to this policy and assuming unit packet values and cost of
transmission, every incoming packet is accepted, whereas if the shared memory
becomes full, one or more packets belonging to the longest queue are preempted,
in order to make space for the newly arrived packets. It was proved in 2001
[Hahne et al., SPAA '01] that the Longest Queue Drop policy is 2-competitive
and at least $\sqrt{2}$-competitive. It remained an open question whether a
(2-\epsilon) upper bound for the competitive ratio of this policy could be
shown, for any positive constant \epsilon. We show that the Longest Queue Drop
online policy is 1.5-competitive.

In this work, we propose an adaptation mechanism to segment medical images at scale by learning from past image distributions and by adapting to new data based on multiple optimization procedures and statistical algorithms. Our framework provides novel results in both classification and regression problems. We implemented our framework using a generative adversarial network with two hidden layers (CNN/HDFN layer). The second hidden layer performs a simple feature selection process, which we called adaptive model learning technique (AML), over two categories based on previous training data samples. For each category, it learns the best parameters that maximize accuracy when applied on new training data sample, and selects the weights that minimize error loss to infer the target class label given the original data set (shown in Fig 2 ). After applying AML with new training data, we evaluated the performance through experimental validation (Fig 3 ) based on one classification problem that captures all three main aspects needed in practice. One classification problem, which relies on four predictors (a measure of shape, color distance, surface normal, density) was chosen because its complexity is easy to parallelize and test our approach against. This task could be performed at scale in large populations as well as by a single machine by combining several models into larger units. Interestingly, our overall average score increased linearly across all categories, indicating that the ability to make more advanced distinctions between species as they are identified was retained via AML even with relatively small amount of data augmentation.

In this paper, we investigate the multimodal transition and excitability of a neural oscillator using a combination of analytical and numerical techniques. Our study focuses on a paradigmatic model of neuronal activity, the Wilson-Cowan oscillator, which exhibits slow and fast oscillations in response to external stimuli.

We first derive an analytical solution for the steady-state behavior of the oscillator as a function of the coupling strength between its components, revealing a rich phase diagram that includes regions of multistability and resonance. We then perform a linear stability analysis around each stable steady state, demonstrating how the emergence of unstable modes can lead to transitions between different dynamical regimes.

Using numerical simulations, we explore the nonlinear regime of the oscillator and demonstrate the existence of a threshold for the onset of spiking activity, below which the system remains quiescent. Above this threshold, we identify multiple dynamical regimes, including periodic and chaotic states, and assess their dependence on the model parameters.

Our results shed light on the role of multimodality in the dynamics of neural oscillators and provide insights into mechanisms underlying the generation of complex spatiotemporal patterns in neural systems. The findings also have implications for our understanding of the neural code and suggest strategies for controlling and manipulating neural activity through external Stimulation.

High resolution urban spatial information has been an absolute challenge in many fields including image and speech recognition, mapping, geospatial analysis, surveillance, location based services, disaster management and social robotics, among others. While both natural language processing (NLP) and NGS use methods that generate dense temporal data sets, these computational approaches tend to rely on hierarchical models with a great deal of domain specific training data. In this paper, we propose a novel approach at building robust neural networks by combining local spatial context to maximize generalization efficiency via hybrid reconstruction algorithms [6,10]. Our algorithm starts by learning an initial global grid state as input to model all images in an annotated dataset. The purpose of the second layer is to re-train an unsupervised version of the network using a locally oriented dataset as global reference frame, which it uses to predict future images [11]. The local orientation is achieved since we choose the nearest pixel value along the direction of interest; the optimal solution can be determined given our global reference grid. This design enables rapid convergence between our global prediction results during offline training as well as their use to improve the quality and accuracy of subsequent inference/model selection tasks offline. Additionally, this process reduces overfitting bias significantly [4,10] while avoiding overgeneralization errors due to sparse data. We also demonstrate an improvement on the current state of the art at learning multiple different local orientations simultaneously, demonstrating higher performance than traditional approaches [12]. Thus our hybrid system demonstrates better flexibility with flexible architecture. It represents a new paradigm change where the goal was to learn a hierarchical structure without having to train additional classes or back-propagator steps. We introduce a dynamic mechanism design problem in which the designer wants
to offer for sale an item to an agent, and another item to the same agent at
some point in the future. The agent's joint distribution of valuations for the
two items is known, and the agent knows the valuation for the current item (but
not for the one in the future). The designer seeks to maximize expected
revenue, and the auction must be deterministic, truthful, and ex post
individually rational. The optimum mechanism involves a protocol whereby the
seller elicits the buyer's current valuation, and based on the bid makes two
take-it-or-leave-it offers, one for now and one for the future. We show that
finding the optimum deterministic mechanism in this situation - arguably the
simplest meaningful dynamic mechanism design problem imaginable - is NP-hard.
We also prove several positive results, among them a polynomial linear
programming-based algorithm for the optimum randomized auction (even for many
bidders and periods), and we show strong separations in revenue between
non-adaptive, adaptive, and randomized auctions, even when the valuations in
the two periods are uncorrelated. Finally, for the same problem in an
environment in which contracts cannot be enforced, and thus perfection of
equilibrium is necessary, we show that the optimum randomized mechanism
requires multiple rounds of cheap talk-like interactions.

Clustering is an important facet of explorative data mining and finds
extensive use in several fields. In this paper, we propose an extension of the
classical Fuzzy C-Means clustering algorithm. The proposed algorithm,
abbreviated as VFC, adopts a multi-dimensional membership vector for each data
point instead of the traditional, scalar membership value defined in the
original algorithm. The membership vector for each point is obtained by
considering each feature of that point separately and obtaining individual
membership values for the same. We also propose an algorithm to efficiently
allocate the initial cluster centers close to the actual centers, so as to
facilitate rapid convergence. Further, we propose a scheme to achieve crisp
clustering using the VFC algorithm. The proposed, novel clustering scheme has
been tested on two standard data sets in order to analyze its performance. We
also examine the efficacy of the proposed scheme by analyzing its performance
on image segmentation examples and comparing it with the classical Fuzzy
C-means clustering algorithm.

In this paper, we investigate the potential of multiuser diversity for secrecy communications in the presence of an opportunistic jammer. We propose a novel approach that leverages opportunistic jammer selection to enhance the security of wireless communication systems. Our approach maximizes the secure degrees of freedom (DoF) and unveils a scaling law for jammer deployment.

We first model the system as a multiple-input single-output broadcast channel with an external eavesdropper and an internal jammers' network. We then introduce a new notion of "jammer-induced interference" and show how it can be exploited to degrade the eavesdropper's performance. By optimizing the placement and transmission powers of the jammers, our scheme achieves a higher level of security compared to traditional jamming strategies.

Our results demonstrate that the proposed approach attains a substantial increase in secure DoF, especially when the number of jammers is large. Moreover, we show that the optimal jammer density scales optimally with the number of active users, which has significant implications for practical system design.

The main contributions of this work are:

1. A novel approach to securing wireless communications using opportunistic jammer selection.
2. An analytical framework for computing the secure DoF and jammer scaling law.
3. Numerical results illustrating the effectiveness of our approach against various jamming strategies.

These findings have far-reaching consequences for the design of robust and reliable wireless networks, particularly those operating in hostile environments where security is paramount.

Longitudinal reproducibility is an essential concern in automated medical
image segmentation, yet has proven to be an elusive objective as manual brain
structure tracings have shown more than 10% variability. To improve
reproducibility, lon-gitudinal segmentation (4D) approaches have been
investigated to reconcile tem-poral variations with traditional 3D approaches.
In the past decade, multi-atlas la-bel fusion has become a state-of-the-art
segmentation technique for 3D image and many efforts have been made to adapt it
to a 4D longitudinal fashion. However, the previous methods were either limited
by using application specified energy function (e.g., surface fusion and multi
model fusion) or only considered tem-poral smoothness on two consecutive time
points (t and t+1) under sparsity as-sumption. Therefore, a 4D multi-atlas
label fusion theory for general label fusion purpose and simultaneously
considering temporal consistency on all time points is appealing. Herein, we
propose a novel longitudinal label fusion algorithm, called 4D joint label
fusion (4DJLF), to incorporate the temporal consistency modeling via non-local
patch-intensity covariance models. The advantages of 4DJLF include: (1) 4DJLF
is under the general label fusion framework by simul-taneously incorporating
the spatial and temporal covariance on all longitudinal time points. (2) The
proposed algorithm is a longitudinal generalization of a lead-ing joint label
fusion method (JLF) that has proven adaptable to a wide variety of
applications. (3) The spatial temporal consistency of atlases is modeled in a
prob-abilistic model inspired from both voting based and statistical fusion.
The pro-posed approach improves the consistency of the longitudinal
segmentation while retaining sensitivity compared with original JLF approach
using the same set of atlases. The method is available online in open-source.

most of the known non-vanishing results for the derivatives of the Riemann zeta
function by establishing the existence of an infinite sequence of regions in
the right half-plane where these derivatives cannot have any zeros; and then,
in the rare regions of the complex plane that do contain zeros of the k-th
derivative of the zeta function, we describe a unexpected phenomenon, which

In this paper, we present a systematic approach for evaluating the suitability of different measures of quantum correlations in various scenarios. Quantum correlations are a fundamental aspect of quantum mechanics and have been found to play a crucial role in various quantum information processing tasks. However, there is no universally accepted measure of quantum correlations, and different measures have been proposed in different contexts.

We identify several desirable criteria that a measure of quantum correlations should satisfy, including:

1. Non-negativity: The measure should be non-negative and zero only for completely uncorrelated states.
2. Symmetry: The measure should be symmetric under the exchange of the systems being correlated.
3. Additivity: The measure should be additive over independent subsystems.
4. Scalability: The measure should be scalable to larger systems.
5. Normalization: The measure should be normalized to a maximum value that represents the maximum possible correlation.
6. Consistency: The measure should be consistent with the quantum mechanical description of correlations.

We evaluate several commonly used measures of quantum correlations, including entanglement entropy, mutual information, and Bell violation, against these criteria. We find that each measure satisfies some but not all of the criteria, and that there is no single measure that satisfies all the criteria in all scenarios.

We also discuss the implications of our results for the study of quantum correlations and the development of quantum information processing protocols. We show that the choice of measure can significantly affect the results of quantum information processing tasks, and that a careful choice of measure can lead to more efficient and robust protocols.

Our work provides a framework for evaluating and understanding the properties of different measures of quantum correlations, and can guide the development of new measures that are better suited to specific applications.

Accurate medical image segmentation is essential for diagnosis, surgical
planning and many other applications. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have
become the state-of-the-art automatic segmentation methods. However, fully
automatic results may still need to be refined to become accurate and robust
enough for clinical use. We propose a deep learning-based interactive
segmentation method to improve the results obtained by an automatic CNN and to
reduce user interactions during refinement for higher accuracy. We use one CNN
to obtain an initial automatic segmentation, on which user interactions are
added to indicate mis-segmentations. Another CNN takes as input the user
interactions with the initial segmentation and gives a refined result. We
propose to combine user interactions with CNNs through geodesic distance
transforms, and propose a resolution-preserving network that gives a better
dense prediction. In addition, we integrate user interactions as hard
constraints into a back-propagatable Conditional Random Field. We validated the
proposed framework in the context of 2D placenta segmentation from fetal MRI
and 3D brain tumor segmentation from FLAIR images. Experimental results show
our method achieves a large improvement from automatic CNNs, and obtains
comparable and even higher accuracy with fewer user interventions and less time
compared with traditional interactive methods.

Myocardial contrast echocardiography (MCE) is an imaging technique that
assesses left ventricle function and myocardial perfusion for the detection of
coronary artery diseases. Automatic MCE perfusion quantification is challenging
and requires accurate segmentation of the myocardium from noisy and
time-varying images. Random forests (RF) have been successfully applied to many
medical image segmentation tasks. However, the pixel-wise RF classifier ignores
contextual relationships between label outputs of individual pixels. RF which
only utilizes local appearance features is also susceptible to data suffering
from large intensity variations. In this paper, we demonstrate how to overcome
the above limitations of classic RF by presenting a fully automatic
segmentation pipeline for myocardial segmentation in full-cycle 2D MCE data.
Specifically, a statistical shape model is used to provide shape prior
information that guide the RF segmentation in two ways. First, a novel shape
model (SM) feature is incorporated into the RF framework to generate a more
accurate RF probability map. Second, the shape model is fitted to the RF
probability map to refine and constrain the final segmentation to plausible
myocardial shapes. We further improve the performance by introducing a bounding
box detection algorithm as a preprocessing step in the segmentation pipeline.
Our approach on 2D image is further extended to 2D+t sequence which ensures
temporal consistency in the resultant sequence segmentations. When evaluated on
clinical MCE data, our proposed method achieves notable improvement in
segmentation accuracy and outperforms other state-of-the-art methods including
the classic RF and its variants, active shape model and image registration.

We then use this information to generate a photorealistic image of the vehicle that appears naturally integrated with its surroundings.

Our approach consists of three main stages: surroundings analysis, vehicle segmentation, and image synthesis. In the first stage, we use a deep neural network to analyze the surroundings of the vehicle and extract relevant features such as road texture, lighting, and object detection. In the second stage, we segment the vehicle from the rest of the image using a instance segmentation algorithm, allowing us to focus on the vehicle and its immediate surroundings. Finally, in the third stage, we use a generative adversarial network (GAN) to synthesize a realistic image of the vehicle that takes into account the extracted surroundings features and the vehicle's segmentation mask.

We evaluate our method on a large dataset of real-world images and demonstrate its effectiveness in generating high-quality vehicle images that accurately reflect the surrounding environment. Our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of image quality and computational efficiency, making it a promising solution for a wide range of applications such as virtual try-on, vehicle rendering, and autonomous driving.

In this paper, we explore the concept of generalized trees and provide both algebraic and logical descriptions of these structures. Generalized trees are a natural generalization of trees, allowing for the representation of more complex and diverse structures, such as networks and hierarchies.

Our algebraic description of generalized trees is based on the use of a novel algebraic structure, called a "tree algebra," which encodes the structure of a generalized tree in a compact and efficient way. We show that tree algebras can be used to represent a wide range of generalized trees, including those with multiple parents, siblings, and children, as well as those with cycles and other non-tree-like structures. We also demonstrate how tree algebras can be used to perform queries and computations on generalized trees, making them a useful tool for a variety of applications.

In addition to our algebraic description, we also provide a logical description of generalized trees using description logic. Description logic is a formalism for representing and reasoning about ontologies and other knowledge representations, and it provides a natural way to describe the structure and properties of generalized trees. We show how description logic can be used to define and reason about generalized trees, and how it can be used to express queries and constraints on these structures.

Our work provides a new and powerful way to represent and reason about generalized trees, and it has a wide range of applications in fields such as computer science, biology, and social network analysis. The algebraic and logical descriptions we provide can be used independently or in combination, depending on the specific needs of the application. Overall, our work provides a significant contribution to the field of generalized trees and their applications.

This academic paper presents a verification of the Nernst theorem for the Casimir-Lifshitz free energy. The Nernst theorem is a fundamental result in thermodynamics that relates the change in entropy of a system to the heat exchanged with its surroundings. The Casimir-Lifshitz free energy is a quantum mechanical effect that arises due to fluctuations in the electromagnetic field. The paper discusses the mathematical derivation of the Nernst theorem for the Casimir-Lifshitz free energy and presents numerical results that confirm the validity of the theorem. The findings of this study have important implications for the understanding of quantum thermodynamics and the Casimir effect.

We introduce publicly available and computationally efficient automatic reconstructions. These reconstructions are driven by user-initiated data flows. They contain no source code or hardware information and hence cannot be altered easily by hostile parties. Moreover, these recoveries do not require external input. This makes them very attractive because they are safe, anonymous, fast, reliable and low-latency. Users can even make open use of each reconstruction freely if they so wish (i.e., without any central control). Each reconstructed entity may have its own associated name using a unique string such as an unencrypted password that the user generates before performing the reconfiguration event. Hence user privacy remains intact. A single reconstruction performs several actions and we propose our system architecture with the intent of facilitating multiple reconstructions. Such an architecture eliminates problems related to the current state of the art. For instance, it enables users to have simultaneous open and closed reconstructions without breaking out of the common interface. Furthermore, we provide a simple way of implementing some core operations on reconstructed entities, such as deletion, search etc. These new capabilities will likely make open-set re-identifications safer, less expensive and less error prone than previous approaches based exclusively on closed sets of targets.

In this paper, we present a novel approach to solving fluid-structure systems with thermal fluctuations using spatially adaptive stochastic multigrid methods. Fluid-structure systems are critical in various engineering and scientific applications, such as ocean and atmospheric flows, blood flow, and turbulent flows. However, their simulation is challenging due to the complex interactions between the fluid and structure, particularly when thermal fluctuations are considered.

To address these challenges, we propose a spatially adaptive stochastic multigrid method that leverages recent advances in uncertainty quantification, numerical analysis, and computational algorithms. The proposed method combines the strengths of stochastic Galerkin methods, which model the thermal fluctuations via random perturbations, with the efficiency of adaptive multi grid methods, which concentrate computational resources where they are most needed.

The key feature of our approach is the use of a spatial adaptation strategy based on error estimators to simultaneously resolve the large gradients in the solution and optimize computational resources. This allows us to effectively capture the physics of the problem while minimizing computational costs. We demonstrate the performance and accuracy of the proposed method through several case studies of increasing complexity, including coupled heat transfer and fluid dynamics problems. Our results show significant improvements in accuracy and computational efficiency compared to traditional deterministic and stochastic methods.

The main contributions of the paper can be summarized as follows: (1) development of a novel spatially adaptive stochastic multigrid method for solving fluid-structure systems with thermal fluctuations; (2) embedding of the stochastic Galerkin method within the multigrid framework to efficiently solve the resulting large-scale linear systems; (3) introduction of an error estimation technique to guide the spatial adaptation of the mesh refinement; and (4) thorough numerical validation of the proposed method through various benchmark problems.

Our findings have important implications for the efficient and accurate simulation of complex fluid-structure systems with thermal fluctuations. The developed method has far-reaching potential in many fields, including environmental simulations, aircraft design, turbulence modeling, chemical reactions, and biomedical research.

In this paper, we investigate harmonic maps of finite uniton type into inner symmetric spaces. We first establish the existence and uniqueness of such maps, and then proceed to study their properties and characteristics.

We begin by defining the concept of a harmonic map and explaining its relevance to the study of differential geometry and partial differential equations. We then introduce the concept of a uniton, which is a special type of harmonic map that is defined on a simply-connected domain and has a certain type of singularity.

Next, we turn our attention to inner symmetric spaces, which are a class of Riemannian manifolds that have a certain type of symmetry. We explain the definition and properties of inner symmetric spaces, and discuss their importance in differential geometry and physics.

We then state the main result of the paper, which establishes the existence and uniqueness of harmonic maps of finite uniton type into inner symmetric spaces. We prove this result using a combination of geometric and analytic techniques, including the use of differential equations and the study of the properties of harmonic maps.

Finally, we discuss the implications of our result and its applications in various fields, including differential geometry, partial differential equations, and physics. We also suggest directions for future research and open problems in this area.

Overall, this paper provides a significant contribution to the study of harmonic maps and their applications, and will be of interest to researchers in differential geometry, partial differential equations, and related fields.

In this paper, we present a novel approach for isolating relativistic effects in large-scale structure (LSS) observations. The standard model of cosmology is based on general relativity, which predicts that gravitational phenomena should be described by curvatures and distortions of spacetime. However, on large scales, dark matter and dark energy dominate the dynamics, and their behavior can be approximated using simple Newtonian dynamics.

Previous studies have shown that incorporating relativistic corrections into LSS analyses can lead to significant improvements in the accuracy of cosmic parameter estimates. However, a full treatment of relativism in LSS observations is challenging due to the complexity of calculating these corrections over vast distances and high densities.

Our method utilizes techniques from image processing and machine learning to separate relativistic effects from the dominant Newtonian signal in galaxy surveys. By creating a set of filters specifically designed to capture the unique signatures of relativity, we are able to extract the associated signals from the data without needing to knowingly construct complex models of the underlying physics.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our technique using simulations of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS III). Our analysis procedure successfully recovers theoretical expectations for the scale-dependent redshift space distortion kernel, as well as contributions from lensing and Doppler distortions. When applied jointly with standard likelihoods for cosmological parameters, our filter greatly improves constraints on several key parameters, including the neutrino mass scale, spatial flatness, and the equation of state of dark energy.

Overall, this work represents an important step towards better understanding how relativistic corrections affect LSS data. Future surveys will benefit significantly from improved control of such nonlinear effects, allowing us to probe even deeper into the nature of gravity and cosmic evolution.

In this paper, we propose a novel method for estimating the inverse covariance matrix of a multivariate distribution, which we term L0 sparse inverse covariance estimation. This method is based on the idea of using L0 regularization, which is a technique that promotes sparse solutions by adding a penalty term to the objective function that is proportional to the absolute value of the coefficients.

We demonstrate that L0 sparse inverse covariance estimation can be used to estimate the inverse covariance matrix of a multivariate normal distribution, as well as the inverse covariance matrix of a multivariate Student's t-distribution. We show that the proposed method outperforms existing methods in terms of computational efficiency and accuracy, and is particularly useful when the number of variables is large and the sample size is small.

We also explore the theoretical properties of L0 sparse inverse covariance estimation, including its consistency and asymptotic normality. We show that the proposed method is consistent and asymptotically normal, which ensures that it can accurately estimate the inverse covariance matrix in large samples.

Finally, we illustrate the practical application of L0 sparse inverse covariance estimation using real-data examples. We demonstrate that the proposed method can be used to estimate the inverse covariance matrix of a variety of multivariate distributions, including financial returns, gene expression data, and image features.

Overall, this paper makes a significant contribution to the field of statistics and machine learning by introducing a novel method for estimating the inverse covariance matrix that is computationally efficient, accurate, and easy to implement. The proposed method has important applications in various fields, including finance, biology, and computer vision, and is likely to be of interest to researchers and practitioners in these areas.

Food image segmentation is a critical and indispensible task for developing
health-related applications such as estimating food calories and nutrients.
Existing food image segmentation models are underperforming due to two reasons:
(1) there is a lack of high quality food image datasets with fine-grained
ingredient labels and pixel-wise location masks -- the existing datasets either
carry coarse ingredient labels or are small in size; and (2) the complex
appearance of food makes it difficult to localize and recognize ingredients in
food images, e.g., the ingredients may overlap one another in the same image,
and the identical ingredient may appear distinctly in different food images. In
this work, we build a new food image dataset FoodSeg103 (and its extension
FoodSeg154) containing 9,490 images. We annotate these images with 154
ingredient classes and each image has an average of 6 ingredient labels and
pixel-wise masks. In addition, we propose a multi-modality pre-training
approach called ReLeM that explicitly equips a segmentation model with rich and
semantic food knowledge. In experiments, we use three popular semantic
segmentation methods (i.e., Dilated Convolution based, Feature Pyramid based,
and Vision Transformer based) as baselines, and evaluate them as well as ReLeM
on our new datasets. We believe that the FoodSeg103 (and its extension
FoodSeg154) and the pre-trained models using ReLeM can serve as a benchmark to
facilitate future works on fine-grained food image understanding. We make all
these datasets and methods public at
\url{https://xiongweiwu.github.io/foodseg103.html}.

This paper formulates an inverse power flow problem which is to infer a nodal
admittance matrix (hence the network structure of a power system) from voltage
and current phasors measured at a number of buses. We show that the admittance
matrix can be uniquely identified from a sequence of measurements corresponding
to different steady states when every node in the system is equipped with a
measurement device, and a Kron-reduced admittance matrix can be determined even
if some nodes in the system are not monitored (hidden nodes). Furthermore, we
propose effective algorithms based on graph theory to uncover the actual
admittance matrix of radial systems with hidden nodes. We provide theoretical
guarantees for the recovered admittance matrix and demonstrate that the actual
admittance matrix can be fully recovered even from the Kron-reduced admittance
matrix under some mild assumptions. Simulations on standard test systems
confirm that these algorithms are capable of providing accurate estimates of
the admittance matrix from noisy sensor data.

In addition to being a functional machine model it produces general representations of a scene (e.g., pose or activity), that can then provide useful information about the observed changes (e.g., brightness), to classify new frames of an images. Introduction There has been much hype around machine learning as an alternative to traditional approaches, and in particular we see semantic segmentation as something that will help solve some key open problems in natural language processing in general. It may be very useful to improve our understanding of how language works and what it could reveal about the human mind, not only in health sciences but also in fields like e-commerce and robotics. In this post, I focus on how meta-learning approaches can address many of these issues, by providing flexible mechanisms to compute the structure of arbitrary objects so that different machine learning methods converge over these structural characteristics together on a final structure which best explains the data. While there are several existing tools already available for applying various type of graph based classification techniques for the problem (namely GraphLab[1] ), these tools are typically used just to detect features and do no attempt at automatically constructing semantic features between related data components. This means that they require knowledge of what types of relationships exist between the items within the set. To make a specific example from a research field we're studying here: Automatic Grammatical Identification. Our project at NYU School of Medicine involves a novel method of parsing words in spoken or written documents via hierarchical probabilistic models based on a variety of prior assumptions about their interrelationships among themselves. These prior relations form a large portion of our training sets in a given session, making interpretation easy. However, some prior relationships fail to hold when dealing with high dimensional word space. We needed some way to recover these missing information without having to reclassify the entire dataset each time we ran an experiment of this sort. If the data was completely structured by default then one task would simply be to derive the relevant probabilities from the model. Such inference would happen across all words with higher or lower probability than expected for those word classes, yielding a more meaningful result than trying to work through the whole dataset. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to image segmentation that leverages the power of meta-learning to learn effective initializations for segmentation models. Our approach, called Meta-Learning Initializations for Image Segmentation (MLIS), is designed to improve the efficiency and accuracy of image segmentation tasks by learning a good initialization for the segmentation model, which can be fine-tuned for a specific task with only a few training examples.

Existing image segmentation methods typically require a large amount of labeled training data to achieve good performance. However, obtaining high-quality labels for medical images can be time-consuming and expensive. In contrast, our MLIS approach learns a good initialization for the segmentation model from a set of related tasks, which can be easily obtained from publicly available datasets. This enables the segmentation model to learn quickly and accurately for a specific task with only a few training examples.

We evaluate the performance of MLIS on several medical image segmentation tasks, including brain tumor segmentation, liver segmentation, and lung segmentation. The results show that MLIS outperforms traditional image segmentation methods, including fully supervised models and transfer learning-based methods, in terms of both accuracy and efficiency. Specifically, MLIS achieves an average segmentation accuracy of 95.2% on the brain tumor segmentation task with only 10 training examples, outperforming the next best method by 12.8%.

Our analysis shows that the learned initialization from MLIS captures important features that are useful for image segmentation, such as edges, textures, and shapes. We also demonstrate that the learned initialization can be used to improve the performance of other segmentation models, such as U-Net and FCN.

Our work has important implications for medical image segmentation, where obtaining large amounts of labeled data can be challenging. By leveraging the power of meta-learning, MLIS provides a promising solution to improve the efficiency and accuracy of image segmentation tasks, which can be applied to a wide range of medical applications.

The CNN-based methods have achieved impressive results in medical image
segmentation, but it failed to capture the long-range dependencies due to the
inherent locality of convolution operation. Transformer-based methods are
popular in vision tasks recently because of its capacity of long-range
dependencies and get a promising performance. However, it lacks in modeling
local context, although some works attempted to embed convolutional layer to
overcome this problem and achieved some improvement, but it makes the feature
inconsistent and fails to leverage the natural multi-scale features of
hierarchical transformer, which limit the performance of models. In this paper,
taking medical image segmentation as an example, we present MISSFormer, an
effective and powerful Medical Image Segmentation tranSFormer. MISSFormer is a
hierarchical encoder-decoder network and has two appealing designs: 1) A feed
forward network is redesigned with the proposed Enhanced Transformer Block,
which makes features aligned adaptively and enhances the long-range
dependencies and local context. 2) We proposed Enhanced Transformer Context
Bridge, a context bridge with the enhanced transformer block to model the
long-range dependencies and local context of multi-scale features generated by
our hierarchical transformer encoder. Driven by these two designs, the
MISSFormer shows strong capacity to capture more valuable dependencies and
context in medical image segmentation. The experiments on multi-organ and
cardiac segmentation tasks demonstrate the superiority, effectiveness and
robustness of our MISSFormer, the exprimental results of MISSFormer trained
from scratch even outperforms state-of-the-art methods pretrained on ImageNet,
and the core designs can be generalized to other visual segmentation tasks. The
code will be released in Github.

In this paper, we introduce a simple, yet powerful pipeline for medical image
segmentation that combines Fully Convolutional Networks (FCNs) with Fully
Convolutional Residual Networks (FC-ResNets). We propose and examine a design
that takes particular advantage of recent advances in the understanding of both
Convolutional Neural Networks as well as ResNets. Our approach focuses upon the
importance of a trainable pre-processing when using FC-ResNets and we show that
a low-capacity FCN model can serve as a pre-processor to normalize medical
input data. In our image segmentation pipeline, we use FCNs to obtain
normalized images, which are then iteratively refined by means of a FC-ResNet
to generate a segmentation prediction. As in other fully convolutional
approaches, our pipeline can be used off-the-shelf on different image
modalities. We show that using this pipeline, we exhibit state-of-the-art
performance on the challenging Electron Microscopy benchmark, when compared to
other 2D methods. We improve segmentation results on CT images of liver
lesions, when contrasting with standard FCN methods. Moreover, when applying
our 2D pipeline on a challenging 3D MRI prostate segmentation challenge we
reach results that are competitive even when compared to 3D methods. The
obtained results illustrate the strong potential and versatility of the
pipeline by achieving highly accurate results on multi-modality images from
different anatomical regions and organs.

In this paper, we present a novel bound on genuine multipartite correlations, which is derived from the principle of information causality. Genuine multipartite correlations refer to the correlations that cannot be explained by any local hidden variable models, and are considered a fundamental resource in quantum information processing tasks such as quantum communication and computation. The bound we derive is based on the idea that the total amount of information that can be transmitted between different parties in a network cannot exceed the total amount of information that is available in the system. We show that this bound can be used to quantify the maximum amount of genuine multipartite correlation that can exist in a given scenario, and can be applied to various types of networks and scenarios, including those with multiple sources of randomness. Our results have important implications for the study of quantum non-locality and the foundations of quantum mechanics, and provide new insights into the power and limitations of quantum communication and computation.

The paper "Computing Valid p-values for Image Segmentation by Selective Inference" presents a novel approach to computing valid p-values for image segmentation techniques. Traditional methods of evaluating segmentation algorithms rely on arbitrarily defined thresholds or subjective visual inspection, which can lead to inconsistent and unreliable results.

In this work, we propose a method based on selective inference that allows for the computation of valid p-values for image segmentation. Our approach leverages recent advances in statistical inference and machine learning to provide a principled way of evaluating the significance of segmentation results. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through experiments on several benchmark datasets, where we show that it provides more accurate and robust assessments of segmentation performance compared to traditional methods.

The key contribution of this paper is the introduction of a new evaluation framework for image segmentation that is grounded in statistical hypothesis testing. By treating segmentation as a hypothesis test, we can compute p-values that indicate the probability that the observed segmentation result occurred by chance. This allows us to quantify the uncertainty in segmentation results and provides a meaningful way to compare the performance of different algorithms.

Our proposed method has important implications for the field of image segmentation, as it enables researchers to evaluate and compare segmentation algorithms in a more objective and reliable manner. It also opens up new avenues for future research, such as investigating the relationship between segmentation performance and underlying factors like image quality or object size. Overall, this work represents an important step towards developing a more rigorous understanding of image segmentation and its limitations.

Abstract The results of this study are presented to investigate whether a computational model based on spatial location could be used to represent the information in cross-modal progressive comprehension (CTP) tasks, one such example being that of referring language referred and categorized by reference words and phonemes with respect to an object. An approach involving using statistical learning methods rather than conventional regression methods had been proposed previously for CTP-like problems [1], but these types of methods have not yet been empirically applied. A hierarchical decision procedure is employed instead to determine which stimulus components provide the highest probability of representing the target word type during a given trial block, while simultaneously accounting for the effects of other elements in task configuration, context, and difficulty. Our preliminary evaluation suggests our method provides efficient representation of cue combinations over the whole set of trial blocks without sacrificing power or accuracy. As we progress further into implementation of our technique it should also prove possible to obtain higher accuracy/power across the different stages of the problem solving process where it may be most optimal. Additionally, it may prove easier to implement and learn our approach due to its modular structure, which allows simultaneous selection of features as needed at specific periods and phases of task design. Although we did not apply the approaches shown above in a real-life task and only simulated models were evaluated herein, much more work needs to be done before it can be considered for use directly as a practice aid. However, there is no immediate practical obstacle in attempting to incorporate this toolbox within existing CTP systems currently utilized by the profession.

This paper proposes a novel approach to remote sensing imagery semantic segmentation, called boundary loss. The proposed method is designed to improve the accuracy of semantic segmentation models by leveraging the information from object boundaries in remote sensing images.

Existing methods for remote sensing imagery semantic segmentation mainly focus on using fully convolutional networks (FCNs) or encoder-decoder architectures, which often produce blurry or incomplete segmentation results due to the lack of explicit boundary information. In contrast, this work introduces a new boundary loss function that incorporates the spatial and spectral information of object boundaries into the training process.

The proposed boundary loss function consists of two components: a boundary detection term and a boundary consistency term. The boundary detection term encourages the model to predict accurate boundaries between different objects or land cover classes while considering both local and global contextual information. Meanwhile, the boundary consistency term enforces the model to generate consistent boundary predictions across multiple scales by aggregating multi-scale features with a specially designed hierarchical fusion module.

The effectiveness of the proposed boundary loss was evaluated using several benchmark datasets including PASCAL VOC dataset, Cityscapes dataset, and a large-scale high-resolution remote sensing image dataset. We introduce a new light-field dataset of materials, and take advantage of
the recent success of deep learning to perform material recognition on the 4D
light-field. Our dataset contains 12 material categories, each with 100 images
taken with a Lytro Illum, from which we extract about 30,000 patches in total.

information in a light-field (such as multiple sub-aperture views and
view-dependent reflectance effects) can aid material recognition. Since
recognition networks have not been trained on 4D images before, we propose and
compare several novel CNN architectures to train on light-field images. In our
experiments, the best performing CNN architecture achieves a 7% boost compared
with 2D image classification (70% to 77%). These results constitute important
baselines that can spur further research in the use of CNNs for light-field
applications. Upon publication, our dataset also enables other novel
applications of light-fields, including object detection, image segmentation

This paper presents an adaptive strategy for superpixel-based region-growing image segmentation. The proposed approach utilizes superpixels to initialize the region-growing process and then adaptively adjusts the size and shape of the growing regions based on the image features and context. The experimental results demonstrate that the adaptive strategy significantly improves the segmentation accuracy and robustness compared to traditional region-growing methods. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have achieved state-of-the-art
performance for automatic medical image segmentation. However, they have not
demonstrated sufficiently accurate and robust results for clinical use. In
addition, they are limited by the lack of image-specific adaptation and the
lack of generalizability to previously unseen object classes. To address these
problems, we propose a novel deep learning-based framework for interactive
segmentation by incorporating CNNs into a bounding box and scribble-based
segmentation pipeline. We propose image-specific fine-tuning to make a CNN
model adaptive to a specific test image, which can be either unsupervised
(without additional user interactions) or supervised (with additional
scribbles). We also propose a weighted loss function considering network and
interaction-based uncertainty for the fine-tuning. We applied this framework to
two applications: 2D segmentation of multiple organs from fetal MR slices,
where only two types of these organs were annotated for training; and 3D
segmentation of brain tumor core (excluding edema) and whole brain tumor
(including edema) from different MR sequences, where only tumor cores in one MR
sequence were annotated for training. Experimental results show that 1) our
model is more robust to segment previously unseen objects than state-of-the-art
CNNs; 2) image-specific fine-tuning with the proposed weighted loss function
significantly improves segmentation accuracy; and 3) our method leads to
accurate results with fewer user interactions and less user time than
traditional interactive segmentation methods.

Superpixel segmentation has become an important research problem in image
processing. In this paper, we propose an Iterative Spanning Forest (ISF)
framework, based on sequences of Image Foresting Transforms, where one can
choose i) a seed sampling strategy, ii) a connectivity function, iii) an
adjacency relation, and iv) a seed pixel recomputation procedure to generate
improved sets of connected superpixels (supervoxels in 3D) per iteration. The
superpixels in ISF structurally correspond to spanning trees rooted at those
seeds. We present five ISF methods to illustrate different choices of its
components. These methods are compared with approaches from the
state-of-the-art in effectiveness and efficiency. The experiments involve 2D
and 3D datasets with distinct characteristics, and a high level application,
named sky image segmentation. The theoretical properties of ISF are
demonstrated in the supplementary material and the results show that some of
its methods are competitive with or superior to the best baselines in
effectiveness and efficiency.
