an end-to-end text detection strategy combining a segmentation algorithm and an
ensemble of multiple text detectors of different types to detect text in every
individual image segments independently. The proposed strategy involves a
super-pixel based image segmenter which splits an image into multiple regions.

This paper proposes a novel approach to food image segmentation, which is a fundamental step in various applications such as nutrition analysis, meal planning, and food recognition. Existing methods for food image segmentation primarily rely on class-specific models that are trained on individual classes (e.g., rice, meat, vegetables) separately, resulting in limited generalization ability to unseen classes or variations in cooking styles.

In this work, we introduce a saliency-aware class-agnostic food image segmentation method that simultaneously separates all present classes in an image without requiring explicit classification. Our approach leverages a self-paced learning strategy that gradually refines the model's sensitivity to different levels of salient features. The core idea is to iteratively identify and emphasize the most discriminative regions within each image while suppressing less relevant areas. By doing so, our model can efficiently capture intrinsic structures among diverse food categories and handle occlusions, clutters, and uneven illumination.

Extensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art class-agnostic segmentation methods and even surpasses class-specific models in certain cases. Notably, it shows superior performance when dealing with low-quality images, manifesting its robustness and versatility. We also perform a thorough ablation study and visual analysis to provide insights into the effectiveness of our design choices.

The main contributions of this paper are:

1. A novel class-agnostic food image segmentation approach based on saliency awareness.
2. An effective self-paced learning framework to adaptively highlight informative features.
3. State-of-the-art performance on several benchmark datasets.
4. Demonstrated robustness against adversarial scenarios and realistic application scenarios like meal planning and dietary assessment.

This work has significant implications for expanding the scope of computer vision applications related to food, promoting healthy eating habits, and streamlining food-related industries.

Crop and weeds detection is a crucial task in agriculture, as it enables farmers to identify areas where weeds are competing with crops for resources and take appropriate action to control their spread. However, manual detection is time-consuming and labor-intensive, leading to a need for automated methods. In this paper, we propose a novel approach for fast and accurate crop and weeds detection using automatic model-based dataset generation. Our approach leverages a combination of machine learning algorithms and image processing techniques to generate a large dataset of labeled images, which are then used to train a deep learning model for crop and weeds detection.

We evaluate the performance of our approach using a variety of metrics and compare it to traditional manual annotation methods. Our results show that our approach achieves higher accuracy and faster processing times than manual annotation, while also reducing the cost and effort required for dataset creation. We also perform a series of ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of different components of our approach, providing insights into the strengths and limitations of our method.

Our work has significant implications for the development of automated crop and weeds detection systems, and demonstrates the potential for machine learning and computer vision techniques to revolutionize the agriculture industry. With the ability to quickly and accurately detect weeds, farmers can take targeted action to control their spread, reducing the use of herbicides and improving crop yields. Our approach can also be adapted for use in other applications, such as autonomous farming and precision agriculture, where accurate detection of crops and weeds is critical.

We construct and test a keypoints dataset, which exhibits strong autocorrelation and high variance and contains at least one pathologically significant feature, including (1) an unusual set of highly abnormal features that are all positively associated with disease, such as thickening or branching, or two outlier features (high or low spore number), and (2) very rare negative features, which may be either positive (large vacuolar content, or small pores) or negatively correlated (small void per cell), in contrast to healthy cells or tissue samples (unusual large vacuoles, unusually thin tissues and so on). We find strong evidence, consistent in several studies, that certain parameters of this critical set provide a reasonable approximation for predicting pathologic progression, particularly with respect to lung cancer risk, especially for milder cancers. In particular, the optimal subset sizes of all features in our sample can vary by between 2 (the minimum value, as determined through experiments, suggests no pathologic change) to 100 (the maximum amount of data observed over 90 experiments yields the optimal subset size estimated here and tested qualitatively). Results of statistical analyses confirm that both subsets were optimal for determining the significance of pathologic changes, even under severe uncertainty, when only a few values are present (i.e., small samples). Thus in practice pathological prediction does not require large datasets: with extremely weak measurements only few parameters represent real differences between patients who do remain alive after treatment versus those who die.

Near-field aperture synthesis imaging is a technique that allows for the creation of high-resolution images of objects or scenes using a large number of low-resolution images taken from different viewpoints. One of the key factors that determines the quality of the reconstructed image is the field of view (FOV) of the imaging system. In this paper, we investigate the relationship between the FOV and the quality of the reconstructed image in the context of near-field aperture synthesis imaging.

We present a theoretical analysis of the impact of FOV on the reconstruction process, and demonstrate that a larger FOV can result in higher-quality images. However, we also show that increasing the FOV comes at the cost of increased computational complexity and a reduced signal-to-noise ratio. We propose several strategies for optimizing the FOV for near-field aperture synthesis imaging, including the use of novel optical designs and image processing techniques.

Our results demonstrate that the FOV is a critical parameter in near-field aperture synthesis imaging, and that careful selection of the FOV can significantly improve the quality of the reconstructed image. Our findings have important implications for the development of high-resolution imaging systems, and could potentially enable new applications in fields such as surveillance, microscopy, and astronomy.

We aim at understanding a surprising fact about linguistic regularities in the most complex ideal languages: Their construction. The construction of an ideal language by an ideal constructor can be decomposed into two phases, i) the specification and execution; ii) the exploration. We have found that (I) the exploration phase corresponds closely to the prototypical algorithm of Chomsky and Yablo (1976): A natural-language learner makes progress with a recursive description of ideal language syntax when she starts out using the minimal set of terms required to generate the entire grammar, called its initial model. She must then revisit or refine her initial model via further lexical exploration. An extreme form of this exploration will eventually yield (II), a complete representation of the grammatical structure of all languages with the minimum number of terms used. This gives rise to the paradox of minimal information requirements in the smallest possible feasible human language construction system. Our findings contribute to understanding how the world works to make up what we think we know. Further studies should aim, moreover, at investigating which details of our linguistic structures are the products simply by their correspondence with optimal search behaviour in computer science—as opposed to purely random—which might provide even more fundamental insight into how grammars are conceived and constructed.

This work exploits two features inherent in images to provide unique information about their scene boundaries in realtime with minimal information bias for human perception: super-resolution and local detection resolution. In this paper, we study convolutions implemented on multi-channel image sequences (the GIFs in the Internet archive) with arbitrary spatial frequency tuning parameters, called bidirectional filters. To maximize accuracy during localization tasks, a bilinear filter was chosen over a quadratic one as the best candidate for super-convergence. After fitting our model to the training data along with a test set (GIFs from the Internet Archive), we observe that our results closely match those obtained by previous network architectures when the number of input channels was increased to 8 or 16. Additionally, since the entire set of the GIF files was used as training data, it allows us directly compare performance for both types of filters. Using the proposed architecture, we observe a dramatic increase in decoding accuracies for more complicated scenes compared to simple scenes. Our results open a number of interesting directions on how to reduce the computational cost of a network that can recognize objects within a constrained feature space, even while simultaneously improving decoder quality.

In this paper, we investigate ion transport in macroscopic radio-frequency (RF) linear traps, which are widely used in various applications such as mass spectrometry, plasma etching, and ion implantation. Ion transport is a critical aspect of these applications as it affects the efficiency, accuracy, and stability of the processes involved.

We present a theoretical analysis of ion transport in macroscopic RF linear traps, taking into account the effects of thermal motion, diffusion, and electric field variations along the trap axis. Our model accounts for the motion of ions within the trap, their interactions with the gas molecules and surfaces, and the influence of external fields on the ion dynamics. We use Monte Carlo simulations to solve the resulting set of equations and study the behavior of ions inside the trap under different operational conditions.

Our results show that there exists an optimal value of the RF frequency that maximizes ion confinement and minimizes losses due to collisions. We also find that the axial distribution of ions inside the trap can be affected by factors such as injection parameters, thermal motion, and surface potential. By optimizing certain operating conditions, we demonstrate that ion loss can be significantly reduced, leading to improved ion beam quality and enhanced process performance.

The insights gained from our study will aid in optimizing existing RF linear traps and guide the development of next-generation devices for ion-based applications. The understanding of ion transport behavior presented here has far-reaching implications for areas like advanced material synthesis, plasma processing, and bio-imaging.

The quality of images captured in outdoor environments can be affected by
poor weather conditions such as fog, dust, and atmospheric scattering of other
particles. This problem can bring extra challenges to high-level computer
vision tasks like image segmentation and object detection. However, previous
studies on image dehazing suffer from a huge computational workload and
corruption of the original image, such as over-saturation and halos. In this
paper, we present a novel image dehazing approach based on the optical model
for haze images and regularized optimization. Specifically, we convert the
non-convex, bilinear problem concerning the unknown haze-free image and light
transmission distribution to a convex, linear optimization problem by
estimating the atmosphere light constant. Our method is further accelerated by
introducing a multilevel Haar wavelet transform. The optimization, instead, is
applied to the low frequency sub-band decomposition of the original image. This
dimension reduction significantly improves the processing speed of our method
and exhibits the potential for real-time applications. Experimental results
show that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art dehazing algorithms in
terms of both image reconstruction quality and computational efficiency. For
implementation details, source code can be publicly accessed via
http://github.com/JiaxiHe/Image-and-Video-Dehazing.

In this paper, we explore the complexity of improving all-switches strategies in various games. All- switches strategies are plans of action that involve switching between different options or paths in a given scenario to maximize payoffs or rewards. We examine the computational difficulties involved in devising efficient methods for enhancing such strategies and demonstrate that many well-known algorithms fail to achieve optimal performance when faced with large problem instances.

Through a series of case studies and theoretical analyses, we show that even simple games can exhibit an exponential increase in the size of the search space as the number of switches increases, rendering traditional approaches ineffective. To address these challenges, we propose several new algorithmic techniques that leverage ideas from combinatorial optimization, machine learning, and heuristic search. Our results demonstrate significant improvements over previous state-of-the-art methods in various domains.

We also consider the impact of uncertainty on all-switches strategy improvement and investigate the use of reinforcement learning methods to learn near-optimal policies in situations where precise model knowledge is unavailable. Our findings highlight the importance of carefully selecting exploration protocols and reward shaping techniques when dealing with high-dimensional state spaces.

Finally, we discuss the applicability of our insights to real-world scenarios, including resource allocation, scheduling, and finance. The paper concludes by outlining promising directions for future research aimed at further advancing the efficiency and effectiveness of all-switches strategy improvement approaches.

Despite popular scientific knowledge suggesting that self awareness involves visual processing across multiple sensory modalities, not much information exists regarding how the observed brain activity reveals these key features when subjects report being consciously aware. Here we report on using state-of-the-art multi-server fMRI techniques to learn neural representations from human fMRI data of individual-level awareness (i.e., knowing what part of an image was seen at a given time). We show that with sufficient training all seven classes of high resolution linear segmentation in one subject revealed detailed representations of awareness, such as where parts of the scene were actually at a glance. Also, the ability to map recognition performance over the same period of learning suggests that our approach can produce statistically meaningful estimates for task performance beyond just recognizing where parts are visible. Our results strongly suggest that future work should focus on improving current models of the mechanisms underpinning complex perceptual functions like conscious perception. In conclusion, our results indicate that large numbers of hidden units on the principal surface may play crucial roles in processing information about surrounding structures and regions. Further studies will benefit by systematically probing their properties and dynamics and exploring alternative computational strategies.

We show that classical chaining bounds on the suprema of random processes in
terms of entropy numbers can be systematically improved when the underlying set
is convex: the entropy numbers need not be computed for the entire set, but
only for certain "thin" subsets. This phenomenon arises from the observation
that real interpolation can be used as a natural chaining mechanism. Unlike the
general form of Talagrand's generic chaining method, which is sharp but often
difficult to use, the resulting bounds involve only entropy numbers but are
nonetheless sharp in many situations in which classical entropy bounds are
suboptimal. Such bounds are readily amenable to explicit computations in
specific examples, and we discover some old and new geometric principles for
the control of chaining functionals as special cases.

The design of neural network architectures is an important component for
achieving state-of-the-art performance with machine learning systems across a
broad array of tasks. Much work has endeavored to design and build
architectures automatically through clever construction of a search space
paired with simple learning algorithms. Recent progress has demonstrated that
such meta-learning methods may exceed scalable human-invented architectures on
image classification tasks. An open question is the degree to which such
methods may generalize to new domains. In this work we explore the construction
of meta-learning techniques for dense image prediction focused on the tasks of
scene parsing, person-part segmentation, and semantic image segmentation.
Constructing viable search spaces in this domain is challenging because of the
multi-scale representation of visual information and the necessity to operate
on high resolution imagery. Based on a survey of techniques in dense image
prediction, we construct a recursive search space and demonstrate that even
with efficient random search, we can identify architectures that outperform
human-invented architectures and achieve state-of-the-art performance on three
dense prediction tasks including 82.7\% on Cityscapes (street scene parsing),
71.3\% on PASCAL-Person-Part (person-part segmentation), and 87.9\% on PASCAL
VOC 2012 (semantic image segmentation). Additionally, the resulting
architecture is more computationally efficient, requiring half the parameters
and half the computational cost as previous state of the art systems.

aware of, the first practical attempt towards joint decoding. The
discriminative feature of the scores benefits on one hand from the
side-information of previously accused users, and on the other hand, from

previous state-of-the-art decoders.

In this paper, we investigate the electronic properties of bilayer tungsten disulfide (WS2) and observe anomalously robust valley polarization and valley coherence. By using a combination of experimental techniques such as optical spectroscopy and theoretical models, we find that the valleys in the bandstructure of WS2 exhibit an unusually strong splitting, which leads to enhanced valley polarization and coherence.

Our results demonstrate that the valley polarization in WS2 is significantly stronger than what is typically observed in other 2D materials, and that it persists even at high temperatures. Additionally, we show that the valley coherence time is longer than expected, indicating that the electrons in WS2 can maintain their valley pseudospin orientation over a relatively long distance.

We attribute these phenomena to the unique stacking structure of WS2 bilayers, which gives rise to a moiré pattern that modulates the interlayer interaction and enhances the valley-dependent electron-electron interactions. Our findings have important implications for the development of next-generation electronic devices, including valleytronics and spintronics applications.

Abstract We present one-path systems consisting of an edge graph that produces continuous non-uniform graphs by two or three of its edges. This allows us to represent two-edge subgraphs of graphs such as "tree diagrams"; to generate arbitrarily complex 2D (or 3D) shapes through several path segments. Therefore, our results reveal the promise of discrete graph construction using only one point method, at least when path segments are very simple.

* A thorough analysis of the effectiveness of MDAN in different scenarios, providing insights into its robustness and adaptability.

Overall, this paper makes an important contribution to the field of network diffusion, and demonstrates the potential of MDAN for improving the efficiency and effectiveness of information dissemination over complex networks.

Abstract This work aims to discover, within an experimental framework, whether there exists an effective information-storage mechanism of particles existing as quantum
momentum entanglement with their classical state. From this conclusion one should arrive at three important conclusions about how particles are stored and accessed. First, while individual particles may store some information and access other information (the same information but in different forms), the process of retrieving stored information depends on many factors and in particular on its degree of uncertainty and that of access. In particular, in situations when storing large quantities (or, which increases with the level of computing energy) entangling several particles will lead to an efficient algorithm. Second, the quantum memory would be able to store the correlations between qubit values even if the computation power of entangled qubits reduces drastically. Third, although some types of measurement fail, entanglement preserves a state 'in' time if its future value is known and can thus lead to a reliable prediction of past events. At present, quantum computers have not succeeded in showing any convincing use cases for using quantum computers over large scale problems without also solving very small scenarios or without also showing many useful applications based purely
on calculations conducted by classical computers before doing them with quantum computers. The problem which remains is determining just how far entanglement scales up when applied directly to quantum systems to produce what we call reliable quantum simulation and/or simulations of quantum systems on larger computer networks. It does seem reasonably likely that if this could be done we would be close to an ideal and accurate quantum simulator. We believe that our results open the door to such a design, which could greatly advance fundamental physics and allow us to address the issues we care most about on the largest possible scales.

In this paper, we propose a deep learning approach for multi-task medical image segmentation in multiple modalities. Our approach leverages the strengths of deep neural networks to simultaneously segment various organs and structures across different imaging modalities, such as CT, MRI, and PET. By jointly training a single network on multiple tasks and modalities, we improve upon traditional single-modality and single-task segmentation methods, which often require separate models and training processes.

Our proposed method is based on a novel architecture that incorporates a shared encoder and modality-specific decoders, allowing the network to learn shared representations across modalities and tasks. We also introduce a novel loss function that combines task-specific losses with a modality-specific regularization term, ensuring that the network learns to segment each modality effectively while still sharing knowledge across modalities.

We evaluate our approach on several publicly available datasets, including the Medical Segmentation Decathlon dataset, which contains images from multiple modalities and tasks. Our results show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art single-modality and single-task segmentation methods, demonstrating the effectiveness of our multi-task and multi-modality approach.

Furthermore, we perform an ablation study to analyze the contributions of different components of our method, providing insights into the benefits of joint training and modality-specific regularization. Our findings suggest that the shared encoder and modality-specific decoders are crucial for improving segmentation performance, while the regularization term helps to reduce overfitting and improve generalization to unseen data.

Overall, our work demonstrates the potential of deep learning for multi-task medical image segmentation in multiple modalities, paving the way for more accurate and efficient segmentation methods in various medical imaging applications.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to constructing prediction sets that are distribution-free and risk-controlling. Existing methods for constructing prediction sets typically rely on assuming a specific distribution for the data, which can be limiting in many real-world applications where the underlying distribution is unknown or complex. Our proposed method, on the other hand, does not require any distributional assumptions and instead relies on a robust optimization framework to construct prediction sets with guaranteed coverage probabilities. Additionally, our approach allows for controlling the risk of the prediction set, ensuring that the error probability is upper bounded by a specified level.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through simulations and real-data experiments, showcasing its ability to provide accurate predictions while maintaining rigorous control over the risk level. We also compare our approach with existing state-of-the art methods, and show that it provides better performance in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. Moreover, we discuss the implementation details of our algorithm and illustrate how it can be applied to various machine learning models, including neural networks and decision trees.

Our main contribution is thus a powerful tool for constructing reliable prediction sets that do not impose any distributional assumptions, enabling their application in diverse domains such as medical diagnosis, financial forecasting, and autonomous systems, among others. By providing a principled way to balance accuracy and risk, our work advances the field of uncertainty quantification and decision making under uncertainty.

images. Staging of lung cancer is a major factor of prognosis. Measuring the

conventional k-means to the representations extracted by the centroids and then
project cluster labels to the target images. We evaluated our methods on
pathology images of lung cancer specimen. Our experiments showed that the
proposed method outperforms traditional k-means segmentation and the
multithreshold Otsu method both quantitatively and qualitatively with an
improved normalized mutual information (NMI) score of 0.626 compared to 0.168
and 0.167, respectively. Furthermore, we found that the centroids can be
applied to the segmentation of other slices from the same sample.

In this paper, we consider the problem of simultaneous inference for misaligned multivariate functional data, where multiple variables are measured over time or across different subjects, and the observations are not aligned in a straightforward manner. This type of data is increasingly common in many fields, including neuroscience, finance, and healthcare, but poses significant challenges for statistical analysis due to the lack of synchronization and potential differences in scales and distributions.

To address these challenges, we propose a novel approach that combines techniques from functional data analysis and inference methods to enable simultaneous estimation and testing of relationships between the variables while accounting for the misalignment. Our approach uses a combination of smoothing splines and Gaussian process regression to model each variable as a function of time or subject, followed by a comparison of the modes of variation captured by each curve using a non-parametric distance metric. This allows us to identify both shared patterns of activity across variables and differences in their temporal or spatial characteristics in a robust and flexible framework.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on several real datasets representing various forms of misaligned mulitvariate functional data, including EEG recordings from cognitive tasks, stock prices, and brain imaging sessions. The results show that our method can accurately capture complex dependencies and contrasts between variables despite their misalignment, outperforming widely used baseline approaches. Additionally, we provide theoretical guarantees for the consistency and asymptotic normality of our estimator under mild regularity conditions, ensuring its validity and reliability.

Our proposed method has important implications for researchers working with multivariate functional data, allowing them to explore richer and more nuanced questions about how variables interact with one another in the presence of misalignment. More broadly, it contributes to the development of powerful tools for understanding and analyzing high-dimensional dependent data, which arise increasingly often in modern scientific studies.

In this paper, we present a novel approach to scene parsing, called Deep Multiphase Level Set (DMLS), which leverages the power of deep learning and level set methods to accurately segment objects in complex scenes. Existing scene parsing techniques suffer from limited performance due to their reliance on hand-crafted features, shallow neural networks, or simplistic segmentation strategies. In contrast, DMLS adopts a deep and multiphase approach to sceneflow estimation, where each phase focuses on a distinct aspect of the scene, enabling the network to capture a richer representation of the visual data.

The proposed method consists of three main components: (1) a Deep Feature Extractor (DFE) that generates high-level features from the input image, (2) a Multiphase Level Set (MLS) formulation that separates the scene into multiple regions based on the feature similarity, and (3) a Segmentation Refining Module (SRM) that fine-tunes the boundaries of the obtained segments using local information. We train the entire network end-to-end using a large dataset of annotated images.

Extensive experiments demonstrate that our DMLS model outperforms state-of-the-art scene parsing methods by a significant margin, achieving an overall accuracy rate of 86.5% on the challenging Cityscapes dataset. Moreover, we perform ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of the individual components and provide insights into the working mechanisms of DMLS. The code and models are made publicly available to facilitate further research in this area.

Our contribution can be summarized as follows:

* We propose a novel deep learning framework for scene parsing, called Deep Multiphase Level Set (DMLS), which combines the strengths of deep feature extraction and level set methods.
* Our approach outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods on several benchmark datasets, showcasing its superiority in handling complex scenarios with multiple objects, varying lighting conditions, and occlusions.
* Through thorough experimentation and analysis, we demonstrate the efficacy of the individually designed components and their synergistic effects in achieving excellent scene understanding results.

Automated segmentation in medical image analysis is a challenging task that
requires a large amount of manually labeled data. However, most existing
learning-based approaches usually suffer from limited manually annotated
medical data, which poses a major practical problem for accurate and robust
medical image segmentation. In addition, most existing semi-supervised
approaches are usually not robust compared with the supervised counterparts,
and also lack explicit modeling of geometric structure and semantic
information, both of which limit the segmentation accuracy. In this work, we
present SimCVD, a simple contrastive distillation framework that significantly
advances state-of-the-art voxel-wise representation learning. We first describe
an unsupervised training strategy, which takes two views of an input volume and
predicts their signed distance maps of object boundaries in a contrastive
objective, with only two independent dropout as mask. This simple approach
works surprisingly well, performing on the same level as previous fully
supervised methods with much less labeled data. We hypothesize that dropout can
be viewed as a minimal form of data augmentation and makes the network robust
to representation collapse. Then, we propose to perform structural distillation
by distilling pair-wise similarities. We evaluate SimCVD on two popular
datasets: the Left Atrial Segmentation Challenge (LA) and the NIH pancreas CT
dataset. The results on the LA dataset demonstrate that, in two types of
labeled ratios (i.e., 20% and 10%), SimCVD achieves an average Dice score of
90.85% and 89.03% respectively, a 0.91% and 2.22% improvement compared to
previous best results. Our method can be trained in an end-to-end fashion,
showing the promise of utilizing SimCVD as a general framework for downstream
tasks, such as medical image synthesis and registration.

Electrostatic modification of functional materials by electrolytic gating has
demonstrated a remarkably wide range of density modulation, a condition crucial
for developing novel electronic phases in systems ranging from complex oxides
to layered chalcogenides. Yet little is known microscopically when carriers are
modulated in electrolyte-gated electric double-layer transistors (EDLTs) due to

interface. Here, we demonstrate the real-space mapping of the channel
conductance in ZnO EDLTs using a cryogenic microwave impedance microscope. A
spin-coated ionic gel layer with typical thicknesses below 50 nm allows us to
perform high resolution (on the order of 100 nm) sub-surface imaging, while
maintaining the capability of inducing the metal-insulator transition under a
gate bias. The microwave images vividly show the spatial evolution of channel
conductance and its local fluctuations through the transition, as well as the
uneven conductance distribution established by a large source-drain bias. The
unique combination of ultra-thin ion-gel gating and microwave imaging offers a
new opportunity to study the local transport and mesoscopic electronic
properties in EDLTs.

This paper presents a novel approach to synthetic aperture sonar (SAS) image segmentation, which is a fundamental step in various underwater applications such as object detection, tracking, and seafloor mapping. Our proposed method leverages the strengths of iterative, deep, and unsupervised learning to effectively segment SAS images.

Firstly, we introduce a novel iterative scheme that progressively refines the segmentation results, allowing for accurate handling of complex scenes with varying textures and artifacts. This iterative approach is built upon a deep neural network architecture that incorporates a custom-designed convolutional neural network (CNN) tailored to the unique characteristics of SAS images.

Furthermore, we propose an unsupervised segmentation method that eliminates the need for labeled data, which is challenging to obtain in the underwater environment. Our approach utilizes a self-supervised loss function that encourages the network to learn meaningful features and segmentation results without the need for manual annotations.

The proposed method is extensively evaluated on a large dataset of SAS images, showcasing its superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. Our experiments demonstrate improved segmentation accuracy, robustness to varying environmental conditions, and reduced computational complexity.

The main contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows:

1. An iterative deep learning framework for SAS image segmentation that progressively refines the segmentation results.
2. A custom-designed CNN architecture tailored to the unique characteristics of SAS images.
3. An unsupervised segmentation method that eliminates the need for labeled data, using a self-supervised loss function.
4. Extensive evaluation and comparison with state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating the superior performance of our proposed approach.

This paper has important implications for various underwater applications that rely on SAS image segmentation, such as object detection, tracking, and seafloor mapping. The proposed method has the potential to significantly improve the accuracy and efficiency of these applications, enabling more effective and reliable underwater operations.

In this paper, we establish a correspondence between the dynamics of unicritical polynomial maps and the arithmetic of their associated Galois groups. We show that the behavior of the map near its critical point can be completely determined by the structure of the Galois group, and conversely, that the Galois group encodes information about the local dynamics of the map.

First, we introduce a new technique for studying the local dynamics of unicritical polynomial maps, which involves associating a “decorated tree" to each critical point. This decorated tree captures the combinatorialinformation about the Julia set and the Fatou set near the critical point, as well as the way in which they intersect the boundary of the disk.

Next, we define a correspondence between the decorated trees associated with two different critical points, which corresponds to the action of the Galois group on the set of critical points. We show that this correspondence preserves the dynamical information encoded in the decorated trees, and hence provides a way to translate information between different critical points.

We then investigate the properties of this correspondence, and show that it has deep connections to both arithmetic and geometry. For example, we prove that the correspondence respects the natural symmetry of the function field ofthe Riemann sphere, and that it is compatible with the action of the modular group on the spaceof unicritical polynomial maps.

Finally, we demonstrate thepower and flexibility of our approach by applying it to several examples of unicritical polynomial maps, including those with complex multiplication and those arising from elliptic curves. In particular,we use the correspondence to calculate the precise asymptotics of certain distinguished orbits under iteration, and to study the arithmetic obstructions that prevent such orbits from being periodic.

Overall, our workestablishes a powerful connection between the arithmetic of Galois groups and thelocal dynamics of unicritical polynomial maps, and opens up a rich new direction for research at the intersection of numbertheoryand dynamical systems.

The authors explore the concept of Quantum Zeno Effect (QZE) through a thought experiment involving Shakespeare's play 'Hamlet'. By analyzing the similarities between QZE and situations depicted in the play, they demonstrate how frequently measuring an electron’s polarization can prevent it from undergoing a transformation. The study emphasizes that while such phenomena may appear counterintuitive at first glance, their underlying principles are rooted in quantum mechanics' unique properties. Overall, this engaging narrative offers insights into both literary analysis and cutting-edge physics research.

Abstract: I have obtained single-photon and superposition-busting effects resulting in optical memory  with quantum-dot devices based on resonant cavity methods using the  laser. In particular, it has been shown that  these systems can be used to store and manipulate single photon entanglement at quantum state  inflection point, as well as two-photon and superposition-busting effects (with an expected gain) from  the quantum-dot storage   regime where a qubit may be located along with its associated photon. The experiments involve storing and manipulating both coherent  and coherently mixed states within the  resonant cavity system. The purpose of this study is to present a novel approach to image segmentation called Compassionate Conservatism, which combines conservative and balanced cuts into a single algorithm. This new method aims to optimize computational efficiency without sacrificing accuracy or precision in segmenting images. We demonstrate its effectiveness through extensive testing on various datasets and compare it with other state-of-the-art algorithms. Our results show that CC outperforms existing methods by achieving greater speed while maintaining high levels of quality and fidelity in segmented outputs. Overall, we believe our proposed technique offers significant advantages over traditional approaches and has great potential for wide adoption across diverse fields such as computer vision biomedical imaging research robotics etc.

Conventional transfer learning leverages weights of pre-trained networks, but
mandates the need for similar neural architectures. Alternatively, knowledge
distillation can transfer knowledge between heterogeneous networks but often
requires access to the original training data or additional generative
networks. Knowledge transfer between networks can be improved by being agnostic
to the choice of network architecture and reducing the dependence on original
training data. We propose a knowledge transfer approach from a teacher to a
student network wherein we train the student on an independent transferal
dataset, whose annotations are generated by the teacher. Experiments were
conducted on five state-of-the-art networks for semantic segmentation and seven
datasets across three imaging modalities. We studied knowledge transfer from a
single teacher, combination of knowledge transfer and fine-tuning, and
knowledge transfer from multiple teachers. The student model with a single
teacher achieved similar performance as the teacher; and the student model with
multiple teachers achieved better performance than the teachers. The salient
features of our algorithm include: 1)no need for original training data or
generative networks, 2) knowledge transfer between different architectures, 3)
ease of implementation for downstream tasks by using the downstream task
dataset as the transferal dataset, 4) knowledge transfer of an ensemble of
models, trained independently, into one student model. Extensive experiments
demonstrate that the proposed algorithm is effective for knowledge transfer and
easily tunable.

This paper proposes a novel approach to skin lesion segmentation, which combines k-means clustering and ensemble regressions to achieve state-of-the-art performance in the ISIC 2017 Skin Lesion Segmentation Challenge. The proposed method first applies k-means clustering to the input image, where each cluster is associated with a distinct skin lesion class. Then, an ensemble of regressors is trained to predict the class label for each cluster, leveraging the spatial information from the clusters.

The proposed algorithm was evaluated on the challenge dataset and achieved an F1 score of 93.5%, outperforming other competing methods. In addition, we performed a series of ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of different components of our algorithm. The results show that both k-means clustering and ensemble regressions contribute significantly to the improved performance.

Our work demonstrates the potential of combining unsupervised and supervised learning techniques for skin lesion segmentation tasks, and provides a new perspective on how to leverage the spatial information in the images. The proposed algorithm has important implications for improving the accuracy and efficiency of skin cancer detection systems, and could potentially be applied to other medical imaging applications.

In this paper, we investigate the maximum size of a subset of asunflower-free set in a graph. A sunflower is a collection of pairs of nodes such that each pair has at least one neighbor in common, and a sunflower-free set is a set of nodes with no two nodes having more than one common neighbor. Our main result provides an upper bound on the size of the largest sunflower-free set in terms of the total number of edges in the graph. Specifically, we show that for any positive integer k, there exists a constant c(k) such that every graph with n vertices and m edges contains either a sunflower or a sunflower-free set with at least (1 - o(1))m/n^2 fraction of the vertices, where the function o(1) tends to zero as k grows.

Our upper bound improves upon previous results, which were limited to logsplitting families of graphs. We also demonstrate the tightness of our bound by constructing explicit families of graphs that achieve it. Finally, we discuss potential applications of our result in other areas, such as property testing and streaming algorithms. By understanding the maximum size of a sunflower-free set, our work sheds light on the structural properties of graphs that are free from certain types of anomalous substructures.

In this paper, we present a novel approach for interactive medical image segmentation, which combines point-based interaction and sequential patch learning. Our method enables users to interact with the segmentation process through intuitive point-based inputs, allowing for real-time feedback and adjustments.

We propose a sequential patch learning framework, where the image is divided into small patches, and the segmentation model is trained on each patch sequentially. This allows for efficient learning and adaptation to local image features. The user's interactions are incorporated into the training process, enabling the model to learn from the user's feedback and improve the segmentation accuracy.

We evaluate our approach on several medical image datasets, including brain tumor segmentation and lung nodule detection. The results show that our method outperforms traditional interactive segmentation methods in terms of both accuracy and efficiency. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in handling complex medical images with varying levels of noise and artifacts.

Our approach has the potential to significantly improve the accuracy and efficiency of medical image segmentation, and could have a major impact on a wide range of medical applications, including disease diagnosis, treatment planning, and monitoring.

Deep co-training has recently been proposed as an effective approach for
image segmentation when annotated data is scarce. In this paper, we improve
existing approaches for semi-supervised segmentation with a self-paced and
self-consistent co-training method. To help distillate information from
unlabeled images, we first design a self-paced learning strategy for
co-training that lets jointly-trained neural networks focus on
easier-to-segment regions first, and then gradually consider harder ones.This
is achieved via an end-to-end differentiable loss inthe form of a generalized
Jensen Shannon Divergence(JSD). Moreover, to encourage predictions from
different networks to be both consistent and confident, we enhance this
generalized JSD loss with an uncertainty regularizer based on entropy. The
robustness of individual models is further improved using a self-ensembling
loss that enforces their prediction to be consistent across different training
iterations. We demonstrate the potential of our method on three challenging
image segmentation problems with different image modalities, using small
fraction of labeled data. Results show clear advantages in terms of performance
compared to the standard co-training baselines and recently proposed
state-of-the-art approaches for semi-supervised segmentation

Given a natural language expression and an image/video, the goal of referring
segmentation is to produce the pixel-level masks of the entities described by
the subject of the expression. Previous approaches tackle this problem by
implicit feature interaction and fusion between visual and linguistic
modalities in a one-stage manner. However, human tends to solve the referring
problem in a progressive manner based on informative words in the expression,
i.e., first roughly locating candidate entities and then distinguishing the
target one. In this paper, we propose a Cross-Modal Progressive Comprehension
(CMPC) scheme to effectively mimic human behaviors and implement it as a CMPC-I
(Image) module and a CMPC-V (Video) module to improve referring image and video
segmentation models. For image data, our CMPC-I module first employs entity and
attribute words to perceive all the related entities that might be considered
by the expression. Then, the relational words are adopted to highlight the
target entity as well as suppress other irrelevant ones by spatial graph
reasoning. For video data, our CMPC-V module further exploits action words
based on CMPC-I to highlight the correct entity matched with the action cues by
temporal graph reasoning. In addition to the CMPC, we also introduce a simple
yet effective Text-Guided Feature Exchange (TGFE) module to integrate the
reasoned multimodal features corresponding to different levels in the visual
backbone under the guidance of textual information. In this way, multi-level
features can communicate with each other and be mutually refined based on the
textual context. Combining CMPC-I or CMPC-V with TGFE can form our image or
video version referring segmentation frameworks and our frameworks achieve new
state-of-the-art performances on four referring image segmentation benchmarks
and three referring video segmentation benchmarks respectively.

Automatic face recognition has received significant performance improvement
by developing specialised facial image representations. On the other hand,
generic object recognition has rarely been applied to the face recognition.
Spatial pyramid pooling of features encoded by an over-complete dictionary has
been the key component of many state-of-the-art image classification systems.
Inspired by its success, in this work we develop a new face image
representation method inspired by the second-order pooling in Carreira et al.
[1], which was originally proposed for image segmentation. The proposed method
differs from the previous methods in that, we encode the densely extracted
local patches by a small-size dictionary; and the facial image signatures are
obtained by pooling the second-order statistics of the encoded features. We
show the importance of pooling on encoded features, which is bypassed by the
original second-order pooling method to avoid the high computational cost.
Equipped with a simple linear classifier, the proposed method outperforms the
state-of-the-art face identification performance by large margins. For example,
on the LFW databases, the proposed method performs better than the previous
best by around 13% accuracy.

In this paper, we present an information-theoretic framework for deriving min-cut based clustering methods. We start by formulating a probabilistic graphical model that represents the observed data as afunction of the underlying cluster assignments and the noise variables. Using concepts from information theory, we define a distance measure between clusters based on their mutual information, which leads to a novel objective function for clustering.

We then show that the proposed objective function is equivalent to the min-cut problem, which is a widely used criterion in Graph Theory for partitioning graphs into disjoint subsets. By solving this optimization problem, we obtain the optimal cluster assignment for the given data. Our approach has several advantages over traditional clustering methods, including its foundation ininformation theory, its ability to handle noisy data, and its scalability to large datasets.

Through simulations and real-world case studies, we demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our algorithm compared to state-of-art methods such as k-means and spectral clustering. Furthermore, we provide theoretical analysis of the convergence properties of our algorithm.

Our work provides a new perspective on min-cut based clustering methods, casting them as an exercise in information compression, rather than graph separation. This insight highlights the fundamental relationship between information theory and clustering, and offers a fresh way of thinking about the design and evaluation of clustering algorithms.

This paper presents a novel approach to keypoint sampling for fast pathological lung segmentation, which is a crucial step in computer-aided diagnosis and treatment planning for lung diseases. Existing methods for keypoint sampling are often limited by their reliance on hand-crafted features and manual parameter tuning, resulting in suboptimal performance and slow processing times.

In this paper, we propose a near-optimal keypoint sampling method that leverages recent advances in machine learning and computer vision to efficiently and accurately segment pathological lung regions. Our approach uses a deep neural network to learn a mapping between medical images and their corresponding keypoints, allowing for automatic and robust feature extraction. We also introduce a novel sampling strategy that adaptively selects the most informative keypoints based on their similarity to the input image, leading to improved accuracy and reduced computational cost.

We evaluate our method on a large dataset of lung CT scans and compare it to state-of-the-art keypoint sampling methods. Our results show that our approach significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of segmentation accuracy and processing speed, while also providing improved robustness to variations in image quality and artifacts.

The main contributions of this paper are:

* A deep learning-based approach for keypoint sampling that learns a mapping between medical images and their corresponding keypoints
* A novel adaptive sampling strategy that selects the most informative keypoints based on their similarity to the input image
* State-of-the-art performance on a large dataset of lung CT scans, outperforming existing methods in terms of segmentation accuracy and processing speed

Overall, our proposed method has the potential to significantly improve the efficiency and accuracy of pathological lung segmentation, and could enable real-time segmentation in clinical settings.

In this work, we study hole transport in a planar silicon
metal-oxide-semiconductor based double quantum dot. We demonstrate Pauli spin
blockade in the few hole regime and map the spin relaxation induced leakage
current as a function of inter-dot level spacing and magnetic field. With
varied inter-dot tunnel coupling we can identify different dominant spin
relaxation mechanisms. Applying a strong out-of-plane magnetic field causes an
avoided singlet-triplet level crossing, from which the heavy hole g-factor
$\sim$ 0.93, and the strength of spin-orbit interaction $\sim$ 110 $\mu$eV, can
be obtained. The demonstrated strong spin-orbit interaction of heavy hole
promises fast local spin manipulation using only electrical fields, which is of
great interest for quantum information processing.

This paper proposes a novel semi-supervised video segmentation approach that leverages temporality in videos to improve segmentation performance. The proposed method utilizes both labeled and unlabeled frames in a video to learn a robust segmentation model. Experimental results on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, achieving state-of-the-art performance while requiring fewer labeled frames for training.

The academic paper titled "Compassionately Conservative Balanced Cuts for Image Segmentation" proposes a new algorithm for image segmentation that combines conservative cuts with a balanced force approach. The algorithm is designed to prioritize the preservation of important features in the image while also ensuring that the segmentation results are accurate. The paper presents a detailed analysis of the algorithm's performance and compares it to other existing methods in the field. Overall, the proposed algorithm demonstrates promising results and has the potential to be a valuable tool for image segmentation applications.

This paper investigates the properties of harmonic maps of finite uniton type into inner symmetric spaces. We provide a comprehensive analysis of the behavior of these maps and their relationship to the underlying geometry of the target space. Our results shed new light on the structure of harmonic maps and have important implications for the study of geometric analysis and differential geometry.

This study proposes a novel image segmentation method using Kernelized Weighted SUSAN (Spatially Uncorrelated Sampling Based Error Estimation) and fuzzy c-means clustering. The proposed approach employs a kernel function to transform data into higher dimensions, which enhances cluster separability while reducing computational complexity. Additionally, weighted SUSAN is used to improve the stability of the clustered results by considering both local contrast information and spatial correlation in an adaptive manner. Experimental evaluations on various noisy images demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art algorithms in terms of segmentation accuracy, robustness, and computation time. Overall, this research provides a promising solution for efficient and accurate image segmentation tasks plagued by noise interference.

This paper explores the use of retrainined off-the-shelf deep neural networks (DNNs) for iris recognition with image segmentation. Iris recognition is a widely used biometric modality that offers high accuracy and resistance to fraud. However, accurate iris recognition requires precise image segmentation to extract the iris region from the eye image. Traditional methods rely on hand-crafted features and manual feature extraction, which can be time-consuming and achieve limited performance.

In this work, we propose a novel approach using DNNs to perform iris segmentation and recognition. We employ a pre-trained convolutional neural network (CNN) to learn a robust representation of the iris region from a large dataset of images. Domain Adaptation (DA) methods are widely used in medical image segmentation
tasks to tackle the problem of differently distributed train (source) and test
(target) data. We consider the supervised DA task with a limited number of
annotated samples from the target domain. It corresponds to one of the most
relevant clinical setups: building a sufficiently accurate model on the minimum
possible amount of annotated data. Existing methods mostly fine-tune specific
layers of the pretrained Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). However, there is
no consensus on which layers are better to fine-tune, e.g. the first layers for
images with low-level domain shift or the deeper layers for images with
high-level domain shift. To this end, we propose SpotTUnet - a CNN architecture
that automatically chooses the layers which should be optimally fine-tuned.
More specifically, on the target domain, our method additionally learns the
policy that indicates whether a specific layer should be fine-tuned or reused
from the pretrained network. We show that our method performs at the same level
as the best of the nonflexible fine-tuning methods even under the extreme
scarcity of annotated data. Secondly, we show that SpotTUnet policy provides a
layer-wise visualization of the domain shift impact on the network, which could
be further used to develop robust domain generalization methods. In order to
extensively evaluate SpotTUnet performance, we use a publicly available dataset
of brain MR images (CC359), characterized by explicit domain shift. We release
a reproducible experimental pipeline.

We present an end-to-end trainable deep convolutional neural network (DCNN)
for semantic segmentation with built-in awareness of semantically meaningful
boundaries. Semantic segmentation is a fundamental remote sensing task, and
most state-of-the-art methods rely on DCNNs as their workhorse. A major reason
for their success is that deep networks learn to accumulate contextual
information over very large windows (receptive fields). However, this success
comes at a cost, since the associated loss of effecive spatial resolution
washes out high-frequency details and leads to blurry object boundaries. Here,
we propose to counter this effect by combining semantic segmentation with
semantically informed edge detection, thus making class-boundaries explicit in
the model, First, we construct a comparatively simple, memory-efficient model
by adding boundary detection to the Segnet encoder-decoder architecture.
Second, we also include boundary detection in FCN-type models and set up a
high-end classifier ensemble. We show that boundary detection significantly
improves semantic segmentation with CNNs. Our high-end ensemble achieves > 90%
overall accuracy on the ISPRS Vaihingen benchmark.

We introduce the notions of a differentiable groupoid and a differentiable
stratified groupoid, generalizations of Lie groupoids in which the spaces of
objects and arrows have the structures of differentiable spaces, respectively
differentiable stratified spaces, compatible with the groupoid structure. After
studying basic properties of these groupoids including Morita equivalence, we
prove a de Rham theorem for locally contractible differentiable stratified
groupoids. We then focus on the study of the inertia groupoid associated to a
proper Lie groupoid. We show that the loop and the inertia space of a proper
Lie groupoid can be endowed with a natural Whitney B stratification, which we
call the orbit Cartan type stratification. Endowed with this stratification,
the inertia groupoid of a proper Lie groupoid becomes a locally contractible
differentiable stratified groupoid.

We evaluate our approach on several challenging datasets captured in adverse weather conditions, including rain, fog, and nighttime scenarios. Additionally, our method is computationally efficient, with an average processing speed of 30.2 frames per second.

In this paper, we investigate the concept of irreversible 2-conversion sets in graphs of bounded degree. A 2-conversion set is a set of vertices in a graph that can be transformed into a dominating set by repeatedly adding or removing edges between pairs of vertices. The irreversibility of a 2-conversion set refers to the fact that once a vertex is added to the set, it cannot be removed without disrupting the connectivity of the remaining vertices.

We prove that for any bounded degree graph, there exists an irreversible 2-conversion set of size O(n), where n is the number of vertices in the graph. This result is tight, as we also show that there are graphs with bounded degree that require an irreversible 2-conversion set of size Omega(n).

Our proof techniques involve a combination of combinatorial arguments and the use of linear programming relaxations. We first show that a minimum-size irreversible 2-conversion set must have a certain structural property, which we call a "good" structure. We then use linear programming relaxations to find a good structure in a graph, and show that this structure can be used to construct an irreversible 2-conversion set of size O(n).

We also consider the algorithmic implications of our results, and show that our construction of an irreversible 2-conversion set can be used to design efficient algorithms for various graph optimization problems, such as minimum edge cover and maximum flow problems.

Overall, our paper provides new insights into the structure and properties of irreversible 2-conversion sets in graphs of bounded degree, and demonstrates their applications in algorithmic design.

Accurate segmentation of nuclei in microscopy images is a crucial step in various biomedical applications, including cancer diagnosis, cell counting, and cell classification. However, the task is challenging due to variations in image quality, staining, and nuclear morphology. In this paper, we propose a novel approach for segmenting nuclei in divergent microscopy images. Our method combines a deep learning-based framework with a novel pre-processing technique, which enhances the contrast and separation between nuclei and background.

The proposed approach consists of three stages: (1) pre-processing, (2) segmentation, and (3) post-processing. In the pre-processing stage, we apply a novel technique that combines histogram equalization, contrast stretching, and morphological operations to enhance the contrast and separation between nuclei and background. In the segmentation stage, we use a deep learning-based framework, specifically a U-Net architecture, to segment the nuclei. Finally, in the post-processing stage, we apply a series of filters to refine the segmentation masks and remove any remaining artifacts.

We evaluate our approach on a dataset of microscopy images with diverse staining and image quality. The results show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art segmentation methods in terms of accuracy, efficiency, and robustness. We also demonstrate the applicability of our approach to various biomedical applications, including cancer diagnosis and cell classification.

Our main contributions are:

* A novel pre-processing technique that enhances the contrast and separation between nuclei and background, leading to improved segmentation accuracy.
* A deep learning-based segmentation framework that effectively handles diverse staining and image quality.
* A comprehensive evaluation of our approach on a large dataset of microscopy images, demonstrating its superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods.

The proposed method has the potential to significantly improve the accuracy and efficiency of various biomedical applications that rely on nuclei segmentation in microscopy images.

Videos can be viewed as unique objects in an image space on the screen, but their structure and arrangement cannot easily be captured or understood by conventional video and image processing algorithms used today, such as edge detection [26]. At the same time, they are not static and do not need to conform exactly to any particular representation of the scene – many videos may simply consist of repeating visual patterns where repeated motions of characters are played out with different camera angles within a scene [4], or simply have no apparent story at all without dialogue or narration (for example), but all of these structures remain hidden to human perception. An ambitious project has been undertaken to quantify some of these features which were previously unseen, enabling video segmentation programs to accurately render videos which would otherwise escape classification or other automated analysis. The goal was to produce real VAS scores representing this hidden structure via a novel video object model that combines low-level features into high-level abstractions of what happens in these videos. We use YouTube-vos [7] to explore how good VAS estimators based on traditional, image-based segmentation techniques perform once applied against large videos whose size permits visualization, and how these results are related to a theoretical machine modeling approach, called 'Video VOS'. Our experiments show that YouTube-vos could identify certain key properties of the video footage while allowing for different interpretation. These results help to distinguish approaches which can successfully classify complex videos from those which will ultimately fail due to insufficient understanding how the relevant video representations change over time. We also demonstrate the potential benefits of using YouTube-vos to apply new learning methods in areas of artificial intelligence where image/video classifier systems might already excel. In this paper, we present a novel approach for interactive segmentation of medical images using fully convolutional neural networks (FCNs). Traditional image segmentation methods rely on manually defined boundaries or manual interaction, which can be time-consuming and subjective. Our proposed method leverages FCNs to learn the underlying patterns in medical images and allow for real-time user interaction to refine the segmentation results.

We propose a two-stage framework, consisting of a coarse segmentation stage followed by a fine-tuning stage. The coarse segmentation stage uses a FCN to generate an initial segmentation mask, which is then refined through user interaction in the fine-tuning stage. We introduce a novel loss function that incorporates both image-based and user-interaction based features, allowing the network to adapt to changing user input.

Our experiments on several publicly available medical imaging datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. Compared to traditional segmentation methods, our method produces more accurate and robust segmentation results, while also providing improved efficiency and usability. Additionally, we conduct a user study to evaluate the performance of our method in various clinical scenarios, demonstrating its potential for widespread application in medical imaging analysis.

Overall, this work presents a significant step towards improving the accuracy and efficiency of medical image segmentation, and has important implications for a wide range of applications including disease diagnosis, treatment planning, and monitoring.

Moreover, the reduced number of parameters also leads to faster training times, making it easier to fine-tune models on specific tasks.

In summary, this paper presents an effective technique to improve the efficiency of CNNs for pixelwise classification tasks. The problem of multiple sensors simultaneously acquiring measurements of a
single object can be found in many applications. In this paper, we present the
optimal recovery guarantees for the recovery of compressible signals from
multi-sensor measurements using compressed sensing. In the first half of the
paper, we present both uniform and nonuniform recovery guarantees for the
conventional sparse signal model in a so-called distinct sensing scenario. In
the second half, using the so-called sparse and distributed signal model, we
present nonuniform recovery guarantees which effectively broaden the class of
sensing scenarios for which optimal recovery is possible, including to the
so-called identical sampling scenario. To verify our recovery guarantees we
provide several numerical results including phase transition curves and
numerically-computed bounds.

Abstract Recently, applications such as Google Map Maker (GM) have been developing into very powerful algorithms that solve many mapping data analysis problems including spatial features recognition, local area image segmentation and localization, high-resolution orthorectification, scene understanding such as to map out complex spatial environments and more. The main challenge to these general purpose learning systems has frequently been performance on datasets with high dimensionality. We propose a new approach based on aerial imagery that can potentially improve quality by several orders of magnitude by using multiple maps to segment images in a similar way to human image segmentation with high resolution multi-view 3D stereo-scanning technology. In one embodiment we develop an algorithm through which two or more sources are used simultaneously and combined directly for their contribution to model the output set of our proposed joint learning process. Using this hybrid solution, we are able to extract both spatio-temporal dimensions in addition to relative position information when performing image segmenting in a relatively expensive manner. Finally, we demonstrate its effectiveness in realtime detection and detection accuracy improvement on a diverse array of image classification tasks with a variety of target classes such indoor scenes.

Our findings point towards a possible future direction toward better optimization techniques for complex systems management such as ASSO during deployment.

3D Convolution Neural Networks (CNNs) have been widely applied to 3D scene
understanding, such as video analysis and volumetric image recognition.
However, 3D networks can easily lead to over-parameterization which incurs
expensive computation cost. In this paper, we propose Channel-wise Automatic
KErnel Shrinking (CAKES), to enable efficient 3D learning by shrinking standard
3D convolutions into a set of economic operations e.g., 1D, 2D convolutions.
Unlike previous methods, CAKES performs channel-wise kernel shrinkage, which
enjoys the following benefits: 1) enabling operations deployed in every layer
to be heterogeneous, so that they can extract diverse and complementary
information to benefit the learning process; and 2) allowing for an efficient
and flexible replacement design, which can be generalized to both
spatial-temporal and volumetric data. Further, we propose a new search space
based on CAKES, so that the replacement configuration can be determined
automatically for simplifying 3D networks. CAKES shows superior performance to
other methods with similar model size, and it also achieves comparable
performance to state-of-the-art with much fewer parameters and computational
costs on tasks including 3D medical imaging segmentation and video action
recognition. Codes and models are available at

High-resolution satellite imagery captured over Asia, Europe, North America, Africa and Europe (PERSIANN-CCS) has become very popular when working with civil disturbance preparedness and emergency services planning. It includes some valuable information about how people are moving in urban environments. A main reason for this popularity is that high resolution images can be acquired quickly which allows rapid analysis and response. This paper presents a method to detect human movement at high spatial frequency using a discrete component approach applied to a low altitude segment of PERSIANN-CCS images. We demonstrate effective detection of human movement over large urban areas with a 3D Gaussian Kernel FFT process that minimizes image distortion. Our model results provide promising insights into human mobility behavior, including possible implications on public safety.

Mandible bone segmentation from computed tomography (CT) scans is challenging
due to mandible's structural irregularities, complex shape patterns, and lack
of contrast in joints. Furthermore, connections of teeth to mandible and
mandible to remaining parts of the skull make it extremely difficult to
identify mandible boundary automatically. This study addresses these challenges
by proposing a novel framework where we define the segmentation as two
complementary tasks: recognition and delineation. For recognition, we use
random forest regression to localize mandible in 3D. For delineation, we
propose to use 3D gradient-based fuzzy connectedness (FC) image segmentation
algorithm, operating on the recognized mandible sub-volume. Despite heavy CT
artifacts and dental fillings, consisting half of the CT image data in our
experiments, we have achieved highly accurate detection and delineation
results. Specifically, detection accuracy more than 96% (measured by union of
intersection (UoI)), the delineation accuracy of 91% (measured by dice
similarity coefficient), and less than 1 mm in shape mismatch (Hausdorff
Distance) were found.

Our method, called FedDG-EPS, aims to address the challenges of domain shift and data heterogeneity in distributed medical imaging datasets, where data from different domains may have varying modalities, resolutions, and qualities.

In this paper, we present EdgeFlow, a novel approach to interactive segmentation that leverages the concept of edge-guided flow to achieve practical and efficient segmentation of images. Interactive segmentation is a fundamental task in computer vision that involves allowing a user to interact with an image to indicate the regions of interest. However, existing methods for interactive segmentation are often limited by their reliance on iterative user input, which can be time-consuming and may not accurately capture the user's intended segmentation.

EdgeFlow addresses these limitations by introducing a new approach that combines the efficiency of edge-guided segmentation with the practicality of interactive segmentation. Our approach uses a novel edge-guided flow algorithm that propagates user input along the edges of an image, allowing for fast and accurate segmentation of complex images. We demonstrate the effectiveness of EdgeFlow through extensive experiments on several benchmark datasets, showing that it outperforms state-of-the-art interactive segmentation methods in terms of both efficiency and accuracy.

In addition, we explore the versatility of EdgeFlow by applying it to a variety of applications, including object segmentation, medical image segmentation, and video segmentation. Our results show that EdgeFlow can handle a wide range of scenarios, from simple object segmentation to complex medical image segmentation, and can accurately segment objects in real-time.

Overall, EdgeFlow represents a significant advancement in the field of interactive segmentation, providing a practical and efficient approach that can be used in a variety of applications. Its ability to accurately segment images with minimal user input makes it an ideal tool for a wide range of users, from researchers to practitioners.
