Abstract: A robust quantular subspace measure in a semidefinite field provides an essential foundation on which to construct and validate new tools using constructive geometry. This theorem has recently been investigated with respect to geometry, especially of manifolds and Lie groups. In this study we extend it to non-geometrical fields by showing that a generalization of general topology rules can be carried out over a wide class of natural numbers and their analogues. Since our proof does not rely upon any additional mathematical theory, we see no fundamental reason either why such an extension should have been conjectured or demonstrated in the past. To address these questions, we present the first formal proofs of two important results: a weak formula (of three components) showing the unique geometric structure of a homotopy type group G g that satisfies the quasilinearity of this definition of the type object; and our proof linking the discrete subspaces approach as well as a complete axiomatisation and construction system of arithmetic on finite fields derived from one such proof. Our argument shows how this framework can be extended to more complicated classes of complex structures—including algebraic structures—and leads us towards extending other existing extensions like those related to rings. Finally, the conjecture itself is presented using proofs derived from our analysis as well as new insights derived solely from the recent developments in geometry. To summarize what we've shown here, at minimum there exist two ways of defining the category of sets for some natural number k with the same set theory. One way was realized recently through construction systems based purely on the result from the section of the conjecture relating the concept of 'number' to the notion of 'elementary'. The second possible way requires a novel kind of mathematics and allows the real dimension of all open families of measurable subsets to be used together with a powerful and non-trivial construction scheme in some cases.

In this paper, we propose a novel technique called Concurrent Spatial and Channel Squeeze & Excitation (CSCSE) to improve the performance of fully convolutional networks (FCNs) in image classification tasks. FCNs are widely used for image classification due to their ability to learn spatial hierarchies of features, but they often suffer from two limitations: (1) the computational cost of processing high-resolution images and (2) the difficulty in capturing long-range dependencies between distant parts of an image.

Our proposed CSCSE method addresses these limitations by introducing a lightweight mechanism that jointly reduces the spatial dimensions and number of channels of feature maps within FCNs, while concurrently enhancing the representation capabilities of the network. Specifically, our approach consists of three key components: (i) channel-wise depthwise separable convolutions, which reduce the number of parameters and computations required while preserving spatial information; (ii) spatial squeeze-and-excite operations, which adaptively adjust the spatial resolution of feature maps based on their importance; and (iii) a multi-scale feature fusion module, which enables the network to capture both local and global contextual relationships.

We comprehensively evaluate the effectiveness of our CSCSE method on several benchmark datasets, including CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. Our experimental results demonstrate that CSCSE achieves state-of-the-art performance with significantly fewer parameters and computations compared to existing state-of-the-art models. Moreover, we perform ablation studies to analyze the contributions of each component of CSCSE, providing insights into the efficacy of our approach.

The main contribution of this work is the introduction of Concurrent Spatial and Channel Squeeze & Excitation, which not only improves the accuracy of Fully Convolutional Networks but also provides a computationally efficient way to process high-resolution images. This technique has important implications for applications where real-time performance and computational efficiency are crucial, such as autonomous driving, robotics, and medical imaging analysis.

In this paper, we present a novel approach for noise reduction and hyperfine level coherence in spontaneous noise spectroscopy of atomic vapor. Spontaneous noise spectroscopy is a technique that uses the random fluctuations in the absorption of light by atoms to measure the absorption spectrum of a sample. However, the accuracy of this technique is limited by the inherent noise present in the measurement process.

To overcome this limitation, we have developed a new method that utilizes a combination of optical and magnetic field manipulation to suppress the noise and enhance the hyperfine level coherence in the atomic vapor. By applying a carefully designed magnetic field, we are able to Zeeman split the hyperfine levels of the atoms, allowing us to selectively manipulate the population of the individual hyperfine levels.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by measuring the absorption spectrum of a rubidium vapor cell using spontaneous noise spectroscopy. Our results show a significant reduction in the noise floor and an increase in the signal-to-noise ratio, allowing us to observe previously unresolvable hyperfine structure in the absorption spectrum.

Our approach has important implications for a wide range of applications, including atomic clocks, magnetometry, and quantum information processing. By improving the sensitivity and resolution of spontaneous noise spectroscopy, we can enable new capabilities for these applications and further our understanding of the behavior of atoms and molecules at the quantum level.

In this paper, we present a novel approach to dense 3D visual mapping that leverages semantic simplification to efficiently represent complex environments. Existing methods often struggle with the trade-off between detail and efficiency, either providing highly detailed but computationally expensive maps or simplified but incomplete representations. Our proposed method addresses this challenge by introducing asemantic simplification step that extracts the most important features of the environment while reducing the computational cost.

We evaluate our approach on several publicly available datasets and demonstrate its superior performance in terms of both accuracy and efficiency compared to state-of-the-art methods. Specifically, our method achieves higher point cloud segmentation accuracy and more efficient map construction, while also providing a more compact representation of the environment. Additionally, we showcase the versatility of our approach by applying it to various applications such as object recognition, scene understanding, and autonomous navigation.

Our main contributions can be summarized as follows:

* A novel approach to dense 3D visual mapping that combines semantic simplification with efficient map construction
* APointNet-like network architecture that integrates semantic information into the mapping process
* An effective simplification strategy that reduces the computational cost while preserving essential details of the environment
* State-of-the-art performance in both accuracy and efficiency on several benchmark datasets
* Demonstration of the versatility of our approach through various applications

The rest of the paper is organized as follows: related work is reviewed in Section 2, followed by the methodology description in Section 3. Results and evaluations are presented in Section 4, while Section 5 concludes the paper and outlines future work directions.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to improve the performance of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) by introducing a hierarchical-split block called HS-ResNet. The proposed block is designed to address the limitations of traditional CNNs, which suffer from the vanishing gradient problem and limited representation capacity.

The HS-ResNet block consists of three main components: a spatial pyramid pooling module, a feature fusion module, and a residual connection module. The spatial pyramid pooling module hierarchically splits the input feature maps into multiple scales, allowing the network to capture multiscale contextual information. The feature fusion module combines the split features through concatenation and channel-wise attention, enhancing the representational capacity of the network. Finally, the residual connection module ensures the stability of the training process and improves the overall performance by incorporating skip connections.

We evaluate the efficacy of HS-ResNet on several benchmark datasets, including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed architecture achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing CNN models. Specifically, HS-ResNet50 achieves an error rate of 3.27% on CIFAR-10 and 19.48% on CIFAR-100, outperforming other CNN models with similar complexity. On ImageNet, HS-ResNet reaches a Top-5 accuracy of 86.1%, surpassing other ResNet variants.

Our extensive ablation studies reveal that the hierarchical-split design and feature fusion module are crucial for the improved performance of HS-ResNet. We also analyze the effectiveness of different component combinations and provide insights into their roles in the network's behavior.

In summary, this paper presents HS-ResNet, a novel CNN architecture that leverages hierarchical splitting and feature fusion to enhance the representational capacity and alleviate the vanishing gradient issue. Our experimental results prove its superiority over existing CNN models and provide valuable guidelines for future architectural advancements in computer vision tasks.

This paper presents a novel approach to image segmentation, Learning to Segment from Scribbles using Multi-scale Adversarial Attention Gates (MSAAG). The proposed method leverages the power of adversarial attention mechanisms to learn a robust and accurate segmentation model from sparse annotated data.

Existing methods rely heavily on fully supervised learning, requiring large amounts of manually labeled data. In contrast, MSAAG uses scribble annotations, which are significantly easier and faster to obtain, yet still provide valuable information about the location of objects in an image. By incorporating multi-scale features and adaptive attention gates, our model is able to effectively focus on the most relevant regions of an image and learn rich semantic representations.

The key innovation of MSAAG lies in its ability to integrate spatial and channel-wise attention into a single module. This enables the model to learn both local and global context, leading to improved performance compared to traditional attention-based approaches. Additionally, we introduce a new loss function that encourages the model to produce smooth and consistent segmentation masks, further enhancing overall accuracy.

Extensive experiments demonstrate that MSAAG outperforms state-of-the-art weakly supervised segmentation models on several benchmark datasets. Our approach achieves superior performance with fewer annotated examples, exhibiting its capability to efficiently leverage limited annotation resources. Moreover, we perform ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of different components within the MSAAG framework, providing insights into the contributions of each component to the overall performance gain.

In summary, this work introduces a novel image segmentation approach that leverages scribble annotations and advances in adversarial attention mechanisms to achieve high accuracy with minimal manual effort. The proposed MSAAG model has important implications for applications where labeling data is costly or challenging, such as medical imaging, autonomous driving, and robotics.

This paper addresses the automatic image segmentation problem in a region
merging style. With an initially over-segmented image, in which the many
regions (or super-pixels) with homogeneous color are detected, image
segmentation is performed by iteratively merging the regions according to a
statistical test. There are two essential issues in a region merging algorithm:
order of merging and the stopping criterion. In the proposed algorithm, these
two issues are solved by a novel predicate, which is defined by the sequential
probability ratio test (SPRT) and the maximum likelihood criterion. Starting
from an over-segmented image, neighboring regions are progressively merged if
there is an evidence for merging according to this predicate. We show that the
merging order follows the principle of dynamic programming. This formulates
image segmentation as an inference problem, where the final segmentation is
established based on the observed image. We also prove that the produced
segmentation satisfies certain global properties. In addition, a faster
algorithm is developed to accelerate the region merging process, which
maintains a nearest neighbor graph in each iteration. Experiments on real
natural images are conducted to demonstrate the performance of the proposed
dynamic region merging algorithm.

This research examines different approaches to approximate solutions in Integer Programming. Through theoretical analysis and computational experiments, we demonstrate that this approach can lead to improved performance compared with traditional methods when dealing with large-scale or complex problems. Overall, our findings highlight the potential benefits of incorporating multiple criteria into decision making within Optimization Theory.

Quantum mechanics is not the unique no-signaling theory which is endowed with
stronger-than-classical correlations, and there exists a broad class of
no-signaling theories allowing even stronger-than-quantum correlations. The
principle of information causality has been suggested to distinguish quantum
theory from these nonphysical theories, together with an elegant
information-theoretic proof of the quantum bound of two-particle correlations.
In this work, we extend this to genuine $N$-particle correlations that cannot
be reduced to mixtures of states in which a smaller number of particles are
entangled. We first express Svetlichny's inequality in terms of multipartite
no-signaling boxes, then prove that the strongest genuine multipartite
correlations lead to the maximal violation of information causality. The
maximal genuine multipartite correlations under the constraint of information
causality is found to be equal to the quantum mechanical bound. This result
consolidates information causality as a physical principle defining the
possible correlations allowed by nature, and provides intriguing insights into
the limits of genuine multipartite correlations in quantum theory.

We investigate the structural, electronic, and thermodynamic properties of these materials using a range of vdW-DFT functionals and compare our results to experimental data and other theoretical calculations.

Our results show that the choice of vdW-DFT functional has a significant impact on the predicted properties of these materials, with some functionals performing better than others for specific properties. We find that the optB88-vdW and Grimme functionals provide a good balance between accuracy and computational cost for the systems studied.

We also examine the effect of van der Waals interactions on the structural and thermodynamic properties of these materials and find that they play a significant role in determining their properties. Our results demonstrate the importance of including van der Waals interactions in DFT calculations for accurate predictions of the properties of bulk solids with BCC, FCC, and diamond structures.

Overall, this study provides a comprehensive assessment of the performance of vdW-DFT functionals for the study of bulk solids with BCC, FCC, and diamond structures and highlights the importance of considering van der Waals interactions in DFT calculations for accurate predictions of material properties.

The main idea is to have different classes of unknown object objects with arbitrary properties and then infer the features of these object models, either through direct evaluation or by using a model comparison toolbox that builds inference structures dynamically according to class constraints. Then the user asks how they expect each new learning step should look like, such as selecting the best fitting structure, comparing its quality against each potential alternative model or just giving some advice on which model he/she likes most and will probably use more often. In this paper, we present SwipeCut, a novel interactive segmentation method that leverages diversified seed proposals to improve the accuracy and efficiency of segmenting objects in images. Existing interactive segmentation methods rely on a single seed point or a small set of seed points to initiate the segmentation process, which can lead to suboptimal segmentation results, especially in cases where the object boundaries are complex or unclear.

SwipeCut addresses this limitation by introducing a diversified seed proposal generation step that produces a large set of candidate seed points, each with a different orientation and location. These seed proposals are then used to initialize a novel optimization framework that refines the segmentation mask through a series of iterative updates. The optimization framework incorporates both image-level and user-level feedback to ensure that the resulting segmentation mask accurately reflects the user's intent.

We evaluate SwipeCut on several benchmark datasets and compare it to state-of-the-art interactive segmentation methods. Our results show that SwipeCut achieves significantly better segmentation accuracy and faster convergence rates than existing methods, while also providing a more intuitive and user-friendly experience. We also demonstrate the versatility of SwipeCut by applying it to a variety of applications, including object segmentation, instance segmentation, and semantic segmentation.

Our key contributions can be summarized as follows:

* We introduce a novel interactive segmentation method called SwipeCut that leverages diversified seed proposals to improve segmentation accuracy and efficiency.

In this paper, we explore the relationship between similar submodules and coincidence site modules in various algebraic structures. We introduce a new notion of similarity between submodules, which is based on the idea of aligning the basis elements of two submodules in a way that maximizes their overlap. This allows us to define a distance metric between submodules, which can be used to compare their similarity.

We then investigate the properties of similar submodules and show that they have several important applications in algebra and combinatorics. For example, we prove that any module with a finite number of similar submodules must have a finite composition series, and that the existence of similar submodules implies the existence of abelian subalgebras in certain algebras.

Furthermore, we study the connection between similar submodules and coincidence site modules, which are submodules that share a common subset of basis elements. We show that every coincidence site module is a direct sum of similar submodules, and that this decomposition is unique up to reordering of the factors. This result provides a new characterization of coincidence site modules, which had previously been defined using different criteria.

Finally, we discuss some potential applications of our results in coding theory and cryptography. Specifically, we demonstrate how similar submodules can be used to construct error-correcting codes with good parameters, and how the theory of coincidence site modules can be applied to the analysis of secret sharing schemes.

Overall, this paper presents a significant contribution to the field of algebraic combinatorics, and it highlights the importance of studying similarity relationships between submodules in various algebraic contexts. The novel techniques and results presented here open up new possibilities for further research in this area, and they provide valuable tools for solving problems arising in algebra, combinatorics, and computer science.

In software systems, missing method calls can indicate errors or inconsistencies in the code that can lead to unexpected behavior and bugs. Detecting these missing method calls is crucial for ensuring the reliability and maintainability of software systems. In this paper, we propose a novel approach for detecting missing method calls based on the majority rule.

Our approach leverages the observation that in well-designed software systems, method calls tend to follow a majority rule, where the majority of methods in a class are typically called from other methods in the same class. We use this property to detect missing method calls by analyzing the call graph of a program and identifying methods that are not called by any other methods in the same class.

We evaluate our approach on several real-world software systems and compare it to existing techniques for detecting missing method calls. Our results show that our approach is effective in detecting missing method calls and outperforms existing techniques in terms of accuracy and efficiency. We also demonstrate the practicality of our approach by applying it to several real-world software systems and identifying missing method calls that were not detected by existing techniques.

Our work makes several contributions to the field of software engineering. First, we introduce a novel approach for detecting missing method calls based on the majority rule. Second, we provide a thorough evaluation of our approach and demonstrate its effectiveness in detecting missing method calls. Finally, we show the practicality of our approach by applying it to real-world software systems and identifying missing method calls that were not detected by existing techniques.

Our approach can be used as a tool for software developers and maintainers to identify potential errors and inconsistencies in their code, improving the overall quality and reliability of software systems.

Au triangular nano-antennas have shown great promise for enhancing the efficiency of various optical processes, including surface-enhanced Raman scattering, fluorescence, and sensing. Here, we use CL spectroscopy to excite and image the resonant optical modes of Au triangular nano-antennas with high spatial and spectral resolution. By using a focused electron beam to excite the nano-antennas, we are able to selectively excited their resonant modes and measure their emission spectra. We demonstrate that the CL spectra of the nano-antennas exhibit a strong dependence on their size, shape, and arrangement, which allows us to infer their resonant modes and spatial distribution.

We also demonstrate the ability to image the resonant modes of the nano-antennas with high spatial resolution using a scanning transmission electron microscope (STEM). By combining the CL spectroscopy with STEM imaging, we are able to correlate the resonant modes with the morphology of the nano-antennas and gain insights into their optical properties.

Our results demonstrate the potential of CL spectroscopy for studying the optical properties of Au triangular nano-antennas and other plasmonic nanostructures. The ability to excite and image their resonant modes with high spatial and spectral resolution opens up new opportunities for optimizing their performance for various applications, including sensing, spectroscopy, and photovoltaics.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach for segmenting kidneys in ultrasound images using a dynamic graph-cuts method with integrated multiple feature maps. Accurate segmentation of kidneys is crucial for diagnosis and treatment of various renal diseases, but it remains a challenging task due to the complexity of ultrasound images. Our proposed method combines the strengths of graph-based segmentation and feature map integration to overcome previous limitations.

Firstly, we introduce a new feature extraction strategy that incorporates both intensity and texture information from ultrasound images. By integrating multiple features at different scales, our approach better captures the intricate details of the kidney structure. Subsequently, we employ a dynamic graph-cuts algorithm that leverages the spatial coherence of the image data to separate the kidney region from the background and irrelevant structures. The proposed algorithm iteratively updates the graph weights based on the evolving segmentation, ensuring optimum accuracy.

The key contribution of our work lies in the seamless integration of multi-scale feature mapping and dynamic graph-cuts, which results in improved performance compared to existing methods. We evaluate our approach on a dataset of 40 ultrasound images and achieve an average Dice similarity coefficient of 86.5%, outperforming state-of-the-art techniques. Additionally, we demonstrate the robustness of our method by applying it to images with varying imaging conditions and artifacts.

Our study demonstrates the potential of the proposed method for clinical applications where accurate kidney segmentation is critical. Future work involves further refinement of the technique to automate the entire process, reducing manual effort, and exploring its applicability to other medical imaging modalities.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to medical image segmentation using semi-supervised contrastive learning. Our method leverages the vast amount of unlabeled data available in medical imaging datasets to improve segmentation performance, while minimizing the need for labeled data.

Existing approaches to medical image segmentation rely heavily on supervised learning methods that require large quantities of labeled data. However, labeling medical images is a time-consuming and expensive process, making it challenging to collect sufficient amounts of labeled data. In contrast, contrastive learning methods have shown promising results in various computer vision tasks by utilizing large amounts of unlabeled data to learn robust representations.

Our proposed method combines semi-supervised contrastive learning with a novel self-paced learning strategy to effectively leverage both labeled and unlabled data. The self-paced learning strategy gradually increases the proportion of labeled data during training, allowing the model to adapt to the limited availability of labels. We evaluate our method on several publicly available medical image segmentation benchmarks, including brain tumor segmentation and liver segmentation.

The experimental results show that our proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art segmentation models while requiring significantly less labeled data. Additionally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in dealing with imbalanced class distribution, which is a common issue in medical image segmentation tasks.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

* A novel semi-supervised contrastive learning approach for medical image segmentation that leverages large amounts of unlabeled data.
* A self-paced learning strategy that adaptively incorporates labeled data into training, reducing the requirement for annotated data.
* State-of-the-art performance on multiple medical image segmentation benchmarks, outperforming fully supervised models while using fewer labels.
* Robustness to class imbalance, a critical issue in medical image segmentation.

This work has significant implications for improving the efficiency and accuracy of medical image segmentation tasks, enabling clinicians and researchers to make more informed decisions with reduced annotation effort.

A BRCA2 mutation that results in an atrazine resistance allele was detected and confirmed using BESPs (BEsp) (1). The mutations cause a loss of heterozygosity and lead to >10-fold increase in frequency of the mutant allele on chromosome 16q28 (chromosome rearrangement region), resulting in double amplification by base pair mismatch from three sources, both in vitro-based assays and by DNA mapping (2). Analysis of these data suggest that genomic rearrangements are common in human populations caused by mutations in atrazine resistant alleles. However, their effects can't be explained solely by base pair mismatches and a few cases were not observed under appropriate conditions, so chromosomal rearrangement will always exist until complete sequencing becomes available in a clinical situation. This represents another example illustrating how a very robust molecular marker could help explain biological variation. We used the ATRANO project (3) database (4–11) as our reference genome sequence with 838 ATs per million mapped regions and 23,890 positions between chromosomes 1 and 4. We studied the first 150 bp, excluding homologous recombination hotspots. Sequence analysis showed at least 33 additional insertion and deletion events, some affecting amino acids but most containing multiple insertions, deletions or whole-genome displacement. Using this information, we applied two approaches aimed to identify mutations responsible for BCS. (i) By modeling a combination of the ATRS and ATAP proteins and finding the sequences which encode them; (ii) by finding the bases with a major effect based on the nucleotide composition. These strategies uncovered nine different types of mutations, each contributing to one end of the spectrum and four different mutations at either extreme: the ATRS(+)/ATAP(−) substitution, G→A transversions and other combinations of nucleotides. Our results show that these alterations affect more than just the ATRS protein in humans, and thus could well provide a key mechanism in explaining why some people get BCS mutations while others do not, and provide us with new targets that may represent an evolutionary target of BCS mutations.

We present the first method to handle curvature regularity in region-based
image segmentation and inpainting that is independent of initialization.
  To this end we start from a new formulation of length-based optimization
schemes, based on surface continuation constraints, and discuss the connections
to existing schemes. The formulation is based on a \emph{cell complex} and
considers basic regions and boundary elements. The corresponding optimization
problem is cast as an integer linear program.
  We then show how the method can be extended to include curvature regularity,
again cast as an integer linear program. Here, we are considering pairs of
boundary elements to reflect curvature. Moreover, a constraint set is derived
to ensure that the boundary variables indeed reflect the boundary of the
regions described by the region variables.
  We show that by solving the linear programming relaxation one gets quite
close to the global optimum, and that curvature regularity is indeed much
better suited in the presence of long and thin objects compared to standard
length regularity.

In an online computer vision experiment, we investigated the performance and robustness benefits of detecting objects in fast non-linear images with super-bended boundary to pixel direction by means of convolutional neural networks (CNNs). In this application, three CNN classes with different levels of optimization of the nonlinearities between inputs, hidden layers and output were implemented. We obtained a training result of 93% (CV_max) on a dataset of 3,056 images, where each class of networks was trained on 20 epochs of 200 seconds each. In each convolutional layer there exist two sub layers which are connected to a single input by a simple, line-like connecting plane, thereby ensuring that every image segment represents only one object, while the other images represent many more objects. In the end, after multiple trainings such a segmentation network can predict exactly what the entire dataset of 4,560 images represented of human faces, based on the feature extraction process that takes less than 150 milliseconds. Here, the CNN architecture consists of 5 stages: object detection, feature extraction, clustering and recognition. The model-specific parameters and hyperparameters are revealed within each of these parts of the task. Our results indicate that the best performing training model had no single learning curve but was tuned to perform significantly better than the most complicated ones, indicating a strong connection between efficient implementation of the CNN algorithms and its ability to improve the performance. Using this general design scheme, such as the one described here, it has also possible to reduce training time drastically compared with conventional state-of-art approaches such as deep LSTMs or conv2d1 networks

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have been widely and successfully used
for medical image segmentation. However, CNNs are typically considered to
require large numbers of dedicated expert-segmented training volumes, which may
be limiting in practice. This work investigates whether clinically obtained
segmentations which are readily available in picture archiving and
communication systems (PACS) could provide a possible source of data to train a
CNN for segmentation of organs-at-risk (OARs) in radiotherapy treatment
planning. In such data, delineations of structures deemed irrelevant to the
target clinical use may be lacking. To overcome this issue, we use multi-label
instead of multi-class segmentation. We empirically assess how many clinical
delineations would be sufficient to train a CNN for the segmentation of OARs
and find that increasing the training set size beyond a limited number of
images leads to sharply diminishing returns. Moreover, we find that by using
multi-label segmentation, missing structures in the reference standard do not
have a negative effect on overall segmentation accuracy. These results indicate
that segmentations obtained in a clinical workflow can be used to train an
accurate OAR segmentation model.

improve the matting performance. Evaluated on these datasets, the proposed

Dense 3D visual mapping estimates as many as possible pixel depths, for each
image. This results in very dense point clouds that often contain redundant and
noisy information, especially for surfaces that are roughly planar, for
instance, the ground or the walls in the scene. In this paper we leverage on
semantic image segmentation to discriminate which regions of the scene require
simplification and which should be kept at high level of details. We propose
four different point cloud simplification methods which decimate the perceived
point cloud by relying on class-specific local and global statistics still
maintaining more points in the proximity of class boundaries to preserve the
infra-class edges and discontinuities. 3D dense model is obtained by fusing the
point clouds in a 3D Delaunay Triangulation to deal with variable point cloud
density. In the experimental evaluation we have shown that, by leveraging on
semantics, it is possible to simplify the model and diminish the noise
affecting the point clouds.

called the (edge) clique cover number of $ G $ and is denoted by $ cc(G) $. It
is an easy observation that for every line graph $ G $ with $ n $ vertices,
$cc(G)\leq n $. G. Chen et al. [Discrete Math. 219 (2000), no. 1--3, 17--26;
MR1761707] extended this observation to all quasi-line graphs and questioned if
the same assertion holds for all claw-free graphs. In this paper, using the
celebrated structure theorem of claw-free graphs due to Chudnovsky and Seymour,
we give an affirmative answer to this question for all claw-free graphs with
independence number at least three. In particular, we prove that if $ G $ is a
connected claw-free graph on $ n $ vertices with $ \alpha(G)\geq 3 $, then $
cc(G)\leq n $ and equality holds if and only if $ G $ is either the graph of
icosahedron, or the complement of a graph on $10$ vertices called twister or
the $p^{th}$ power of the cycle $ C_n $, for $1\leq p \leq \lfloor
(n-1)/3\rfloor $.

manually traced images in one imaging modality (e.g., MRI) are able to train a
segmentation network for another imaging modality (e.g., CT). In this paper, we
propose an end-to-end synthetic segmentation network (SynSeg-Net) to train a
segmentation network for a target imaging modality without having manual
labels. SynSeg-Net is trained by using (1) unpaired intensity images from
source and target modalities, and (2) manual labels only from source modality.
SynSeg-Net is enabled by the recent advances of cycle generative adversarial
networks (CycleGAN) and DCNN. We evaluate the performance of the SynSeg-Net on
two experiments: (1) MRI to CT splenomegaly synthetic segmentation for
abdominal images, and (2) CT to MRI total intracranial volume synthetic
segmentation (TICV) for brain images. The proposed end-to-end approach achieved
superior performance to two stage methods. Moreover, the SynSeg-Net achieved
comparable performance to the traditional segmentation network using target
modality labels in certain scenarios. The source code of SynSeg-Net is publicly
available (https://github.com/MASILab/SynSeg-Net).

This paper presents a comprehensive survey of data mining techniques used for social media analysis. The survey covers various aspects of social media, including text mining, sentiment analysis, opinion mining, and network analysis. The paper also discusses the challenges and opportunities associated with social media data and highlights the potential applications of data mining techniques in this domain. Overall, this survey provides a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners interested in leveraging data mining for social media analysis.

In this paper, we investigate the equivalence of multi-letter quantum finite automata (QLA) and their ability to recognize certain languages. We present several results that establish connections between various types of QLA and their classical counterparts, including the well-known notion of non-deterministic finite automata (NFA).

Firstly, we show that every deterministic QLA can be simulated by a NFA, providing a characterization of the class of languages recognizable by these devices. Subsequently, we extend this result to the probabilistic setting, demonstrating that any probabilistic QLA can be approximated by a probabilistic NFA with comparable performance guarantees. Notably, our methods in this section rely on an intricate combination of techniques from linear programming relaxations and Markov chain analysis.

Furthermore, we explore the connection between QLA and memoryless symmetries in language recognition. By introducing a suitable adaptation of the Myhill-Nerode theorem, we prove that a language is recognizable by a QLA if and only if it possesses specific properties related to spectral symmetry. This fundamental insight enables us to generalize celebrated results from algebraic combinatorics to the realm of quantum computing, ultimately leading to new insights into the computational capabilities and limitations of QLAs.

Our findings contribute significantly towards a deeper understanding of quantum formal language theory and its relationships to other areas within theoretical computer science. Particularly, they shed light on the role of quantum effects when dealing with complex patterns in data streams, with potential implications for applications such as natural language processing or information security.

The curvature tensors play an important role in understanding the geometry of a manifold. In this paper, we explore the properties and behavior of curvature tensors on Hermitian manifolds, which are complex manifolds equipped with an additional holomorphic symplectic structure. We derive expressions for various components of the Riemann tensor and analyze their significance from both mathematical and physical perspectives. Our results provide insight into the geometric structures underlying these manifolds and shed light on potential applications to fields such as string theory and condensed matter physics.

Infrared (IR) image segmentation is essential in many urban defence
applications, such as pedestrian surveillance, vehicle counting, security
monitoring, etc. Active contour model (ACM) is one of the most widely used
image segmentation tools at present, but the existing methods only utilize the
local or global single feature information of image to minimize the energy
function, which is easy to cause false segmentations in IR images. In this
paper, we propose a multi-feature driven active contour segmentation model to
handle IR images with intensity inhomogeneity. Firstly, an especially-designed
signed pressure force (SPF) function is constructed by combining the global
information calculated by global average gray information and the local
multi-feature information calculated by local entropy, local standard deviation
and gradient information. Then, we draw upon adaptive weight coefficient
calculated by local range to adjust the afore-mentioned global term and local
term. Next, the SPF function is substituted into the level set formulation
(LSF) for further evolution. Finally, the LSF converges after a finite number
of iterations, and the IR image segmentation result is obtained from the
corresponding convergence result. Experimental results demonstrate that the
presented method outperforms the state-of-the-art models in terms of precision
rate and overlapping rate in IR test images.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) have recently seen tremendous success in
various computer vision tasks. However, their application to problems with high
dimensional input and output, such as high-resolution image and video
segmentation or 3D medical imaging, has been limited by various factors.
Primarily, in the training stage, it is necessary to store network activations
for back propagation. In these settings, the memory requirements associated
with storing activations can exceed what is feasible with current hardware,
especially for problems in 3D. Motivated by the propagation of signals over
physical networks, that are governed by the hyperbolic Telegraph equation, in
this work we introduce a fully conservative hyperbolic network for problems
with high dimensional input and output. We introduce a coarsening operation
that allows completely reversible CNNs by using a learnable Discrete Wavelet
Transform and its inverse to both coarsen and interpolate the network state and
change the number of channels. We show that fully reversible networks are able
to achieve results comparable to the state of the art in 4D time-lapse hyper
spectral image segmentation and full 3D video segmentation, with a much lower
memory footprint that is a constant independent of the network depth. We also
extend the use of such networks to Variational Auto Encoders with high
resolution input and output.

The requirements to achieve high detection efficiency (above 50\%) and
gigahertz (GHz) frame rate for the proposed 42-keV X-ray free-electron laser
(XFEL) at Los Alamos are summarized. Direct detection scenarios using C
(diamond), Si, Ge and GaAs semiconductor sensors are analyzed. Single-photon
counting (SPC) mode and weak SPC mode using Si can potentially meet the
efficiency and frame rate requirements and be useful to both photoelectric
absorption and Compton physics as the photon energy increases. Multilayer
three-dimensional (3D) detector architecture, as a possible means to realize
SPC modes, is compared with the widely used two-dimensional (2D) hybrid planar
electrode structure and 3D deeply entrenched electrode architecture.
Demonstration of thin film cameras less than 100-$\mu$m thick with onboard thin
ASICs could be an initial step to realize multilayer 3D detectors and SPC modes
for XFELs.

The BEC-BCS crossover for a NJL model with diquark interactions is studied in
the presence of an external magnetic field. Particular attention is paid to
different regularization schemes used in the literature. A thorough comparison
of results is performed for the case of a cold and magnetized two-color NJL
model. According to our results, the critical chemical potential for the BEC
transition exhibits a clear inverse magnetic catalysis effect for magnetic
fields in the range $ 1 \lesssim eB/m_\pi^2 \lesssim 20 $. As for the BEC-BCS
crossover, the corresponding critical chemical potential is very weakly
sensitive to magnetic fields up to $eB \sim 9\ m_\pi^2$, showing a much smaller
inverse magnetic catalysis as compared to the BEC transition, and displays a
strong magnetic catalysis from this point on.

This academic paper proposes a new method for measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution (QKD) using modified coherent states. The approach eliminates the need for traditional measuring devices, thereby enhancing security and overcoming limitations associated with previous QKD protocols. The authors demonstrate the feasibility of this technique through theoretical analysis and simulations, paving the way for practical implementation in future quantum communication systems.

``continuous action'' of $\operatorname {Ham} (M, \omega) $ on the Fukaya
category of a closed monotone symplectic manifold. Here we show that this
action is generally homotopically non-trivial, i.e implicitly the main part of
a conjecture of Teleman. We use this to give various applications. For example
we find new curvature constraint phenomena for smooth and singular
$\mathcal{G}$-connections on principal $\mathcal{G}$-bundles over $S ^{4}$,
where $\mathcal{G}$ is $\operatorname {PU} (2)$ or $\operatorname {Ham} (S ^{2}
)$. Even for the classical group $\operatorname {PU} (2)$, these phenomena are

In this paper, we propose a novel approach for estimating food portion sizes from monocular images using cross-domain feature adaptation. Existing methods for food portion estimation rely on manual annotation of portion sizes, which can be time-consuming and expensive to obtain. In contrast, our approach leverages large-scale datasets of images with object annotations to learn a model that can accurately estimate portion sizes from a single monocular image.

We address the challenge of adapting features from object-annotated images to the target task of portion estimation by proposing a domain adaptation technique that aligns features across domains using a shared embedding space. Our approach consists of two stages: 1) pre-training a feature extractor on a large-scale object detection dataset, and 2) fine-tuning the feature extractor on a smaller dataset of images with annotated portion sizes.

We evaluate our approach on several datasets with varying levels of complexity and show that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods for food portion estimation. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of cross-domain feature adaptation for addressing the challenge of limited annotated data in the target domain. We also perform a thorough analysis of the contribution of different components of our approach, providing insights into the importance of domain adaptation and the choice of feature extractor architecture.

Our work has important implications for the development of automated food portion estimation systems, which can help address issues related to food waste, nutrition, and health. The proposed approach can be applied to a wide range of applications, including food portion estimation in restaurants, cafeterias, and home environments.

In this paper, we present YouTube-VOS, a large-scale video object segmentation benchmark that provides a comprehensive evaluation framework for video object segmentation (VOS) algorithms. VOS is an important task in computer vision that involves separating objects of interest from their background and other objects in a video sequence. Despite its significance, there is a lack of large-scale benchmarks for VOS, which hinders the development and evaluation of VOS algorithms.

YouTube-VOS addresses this issue by providing a dataset of 4,417 video clips, totaling 150,000 frames, with annotated objects across various categories, including animals, vehicles, and humans. The dataset is diverse, covering various scenarios such as object movement, occlusion, and cluttered backgrounds. We also introduce a new evaluation metric, called Video Object Segmentation Quality (VOSQ), which combines both temporal and spatial metrics to provide a comprehensive measure of VOS performance.

We evaluate several state-of-the-art VOS algorithms on YouTube-VOS and analyze their performance. Our results show that existing VOS algorithms struggle with objects that undergo significant motion or deformation, and that there is a need for better algorithms that can handle these challenges. We also demonstrate the utility of YouTube-VOS in evaluating the performance of VOS algorithms under different scenarios and provide insights into the strengths and weaknesses of various approaches.

YouTube-VOS is a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners working on VOS, and we believe it will play an important role in advancing the field of video object segmentation. Our hope is that YouTube-VOS will encourage the development of more sophisticated VOS algorithms that can handle the challenges of real-world videos and contribute to various applications such as video surveillance, autonomous driving, and video editing.

Abstract: Simultaneous core partition algorithms are used to identify which physical regions may be partitioned onto a chip, either manually or automatically using various threshold constraints that enforce separation of memory and data space within the computer circuit. The present work presents CorePairs, an efficient but complex algorithm based on coherency principles and in the context of symmetric multiprocessing (SMP) software defined networking. CorePairs finds all possible cores within a set of constraints, with an algorithm that can effectively discover concurrent execution as long it has access to many different instructions in parallel. In particular, CorePairs can avoid memory leaks by finding all memory references that lead to multiple core operations without also taking into account shared caches. Finally, CorePairs provides several interesting benchmark results and provides clear guidance regarding the efficiency requirements of future performance-oriented ASIC solutions. Key words: corepairs, synchronously coherent software virtual machines.

With the recent advances in complex networks theory, graph-based techniques
for image segmentation has attracted great attention recently. In order to
segment the image into meaningful connected components, this paper proposes an
image segmentation general framework using complex networks based community
detection algorithms. If we consider regions as communities, using community
detection algorithms directly can lead to an over-segmented image. To address
this problem, we start by splitting the image into small regions using an
initial segmentation. The obtained regions are used for building the complex
network. To produce meaningful connected components and detect homogeneous
communities, some combinations of color and texture based features are employed
in order to quantify the regions similarities. To sum up, the network of
regions is constructed adaptively to avoid many small regions in the image, and
then, community detection algorithms are applied on the resulting adaptive
similarity matrix to obtain the final segmented image. Experiments are
conducted on Berkeley Segmentation Dataset and four of the most influential
community detection algorithms are tested. Experimental results have shown that
the proposed general framework increases the segmentation performances compared
to some existing methods.

This paper proposes a novel approach to image segmentation using an efficient evolutionary algorithm. The proposed method utilizes the principles of natural selection and genetics to search for the optimal segmentation of an image. The evolutionary process is guided by a fitness function that rewards segments with high accuracy and convergence, leading to improved performance compared to traditional segmentation methods.

The proposed method consists of three stages: (1) initialization, where the image is divided into random regions, (2) evolution, where the regions are evolved through a process of mutation and crossover, and (3) refinement, where the resulting segments are fine-tuned using a conventional segmentation technique.

Experiments conducted on several benchmark images demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in terms of both efficiency and accuracy. The results show that the proposed method outperforms traditional methods in terms of computational time and produces segments with higher accuracy. Additionally, the method is robust to noise and varying illumination conditions, making it suitable for real-world applications.

The main contribution of this work lies in its ability to efficiently explore the vast solution space of image segmentation problems using an evolutionary algorithm. By leveraging the power of natural selection, the proposed method can find good solutions quickly and accurately, even for complex images. As such, the proposed method represents a significant advancement in the field of image segmentation and has important implications for applications such as object recognition, tracking, and scene understanding.

We characterize Leavitt path algebras which are Rickart, Baer, and Baer
$*$-rings in terms of the properties of the underlying graph. In order to treat
non-unital Leavitt path algebras as well, we generalize these
annihilator-related properties to locally unital rings and provide a more
general characterizations of Leavitt path algebras which are locally Rickart,
locally Baer, and locally Baer $*$-rings. Leavitt path algebras are also graded
rings and we formulate the graded versions of these annihilator-related
properties and characterize Leavitt path algebras having those properties as
well.
  Our characterizations provide a quick way to generate a wide variety of
examples of rings. For example, creating a Baer and not a Baer $*$-ring, a
Rickart $*$-ring which is not Baer, or a Baer and not a Rickart $*$-ring, is
straightforward using the graph-theoretic properties from our results. In
addition, our characterizations showcase more properties which distinguish
behavior of Leavitt path algebras from their $C^*$-algebra counterparts. For
example, while a graph $C^*$-algebra is Baer (and a Baer $*$-ring) if and only
if the underlying graph is finite and acyclic, a Leavitt path algebra is Baer
if and only if the graph is finite and no cycle has an exit, and it is a Baer
$*$-ring if and only if the graph is a finite disjoint union of graphs which
are finite and acyclic or loops.

In this work, we explore the issue of the inter-annotator agreement for
training and evaluating automated segmentation of skin lesions. We explore what
different degrees of agreement represent, and how they affect different use
cases for segmentation. We also evaluate how conditioning the ground truths
using different (but very simple) algorithms may help to enhance agreement and
may be appropriate for some use cases. The segmentation of skin lesions is a
cornerstone task for automated skin lesion analysis, useful both as an
end-result to locate/detect the lesions and as an ancillary task for lesion
classification. Lesion segmentation, however, is a very challenging task, due
not only to the challenge of image segmentation itself but also to the
difficulty in obtaining properly annotated data. Detecting accurately the
borders of lesions is challenging even for trained humans, since, for many
lesions, those borders are fuzzy and ill-defined. Using lesions and annotations
from the ISIC Archive, we estimate inter-annotator agreement for skin-lesion
segmentation and propose several simple procedures that may help to improve
inter-annotator agreement if used to condition the ground truths.

In this paper, we present a novel approach for reconstructing the intrinsic $B$-mode power of a signal from its spectral levels. The $B$-mode power, which represents the power spectral density of a signal in the frequency domain, is a crucial aspect of signal analysis in various fields such as signal processing, communication systems, and biomedical engineering.

Traditional methods for estimating the $B$-mode power rely on the assumption that the signal is stationary and ergodic, and often require a large amount of data to achieve accurate estimates. However, in many real-world applications, signals are non-stationary and/or non-ergodic, and the available data may be limited.

Our proposed method, called spectral level reconstruction, addresses these limitations by exploiting the properties of the spectral levels of a signal. We demonstrate that the $B$-mode power can be accurately reconstructed from the spectral levels, without assuming stationarity or ergodicity, and with a reduced amount of data.

The proposed method is validated through simulations and real-world signal processing examples, including the analysis of electroencephalography (EEG) signals and speech signals. The results show that our method outperforms traditional methods in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency, especially when dealing with non-stationary and/or non-ergodic signals.

The paper also provides a theoretical analysis of the proposed method, including the convergence properties of the reconstruction algorithm and the relationship between the spectral levels and the $B$-mode power.

Overall, this paper presents a novel and effective approach for reconstructing the intrinsic $B$-mode power of a signal from its spectral levels, which can be useful in various applications where signal analysis is crucial.

> We present a new method for enforcing statistics in a generative model. Our method is based on a new energy function that is a lower bound on the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the model and the target distribution. The energy function is convex and can be minimized efficiently. We show that the energy function is a lower bound on the Kullback-Leibler divergence for any distribution that is a mixture of Gaussians. We also show that the energy function is a lower bound on the Kullback-Leibler divergence for any distribution that is a mixture of Gaussians and a uniform distribution. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on a variety of tasks, including image generation, image-to-image translation, and text generation.

## 2. Introduction

Generative models are a class of machine learning models that are used to generate new data that is similar to the training data. They are often used in applications such as image generation, text generation, and speech synthesis. One of the key challenges in generative modeling is to enforce the desired statistics of the generated data. For example, in image generation, it is often desired to enforce the distribution of the generated images to be similar to the distribution of the training images. This paper proposes a novel image segmentation framework, called Co-Seg, that is robust against label corruption. Existing segmentation methods rely heavily on high-quality annotated data, which can be difficult to obtain, especially in medical imaging. However, these annotations can become corrupted during the annotation process or when dataset are merged, leading to significant degradations in performance. In this work, we address this problem by introducing a co-segmentation approach that jointly learns image segmentation and robustness againstlabel noise. Our method consists of two main components: (1) a noise-invariant feature learning module that extracts features insensitive to label noise, and (2) a robust loss function that adaptively adjusts the penalty term based on the confidence of the prediction.

We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets with various types of label corruptions and demonstrate its superiority over state-of-the-art methods. Notably, Co-Seg achieved an average dice similarity coefficient of 0.853 on Liver-trasined Dataset, outperforming the second-best method by a margin of 6.4%. Furthermore, our ablation studies show that both modules contribute significantly to the improvement in robustness and accuracy. 

Our work has important implications for real-world applications where labeled data may not always be reliable. With Co-seg, we can reduce the risk of propagating errors in scenarios such as autonomous driving, medical diagnosis, and robotics, providing a safer and more trustworthy solution for image segmentation tasks.

In this paper, we present a novel approach to semi-supervised 3D semantic segmentation of medical images, which leverages shape information to improve accuracy. Our proposed method, called Shape-Aware Semi-Supervised 3D Semantic Segmentation (SASS), incorporates shape prior knowledge into the segmentation process through a novel graph convolutional network architecture. SASS takes advantage of both sparse annotated data and abundant unannotated data to learn a robust representation of the underlying anatomy, leading to improved performance compared to traditional fully supervised or semi-supervised segmentation approaches.

Notably, as few as 10% labeled examples are required to achieve high performance on some tasks, making it particularly useful for applications where manual annotations are difficult and expensive to obtain.

The main contributions of this work are twofold: first, the introduction of a novel graph convolutional network architecture that fuses instance-wise shape information with image features; second, the development of an effective training strategy that combines adversarial and self-supervised learning objectives to optimize the segmentation model using limited annotated data. This study has important implications for future research in medical image analysis, and more broadly, for developing AI algorithms that can effectively leverage large amounts of weakly labeled data for complex task automation.

We present a study on the large scale pattern of optical quasar polarization vectors using a sample of over 10,000 quasars from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) DR7 catalog. Our analysis reveals a striking correlation between the orientation of quasar polarization vectors and the distribution of galaxies in the universe. We find that the polarization vectors are preferentially aligned with the surrounding galactic structures, showing a strong correlation signal on scales of up to several hundred megaparsecs. This phenomenon is observed to be more pronounced in regions of high galaxy density and appears to be independent of redshift or quasar luminosity. The observed large scale pattern suggests that quasar activity may be influenced by the global structure of the universe, potentially linked to the formation and evolution of galaxy clusters. These results provide new insights into the role of quasars as tracers of cosmic history and offer opportunities for novel tests of cosmological models.

Our findings indicate that the PCQM offers a computationally economical alternative to conventional statistical analyses without sacrificing accuracy, rendering it particularly useful when dealing with big data or limited computing resources.

We apply the Zipf power law to financial time series of WIG20 index daily
changes (open-close). Thanks to the mapping of time series signal into the
sequence of 2k+1 'spin-like' states, where k=0, 1/2, 1, 3/2, ..., we are able
to describe any time series increments, with almost arbitrary accuracy, as the
one of such 'spin-like' states. This procedure leads in the simplest
non-trivial case (k = 1/2) to the binary data projection. More sophisticated
projections are also possible and mentioned in the article. The introduced
formalism allows then to use Zipf power law to describe the intrinsic structure
of time series. The fast algorithm for this implementation was constructed by
us within Matlab^{TM} software. The method, called Zipf strategy, is then
applied in the simplest case k = 1/2 to WIG 20 open and close daily data to
make short-term predictions for forthcoming index changes. The results of
forecast effectiveness are presented with respect to different time window
sizes and partition divisions (word lengths in Zipf language). Finally, the
various investment strategies improving ROI (return of investment) for WIG20
futures are proposed. We show that the Zipf strategy is the appropriate and
very effective tool to make short-term predictions and therefore, to evaluate
short-term investments on the basis of historical stock index data. Our
findings support also the existence of long memory in financial data, exceeding
the known in literature 3 days span limit.

systematic study of almost Abelian Lie groups and algebras from mathematics

ideals, automorphisms and derivations, Lie orthogonal operators and quadratic
Casimir elements are described exactly.

This paper studies the context aggregation problem in semantic image
segmentation. The existing researches focus on improving the pixel
representations by aggregating the contextual information within individual
images. Though impressive, these methods neglect the significance of the
representations of the pixels of the corresponding class beyond the input
image. To address this, this paper proposes to mine the contextual information
beyond individual images to further augment the pixel representations. We first
set up a feature memory module, which is updated dynamically during training,
to store the dataset-level representations of various categories. Then, we
learn class probability distribution of each pixel representation under the
supervision of the ground-truth segmentation. At last, the representation of
each pixel is augmented by aggregating the dataset-level representations based
on the corresponding class probability distribution. Furthermore, by utilizing
the stored dataset-level representations, we also propose a representation
consistent learning strategy to make the classification head better address
intra-class compactness and inter-class dispersion. The proposed method could
be effortlessly incorporated into existing segmentation frameworks (e.g., FCN,
PSPNet, OCRNet and DeepLabV3) and brings consistent performance improvements.
Mining contextual information beyond image allows us to report state-of-the-art
performance on various benchmarks: ADE20K, LIP, Cityscapes and COCO-Stuff.

We discuss the development, verification, and performance of a GPU

instruction multiple data (SIMD) architecture of graphic processing units. The
time integration is accelerated by local time stepping based on a multi-rate
Adams-Bashforth scheme. A total variational bounded limiter is adopted for
nonlinear stability of the numerical scheme. This limiter is coupled with a
mass and momentum conserving positivity preserving limiter for the special
treatment of a dry or partially wet element in the triangulation. Accuracy,

compare the performance of the kernels expressed in a portable threading
language OCCA, when cross compiled with OpenCL, CUDA, and OpenMP at runtime.

Strategy improvement is a widely-used and well-studied class of algorithms
for solving graph-based infinite games. These algorithms are parameterized by a
switching rule, and one of the most natural rules is "all switches" which
switches as many edges as possible in each iteration. Continuing a recent line
of work, we study all-switches strategy improvement from the perspective of
computational complexity. We consider two natural decision problems, both of
which have as input a game $G$, a starting strategy $s$, and an edge $e$. The
problems are: 1.) The edge switch problem, namely, is the edge $e$ ever
switched by all-switches strategy improvement when it is started from $s$ on
game $G$? 2.) The optimal strategy problem, namely, is the edge $e$ used in the
final strategy that is found by strategy improvement when it is started from
$s$ on game $G$? We show $\mathtt{PSPACE}$-completeness of the edge switch
problem and optimal strategy problem for the following settings: Parity games
with the discrete strategy improvement algorithm of V\"oge and Jurdzi\'nski;
mean-payoff games with the gain-bias algorithm [14,37]; and discounted-payoff
games and simple stochastic games with their standard strategy improvement
algorithms. We also show $\mathtt{PSPACE}$-completeness of an analogous problem
to edge switch for the bottom-antipodal algorithm for finding the sink of an
Acyclic Unique Sink Orientation on a cube.

We present a time series classification algorithm similar to one proposed by Yang et al. (2014) with three main differences: 1) A high precision image segmentations are made in the presence of blood vessels, where the model takes only an edge between two adjacent images of liver tissue and identifies the region containing the lesion or tumors. It performs well in practice but does not consider non-bifurcated images like intraabdominal or hepatic veins as they cannot be detected using the same approach but could yield very useful information about disease evolution within a specimen. Therefore it is considered important that a comprehensive study on these regions needs to be performed, especially when doing more complicated time series graphs such as log scale graphs of tumor burden, since the latter can have thousands of nodes. 2) The current method involves some image preprocessing steps prior to identifying an individual node or clusters of node values. These may include filtering out undesirable background objects (blobs, stripes) either due to their pixelization in the resulting output, or for better performance if the training data contains low frequency noise, so all possible combinations are potentially examined before finding relevant clusters and thus provide for better error recovery after computing many small number of image segments. These features should improve the performance further although we are currently investigating ways how to avoid this cost while still providing good results. 3) In contrast to previous approaches our model learns through feedback from its users - it produces classification labels automatically by evaluating each new instance against a calibration distribution and also penalizes any incorrect responses by reclassifying them again until learning rules converge. We demonstrate several applications related to the use of the trained model to identify cancerous tumours based on multiple levels of histology and images, including analysis of time trends over whole liver samples, visualization of tumor burden in time histograms and evaluation of the accuracy and confidence among various algorithms applied to the extracted datasets.

Deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have been shown to perform
extremely well at a variety of tasks including subtasks of autonomous driving
such as image segmentation and object classification. However, networks
designed for these tasks typically require vast quantities of training data and
long training periods to converge. We investigate the design rationale behind
end-to-end driving network designs by proposing and comparing three small and
computationally inexpensive deep end-to-end neural network models that generate
driving control signals directly from input images. In contrast to prior work
that segments the autonomous driving task, our models take on a novel approach
to the autonomous driving problem by utilizing deep and thin Fully
Convolutional Nets (FCNs) with recurrent neural nets and low parameter counts
to tackle a complex end-to-end regression task predicting both steering and
acceleration commands. In addition, we include layers optimized for
classification to allow the networks to implicitly learn image semantics. We
show that the resulting networks use 3x fewer parameters than the most recent
comparable end-to-end driving network and 500x fewer parameters than the
AlexNet variations and converge both faster and to lower losses while
maintaining robustness against overfitting.

In the second stage, the trained FCN is used to segment new, unseen images in an interactive manner. The user interacts with the system by providing rough annotations of the object boundaries, which are then used to fine-tune the FCN's predictions.

We evaluate our approach on several datasets of medical images, including MRI scans, CT scans, and microscopy images. The results show that our method outperforms traditional segmentation methods in terms of both accuracy and efficiency. We also demonstrate the versatility of our approach by applying it to various medical image segmentation tasks, such as tumor detection, organ segmentation, and cell detection.

Our main contribution is the development of a fully convolutional neural network that can learn to segment medical images through interactive user feedback. The proposed method has the potential to significantly reduce the time and effort required for medical image segmentation, making it a valuable tool for researchers, clinicians, and practitioners in the field.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach for top-down salient object detection (SOD) that combines the strengths of classifier-based and gradient-based methods. 4. Flexibility: Our top-down design allows for natural extensions towards video SOD, instance segmentation, and other related tasks.

In this paper, we demonstrate a novel approach to spectral engineering using coupled microcavities, enabling active control of resonant mode-splitting. By harnessing the interplay between cavity-coupling and nonlinearity, we show that the resonant modes of the system can be actively controlled, leading to a significant enhancement of the splitting phenomenon.

Using a theoretical model, we first investigate the underlying physics of the coupled microcavity system and reveal the key mechanisms responsible for the observed mode-splitting behavior. We then experimentally validate our findings using a state-of-the-art coupled microcavity platform, and demonstrate the ability to actively control the splitting phenomenon through careful tuning of the cavity-coupling strength and nonlinearity.

Our results have significant implications for the development of novel optical devices and applications, including tunable filters, sensors, and nonlinear optical sources. By enabling active control of resonant mode-splitting, our approach offers a promising route towards the realization of highly efficient and versatile photonic devices that can be dynamically reconfigured to meet specific performance requirements.

In addition, our work sheds new light on the fundamental physics of coupled cavity systems, and highlights the potential of exploiting nonlinearity and coupling effects for tailoring the spectral properties of photonic devices. The insights gained from this study are expected to inspire new avenues of research in the field of photonics, and contribute to the development of novel technologies with significant societal impact.

Selective weeding is one of the key challenges in the field of agriculture
robotics. To accomplish this task, a farm robot should be able to accurately
detect plants and to distinguish them between crop and weeds. Most of the
promising state-of-the-art approaches make use of appearance-based models
trained on large annotated datasets. Unfortunately, creating large agricultural
datasets with pixel-level annotations is an extremely time consuming task,
actually penalizing the usage of data-driven techniques. In this paper, we face
this problem by proposing a novel and effective approach that aims to
dramatically minimize the human intervention needed to train the detection and
classification algorithms. The idea is to procedurally generate large synthetic
training datasets randomizing the key features of the target environment (i.e.,
crop and weed species, type of soil, light conditions). More specifically, by
tuning these model parameters, and exploiting a few real-world textures, it is
possible to render a large amount of realistic views of an artificial
agricultural scenario with no effort. The generated data can be directly used
to train the model or to supplement real-world images. We validate the proposed
methodology by using as testbed a modern deep learning based image segmentation
architecture. We compare the classification results obtained using both real
and synthetic images as training data. The reported results confirm the
effectiveness and the potentiality of our approach.
