This paper proposes an innovative approach to automatic color image segmentation, leveraging a square elemental region-based seeded region growing and merging method. The proposed technique divides the image into small regions, known as seed regions, which are used as starting points for the segmentation process. These seed regions are then grown and merged using a carefully designed algorithm that takes into account both spatial and spectral information from the image.

The proposed method is robust to noise and can handle images with varying levels of complexity and texture. It also does not require any prior knowledge about the number of classes or boundaries in the image, making it highly versatile and applicable to a wide range of applications.

Experiments were conducted on several benchmark datasets, including natural scenes and objects, and the results demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed method compared to existing techniques. The obtained segmentation accuracy and computational time are superior to those of other approaches, particularly when dealing with large images.

This research contributes to the field of computer vision by introducing a novel solution forautomatic color image segmentation that combines the benefits of region-growing and merging methods while overcoming their limitations. The presented technique has significant potential for applications such as object recognition, tracking, and classification.

Deep convolutional neural networks have driven substantial advancements in
the automatic understanding of images. Requiring a large collection of images
and their associated annotations is one of the main bottlenecks limiting the
adoption of deep networks. In the task of medical image segmentation, requiring
pixel-level semantic annotations performed by human experts exacerbate this
difficulty. This paper proposes a new framework to train a fully convolutional
segmentation network from a large set of cheap unreliable annotations and a
small set of expert-level clean annotations. We propose a spatially adaptive
reweighting approach to treat clean and noisy pixel-level annotations
commensurately in the loss function. We deploy a meta-learning approach to
assign higher importance to pixels whose loss gradient direction is closer to
those of clean data. Our experiments on training the network using segmentation
ground truth corrupted with different levels of annotation noise show how
spatial reweighting improves the robustness of deep networks to noisy
annotations.

The article "O-minimal Hauptvermutung for Polyhedra II" presents a continuation of the study initiated in the first part of the paper, focusing on the O-minimal hypothesis for polyhedra. The authors delve deeper into the investigation of the topological and combinatorial properties of polyhedral varieties, exploiting the versatile framework of O-minimality.

The paper's main objectives are twofold. Firstly, the authors strive to advance the understanding of the structure of polynomial equations defining polyhedral varieties by leveraging tools from O-minimal geometry. Secondly, they aim to demonstrate how this theory can be applied to tackle complex problems in enumerative combinatorics and algebraic geometry that involve polyhedra.

To achieve these goals, the authors engage in an intricate process of refining their predecessors' work. They introduce novel techniques and sharpen existing ones, leading to significant advancements in the field. Specifically, they provide new evidence supporting the O-minimal Hauptvermutung for a broader class of polyhedra than previously considered. This contribution has far-reaching consequences, as it tightens the connections between disparate areas of mathematics and deepens our knowledge of their interplay.

Ultimately, the findings scattered throughout "O-minimal Hauptvermutung for Polyhedra II" have profound implications surpassing the realm of polyhedra alone. They illuminate fundamental aspects of algebraic geometry, combinatorics, and geometric model theory, paving the way for fresh research opportunities and stimulating further developments within these densely connected fields.

The segmentation of nanoscale electron microscopy (EM) images is crucial but
challenging in connectomics. Recent advances in deep learning have demonstrated
the significant potential of automatic segmentation for tera-scale EM images.
However, none of the existing segmentation methods are error-free, and they
require proofreading, which is typically implemented as an interactive,
semi-automatic process via manual intervention. Herein, we propose a fully
automatic proofreading method based on reinforcement learning. The main idea is
to model the human decision process in proofreading using a reinforcement agent
to achieve fully automatic proofreading. We systematically design the proposed
system by combining multiple reinforcement learning agents in a hierarchical
manner, where each agent focuses only on a specific task while preserving
dependency between agents. Furthermore, we also demonstrate that the episodic
task setting of reinforcement learning can efficiently manage a combination of
merge and split errors concurrently presented in the input. We demonstrate the
efficacy of the proposed system by comparing it with state-of-the-art
proofreading methods using various testing examples.

Automatic parsing of anatomical objects in X-ray images is critical to many
clinical applications in particular towards image-guided invention and workflow
automation. Existing deep network models require a large amount of labeled
data. However, obtaining accurate pixel-wise labeling in X-ray images relies
heavily on skilled clinicians due to the large overlaps of anatomy and the
complex texture patterns. On the other hand, organs in 3D CT scans preserve
clearer structures as well as sharper boundaries and thus can be easily
delineated. In this paper, we propose a novel model framework for learning
automatic X-ray image parsing from labeled CT scans. Specifically, a Dense
Image-to-Image network (DI2I) for multi-organ segmentation is first trained on
X-ray like Digitally Reconstructed Radiographs (DRRs) rendered from 3D CT
volumes. Then we introduce a Task Driven Generative Adversarial Network
(TD-GAN) architecture to achieve simultaneous style transfer and parsing for
unseen real X-ray images. TD-GAN consists of a modified cycle-GAN substructure
for pixel-to-pixel translation between DRRs and X-ray images and an added
module leveraging the pre-trained DI2I to enforce segmentation consistency. The
TD-GAN framework is general and can be easily adapted to other learning tasks.
In the numerical experiments, we validate the proposed model on 815 DRRs and
153 topograms. While the vanilla DI2I without any adaptation fails completely
on segmenting the topograms, the proposed model does not require any topogram
labels and is able to provide a promising average dice of 85% which achieves
the same level accuracy of supervised training (88%).

In this study, we investigate Coulomb screening effects on nuclear reactions during linear coasting nucleosynthesis. Our results highlight the importance of including electromagnetic interaction physics in models of heavy element formation in stellar environments. The implications of our findings are discussed with respect to current observations and future experiments aimed at probing the early universe's chemical composition.

America has a massive railway system. As of 2006, U.S. freight railroads have
140,490 route- miles of standard gauge, but maintaining such a huge system and
eliminating any dangers, like reduced track stability and poor drainage, caused
by railway ballast degradation require huge amount of labor. The traditional
way to quantify the degradation of ballast is to use an index called Fouling
Index (FI) through ballast sampling and sieve analysis. However, determining
the FI values in lab is very time-consuming and laborious, but with the help of
recent development in the field of computer vision, a novel method for a
potential machine-vison based ballast inspection system can be employed that
can hopefully replace the traditional mechanical method. The new machine-vision
approach analyses the images of the in-service ballasts, and then utilizes
image segmentation algorithm to get ballast segments. By comparing the segment
results and their corresponding FI values, this novel method produces a
machine-vision-based index that has the best-fit relation with FI. The
implementation details of how this algorithm works are discussed in this
report.

The exchange graph of a cluster algebra encodes the combinatorics of
mutations of clusters. Through the recent "categorifications" of cluster
algebras using representation theory one obtains a whole variety of exchange
graphs associated with objects such as a finite-dimensional algebra or a
differential graded algebra concentrated in non-positive degrees. These
constructions often come from variations of the concept of tilting, the
vertices of the exchange graph being torsion pairs, t-structures, silting
objects, support $\tau$-tilting modules and so on. All these exchange graphs
stemming from representation theory have the additional feature that they are
the Hasse quiver of a partial order which is naturally defined for the objects.
In this sense, the exchange graphs studied in this article can be considered as
a generalization or as a completion of the poset of tilting modules which has
been studied by Happel and Unger. The goal of this article is to axiomatize the
thus obtained structure of an ordered exchange graph, to present the various
constructions of ordered exchange graphs and to relate them among each other.

We consider inference for misaligned multivariate functional data that
represents the same underlying curve, but where the functional samples have
systematic differences in shape. In this paper we introduce a new class of
generally applicable models where warping effects are modeled through nonlinear
transformation of latent Gaussian variables and systematic shape differences
are modeled by Gaussian processes. To model cross-covariance between sample
coordinates we introduce a class of low-dimensional cross-covariance structures
suitable for modeling multivariate functional data. We present a method for
doing maximum-likelihood estimation in the models and apply the method to three
data sets. The first data set is from a motion tracking system where the
spatial positions of a large number of body-markers are tracked in
three-dimensions over time. The second data set consists of height and weight
measurements for Danish boys. The third data set consists of three-dimensional
spatial hand paths from a controlled obstacle-avoidance experiment. We use the
developed method to estimate the cross-covariance structure, and use a
classification setup to demonstrate that the method outperforms
state-of-the-art methods for handling misaligned curve data.

In this paper, we present a purely algebraic approach to the generalized Jacobian conjecture, which states that for a smooth projective variety X over a field k, the Albanese variety of X is isogenous to a product of simpler algebraic varieties, called the Jacobian factors. Our approach avoids the use of complex analytic tools, such as Hodge theory and harmonic representatives, and instead relies solely on algebraic geometry and number theory.

We first establish a new criterion for the existence of Jacobian factors, which allows us to construct them explicitly in terms of the cohomology ring of X. We then show that these factors are compatible with the Albanese variety, in the sense that they induce a morphism from the Albanese variety to the product of the Jacobian factors.

Our main result is the proof of the generalized Jacobian conjecture for a large class of varieties, including all smooth projective surfaces and all varieties with a rational singularity. We also provide examples of varieties that do not satisfy the conjecture, demonstrating its optimality.

Our approach has several advantages over previous work on the subject. First, it provides a conceptual understanding of the generalized Jacobian conjecture, highlighting its deep connections to algebraic geometry and number theory. Second, it offers a new perspective on the structure of the Albanese variety, which we believe will be useful in the study of other questions in algebraic geometry. Finally, our results provide a solid foundation for further research in this area, opening up new avenues for investigation and generalization.

In conclusion, our paper presents a significant advancement in the study of the generalized Jacobian conjecture, providing a purely algebraic approach that is both conceptually satisfying and technically powerful. We believe that our results will be of interest to researchers in algebraic geometry, number theory, and related fields, and that they will contribute to a deeper understanding of the rich and fascinating interplay between these areas of mathematics.

We study the phase diagram of the spin-3/2 Blume-Emery-Griffiths model on a
honeycomb lattice by Monte Carlo simulations in order to verify the presence of
some peculiar features predicted by the effective field theory (EFT) with
correlations. The locations of the order-disorder phase boundaries are
estimated from thermal variations of the magnetic susceptibility curves. It is
found that for positive values of the biquadratic interactions the critical
boundary shows a discontinuous character as a function of the single-ion
anisotropy strength, in line with the EFT expectations. However, for negative
values of the biquadratic interactions the step-like variation of the critical
frontier predicted by EFT was not reproduced.

Pre-training a recognition model with contrastive learning on a large dataset
of unlabeled data has shown great potential to boost the performance of a
downstream task, e.g., image classification. However, in domains such as
medical imaging, collecting unlabeled data can be challenging and expensive. In
this work, we propose to adapt contrastive learning to work with meta-label
annotations, for improving the model's performance in medical image
segmentation even when no additional unlabeled data is available. Meta-labels
such as the location of a 2D slice in a 3D MRI scan or the type of device used,
often come for free during the acquisition process. We use the meta-labels for
pre-training the image encoder as well as to regularize a semi-supervised
training, in which a reduced set of annotated data is used for training.
Finally, to fully exploit the weak annotations, a self-paced learning approach
is used to help the learning and discriminate useful labels from noise. Results
on three different medical image segmentation datasets show that our approach:
i) highly boosts the performance of a model trained on a few scans, ii)
outperforms previous contrastive and semi-supervised approaches, and iii)
reaches close to the performance of a model trained on the full data.

Recently, state-of-the-art results have been achieved in semantic
segmentation using fully convolutional networks (FCNs). Most of these networks
employ encoder-decoder style architecture similar to U-Net and are trained with
images and the corresponding segmentation maps as a pixel-wise classification
task. Such frameworks only exploit class information by using the ground truth
segmentation maps. In this paper, we propose a multi-task learning framework
with the main aim of exploiting structural and spatial information along with
the class information. We modify the decoder part of the FCN to exploit class
information and the structural information as well. We intend to do this while
also keeping the parameters of the network as low as possible. We obtain the
structural information using either of the two ways: i) using the contour map
and ii) using the distance map, both of which can be obtained from ground truth
segmentation maps with no additional annotation costs. We also explore
different ways in which distance maps can be computed and study the effects of
different distance maps on the segmentation performance. We also experiment
extensively on two different medical image segmentation applications: i.e i)
using color fundus images for optic disc and cup segmentation and ii) using
endoscopic images for polyp segmentation. Through our experiments, we report
results comparable to, and in some cases performing better than the current
state-of-the-art architectures and with an order of 2x reduction in the number
of parameters.

Abstract This study addresses the problem of medical image segmentation through cross modality convolutional neural networks (CNNs). In particular, it presents an algorithm known as MRI Medical Imaging Stitch that combines multiple MRIs to generate images that are automatically aligned so they form a similar look throughout and thereby assist in obtaining useful image matches. The CNN algorithm was trained by pre-training the weights over a large database comprising multiple MRI scans, each with their respective morphological changes in tissues. The resulting CNN resulted in faster matching than techniques using multi-parametric logistic regression and traditional single linear regression. Further, this approach could handle complicated medical cases where individual anatomic features like different types of tissue were represented or which images involved many body parts. We demonstrate that these approaches can be used to reduce error rates for image-specific training but do not work across all image categories and should not otherwise replace more traditional image segmentation methods. We also discuss the limitations inherent among the various techniques, although our results suggest such limitations have a limited impact. More specifically, our study provides validation that existing techniques for manual image segmenting can often achieve better quality, faster speed and significantly higher precision compared to CNN based algorithms. It demonstrates also the applicability of various non-uniform probability pooling techniques, such as conditional random fields models, and reveals how several common modeling choices affect both quality and performance. Although we still need other algorithms specifically tasked to image processing tasks, we recommend that more effort is required to integrate these algorithms into current commercial image-processing stacks to address the problems they solve and improve ease of use in a global industry standard way.

In this paper, we present a novel approach for 3D semantic segmentation of medical images, which combines the strengths of shape-aware and semi-supervised learning. Our proposed method leverages the rich spatial and semantic information present in medical images to improve segmentation accuracy, while minimizing the need for annotated data.

Existing 3D semantic segmentation methods rely heavily on fully-supervised learning, which requires a large amount of annotated data to achieve high accuracy. However, annotating medical images is a time-consuming and expensive process, and the lack of annotated data can limit the performance of these methods. In contrast, our proposed method exploits the shape information present in medical images to guide the segmentation process, even in the absence of annotated data.

Our approach consists of two main components: a shape-aware loss function and a semi-supervised learning framework. The shape-aware loss function encourages the segmentation model to produce smooth and consistent predictions that align with the underlying anatomy, while the semi-supervised learning framework leverages both labeled and unlabeled data to improve segmentation accuracy.

We evaluate our method on several publicly available medical image datasets, including brain MRI and CT scans. Our results show that our proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art semi-supervised and fully-supervised 3D semantic segmentation methods, while requiring significantly less annotated data. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in segmenting various medical structures, such as tumors, organs, and vessels, and show that it can handle complex cases with multiple structures and low contrast.

Our work has important implications for medical image analysis, as it provides a more efficient and accurate approach to 3D semantic segmentation, which can be used for a variety of applications, such as disease diagnosis, treatment planning, and monitoring. Additionally, our method has the potential to be adapted to other medical imaging modalities and tasks, such as 2D image segmentation and image registration.

In summary, our paper presents a novel approach to 3D semantic segmentation of medical images that combines the strengths of shape-aware and semi-supervised learning.

This paper presents an innovative approach to real-time pricing in regional electricity networks, based on an automated linear function submission-based double auction mechanism. The proposed method enables prosumers (producer-consumers) to participate in the auction process and maximize their economic benefits by optimizing their energy trading strategies.

The proposed mechanism utilizes advanced data analytics and machine learning algorithms to predict demand and supply patterns, ensuring efficient price discovery and reducing market volatility. Additionally, it allows for real-time adjustments of bids and asks, enabling participants to react quickly to changes in market conditions.

The study demonstrates the effectiveness of the automated linear function submission-based double auction through simulations and case studies, showcasing its potential to improve the efficiency and reliability of regional electricity markets. By providing a bottom-up approach that empowers prosumers to take an active role in shaping the market, this research offers an important contribution to the transition towards more decentralized and sustainable energy systems.

Moreover, the automatic nature of the auction system reduces the need for intermediaries, lowering transaction costs and increasing transparency. As such, the presented approach has significant practical implications for energy retailers, distribution system operators, and regulatory bodies interested in fostering the development of smart grids and community energy management systems.

Overall, the paper provides solid theoretical foundations and empirical evidence supporting the use of automated linear function submission-based double auctions as a suitable solution for real-time pricing in regional prosumers' electricity networks. It paves the way for further investigations into this promising area of research, which can help address some of the key challenges facing modern power systems.

Today, deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have demonstrated state of
the art performance for supervised medical image segmentation, across various
imaging modalities and tasks. Despite early success, segmentation networks may
still generate anatomically aberrant segmentations, with holes or inaccuracies
near the object boundaries. To mitigate this effect, recent research works have
focused on incorporating spatial information or prior knowledge to enforce
anatomically plausible segmentation. If the integration of prior knowledge in
image segmentation is not a new topic in classical optimization approaches, it
is today an increasing trend in CNN based image segmentation, as shown by the
growing literature on the topic. In this survey, we focus on high level prior,
embedded at the loss function level. We categorize the articles according to
the nature of the prior: the object shape, size, topology, and the
inter-regions constraints. We highlight strengths and limitations of current
approaches, discuss the challenge related to the design and the integration of
prior-based losses, and the optimization strategies, and draw future research
directions.

In this paper, we propose an efficient and generic interactive segmentation framework to correct mispredictions during clinical evaluation of medical images. Our approach leverages the strengths of both machine learning algorithms and human expertise to improve the accuracy of image segmentation models. We present a novel method that enables domain-expert annotators to interact with a deep neural network through user-friendly interfaces, allowing them to correct errors in real-time while providing feedback to the model.

Our proposed framework is capable of adapting to various types of medical images and segmentation tasks, making it a versatile tool for clinical applications. The key components of our method include an intuitive interface design, a robust data storage system, and an algorithm that utilizes user input to refine the segmentation output. Through extensive experiments on several datasets, we demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our approach in reducing mispredictions and improving overall segmentation accuracy.

We evaluate our framework by comparing its performance against state-of-the-art methods as well as existing approaches that rely solely on machine learning or manual annotation. Our results show that the incorporation of human expertise significantly enhances the precision and recall of the segmented regions. Furthermore, we conduct a usability study that shows the feasibility and practicality of using our framework in real-world scenarios.

The main contributions of this work are: (1) the development of an efficient and generic interactive segmentation framework that combines the strengths of deep learning and human expertise; (2) the creation of a user-Friendly interface that allows domain experts to correct errors in real-time; (3) the demonstration of improved segmentation accuracy compared to traditional machine learning or manual annotation methods; and (4) the potential applicability of our framework across various medical imaging domains.

Overall, this paper offers significant insights into the design and implementation of interactive segmentation frameworks and their ability to improve the accuracy of medical image analysis. It highlights the importance of integrating domain knowledge into the process and provides evidence that such collaboration can lead to better outcomes than relying solely on computational techniques.

We consider an ordinary differential equation with a unique hyperbolic
attractor at the origin, to which we add a small random perturbation. It is
known that under general conditions, the solution of this stochastic
differential equation converges exponentially fast to an equilibrium
distribution. We show that the convergence occurs abruptly: in a time window of
small size compared to the natural time scale of the process, the distance to
equilibrium drops from its maximal possible value to near zero, and only after
this time window the convergence is exponentially fast. This is what is known
as the cut-off phenomenon in the context of Markov chains of increasing
complexity. In addition, we are able to give general conditions to decide
whether the distance to equilibrium converges in this time window to a
universal function, a fact known as profile cut-off.

In the recent years, researchers proposed a number of successful methods to
perform out-of-distribution (OOD) detection in deep neural networks (DNNs). So
far the scope of the highly accurate methods has been limited to image level
classification tasks. However, attempts for generally applicable methods beyond
classification did not attain similar performance. In this paper, we address
this limitation by proposing a simple yet effective task-agnostic OOD detection
method. We estimate the probability density functions (pdfs) of intermediate
features of a pre-trained DNN by performing kernel density estimation (KDE) on
the training dataset. As direct application of KDE to feature maps is hindered
by their high dimensionality, we use a set of lower-dimensional marginalized
KDE models instead of a single high-dimensional one. At test time, we evaluate
the pdfs on a test sample and produce a confidence score that indicates the
sample is OOD. The use of KDE eliminates the need for making simplifying
assumptions about the underlying feature pdfs and makes the proposed method
task-agnostic. We perform extensive experiments on classification tasks using
benchmark datasets for OOD detection. Additionally, we perform experiments on
medical image segmentation tasks using brain MRI datasets. The results
demonstrate that the proposed method consistently achieves high OOD detection
performance in both classification and segmentation tasks and improves
state-of-the-art in almost all cases. Code is available at
\url{https://github.com/eerdil/task_agnostic_ood}

The spectral ergodic Banach problem, which asks whether every bounded sequence of positive integers contains a subsequence that is both thin and frequent, has been a longstanding open question in additive combinatorics. In this paper, we make progress on this problem by introducing a new tool from algebraic combinatorics: flat polynomials.

Flat polynomials are a generalization of the notion of polynomial sequences, and they have a rich theory that allows us to study their properties with greater precision than traditional polynomial sequences. We show how to use flat polynomials to construct examples of thin and frequent subsequences of boundeds sequences of positive integers, making progress towards resolving the spectral ergodic Banach problem.

Our main result shows that there exists a constant c such that any bounded sequence of positive integers contains a subsequence that grows at least as fast as cx^2, where x is the length of the subsequence. This improves upon previous results, which only provided lower bounds of the form O(x^c) for some constant c.

We also explore the connections between flat polynomials and other areas of mathematics, including harmonic analysis, graph theory, and optimization. Our work provides a new perspective on these areas and demonstrates the power of using algebraic tools to solve problems in combinatorics and analysis.

Overall, our paper makes significant contributions to the study of the spectral ergodic Banach problem and introduces a new tool from algebraic combinatorics that can be used to tackle challenging questions in several fields.

This paper presents a theoretical analysis of active contours on graphs, which are used to model complex shapes and structures in computer vision and image processing. The active contour model is based on the minimization of an energy functional that incorporates both internal and external forces. We derive the Euler-Lagrange equations for the energy functional and show that they can be interpreted as a dynamic system on the graph. We also discuss the numerical implementation of the active contour model on graphs and provide examples of its application to image segmentation and shape analysis.

Abstract Ionic flow through electromagnetic (EM) devices has been a common mechanism for controlling and measuring the properties of semiconductor elements since the introduction of magnetic bearings in the 19th century. An example of this behavior is provided by ion-propagating EM drives with embedded linear trap arrays that can be tuned to generate, modulate, or monitor flows along different paths without additional control electronics or software. We present microprocessor based interfaces for configuring multiple such traps and quantifying them through standard measurements methods, including time domain, Fourier transform frequency domain, voltage versus current, and magnetostriction torque force on noncoiled surfaces in bulk metal foils or semiconductors. Two examples show dynamic features of low-noise high quality inductor coils measured at room temperature within ~5 nanometer dimensions. We estimate the magnetic flux density due to an 8 μT looped conductor coil at 5 T using Euler's law rather than standard resistivity values and compare these results with data from real systems. Using data from our experimental setups we also discuss how the characteristics of individual traps have changed over time as various environmental variables (temperature/current range) are varied. These results provide new opportunities related to large scale integration and optimization of traps in near space environments with complex geometries. Furthermore they will be useful when building future MEMS accelerators because their dynamic geometry simplifications would allow high fidelity, reliable electrical measurements within thin films and other metallic materials not possible with previous approaches. It should be noted, however, that trapping ion concentrations requires special device engineering considerations, which may limit its use inside a vacuum chamber.

Radiological imaging offers effective measurement of anatomy, which is useful
in disease diagnosis and assessment. Previous study has shown that the left
atrial wall remodeling can provide information to predict treatment outcome in
atrial fibrillation. Nevertheless, the segmentation of the left atrial
structures from medical images is still very time-consuming. Current advances
in neural network may help creating automatic segmentation models that reduce
the workload for clinicians. In this preliminary study, we propose automated,
two-stage, three-dimensional U-Nets with convolutional neural network, for the
challenging task of left atrial segmentation. Unlike previous two-dimensional
image segmentation methods, we use 3D U-Nets to obtain the heart cavity
directly in 3D. The dual 3D U-Net structure consists of, a first U-Net to
coarsely segment and locate the left atrium, and a second U-Net to accurately
segment the left atrium under higher resolution. In addition, we introduce a
Contour loss based on additional distance information to adjust the final
segmentation. We randomly split the data into training datasets (80 subjects)
and validation datasets (20 subjects) to train multiple models, with different
augmentation setting. Experiments show that the average Dice coefficients for
validation datasets are around 0.91 - 0.92, the sensitivity around 0.90-0.94
and the specificity 0.99. Compared with traditional Dice loss, models trained
with Contour loss in general offer smaller Hausdorff distance with similar Dice
coefficient, and have less connected components in predictions. Finally, we
integrate several trained models in an ensemble prediction to segment testing
datasets.

Overall, DAMMs are a powerful tool for analyzing complex data and can be used in a variety of fields, including finance, healthcare, and social sciences.

We study the structure of multiple correlation sequences defined by measure
preserving actions of commuting transformations. When the iterates of the
transformations are integer polynomials we prove that any such correlation
sequence is the sum of a nilsequence and an error term that is small in uniform
density; this was previously known only for measure preserving actions of a
single transformation. We then use this decomposition result to give
convergence criteria for multiple ergodic averages involving iterates that grow
linearly, and prove the rather surprising fact that for such sequences,
convergence results for actions of commuting transformations follow
automatically from the special case of actions of a single transformation. Our
proof of the decomposition result differs from previous works of V. Bergelson,
B. Host, B. Kra, and A. Leibman, as it does not rely on the theory of
characteristic factors. It consists of a simple orthogonality argument and the
main tool is an inverse theorem of B. Host and B. Kra for general bounded
sequences.

This paper presents a novel approach to seismic source inversion, entitled Fast Bayesian Optimal Experimental Design (FBOED), which combines the strengths of Bayesian optimization and optimal experimental design to efficiently explore the parameter space of seismic sources. The proposed method is designed to overcome the computational expense and limitations of traditional iterative methods by leveraging the advantages of Gaussian processes and parallel computing.

The FBOED algorithm is developed to optimize the experimental design parameters, such as source location, moment tensor, and amplitude, that maximize the posterior probability of the source parameters given the observed data. The algorithm uses an acquisition function that quantifies the expected information gain about the source parameters upon collecting additional data. The acquisition function is constructed using a Gaussian process surrogate model updated at each iteration with new observations, allowing for efficient exploration of the parameter space.

The effectiveness of FBOED is demonstrated through synthetic experiments on simple and complex geophysical scenarios, where it outperforms existing methods in terms of computational efficiency and accuracy. Additionally, we show that FBOED can be applied to real-world problems by utilizing large-scale simulations of seismic data from Earth's subsurface. This academic paper presents a novel approach for fast pathological lung segmentation using near-optimal keypoint sampling. The proposed method significantly reduces the computational complexity while maintaining high accuracy, making it suitable for real-time applications. The approach is evaluated on a large dataset of pathological lung images, demonstrating its effectiveness and efficiency compared to existing methods. In this paper, we present a novel approach for improving the accuracy of pancreas segmentation in medical images using a technique called Attention U-Net. Pancreas segmentation is a crucial step in the diagnosis and treatment of pancreatic diseases, but it can be challenging due to the organ's complex shape and location.

Existing methods for pancreas segmentation rely on fully convolutional networks (FCNs) that learn to identify the pancreas based on its visual features. However, these methods often struggle to accurately segment the pancreas in cases where it is difficult to distinguish from surrounding tissues or when there is significant variation in the size, shape, and location of the organ.

To address these challenges, we propose the Attention U-Net, which incorporates an attention mechanism into the U-Net architecture to learn where to look for the pancreas. The attention mechanism allows the network to selectively focus on the most relevant regions of the image when making predictions, improving its ability to accurately segment the pancreas.

We evaluate the Attention U-Net on a dataset of 100 CT scans and compare its performance to a baseline U-Net and a state-of-the-art FCN. Our results show that the Attention U-Net significantly outperforms both comparison methods, with an average Dice score of 0.86 compared to 0.78 and 0.79, respectively.

We also perform a series of ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of the attention mechanism and demonstrate its ability to adapt to different types of variations in the pancreas. Our findings suggest that the Attention U-Net is a promising approach for improving the accuracy of pancreas segmentation, and has the potential to be applied to other medical image segmentation tasks where accurate localization is crucial.

With the introduction of fully convolutional neural networks, deep learning
has raised the benchmark for medical image segmentation on both speed and
accuracy, and different networks have been proposed for 2D and 3D segmentation
with promising results. Nevertheless, most networks only handle relatively
small numbers of labels (<10), and there are very limited works on handling
highly unbalanced object sizes especially in 3D segmentation. In this paper, we
propose a network architecture and the corresponding loss function which
improve segmentation of very small structures. By combining skip connections
and deep supervision with respect to the computational feasibility of 3D
segmentation, we propose a fast converging and computationally efficient
network architecture for accurate segmentation. Furthermore, inspired by the
concept of focal loss, we propose an exponential logarithmic loss which
balances the labels not only by their relative sizes but also by their
segmentation difficulties. We achieve an average Dice coefficient of 82% on
brain segmentation with 20 labels, with the ratio of the smallest to largest
object sizes as 0.14%. Less than 100 epochs are required to reach such
accuracy, and segmenting a 128x128x128 volume only takes around 0.4 s.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach for gray image extraction using fuzzy logic. Gray images are widely used in various fields such as medical imaging, remote sensing, and computer vision. However, extracting gray images from color images can be a challenging task, especially when the colors are not well-defined or have similar intensity levels.

Fuzzy logic is a mathematical method that allows to handle imprecise data by assigning membership values to each pixel of an image. This approach enables us to extract gray images with higher accuracy than traditional thresholding methods. We use a Mamdani inference system, which is a type of fuzzy logic controller, to extract the gray level of each pixel based on the intensities of the neighboring pixels.

The proposed method consists of three stages: preprocessing, fuzzification, and defuzzification. In the preprocessing stage, we apply a histogram equalization technique to enhance the contrast of the input image. In the fuzzification stage, we use a Gaussian membership function to assign membership values to each pixel. Finally, in the defuzzification stage, we use a center of gravity method to compute the crisp gray level of each pixel.

We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets and compare it with other state-of-the-art gray image extraction techniques. The results show that our method outperforms the others in terms of both accuracy and efficiency. Moreover, we perform a series of experiments to analyze the effectiveness of different parameters of the proposed method and provide guidelines for selecting optimal parameters.

Our contribution lies in proposing a robust and efficient gray image extraction technique using fuzzy logic, which can handle variations in lighting conditions, shadows, and noise. The proposed method has numerous applications in areas such as object recognition, image compression, and medical diagnosis.

In this paper, we investigate the concept of local quantum uncertainty in two-qubit separable states. We consider a specific case study where we examine the behavior of local quantum uncertainty under various types of noise and perturbations.

Starting with the theoretical framework of quantum entanglement and uncertainty principles, we derive explicit expressions for the quantum uncertainties associated with each qubit in a two-qubit system when the state is separable. We then introduce different types of noise and perturbations to the system and analyze how they affect the local quantum uncertainty.

Our results show that local quantum uncertainty is not robust against certain types of noise and can exhibit non-intuitive behavior in some cases. Specifically, we demonstrate instances where local quantum uncertainty increases despite the presence of classical correlations between the qubits. This challenges the conventional view that classical correlations are sufficient to reduce quantum uncertainty.

Furthermore, we find that certaintypes of perturbations can transform pure entangled states into separable states while preserving low levels of local quantum uncertainty, which may have implications for quantum information processing protocols that rely on such resources. Our study also highlightsthe role of complementarity relations in understanding the interplay between local and global properties of quantum systems.

The results of our case study contribute to the growing body of research on the foundational aspects of quantum mechanics, specifically, the exploration of local quantum uncertainty in multi-particle systems. They also underscore the importance of considering the joint dynamics of multiple observables, rather than just individual ones, when analyzinquantumi systems.

This paper studies the coordinated beamforming (CoBF) design for the
multiple-input single-output interference channel, provided that only channel
distribution information is known to the transmitters. The problem under
consideration is a probabilistically constrained optimization problem which
maximizes a predefined system utility subject to constraints on rate outage
probability and power budget of each transmitter. Our recent analysis has shown
that the outage-constrained CoBF problem is intricately difficult, e.g.,
NP-hard. Therefore, the focus of this paper is on suboptimal but
computationally efficient algorithms. Specifically, by leveraging on the block
successive upper bound minimization (BSUM) method in optimization, we propose a
Gauss-Seidel type algorithm, called distributed BSUM algorithm, which can
handle differentiable, monotone and concave system utilities. By exploiting a
weighted minimum mean-square error (WMMSE) reformulation, we further propose a
Jocobi-type algorithm, called distributed WMMSE algorithm, which can optimize
the weighted sum rate utility in a fully parallel manner. To provide a
performance benchmark, a relaxed approximation method based on polyblock outer
approximation is also proposed. Simulation results show that the proposed
algorithms are significantly superior to the existing successive convex
approximation method in both performance and computational efficiency, and can
yield promising approximation performance.

An important issue with oversampled FIR analysis filter banks (FBs) is to
determine inverse synthesis FBs, when they exist. Given any complex oversampled
FIR analysis FB, we first provide an algorithm to determine whether there
exists an inverse FIR synthesis system. We also provide a method to ensure the
Hermitian symmetry property on the synthesis side, which is serviceable to
processing real-valued signals. As an invertible analysis scheme corresponds to
a redundant decomposition, there is no unique inverse FB. Given a particular
solution, we parameterize the whole family of inverses through a null space
projection. The resulting reduced parameter set simplifies design procedures,
since the perfect reconstruction constrained optimization problem is recast as
an unconstrained optimization problem. The design of optimized synthesis FBs
based on time or frequency localization criteria is then investigated, using a
simple yet efficient gradient algorithm.

In this paper, we present a novel approach to describing generalized trees using algebraic and logical techniques. Generalized trees are a generalization of traditional trees that allow for multiple edges between nodes, providing a more flexible and realistic representation of complex systems.

Our approach is based on the idea of associating a set of rails with each node in the tree, which enables us to represent the connectivity of the system in a compact and efficient way. We develop an algebraic structure, called a rail-tree algebra, that allows us to manipulate and reason about these rails in a formal and systematic manner.

Using this algebra, we prove the existence of a logic that can be used to query and verify properties of generalized trees. This logic provides a powerful tool for analyzing and understanding the structural properties of arbitrary large networks, and it has applications in various fields such as computer science, physics, biology, and social network analysis.

We also demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to several case studies, including a study of scale-free networks and a study of hierarchical organizational structures. Our results show that our method can efficiently identify interesting patterns and substructures in these networks, outperforming existing methods in terms of computational complexity and interpretability.

Overall, our work opens up new possibilities for studying generalized trees and their applications, and it demonstrates the power of combining algebraic and logical methods for analyzing complex systems.

In this paper, we present a novel approach to tunable coupled-mode dispersion compensation and demonstrate its application in on-chip resonant four-wave mixing. Dispersion effects are a significant challenge in high-speed optical communication systems, particularly in chip-scale devices where spatial constraints limit the amount of dispersive material that can be used for compensation. By leveraging the concept of coupled-mode theory, we develop a compact and highly efficient method for tunably compensating dispersion in on-chip waveguides. The proposed technique relies on introducing two or more closely spaced modes with unequal propagation speeds into a single waveguide, creating a coupled-mode system tunable by adjusting the mode coupling strength. We show that the dispersion coefficient can be significantly reduced using a low-power tuning laser, allowing for precise control over the phase front of the signal beam. We experimentally demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in a silicon slot-waveguide platform, achieving 20 dB reduction in residual dispersion at telecommunications wavelengths.

Furthermore, we explore the potential of this technology in on-chip nonlinear optics, specifically four-wave mixing (FWM). By applying the tunable coupled-mode dispersion compensation technique to a pair of pump and Stokes waves, we observe intense generation of the lower-frequency idler wave at variable rates depending on the pump power and detuning from degeneracy. This contributes to a better understanding of FWM dynamics under strongly interacting conditions, unlocking new routes towards chip-based nonlinear frequency conversion applications. Our work highlights the versatility and scalability of integrated photonics tools enabled by this breakthrough technique.

The "bag-of-frames" approach (BOF), which encodes audio signals as the
long-term statistical distribution of short-term spectral features, is commonly
regarded as an effective and sufficient way to represent environmental sound
recordings (soundscapes) since its introduction in an influential 2007 article.
The present paper describes a concep-tual replication of this seminal article
using several new soundscape datasets, with results strongly questioning the
adequacy of the BOF approach for the task. We show that the good accuracy
originally re-ported with BOF likely result from a particularly thankful
dataset with low within-class variability, and that for more realistic
datasets, BOF in fact does not perform significantly better than a mere
one-point av-erage of the signal's features. Soundscape modeling, therefore,
may not be the closed case it was once thought to be. Progress, we ar-gue,
could lie in reconsidering the problem of considering individual acoustical
events within each soundscape.

Our results provide compelling evidence for parallelization and inference via two common architectures: conv1d-based architectures based on convolutionality decomposition and LSTM recurrent architectures combined with attentional capture. Timed systems, such as timed automata, are usually analyzed using their
operational semantics on timed words. The classical region abstraction for
timed automata reduces them to (untimed) finite state automata with the same
time-abstract properties, such as state reachability. We propose a new
technique to analyze such timed systems using finite tree automata instead of
finite word automata. The main idea is to consider timed behaviors as graphs
with matching edges capturing timing constraints. When a family of graphs has
bounded tree-width, they can be interpreted in trees and MSO-definable
properties of such graphs can be checked using tree automata. The technique is
quite general and applies to many timed systems. In this paper, as an example,
we develop the technique on timed pushdown systems, which have recently
received considerable attention. Further, we also demonstrate how we can use it
on timed automata and timed multi-stack pushdown systems (with boundedness
restrictions).

If $\Sigma=(X,\sigma)$ is a topological dynamical system, where $X$ is a
compact Hausdorff space and $\sigma$ is a homeomorphism of $X$, then a crossed
product Banach $\sp{*}$-algebra $\ell^1(\Sigma)$ is naturally associated with
these data. If $X$ consists of one point, then $\ell^1(\Sigma)$ is the group
algebra of the integers. The commutant $C(X)'_1$ of $C(X)$ in $\ell^1(\Sigma)$
is known to be a maximal abelian subalgebra which has non-zero intersection
with each non-zero closed ideal, and the same holds for the commutant $C(X)'_*$
of $C(X)$ in $C^*(\Sigma)$, the enveloping $C^*$-algebra of $\ell^1(\Sigma)$.
This intersection property has proven to be a valuable tool in investigating
these algebras. Motivated by this pivotal role, we study $C(X)'_1$ and
$C(X)'_*$ in detail in the present paper. The maximal ideal space of $C(X)'_1$
is described explicitly, and is seen to coincide with its pure state space and
to be a topological quotient of $X\times\mathbb{T}$. We show that $C(X)'_1$ is
hermitian and semisimple, and that its enveloping $C^*$-algebra is $C(X)'_*$.
Furthermore, we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for projections
onto $C(X)'_1$ and $C(X)'_*$ to exist, and give explicit formulas for such
projections, which we show to be unique. In the appendix, topological results
for the periodic points of a homeomorphism of a locally compact Hausdorff space
are given.

threshold-based approach for the overwhelming majority of cases examined.

elegans' segmentation and `skeletonizing' across a wide range of motility
assays.

Abstract

There has been much recent interest towards real-time information about traffic, which could be used to inform decisions affecting vehicles (e.g. traffic lights). This work identifies how it might look if one's car became able to select its preferred route. It demonstrates that it can provide information such as the speed limit on a road when driven by a vehicle or its proximity to other roadways, allowing an evaluation of signals priorities and their effects on speeds. We demonstrate two distinct methods from machine learning and statistics that allow us to make optimal selection of priority lines via dynamic optimization. These methods are useful for the following purposes in a highly-urbanized setting with numerous lane closures during rush hours: 1) identifying and maximizing the number of open lanes of travel; 2) evaluating routes by choosing among different levels of priority between two or more road users; and 3) finding where those locations best intersect eachother.

In this paper, we analyze the impact of compressed sensing with complex
random matrices on Fisher information and the Cram\'{e}r-Rao Bound (CRB) for
estimating unknown parameters in the mean value function of a complex
multivariate normal distribution. We consider the class of random compression
matrices whose distribution is right-orthogonally invariant. The compression
matrix whose elements are i.i.d. standard normal random variables is one such

be efficiently used for vehicle localization without the need for detailed

segmenter. The resulting map takes up much less storage space compared to a

solution is compared to one based on SIFT-features, and even with large
seasonal variations over the year we perform on par with the larger and more
descriptive SIFT-features, and are able to localize with an error below 1 m
most of the time.

Current state-of-the-art methods for image segmentation form a dense image
representation where the color, shape and texture information are all processed
together inside a deep CNN. This however may not be ideal as they contain very
different type of information relevant for recognition. Here, we propose a new
two-stream CNN architecture for semantic segmentation that explicitly wires
shape information as a separate processing branch, i.e. shape stream, that
processes information in parallel to the classical stream. Key to this
architecture is a new type of gates that connect the intermediate layers of the
two streams. Specifically, we use the higher-level activations in the classical
stream to gate the lower-level activations in the shape stream, effectively
removing noise and helping the shape stream to only focus on processing the
relevant boundary-related information. This enables us to use a very shallow
architecture for the shape stream that operates on the image-level resolution.
Our experiments show that this leads to a highly effective architecture that
produces sharper predictions around object boundaries and significantly boosts
performance on thinner and smaller objects. Our method achieves
state-of-the-art performance on the Cityscapes benchmark, in terms of both mask
(mIoU) and boundary (F-score) quality, improving by 2% and 4% over strong
baselines.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach for learning tree potentials in Conditional Random Fields (CRF) for image segmentation. CRF is a popular framework for segmenting images, but the learning of tree potentials, which capture the relationships between neighboring pixels, remains a challenging task. Existing methods rely on hand-crafted features or unstructured learning methods, which can be limited in their ability to capture complex contextual relationships.

Our proposed approach, called Structured Learning of Tree Potentials (SLTP), addresses this limitation by incorporating structured learning techniques to improve the representation of tree potentials. Specifically, we introduce a new feature extraction method that captures the structural information of the image, and use a structured learning algorithm to learn a set of basis functions that can be used to represent the tree potentials.

We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets and show that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of segmentation accuracy. We also perform a series of ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of different components of our approach, and demonstrate that the use of structured learning techniques and the incorporation of structural information are crucial for improving the learning of tree potentials.

Our work has important implications for image segmentation tasks, and demonstrates the potential of structured learning methods for improving the performance of CRF models. We believe that our approach can be applied to a wide range of applications, including object recognition, scene understanding, and autonomous driving.

This paper tackles the issue of linear regressions with errors in all variables, a common problem in many fields such as finance, economics, and engineering. We present a novel approach to identifying linear regressions with errors in all variables using a combination of statistical tools and machine learning algorithms. Our method involves first detecting outliers and influential observations, and then applying principal component regression (PCR) to reduce the dimensionality of the data. Next, we use a ensemble of decision trees to identify the most important features and their relationships with the response variable. Finally, we employ a regularized least squares method to estimate the coefficients of the linear regression model.

We evaluate our method on several synthetic and real-world datasets and compare its performance to existing methods. The results show that our approach can accurately identify linear regressions with errors in all variables and outperform other methods in terms of prediction accuracy and computational efficiency. Additionally, we demonstrate how our method can be used for feature selection and variable selection, which is particularly useful when dealing with high-dimensional data.

Our work has important implications for various applications where linear regressions with errors in all variables are prevalent. It enables researchers and practitioners to more accurately model complex systems, make predictions, and make informed decisions based on reliable estimates.

Functional integrals can be defined on topological groups in terms of
families of locally compact topological groups and their associated
Banach-valued Haar integrals. The definition forgoes the goal of constructing a
genuine measure on a space of functions, and instead provides for a topological
realization of localization in the infinite-dimensional domain. This yields
measurable subspaces that characterize meaningful functional integrals and a
scheme that possesses significant potential for representing non-commutative
Banach algebras suitable for mathematical physics applications. The framework
includes, within a broader structure, other successful approaches to define
functional integrals in restricted cases, and it suggests new and potentially
useful functional integrals that go beyond the standard Gaussian case. In
particular, functional integrals based on skew-Hermitian and K\"{a}hler
quadratic forms are defined and developed. Also defined are gamma-type and
Poisson-type functional integrals based on linear forms suggested by the gamma
probability distribution. These are expected to play an important role in
generating $C^\ast$-algebras of quantum systems. Several applications and
implications are presented.

Traditionally, the Bayesian optimal auction design problem has been

but there are many instances where the classification of bidders is a
continuum. For example, the classification of the bidders may be based on their
annual income, their propensity to buy an item based on past behavior, or in
the case of ad auctions, the click through rate of their ads. We introduce an
alternate model that captures this aspect, where bidders are \emph{a priori}
identical, but can be distinguished based (only) on some side information the
auctioneer obtains at the time of the auction.
  We extend the sample complexity approach of Dhangwatnotai, Roughgarden, and

matching upper and lower bounds. As an aside, we obtain a revenue monotonicity

Risk Minimization techniques to improve the sample complexity bound of Cole and
Roughgarden (2014) for the non-identical but independent value distribution
case.

Aggregating multi-level feature representation plays a critical role in
achieving robust volumetric medical image segmentation, which is important for
the auxiliary diagnosis and treatment. Unlike the recent neural architecture
search (NAS) methods that typically searched the optimal operators in each
network layer, but missed a good strategy to search for feature aggregations,
this paper proposes a novel NAS method for 3D medical image segmentation, named
UXNet, which searches both the scale-wise feature aggregation strategies as
well as the block-wise operators in the encoder-decoder network. UXNet has
several appealing benefits. (1) It significantly improves flexibility of the
classical UNet architecture, which only aggregates feature representations of
encoder and decoder in equivalent resolution. (2) A continuous relaxation of
UXNet is carefully designed, enabling its searching scheme performed in an
efficient differentiable manner. (3) Extensive experiments demonstrate the
effectiveness of UXNet compared with recent NAS methods for medical image
segmentation. The architecture discovered by UXNet outperforms existing
state-of-the-art models in terms of Dice on several public 3D medical image
segmentation benchmarks, especially for the boundary locations and tiny
tissues. The searching computational complexity of UXNet is cheap, enabling to
search a network with the best performance less than 1.5 days on two TitanXP
GPUs.

Recently, Landau, Reid and Yershov provided a novel solution to the problem
of redistricting. Instead of trying to ensure fairness by restricting the shape
of the possible maps or by assigning the power to draw the map to nonbiased
entities, the solution ensures fairness by balancing competing interests
against each other. This kind of solution is an example of what are known as
"fair division" solutions--- such solutions involve the preferences of all
parties and are accompanied by rigorous guarantees of a specified well-defined
notion of fairness. In this expository article, we give an introduction to the
ideas of fair division in the context of this redistricting solution. Through
examples and discussion we clarify how fair division methods can play an
important role in a realistic redistricting solution by introducing an
interactive step that incorporates a certain kind of fairness that can be used
in concert with, and not a substitute for, other necessary or desired criteria
for a good redistricting solution.

We investigate Referring Image Segmentation (RIS), which outputs a
segmentation map corresponding to the given natural language description. To
solve RIS efficiently, we need to understand each word's relationship with
other words, each region in the image to other regions, and cross-modal
alignment between linguistic and visual domains. We argue that one of the
limiting factors in the recent methods is that they do not handle these
interactions simultaneously. To this end, we propose a novel architecture
called JRNet, which uses a Joint Reasoning Module(JRM) to concurrently capture
the inter-modal and intra-modal interactions. The output of JRM is passed
through a novel Cross-Modal Multi-Level Fusion (CMMLF) module which further
refines the segmentation masks by exchanging contextual information across
visual hierarchy through linguistic features acting as a bridge. We present
thorough ablation studies and validate our approach's performance on four
benchmark datasets, showing considerable performance gains over the existing
state-of-the-art methods.

The NA62 experiment at CERN requires a high-resolution trigger and data acquisition system to accurately detect and measure the properties of rare particles produced in high-energy collisions. In this paper, we present the development of a high-resolution TDC-based board for a fully digital trigger and data acquisition system in the NA62 experiment.

The board is designed to provide high-precision timing and digitization of signals from detectors in the NA62 experiment, allowing for accurate identification and measurement of particles with nanosecond-level timing resolution. The board utilizes a Time-to-Digital Converter (TDC) to convert the analog signals from the detectors into digital signals, which are then processed and analyzed by a Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA).

The board is designed to operate in a high-radiation environment and is equipped with several features to improve its performance and reliability, including radiation-hardened components, data validation and error correction, and a scalable architecture that allows for easy integration with other boards and systems.

We evaluate the performance of the board using a test bench and demonstrate its ability to accurately measure the timing of signals with high precision. We also demonstrate the board's ability to handle high-speed data acquisition and processing, with a maximum data transfer rate of 100 Gb/s.

The high-resolution TDC-based board presented in this paper represents a significant advancement in the field of digital trigger and data acquisition systems, and will play a critical role in the success of the NA62 experiment at CERN. Its high-precision timing and digitization capabilities, combined with its scalability and reliability, make it an ideal solution for a wide range of high-energy physics experiments.

We demonstrate a method that allows visual mapping using only small image samples for low polygon meshes, reducing texture consumption substantially and allowing better quality maps for user interface elements without additional shader execution times or significant memory requirements. The resulting images retain all important functionality such as edge definition, color blending/sharpening effects, transparency coloring and texture painting and also provide extremely compact, simple 3D visualization. We study the lexicographically least infinite $a/b$-power-free word on the
alphabet of non-negative integers. Frequently this word is a fixed point of a
uniform morphism, or closely related to one. For example, the lexicographically
least $7/4$-power-free word is a fixed point of a $50847$-uniform morphism. We
identify the structure of the lexicographically least $a/b$-power-free word for
three infinite families of rationals $a/b$ as well many "sporadic" rationals
that do not seem to belong to general families. To accomplish this, we develop
an automated procedure for proving $a/b$-power-freeness for morphisms of a
certain form, both for explicit and symbolic rational numbers $a/b$. Finally,
we establish a connection to words on a finite alphabet. Namely, the
lexicographically least $27/23$-power-free word is in fact a word on the finite
alphabet $\{0, 1, 2\}$, and its sequence of letters is $353$-automatic.

Difference-in-differences (DID) is a method to evaluate the effect of a
treatment. In its basic version, a "control group" is untreated at two dates,
whereas a "treatment group" becomes fully treated at the second date. However,
in many applications of the DID method, the treatment rate only increases more
in the treatment group. In such fuzzy designs, a popular estimator of treatment
effects is the DID of the outcome divided by the DID of the treatment. We show
that this ratio identifies a local average treatment effect only if two
homogeneous treatment effect assumptions are satisfied. We then propose two
alternative estimands that do not rely on any assumption on treatment effects,
and that can be used when the treatment rate does not change over time in the
control group. We prove that the corresponding estimators are asymptotically
normal. Finally, we use our results to revisit Duflo (2001).

We present a powerful and cost-effective method for active illumination using
a digital micromirror device (DMD) for quantitative phase imaging techniques.
Displaying binary illumination patterns on a DMD with appropriate spatial
filtering, plane waves with various illumination angles are generated and
impinged onto a sample. Complex optical fields of the sample obtained with
various incident angles are then measured via Mach-Zehnder interferometry, from
which a high-resolution two-dimensional synthetic aperture phase image and a
three-dimensional refractive index tomogram of the sample are reconstructed. We
demonstrate the fast and stable illumination control capability of the proposed
method by imaging colloidal spheres and biological cells, including a human red
blood cell and a HeLa cell.

We begin by discussing the limitations of classical computing and the promises of quantum computing, highlighting the challenges and opportunities that arise from their integration. We then introduce the concept of hybrid hypercomputing and its key components, including a novel quantum-inspired classical algorithm and a quantum coprocessor that leverages the power of quantum parallelism.

We evaluate the performance of hybrid hypercomputing through a series of experiments on various problem sets, demonstrating its ability to solve complex optimization problems, machine learning tasks, and simulations that are beyond the capabilities of classical or quantum computing alone. We also discuss the potential applications of hybrid hypercomputing in fields such as cryptography, drug discovery, and climate modeling.

Our results demonstrate that hybrid hypercomputing offers a promising path forward for solving complex problems that are currently intractable with existing computational methods. By combining the strengths of quantum and classical computing, hybrid hypercomputing has the potential to revolutionize a wide range of fields and industries, opening up new avenues for scientific inquiry and technological innovation.

In conclusion, this paper provides a comprehensive overview of hybrid hypercomputing, its potential applications, and its implications for the future of computing. We envision that hybrid hypercomputing will play a critical role in addressing some of the most pressing challenges facing society today, and we look forward to exploring its full potential in the years to come.

Training deep convolutional neural networks usually requires a large amount
of labeled data. However, it is expensive and time-consuming to annotate data
for medical image segmentation tasks. In this paper, we present a novel
uncertainty-aware semi-supervised framework for left atrium segmentation from
3D MR images. Our framework can effectively leverage the unlabeled data by
encouraging consistent predictions of the same input under different
perturbations. Concretely, the framework consists of a student model and a
teacher model, and the student model learns from the teacher model by
minimizing a segmentation loss and a consistency loss with respect to the
targets of the teacher model. We design a novel uncertainty-aware scheme to
enable the student model to gradually learn from the meaningful and reliable
targets by exploiting the uncertainty information. Experiments show that our
method achieves high performance gains by incorporating the unlabeled data. Our
method outperforms the state-of-the-art semi-supervised methods, demonstrating
the potential of our framework for the challenging semi-supervised problems.

Although spatial information of images usually enhance the robustness of the
Fuzzy C-Means (FCM) algorithm, it greatly increases the computational costs for
image segmentation. To achieve a sound trade-off between the segmentation
performance and the speed of clustering, we come up with a Kullback-Leibler
(KL) divergence-based FCM algorithm by incorporating a tight wavelet frame
transform and a morphological reconstruction operation. To enhance FCM's
robustness, an observed image is first filtered by using the morphological
reconstruction. A tight wavelet frame system is employed to decompose the
observed and filtered images so as to form their feature sets. Considering
these feature sets as data of clustering, an modified FCM algorithm is
proposed, which introduces a KL divergence term in the partition matrix into
its objective function. The KL divergence term aims to make membership degrees
of each image pixel closer to those of its neighbors, which brings that the
membership partition becomes more suitable and the parameter setting of FCM
becomes simplified. On the basis of the obtained partition matrix and
prototypes, the segmented feature set is reconstructed by minimizing the
inverse process of the modified objective function. To modify abnormal features
produced in the reconstruction process, each reconstructed feature is
reassigned to the closest prototype. As a result, the segmentation accuracy of
KL divergence-based FCM is further improved. What's more, the segmented image
is reconstructed by using a tight wavelet frame reconstruction operation.
Finally, supporting experiments coping with synthetic, medical and color images
are reported. Experimental results exhibit that the proposed algorithm works
well and comes with better segmentation performance than other comparative
algorithms. Moreover, the proposed algorithm requires less time than most of
the FCM-related algorithms.

In this paper, we investigate the concept of Cauchy sequences in fuzzy metric spaces and their relationship to fixed point theorems. We first introduce the basic definitions and properties of fuzzy metric spaces, including the notion of a fuzzification of a classical metric space and the associated fuzzy distance and neighborhood functions. We then define Cauchy sequences in these spaces and establish their fundamental properties, such as the existence of monotone and bounded Cauchy sequences.

Our main result is the establishment of fixed point theorems for Cauchy sequences in fuzzy metric spaces. Specifically, we prove that any monotone and bounded Cauchy sequence in a complete fuzzy metric space has a unique fixed point, which is also the limit of the sequence. We further show that this result can be extended to more general cases, including non-monotone sequences and sequences that are only bounded above or below.

We also explore the connections between our results and existing work on fixed point theorems in classical metric spaces, highlighting the novel features that arise due to the fuzziness of the metrics. Finally, we provide examples of applications of our results in various fields, such as image processing, control theory, and decision making under uncertainty.

Overall, our study deepens the understanding of convergence and fixed points in fuzzy metric spaces, providing new tools for analyzing and modeling complex systems with inherent uncertainties.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to real-time semantic segmentation using a revised version of the Bisection Network (BiSeNet). Our proposed method leverages the strengths of both fully convolutional networks (FCNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to improve performance in real-world scenarios.

Semantic segmentation is an essential task in computer vision that involves assigning a class label to each pixel in an image. However, achieving high accuracy in real-time remains a significant challenge, particularly when dealing with high-resolution images or videos. To address this issue, we revisit the BiSeNet architecture and introduce several key modifications that enhance its performance and efficiency.

The original BiSeNet was designed as a two-stage framework consisting of a base network followed by a bifurcated branch. The base network generates coarse features, which are then passed through the bifurcated branch to produce fine-grained features. While effective, this approach suffers from several limitations. Firstly, the separate branches result in increased computational complexity, leading to slower processing times. Secondly, the disjoint nature of the branches hinders the sharing of information between different scales, resulting in suboptimal feature extraction.

To overcome these issues, we propose a novel integration mechanism that combines the strengths of FCNs and RNNs within the BiSeNet architecture. Specifically, we incorporate 1x1 convolutions and gating mechanisms to selectively focus on relevant spatial locations and channel dimensions. This allows our model to adapt to various input sizes without sacrificing performance. We also employ dilated convolutions to increase the receptive field while maintaining a compact model size.

Our extensive experiments show that the proposed method surpasses state-of-the-art real-time semantic segmentation models on multiple benchmark datasets (Cityscapes, PASCAL VOC, and COCO). Notably, we achieve an F1-score of 78.6% on Cityscapes at 30 frames per second (FPS), outperforming the previous state-of-the-art method by 5.9%.
