Machine learning has revolutionized numerous fields, including computer vision, natural language processing, and predictive analytics. However, a critical examination of the field reveals a lack of diversity in various aspects, including the data used for training, the algorithms employed, and the individuals involved in the development process. This homogeneity can result in biases, discrimination, and limited representation of marginalized groups, which can have severe consequences in areas such as healthcare, finance, and criminal justice.

This paper explores the concept of diversity in machine learning and its importance in ensuring fairness, equity, and inclusivity. We discuss the various dimensions of diversity, including demographic, cognitive, and cultural diversity, and their impact on the development and deployment of machine learning models. We also examine the challenges and barriers that prevent diverse groups from participating in the machine learning ecosystem and propose strategies to address these issues.

Furthermore, we discuss the role of diversity in mitigating bias and ensuring ethical considerations in machine learning. We explore techniques such as data augmentation, debiasing, and inclusive data collection, which can help reduce bias and improve the representativeness of machine learning models. We also discuss the importance of transparency and accountability in ensuring that machine learning models are fair and unbiased.

Finally, we highlight the need for a multidisciplinary approach to address the issue of diversity in machine learning. We argue that diversity should be integrated into the development process, and that individuals from diverse backgrounds should be involved in every stage of the machine learning lifecycle. We also emphasize the importance of creating inclusive environments that foster diversity and encourage diverse perspectives.

In conclusion, this paper emphasizes the urgent need for diversity in machine learning to ensure fairness, equity, and inclusivity. We propose strategies to address the challenges and barriers that prevent diverse groups from participating in the machine learning ecosystem and highlight the importance of a multidisciplinary approach to address this issue. By promoting diversity in machine learning, we can create models that are more representative, fair, and beneficial to society as a whole.

The Matlab implementation allows for real-time processing of images and provides a user-friendly interface for operators to interact with the algorithm. The paper also presents results from field tests conducted on a railway track, demonstrating the effectiveness of the algorithm in accurately evaluating ballast degradation. The implementation of this machine vision algorithm has the potential to significantly improve the efficiency and accuracy of ballast maintenance, reducing the need for manual inspections and improving the overall safety and performance of rail transportation.

Semantic image segmentation aims to obtain object labels with precise
boundaries, which usually suffers from overfitting. Recently, various data
augmentation strategies like regional dropout and mix strategies have been
proposed to address the problem. These strategies have proved to be effective
for guiding the model to attend on less discriminative parts. However, current
strategies operate at the image level, and objects and the background are
coupled. Thus, the boundaries are not well augmented due to the fixed semantic
scenario. In this paper, we propose ObjectAug to perform object-level
augmentation for semantic image segmentation. ObjectAug first decouples the
image into individual objects and the background using the semantic labels.
Next, each object is augmented individually with commonly used augmentation
methods (e.g., scaling, shifting, and rotation). Then, the black area brought
by object augmentation is further restored using image inpainting. Finally, the
augmented objects and background are assembled as an augmented image. In this
way, the boundaries can be fully explored in the various semantic scenarios. In
addition, ObjectAug can support category-aware augmentation that gives various
possibilities to objects in each category, and can be easily combined with
existing image-level augmentation methods to further boost performance.
Comprehensive experiments are conducted on both natural image and medical image
datasets. Experiment results demonstrate that our ObjectAug can evidently
improve segmentation performance.

The Normalized Cut (NCut) objective function, widely used in data clustering
and image segmentation, quantifies the cost of graph partitioning in a way that
biases clusters or segments that are balanced towards having lower values than
unbalanced partitionings. However, this bias is so strong that it avoids any
singleton partitions, even when vertices are very weakly connected to the rest
of the graph. Motivated by the B\"uhler-Hein family of balanced cut costs, we
propose the family of Compassionately Conservative Balanced (CCB) Cut costs,
which are indexed by a parameter that can be used to strike a compromise
between the desire to avoid too many singleton partitions and the notion that
all partitions should be balanced. We show that CCB-Cut minimization can be
relaxed into an orthogonally constrained $\ell_{\tau}$-minimization problem
that coincides with the problem of computing Piecewise Flat Embeddings (PFE)
for one particular index value, and we present an algorithm for solving the
relaxed problem by iteratively minimizing a sequence of reweighted Rayleigh
quotients (IRRQ). Using images from the BSDS500 database, we show that image
segmentation based on CCB-Cut minimization provides better accuracy with
respect to ground truth and greater variability in region size than NCut-based
image segmentation.

In this paper, we investigate homotopy invariants of combings of 3-manifolds. A combing of a 3-manifold is a way of decomposing it into smaller pieces, called teeth, that are glued together along their boundaries in a specific way. We focus on homotopy invariants of combings, which are properties that remain unchanged under continuous deformations of the combing.

We first establish a framework for studying homotopy invariants of combings by defining a notion of homotopy between combings and introducing a category whose objects are combings and whose morphisms are homotopy classes of combings. We then prove that this category is triangulated, meaning that it has well-defined notions of kernels and cokernels, and that these can be used to define homology and cohomology groups of combings.

Next, we explore various homotopy invariants of combings, including the number of teeth, the total space of the combing, and the fundamental group of the complement of the teeth. We show that all of these invariants can be computed using the above-mentioned homology and cohomology groups.

In particular, we prove that the number of teeth is equal to the dimension of the kernel of a certain map from the homology group of the 3-manifold to its cohomology group, while the total space of the combing can be identified with the cokernel of another map between these groups. Finally, we show that the fundamental group of the complement of the teeth can be realized as a quotient of the fundamental group of the 3-manifold modulo a certain normal subgroup that encodes information about the combinatorics of the combing.

Our results provide a new perspective on the study of 3-manifolds and their decompositions, and they have important implications for the understanding of topological and geometric structure of these spaces. They also demonstrate the power of our proposed approach to the study of homotopy invariants of combings, and pave the way for further investigations in this area.

Convolutional neural networks (CNN) have had unprecedented success in medical
imaging and, in particular, in medical image segmentation. However, despite the
fact that segmentation results are closer than ever to the inter-expert
variability, CNNs are not immune to producing anatomically inaccurate
segmentations, even when built upon a shape prior. In this paper, we present a
framework for producing cardiac image segmentation maps that are guaranteed to
respect pre-defined anatomical criteria, while remaining within the
inter-expert variability. The idea behind our method is to use a well-trained
CNN, have it process cardiac images, identify the anatomically implausible
results and warp these results toward the closest anatomically valid cardiac
shape. This warping procedure is carried out with a constrained variational
autoencoder (cVAE) trained to learn a representation of valid cardiac shapes
through a smooth, yet constrained, latent space. With this cVAE, we can project
any implausible shape into the cardiac latent space and steer it toward the
closest correct shape. We tested our framework on short-axis MRI as well as
apical two and four-chamber view ultrasound images, two modalities for which
cardiac shapes are drastically different. With our method, CNNs can now produce
results that are both within the inter-expert variability and always
anatomically plausible without having to rely on a shape prior.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to joint segmentation and localization in videos and images called Foreground Clustering. The proposed method leverages the strengths of both spectral clustering and graph-based algorithms to simultaneously segment objects from their backgrounds and estimate their positions within the scene.

Existing methods often treat these tasks separately, requiring manual parameter tuning and resulting in suboptimal performance when dealing with complex scenes or varying illumination conditions. In contrast, our method treats the problems as interrelated and uses them to mutually improve each other. By iteratively refining object boundaries and motion estimates through careful cluster assignments, Foreground Clustering achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on several benchmark datasets while providing real-time performance.

The key idea is to construct an affinity graph that encodes appearance, spatial, and temporal information across frames and then applies spectral clustering to partition it into coherent foreground structures. These are then used to seed dense trajectory optimization, which revises object boundaries based on motion cues and enforces temporal consistency. This process alternates between clustering and tracking until convergence, where the final output consists of separated objects and their associated motion fields.

Extensive experiments show that Foreground Clustering outperforms existing methods under various scenarios, such as occlusions, cluttered scenes, shadows, and low light conditions. Additionally, its ability to handle irregular object shapes and non-rigid deformations makes it particularly suitable for applications like multi-object tracking, activity recognition, and video surveillance. Overall, the proposed method significantly advances the field by introducing a robust solution that can effectively address challenging scenarios in computer vision.

In this paper, we propose a new method for learning conditional random fields (CRFs) using maximum a posteriori (MAP) decoding. CRFs are popular models for probabilistic graphical models, but learning them from data can be challenging, especially when the structure of the graph is unknown or partially known. Our proposed method leverages the MAP decoding algorithm to optimize the parameters of the CRF by iteratively improving the estimate of the most likely state sequence given the observed data. We show that our method converges to the optimal solution under certain conditions and outperforms other state-of-the-art methods in terms of computational efficiency and accuracy. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several benchmark datasets and apply it to real-world applications such as natural language processing and image segmentation. The main contribution of this work is providing an efficient way to learn CRFs using MAP decoding, which enables their use in more complex and dynamic domains where previous methods were not applicable.

This paper presents a Galois-dynamics correspondence for unicritical polynomials, which are a class of polynomials with a single critical point. The correspondence relates the dynamics of the polynomial to the action of the Galois group on the splitting fields of the polynomial. This result provides a new perspective on the study of unicritical polynomials and their Galois groups, and has potential applications in number theory and the study of dynamical systems.

Medical image segmentation is a fundamental task in healthcare, with the aim of accurately separating the pixels of a medical image into distinct regions of interest. Evaluating the performance of segmentation algorithms is crucial to ensure that the resulting segments are reliable and useful for clinical decision-making. Two commonly used metrics for evaluating segmentation performance are the Dice score and Jaccard index. However, optimizing these metrics can be challenging, especially when dealing with complex medical images.

This paper presents a comprehensive review of the Dice score and Jaccard index, including their theoretical foundations and practical applications in medical image segmentation. We discuss the limitations and drawbacks of these metrics, as well as strategies for optimizing them. We also explore the use of these metrics in deep learning-based segmentation methods, such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs).

Our review covers a range of topics, including:

1. Introduction to medical image segmentation and its importance in healthcare.
2. Overview of the Dice score and Jaccard index, including their mathematical formulations and interpretation.
3. Limitations and drawbacks of the Dice score and Jaccard index, including their sensitivity to class imbalance and spatial overlap.
4. Strategies for optimizing the Dice score and Jaccard index, including data augmentation, ensemble learning, and post-processing techniques.
5. Application of the Dice score and Jaccard index in deep learning-based segmentation methods, including CNNs.
6. Future directions for research and development in medical image segmentation evaluation.

This paper serves as a valuable resource for researchers, practitioners, and students working in the field of medical image segmentation. By providing a comprehensive understanding of the Dice score and Jaccard index, as well as practical strategies for optimizing these metrics, we hope to improve the accuracy and reliability of medical image segmentation and ultimately contribute to better patient outcomes.

We also discuss some open problems and future directions for research in this field. Overall, this paper offers a valuable contribution to the study of modal logic and its applications.

In this study, we present a novel macroscopic acousto-mechanical analogy of a microbubble. Microbubbles are tiny bubbles that are typically on the order of micrometers in size and play important roles in various biomedical applications such as drug delivery and ultrasound imaging. However, their small size makes them difficult to study using conventional experimental techniques. Here, we develop an analogous system at the macroscale, where a large bubble is placed in a cylindrical container filled with a viscoelastic fluid. The bubble's dynamics are driven by applying external forces that mimic the effects of surface tension and gravitational forces experienced by a microbubble. We demonstrate that the macroscopic bubble exhibits behaviors similar to those of a microbubble, including periodic oscillations and nonlinear dynamic behavior. Our findings provide new insights into the physical mechanisms governing microbubble dynamics and have potential applications in the design and optimization of microbubble-based technologies. Additionally, our approach demonstrates the feasibility of using macroscopic analogs to study complex phenomena at the nanoscale, offering a promising way to investigate the behavior of microscopic systems that are difficult to access experimentally.

A total dominating set of a graph $G=(V,E)$ is a subset $D \subseteq V$ such
that every vertex in $V$ is adjacent to some vertex in $D$. Finding a total
dominating set of minimum size is NP-hard on planar graphs and W[2]-complete on
general graphs when parameterized by the solution size. By the meta-theorem of
Bodlaender et al. [J. ACM, 2016], there exists a linear kernel for Total
Dominating Set on graphs of bounded genus. Nevertheless, it is not clear how
such a kernel can be effectively constructed, and how to obtain explicit
reduction rules with reasonably small constants. Following the approach of
Alber et al. [J. ACM, 2004], we provide an explicit kernel for Total Dominating
Set on planar graphs with at most $410k$ vertices, where $k$ is the size of the
solution. This result complements several known constructive linear kernels on
planar graphs for other domination problems such as Dominating Set, Edge
Dominating Set, Efficient Dominating Set, Connected Dominating Set, or Red-Blue
Dominating Set.

We construct a mesoscale model of colloidal suspensions that contain solutes
reversibly adsorbing onto the colloidal particle surfaces. The present model
describes the coupled dynamics of the colloidal particles, the host fluid, and
the solutes through the Newton-Euler equations of motion, the hydrodynamic
equations, and the advection-diffusion equation, respectively. The solute
adsorption is modeled through a square-well potential, which represents a
short-range attractive interaction between a particle and a solute molecule.
The present model is formulated to be solved through direct numerical
simulations. Some numerical results are presented to validate the simulations.
The present model enables investigations of solute adsorption effects in the
presence of a fluid flow and an inhomogeneous solute concentration
distribution.

This paper proposes a novel approach for historical document image segmentation using LDA-initialized deep neural networks. Historical document images are often characterized by their complex layouts, diverse fonts, and degraded quality, making it challenging to extract relevant information using traditional Optical Character Recognition (OCR) techniques. To address this problem, we leverage Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) to initialize a deep neural network for document image segmentation.

LDA is a popular topic modeling technique used in natural language processing, which can effectively capture the underlying topics in a corpus of text documents. In this work, we adapt LDA to learn a set of topics that are relevant to the layout and content of historical document images. These topics are then used to initialize a deep neural network, which is fine-tuned using a small set of labeled document images.

The proposed approach is evaluated on several datasets of historical documents, and the results show that it outperforms state-of-the-art OCR and layout analysis methods. Specifically, our approach achieves an average segmentation accuracy of 93.6% on the challenging "Old Books" dataset, which contains documents from the 15th to 19th centuries.

The main contributions of this paper are:

1. The introduction of LDA-initialized deep neural networks for historical document image segmentation, which leverages the power of topic modeling to improve the accuracy of document image analysis.
2. The development of a novel deep neural network architecture that integrates LDA-learned topics with convolutional and recurrent neural networks for effective feature extraction and segmentation.
3. The establishment of a new benchmark for historical document image segmentation, which includes several datasets of diverse historical documents and a set of evaluation metrics tailored to this task.

Overall, this paper demonstrates the effectiveness of LDA-initialized deep neural networks for historical document image segmentation, and highlights the potential of using topic modeling techniques in document image analysis.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to medical image segmentation using multi-scale self-guided attention. Traditional methods rely on hand-crafted features or deep learning models that are limited by their inability to captured long-range dependencies and contextual information. Our proposed method leverages attention mechanisms to learn hierarchical representations of medical images at multiple scales, allowing for more accurate and robust segmentation results.

We evaluate our method on several publicly available datasets and show that it outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in terms of both accuracy and efficiency. Additionally, we perform ablation studies to demonstrate the effectiveness of different components of our approach, providing insights into the role of each component in improving segmentation performance.

Our key contributions include:

* A novel attention-based architecture for medical image segmentation that captures multi-scale contextual information.
* An efficient and effective way to integrate high-level semantic information with low-level feature maps, leading to improved segmentation performance.
* State-of-the-art results on several challenging medical image segmentation benchmarks, demonstrating the superiority of our approach over existing methods.

This work has important implications for a wide range of applications in healthcare, including disease diagnosis, treatment planning, and monitoring. We anticipate that our approach will serve as a foundation for future research in medical image analysis and inspire new directions in the field.

This paper presents a collaborative sparse regression approach using spatially correlated supports for hyperspectral unmixing. The proposed method leverages the spatial correlation among neighboring pixels to improve the accuracy of the unmixing process. The collaborative sparse regression model is formulated as a joint optimization problem, where the coefficients of the sparse basis functions and the mixing proportions of the endmembers are estimated simultaneously. Experimental results on real hyperspectral data demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in improving the accuracy of the unmixing process compared to state-of-the-art methods.

Accurate segmentation of nuclei in microscopy images is a crucial step in various biomedical applications, including cancer diagnosis and cell counting. However, this task is challenging due to variations in image quality, staining conditions, and nuclear morphology. In this paper, we propose a novel method for segmenting nuclei in divergent microscopy images using a combination of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and traditional computer vision techniques. Our approach consists of three stages: (1) preprocessing, (2) feature extraction, and (3) post-processing. In the preprocessing stage, we apply data augmentation and normalization techniques to enhance the quality of the input images. In the feature extraction stage, we use a CNN to learn hierarchical representations of the images, which are then used to extract relevant features. Finally, in the post-processing stage, we employ traditional computer vision techniques such as thresholding and morphological operations to refine the segmentation results. We evaluate our method on two publicly available datasets, and demonstrate that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency. The proposed method has important implications for automated analysis of microscopy data, and can potentially be applied to other image segmentation tasks in biomedical research.

Additionally, our research may shed light on how certain positions are more important than others within the context of basketball strategy. Overall, this quantitative analysis strives to quantify intangible aspects of sports performance through rigorous mathematical modeling.

This study aims to develop and validate a novel multivariable magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) method for accurately segmenting the thalamic nuclei. The proposed technique leverages multiple contrast weighting schemes, including T1-, proton density-(PD-) weighted, and fluid attenuated inversion recovery -(FLAIR)-weighted images, which are combined using data fusion techniques to create an enhanced image dataset that enhances visibility of structural features relevant to thalamus segmentation. A deep learning model is then trained on this fused dataset with annotations from expert radiologists, allowing it to learn intricate patterns in the MRIs related to thalamocortical connectivity while also accounting for individual subject variation. Through extensive testing comparing our automated methodology against manual tracing by experts and other state-of-the art algorithms, we demonstrate superior accuracy and robustness across diverse datasets containing healthy subjects as well as individuals with neurodegenerative disorders affecting the brain. Our results suggest that integrating advanced imaging technologies with machine learning can significantly enhance clinical decision making by enabling more precise identification and characterization of subcortical structures like the thalamus.

Our approach relies on a combination of advanced algebraic and geometric techniques, including the use of modular forms and the theory of motives. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by providing explicit examples of number fields that satisfy the conjectures, and we also discuss the implications of our results for related problems in arithmetic geometry. Our work represents a significant breakthrough in number theory, and it opens up new avenues for research in this field.

The proposed SFCN is designed to learn hierarchical representations of 3D shapes, allowing it to capture both local and global structural information. We present an algorithm for boundary loss in remote sensing imagery semantic segmentation (IRIS) that provides reliable and high-quality results on all imagery types while reducing data storage, processing and computational demands by about one order of magnitude compared with state-of-the-art approaches. This abstract briefly describes a segmentation algorithm developed for the

using the scores of each region as input. Before using the algorithm these
regression models must be trained using the training set of images and ground
truth masks provided by the Competition. Steps 2 to 4 are repeated with an
increasing number of clusters (and therefore the image is segmented into more
regions) until there is no further improvement of the calculated scores.

In this paper, we present a novel approach for referring image segmentation that incorporates comprehensive multi-modal interactions between the user and the system. Our approach allows users to interact with the system through various modalities, including speech, gesture, and touch, to improve the accuracy and efficiency of the segmentation process.

We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate its superiority compared to traditional single-modal interaction methods. Our experiments show that the proposed approach can significantly improve the segmentation accuracy and reduce the interaction time, making it more efficient and user-friendly.

The main contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows:

* We propose a comprehensive multi-modal interaction framework for referring image segmentation that integrates speech, gesture, and touch modalities.
* We develop a deep learning-based model that fuses the complementary information from multiple modalities to improve the segmentation performance.

Thalamic alterations are relevant to many neurological disorders including
Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease and multiple sclerosis. Routine
interventions to improve symptom severity in movement disorders, for example,
often consist of surgery or deep brain stimulation to diencephalic nuclei.
Therefore, accurate delineation of grey matter thalamic subregions is of the
upmost clinical importance. MRI is highly appropriate for structural
segmentation as it provides different views of the anatomy from a single
scanning session. Though with several contrasts potentially available, it is
also of increasing importance to develop new image segmentation techniques that
can operate multi-spectrally. We hereby propose a new segmentation method for
use with multi-modality data, which we evaluated for automated segmentation of
major thalamic subnuclear groups using T1-, T2*-weighted and quantitative
susceptibility mapping (QSM) information. The proposed method consists of four
steps: highly iterative image co-registration, manual segmentation on the
average training-data template, supervised learning for pattern recognition,
and a final convex optimisation step imposing further spatial constraints to
refine the solution. This led to solutions in greater agreement with manual
segmentation than the standard Morel atlas based approach. Furthermore, we show
that the multi-contrast approach boosts segmentation performances. We then
investigated whether prior knowledge using the training-template contours could
further improve convex segmentation accuracy and robustness, which led to
highly precise multi-contrast segmentations in single subjects. This approach
can be extended to most 3D imaging data types and any region of interest
discernible in single scans or multi-subject templates.

Automatic segmentation of organs-at-risk (OAR) in computed tomography (CT) is
an essential part of planning effective treatment strategies to combat lung and
esophageal cancer. Accurate segmentation of organs surrounding tumours helps
account for the variation in position and morphology inherent across patients,
thereby facilitating adaptive and computer-assisted radiotherapy. Although
manual delineation of OARs is still highly prevalent, it is prone to errors due
to complex variations in the shape and position of organs across patients, and
low soft tissue contrast between neighbouring organs in CT images. Recently,
deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have gained tremendous traction and
achieved state-of-the-art results in medical image segmentation. In this paper,
we propose a deep learning framework to segment OARs in thoracic CT images,
specifically for the: heart, esophagus, trachea and aorta. Our approach employs
dilated convolutions and aggregated residual connections in the bottleneck of a
U-Net styled network, which incorporates global context and dense information.
Our method achieved an overall Dice score of 91.57% on 20 unseen test samples
from the ISBI 2019 SegTHOR challenge.

In image segmentation, there is often more than one plausible solution for a
given input. In medical imaging, for example, experts will often disagree about
the exact location of object boundaries. Estimating this inherent uncertainty
and predicting multiple plausible hypotheses is of great interest in many
applications, yet this ability is lacking in most current deep learning
methods. In this paper, we introduce stochastic segmentation networks (SSNs),
an efficient probabilistic method for modelling aleatoric uncertainty with any
image segmentation network architecture. In contrast to approaches that produce
pixel-wise estimates, SSNs model joint distributions over entire label maps and
thus can generate multiple spatially coherent hypotheses for a single image. By
using a low-rank multivariate normal distribution over the logit space to model
the probability of the label map given the image, we obtain a spatially
consistent probability distribution that can be efficiently computed by a
neural network without any changes to the underlying architecture. We tested
our method on the segmentation of real-world medical data, including lung
nodules in 2D CT and brain tumours in 3D multimodal MRI scans. SSNs outperform
state-of-the-art for modelling correlated uncertainty in ambiguous images while
being much simpler, more flexible, and more efficient.

Segmentation of magnetic resonance (MR) images is a fundamental step in many
medical imaging-based applications. The recent implementation of deep
convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in image processing has been shown to have
significant impacts on medical image segmentation. Network training of
segmentation CNNs typically requires images and paired annotation data
representing pixel-wise tissue labels referred to as masks. However, the
supervised training of highly efficient CNNs with deeper structure and more
network parameters requires a large number of training images and paired tissue
masks. Thus, there is great need to develop a generalized CNN-based
segmentation method which would be applicable for a wide variety of MR image
datasets with different tissue contrasts. The purpose of this study was to
develop and evaluate a generalized CNN-based method for fully-automated
segmentation of different MR image datasets using a single set of annotated
training data. A technique called cycle-consistent generative adversarial
network (CycleGAN) is applied as the core of the proposed method to perform
image-to-image translation between MR image datasets with different tissue
contrasts. A joint segmentation network is incorporated into the adversarial
network to obtain additional segmentation functionality. The proposed method
was evaluated for segmenting bone and cartilage on two clinical knee MR image
datasets acquired at our institution using only a single set of annotated data
from a publicly available knee MR image dataset. The new technique may further
improve the applicability and efficiency of CNN-based segmentation of medical
images while eliminating the need for large amounts of annotated training data.

both images and videos. Given a novel image or video, our approach produces a
pixel-level mask for all "object-like" regions---even for object categories

appearance and motion and attempts to extract all prominent objects whether

results and improves the state-of-the-art for fully automatic segmentation of

In this paper, we propose a novel approach for semi-supervised medical image segmentation that enforces mutual consistency of hard regions. Our approach leverages a combination of supervised and unsupervised learning techniques to improve the accuracy and robustness of the segmentation model.

In semi-supervised learning, the lack of labeled data can lead to overfitting and inconsistent segmentation results. To address this challenge, we introduce a regularization term that encourages the model to produce consistent segmentation masks for images with similar features. Specifically, we define a hard region consistency loss that penalizes the model for deviating from the majority vote of the segmentation masks produced by the model for a set of images with similar features.

We evaluate our approach on several medical image segmentation tasks, including brain tumor segmentation and liver segmentation. Our results show that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art semi-supervised segmentation methods, and achieves performance comparable to fully-supervised methods while using significantly less labeled data.

Our main contributions are:

* A novel approach for semi-supervised medical image segmentation that enforces mutual consistency of hard regions
* A hard region consistency loss function that encourages the model to produce consistent segmentation masks for images with similar features
* An extensive evaluation of our approach on several medical image segmentation tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness and robustness.

Our work has important implications for medical image segmentation tasks, where labeled data is scarce and expensive to obtain. Our approach can help improve the accuracy and efficiency of segmentation models, and enable their use in a wider range of applications.

In this paper, we numerically study the ground and first excited states of
the fractional Schrodinger equation in an infinite potential well. Due to the
non-locality of the fractional Laplacian, it is challenging to find the
eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of the fractional Schrodinger equation either
analytically or numerically. We first introduce a fractional gradient flow with
discrete normalization and then discretize it by using the trapezoidal type
quadrature rule in space and the semi-implicit Euler method in time. Our method
can be used to compute the ground and first excited states not only in the
linear cases but also in the nonlinear cases. Moreover, it can be generalized
to solve the fractional partial differential equations (PDEs) with Riesz
fractional derivatives in space. Our numerical results suggest that the
eigenfunctions of the fractional Schrodinger equation in an infinite potential
well are significantly different from those of the standard (non-fractional)
Schrodinger equation. In addition, we find that the strong nonlocal
interactions represented by the fractional Laplacian can lead to a large
scattering of particles inside of the potential well. Compared to the ground
states, the scattering of particles in the first excited states is larger.
Furthermore, boundary layers emerge in the ground states and additionally inner
layers exist in the first excited states of the fractional nonlinear
Schrodinger equation.

the model/algorithm could guide users for annotation of a set of data points

primary advantage being that active learning frameworks select data points that
can accelerate the learning process of a model and can reduce the amount of
data needed to achieve full accuracy as compared to a model trained on a
randomly acquired data set. Multiple frameworks for active learning combined
with deep learning have been proposed, and the majority of them are dedicated

segmentation of medical imaging data sets. We investigate our proposed
framework using two datasets: 1.) MRI scans of the hippocampus, 2.) CT scans of
pancreas and tumors. This work presents a query-by-committee approach for
active learning where a joint optimizer is used for the committee. At the same
time, we propose three new strategies for active learning: 1.) increasing
frequency of uncertain data to bias the training data set; 2.) Using mutual
information among the input images as a regularizer for acquisition to ensure
diversity in the training dataset; 3.) adaptation of Dice log-likelihood for
Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD). The results indicate an improvement
in terms of data reduction by achieving full accuracy while only using 22.69 %

Medical image segmentation is a critical task in healthcare, as it enables clinicians to diagnose and treat various diseases. However, annotating medical images for training machine learning models can be time-consuming and expensive, limiting the availability of large-scale labeled datasets. In this review, we discuss deep network models that address the challenge of medical image segmentation with limited supervision. We explore different approaches, including self-supervised learning, weakly supervised learning, and semi-supervised learning, which leverage unlabeled or low-quality labeled data to improve segmentation performance. Our review highlights the potential of these methods in various medical imaging modalities, such as computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and positron emission tomography (PET). Furthermore, we discuss the challenges and limitations of limited supervision in medical image segmentation and identify future research directions, including the need for better evaluation metrics and domain adaptation techniques. This review provides insights into the state-of-the-art strategies for medical image segmentation with limited supervision and their applications in clinical settings where labeled data is scarce.

This work proposes the use of Bayesian approximations of uncertainty from
deep learning in a robot planner, showing that this produces more cautious
actions in safety-critical scenarios. The case study investigated is motivated
by a setup where an aerial robot acts as a "scout" for a ground robot. This is
useful when the below area is unknown or dangerous, with applications in space
exploration, military, or search-and-rescue. Images taken from the aerial view
are used to provide a less obstructed map to guide the navigation of the robot
on the ground. Experiments are conducted using a deep learning semantic image
segmentation, followed by a path planner based on the resulting cost map, to
provide an empirical analysis of the proposed method. A comparison with similar
approaches is presented to portray the usefulness of certain techniques, or
variations within a technique, in similar experimental settings. The method is
analyzed to assess the impact of variations in the uncertainty extraction, as
well as the absence of an uncertainty metric, on the overall system with the
use of a defined metric which measures surprise to the planner. The analysis is
performed on multiple datasets, showing a similar trend of lower surprise when

The energy functional combines a data term, which encourages the segmentation to be consistent with the image data, and a regularization term, which promotes spatial smoothness and adaptive similarity between neighboring pixels.

The key innovation of the proposed model is the use of adaptive similarity, which allows the model to adapt to the local image structure and capture finer details in the segmentation. The adaptive similarity is achieved by learning a set of similarity weights that are spatially varying and take into account the local image features.

The proposed model also incorporates spatial regularization, which helps to smooth the segmentation boundaries and reduce artifacts. The spatial regularization term is designed to be flexible and can be adjusted based on the complexity of the image structure.

The model is optimized using a efficient optimization algorithm, which enables fast and accurate segmentation of large images. The proposed model is evaluated on several benchmark datasets, and the results demonstrate its superior performance compared to state-of-the-art segmentation techniques.

* An efficient optimization algorithm that enables fast and accurate segmentation of large images.

In this paper, we investigate the concept of regular ideal languages and their properties. We present a novel approach to constructing regular ideal languages that are provably more complex than any previously known examples. Our construction technique leverages recent advances in combinatorial number theory and algebraic geometry to generate languages with unprecedented levels of complexity.

We begin by exploring the fundamental properties of regular ideal languages and their relationships to other classes of formal languages. We then introduce our new construction method, which involves embedding hierarchical structures within the language and exploiting the properties of certain algebraic functions.

Our main result shows that the regular ideal languages constructed using our technique have maximum likelihood normalized entropy (MLNE) values that grow exponentially with the length of the input sequence. This implies that these languages exhibit an extreme form of randomness, making them among the most complex regular languages known to date.

Furthermore, we demonstrate that our constructions can be used to obtain optimal lower bounds on the size of finite automata recognizing such languages, shedding light on the intrinsic difficulty of recognizing highly complex regular languages.

Finally, we discuss potential applications of our results in various fields, including cryptography, coding theory, and natural language processing. Our work highlights the richness and beauty of regular ideal languages and opens up new avenues for research at the intersection of theoretical computer science, mathematics, and linguistics.

In this paper, we investigate the generalized colouring numbers of graphs that exclude a fixed minor. Specifically, we consider the class of graphs that excludes a fixed graph H as a minor, and study the behaviour of the chromatic number, fractional chromatic number, and list chromatic number of these graphs under various constraints.

We first show that the chromatic number of graphs that exclude a fixed minor is always bounded above by a constant that depends on the minor. We then prove that this bound is tight by constructing a family of graphs that achieve the bound for all possible minors.

Next, we turn our attention to fractional colourings and show that the fractional chromatic number of graphs that exclude a fixed minor can be strictly smaller than the chromatic number. We provide an example of a graph that has a fractional chromatic number strictly smaller than its chromatic number, demonstrating that the fractional chromatic number cannot be inferred from the chromatic number alone.

Finally, we examine the list chromatic number of graphs that exclude a fixed minor and show that it can also be strictly smaller than the chromatic number. However, we prove that the list chromatic number is always within a logarithmic factor of the chromatic number, establishing a tight upper bound on the ratio between the two quantities.

Our results demonstrate that the generalized colouring numbers of graphs that exclude a fixed minor exhibit rich and interesting behaviours, highlighting the importance of considering multiple colouring models when studying graph families with structural restrictions.

In this work, we demonstrate joint processing of medical image features such as brightness, rotation, color, etc., in a manner that resembles standard approaches to face recognition and object localization and thus provide an efficient and tractable basis for future work on training image-guided methods. The state-of-the-art state-of-the art methods do not explicitly embed feature representations such as features into the networks; instead they use linear activation function (LF) schemes, which lead to significant overfitting as described by [Caklinas et al., 2011]. In contrast, our system utilizes three basic feature structures directly learned directly from human perception, i.e., luminance, rotation, color, sharpness, etc., and embeds them in the neural network itself. These constructions are then embedded into the underlying convolutional neural network as unsupervised feature extractors. It results in highly flexible, highly useful CNN based models with few assumptions and very little generalization requirements beyond what could be applied to previously trained CNNs—resulting in rapid adoption by many healthcare applications and even by vision systems.

This study presents a learning-based approach to cost function design for multi-surface, multi-object segmentation of knee magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data from the Osteoarthritis Initiative. The proposed method uses deep neural networks to learn an optimal combination of image coherence and contour plausibility metrics that are tailored to the specific task of segmenting multiple surfaces and objects in 3D and 4D MRI datasets. Experimental results on a publicly available dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach compared to standard manual annotation techniques, with significant improvements in both inter-observer variability and overall segmentation accuracy. We report on the anisotropic magnetic properties of the URhIn$_{5}$ compound, which exhibits a complex magnetic phase diagram with multiple magnetic transitions. The magnetic susceptibility, specific heat, and neutron scattering measurements reveal a rich magnetic structure, including a low-temperature spiral phase and a high-temperature paramagnetic phase. The anisotropic magnetic properties of URhIn$_{5}$ are found to be strongly dependent on the crystal field and spin-orbit coupling, leading to a highly non-trivial magnetic phase diagram. Our results provide new insights into the interplay between lattice geometry, spin-orbit coupling, and magnetic interactions in actinide compounds, and highlight the potential of URhIn$_{5}$ as a model system for the study of anisotropic magnetic phenomena.

In this paper, we present a novel approach for solving the classical problem of finding the optimal move in a general non-submodular pairwise energy system. Our proposed algorithm, called the Tiered Move-making Algorithm (TMA), is designed to efficiently explore the solution space and identify high-quality moves that minimize the energy function.

Unlike traditional methods that rely on iterative local search or linear programming relaxations, TMA employs a tiered structure to guide the search process. The algorithm starts by initializing a set of tiers, each containing a subset of the particles in the system. It then iteratively performs moves that exchange particles between tiers, following a carefully designed set of rules that ensure the energy function is non-increasing.

The key insight behind TMA is that the tiers serve as a coarse-graining of the solution space, allowing the algorithm to quickly explore the space and identify promising regions. By exchanging particles between tiers, TMA can effectively navigate the complex landscape of the energy function and avoid getting stuck in local minima.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of TMA through extensive simulations on a variety of non-submodular pairwise energy functions. Our results show that TMA significantly outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms in terms of computational efficiency and solution quality. In particular, we show that TMA can find better solutions than existing methods in a fraction of the time, and is able to solve instances that were previously unsolvable.

Overall, our work presents a major advancement in the field of non-submodular pairwise energy optimization, and demonstrates the power of using tiered structures to solve complex optimization problems. The Tiered Move-making Algorithm provides a new and effective approach for solving a wide range of problems in computer science and related fields, and has important implications for the design of efficient algorithms for solving hard optimization problems.

Residual amplitude modulation (RAM) is a phenomenon that can affect the performance of interferometric gravitational wave detectors, such as those used in the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO) and Virgo. RAM refers to any variation in the amplitude of the laser light that propagates through the interferometer's arms, which can cause errors in the measurement of the phase difference between the two beams. In this paper, we investigate the effects of RAM on these measurements and develop methods for mitigating its impact.

Using analytical and numerical models, we demonstrate how RAM introduces frequency-dependent errors into the measured phase difference, leading to false signals that cannot be easily distinguished from genuine gravitational waves. We also present a detailed analysis of the sources of RAM in LIGO-like interferometers, including mirror motion, thermal fluctuations, and shot noise.

To address the issue of RAM, we propose several approaches for suppressing its impact. These include using optimal filtering techniques to remove the residual amplitude modulation from the data, developing more sophisticated vibration isolation systems to reduce mirror motion, and implementing better noise reduction strategies to minimize thermal fluctuations and shot noise.

Our results show that with proper mitigation techniques, it is possible to significantly improve the accuracy of ground-based gravitational wave detectors, enabling them to reach their full potential for detecting and characterizing gravitational waves from astrophysical sources. This work has important implications not only for current and future generation gravitational wave observatories but also for other fields where interferometry is used, such as optical metrology and telecommunications.

This paper proposes a novel algorithm for the problem of structural image
segmentation through an interactive model-based approach. Interaction is
expressed in the model creation, which is done according to user traces drawn
over a given input image. Both model and input are then represented by means of
attributed relational graphs derived on the fly. Appearance features are taken
into account as object attributes and structural properties are expressed as
relational attributes. To cope with possible topological differences between
both graphs, a new structure called the deformation graph is introduced. The
segmentation process corresponds to finding a labelling of the input graph that
minimizes the deformations introduced in the model when it is updated with
input information. This approach has shown to be faster than other segmentation
methods, with competitive output quality. Therefore, the method solves the
problem of multiple label segmentation in an efficient way. Encouraging results
on both natural and target-specific color images, as well as examples showing
the reusability of the model, are presented and discussed.

In this paper, we present a novel approach for fully-automatic synapse prediction and validation on a large data set. Synapses are critical structures in the brain that facilitate communication between neurons, and their accurate identification is essential for understanding brain function and disease. However, current methods for synapse identification are time-consuming, labor-intensive, and prone to errors, limiting the scale and accuracy of synapse research.

To address these limitations, we developed a fully-automatic method for synapse prediction and validation, leveraging recent advances in machine learning and high-performance computing. Our approach uses a deep neural network to identify synapses in large-scale electron microscopy (EM) data sets, and validates them using a combination of automated and manual methods.

We evaluated our method on a large data set of EM images and compared the results to those obtained using manual annotation. Our results show that our method accurately identifies synapses with high precision and recall, and outperforms manual annotation in terms of speed and scalability. We also demonstrate the utility of our method for identifying synapses in a variety of brain regions and experimental conditions.

Overall, our work represents a significant step forward in the field of synapse research, providing a powerful tool for studying synaptic connectivity at unprecedented scale and resolution. The fully-automatic nature of our method makes it accessible to researchers without expertise in machine learning or image analysis, and its high accuracy and throughput enable the analysis of large-scale data sets that were previously inaccessible. Our method has the potential to enable new discoveries in the field of neuroscience and to accelerate the development of treatments for neurological and psychiatric disorders.

A large labeled dataset is a key to the success of supervised deep learning,
but for medical image segmentation, it is highly challenging to obtain
sufficient annotated images for model training. In many scenarios, unannotated
images are abundant and easy to acquire. Self-supervised learning (SSL) has
shown great potentials in exploiting raw data information and representation
learning. In this paper, we propose Hierarchical Self-Supervised Learning
(HSSL), a new self-supervised framework that boosts medical image segmentation
by making good use of unannotated data. Unlike the current literature on
task-specific self-supervised pretraining followed by supervised fine-tuning,
we utilize SSL to learn task-agnostic knowledge from heterogeneous data for
various medical image segmentation tasks. Specifically, we first aggregate a
dataset from several medical challenges, then pre-train the network in a
self-supervised manner, and finally fine-tune on labeled data. We develop a new
loss function by combining contrastive loss and classification loss and
pretrain an encoder-decoder architecture for segmentation tasks. Our extensive
experiments show that multi-domain joint pre-training benefits downstream
segmentation tasks and outperforms single-domain pre-training significantly.
Compared to learning from scratch, our new method yields better performance on
various tasks (e.g., +0.69% to +18.60% in Dice scores with 5% of annotated
data). With limited amounts of training data, our method can substantially
bridge the performance gap w.r.t. denser annotations (e.g., 10% vs.~100% of
annotated data).

image segmentation, we introduce an end-to-end trainable model for face mask
extraction in video sequence. Comparing to landmark-based sparse face shape
representation, our method can produce the segmentation masks of individual
facial components, which can better reflect their detailed shape variations. By
integrating Convolutional LSTM (ConvLSTM) algorithm with Fully Convolutional

takes advantage of the temporal correlation in video clips. In addition, we
also propose a novel loss function, called Segmentation Loss, to directly

further increase segmentation accuracy, one primary model and two additional

There are now many open source tools for analyzing microarrays using various image processors such as ImageJ. This paper outlines an approach that provides access to environmental monitoring and diagnostic databases to obtain integrated molecular images for microbial biomass analysis. We developed this work based on four main concepts: 1) The use of large amounts of realtime DNA sequences, and their associated read mapping information, not only for the visualization but also for statistical, computational or biological methods. 2) We create a dataset with the highest number of sequenced individual bacteria/organisms representing all major phyla (e.g., Prokaryotes, Bacteria, Viruses, Spirochetes, Eukarya) at different time points over several months. This paper presents a Bayesian Logistic Shape Model Inference approach for cochlea image segmentation. The proposed method utilizes a logistic shape model to represent the cochlea structure and employs a Bayesian framework to infer the model parameters from the image data. The effectiveness of the approach is demonstrated through extensive experiments on a dataset of cochlea images, showing significant improvement in segmentation accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods. The paper provides a valuable contribution to the field of medical image analysis by offering a robust and accurate method for cochlea segmentation.

In this paper, we investigate the phenomenon of degree of radiation damping in inversion recovery measurements and propose several characterization and suppression techniques to mitigate its impact. Degree of radiation damping refers to the loss of magnetization that occurs during the measurement process, leading to inaccurate recovery of the equilibrium signal. We first analyze the factors contributing to degree of radiation damping in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) systems and identify the most significant sources of errors. Next, we propose a set of techniques to characterize and correct for these effects, including:

1. Empirical correction methods based on referenced measurements
2. Signal enhancement algorithms exploiting the spatial sensitivity profile of the coil
3. Optimized radiofrequency pulse designs minimizing the effect of radiation damping
4. Parallel imaging techniques combining data from multiple receivers and coils
5. Advanced reconstruction methods incorporating prior knowledge about the expected signal behavior

We evaluate the performance of each technique using simulations and experimental data acquired on a clinical MRI scanner. Our results show that a combination of these approaches can significantly improve the accuracy and precision of inversion recovery measurements, reducing the artifacts caused by degree of radiation damping. The proposed techniques have the potential to improve image quality and diagnostic confidence in applications such as functional MRI, diffusion-weighted imaging, and molecular imaging.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to semantic segmentation in pathology using an adaptive weighting multi-field-of-view convolutional neural network (CNN). Current state-of-the-art methods for semantic segmentation in pathology are limited by their inability to effectively incorporate multi-scale contextual information and handle varying field-of-view (FOV) sizes. Our proposed method addresses these limitations by introducing an adaptive weighting mechanism that learns to assign appropriate weights to different FOVs based on their relevance to the current image.

The proposed method consists of three main components: 1) a multi-FOV CNN that extracts features from different FOVs, 2) an adaptive weighting module that learns to weight the importance of each FOV, and 3) a fusion module that combines the weighted features to produce the final segmentation mask. We evaluate our method on a large dataset of pathology images and demonstrate its superiority compared to state-of-the-art methods.

Our key contributions include:

* The introduction of an adaptive weighting mechanism to learn the importance of different FOVs for semantic segmentation in pathology.
* The development of a multi-FOV CNN that effectively incorporates contextual information from different scales.
* The proposal of a novel fusion module that combines weighted features from different FOVs to produce accurate segmentation masks.

Our experimental results show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of segmentation accuracy and efficiency. We also perform a series of ablation studies to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed adaptive weighting mechanism and the contribution of each component to the overall performance.

The proposed method has important implications for improving the accuracy and efficiency of semantic segmentation in pathology, and has the potential to be applied to other medical image analysis tasks where multi-scale contextual information is crucial.

This paper investigates the properties of modular curves over finite fields. Specifically, it focuses on the occurrence of curves with many points, which have significant applications in cryptography. By analyzing the structure of these curves, the paper provides insights into their behavior and demonstrates their potential for use in cryptographic systems. The results presented herein contribute to the understanding of modular curves and their role in cryptography, paving the way for further research in this area.

Segmentation of organs of interest in 3D medical images is necessary for
accurate diagnosis and longitudinal studies. Though recent advances using deep
learning have shown success for many segmentation tasks, large datasets are
required for high performance and the annotation process is both time consuming
and labor intensive. In this paper, we propose a 3D few shot segmentation
framework for accurate organ segmentation using limited training samples of the
target organ annotation. To achieve this, a U-Net like network is designed to
predict segmentation by learning the relationship between 2D slices of support
data and a query image, including a bidirectional gated recurrent unit (GRU)
that learns consistency of encoded features between adjacent slices. Also, we
introduce a transfer learning method to adapt the characteristics of the target
image and organ by updating the model before testing with arbitrary support and
query data sampled from the support data. We evaluate our proposed model using
three 3D CT datasets with annotations of different organs. Our model yielded
significantly improved performance over state-of-the-art few shot segmentation
models and was comparable to a fully supervised model trained with more target
training data.

The Riemann Hypothesis (RH) is one of the most famous unsolved problems in mathematics, and has been a subject of intense study for over a century. In recent years, several equivalent formulations of the RH have been proposed, which provide new insights into its nature and potential solutions. This paper reviews and explores these equivalencies, including the Robin inequality, the Lagarias criterion, and other related results. We also discuss the current state of knowledge regarding the RH, and examine the implications of various hypothetical proofs or counterexamples. Our main goal is to shed light on the deep connections between these different approaches, and to highlight their contributions to our understanding of the RH and number theory more broadly. Ultimately, we hope that this work will contribute to ongoing efforts to solve the RH, and to foster further advances in mathematical research.

In this paper, we present efficient approximation algorithms for multicell coordinated beamforming with rate outage constraint. The problem is formulated as a mixed-integer non-linear programming (MINLP) problem, which is computationally intractable for large-scale systems. To address this challenge, we propose two approximation algorithms: a linear programming (LP) relaxation-based algorithm and a successive convex approximation (SCA) algorithm.

The LP relaxation-based algorithm relaxes the integer constraints and solves a linear programming problem that provides a lower bound on the optimal value of the MINLP problem. The solution of the LP problem is then rounded to obtain an approximate solution for the MINLP problem. The SCA algorithm, on the other hand, approximates the non-convex rate outage constraint using a sequence of convex functions, which allows for a tractable optimization problem. The solution of the approximated problem is then refined using a feasibility-based method.

The performance of the proposed algorithms is evaluated using simulations, and the results show that they provide a significant reduction in computational complexity compared to the MINLP problem, while still achieving near-optimal performance. In particular, the LP relaxation-based algorithm provides a good trade-off between computational complexity and performance, while the SCA algorithm achieves better performance at the expense of higher computational complexity.

The results also show that the proposed algorithms outperform existing approximation algorithms in terms of computational complexity and performance. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of the proposed algorithms to a real-world scenario, where they are used to optimize the beamforming vectors in a multicell wireless network.

Overall, this paper provides efficient approximation algorithms for multicell coordinated beamforming with rate outage constraint, which can be used to optimize the performance of wireless networks while reducing the computational complexity of the optimization problem.

In this paper, we present a novel approach for image segmentation using 3D models. Traditional image segmentation methods rely on 2D image information, which can be limited in accurately separating objects with complex shapes and overlapping boundaries. Our proposed method utilizes 3D models to enhance the segmentation process by incorporating depth information and spatial relationships between objects.

Then, the 3D model is used to guide the image segmentation process, where each object in the scene is segmented based on its spatial relationship with other objects and the 3D model. We evaluate our method on several challenging datasets, including scenes with complex objects and varying lighting conditions.

The results show that our 3D model-assisted image segmentation method outperforms traditional image segmentation methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency. We also demonstrate the versatility of our method by applying it to various applications such as object recognition, tracking, and virtual try-on.

We present a method for reconstructing images viewed by observers based only
on their eye movements. By exploring the relationships between gaze patterns
and image stimuli, the "What Are You Looking At?" (WAYLA) system learns to
synthesize photo-realistic images that are similar to the original pictures
being viewed. The WAYLA approach is based on the Conditional Generative
Adversarial Network (Conditional GAN) image-to-image translation technique of
Isola et al. We consider two specific applications - the first, of
reconstructing newspaper images from gaze heat maps, and the second, of
detailed reconstruction of images containing only text. The newspaper image
reconstruction process is divided into two image-to-image translation
operations, the first mapping gaze heat maps into image segmentations, and the
second mapping the generated segmentation into a newspaper image. We validate
the performance of our approach using various evaluation metrics, along with
human visual inspection. All results confirm the ability of our network to
perform image generation tasks using eye tracking data.

In this paper, we present a novel approach for segmenting fluorescence microscopy images using deep neural networks. Our approach leverages the fact that different structures in these images have distinct patterns and arrangements, which can be learned by a deep neural network.

We evaluate our method on several datasets of diverse fluorescence microscopy images and show that it outperforms traditional image segmentation techniques. Specifically, we demonstrate that our method accurately segments various subcellular structures such as mitochondria, lysosomes, and nuclei in cell samples, as well as cells and tissues in whole mount images. Furthermore, we show that our method is able to generalize well to new images and can handle variations in imaging conditions, staining intensities, and artifacts.

Our main contribution is the development of a deep learning architecture that learns meta-structures, which are abstractions of the underlying structure patterns in fluorescence microscopy images. This allows the network to learn from a small set of training examples and generalize to unseen data. We also introduce a novel loss function that takes into account the spatial relationships between neighboring pixels, improving accuracy and robustness.

The proposed method has potential applications in various fields, including biology, medicine, and materials science, where fluorescence microscopy is commonly used to study complex sample morphologies at high resolution. Overall, this work advances the state-of-the-art in fluorescence microscopy image analysis and opens up possibilities for new discoveries in life sciences research.

In the field of medical image analysis, inter-annotator agreement is a crucial aspect in ensuring the accuracy and reliability of automated skin lesion segmentation systems. However, achieving strong agreement between annotators can be challenging, particularly when dealing with complex and variable skin lesions. This paper proposes a novel approach to handling inter-annotator agreement for automated skin lesion segmentation, which combines human annotations with deep learning techniques.

Our proposed method utilizes a dataset of manually annotated images of skin lesions, where multiple annotators have labeled each image with bounding boxes around the lesion areas. We employ a combination of overlap measures and uncertainty-based methods to quantify the level of agreement among annotators and identify instances of disagreement. By leveraging these metrics, we introduce an algorithm that selects the most reliable annotator for each instance and generates a corrected annotation mask that better reflects the true extent of the lesion.

The performance of our approach was evaluated using a test set of images, demonstrating significant improvement in segmentation accuracy compared to using a single annotator's labels or a simple majority voting strategy. Additionally, we investigate the impact of different factors on inter-annotator agreement, such as lesion size, complexity, and location, providing valuable insights into the limitations and strengths of current annotation practices.

This work has important implications for improving the quality and consistency of skin lesion segmentation, which can boost the accuracy of downstream tasks like disease diagnosis and monitoring. Our findings also highlight the potential benefits of incorporating multiple annotator perspectives into machine learning models, particularly in situations where ground truth data are limited or subjective.

Additionally, we provide thorough analyses of parameter sensitivity and performance consistency across different scenarios, offering insights into the strengths and limitations of deep, unsupervised SAS image segmentation.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to scene understanding called the Deep Grouping Model (DGM) that unifies perceptual parsing into a single, Trainable framework. Traditional methods rely on hand-crafted features and separate models for each task, leading to suboptimal performance and limited generalization. In contrast, DGM leverages recent advances in deep learning to learn hierarchical representations of images and jointly perform multiple tasks related to perceptual parsing, such as object detection, semantic segmentation, and instance segmentation.

Our key innovation is the use of a grouping module that iteratively refines the output of a backbone network, progressively partitioning the image into more coherent regions. This allows the model to capture complex contextual relationships between objects, leading to improved performance across all tasks. We demonstrate the effectiveness of DGM on several benchmark datasets, achieving state-of-the-art results with significantly fewer parameters than existing methods. Moreover, we show that DGM can be easily adapted to different dataset settings and outperform task-specific baselines.

The main contributions of this work are:

1. A new deep learning architecture that combines perceptual parsing tasks under a unified framework, exploiting their natural connections and improving overall efficiency.
2. An innovative grouping module that enables the model to capture sophisticated contextual information and enhance feature representation.
3. State-of-the-art performance on various benchmarks while using fewer parameters compared to current state-of-the-art methods.
4. Adaptability to diverse dataset settings, validating the versatility and robustness of our proposed approach.

Our findings have important implications for computer vision research, showing that jointly training models for multiple perceptual parsing tasks can lead to better performance and more efficient use of resources. piecewise flat embeddings (PFE) has been proposed for use in image
segmentation; PFE transforms image pixel data into a lower dimensional
representation where similar pixels are pulled close together and dissimilar
pixels are pushed apart. This technique has shown promising results, but its
original formulation is not computationally feasible for large images. We
propose two improvements to the algorithm for computing PFE: first, we
reformulate portions of the algorithm to enable various linear algebra
operations to be performed in parallel; second, we propose utilizing an
iterative linear solver (preconditioned conjugate gradient) to quickly solve a
linear least-squares problem that occurs in the inner loop of a nested
iteration. With these two computational improvements, we show on a publicly
available image database that PFE can be sped up by an order of magnitude
without sacrificing segmentation performance. Our results make this technique
more practical for use on large data sets, not only for image segmentation, but
for general data clustering problems.

This study introduces a novel mask-guided sample selection approach for semi-supervised instance segmentation. Our method utilizes the availability of partially labeled data, where only object masks are provided during training, to improve the overall performance of instance segmentation models in scenarios with limited fully annotated datasets. We demonstrate that our technique can effectively leverage these partial annotations by using them as guidance for selecting informative samples from unlabeled images and incorporating them into the model's learning process via consistency regularization. Extensive experimental results on three benchmark datasets show consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods while reducing labor costs associated with full annotation. Overall, this work highlights the potential benefits of leveraging available partly labelled information towards more efficient use of human expert knowledge in deep learning applications.

In this paper, we present two new types of scheduling primitives, one that uses an adaptive search path to determine whether tasks have been done yet, and another that searches a list of all potentially scheduled tasks using Monte Carlo sampling without needing to make assumptions about the task's prior condition or task performance characteristics, thus removing the potential for non-determinism in our algorithms (a problem commonly solved by recursive routines). We also show how these primitives perform well on three different real world computer systems we evaluated against benchmarks in both time, which accounts for computational demand and utilization as well as average runtime among threads, and throughput, whose effect depends upon several variables such as hardware speed. The first system achieves nearly 70% responsiveness, with an average response time of under 50 ns. Both the adaptive path and the Monte Carlo sampling techniques exhibit significant reductions in execution costs relative to more traditional approaches and provide large scale performance gains that are not only suitable for many common user tasks but also for most critical business processes.

In this paper, we introduce a new invariant of G_2 manifolds, which are 7-dimensional manifolds equipped with a special kind of geometric structure known as a G_2 structure. This invariant is defined using a combination of geometric and analytic techniques, and is shown to be a powerful tool for studying the properties of G_2 manifolds.

We begin by reviewing the basic definitions and properties of G_2 manifolds, and discussing the current state of the art in terms of invariants and classification. We then introduce our new invariant, which is based on the idea of associating a certain kind of differential operator to each G_2 manifold. This operator, which we call the "G_2 operator," encodes information about the geometry and topology of the manifold in a way that is invariant under certain transformations.

We prove that the G_2 operator is well-defined and has a number of desirable properties, including the fact that it is invariant under certain natural transformations of the manifold. We also show that the G_2 operator can be used to distinguish between different G_2 manifolds, and that it can be used to study the properties of G_2 manifolds in a way that is not possible using current methods.

We then apply our invariant to a number of examples of G_2 manifolds, including certain families of manifolds that have been studied extensively in the literature.
