Information-communication technology promotes collaborative environments like
Wikipedia where, however, controversiality and conflicts can appear. To
describe the rise, persistence, and resolution of such conflicts we devise an
extended opinion dynamics model where agents with different opinions perform a
single task to make a consensual product. As a function of the convergence
parameter describing the influence of the product on the agents, the model
shows spontaneous symmetry breaking of the final consensus opinion represented
by the medium. In the case when agents are replaced with new ones at a certain
rate, a transition from mainly consensus to a perpetual conflict occurs, which
is in qualitative agreement with the scenarios observed in Wikipedia.

Class imbalance poses a challenge for developing unbiased, accurate
predictive models. In particular, in image segmentation neural networks may
overfit to the foreground samples from small structures, which are often
heavily under-represented in the training set, leading to poor generalization.
In this study, we provide new insights on the problem of overfitting under
class imbalance by inspecting the network behavior. We find empirically that
when training with limited data and strong class imbalance, at test time the
distribution of logit activations may shift across the decision boundary, while
samples of the well-represented class seem unaffected. This bias leads to a
systematic under-segmentation of small structures. This phenomenon is
consistently observed for different databases, tasks and network architectures.
To tackle this problem, we introduce new asymmetric variants of popular loss
functions and regularization techniques including a large margin loss, focal
loss, adversarial training, mixup and data augmentation, which are explicitly
designed to counter logit shift of the under-represented classes. Extensive
experiments are conducted on several challenging segmentation tasks. Our
results demonstrate that the proposed modifications to the objective function
can lead to significantly improved segmentation accuracy compared to baselines
and alternative approaches.

Fine-grained annotations---e.g. dense image labels, image segmentation and
text tagging---are useful in many ML applications but they are labor-intensive
to generate. Moreover there are often systematic, structured errors in these
fine-grained annotations. For example, a car might be entirely unannotated in
the image, or the boundary between a car and street might only be coarsely
annotated. Standard ML training on data with such structured errors produces
models with biases and poor performance. In this work, we propose a novel
framework of Error-Correcting Networks (ECN) to address the challenge of
learning in the presence structured error in fine-grained annotations. Given a
large noisy dataset with commonly occurring structured errors, and a much
smaller dataset with more accurate annotations, ECN is able to substantially
improve the prediction of fine-grained annotations compared to standard
approaches for training on noisy data. It does so by learning to leverage the
structures in the annotations and in the noisy labels. Systematic experiments
on image segmentation and text tagging demonstrate the strong performance of
ECN in improving training on noisy structured labels.

In this paper, we investigate the use of WS2 (tungsten disulfide) as a saturable absorber for ultrafast photonic applications of mode-locked and Q-switched lasers. We demonstrate that WS2 exhibits a high saturation intensity and a fast recovery time, making it an ideal material for use in high-speed optical switching and modulation applications.

Using a femtosecond laser writing technique, we fabricate high-quality WS2 nanostructures on a silica substrate and integrate them into a fiber-based laser cavity. We experimentally demonstrate that the WS2 nanostructures exhibit strong saturable absorption behavior, with a saturation intensity of 1.5 kW/cm² and a recovery time of less than 1 ps.

We also demonstrate the ability to achieve high-speed modulation of a mode-locked laser using the WS2 saturable absorber, with a modulation frequency of up to 10 GHz. Furthermore, we show that the WS2 absorber can be used to achieve Q-switching of a nanosecond laser, with a switching time of less than 1 ns.

Our results demonstrate the potential of WS2 as a saturable absorber for high-speed photonic applications, and highlight the advantages of using two-dimensional materials in photonic devices. The ultrafast response time and high saturation intensity of WS2 make it an attractive material for a wide range of applications, including high-speed data communication, laser-material processing, and nonlinear optics.

This paper presents a novel approach to image segmentation using multi-scale adversarial attention gates. The proposed method utilizes scribbles, which are simple and easy-to-provide annotations, to train a deep neural network that can accurately segment objects in images. The network is designed to learn from scribbles at multiple scales, allowing it to capture both local and global context. Additionally, attention gates are employed to focus on relevant regions of the image, further improving segmentation accuracy. The effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated through extensive experiments on several benchmark datasets, outperforming state-of-the-art methods for image segmentation from scribbles.

In this paper, we explore the concept of simultaneous core partitions, which are partitions of a set of items into subsets such that each item is contained in at least one subset and each subset contains at least one item from each of k given categories. We consider the problem of finding the maximum number of simultaneous core partitions, and present several parameterizations of this problem that allow us to compute exact solutions or bounds for various special cases. We also investigate the relationship between simultaneous core partitions and other combinatorial structures, such as matroids and transversal matroids, and use these connections to derive new results and techniques for solving the problem. Finally, we present experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of our approaches and discuss potential applications of simultaneous core partitions in fields such as data analysis and optimization.

This paper presents a novel approach to analyzing timed systems using tree automata. Timed systems are systems where events occur at specific points in time, and their behavior is determined by both the logical structure of the system and the timing constraints inherent in the system's operations. The analysis of timed systems is crucial in many applications, such as real-time systems, embedded systems, and control systems, where predictable behavior and response times are critical.

Existing methods for analyzing timed systems include model checking, which can be computationally expensive and may not scale well for large systems, and approximations, which may introduce errors and uncertainty into the analysis. In this paper, we present UNet++, a new, more powerful architecture for
medical image segmentation. Our architecture is essentially a deeply-supervised
encoder-decoder network where the encoder and decoder sub-networks are
connected through a series of nested, dense skip pathways. The re-designed skip
pathways aim at reducing the semantic gap between the feature maps of the
encoder and decoder sub-networks. We argue that the optimizer would deal with
an easier learning task when the feature maps from the decoder and encoder
networks are semantically similar. We have evaluated UNet++ in comparison with
U-Net and wide U-Net architectures across multiple medical image segmentation
tasks: nodule segmentation in the low-dose CT scans of chest, nuclei
segmentation in the microscopy images, liver segmentation in abdominal CT
scans, and polyp segmentation in colonoscopy videos. Our experiments
demonstrate that UNet++ with deep supervision achieves an average IoU gain of
3.9 and 3.4 points over U-Net and wide U-Net, respectively.

Modern computer vision (CV) is often based on convolutional neural networks
(CNNs) that excel at hierarchical feature extraction. The previous generation
of CV approaches was often based on conditional random fields (CRFs) that excel
at modeling flexible higher order interactions. As their benefits are
complementary they are often combined. However, these approaches generally use
mean-field approximations and thus, arguably, did not directly optimize the
real problem. Here we revisit dual-decomposition-based approaches to CRF
optimization, an alternative to the mean-field approximation. These algorithms
can efficiently and exactly solve sub-problems and directly optimize a convex
upper bound of the real problem, providing optimality certificates on the way.
Our approach uses a novel fixed-point iteration algorithm which enjoys
dual-monotonicity, dual-differentiability and high parallelism. The whole
system, CRF and CNN can thus be efficiently trained using back-propagation. We
demonstrate the effectiveness of our system on semantic image segmentation,
showing consistent improvement over baseline models.

Large, fine-grained image segmentation datasets, annotated at pixel-level,
are difficult to obtain, particularly in medical imaging, where annotations
also require expert knowledge. Weakly-supervised learning can train models by
relying on weaker forms of annotation, such as scribbles. Here, we learn to
segment using scribble annotations in an adversarial game. With unpaired
segmentation masks, we train a multi-scale GAN to generate realistic
segmentation masks at multiple resolutions, while we use scribbles to learn
their correct position in the image. Central to the model's success is a novel
attention gating mechanism, which we condition with adversarial signals to act
as a shape prior, resulting in better object localization at multiple scales.
Subject to adversarial conditioning, the segmentor learns attention maps that
are semantic, suppress the noisy activations outside the objects, and reduce
the vanishing gradient problem in the deeper layers of the segmentor. We
evaluated our model on several medical (ACDC, LVSC, CHAOS) and non-medical
(PPSS) datasets, and we report performance levels matching those achieved by
models trained with fully annotated segmentation masks. We also demonstrate
extensions in a variety of settings: semi-supervised learning; combining
multiple scribble sources (a crowdsourcing scenario) and multi-task learning
(combining scribble and mask supervision). We release expert-made scribble
annotations for the ACDC dataset, and the code used for the experiments, at
https://vios-s.github.io/multiscale-adversarial-attention-gates

Incorporating a human-in-the-loop system when deploying automated decision
support is critical in healthcare contexts to create trust, as well as provide
reliable performance on a patient-to-patient basis. Deep learning methods while
having high performance, do not allow for this patient-centered approach due to
the lack of uncertainty representation. Thus, we present a framework of
uncertainty representation evaluated for medical image segmentation, using
MCU-Net which combines a U-Net with Monte Carlo Dropout, evaluated with four
different uncertainty metrics. The framework augments this by adding a
human-in-the-loop aspect based on an uncertainty threshold for automated
referral of uncertain cases to a medical professional. We demonstrate that
MCU-Net combined with epistemic uncertainty and an uncertainty threshold tuned
for this application maximizes automated performance on an individual patient
level, yet refers truly uncertain cases. This is a step towards uncertainty
representations when deploying machine learning based decision support in
healthcare settings.

In this paper, we investigate the edge clique cover problem in claw-free graphs, which is a fundamental problem in graph theory and has applications in various fields such as social network analysis, web graph analysis, and database design. A clique cover of a graph is a set of cliques (maximal cliques) that covers all the edges of the graph. The minimum size of a clique cover is called the edge clique cover number of the graph.

We present a new algorithm that finds an edge clique cover of a claw-free graph with a guaranteed performance ratio. Our approach is based on a combination of spectral methods and combinatorial techniques. We first compute a sparse approximation of the graph's adjacency matrix and then use a linear programming relaxation to find an approximate solution. We then round the solution to obtain a clique cover.

We prove that our algorithm produces an edge clique cover of size at most (1+ε) times the optimal edge clique cover number, for any ε>0. This is the first algorithm that achieves a guaranteed performance ratio for the edge clique cover problem in claw-free graphs.

Our results have important implications for the design and analysis of algorithms for various graph problems. In particular, our technique can be applied to other graph problems that can be formulated as linear programs, such as the maximum flow problem and the minimum cut problem.

We also perform extensive experiments on real-world graphs to evaluate the performance of our algorithm. Our results show that our algorithm significantly outperforms existing algorithms in terms of both computational efficiency and solution quality.

Overall, our paper makes a significant contribution to the study of the edge clique cover problem in claw-free graphs, and demonstrates the power of combining spectral methods and combinatorial techniques for solving graph optimization problems.

We introduce a parametrized version of the Wadge game for functions and show
that each lower cone in the Weihrauch degrees is characterized by such a game.
These parametrized Wadge games subsume the original Wadge game, the eraser and
backtrack games as well as Semmes's tree games. In particular, we propose that
the lower cones in the Weihrauch degrees are the answer to Andretta's question
on which classes of functions admit game characterizations.

For the purpose of this paper we show that for four‐wavelength mode mixers such as multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs), tuning does not influence a resonant state under one full cycle pulse with a wavelength length equivalent to that of the CW carrier. This same technology has now been implemented and tested utilizing several large 1–2 cm radius samples. In this paper, we present an information-theoretic derivation of min-cut based clustering, a popular method for partitioning a graph into clusters. Our approach is based on the idea of maximizing the mutual information between clusters, which is a measure of the similarity between the clusters. We show that the min-cut algorithm can be interpreted as a method for finding the optimal clustering that maximizes the mutual information, subject to a constraint on the total edge weight between clusters.

We begin by defining a probabilistic model for the graph, in which each node is assigned a random variable representing its cluster membership. We then derive an expression for the mutual information between clusters, which is a function of the cluster assignments and the edge weights between nodes. We show that the min-cut algorithm can be seen as a method for finding the cluster assignments that maximize the mutual information, subject to the constraint that the total edge weight between clusters is minimized.

We also prove that the min-cut algorithm is equivalent to a variational inference algorithm, which is a method for approximating the true posterior distribution over the cluster assignments. This equivalence provides a theoretical justification for the use of min-cut clustering, and suggests that it can be seen as a form of approximate inference in a probabilistic model.

Our results provide a new perspective on min-cut clustering, and demonstrate its connection to information-theoretic principles. They also suggest that the algorithm can be used in a wider range of applications, such as image segmentation, natural language processing, and recommendation systems.

Overall, our paper provides a theoretical foundation for min-cut clustering, and demonstrates its relationship to information-theoretic principles. The results have important implications for the design and analysis of clustering algorithms, and provide a new perspective on the use of graph-based methods in machine learning.

In this paper, we present Segmenter, a novel approach to semantic segmentation that leverages the power of Transformers to accurately and efficiently segment images into their constituent parts. Semantic segmentation is a fundamental task in computer vision, with applications in a wide range of domains, including autonomous driving, medical imaging, and robotics.

Existing approaches to semantic segmentation rely on convolutional neural networks (CNNs), which are limited in their ability to capture long-range dependencies and contextual information. In contrast, Transformers have proven highly effective in natural language processing tasks, where long-range dependencies are crucial. We hypothesize that Transformers can similarly improve performance in semantic segmentation tasks.

Our Segmenter model replaces traditional CNNs with Transformers, using self-attention mechanisms to capture contextual information and long-range dependencies between image pixels. We evaluate Segmenter on several benchmark datasets, including Cityscapes, PASCAL VOC, and COCO, and show that it outperforms state-of-the-art CNN-based models in terms of both accuracy and efficiency.

In addition to its improved performance, Segmenter has several advantages over traditional CNN-based models. It requires fewer parameters and computations, making it more computationally efficient and easier to train. It is also more scalable, allowing for larger input sizes and faster inference times.

Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of Transformers in semantic segmentation tasks, and highlight the potential of Segmenter as a valuable tool for a wide range of applications. We further analyze the contributions of different components of the Segmenter model, providing insights into the role of self-attention and other design choices in its performance.

Overall, our work represents a significant step forward in the field of semantic segmentation, and demonstrates the versatility and power of Transformers in computer vision tasks.

This study examines the relationship between societal individualism and tobacco use over the past century, using data from the United States. We employed time series analysis techniques to model the prevalence of smoking among adults, considering factors such as urbanization, income, education, and media exposure. Our results indicate that societal individualism has played a significant role in shaping tobacco use patterns during this period. Specifically, we found that increases in individualism were associated with higher rates of smoking initiation, particularly among young people, and that this effect was strongest in environments where individual freedom and autonomy are highly valued. Conversely, reductions in individualism corresponded with decreases in smoking prevalence, especially among older adults. These findings suggest that public health initiatives aiming to reduce tobacco use should consider addressing broader sociocultural factors, including social norms and values related to individualism. By acknowledging and addressing these influences, policymakers may achieve greater success in reducing the burden of tobacco-related diseases.

In this paper, we present a novel approach towards clustering-based image segmentation that leverages the strengths of both hierarchical and density-based clustering methods. Our proposed method, called HDP-DBSCAN, combines the probabilistic nature of Hierarchical Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (HDP-clustering) with the robustness of Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN). This hybrid approach enables us to capture the spatial heterogeneity of images while efficiently handling noise and outliers.

We evaluate the performance of HDP-DBSCAN on several benchmark datasets, including synthetic and real-world images, and compare it with state-of-the-art clustering-based image segmentation methods. The results show that our proposed method outperforms existing approaches in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency. Specifically, HDP-DBSCAN achieves an average silhouette coefficient of 0.85 and accurately segments images with varying levels of noise and complexity.

The key contribution of this paper is the introduction of a novel clustering framework that seamlessly integrates the advantages of HDP-clustering and DBSCAN. By combining the probabilistic nature of HDP-clustering with the robustness of DBSCAN, we develop a method that can effectively handle diverse types of noise and irregularities in images. Additionally, we propose a new evaluation metric, called the Adjusted Rand Index with Noise (ARIN), which better captures the performance of clustering algorithms in the presence of noise.

Our findings have significant implications for various computer vision applications, such as object recognition, tracking, and scene understanding. The proposed method has the potential to improve the accuracy and efficiency of clustering-based image segmentation techniques, making them more viable for real-world scenarios where data is often noisy and complex.

In this paper, we investigate the problem of graph differentiation in first-order logic (FOL) and establish upper bounds on the quantifier depth required to differentiate between two graphs. We consider the class of graphs that can be represented using FOL formulas with a fixed set of predicate symbols and show that the quantifier depth needed to distinguish between any two such graphs is at most $k$, where $k$ is a constant that depends only on the number of predicate symbols used.

Our main result demonstrates that the quantifier depth required for graph differentiation in FOL grows logarithmically with the size of the input graphs. Specifically, we prove that there exists a function $f$ such that the quantifier depth needed to differentiate between two graphs of size $n$ is at most $f(n)$, where $f(n)$ is a logarithmic function of $n$. This Upper bound holds even when the formulae are allowed to have multiple variables per edge, which greatly increases their expressive power.

We also explore related results and extensions of our main theorem, including the case of graphs with bounded degree, the relationship between quantifier depth and other complexity measures, and connections to similar results in the literature. Our findings provide new insights into the limitations and capabilities of FOL for reasoning about graph structures and contribute to a deeper understanding of the fundamental limits of logical reasoning in artificial intelligence.

Unsupervised Domain Adaptation Network with Category-Centric Prototype Aligner for Biomedical Image Segmentation

Abstract: Biomedical image segmentation is a fundamental task in medical image analysis. However, the performance of deep learning-based segmentation methods is often limited by the lack of annotated training data. To address this issue, we propose a novel unsupervised domain adaptation network with category-centric prototype aligner (CCPA) for biomedical image segmentation. a new multi-attention learning model based on adaptive boosting. AttentionBoost
designs a multi-stage network and introduces a new loss adjustment mechanism
for a dense prediction model to adaptively learn what to attend at each stage
directly on image data without necessitating any prior definition about what to
attend. This mechanism modulates the attention of each stage to correct the
mistakes of previous stages, by adjusting the loss weight of each pixel
prediction separately with respect to how accurate the previous stages are on
this pixel. This mechanism enables AttentionBoost to learn different attentions
for different pixels at the same stage, according to difficulty of learning
these pixels, as well as multiple attentions for the same pixel at different
stages, according to confidence of these stages on their predictions for this
pixel. Using gland segmentation as a showcase application, our experiments
demonstrate that AttentionBoost improves the results of its counterparts.

We then use a fully connected CRF to refine the output of the CNN, enforcing spatial consistency and incorporating contextual information from neighboring pixels.

Experiments on several benchmark datasets demonstrate that DeepLab outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of segmentation accuracy while maintaining a high processing speed. Our work advances the field of semantic image segmentation by introducing a powerful and efficient approach that can accurately handle complex scenes with fine boundaries and various object scales. The combination of CNNs, atrous convolution, and fully connected CRFs in DeepLab establishes a new standard for segmentation models, paving the way for further improvements and applications in computer vision.

medical image computing and analysis, its paradigm of supervised learning
demands a large number of annotations for training to avoid overfitting and
achieving promising results. In clinical practices, massive semantic
annotations are difficult to acquire in some conditions where specialized

segmentation model to fast generalize to an unseen class with few training
images. We construct our few-shot image segmentor using a deep convolutional
network trained episodically. Motivated by the spatial consistency and
regularity in medical images, we developed an efficient global correlation
module to capture the correlation between a support and query image and
incorporate it into the deep network called global correlation network.
Moreover, we enhance discriminability of deep embedding to encourage clustering
of the feature domains of the same class while keep the feature domains of
different organs far apart. Ablation Study proved the effectiveness of the
proposed global correlation module and discriminative embedding loss. Extensive
experiments on anatomical abdomen images on both CT and MRI modalities are
performed to demonstrate the state-of-the-art performance of our proposed
model.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to image segmentation that combines the strengths of variational image segmentation with the advances in image restoration. Our proposed model leverages the ability of Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) to learn a probabilistic representation of images and couples it with an image restoration module to improve the accuracy and efficiency of image segmentation.

Experiments on several benchmark datasets demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art image segmentation models, including fully supervised models, in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency. We also show that our model is robust to various types of noise and corruptions, making it suitable for real-world applications where images are often degraded or imperfect.

Our main contribution is the introduction of an image restoration module into the traditional VAE architecture, which enables the model to refine its learned representations and produce more accurate segmentations. This is achieved by incorporating a feedback loop that allows the model to iteratively refine its predictions based on the restored images.

The key advantage of our proposed method lies in its ability to jointly optimize image segmentation and restoration tasks, leading to improved performance in both tasks. The experimental results demonstrate that our approach not only produces accurate segmentations but also effectively removes noise and artifacts from the input images.

This work has important implications for a wide range of applications, such as medical imaging, autonomous driving, and robotics, where both accurate image segmentation and restoration are crucial. Our proposed method offers a promising solution for scenarios where labeled data is scarce or difficult to obtain, while still achieving high accuracy and robustness.

Our results show that the electrode density of states has a significant impact on the transport properties of pyridine-linked single molecule junctions. We find that the density of states of the electrodes can alter the electronic structure of the molecule, leading to changes in the molecular orbitals and the bonding between the molecule and the electrodes. This, in turn, affects the transport behavior, including the current-voltage characteristics and the stability of the junction.

We also find that the impact of the electrode density of states on transport is strongly dependent on the type of electrodes used. For example, we show that using noble metal electrodes with high density of states leads to a significant increase in the current flowing through the junction, while using electrodes with lower density of states results in a decrease in current.

Our results have important implications for the design and optimization of single molecule junctions for electronic applications. By controlling the electrode density of states, we can tune the transport properties of these junctions and enhance their performance. This work provides a new avenue for the development of high-performance single molecule electronic devices.

Overall, our study demonstrates the importance of considering the electrode density of states in the design and optimization of single molecule junctions. By understanding the impact of this parameter on transport behavior, we can develop new strategies for improving the performance of these junctions and advancing the field of molecular electronics.

predicted SDMs of labeled and unlabeled data so that our network is able to

state-of-the-art approaches with improved shape estimation, which validates its

In recent years researchers have gravitated to social media platforms,
especially Twitter, as fertile ground for empirical analysis of social
phenomena. Social media provides researchers access to trace data of
interactions and discourse that once went unrecorded in the offline world.

particular to social media and applicable to the broader social world. This
paper offers a minireview of Twitter-based research on political crowd
behavior. This literature offers insight into particular social phenomena on
Twitter, but often fails to use standardized methods that permit interpretation
beyond individual studies. Moreover, the literature fails to ground
methodologies and results in social or political theory, divorcing empirical
research from the theory needed to interpret it. Rather, papers focus primarily
on methodological innovations for social media analyses, but these too often
fail to sufficiently demonstrate the validity of such methodologies. This
minireview considers a small number of selected papers; we analyze their (often
lack of) theoretical approaches, review their methodological innovations, and
offer suggestions as to the relevance of their results for political scientists
and sociologists.

Contemporary deep learning based medical image segmentation algorithms
require hours of annotation labor by domain experts. These data hungry deep
models perform sub-optimally in the presence of limited amount of labeled data.
In this paper, we present a data efficient learning framework using the recent
concept of Generative Adversarial Networks; this allows a deep neural network
to perform significantly better than its fully supervised counterpart in low
annotation regime. The proposed method is an extension of our previous work
with the addition of a new unsupervised adversarial loss and a structured
prediction based architecture. To the best of our knowledge, this work is the
first demonstration of an adversarial framework based structured prediction
model for medical image segmentation. Though generic, we apply our method for
segmentation of blood vessels in retinal fundus images. We experiment with
extreme low annotation budget (0.8 - 1.6% of contemporary annotation size). On
DRIVE and STARE datasets, the proposed method outperforms our previous method
and other fully supervised benchmark models by significant margins especially
with very low number of annotated examples. In addition, our systematic
ablation studies suggest some key recipes for successfully training GAN based
semi-supervised algorithms with an encoder-decoder style network architecture.

Segmentation of colorectal cancerous regions from 3D Magnetic Resonance (MR)
images is a crucial procedure for radiotherapy which conventionally requires
accurate delineation of tumour boundaries at an expense of labor, time and
reproducibility. While deep learning based methods serve good baselines in 3D
image segmentation tasks, small applicable patch size limits effective
receptive field and degrades segmentation performance. In addition, Regions of
interest (RoIs) localization from large whole volume 3D images serves as a
preceding operation that brings about multiple benefits in terms of speed,
target completeness, reduction of false positives. Distinct from sliding window
or non-joint localization-segmentation based models, we propose a novel
multitask framework referred to as 3D RoI-aware U-Net (3D RU-Net), for RoI
localization and in-region segmentation where the two tasks share one backbone
encoder network. With the region proposals from the encoder, we crop
multi-level RoI in-region features from the encoder to form a GPU
memory-efficient decoder for detailpreserving segmentation and therefore
enlarged applicable volume size and effective receptive field. To effectively
train the model, we designed a Dice formulated loss function for the
global-to-local multi-task learning procedure. Based on the efficiency gains,
we went on to ensemble models with different receptive fields to achieve even
higher performance costing minor extra computational expensiveness. Extensive
experiments were conducted on 64 cancerous cases with a four-fold
cross-validation, and the results showed significant superiority in terms of
accuracy and efficiency over conventional frameworks. In conclusion, the
proposed method has a huge potential for extension to other 3D object
segmentation tasks from medical images due to its inherent generalizability.
The code for the proposed method is publicly available.

Deep fully convolutional neural network (FCN) based architectures have shown
great potential in medical image segmentation. However, such architectures
usually have millions of parameters and inadequate number of training samples
leading to over-fitting and poor generalization. In this paper, we present a
novel highly parameter and memory efficient FCN based architecture for medical
image analysis. We propose a novel up-sampling path which incorporates long
skip and short-cut connections to overcome the feature map explosion in FCN
like architectures. In order to processes the input images at multiple scales
and view points simultaneously, we propose to incorporate Inception module's
parallel structures. We also propose a novel dual loss function whose weighting
scheme allows to combine advantages of cross-entropy and dice loss. We have
validated our proposed network architecture on two publicly available datasets,
namely: (i) Automated Cardiac Disease Diagnosis Challenge (ACDC-2017), (ii)
Left Ventricular Segmentation Challenge (LV-2011). Our approach in ACDC-2017
challenge stands second place for segmentation and first place in automated
cardiac disease diagnosis tasks with an accuracy of 100%. In the LV-2011
challenge our approach attained 0.74 Jaccard index, which is so far the highest
published result in fully automated algorithms. From the segmentation we
extracted clinically relevant cardiac parameters and hand-crafted features
which reflected the clinical diagnostic analysis to train an ensemble system
for cardiac disease classification. Our approach combined both cardiac
segmentation and disease diagnosis into a fully automated framework which is
computational efficient and hence has the potential to be incorporated in
computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) tools for clinical application.

The ability to detect change-points in a dynamic network or a time series of
graphs is an increasingly important task in many applications of the emerging
discipline of graph signal processing. This paper formulates change-point
detection as a hypothesis testing problem in terms of a generative latent
position model, focusing on the special case of the Stochastic Block Model time
series. We analyze two classes of scan statistics, based on distinct underlying
locality statistics presented in the literature. Our main contribution is the
derivation of the limiting distributions and power characteristics of the
competing scan statistics. Performance is compared theoretically, on synthetic
data, and on the Enron email corpus. We demonstrate that both statistics are
admissible in one simple setting, while one of the statistics is inadmissible a
second setting.

We present a novel method to study the polarisation distribution patterns in a large class of quasars. We use the spectral composition of a single quasar, CMB 1386+648 as described by Riekel et al. [2013] and apply it to detect and analyze numerous polarisers detected using HST/GALEX filters (Figure 1). These spectra provide data to confirm that there are hundreds or even thousands of polarising objects present at any object distance of interest. In the analysis phase we apply two parametric methods that combine the optical, spectroscopic and statistical constraints on the polarisations of quasars to determine their polarizabilities. Firstly we plot each spectral profile against luminosity, which gives a good indication for the density of nearby objects; secondly we calculate the spatial distribution of polariser properties by measuring them with several different tools. These results enable us to make inferences about object size and structure, stellar mass distribution and magnetic field strength (i.e. flux lines) – providing evidence for dark matter, normal matter or both at multiple redshifts. To find out how these properties change over different brightness levels such as quasar redshift z ~10, they also need to be estimated at quasar distances, where the resulting variation gives significant information about the structure and the host galaxy hosting the quasar. Finally, this technique reveals some interesting observations around very rapidly-brightening bright quasars that only appeared within months and years of the discovery, thus hinting towards distant population structures.

We also introduce a new regularization term that encourages the dictionary atoms to be sparse, leading to better generalization performance.

We evaluate our algorithm on several benchmark datasets and compare it to state-of-the-art methods for online learning with kernels. Our results show that our algorithm achieves better performance in terms of accuracy and efficiency, particularly in high-dimensional settings. We also provide an analysis of the effect of the key hyperparameters on the performance of our algorithm, providing insights into the best practices for using sparse dictionaries for online learning with kernels.

Our work has important implications for a wide range of applications, including image and text classification, bioinformatics, and recommender systems. When mathematical/computational problems reach infinity, extending analysis
and/or numerical computation beyond it becomes a notorious challenge. We
suggest that, upon suitable singular transformations (that can in principle be
computationally detected on the fly) it becomes possible to go beyond infinity
to the other side, with the solution becoming again well behaved and the
computations continuing normally. In our lumped, Ordinary Differential Equation
(ODE) examples this infinity crossing can happen instantaneously; at the
spatially distributed, Partial Differential Equation (PDE) level the crossing
of infinity may even persist for finite time, necessitating the introduction of

Contour detection has been a fundamental component in many image segmentation
and object detection systems. Most previous work utilizes low-level features
such as texture or saliency to detect contours and then use them as cues for a
higher-level task such as object detection. However, we claim that recognizing
objects and predicting contours are two mutually related tasks. Contrary to
traditional approaches, we show that we can invert the commonly established
pipeline: instead of detecting contours with low-level cues for a higher-level
recognition task, we exploit object-related features as high-level cues for
contour detection.
  We achieve this goal by means of a multi-scale deep network that consists of
five convolutional layers and a bifurcated fully-connected sub-network. The
section from the input layer to the fifth convolutional layer is fixed and
directly lifted from a pre-trained network optimized over a large-scale object
classification task. This section of the network is applied to four different
scales of the image input. These four parallel and identical streams are then
attached to a bifurcated sub-network consisting of two independently-trained
branches. One branch learns to predict the contour likelihood (with a
classification objective) whereas the other branch is trained to learn the
fraction of human labelers agreeing about the contour presence at a given point
(with a regression criterion).
  We show that without any feature engineering our multi-scale deep learning
approach achieves state-of-the-art results in contour detection.

In this paper, we investigate the concept of field of view (FOV) in the context of near-field aperture synthesis imaging. Near-field aperture synthesis is a technique that allows for the creation of high-resolution images of objects or scenes using a large number of low-resolution images taken from different viewpoints. The FOV refers to the region of space that can be observed by an imaging system at a given time.

We analyze the relationship between the FOV and the size and shape of the near-field aperture, as well as the impact of FOV on the quality of the reconstructed image. We demonstrate through simulations and experiments that the FOV has a significant effect on the resolution and artifacts present in the reconstruction, and that carefully designing the FOV can improve the overall performance of the imaging system.

Our results have important implications for the development of high-resolution imaging systems using near-field aperture synthesis, particularly in applications where the object being imaged is too small to be captured within a single exposure, such as in microscopy, surveillance, and telescopy. By optimizing the FOV, these systems can achieve higher resolution and improved image quality, enabling new opportunities for scientific research and other applications.

[Abstract] The concept of vector spaces is widely used in theoretical computer science [1]. This has led to many articles that describe it, while there are essentially no such books on the subject (for example I could find only one book that describes a formal way to visualize generalization laws). On average, we cannot distinguish between the different kinds of convex-concave transformations. To illustrate our point, we extend the conventional notion of a vector space to include congruent and conversely congruential transformations, so called convex interleaveings [2, 3 ]. We show that in such an environment, it makes sense not to expect any particular property called "power", which normally characterises the congruential transformation as well as all other nonlinear conjugate pairs (LIPs) [4], because our definition includes all subspace invariants that can be proved either by convex interleaving or LIP-equations; hence our definitions require no special power argument. A generalisation of this idea leads to new methods for solving nonstandard linear equations with high convergence when their solution is unconstrained [5]. However, these new methods remain under active development and should soon provide us with more sophisticated tools. In addition, the concept is now relevant to algebraic geometry, where the non-Gaussian group ZFC is often known to form an ordinary matrix, whose dimension n (also denoted n0, meaning no diagonal element) measures its Convexity Property as ε(n), defined simply on the product-column vector space over a unit sphere [6]. Such groups were recently discussed by Karpov [7–9]; but they do not correspond well to a real world model with high dimensionality. Our method is based exclusively on the idea of congruency matrices. We observe several properties that may be useful for understanding convex analysis – namely power, complementarity and connectivity.

In this paper, we present a novel approach to electron microscopy image segmentation using a semi-supervised hierarchical merge tree (SSHMT). Electromicroscopy imaging is a widely used technique in materials science and biology for observing the morphology of samples at the nanoscale. However, automatic segmentation of these images remains a challenging task due to the complexity of the structures and the large amount of data generated by modern electron microscopes.
Existing methods for electron microscopy image segmentation rely on supervised learning techniques that require manual annotations of large numbers of training examples, which can be time-consuming and expensive to obtain. In contrast, our SSHMT method leverages both labeled and unlabeled data to train a hierarchy of merged trees that progressively segment the input images. We demonstrate the effectiveness of SSHMT using several experimental datasets and show that it outperforms state-of-the-art segmentation techniques in terms of accuracy and efficiency. Moreover, our method is robust against various types of noise and artifacts commonly encountered in electron microscopy imaging. The proposed SSHMT algorithm has important implications for many applications including but not limited to fault detection and classification in electronics , particle detection in biomedical research, and grain boundary characterization in materials science.
To summarize, in this work , we put forward an innovative solution for electron microscopy image segmentation utilizing a semi-supervised hierarchical merge tree(SSHMT), which takes advantage of both labeled and unlabelled information from gigantic datasets, demonstrating superior performance and stability compared with prior arts. Our findings open up new possibilities for automated analysis of massive amounts of electron microscopy pictures. This may have far-reaching consequences in fields such as material science, biology, and electronics.

We present a method to correct the timing jitter of a femtosecond laser system
  for pump-probe experiments at the Linac Coherent Light Source (LCLS).
  The method is based on the measurement of the timing jitter of the laser
  system using a fast photodiode and a time-to-digital converter (TDC).
  The jitter is measured by comparing the laser pulse arrival time with
  the arrival time of a reference pulse. The reference pulse is generated
  by a second laser system, which is synchronized to the first laser system
  by a common master clock. The jitter is corrected by delaying the laser
  pulse by the measured jitter. The method is demonstrated on a Ti:sapphire
  laser system with a pulse duration of 100 fs and a repetition rate of
  1 kHz. The jitter is measured to be less than 1 fs. The jitter correction
  is demonstrated by measuring the time-resolved photoluminescence of a
  semiconductor sample. The jitter correction is shown to improve the
  signal-to-noise ratio of the photoluminescence signal by a factor of 2.

This paper addresses the problem of identifying linear regressions with errors in all variables, a common issue in many fields such as finance, economics, and social sciences. Existing methods for linear regression assume that the independent variables are error-free, which can lead to biased estimates and incorrect inference when errors are present in all variables.

We propose a new method that can identify linear regressions with errors in all variables by exploiting the redundancy in the regression equation. Our method uses a combination of dimensionality reduction techniques and robust regression methods to estimate the regression coefficients and their standard errors.

We evaluate the performance of our method using simulations and real-data examples, and compare it to existing methods. The results show that our method outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and robustness, especially when the errors in the independent variables are large.

Our method has important implications for many fields where data is often subject to errors, and will enable researchers and practitioners to draw more reliable conclusions from their data.

This article presents experiments with real-time variant detection and image reconstruction in the context of detecting variants in genomic data. The experiments use several popular deep neural network architectures, such as convolutional networks, LSTMs and autoencoders, along with different number of hidden layers (1 to 8) and their default activation functions. In each experiment the detector performs two task instances -- a background instance and a feature domain where the detected variant was predicted to exist. These operations combine to produce an individual model that combines the training set with a global validation sample while detecting changes between the two trials. Our aim is to investigate how we can improve the performance of the resulting model by optimizing the parameters of this classifier. We test various methods on a standard dataset including both normal datasets where there are no predictions made and images selected with known regions of noise; these samples have been processed using the following method: the feature map from the detector's loss function at each pixel location is normalized into one parameter vector that encodes all possible features (e.g., 3 different colors), then added up over some range of pixels, weighted by their importance relative to the baseline color. The difference with the background-predicted value is averaged across pixels in the image or over several images, and these results are averaged out separately before calling the trained model. We also compare our experimental setup against our previous results when testing other deep kernel learning models on the same dataset. By doing so, we identify significant advantages over state-of-the-art implementations for various kinds of applications. To achieve high levels of quality, we implement the convnet architecture through a combination of a custom kernel-based implementation and the optimized kernels of many large Deep Learning frameworks used in computer vision in order to obtain best image similarity ratings based on the original input data.

Advances in object-centric generative models (OCGMs) have culminated in the
development of a broad range of methods for unsupervised object segmentation
and interpretable object-centric scene generation. These methods, however, are
limited to simulated and real-world datasets with limited visual complexity.
Moreover, object representations are often inferred using RNNs which do not
scale well to large images or iterative refinement which avoids imposing an
unnatural ordering on objects in an image but requires the a priori
initialisation of a fixed number of object representations. In contrast to
established paradigms, this work proposes an embedding-based approach in which
embeddings of pixels are clustered in a differentiable fashion using a
stochastic, non-parametric stick-breaking process. Similar to iterative
refinement, this clustering procedure also leads to randomly ordered object
representations, but without the need of initialising a fixed number of
clusters a priori. This is used to develop a new model, GENESIS-V2, which can
infer a variable number of object representations without using RNNs or
iterative refinement. We show that GENESIS-V2 outperforms previous methods for
unsupervised image segmentation and object-centric scene generation on
established synthetic datasets as well as more complex real-world datasets.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to interactive medical image segmentation that combines point-based interaction and sequential patch learning. Our method enables users to interact with the segmentation process through intuitive point-based input, allowing them to indicate the location of relevant structures within the image. This information is then used to iteratively refine the segmentation mask, leveraging the strengths of both fully supervised and unsupervised learning methods.

We evaluate our approach on several datasets of varying modalities and complexity, including brain MRIs, lung CT scans, and fundus images. The results demonstrate that our method achieves high accuracy and efficiency in segmenting complex anatomical structures while also providing a user-friendly experience. Furthermore, we show that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art interactive segmentation techniques in terms of both accuracy and computational cost.

The main contributions of this work are:

1. A novel framework for interactive medical image segmentation that integrates point-based interaction and sequential patch learning.
2. An efficient algorithm that utilizes point-based feedback to progressively refine the segmentation mask, leveraging the advantages of both supervised and unsupervised learning methods.
3. Thorough evaluations demonstrating the effectiveness and efficiency of our approach compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.
4. A detailed analysis of the impact of different design choices and parameters on performance, providing insights into optimal usage scenarios.

Our work has important implications for various applications that require accurate and efficient medical image segmentation, such as disease diagnosis, treatment planning, and monitoring. By enabling users to actively guide the segmentation process, our approach can improve the accuracy and reliability of downstream analyses, ultimately supporting better patient care and clinical decision-making.

This paper presents local spectral radius formulas for a class of unbounded operators on Banach spaces. The local spectral radius is a measure of the growth rate of the operator, and the formulas provide a way to estimate this growth rate in a local sense. The class of operators considered includes those that are not necessarily compact or even bounded, but still have certain regularity properties. The formulas are derived using functional analysis techniques, and their validity is demonstrated through a series of examples and counterexamples. The results presented in this paper have implications for the study of dynamical systems and partial differential equations, among other areas of mathematics.

This survey provides an overview of recent research in computer-aided knee joint magnetic resonance image segmentation, a critical step in diagnosing and treating knee injuries and diseases. We discuss the challenges associated with manual segmentation, which can be time-consuming and subjective, and highlight the need for accurate and efficient automated methods.

We review state-of-the-art algorithms and techniques used in computer-aided knee joint MRI segmentation, including machine learning approaches, active contours, level sets, and graph-based methods. We also examine the use of transfer learning, atlas-based segmentation, and multi-modal imaging fusion to improve segmentation accuracy. Specifically, we discuss the application of deep learning techniques such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) for image segmentation and feature extraction. Additionally, we explore the role of hyperparameter optimization and validation methodologies in achieving robust performance.

Accurate segmentation and reconstruction of cardiac walls from computed tomography (CT) data are crucial steps in various clinical applications, such as diagnosis, treatment planning, and monitoring of heart diseases. However, the task is challenging due to factors like image quality, motion artifacts, and complex anatomy. In this work, we propose PC-U Net, a deep learning framework that jointly learns to reconstruct and segment cardiac walls in 3D from raw CT data. Our approach leverages a combination of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with physics constraints to improve accuracy, efficiency, and robustness. The proposed method consists of two parts: 1) PC-Net, which generates initial wall boundaries using a fully convolutional network, and 2) U-Net, which refines the borders via skip connections and incorporates user interactions. We evaluate our method on a dataset containing 40 diverse patients using both qualitative and quantitative metrics. Experimental results show superior performance when compared to state-of-the-art methods regarding Dice similarity coefficient, average surface distance, and processing time. Additionally, we demonstrate the feasibility of integrating our method into real-time scenarios through synchronization with commercial software. By providing accurate and efficient reconstruction and segmentation, PC-U Net can significantly aid interventionalists and researchers in their endeavors involving cardiac care.

In this paper, we explore the use of graphical structures for the design and verification of quantum error correction (QEC) codes. QEC codes are a crucial component of fault-tolerant quantum computing, as they enable the protection of quantum information against errors caused by noise in quantum systems. However, the design and verification of these codes remain challenging tasks due to their complex algebraic structure.

To address these challenges, our work leverages the power of graph theory to represent and manipulate QEC codes in a visually intuitive way. We introduce several Graphical Structures for Quantum Error Correction (GQECs), which provide a compact representation of QEC codes that can be easily navigated and analyzed using graphical tools. We demonstrate the effectiveness of GQECs by applying them to several examples of QEC codes, including surface codes and color codes.

Our results show that GQECs offer significant advantages over traditional methods for designing and verifying QEC codes. They allow for efficient simulation, visualization, and analysis of QEC codes, enabling rapid prototyping and optimization of code designs. Furthermore, GQECs facilitate the understanding oferror thresholds and fault tolerance limits, providing valuable insights into the behavior of QEC codes under various noise models.

We also investigate the theoretical foundations of GQECs, establishing connections between graphical representations and the underlying algebraic properties of QEC codes. This enables us to develop a systematic approach for constructing GQECs from arbitrary QEC codes, paving the way for future research on more sophisticated GQEC designs.

Overall, our work presents a novel, graphically-driven framework for the design and verification of QEC codes that has the potential to significantly improve the efficiency and accuracy of quantum error correction techniques. The introduced GQECs offer an accessible entry point for researchers and practitioners interested in exploring the rich landscape of QEC codes and their applications in quantum computing.

Fuzzing methods such as kernelized weighted statistics (WBS), clustering trees, and other machine learning algorithms are popular in many areas of data science and engineering, but they often rely on pre-trained models and assumptions to achieve high accuracy. Because neural networks lack some of these features (e.g., cross validation), robust analysis on non-human datasets relies largely on pre-processing tasks to identify important properties that differentiate images by using techniques like discriminant analyses, clustering tree techniques, clustering analysis or random forest techniques. While these approaches allow researchers to learn new features via reinforcement learning that can be useful with more complex cases, they are insufficient tools when working on noisy human datasets or unsupervised machine learning tasks which often only require classification and clustering with very limited feature selection. We present two implementations of Kernelized Weighted Syste(er) Analysis (SUSAN) and apply them to three different tasks where there is no formal model training at all: clustering (unsupervised task); image segmentation through fMRI [1]; and class recognition via Naive Bayes Classifier (NBCC). Our method achieves higher scores than previously reported kernel analysis systems within each task with over 95% accuracy; however, this result was obtained without model optimization as we performed our analysis with just two dimensions—a binary classification filter and an eigenvector length predictor. Finally, we show how SUSAN can also be used with the Leaps API to obtain additional statistical accuracy at no additional computation cost compared to regular analysis. However, since Leaps uses machine learning frameworks with well known implementation details as input for these kernels rather than introducing his own kernels and tuning settings, it is possible on the larger dataset of 1000 images that SUSAN may perform better for certain kinds of tasks such as regression and classification rather than Leaps.[[pdf]]

A group-specific neural representation underlying complex, hierarchical percepts has been proposed for vision, speech, reading and other perceptual processing in monkeys [1], dogs [4] and human beings [3]. In contrast to more specialized representations used by other primates [5], monkeys' groups are hierarchically organized; with each monkey forming its own cluster of neurons with minimal interconnections with neighboring clusters or other monkeys [2]. To explore what might be meant by this notion of hierarchical representation with respect to perceptual processing, we constructed a model based on hierarchical neuron coding (HNC) that incorporates these properties and exploits them to represent visual spatial relationships among objects [6]. This hierarchical encoding can simultaneously extract relevant features to recognize an object at low levels of abstraction and retain discriminative power even when higher levels of abstraction are required to perform a matching action on the extracted feature.

In this paper, we investigate the universality of luminosity-metallicity and mass-metallicity relations for compact star-forming galaxies at redshifts 0 < z < 3. By analyzing a large sample of galaxies from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey and the Hubble Space Telescope, we find that the luminosity-metallicity relation exhibits a strong correlation between galaxy luminosity and metallicity, with more luminous galaxies displaying higher metallicities. Similarly, the mass-metallicity relation shows a positive correlation between galaxy mass and metallicity.

We find that these relations hold universally for compact star-forming galaxies across the entire redshift range, with no significant evolution in the normalization or slope of the relations over cosmic time. Our results suggest that the physical processes driving galaxy evolution, such as gas accretion and star formation, are remarkably consistent across the universe, and that the underlying physical principles governing these processes are well-described by current theoretical models.

Our findings have important implications for the study of galaxy evolution and the interpretation of observations from high-redshift galaxies. They demonstrate that the luminosity-metallicity and mass-metallicity relations can be used as reliable tools for studying galaxy evolution and for constraining models of galaxy formation and evolution. Additionally, our results provide a valuable benchmark for comparing the properties of galaxies at different redshifts and for understanding the role of environment and other external factors in shaping galaxy evolution.

Overall, our study provides new insights into the universality of galaxy evolution and highlights the power of large-scale spectroscopic surveys for understanding the properties and behavior of galaxies across the universe.

Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm remains one of the most popular ways to

techniques. In simulation experiments, the proposed method is shown to

estimation performance. The proposed method is applied to cluster Multiple
sclerosis (MS) patients based on their treatment sequences of disease-modifying
therapies (DMTs). We also propose a novel method to cluster people with MS
based on DMT prescriptions and associated clinical features (covariates) using

Let s_q(n) denote the base q sum of digits function, which for n<x, is
centered around (q-1)/2 log_q x. In Drmota, Mauduit and Rivat's 2009 paper,
they look at sum of digits of prime numbers, and provide asymptotics for the
size of the set {p<x, p prime : s_q(p)=alpha(q-1)log_q x} where alpha lies in a
tight range around 1/2. In this paper, we examine the tails of this
distribution, and provide the lower bound |{p < x, p prime :
s_q(p)>alpha(q-1)log_q x}| >>x^{2(1-alpha)}e^{-c(log x)^{1/2+epsilon}} for
1/2<alpha<0.7375. To attain this lower bound, we note that the multinomial
distribution is sharply peaked, and apply results regarding primes in short
intervals. This proves that there are infinitely many primes with more than
twice as many ones than zeros in their binary expansion.

In the deep metric learning approach to image segmentation, a convolutional
net densely generates feature vectors at the pixels of an image. Pairs of
feature vectors are trained to be similar or different, depending on whether
the corresponding pixels belong to same or different ground truth segments. To
segment a new image, the feature vectors are computed and clustered. Both
empirically and theoretically, it is unclear whether or when deep metric
learning is superior to the more conventional approach of directly predicting
an affinity graph with a convolutional net. We compare the two approaches using
brain images from serial section electron microscopy images, which constitute
an especially challenging example of instance segmentation. We first show that
seed-based postprocessing of the feature vectors, as originally proposed,
produces inferior accuracy because it is difficult for the convolutional net to
predict feature vectors that remain uniform across large objects. Then we
consider postprocessing by thresholding a nearest neighbor graph followed by
connected components. In this case, segmentations from a "metric graph" turn
out to be competitive or even superior to segmentations from a directly
predicted affinity graph. To explain these findings theoretically, we invoke
the property that the metric function satisfies the triangle inequality. Then
we show with an example where this constraint suppresses noise, causing
connected components to more robustly segment a metric graph than an
unconstrained affinity graph.

The work reported in this article presents a high-order, stable, and
efficient Gegenbauer pseudospectral method to solve numerically a wide variety
of mathematical models. The proposed numerical scheme exploits the stability
and the well-conditioning of the numerical integration operators to produce
well-conditioned systems of algebraic equations, which can be solved easily
using standard algebraic system solvers. The core of the work lies in the
derivation of novel and stable Gegenbauer quadratures based on the stable
barycentric representation of Lagrange interpolating polynomials and the
explicit barycentric weights for the Gegenbauer-Gauss (GG) points. A rigorous
error and convergence analysis of the proposed quadratures is presented along
with a detailed set of pseudocodes for the established computational
algorithms. The proposed numerical scheme leads to a reduction in the
computational cost and time complexity required for computing the numerical
quadrature while sharing the same exponential order of accuracy achieved by
Elgindy and Smith-Miles (2013). The bulk of the work includes three numerical
test examples to assess the efficiency and accuracy of the numerical scheme.
The present method provides a strong addition to the arsenal of numerical
pseudospectral methods, and can be extended to solve a wide range of problems
arising in numerous applications.

The problem of determining the number of "flooding operations" required to
make a given coloured graph monochromatic in the one-player combinatorial game
Flood-It has been studied extensively from an algorithmic point of view, but
basic questions about the maximum number of moves that might be required in the
worst case remain unanswered. We begin a systematic investigation of such
questions, with the goal of determining, for a given graph, the maximum number
of moves that may be required, taken over all possible colourings. We give
several upper and lower bounds on this quantity for arbitrary graphs and show
that all of the bounds are tight for trees; we also investigate how much the
upper bounds can be improved if we restrict our attention to graphs with higher
edge-density.

Advances in image-based dietary assessment methods have allowed nutrition
professionals and researchers to improve the accuracy of dietary assessment,
where images of food consumed are captured using smartphones or wearable
devices. These images are then analyzed using computer vision methods to
estimate energy and nutrition content of the foods. Food image segmentation,
which determines the regions in an image where foods are located, plays an
important role in this process. Current methods are data dependent, thus cannot
generalize well for different food types. To address this problem, we propose a
class-agnostic food image segmentation method. Our method uses a pair of eating
scene images, one before start eating and one after eating is completed. Using
information from both the before and after eating images, we can segment food
images by finding the salient missing objects without any prior information
about the food class. We model a paradigm of top down saliency which guides the
attention of the human visual system (HVS) based on a task to find the salient
missing objects in a pair of images. Our method is validated on food images
collected from a dietary study which showed promising results.

Bilateral filters have wide spread use due to their edge-preserving
properties. The common use case is to manually choose a parametric filter type,
usually a Gaussian filter. In this paper, we will generalize the
parametrization and in particular derive a gradient descent algorithm so the
filter parameters can be learned from data. This derivation allows to learn
high dimensional linear filters that operate in sparsely populated feature
spaces. We build on the permutohedral lattice construction for efficient
filtering. The ability to learn more general forms of high-dimensional filters
can be used in several diverse applications. First, we demonstrate the use in
applications where single filter applications are desired for runtime reasons.
Further, we show how this algorithm can be used to learn the pairwise
potentials in densely connected conditional random fields and apply these to
different image segmentation tasks. Finally, we introduce layers of bilateral
filters in CNNs and propose bilateral neural networks for the use of
high-dimensional sparse data. This view provides new ways to encode model
structure into network architectures. A diverse set of experiments empirically
validates the usage of general forms of filters.

In this paper, we investigate the structure of almost Abelian Lie algebras, a class of Lie algebras that are nearly Abelian but not necessarily so. We provide a detailed analysis of the properties and characteristics of these algebras, and demonstrate their applications in various areas of mathematics and physics.

We begin by defining almost Abelian Lie algebras and discussing their basic properties, such as the existence of a maximal Abelian subalgebra and the presence of a non-trivial center. We then examine the relationship between almost Abelian Lie algebras and other classes of Lie algebras, including solvable and nilpotent Lie algebras.

Next, we focus on the structure of almost Abelian Lie algebras, particularly their decomposition into simpler subalgebras. We show that every almost Abelian Lie algebra can be decomposed into a direct sum of a maximal Abelian subalgebra and a complementary subalgebra, which is either Abelian or a Heisenberg algebra. We also explore the possibility of decomposing an almost Abelian Lie algebra into a product of simpler algebras, and discuss the conditions under which this is possible.

The paper also includes a discussion of the representations of almost Abelian Lie algebras, including their irreducible representations and the structure of their representation algebras. We show that the representation theory of almost Abelian Lie algebras is closely related to that of Abelian Lie algebras, but with some important differences.

Finally, we explore the applications of almost Abelian Lie algebras in various areas of mathematics and physics, including differential geometry, algebraic geometry, and quantum mechanics. We demonstrate how almost Abelian Lie algebras can be used to study certain types of differential equations and symmetries, and how they can be used to construct solvable models in physics.

Overall, this paper provides a comprehensive study of almost Abelian Lie algebras, shedding light on their structure, properties, and applications. Our results demonstrate the importance of these algebras in various areas of mathematics and physics, and provide a foundation for further research in this area.

This paper proposes a novel approach to texture segmentation of images based on graph entropies. Texture segmentation is a fundamental task in computer vision that involves dividing an image into its constituent textures or materials. Traditional methods rely on hand-crafted features and heuristics, which can be limited in their ability to handle complex textures and varying lighting conditions.

In this paper, we leverage the concept of graph entropies to develop a more robust and flexible approach to texture segmentation. We represent an image as a graph, where each pixel is a node, and edges connect pixels with similar texture features. We then compute the entropy of this graph, which captures the uncertainty or randomness in the texture patterns.

We propose a novel algorithm that iteratively updates the graph structure and computes the graph entropy at each iteration. The algorithm starts with an initial graph constructed from the image pixels and their similarity measures. At each iteration, it updates the graph structure by adding, removing, or modifying edges based on the local texture features and the current graph entropy. The process continues until the graph entropy converges or reaches a minimum threshold.

We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets, including natural images, texture synthesis datasets, and real-world scenarios. The results show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art texture segmentation methods in terms of accuracy, efficiency, and robustness. We also perform a series of ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of different components of our method and demonstrate its interpretability.

Our main contributions can be summarized as follows:

* We introduce a novel approach to texture segmentation based on graph entropies, which provides a more robust and flexible way to handle complex textures and varying lighting conditions.
* We propose a novel algorithm that iteratively updates the graph structure and computes the graph entropy, leading to improved accuracy and efficiency in texture segmentation.
* We demonstrate the effectiveness and interpretability of our method through extensive experiments and ablation studies.

Overall, this paper provides a significant step towards more accurate and efficient texture segmentation, and paves the way for further research in this area.

alcohol (PVA) thin film for the practical usage. Saturable absorption was
observed in the WS2-PVA SA at the telecommunication waveband near 1550 nm. By

purity in the radio frequency spectrum. In the Q-switching operation, the laser
had tunable repetition rate and output pulse energy of a few tens of nano
joule. Our findings suggest that few-layer WS2 nanosheets embedded in PVA thin
film are promising nonlinear optical materials for ultrafast photonic
applications as a mode locker or Q-switcher.
