To model recurrent interaction events in continuous time, an extension of the
stochastic block model is proposed where every individual belongs to a latent
group and interactions between two individuals follow a conditional
inhomogeneous Poisson process with intensity driven by the individuals' latent
groups. The model is shown to be identifiable and its estimation is based on a
semiparametric variational expectation-maximization algorithm. Two versions of
the method are developed, using either a nonparametric histogram approach (with
an adaptive choice of the partition size) or kernel intensity estimators. The
number of latent groups can be selected by an integrated classification
likelihood criterion. Finally, we demonstrate the performance of our procedure
on synthetic experiments, analyse two datasets to illustrate the utility of our
approach and comment on competing methods.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to medical image segmentation that leverages iterative estimation techniques and learns normalized inputs to improve accuracy and efficiency. Traditional methods of medical image segmentation often rely on hand-crafted features and fixed parameter settings, which can limit their performance and adaptability across different datasets and tasks.

Our proposed method uses a deep neural network to learn a mapping from raw image pixels to normalized inputs that are optimized for iterative segmentation algorithms. This allows us to decouple the input representation from the segmentation algorithm, enabling the use of different algorithms and parameters for different images and tasks. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several benchmark medical image segmentation datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance with improved computational efficiency compared to traditional methods.

We also conduct an ablation study to analyze the contributions of different components of our approach, providing insights into the role of each component in improving segmentation performance. Our results show that learning normalized inputs can significantly enhance the robustness and adaptability of iterative segmentation algorithms, leading to better overall performance and more accurate segmentations.

The main contributions of this paper are:

* A novel approach to medical image segmentation that combines learned normalized inputs with iterative estimation techniques.
* An effective deep neural network architecture for learning normalized inputs that are optimal for segmentation tasks.
* State-of-the-art performance on several benchmark medical image segmentation datasets, demonstrating the superiority of our approach over traditional methods.
* An analysis of the contributions of different components of our approach, providing valuable insights into the design of effective segmentation systems.

Overall, our work has important implications for the development of efficient and accurate medical image segmentation systems, and highlights the potential benefits of combining learned representations with iterative algorithms for image processing tasks.

Our results show that the graphs exhibit interesting structural properties, such as connectivity, planarity, and Hamiltonicity, which are not observed in traditional grid graphs. We also investigate the computational complexity of computing shortest paths and longest paths in these graphs, and provide empirical evidence supporting our theoretical findings. The study contributes to the understanding of grid graph theory and its applications in various fields, including computer science, mathematics, engineering, and architecture.

Fluorescence microscopy images play the critical role of capturing spatial or
spatiotemporal information of biomedical processes in life sciences. Their
simple structures and semantics provide unique advantages in elucidating
learning behavior of deep neural networks (DNNs). It is generally assumed that
accurate image annotation is required to train DNNs for accurate image
segmentation. In this study, however, we find that DNNs trained by label images
in which nearly half (49%) of the binary pixel labels are randomly flipped
provide largely the same segmentation performance. This suggests that DNNs
learn high-level structures rather than pixel-level labels per se to segment
fluorescence microscopy images. We refer to these structures as
meta-structures. In support of the existence of the meta-structures, when DNNs
are trained by a series of label images with progressively less meta-structure
information, we find progressive degradation in their segmentation performance.
Motivated by the learning behavior of DNNs trained by random labels and the
characteristics of meta-structures, we propose an unsupervised segmentation
model. Experiments show that it achieves remarkably competitive performance in
comparison to supervised segmentation models.

We propose a device that combines the functionalities of an entangler and an analyzer, allowing for the efficient generation and characterization of high-dimensional entangled states.

The entangler component of the device utilizes a weak nonlinear process to generate a pair of photons that are entangled in a high-dimensional quantum state. The analyzer component then measures the entangled state, projecting it onto a set of orthogonal bases, and allowing for the efficient characterization of the entangled state.

We demonstrate the efficacy of our device by simulating the generation and analysis of a four-photon maximally entangled state. Our results show that the device is able to generate and analyze the entangled state with high fidelity, and that the entangled state can be used for various quantum information processing tasks, such as quantum teleportation and superdense coding.

Our work has significant implications for the development of quantum technologies, as it provides a new way to generate and characterize high-dimensional entangled states using weak nonlinearities, which are readily available in many experimental systems. This could enable the development of more efficient and robust quantum communication and computation protocols, and help to advance the field of quantum information science.

errors in all the variables. First, we provide necessary and sufficient
conditions for identification of the coefficients. We show that the
coefficients are not identified if and only if an independent normally
distributed linear combination of regressors can be transferred from the
regressors to the errors. Second, we introduce a new estimator for the

firm investment decisions, the estimates are similar to those produced by a
generalized method of moments estimator based on third to fifth moments.

STECKMAP stands for STEllar Content and Kinematics via Maximum A Posteriori
likelihood. It is a tool for interpreting galaxy spectra in terms of their
stellar populations, through the derivation of their star formation history,
age-metallicity relation, kinematics and extinction. To do so, the observed
spectrum is projected onto a temporal sequence of models of single stellar
populations, so as to determine a linear combination of these models, that fit
the observed spectrum best. The weights of the various components of this
linear combination indicate the stellar content of the population. This
procedure is regularized using various penalizing functions. The principles of
the method are detailed in Ocvirk et al. 2006a,b. The STECKMAP software package
is public and freely available at https://github.com/pocvirk/STECKMAP. A number
of authors have already adopted it and use it in their daily research. This
user guide aims at accompanying the user through the setup and first runs of
STECKMAP. The last chapter will help the user to understand and improve his
results and experience with the code.

However, as antenna size increases, so too does complexity with regard to all aspects of control : antenna path length/angle, diameter and position among them ; antenna gain factor [1], power dissipation [2], radiation resistance [3], mechanical strength [4], structural accuracy [5] and weight. An array's limited dynamic range becomes one more obstacle in improving radio transceivers' performance and making it possible to make many, relatively inexpensive directional antennas from compact arrays. This paper presents a novel method that exploits the inherent advantages of array reflective microlens designs. In contrast with conventional arrays that can be easily altered via shaping or assembly, our method allows fabrication and assembly only when necessary, requiring less complicated construction techniques than have been previously applied. The resulting system incorporates advanced adaptive reflectivity properties such as increased scattering coefficient [6], effective beam resolution of ~25° (with linearity), high reflection coefficient under most beam angles (with 1/ω = 0.45), fast adaptation capacity during flight [7–9], and wide tuning over a broad operating span with minimal loss and substantial efficiency gains [10]. Such properties are expected to produce improved scalability, reduced dimensional requirements (e.g., larger modules for greater payload mass), greater integration of multi-beam antenna systems, and the potential to enable higher throughput and better signal quality at smaller space scales for lower cost overall, thereby driving improvements in many applications.

We introduce $\textit{InExtremIS}$, a weakly supervised 3D approach to train
a deep image segmentation network using particularly weak train-time
annotations: only 6 extreme clicks at the boundary of the objects of interest.
Our fully-automatic method is trained end-to-end and does not require any
test-time annotations. From the extreme points, 3D bounding boxes are extracted
around objects of interest. Then, deep geodesics connecting extreme points are
generated to increase the amount of "annotated" voxels within the bounding
boxes. Finally, a weakly supervised regularised loss derived from a Conditional
Random Field formulation is used to encourage prediction consistency over
homogeneous regions. Extensive experiments are performed on a large open
dataset for Vestibular Schwannoma segmentation. $\textit{InExtremIS}$ obtained
competitive performance, approaching full supervision and outperforming
significantly other weakly supervised techniques based on bounding boxes.
Moreover, given a fixed annotation time budget, $\textit{InExtremIS}$
outperforms full supervision. Our code and data are available online.

In this paper, we proposed a novel mutual consistency network (MC-Net+) to
effectively exploit the unlabeled hard regions for semi-supervised medical
image segmentation. The MC-Net+ model is motivated by the observation that deep
models trained with limited annotations are prone to output highly uncertain
and easily mis-classified predictions in the ambiguous regions (e.g. adhesive
edges or thin branches) for the image segmentation task. Leveraging these
region-level challenging samples can make the semi-supervised segmentation
model training more effective. Therefore, our proposed MC-Net+ model consists
of two new designs. First, the model contains one shared encoder and multiple
sightly different decoders (i.e. using different up-sampling strategies). The
statistical discrepancy of multiple decoders' outputs is computed to denote the
model's uncertainty, which indicates the unlabeled hard regions. Second, a new
mutual consistency constraint is enforced between one decoder's probability
output and other decoders' soft pseudo labels. In this way, we minimize the
model's uncertainty during training and force the model to generate invariant
and low-entropy results in such challenging areas of unlabeled data, in order
to learn a generalized feature representation. We compared the segmentation
results of the MC-Net+ with five state-of-the-art semi-supervised approaches on
three public medical datasets. Extension experiments with two common
semi-supervised settings demonstrate the superior performance of our model over
other existing methods, which sets a new state of the art for semi-supervised
medical image segmentation.

Inspired by classic generative adversarial networks (GAN), we propose a novel
end-to-end adversarial neural network, called SegAN, for the task of medical
image segmentation. Since image segmentation requires dense, pixel-level
labeling, the single scalar real/fake output of a classic GAN's discriminator
may be ineffective in producing stable and sufficient gradient feedback to the
networks. Instead, we use a fully convolutional neural network as the segmentor
to generate segmentation label maps, and propose a novel adversarial critic
network with a multi-scale $L_1$ loss function to force the critic and
segmentor to learn both global and local features that capture long- and
short-range spatial relationships between pixels. In our SegAN framework, the
segmentor and critic networks are trained in an alternating fashion in a
min-max game: The critic takes as input a pair of images, (original_image $*$
predicted_label_map, original_image $*$ ground_truth_label_map), and then is
trained by maximizing a multi-scale loss function; The segmentor is trained
with only gradients passed along by the critic, with the aim to minimize the
multi-scale loss function. We show that such a SegAN framework is more
effective and stable for the segmentation task, and it leads to better
performance than the state-of-the-art U-net segmentation method. We tested our
SegAN method using datasets from the MICCAI BRATS brain tumor segmentation
challenge. Extensive experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the
proposed SegAN with multi-scale loss: on BRATS 2013 SegAN gives performance
comparable to the state-of-the-art for whole tumor and tumor core segmentation
while achieves better precision and sensitivity for Gd-enhance tumor core
segmentation; on BRATS 2015 SegAN achieves better performance than the

Deep neural networks have been a prevailing technique in the field of medical
image processing. However, the most popular convolutional neural networks
(CNNs) based methods for medical image segmentation are imperfect because they
model long-range dependencies by stacking layers or enlarging filters.
Transformers and the self-attention mechanism are recently proposed to
effectively learn long-range dependencies by modeling all pairs of word-to-word
attention regardless of their positions. The idea has also been extended to the
computer vision field by creating and treating image patches as embeddings.
Considering the computation complexity for whole image self-attention, current
transformer-based models settle for a rigid partitioning scheme that
potentially loses informative relations. Besides, current medical transformers
model global context on full resolution images, leading to unnecessary
computation costs. To address these issues, we developed a novel method to
integrate multi-scale attention and CNN feature extraction using a pyramidal
network architecture, namely Pyramid Medical Transformer (PMTrans). The PMTrans
captured multi-range relations by working on multi-resolution images. An
adaptive partitioning scheme was implemented to retain informative relations
and to access different receptive fields efficiently. Experimental results on
three medical image datasets (gland segmentation, MoNuSeg, and HECKTOR
datasets) showed that PMTrans outperformed the latest CNN-based and
transformer-based models for medical image segmentation.

The ability of neural networks to continuously learn and adapt to new tasks
while retaining prior knowledge is crucial for many applications. However,
current neural networks tend to forget previously learned tasks when trained on
new ones, i.e., they suffer from Catastrophic Forgetting (CF). The objective of
Continual Learning (CL) is to alleviate this problem, which is particularly
relevant for medical applications, where it may not be feasible to store and
access previously used sensitive patient data. In this work, we propose a
Continual Learning approach for brain segmentation, where a single network is
consecutively trained on samples from different domains. We build upon an
importance driven approach and adapt it for medical image segmentation.
Particularly, we introduce learning rate regularization to prevent the loss of
the network's knowledge. Our results demonstrate that directly restricting the
adaptation of important network parameters clearly reduces Catastrophic
Forgetting for segmentation across domains.

In this work, we address the task of referring image segmentation (RIS),
which aims at predicting a segmentation mask for the object described by a
natural language expression. Most existing methods focus on establishing
unidirectional or directional relationships between visual and linguistic
features to associate two modalities together, while the multi-scale context is
ignored or insufficiently modeled. Multi-scale context is crucial to localize
and segment those objects that have large scale variations during the
multi-modal fusion process. To solve this problem, we propose a simple yet
effective Cascaded Multi-modal Fusion (CMF) module, which stacks multiple
atrous convolutional layers in parallel and further introduces a cascaded
branch to fuse visual and linguistic features. The cascaded branch can
progressively integrate multi-scale contextual information and facilitate the
alignment of two modalities during the multi-modal fusion process. Experimental
results on four benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms most
state-of-the-art methods. Code is available at

Cardiac image segmentation is a critical process for generating personalized
models of the heart and for quantifying cardiac performance parameters. Several
convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures have been proposed to segment
the heart chambers from cardiac cine MR images. Here we propose a multi-task
learning (MTL)-based regularization framework for cardiac MR image
segmentation. The network is trained to perform the main task of semantic
segmentation, along with a simultaneous, auxiliary task of pixel-wise distance
map regression. The proposed distance map regularizer is a decoder network
added to the bottleneck layer of an existing CNN architecture, facilitating the
network to learn robust global features. The regularizer block is removed after
training, so that the original number of network parameters does not change. We
show that the proposed regularization method improves both binary and
multi-class segmentation performance over the corresponding state-of-the-art
CNN architectures on two publicly available cardiac cine MRI datasets,
obtaining average dice coefficient of 0.84$\pm$0.03 and 0.91$\pm$0.04,
respectively. Furthermore, we also demonstrate improved generalization
performance of the distance map regularized network on cross-dataset
segmentation, showing as much as 42% improvement in myocardium Dice coefficient
from 0.56$\pm$0.28 to 0.80$\pm$0.14.

In this paper, we develop a limit distribution theory for maximum likelihood estimation of a log-concave density. We show that the maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) of a log-concave density converges in distribution to a random probability measure on the real line, which we term the "limiting distribution." We prove that the limiting distribution is unique and has several desirable properties, including being continuous and having a density function that is also log-concave. We also establish the convergence rate of the MLE to the limiting distribution, showing that it converges at the optimal rate of $O\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log\log n}{n}}\right)$, where $n$ is the sample size. Our results have important implications for statistical inference and Learning Theory, as they provide a theoretical foundation for using maximum likelihood methods to estimate log-concave densities. Furthermore, our techniques can be used to study the behavior of other estimators, such as Bayesian estimators or Method of Moments estimators, and provide insights into their performance in settings where the true density is log-concave.

The Ott-Antonsen (OA) ansatz [Chaos 18, 037113 (2008), Chaos 19, 023117
(2009)] has been widely used to describe large systems of coupled phase
oscillators. If the coupling is sinusoidal and if the phase dynamics does not
depend on the specific oscillator, then the macroscopic behavior of the systems
can be fully described by a low-dimensional dynamics. Does the corresponding
manifold remain attractive when introducing an intrinsic dependence between an
oscillator's phase and its dynamics by additional, oscillator specific
parameters? To answer this we extended the OA ansatz and proved that
parameter-dependent oscillatory systems converge to the OA manifold given
certain conditions. Our proof confirms recent numerical findings that already
hinted at this convergence. Furthermore we offer a thorough mathematical
underpinning for networks of so-called theta neurons, where the OA ansatz has
just been applied. In a final step we extend our proof by allowing for
time-dependent and multi-dimensional parameters as well as for network
topologies other than global coupling. This renders the OA ansatz an excellent
starting point for the analysis of a broad class of realistic settings.

intersection-over-union score of 78.0 on the challenging PASCAL VOC 2012
dataset.

This work implements a stereo-based terrain traversability analysis that can be used to characterize how complex surfaces tend to appear on simple flat maps. One way is to compute the geometric distance between successive views taken from an arbitrary viewpoint, where this metric measures the change in elevation seen from a point along a path divided by the time difference traversed between every two successive shots.

We show, first, that a map with many small sections (e.g. only 12 kilometers) which has no curvature would have many distinct "shallow paths", if it were viewed from multiple vantage points at different elevations. This is shown experimentally using Google Earth with several maps with a variety of steep slopes. Then we consider what an idealized image from one viewpoint at the top of the globe would look like from different directions, based on various possible perspective transformations. The results indicate that a stereoscopic camera will capture an illusion of depth when used against large or shallowly sloped terrains but not when the horizon is too close, so that objects appearing close to the viewer do appear closer than an equal distance of distant objects seen in normal view. In addition, these data point out some constraints imposed by our physical theories – namely – the speed limits, the viewing angle, and the spatial resolution necessary to use depth information efficiently is quite low. We show further that if we allow free navigation in each direction, then the apparent positions relative to other objects also move over the world. Thus, some terrain features such as mountain tops are best observed with higher vantage points while regions of smooth terrains may need narrower looking perspectives to properly traverse them. To ensure that viewers do not lose their experience due to perspective changes between shots of the same piece of territory, a rotation matrix needs to be built up before and after each shot for each viewpoint, so as not to bias observers towards any particular viewpoint. Finally, it seems desirable for us to allow realistic movement within a scene; nevertheless, it should be avoided so long as this doesn't result in too unnatural looking contours or objects being removed from view. We believe that this approach achieves all necessary goals.

In this paper, we present a novel approach to semantic segmentation of 3D magnetic resonance (MR) images called holistic decomposition convolution (HDC). This method combines the strengths of traditional convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with the representational power of dimensionality reduction techniques to improve the accuracy and efficiency of semantic segmentation in medical imaging.

Existing methods for semantic segmentation of 3D MR images often rely on voxel-wise classification, which can be computationally expensive and may not fully capture the spatial relationships between different structures within the image. HDC addresses these limitations by decomposing the input volume into a set of lower-dimensional, non-overlapping feature maps that encode spatial information at multiple scales. These feature maps are then fed into a hierarchical CNN to learn high-level representations of the input data.

The key innovation of HDC is the use of a novel activation function that allows the network to selectively emphasize or suppress certain features based on their relevance to the task at hand. This results in improved performance compared to traditional CNNs, as well as reduced computational cost due to the fewer number of parameters required to represent the input data.

We evaluate HDC using several experiments on publicly available datasets of 3D MR images. Our results demonstrate significant improvements in segmentation accuracy compared to state-of-the-art baselines, as well as faster training times due to the reduced number of parameters. We also perform an ablation study to analyze the effectiveness of the proposed activation function and provide insights into its behavior.

Our main contributions include:

* The introduction of HDC, a novel method for efficient and accurate semantic segmentation of 3D MR images
* A new activation function that selectively emphasizes relevant features and reduces the computational cost of the network
* An extensive evaluation of HDC using several experiments on publicly available datasets, demonstrating its superior performance and efficiency compared to existing methods

Overall, our work has important implications for improving the diagnosis and treatment of various neurological disorders, where accurate segmentation of brain structures from MR images is critical.

In this paper, we present a mesoscale modeling approach for colloidal suspensions with adsorbing solutes. Colloidal suspensions are complex fluids that consist of particles suspended in a liquid, and they are commonly encountered in a variety of industrial and environmental applications. Adsorption of solutes onto colloidal particles can significantly impact the suspension's properties and behavior, yet it remains a challenging aspect to model.

Our approach combines the lattice Boltzmann method with a novel adsorption algorithm to simulate the mesoscale behavior of colloidal suspensions with adsorbing solutes. The lattice Boltzmann method is a computational fluid dynamics technique that can efficiently simulate the hydrodynamic behavior of complex fluids at the mesoscale. The adsorption algorithm, on the other hand, is based on a set of rules that govern the adsorption and desorption of solutes onto and off of colloidal particles.

We validate our model by comparing the simulation results with experimental data and other numerical models. Our results show good agreement with the experimental data and demonstrate the ability of our model to capture the effects of adsorption on the suspension's behavior. We also investigate the impact of various parameters, such as particle size, solute concentration, and adsorption affinity, on the suspension's behavior.

Our findings have important implications for the understanding and prediction of colloidal suspensions' behavior in various applications, such as water treatment, drug delivery, and energy storage. The mesoscale modeling approach presented in this paper can be used to optimize the design and operation of colloidal suspension-based systems, and it provides a valuable tool for exploring the complex interplay between adsorption and hydrodynamics in these systems.

Now that so much of collective action takes place online, web-generated data
can further understanding of the mechanics of Internet-based mobilisation. This
trace data offers social science researchers the potential for new forms of
analysis, using real-time transactional data based on entire populations,
rather than sample-based surveys of what people think they did or might do.
This paper uses a `big data' approach to track the growth of over 8,000
petitions to the UK Government on the No. 10 Downing Street website for two
years, analysing the rate of growth per day and testing the hypothesis that the
distribution of daily change will be leptokurtic (rather than normal) as
previous research on agenda setting would suggest. This hypothesis is
confirmed, suggesting that Internet-based mobilisation is characterized by
tipping points (or punctuated equilibria) and explaining some of the volatility
in online collective action. We find also that most successful petitions grow
quickly and that the number of signatures a petition receives on its first day
is a significant factor in explaining the overall number of signatures a
petition receives during its lifetime. These findings have implications for the
strategies of those initiating petitions and the design of web sites with the
aim of maximising citizen engagement with policy issues.

The resulting model enables visual localization capabilities as large or larger than those used in traditional linear image sequence classification. Existing methods often rely on hand-crafted features or shallow neural networks, which may not capture the underlying structure of the images effectively.

In this paper, we propose a deep neural convolution network (CNN) that incorporates a convex shape prior to improve the segmentation accuracy. The convex shape prior is used to regularize the CNN's output, encouraging it to produce a smooth and convex segmentation mask. We also introduce a novel loss function that combines the traditional cross-entropy loss with a term that enforces the convexity of the segmentation mask.

Our experiments on a publicly available dataset show that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art segmentation methods, including those that use hand-crafted features or shallow CNNs. We also perform a series of ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of the convex shape prior and the novel loss function. The results demonstrate that the convex shape prior helps to improve the smoothness and accuracy of the segmentation mask, while the novel loss function helps to refine the boundaries of the segmented structures.

The main contributions of this paper are:

* A deep CNN with a convex shape prior for eye fundus images segmentation
* A novel loss function that combines cross-entropy loss with a convexity regularization term
* Experimental results that demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method and its superiority over state-of-the-art methods

space $Q$ are acyclic, then there are three types of homology classes in $X$:
(1) classes of face submanifolds; (2) $k$-dimensional classes of $Q$ swept by
actions of subtori of dimensions $<k$; (3) relative $k$-classes of $Q$ modulo
$\partial Q$ swept by actions of subtori of dimensions $\geqslant k$. The

respect to the intersection product. It is isomorphic to
$(\mathbb{Z}[S_Q]/\Theta)/W$, where $\mathbb{Z}[S_Q]$ is the face ring of the
Buchsbaum simplicial poset $S_Q$ dual to $Q$; $\Theta$ is the linear system of
parameters determined by the characteristic function; and $W$ is a certain
submodule, lying in the socle of $\mathbb{Z}[S_Q]/\Theta$. Intersections of
homology classes different from face submanifolds are described in terms of
intersections on $Q$ and $T^n$.

Recent progress in biomedical image segmentation based on deep convolutional
neural networks (CNNs) has drawn much attention. However, its vulnerability
towards adversarial samples cannot be overlooked. This paper is the first one
that discovers that all the CNN-based state-of-the-art biomedical image
segmentation models are sensitive to adversarial perturbations. This limits the
deployment of these methods in safety-critical biomedical fields. In this
paper, we discover that global spatial dependencies and global contextual
information in a biomedical image can be exploited to defend against
adversarial attacks. To this end, non-local context encoder (NLCE) is proposed
to model short- and long range spatial dependencies and encode global contexts
for strengthening feature activations by channel-wise attention. The NLCE
modules enhance the robustness and accuracy of the non-local context encoding
network (NLCEN), which learns robust enhanced pyramid feature representations
with NLCE modules, and then integrates the information across different levels.
Experiments on both lung and skin lesion segmentation datasets have
demonstrated that NLCEN outperforms any other state-of-the-art biomedical image
segmentation methods against adversarial attacks. In addition, NLCE modules can
be applied to improve the robustness of other CNN-based biomedical image
segmentation methods.

Our approach, called Compassionately Conservative Balanced Cuts (CCBC), is designed to address the limitations of traditional segmentation methods that often rely on aggressive boundary detection and neglect the importance of preserving the integrity of the image.

CCBC is based on the idea of compassionate conservation, which aims to preserve the coherence and structure of the image while segmenting it into meaningful regions. We achieve this by introducing a novel optimization framework that balances the segmentation criteria with a compassionate conservation term that encourages the preservation of the image's integrity. The resulting optimization problem is solved using a efficient algorithm that combines graph cuts and linear programming.

Experiments on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of CCBC in comparison to state-of-the-art segmentation methods. Our approach achieves high accuracy while preserving the coherence and structure of the image, making it particularly useful for applications where image segmentation is a crucial step, such as object recognition, tracking, and scene understanding.

* We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several benchmark datasets, outperforming state-of-the-art segmentation methods.

Overall, CCBC offers a new perspective on image segmentation that prioritizes the preservation of the image's integrity and structure, leading to more accurate and informative segmentation results. We also demonstrate the versatility of DMLS by applying it to various computer vision tasks, such as object proposal generation, instance segmentation, and semantic segmentation.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to constructing prediction sets that do not rely on any distributional assumptions and simultaneously control the risk of over-prediction. Our method, called distribution-free, risk-controlling prediction sets (DFRCPS), is based on a non-parametric, data-driven approach that leverages the concept of conformal prediction. We demonstrate that DFRCPS can be used to construct prediction sets with a guaranteed level of confidence, while also providing a risk-controlling mechanism to prevent over-prediction.

We evaluate the performance of DFRCPS through simulations and real-world case studies, comparing it to existing methods such as conformal prediction and Bayesian prediction. Our results show that DFRCPS outperforms these methods in terms of both accuracy and risk control, particularly in situations where the underlying distribution is complex or unknown.

The key contribution of this paper is the development of a distribution-free, risk-controlling approach to prediction set construction that does not require any distributional assumptions. Our method provides a principled way to balance the trade-off between accuracy and risk control, and can be applied to a wide range of prediction problems, including classification, regression, and time-series forecasting.

The paper is organized as follows: In Section 2, we review the related work on prediction sets and conformal prediction. In Section 3, we introduce the concept of DFRCPS and its construction method. In Section 4, we present the theoretical properties of DFRCPS, including its risk control and confidence guarantees. In Section 5, we evaluate the performance of DFRCPS through simulations and case studies. Finally, we conclude with a discussion of the results and future directions in Section 6.

Overall, this paper provides a novel approach to prediction set construction that addresses the limitations of existing methods and provides a distribution-free, risk-controlling alternative. The proposed method has broad applications in fields such as machine learning, statistics, and decision-making under uncertainty.

Abstract : The recent increase in computing power has given us an opportunity to examine the relationship between a highly asymptotic approximation and a well-defined problem domain, which would otherwise be impossible (in principle) with classical computing facilities. We examined whether it makes sense, on average, to use higher than traditional high-precision computers during data recovery tasks. In particular, we compared the degree of reduction from the current highest asymptotic result achieved using supercomputers to what could be achieved using more common desktop CPUs/GPUs without running out of memory or resources. Our results indicate that, despite this increased computational capability, one can expect little advantage to be gained through using faster hardware, unless high enough precision computation can be obtained (using other approaches such as approximate methods).

Intentional image segmentation is an important problem in machine learning and data mining. In natural images, simple object detection methods have been used to extract similar objects with low error rates, but these systems can also be used to achieve high accuracy to reveal hidden structures and recognize faces (and other things besides). We present a fully convolutional two-stream fusion network that efficiently unifies low quality and error samples of the task as they appear while training on the test set. Our results show that this system achieves more stable performances than many neural networks based on back propagation, temporal averaging (such as the famous Resnet-101), or semi-supervised classifications. This improvement comes at a cost which may lead to higher data generation costs. While our results are promising, many problems still remain unsolved such as the integration into complex images like video clips. This work has exciting application fields especially for visual search, computer vision applications, augmented reality, etc.

In this paper, we present a novel approach to interactive segmentation called EdgeFlow, which leverages edge information to guide the segmentation process and achieve practical interaction efficiency. Existing methods often suffer from slow convergence or rely on heuristics that limit their accuracy, making them impractical for real-world applications.

EdgeFlow addresses these limitations by introducing an edge-guided flow algorithm that combines the benefits of both boundary-following and gradient-descent-based methods. The proposed method efficiently explores the image space while adaptively adjusting its behavior based on local edge features, ensuring accurate segmentation and minimizing user input.

We evaluate EdgeFlow on several benchmark datasets and compare it to state-of-the-art methods in terms of efficiency, accuracy, and usability. Our results show significant advantages in terms of both computational cost and user effort required to obtain high-quality segmentations. Additionally, we demonstrate the versatility of EdgeFlow through applications in various domains such as object recognition, medical imaging, and video analysis.

The key contributions of this work can be summarized as follows:

* Introducing EdgeFlow, a practical solution for efficient and accurate interactive segmentation guided by edge information.
* Developing a novel edge-guided flow algorithm that adapts to local edge features, promoting accurate and efficient segmentation.
* Showcasing superior performance of EdgeFlow compared to existing methods in terms of both computational cost and user effort required.
* Demonstrating the applicability of EdgeFlow across diverse domains, including object recognition, medical imaging, and video analysis.

In conclusion, our proposed method presents a substantial improvement over traditional interactivesegmentation techniques and has far-reaching implications for applications where precise segmentation is critical. We envision EdgeFlow serving as a valuable tool for researchers, practitioners, and users seeking efficient and reliable segmentation solutions.

To extract information at scale, researchers increasingly apply semantic
segmentation techniques to remotely-sensed imagery. While fully-supervised
learning enables accurate pixel-wise segmentation, compiling the exhaustive
datasets required is often prohibitively expensive. As a result, many non-urban
settings lack the ground-truth needed for accurate segmentation. Existing open
source infrastructure data for these regions can be inexact and non-exhaustive.
Open source infrastructure annotations like OpenStreetMaps (OSM) are
representative of this issue: while OSM labels provide global insights to road
and building footprints, noisy and partial annotations limit the performance of
segmentation algorithms that learn from them. In this paper, we present a novel
and generalizable two-stage framework that enables improved pixel-wise image
segmentation given misaligned and missing annotations. First, we introduce the
Alignment Correction Network to rectify incorrectly registered open source
labels. Next, we demonstrate a segmentation model -- the Pointer Segmentation
Network -- that uses corrected labels to predict infrastructure footprints
despite missing annotations. We test sequential performance on the AIRS
dataset, achieving a mean intersection-over-union score of 0.79; more
importantly, model performance remains stable as we decrease the fraction of
annotations present. We demonstrate the transferability of our method to lower
quality data, by applying the Alignment Correction Network to OSM labels to
correct building footprints; we also demonstrate the accuracy of the Pointer
Segmentation Network in predicting cropland boundaries in California from
medium resolution data. Overall, our methodology is robust for multiple
applications with varied amounts of training data present, thus offering a
method to extract reliable information from noisy, partial data.

In this study, we demonstrate the excitation and imaging of resonant optical modes in au triangular nano-antennas using cathodoluminescence spectroscopy. Our results show that the antennas exhibit strong field concentration and enhancement at specific wavelengths, corresponding to the resonant modes of the structure. We observe a strong correlation between the excited mode and the geometric parameters of the antenna, such as size and shape. By using cathodoluminescence spectroscopy, we are able to map the emitted light from the antennas with high spatial resolution, allowing us to visualize the distribution of the resonant modes on the surface of the material. This work has important implications for the development of plasmonic devices that rely on the manipulation of light at the nanoscale. The ability to accurately excite and image resonant modes in these structures will enable new applications in fields such as surface-enhanced Raman scattering, sensing, and optoelectronics.

Reactive Turing machines extend classical Turing machines with a facility to
model observable interactive behaviour. We call a behaviour (finitely)
executable if, and only if, it is equivalent to the behaviour of a (finite)
reactive Turing machine. In this paper, we study the relationship between
executable behaviour and behaviour that can be specified in the $\pi$-calculus.
We establish that every finitely executable behaviour can be specified in the
$\pi$-calculus up to divergence-preserving branching bisimilarity. The
converse, however, is not true due to (intended) limitations of the model of
reactive Turing machines. That is, the $\pi$-calculus allows the specification
of behaviour that is not finitely executable up to divergence-preserving
branching bisimilarity. We shall prove, however, that if the finiteness
requirement on reactive Turing machines and the associated notion of
executability is relaxed to orbit-finiteness, then the $\pi$-calculus is
executable up to (divergence-insensitive) branching bisimilarity.

when working on SP images. To better mimic human visual perception, we think it
is desirable for the deep learning model to be able to perceive not only raw
images but also SP images. In this paper, we propose a new superpixel-based
data augmentation (SPDA) method for training deep learning models for
biomedical image segmentation. Our method applies a superpixel generation
scheme to all the original training images to generate superpixelized images.
The SP images thus obtained are then jointly used with the original training

biomedical image datasets show that SPDA is effective and can consistently
improve the performance of state-of-the-art fully convolutional networks for
biomedical image segmentation in 2D and 3D images. Additional studies also
demonstrate that SPDA can practically reduce the generalization gap.

Accurate segmentation of objects in images is a fundamental task in computer vision, with applications in various fields such as robotics, autonomous driving, and medical imaging. However, ensuring the quality of segmentation models in real-time remains a challenging problem. In this paper, we propose a novel approach for real-time prediction of segmentation quality, which enables the detection of errors and inconsistencies in segmentation models during the inference process.

Our approach is based on a deep learning framework that leverages the concept of uncertainty estimation in neural networks. We train a dedicated network to predict the uncertainty of the segmentation model's output, which is then used to identify potential errors and inconsistencies. We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate its effectiveness in detecting segmentation errors in real-time.

The main contributions of this paper are:

1. A novel approach for real-time prediction of segmentation quality based on uncertainty estimation in neural networks.
2. A dedicated network architecture for predicting segmentation uncertainty, which can be integrated with existing segmentation models.
3. An extensive evaluation of our approach on several benchmark datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in detecting segmentation errors in real-time.

Our approach has significant implications for applications where segmentation accuracy is critical, such as autonomous driving, medical imaging, and robotics. By enabling real-time detection of segmentation errors, we can improve the overall performance and reliability of these systems, and ultimately enhance their ability to perform complex tasks.

In this paper, we investigate the algebraic dependence of commuting elements in algebras, with a focus on the relationship between the commutativity of elements and their algebraic dependence. We present a series of results that provide a deeper understanding of the interplay between these two concepts, and demonstrate the utility of our approach through a variety of examples.

First, we establish a fundamental result that shows that if a set of elements in an algebra commutes, then they are algebraically dependent. This result has important implications for the study of algebraic independence, as it implies that the existence of a set of algebraically independent elements in an algebra is equivalent to the existence of a set of non-commuting elements.

Next, we explore the converse of this result, and show that algebraic dependence of a set of elements does not necessarily imply their commutativity. We provide examples of algebras in which a set of elements are algebraically dependent, but do not commute. This highlights the subtlety of the relationship between commutativity and algebraic dependence, and underscores the importance of carefully considering both concepts in the study of algebras.

Furthermore, we investigate the relationship between commutativity and algebraic dependence in the context of finite-dimensional algebras. We show that in a finite-dimensional algebra, a set of elements that commute are necessarily algebraically dependent, and provide a bound on the size of the smallest set of algebraically independent elements. This result has important implications for the study of finite-dimensional algebras, and provides a new perspective on the relationship between commutativity and algebraic independence.

Finally, we extend our results to the context of Lie algebras, and show that the same principles hold in this setting. We demonstrate the application of our results to the study of Lie algebras, and provide examples of Lie algebras in which a set of elements are algebraically dependent, but do not commute.

In conclusion, this paper provides a detailed investigation of the relationship between commutativity and algebraic dependence in algebras, and demonstrates the importance of carefully considering both concepts in the study of algebras. Our results provide a new perspective on the interplay between these two concepts, and have important implications for the study of finite-dimensional algebras and Lie algebras.

Performing inference in graphs is a common task within several machine
learning problems, e.g., image segmentation, community detection, among others.
For a given undirected connected graph, we tackle the statistical problem of
exactly recovering an unknown ground-truth binary labeling of the nodes from a
single corrupted observation of each edge. Such problem can be formulated as a
quadratic combinatorial optimization problem over the boolean hypercube, where
it has been shown before that one can (with high probability and in polynomial
time) exactly recover the ground-truth labeling of graphs that have an
isoperimetric number that grows with respect to the number of nodes (e.g.,
complete graphs, regular expanders). In this work, we apply a powerful
hierarchy of relaxations, known as the sum-of-squares (SoS) hierarchy, to the
combinatorial problem. Motivated by empirical evidence on the improvement in
exact recoverability, we center our attention on the degree-4 SoS relaxation
and set out to understand the origin of such improvement from a graph
theoretical perspective. We show that the solution of the dual of the relaxed
problem is related to finding edge weights of the Johnson and Kneser graphs,
where the weights fulfill the SoS constraints and intuitively allow the input
graph to increase its algebraic connectivity. Finally, as byproduct of our
analysis, we derive a novel Cheeger-type lower bound for the algebraic
connectivity of graphs with signed edge weights.

It is well-known that simple type theory is complete with respect to
non-standard set-valued models. Completeness for standard models only holds
with respect to certain extended classes of models, e.g., the class of
cartesian closed categories. Similarly, dependent type theory is complete for
locally cartesian closed categories. However, it is usually difficult to
establish the coherence of interpretations of dependent type theory, i.e., to
show that the interpretations of equal expressions are indeed equal. Several
classes of models have been used to remedy this problem. We contribute to this
investigation by giving a semantics that is standard, coherent, and
sufficiently general for completeness while remaining relatively easy to
compute with. Our models interpret types of Martin-L\"of's extensional
dependent type theory as sets indexed over posets or, equivalently, as
fibrations over posets. This semantics can be seen as a generalization to
dependent type theory of the interpretation of intuitionistic first-order logic
in Kripke models. This yields a simple coherent model theory, with respect to
which simple and dependent type theory are sound and complete.

Although having achieved great success in medical image segmentation, deep

classes from only a few labeled examples. In this work, we propose a new
framework for few-shot medical image segmentation based on prototypical
networks. Our innovation lies in the design of two key modules: 1) a context
relation encoder (CRE) that uses correlation to capture local relation features

module that repeatedly uses the CRE and a prototypical network to recapture the
change of context relationship and refine the segmentation mask iteratively.
Experiments on two abdomen CT datasets and an abdomen MRI dataset show the
proposed method obtains substantial improvement over the state-of-the-art

nonparametric models. The method is based on estimating equations that are
$U$-statistics in the observations. The $U$-statistics are based on higher

the parameter of interest, and represent higher derivatives of this parameter.

slower than $\sqrt n$-rate. In a number of examples the resulting rate can be

In this paper, we investigate the phenomenon of spin-flip reflection of electrons from a potential barrier in heterostructures. Heterostructures are materials composed of alternating layers of different materials, and they have attracted significant interest in recent years due to their potential for applications in a wide range of fields, including electronics, optoelectronics, and spintronics.

One of the key properties of heterostructures is the ability to manipulate the spin of electrons, which is a fundamental property of particles that determines their intrinsic angular momentum. Spin-flip reflection, where an electron's spin is flipped upon reflection from a potential barrier, is a phenomenon that has been observed in heterostructures and has important implications for the design and operation of spintronic devices.

In this paper, we present a theoretical study of spin-flip reflection in heterostructures using a combination of analytical and numerical methods. We develop a model that takes into account the spin-dependent transport properties of the heterostructure and the potential barrier, and we investigate the effects of various parameters, such as the barrier height, width, and spin-orbit coupling, on the spin-flip reflection probability.

Our results show that spin-flip reflection is a strong function of the barrier height and width, and that it can be significantly enhanced by increasing the spin-orbit coupling in the heterostructure. We also find that the spin-flip reflection probability can be controlled by applying an external magnetic field, which offers a way to manipulate the spin properties of electrons in heterostructures.

Our findings have important implications for the design and operation of spintronic devices, such as spin-based transistors and logic gates, which rely on the manipulation of electron spin to perform logical operations. By understanding and controlling spin-flip reflection in heterostructures, we can improve the performance and efficiency of these devices, and pave the way for the development of new spintronic technologies.

In this study, we investigate the universality of luminosity-metallicity (L-Z) and mass-metallicity (M-Z) relations for compact star-forming galaxies at redshifts 0 < z < 3. By analyzing a large sample of galaxies from various survey datasets, we find that both relations exhibit significant dependences on galaxy size, with more compact galaxies showing higher metallicities at fixed stellar mass or luminosity. We also explore how the L-Z and M-Z relations evolve over cosmic time and find that they become tighter and steeper at higher redshift. Our results suggest that gas fraction and star formation efficiency play important roles in shaping these relations, implying that galaxy size is not just a passive observer but an active participant in regulating galactic chemical evolution. The observed universality of the L-Z and M-Z relations has crucial implications for understanding the physical processes driving galaxy evolution across different cosmic epochs.

We also perform experiments to analyze the impact of different components of our method, providing insights into the role of various design choices.

The main contributions of this work can be summarized as follows:

* A novel deep learning-based approach for automatic pixel-level image labeling
* A CNN architecture that integrates local and global contextual information
* An efficient loss function promoting consistency and spatial smoothness
* State-of-the-art performance on several benchmark datasets
* Insights into the importance of different components of our method

This paper's findings have important implications for a wide range of applications, such as scene understanding, object detection, and image restoration. In this paper, we present a novel approach to real-time semantic segmentation using a revised version of the BiseNet architecture. Our proposed method, called Rethinking BiSeNet, leverages the strengths of the original BiSeNet model while addressing its limitations, particularly in terms of computational efficiency and accuracy.

BiSeNet is a popular deep learning architecture for semantic segmentation that uses a combination of binary and multi-class classification to improve performance. However, its computationally intensive nature has limited its use in real-world applications where speed and efficiency are crucial.

Our Rethinking BiSeNet approach significantly improves the efficiency of the original model while maintaining its accuracy. We achieve this through a combination of architectural modifications, including depthwise separable convolutions, channel shuffle operations, and a novel feature pyramid network. These modifications allow us to reduce the computational complexity of the model while preserving its ability to capture subtle contextual information.

We evaluate our Rethinking BiSeNet model on several benchmark datasets, including Cityscapes, PASCAL VOC, and CamVid. Our results show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on these datasets while providing a significant speedup compared to the original BiSeNet model. Specifically, we achieve an improvement of up to 30% in inference speed without sacrificing accuracy.

Our work demonstrates the potential of Rethinking BiSeNet for real-time semantic segmentation applications, such as autonomous driving, robotics, and video surveillance. We believe that our approach provides a valuable contribution to the field of computer vision and deep learning, and we hope to inspire further research in this area.

The task of image segmentation is inherently noisy due to ambiguities
regarding the exact location of boundaries between anatomical structures. We
argue that this information can be extracted from the expert annotations at no
extra cost, and when integrated into state-of-the-art neural networks, it can
lead to improved calibration between soft probabilistic predictions and the
underlying uncertainty. We built upon label smoothing (LS) where a network is
trained on 'blurred' versions of the ground truth labels which has been shown
to be effective for calibrating output predictions. However, LS is not taking
the local structure into account and results in overly smoothed predictions
with low confidence even for non-ambiguous regions. Here, we propose Spatially
Varying Label Smoothing (SVLS), a soft labeling technique that captures the
structural uncertainty in semantic segmentation. SVLS also naturally lends
itself to incorporate inter-rater uncertainty when multiple labelmaps are
available. The proposed approach is extensively validated on four clinical
segmentation tasks with different imaging modalities, number of classes and
single and multi-rater expert annotations. The results demonstrate that SVLS,
despite its simplicity, obtains superior boundary prediction with improved
uncertainty and model calibration.

Dice coefficient of 0.9260 and a median Dice coefficient of 0.9262 using SSNet

This study examines the growth and success rates of petitions uploaded onto the UK No. 10 Downing Street website, a platform that allows citizens to submit their views and demands directly to the Prime Minister's office. Using data from over 2500 petitions created between 2014 and 2019, we analyze the factors that influence the number of signatures attracted by each petition and the likelihood of achieving its desired outcome. Our findings show that petitions related to social issues, such as healthcare and education, tend to receive more support than those focused on economic or political topics. We also find that petitions with simpler language and clear calls-to-action are more successful in garnering public attention and support. Notably, our analysis reveals that while only around 6% of petitions achieved their stated goal, there is a positive correlation between signature count and the likelihood of policy change. These insights can inform decision-making and communication strategies for policymakers and activists seeking to leverage online platforms for public engagement and advocacy.

This paper presents a novel approach to edge detection using structured forests, which are ensembles of decision trees that combine to produce accurate and efficient feature extraction. Our proposed method, called Fast Edge Detection using Structured Forests (FEDS), leverages the strengths ofstructured forests to detect edges in images with high accuracy and speed.

Existing edge detection methods suffer from either high computational complexity or low accuracy, particularly in the presence of noise or complex structures. F ED S addresses these limitations by employing a two-stage approach that first generates a set of candidate edges using a novel sampling strategy and then refines the candidates using a trained structured forest.

The first stage of FEDS involves generating a set of candidate edges using a dense sampling strategy that concentrates on areas of high gradient magnitude. This stage is designed to be fast and efficient, producing a large number of potential edges while minimizing computational overhead.

The second stage refines the candidate edges using a trained structured forest. The forest is trained on a dataset of labeled edges and non-edges, and it learns to identify the features that distinguish edges from non-edges. The forest is then applied to the set of candidate edges, and each edge is classified as an actual edge or a false positive.

We evaluate FEDS on several benchmark datasets, including the Bonn dataset, the Berkeley segmentation dataset, and the MSRA10K dataset. Our experiments show that FEDS outperforms several state-of-the-art edge detection methods in terms of both accuracy and speed. Specifically, we achieve a higher mean AUC than the compared methods on all three datasets while maintaining competitive execution times.

Our main contribution is a novel approach to edge detection that combines the efficiency of dense sampling with the accuracy of structured forests. The resulting algorithm offers a significant improvement over traditional edge detection techniques and demonstrates great promise for applications such as object recognition, image segmentation, and robot vision.

In this paper, we present a novel approach for detecting deepfake-forged contents using separable convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and image segmentation. The proliferation of deepfake technology has made it increasingly challenging to distinguish between genuine and manipulated images or videos, posing significant threats to individual privacy and national security.

Existing methods for detecting deepfakes often rely on complex architectures that require extensive computational resources and exhibit limited performance in real-world scenarios. To address these limitations, our proposed method leverages separable CNNs, which offer improved efficiency and scalability without compromising accuracy.

Our approach consists of two stages: first, we employ image segmentation techniques to isolate the region of interest (ROI) in the input image or video; then, we apply a separable CNN to the ROI, followed by a classification layer that outputs a probability map indicating the likelihood of forgery. We evaluate our method on several datasets, including CelebFaces and DeepFaceLab, and achieve superior detection performances compared to state-of-the-art methods.

The key contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows:

* We propose a novel deep learning architecture combining separable CNNs and image segmentation for detecting deepfake-forged contents.
* Our method demonstrates improved efficiency and scalability compared to existing approaches while maintaining high detection accuracy.
* Extensive experiments on various datasets showcase the effectiveness of our approach in detecting deepfakes generated by different algorithms and under diverse conditions.

This work has important implications for applications where real-time detection of deepfakes is critical, such as news media monitoring, cybersecurity systems, and digital forensics. Our findings also shed light on the potential capabilities and limitations of separable CNNs in dealing with complex image forgery tasks.

We use a Potts model community detection algorithm to accurately and
quantitatively evaluate the hierarchical or multiresolution structure of a
graph. Our multiresolution algorithm calculates correlations among multiple
copies ("replicas") of the same graph over a range of resolutions. Significant
multiresolution structures are identified by strongly correlated replicas. The
average normalized mutual information, the variation of information, and other
measures in principle give a quantitative estimate of the "best" resolutions
and indicate the relative strength of the structures in the graph. Because the
method is based on information comparisons, it can in principle be used with
any community detection model that can examine multiple resolutions. Our
approach may be extended to other optimization problems. As a local measure,
our Potts model avoids the "resolution limit" that affects other popular
models. With this model, our community detection algorithm has an accuracy that
ranks among the best of currently available methods. Using it, we can examine
graphs over 40 million nodes and more than one billion edges. We further report
that the multiresolution variant of our algorithm can solve systems of at least
200000 nodes and 10 million edges on a single processor with exceptionally high
accuracy. For typical cases, we find a super-linear scaling, O(L^{1.3}) for
community detection and O(L^{1.3} log N) for the multiresolution algorithm
where L is the number of edges and N is the number of nodes in the system.

In this paper, we explore the use of sparse dictionaries for online learning tasks with kernel methods. Sparse dictionaries are a promising tool for dimensionality reduction and feature extraction, but their application to online learning settings has been largely overlooked in the literature. We propose an algorithm that leverages the efficiency of kernel methods to learn a sparse dictionary for online learning tasks, and demonstrate its effectiveness on several benchmark datasets.

Our approach is based on the idea of incremental learning, where the dictionary is updated iteratively as new data arrives. We show that by using a kernel-based method, we can efficiently incorporate new data points into the dictionary without having to relearn the entire dataset. This allows for scalable and efficient learning in high-dimensional spaces, even when dealing with large amounts of data.

We evaluate our approach on a variety of datasets and compare it to established online learning algorithms, such as stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and online support vector machines (SVMs). Our results show that our proposed method achieves better performance than these baseline algorithms in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency.

Furthermore, we analyze the properties of the learned dictionaries and provide insights into the relationship between sparsity and generalization ability. Our findings suggest that the sparse dictionaries obtained from our algorithm lead to better generalization performance compared to denser representations.

The main contributions of this work are: (1) proposing an efficient algorithm for online learning with sparse dictionaries and kernels, (2) demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach on various datasets, and (3) providing theoretical analysis of the learned dictionaries. The presented research opens up new possibilities for applying sparse representation techniques to real-world applications, including image and text classification, bioinformatics, and recommender systems.

often mediated by the hydrodynamics of a solvent fluid. At microscopic scales
the elastic structures are also subject to thermal fluctuations. Stochastic

In this paper, we present a comprehensive framework for the global formulation of generalized Einstein-Scalar-Maxwell (GESM) theories. GESM theories are a generalization of the well-known Einstein-Maxwell theory, which describes the interaction between gravity and electromagnetism in the presence of scalar fields. The global formulation of these theories is crucial to understand their properties and physics in a consistent manner.

We develop a novel approach based on the idea of gauge-invariant differentiable structures, which enables us to globally describe the geometry and topology of spacetime in the presence of matter fields. Our framework allows for a unified treatment of all types of matter fields, including scalar, vector, and spinor fields, and accounts for their non-linear couplings with the gravitational field.

Within our framework, we derive the general equations of motion and conservation laws for GESM theories in a manifestly gauge-invariant form. We also discuss the role of boundary conditions and their impact on the physical predictions of the theory. Furthermore, we provide explicit examples of physically interesting solutions, such as black holes and charged cosmological solutions, which demonstrate the richness and diversity of these models.

Our work has significant implications for our understanding of the fundamental forces of nature and their interplay with the structure and evolution of the universe. It provides a solid foundation for further investigations into the phenomenology of GESM theories and its possible applications to observations in cosmology and astrophysics.

Moreover, our results shed light on the mathematical structure of the space of solutions of GESM theories, which will be an essential tool for future studies in the field. Therefore, this work paves the way for new insights into the fascinating realm of strong coupling phenomena, where quantum gravity and high-energy particle physics meet.

A polarization entangled photon pair source is widely used in many quantum
information processing applications such as teleportation, quantum swapping,
quantum computation and high precision quantum metrology. Here, we report on
the generation of a continuous-wave pumped degenerated 1550 nm polarization
entangled photon pair source at telecom wavelength using a type-II
phase-matched periodically poled KTiOPO4 crystal in a Sagnac interferometer.

tomography. The wavelength of photons can be tuned over a broad range by
changing the temperature of crystal or pump power without losing the quality of
entanglement. This source will be useful for building up long-distance quantum
networks.

Traditional NBA player evaluation metrics are based on scoring differential
or some pace-adjusted linear combination of box score statistics like points,
rebounds, assists, etc. These measures treat performances with the outcome of
the game still in question (e.g. tie score with five minutes left) in exactly
the same way as they treat performances with the outcome virtually decided
(e.g. when one team leads by 30 points with one minute left). Because they
ignore the context in which players perform, these measures can result in
misleading estimates of how players help their teams win. We instead use a win
probability framework for evaluating the impact NBA players have on their
teams' chances of winning. We propose a Bayesian linear regression model to
estimate an individual player's impact, after controlling for the other players
on the court. We introduce several posterior summaries to derive rank-orderings
of players within their team and across the league. This allows us to identify
highly paid players with low impact relative to their teammates, as well as
players whose high impact is not captured by existing metrics.

In this survey we give an overview of recent developments on the Quantitative
Subspace Theorem. In particular, we discuss a new upper bound for the number of
subspaces containing the "large" solutions, obtained jointly with Roberto
Ferretti, and sketch the proof of the latter. Further, we prove a new gap
principle to handle the "small" solutions in the system of inequalities
considered in the Subspace Theorem. Finally, we go into the refinement of the
Subspace Theorem by Faltings and Wuestholz, which states that the system of
inequalities considered has only finitely many solutions outside some
effectively determinable proper linear subspace of the ambient solution space.
Estimating the number of these solutions is still an open problem. We give some
motivation that this problem is very hard.

We introduce a new smooth estimator of the ROC curve based on log-concave
density estimates of the constituent distributions. We show that our estimate
is asymptotically equivalent to the empirical ROC curve if the underlying
densities are in fact log-concave. In addition, we empirically show that our
proposed estimator exhibits an efficiency gain for finite sample sizes with
respect to the standard empirical estimate in various scenarios and that it is
only slightly less efficient, if at all, compared to the fully parametric
binormal estimate in case the underlying distributions are normal. The
estimator is also quite robust against modest deviations from the log-concavity
assumption. We show that bootstrap confidence intervals for the value of the
ROC curve at a fixed false positive fraction based on the new estimate are on
average shorter compared to the approach by Zhou & Qin (2005), while
maintaining coverage probability. Computation of our proposed estimate uses the
R package logcondens that implements univariate log-concave density estimation
and can be done very efficiently using only one line of code. These obtained
results lead us to advocate our estimate for a wide range of scenarios.

The paper "Consequences of the existence of Auslander-Reiten triangles with applications to perfect complexes for self-injective algebras" explores the ramifications of the existence of Auslander-Reiten triangles in the context of self-injective algebras. Specifically, the authors investigate the implications of the existence of such triangles on the structure and properties of perfect complexes over self-injective algebras.

The authors begin by establishing a connection between Auslander-Reiten triangles and the theory of perfect complexes, demonstrating that the former can be used to construct the latter. They then examine the consequences of this relationship, including the fact that the existence of an Auslander-Reiten triangle implies the existence of a tilting complex, which is a special type of perfect complex that plays a central role in representation theory.

One of the main results of the paper shows that if an Auslander-Reiten triangle exists for a self-injective algebra, then there exists a bounded t-structure on the derived category of the algebra, which is compatible with the usual t-structure up to some shifts. This has important consequences for the study of homological algebra and the representation theory of self-injective algebras.

Furthermore, the authors demonstrate that the existence of Auslander-Reiten triangles can be used to infer information about the number of indecomposable modules and the depth of the Ext^i groups of the algebra. They also explore connections to other areas of mathematics, such as singularity theory and intersection cohomology, and show how their results have practical applications in these fields.

Overall, the paper provides significant new insights into the interplay between Auslander-Reiten triangles, perfect complexes, and self-injective algebras, contributing substantially to our understanding of the representation theory and homological algebra of these algebraic structures. Its findings are sure to interest mathematicians working in representation theory, homological algebra, and closely related fields.
