In this paper, we introduce YouTube-VOS, a large-scale video object segmentation benchmark that provides a comprehensive evaluation framework for assessing the performance of state-of-the-art object segmentation algorithms in realistic scenarios. With the rapid growth of video data and the increasing demand for automated video analysis tools, there is an urgent need for robust and efficient object segmentation methods that can handle complex scenarios with multiple objects, occlusions, and cluttered backgrounds.

Existing benchmarks for video object segmentation are limited by their small scale, simplicity, or focus on specific application domains. In contrast, YouTube-VOS is built upon a vast collection of videos from YouTube, covering various categories such as sports, music, animation, and educational content. The dataset contains over 130K video clips, each lasting around 10 seconds, resulting in a total of approximately 47 hours of video footage.

We annotated each clip with high-quality object masks, providing extensive coverage of object categories, including humans, animals, vehicles, and indoor/outdoor scenes. This enabled us to create a diverse set of subset benchmarks within the larger dataset, allowing researchers to evaluate their algorithms' performance on specific tasks (e.g., human segmentation, vehicle tracking) while still contributing to the overall goal of improving generalizable object segmentation capabilities.

Alongside the dataset, we also provide a thorough evaluation protocol and metric suite to facilitate comparisons between different approaches. We perform extensive experiments using popular state-of-the-art methods and demonstrate YouTube-VOS's effectiveness in highlighting areas where existing techniques struggle. Our hope is that this benchmark will encourage further advancements in video object segmentation technology and ultimately contribute to more sophisticated and reliable multimedia processing applications.

Shape instantiation which predicts the 3D shape of a dynamic target from one
or more 2D images is important for real-time intra-operative navigation.
Previously, a general shape instantiation framework was proposed with manual
image segmentation to generate a 2D Statistical Shape Model (SSM) and with
Kernel Partial Least Square Regression (KPLSR) to learn the relationship
between the 2D and 3D SSM for 3D shape prediction. In this paper, the two-stage
shape instantiation is improved to be one-stage. PointOutNet with 19
convolutional layers and three fully-connected layers is used as the network
structure and Chamfer distance is used as the loss function to predict the 3D
target point cloud from a single 2D image. With the proposed one-stage shape
instantiation algorithm, a spontaneous image-to-point cloud training and
inference can be achieved. A dataset from 27 Right Ventricle (RV) subjects,
indicating 609 experiments, were used to validate the proposed one-stage shape
instantiation algorithm. An average point cloud-to-point cloud (PC-to-PC) error
of 1.72mm has been achieved, which is comparable to the PLSR-based (1.42mm) and
KPLSR-based (1.31mm) two-stage shape instantiation algorithm.

Recent advances in deep learning based image segmentation methods have
enabled real-time performance with human-level accuracy. However, occasionally
even the best method fails due to low image quality, artifacts or unexpected
behaviour of black box algorithms. Being able to predict segmentation quality
in the absence of ground truth is of paramount importance in clinical practice,
but also in large-scale studies to avoid the inclusion of invalid data in
subsequent analysis.
  In this work, we propose two approaches of real-time automated quality
control for cardiovascular MR segmentations using deep learning. First, we
train a neural network on 12,880 samples to predict Dice Similarity
Coefficients (DSC) on a per-case basis. We report a mean average error (MAE) of
0.03 on 1,610 test samples and 97% binary classification accuracy for
separating low and high quality segmentations. Secondly, in the scenario where
no manually annotated data is available, we train a network to predict DSC
scores from estimated quality obtained via a reverse testing strategy. We
report an MAE=0.14 and 91% binary classification accuracy for this case.
Predictions are obtained in real-time which, when combined with real-time
segmentation methods, enables instant feedback on whether an acquired scan is
analysable while the patient is still in the scanner. This further enables new
applications of optimising image acquisition towards best possible analysis
results.

We develop a generalized active contour formalism for image segmentation
based on shape templates. The shape template is subjected to a restricted
affine transformation (RAT) in order to segment the object of interest. RAT
allows for translation, rotation, and scaling, which give a total of five
degrees of freedom. The proposed active contour comprises an inner and outer
contour pair, which are closed and concentric. The active contour energy is a
contrast function defined based on the intensities of pixels that lie inside
the inner contour and those that lie in the annulus between the inner and outer
contours. We show that the contrast energy functional is optimal under certain
conditions. The optimal RAT parameters are computed by maximizing the contrast
function using a gradient descent optimizer. We show that the calculations are
made efficient through use of Green's theorem. The proposed formalism is
capable of handling a variety of shapes because for a chosen template,
optimization is carried with respect to the RAT parameters only. The proposed
formalism is validated on multiple images to show robustness to Gaussian and
Poisson noise, to initialization, and to partial loss of structure in the
object to be segmented.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach for polyp localisation in colonoscopy videos using ensemble learning and particle swarm optimization. Instead of directly utilizing an observed image including some outliers,
noise or intensity inhomogeneity, the use of its ideal value (e.g. noise-free
image) has a favorable impact on clustering. Hence, the accurate estimation of
the residual (e.g. unknown noise) between the observed image and its ideal
value is an important task. To do so, we propose an $\ell_0$
regularization-based Fuzzy $C$-Means (FCM) algorithm incorporating a
morphological reconstruction operation and a tight wavelet frame transform. To
achieve a sound trade-off between detail preservation and noise suppression,
morphological reconstruction is used to filter an observed image. By combining
the observed and filtered images, a weighted sum image is generated. Since a
tight wavelet frame system has sparse representations of an image, it is
employed to decompose the weighted sum image, thus forming its corresponding
feature set. Taking it as data for clustering, we present an improved FCM
algorithm by imposing an $\ell_0$ regularization term on the residual between
the feature set and its ideal value, which implies that the favorable
estimation of the residual is obtained and the ideal value participates in
clustering. Spatial information is also introduced into clustering since it is
naturally encountered in image segmentation. Furthermore, it makes the
estimation of the residual more reliable. To further enhance the segmentation
effects of the improved FCM algorithm, we also employ the morphological
reconstruction to smoothen the labels generated by clustering. Finally, based
on the prototypes and smoothed labels, the segmented image is reconstructed by
using a tight wavelet frame reconstruction operation. Experimental results
reported for synthetic, medical, and color images show that the proposed
algorithm is effective and efficient, and outperforms other algorithms.

Few-shot segmentation has been attracting a lot of attention due to its
effectiveness to segment unseen object classes with a few annotated samples.
Most existing approaches use masked Global Average Pooling (GAP) to encode an
annotated support image to a feature vector to facilitate query image
segmentation. However, this pipeline unavoidably loses some discriminative
information due to the average operation. In this paper, we propose a simple
but effective self-guided learning approach, where the lost critical
information is mined. Specifically, through making an initial prediction for
the annotated support image, the covered and uncovered foreground regions are
encoded to the primary and auxiliary support vectors using masked GAP,
respectively. By aggregating both primary and auxiliary support vectors, better
segmentation performances are obtained on query images. Enlightened by our
self-guided module for 1-shot segmentation, we propose a cross-guided module
for multiple shot segmentation, where the final mask is fused using predictions
from multiple annotated samples with high-quality support vectors contributing
more and vice versa. This module improves the final prediction in the inference
stage without re-training. Extensive experiments show that our approach
achieves new state-of-the-art performances on both PASCAL-5i and COCO-20i
datasets.

In this study, we investigate the spin-flip reflection of electrons from a potential barrier in heterostructures. We use a theoretical model to analyze the reflection process and demonstrate the influence of the spin-orbit interaction on the reflected electron's spin polarization. Our results show that the spin-flip reflection probability is significantly enhanced in the presence of a strong spin-orbit interaction, leading to a substantial increase in the spin polarization of the reflected electrons. We also find that the spin-flip reflection is strongly dependent on the angle of incidence and the strength of the potential barrier. Our findings have important implications for the design and optimization of spintronic devices, such as spin-based transistors and sensors, which rely on the manipulation of spin currents and their interactions with potential barriers.

Convolutional neural networks have shown to achieve superior performance on
image segmentation tasks. However, convolutional neural networks, operating as
black-box systems, generally do not provide a reliable measure about the
confidence of their decisions. This leads to various problems in industrial
settings, amongst others, inadequate levels of trust from users in the model's
outputs as well as a non-compliance with current policy guidelines (e.g., EU AI
Strategy). To address these issues, we use uncertainty measures based on
Monte-Carlo dropout in the context of a human-in-the-loop system to increase
the system's transparency and performance. In particular, we demonstrate the
benefits described above on a real-world multi-class image segmentation task of
wear analysis in the machining industry. Following previous work, we show that
the quality of a prediction correlates with the model's uncertainty.
Additionally, we demonstrate that a multiple linear regression using the
model's uncertainties as independent variables significantly explains the
quality of a prediction (\(R^2=0.718\)). Within the uncertainty-based
human-in-the-loop system, the multiple regression aims at identifying failed
predictions on an image-level. The system utilizes a human expert to label
these failed predictions manually. A simulation study demonstrates that the
uncertainty-based human-in-the-loop system increases performance for different
levels of human involvement in comparison to a random-based human-in-the-loop
system. To ensure generalizability, we show that the presented approach
achieves similar results on the publicly available Cityscapes dataset.

In this paper, we propose a new approach to estimating high-dimensional models that leverages higher order statistical moments to improve estimation accuracy. Traditional estimators, such as maximum likelihood and Bayesian methods, are based on the first two moments of the data distribution and can be sensitive to their choice. Our proposed method uses higher order moments to derive more robust estimating equations that are less susceptible to moment misspecification.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through simulations and real-data applications in finance, marketing, and genetics. The results show that our method outperforms traditional estimators in terms of forecast accuracy and parameter inference, particularly when data dimensions are high. We also establish the theoretical properties of our estimator under regularity conditions, including consistency and asymptotic normality.

Our work has important implications for fields where high-dimensional modeling is prevalent, providing a reliable alternative to existing methods that may be affected by moment misspecification or poor convergence rates. By harnessing the power of higher order statistics, our approach offers a powerful tool for practitioners and researchers who need accurate estimates and predictions from complex data sets.

The minimal path model based on the Eikonal partial differential equation
(PDE) has served as a fundamental tool for the applications of image
segmentation and boundary detection in the passed three decades. However, the
existing minimal paths-based image segmentation approaches commonly rely on the
image boundary features, potentially limiting their performance in some
situations. In this paper, we introduce a new variational image segmentation
model based on the minimal path framework and the Eikonal PDE, where the
region-based functional that defines the homogeneity criteria can be taken into
account for estimating the associated geodesic paths. This is done by
establishing a geodesic curve interpretation to the region-based active contour
evolution problem. The image segmentation processing is carried out in an
iterative manner in our approach. A crucial ingredient in each iteration is to
construct an asymmetric Randers geodesic metric using a sufficiently small
vector field, such that a set of geodesic paths can be tracked from the
geodesic distance map which is the solution to an Eikonal PDE. The object
boundary can be delineated by the concatenation of the final geodesic paths. We
invoke the Finsler variant of the fast marching method to estimate the geodesic
distance map, yielding an efficient implementation of the proposed Eikonal
region-based active contour model. Experimental results on both of the
synthetic and real images exhibit that our model indeed achieves encouraging
segmentation performance.

One might expect that students playing video games would be less aggressive overall. In fact, some recent studies show a negative correlation between high school game-playing and aggression towards others [1]. The idea seems compelling because video games could represent one way to reduce negative social interaction associated with peer pressure. However, these recent findings are based on self-report measures on aggression. They may not be valid measures due to other variables that can influence people's behavior (e.g., how young an individual is or what environment they spend their time in), which also have been shown to interact with changes in aggression [2–6]. More importantly, they only apply to youth. Adults are more likely than youths to behave aggressively even when they were asked before the survey whether they engaged in video gaming, and adults are more violent as compared with children [3,7]—thus it makes sense to focus on adolescent outcomes when researching this question more comprehensively in adult samples.


However, most previous literature has studied only small subgroups either by adolescents or middle-aged children. Thus, researchers do not always have insight into the larger population effects that can shape adult aggressiveness. Therefore we sought to answer the important question in this regard without making assumptions about age. To meet our goal we randomly selected 5,000 participants enrolled in a longitudinal study designed for examining how early exposure to violent media impacts aggressive and antisocial behaviors. We aimed to assess both violent video game play and subsequent levels of delinquent behavior in these youth over time using data provided by teachers as part of the California Student System assessment protocol administered in 2004 and 2005 [8]. current status of the theory of jet modification in dense matter. We commence
with an outline of the "traditional" observables which may be calculated
without recourse to event generators. These include single and double hadron

transport coefficients. This is followed by a review of the more modern

The aim of this study is to investigate the consistency of various matter models with asymptotically safe quantum gravity. Asymptotically safe quantum gravity is a promising approach to unify general relativity and quantum mechanics, which posits that the gravitational coupling becomes weakly coupled at very high energies or short distances. We explore different matter models, including fermionic and bosonic fields, and analyze their compatibility with asymptotic safety conditions. Our findings suggest that certain matter models are indeed consistent with asymptotically safe quantum gravity, while others may lead to inconsistencies or require further modifications. Overall, our work provides important insights into the interplay between matter and geometry in a non-perturbatively renormalizable theory of quantum gravity.

In this study we provide methods to segment subjects' brains into 1–25 anatomical regions, based on a probabilistic model of their neural activity. This approach allows us to define spatially precise and biologically meaningful metrics to compare subject representations with other experimental data sets. By applying these new measures to functional imaging signals in vivo with fMRI and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) our aim was to validate the application of the modified human brain connectivity metric in behavioral and lesion studies. In addition, by performing structural equation modeling we attempt to quantify the contribution of individual brain networks (neuronal nodes) to individual representation differences in neuroimaging. More specifically, neural network models were used to represent how particular classes of neurons relate to each other in terms of the way they react to certain inputs. If an output for the corresponding neuron falls within some distance interval then it may be given that the input is correct at that location. However, when working memory needs to access a similar sequence of stimuli the model would make further predictions as follows. To do so, the model predicts the response from the current neuron when presented with one stimulus but is expecting two others. Our results show that our method achieves highly precise and accurate classifiers of functional brain networks, providing robust quantitative measurements of neural representations.

This paper proposes a novel gradient-based algorithm for effective cloud detection and segmentation in satellite imagery, with an aim to improve the performance of the PERSIANN-CCS (Persistent Systems' Cloud Coverage and Storm Intensity Estimation) algorithm. The proposed algorithm leverages the gradient information of the image intensity values to separate clouds from the background and to identify the boundaries between clouds and non-cloud regions. The gradient-based approach allows for accurate detection of clouds even in the presence of complex weather conditions, such as overlapping clouds or clouds with varying densities.

The proposed algorithm is evaluated using a dataset of satellite images and shows significant improvement in cloud detection and segmentation accuracy compared to the traditional thresholding-based approach used in PERSIANN-CCS. The gradient-based algorithm is able to accurately detect clouds with an accuracy of 96.5%, while the traditional thresholding-based approach achieves an accuracy of 88.2%. Additionally, the gradient-based algorithm is able to accurately segment clouds with an average intersection over union (IoU) of 0.87, outperforming the traditional approach which achieves an IoU of 0.73.

The improved cloud detection and segmentation accuracy achieved by the proposed algorithm has the potential to significantly improve the performance of PERSIANN-CCS, which is widely used in various applications such as weather forecasting, climate modeling, and environmental monitoring. The algorithm's ability to accurately detect and segment clouds in complex weather conditions makes it particularly useful for applications where accurate cloud information is critical.

In summary, this paper presents a novel gradient-based algorithm for effective cloud detection and segmentation in satellite imagery, which significantly improves the performance of the PERSIANN-CCS algorithm. The proposed algorithm has the potential to improve the accuracy of various applications that rely on cloud information, and its simplicity and efficiency make it a valuable tool for researchers and practitioners in the field of remote sensing and computer vision.

whole volume at once. We introduce a novel objective function, that we optimise
during training, based on Dice coefficient. In this way we can deal with

available for training, we augment the data applying random non-linear
transformations and histogram matching. We show in our experimental evaluation
that our approach achieves good performances on challenging test data while

In this paper we present a general solution for multi-target tracking with
superpositional measurements. Measurements that are functions of the sum of the
contributions of the targets present in the surveillance area are called
superpositional measurements. We base our modelling on Labeled Random Finite
Set (RFS) in order to jointly estimate the number of targets and their
trajectories. This modelling leads to a labeled version of Mahler's
multi-target Bayes filter. However, a straightforward implementation of this
tracker using Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) methods is not feasible due to the
difficulties of sampling in high dimensional spaces. We propose an efficient
multi-target sampling strategy based on Superpositional Approximate CPHD
(SA-CPHD) filter and the recently introduced Labeled Multi-Bernoulli (LMB) and
Vo-Vo densities. The applicability of the proposed approach is verified through
simulation in a challenging radar application with closely spaced targets and
low signal-to-noise ratio.

In this work, we present a simple yet effective framework to address the
domain translation problem between different sensor modalities with unique data
formats. By relying only on the semantics of the scene, our modular generative
framework can, for the first time, synthesize a panoramic color image from a
given full 3D LiDAR point cloud. The framework starts with semantic
segmentation of the point cloud, which is initially projected onto a spherical
surface. The same semantic segmentation is applied to the corresponding camera
image. Next, our new conditional generative model adversarially learns to
translate the predicted LiDAR segment maps to the camera image counterparts.
Finally, generated image segments are processed to render the panoramic scene
images. We provide a thorough quantitative evaluation on the SemanticKitti
dataset and show that our proposed framework outperforms other strong baseline
models.

Image segmentation is a fundamental vision task and a crucial step for many
applications. In this paper, we propose a fast image segmentation method based
on a novel super boundary-to-pixel direction (super-BPD) and a customized
segmentation algorithm with super-BPD. Precisely, we define BPD on each pixel
as a two-dimensional unit vector pointing from its nearest boundary to the
pixel. In the BPD, nearby pixels from different regions have opposite
directions departing from each other, and adjacent pixels in the same region
have directions pointing to the other or each other (i.e., around medial
points). We make use of such property to partition an image into super-BPDs,
which are novel informative superpixels with robust direction similarity for
fast grouping into segmentation regions. Extensive experimental results on
BSDS500 and Pascal Context demonstrate the accuracy and efficency of the
proposed super-BPD in segmenting images. In practice, the proposed super-BPD
achieves comparable or superior performance with MCG while running at ~25fps
vs. 0.07fps. Super-BPD also exhibits a noteworthy transferability to unseen
scenes. The code is publicly available at
https://github.com/JianqiangWan/Super-BPD.

By analyzing the behavior of charged particles in a plasma and considering the impact of Coulomb screening on nuclear reaction rates, this study aims to provide a better understanding of the role of plasma conditions on the outcome of nucleosynthesis processes.

Our method is based on the idea of inpainting, where we train a network to predict the missing parts of a 3D image. We propose a novel inpainting strategy that leverages the region-of-interest (ROI) information to guide the inpainting process. Our method is based on the idea of supervoxel inpainting, where we first segment the image into supervoxels and then inpaint each supervoxel individually. We show that our method can achieve competitive performance compared to fully supervised methods, while requiring no manual annotations. Our method is also more robust to noise and missing data compared to other self-supervised methods. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on two challenging medical image segmentation tasks: brain tumor segmentation and liver segmentation. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on both tasks, while requiring no manual annotations.

We evaluate the performance of our proposed method on several benchmark datasets and compare it with state-of-the-art deepfake detection methods. Our results show that our method outperforms existing approaches in terms of detection accuracy and computational efficiency. We also perform a series of ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of different components of our method and demonstrate its robustness against various attacks.

Our approach has several advantages over existing methods. First, it is lightweight and can be deployed on resource-constrained devices, making it suitable for real-time applications. Second, it is robust against various attacks, including those that aim to manipulate the input image or video. Finally, it can be easily extended to detect deepfakes in other modalities, such as audio and text.

In conclusion, our proposed method represents a significant advancement in the field of deepfake detection. Its lightweight and efficient nature, combined with its robustness and versatility, make it a promising solution for mitigating the risks associated with deepfakes.

Atomic layers of black phosphorus (P) isolated from its layered bulk make a
new two-dimensional (2D) semiconducting crystal with sizable direct bandgap,
high carrier mobility, and promises for 2D electronics and optoelectronics.
However, the integrity of black P crystal could be susceptible to a number of
environmental variables and processes, resulting in degradation in device
performance even before the device optical image suggests so. Here, we perform
a systematic study of the environmental effects on black P electronic devices
through continued measurements over a month under a number of controlled
conditions, including ambient light, air, and humidity, and identify evolution
of device performance under each condition. We further examine effects of
thermal and electrical treatments on inducing morphology and, performance
changes and failure modes in black P devices. The results suggest that
procedures well established for nanodevices in other 2D materials may not
directly apply to black P devices, and improved procedures need to be devised
to attain stable device operation.

An evacuation process is simulated within the Social Force Model. Thousand
pedestrians are leaving a room by one exit. We investigate the stationarity of
the distribution of time lags between instants when two successive pedestrians
cross the exit. The exponential tail of the distribution is shown to gradually
vanish. Taking fluctuations apart, the time lags decrease in time till there
are only about 50 pedestrians in the room, then they start to increase. This
suggests that at the last stage the flow is laminar. In the first stage,
clogging events slow the evacuation down. As they are more likely for larger
crowds, the flow is not stationary. The data are investigated with detrended
fluctuation analysis.

In this paper, we present a comprehensive analysis of exact inference in graphs from the degree-4 sum-of-squares hierarchy. We explore the capabilities and limitations of this powerful inference technique, which has been widely used in various fields, including computer vision, machine learning, and social network analysis.

Our work provides a thorough understanding of the degree-4 sum-of-squares hierarchy, including its theoretical foundations, computational complexity, and applications to graphical models. We demonstrate the versatility of this approach by applying it to a variety of graphical models, including Bayesian networks, Markov random fields, and Gaussian graphical models.

Our main contributions include the development of novel inference algorithms that leverage the degree-4 sum-of-squares hierarchy to perform exact inference in graphs. We also derive tight computational complexity bounds for these algorithms, providing insights into their scalability and performance.

Our experimental evaluation on several real-world datasets demonstrates the effectiveness and efficiency of our proposed methods. We show that they can accurately perform exact inference in large-scale graphs, outperforming existing methods in terms of computational speed and scalability.

Our work has important implications for a wide range of applications, including image segmentation, natural language processing, and recommendation systems. It also provides a foundation for future research in graphical models and exact inference, opening up new avenues for developing more powerful and efficient inference techniques.

In summary, our paper offers a comprehensive view of exact inference in graphs from the degree-4 sum-of-squares hierarchy, providing novel algorithms, computational complexity analysis, and experimental evaluation. Our work has significant implications for both theoretical and practical applications, advancing the state-of-the-art in graphical models and exact inference.

We present an application of multi-mesh finite element methods as part of a
methodology for optimizing settlement layouts. By formulating a multi-objective
optimization problem, we demonstrate how a given number of buildings may be
optimally placed on a given piece of land with respect to both wind conditions
and the view experienced from the buildings. The wind flow is modeled by a
multi-mesh (cut finite element) method. This allows each building to be
embedded in a boundary-fitted mesh which can be moved freely on top of a fixed
background mesh. This approach enables a multitude of settlement layouts to be
evaluated without the need for costly mesh generation when changing the
configuration of buildings. The view is modeled by a measure that takes into
account the totality of unobstructed view from the collection of buildings, and
is efficiently computed by rasterization.

Consider the normal linear regression setup when the number of covariates p
is much larger than the sample size n, and the covariates form correlated
groups. The response variable y is not related to an entire group of covariates
in all or none basis, rather the sparsity assumption persists within and
between groups. We extend the traditional g-prior setup to this framework.
Variable selection consistency of the proposed method is shown under fairly
general conditions, assuming the covariates to be random and allowing the true
model to grow with both n and p. For the purpose of implementation of the
proposed g-prior method to high-dimensional setup, we propose two procedures.
First, a group screening procedure, termed as group SIS (GSIS), and secondly, a
novel stochastic search variable selection algorithm, termed as group informed
variable selection algorithm (GiVSA), which uses the known group structure
efficiently to explore the model space without discarding any covariate based
on an initial screening. Screening consistency of GSIS, and theoretical mixing
time of GiVSA are studied using the canonical path ensemble approach of Yang et
al. (2016). Performance of the proposed prior with implementation of GSIS as
well as GiVSA are validated using various simulated examples and a real data
related to residential buildings.

We construct Hamiltonian Floer complexes associated to continuous, and even
lower semi-continuous, time dependent exhaustion functions on geometrically
bounded symplectic manifolds. We further construct functorial continuation maps
associated to monotone homotopies between them, and operations which give rise
to a product and unit. The work rests on novel techniques for energy
confinement of Floer solutions as well as on methods of Non-Archimedean
analysis. The definition for general Hamiltonians utilizes the notion of
reduced cohomology familiar from Riemannian geometry, and the continuity
properties of Floer cohomology. This gives rise in particular to localized
Floer theory. We discuss various functorial properties as well as some
applications to existence of periodic orbits and to displaceability.

In this paper, we present a novel framework for evaluating non-Gaussian functional integrals, which are ubiquitous in various fields of physics, engineering, and finance. The proposed methodology enables the efficient and accurate computation of these integrals, thereby facilitating the analysis and modeling of complex systems that exhibit non-Gaussian behavior.

Our approach is based on a combination of mathematical techniques, including functional analysis, differential equations, and numerical methods. We first introduce a new class of basis functions, called non-Gaussian basis functions, which are specifically designed to capture the non-Gaussian nature of the integrands. These basis functions are used to expand the integrand, allowing for a more accurate representation of the integral.

We then derive a set of differential equations that govern the behavior of the non-Gaussian basis functions. These equations are solved numerically using a variety of techniques, including finite difference and finite element methods. The solution of these equations provides the values of the non-Gaussian basis functions at different points in the input space, which are then used to compute the functional integral.

The proposed framework is applied to several examples from various fields, including quantum field theory, signal processing, and finance. In each case, we demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of our method by comparing the results obtained using our framework with existing methods and numerical simulations.

Our work provides a significant contribution to the field of functional integration, and it has important implications for the analysis and modeling of complex systems that exhibit non-Gaussian behavior. The proposed framework offers a powerful tool for researchers and practitioners in various fields, enabling them to compute non-Gaussian functional integrals with greater accuracy and efficiency than ever before.

Pixel-wise image segmentation is demanding task in computer vision. Classical
U-Net architectures composed of encoders and decoders are very popular for
segmentation of medical images, satellite images etc. Typically, neural network
initialized with weights from a network pre-trained on a large data set like
ImageNet shows better performance than those trained from scratch on a small
dataset. In some practical applications, particularly in medicine and traffic
safety, the accuracy of the models is of utmost importance. In this paper, we
demonstrate how the U-Net type architecture can be improved by the use of the
pre-trained encoder. Our code and corresponding pre-trained weights are
publicly available at https://github.com/ternaus/TernausNet. We compare three
weight initialization schemes: LeCun uniform, the encoder with weights from
VGG11 and full network trained on the Carvana dataset. This network
architecture was a part of the winning solution (1st out of 735) in the Kaggle:
Carvana Image Masking Challenge.

This paper presents a method for segmenting iris images obtained from the
deceased subjects, by training a deep convolutional neural network (DCNN)
designed for the purpose of semantic segmentation. Post-mortem iris recognition
has recently emerged as an alternative, or additional, method useful in
forensic analysis. At the same time it poses many new challenges from the
technological standpoint, one of them being the image segmentation stage, which
has proven difficult to be reliably executed by conventional iris recognition
methods. Our approach is based on the SegNet architecture, fine-tuned with
1,300 manually segmented post-mortem iris images taken from the
Warsaw-BioBase-Post-Mortem-Iris v1.0 database. The experiments presented in
this paper show that this data-driven solution is able to learn specific
deformations present in post-mortem samples, which are missing from alive
irises, and offers a considerable improvement over the state-of-the-art,
conventional segmentation algorithm (OSIRIS): the Intersection over Union (IoU)
metric was improved from 73.6% (for OSIRIS) to 83% (for DCNN-based presented in
this paper) averaged over subject-disjoint, multiple splits of the data into
train and test subsets. This paper offers the first known to us method of
automatic processing of post-mortem iris images. We offer source codes with the
trained DCNN that perform end-to-end segmentation of post-mortem iris images,
as described in this paper. Also, we offer binary masks corresponding to manual
segmentation of samples from Warsaw-BioBase-Post-Mortem-Iris v1.0 database to
facilitate development of alternative methods for post-mortem iris
segmentation.

Fix coprime $s,t\ge1$. We re-prove, without Ehrhart reciprocity, a conjecture
of Armstrong (recently verified by Johnson) that the finitely many simultaneous
$(s,t)$-cores have average size $\frac{1}{24}(s-1)(t-1)(s+t+1)$, and that the
subset of self-conjugate cores has the same average (first shown by
Chen--Huang--Wang). We similarly prove a recent conjecture of Fayers that the
average weighted by an inverse stabilizer---giving the "expected size of the
$t$-core of a random $s$-core"---is $\frac{1}{24}(s-1)(t^2-1)$. We also prove
Fayers' conjecture that the analogous self-conjugate average is the same if $t$
is odd, but instead $\frac{1}{24}(s-1)(t^2+2)$ if $t$ is even. In principle,
our explicit methods---or implicit variants thereof---extend to averages of
arbitrary powers.
  The main new observation is that the stabilizers appearing in Fayers'
conjectures have simple formulas in Johnson's $z$-coordinates parameterization
of $(s,t)$-cores.
  We also observe that the $z$-coordinates extend to parameterize general
$t$-cores. As an example application with $t := s+d$, we count the number of
$(s,s+d,s+2d)$-cores for coprime $s,d\ge1$, verifying a recent conjecture of
Amdeberhan and Leven.

In this paper, we present a novel result in the field of process calculi, specifically in the context of the $\pi$-calculus. We prove that the $\pi$-calculus is both behaviourally complete and orbit-finitely executable.

Behavioural completeness is a property that ensures that any process calculus can simulate the behaviour of any other process calculus. This means that the $\pi$-calculus is capable of modelling and analysing the behaviour of a wide range of systems, including those that are not directly representable in the calculus itself.

Orbit-finiteness, on the other hand, is a property that guarantees that the calculus has a finite number of possible orbit-equivalence classes, where two processes are considered to be in the same orbit if they have the same observable behaviour. This property is important because it allows for the efficient analysis and verification of processes, as it reduces the number of possible processes that need to be considered.

The combination of behavioural completeness and orbit-finiteness makes the $\pi$-calculus a powerful tool for the analysis and verification of systems. It allows for the modelling and analysis of a wide range of systems, while also providing a finite and manageable number of possible processes to consider.

Our proof of the behavioural completeness and orbit-finiteness of the $\pi$-calculus is based on a series of technical results and constructions, which we present in detail in the paper. Our approach draws on a range of techniques from category theory, logic, and theoretical computer science, and provides a novel and insightful perspective on the $\pi$-calculus and its properties.

Overall, our results demonstrate the versatility and expressive power of the $\pi$-calculus, and provide a solid foundation for its use in a wide range of applications, including the analysis and verification of distributed systems, programming languages, and other systems with complex behaviour.

This study aims to develop a deep learning model called PC-U Net that can jointly reconstruct and segment the cardiac walls in three dimensions using computed tomography (CT) data. Results showed that the proposed method achieved state-of-the-art performance in both myocardial segmentation and left ventricular structure reconstruction tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness and potential clinical utility in improving the accuracy of cardiovascular image analysis.

This application will make use of Exponential-Linear Loss (ELL) to segment 3D scenes into small, consistent object sizes in order to create low resolution video sequences. An initial evaluation of an ELL algorithm on five different size datasets yielded over 95% correct classification accuracy when applied using a quadtree search treebank and 8k GPUs per array dimension in each benchmark case. This can be expected to be improved greatly by leveraging multiple GPU arrays on a cluster or a large number of GPUs per CPU for example if only a small subset of the object space is used as part of the training set. Our model should theoretically allow for much lower false positives due to fewer outliers so this would provide much better generalization performance than other methods such as nearest neighbor feature detection. However, while our experiment shows that LDL seems able to detect more distinct 3D objects than neighboring edges within the same volume then still has significant dropout rates even while scaling linearly or exponentially and provides poor sensitivity to small scale perturbations we show it also lacks sufficient power to find significant differences between objects with identical shapes or similar mass but drastically differing volumes such as those seen in objects like LEGO bricks. For these types of features that are important for image analysis (such as contour maps) we propose combining LAL, and using the average distance of points for further quality control to significantly increase overall accuracy, especially below 10K feature volumes or so. In contrast LDL with constant memory and only single thread cannot exploit any improvements found due to memory contention issues during training. So this work shows the importance of both running many epochs, but also making sure your models scales linearly and exponentially which helps overall system efficiency while at the same time providing higher spatial precision.

Solar Cycle Variability: A Possible Connection to Solar Irradiance Changes? The importance and relevance of variability in sunspot formation, activity and trends is now widely recognized across various scientific studies as well. However, some researchers – such as Thomas Klaassen of BSSI-Institute for Applied Space Physics – have suggested possible connections between sunspot numbers, solar energy output and climate dynamics from time scales up to 10 years or even longer when these variables change together. As such, they propose that variations of the active Sun may result in a modulation, which may alter the climatic impact on planet Earth. Here we discuss a particular study by Karsten Kjaer (Boeing Satellite Systems) and his group using an innovative set of simulations which aimed at studying long-term solar variability by using observations from Hinode: TIE-1 mission and related satellite datasets at ground level, supplemented by numerical model calculations. Their data analysis was recently published in the journal Astrophysical Journal Letters. Our results show no evidence for modulation in sunspot number over the period 1990–2003. However, it appears that the overall solar flux – which varies greatly throughout the year – influences several aspects of regional climate. During periods with stronger solar irradiance fluctuations, it can lead to increased frequency of low sun spots; these are responsible for more extreme climate conditions. Similarly, on shorter timescales, a maximum in intensity may be reached just at decadal timescales. Such patterns can lead to abrupt reductions in northern hemisphere cloud cover, which can exacerbate global warming. It should also be noted that sunspot changes can have different impacts on atmospheric circulation patterns within days; this would seem very important in relation to their influence both at the top-down levels [e.g., by causing jet stream divergence] and top-up levels [such as through changing stratospheric flow]. Further investigation of the significance of such a potential link to planetary climate with better observation and simulations is strongly needed.

Then, we use the masks to select a subset of the unlabeled data that is most likely to contain objects from the target category. We evaluate the effectiveness of our method on several benchmark datasets, including PASCAL VOC and COCO.

The main contributions of this paper are:

In this paper, we present a comprehensive approach to optimizing the Dice score and Jaccard index for medical image segmentation. These two metrics are widely used in the field to evaluate the performance of segmentation algorithms, with the Dice score measuring overlap between the predicted mask and ground truth, and the Jaccard index assessing their similarity. Despite their importance, existing methods for maximizing these metrics often rely on heuristics or intuition rather than a principled optimization framework.

In contrast, our proposed method takes a theoretical approach, leveraging tools from optimization theory to directly optimize the Dice score and Jaccard index. We first derive the optimal transport formulation of the segmentation problem, which enables us to cast the task as minimization of a linear program (LP). By solving this LP, we obtain theoptimal parameters that maximize the Dice score and Jaccard index simultaneously. To ensure computational efficiency, we also propose an approximate solution based on gradient descent with provable guarantees.

Our experimental evaluation on several benchmark datasets demonstrates significant improvements over state-of-the-art segmentation techniques. Moreover, we perform ablation studies to dissect the contributions of various components in our methodology, providing valuable insights into the role of each component in enhancing performance. Our results not only establish new baselines for medical image segmentation tasks but also shed light on the inherent tradeoffs between different objectives, paving the way for more informed design choices in future research.

1. A theoretically grounded approach to optimizing the Dice score and Jaccard index via optimal transport and linear programming.

Abstract

Inversion recovery (IR) is a widely used magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) pulse sequence that is sensitive to the degree of radiation damping (DOR) of the magnetic field. The DOR is a measure of the rate at which the magnetic field decays with time. The DOR is a function of the magnetic field strength, the magnetic field gradient strength, and the magnetic field gradient direction. The DOR is typically characterized by measuring the T1 relaxation time of a sample. The T1 relaxation time is the time it takes for the signal to decay to 37% of its initial value. The T1 relaxation time is inversely proportional to the DOR. The T1 relaxation time can be measured by performing a series of IR measurements at different inversion times. The T1 relaxation time can be calculated from the IR measurements using a mathematical model. The T1 relaxation time can be used to characterize the DOR of the magnetic field. The DOR can be suppressed by using a magnetic field gradient that is oriented in the same direction as the magnetic field. This technique is called parallel imaging (PI). PI can be used to reduce the DOR in IR measurements. PI can also be used to reduce the DOR in other MRI pulse sequences.

In this paper, we explore the notion of additive deformations of Hopf algebras, a generalization of the classical notion of deformations of algebras. We introduce the concept of an additive deformation of a Hopf algebra, which is a one-parameter family of Hopf algebras that share the same underlying vector space and comultiplication, but have different multiplication operations. We study the properties of additive deformations, including their relationship to classical deformations and their behavior under various algebraic operations such as tensor products and homomorphisms.

We also investigate the application of additive deformations to various areas of mathematics and physics, including the study of integrable systems, quantum field theory, and representation theory. In particular, we show how additive deformations can be used to construct new solutions of the Yang-Baxter equation and the quantum Yang-Baxter equation, and how they can be used to study the representation theory of certain deformed algebraic structures.

Our results provide a new perspective on the study of deformations of Hopf algebras and their applications, and demonstrate the power and flexibility of the concept of additive deformations. They also highlight the rich interplay between algebra, geometry, and physics, and open up new avenues for research in these areas.

In this paper, we present a novel approach to 3D medical image segmentation called Elastic Boundary Projection (EBP). EBP is designed to address the challenge of accurately separating complex anatomical structures in 3D medical images, where traditional methods often struggle due to the complexity and variability of boundary shapes.

Our approach leverages the concept of elasticity to create a dynamic boundary that adapts to the underlying anatomy, enabling accurate segmenation even in the presence of large deformations and irregularities. The key idea behind EBP is to establish a continuous boundary that snugly fits around the object of interest, much like a rubber sheet fitting around a irregularly-shaped object.

The proposed method consists of two main components: (1) a deep neural network that learns to project 2D image intensities onto an elastic boundary, and (2) an optimization algorithm that adjusts the boundary's shape and position to minimize an energy functional. We evaluate EBP on several publicly available datasets containing various types of 3D medical images, including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), computed tomography (CT), and positron emission tomography (PET).

Experimental results demonstrate that EBP outperforms state-of-the-art segmentation methods in terms of both accuracy and efficiency. Our approach has important implications for applications such as tumor tracking, organ segmentation, and surgical planning, where accurate separation of anatomical structures is crucial. Moreover, the ability of EBP to handle complex and varying boundary shapes makes it particularly well-suited for cases where traditional methods may struggle or fail.

In summary, our paper introduces a novel, physically informed approach to 3D medical image segmentation that leverages elasticity to achieve accurate and robust separation of anatomical structures. With its ability to adapt to complex boundaries and deformations, EBP holds great promise for improving the accuracy and efficacy of various medical image analysis tasks.

In this paper, we explore the properties and characteristics of two specific types of Snow Leopard permutations: even and odd threads. We present novel techniques for generating and enumerating these permutations, and examine their structural properties, such as descents, ascents, and fixed points.

Our results reveal that even and odd threads exhibit distinct patterns and behavior under certain operations, such as reversal and complementation. Furthermore, we investigate the relationship between these permutations and other well-known families of permutations, including the classic derangements and the more recently introduced randomized permutations. Our findings shed light on the intricate structure of Snow Leopard permutations and contribute to a deeper understanding of their role in various mathematical contexts.

This work has implications not only for theoretical developments in combinatorics but also for practical applications in fields such as data compression, error-correcting codes, and cryptographic protocols. By uncovering new insights into the properties and behaviors of Snow Leopard permutations, our research paves the way for further exploration and innovation in these areas.

In this paper, we explore Bäcklund transformations, a fundamental concept in differential geometry and lie theory. We present both old and new perspectives on this topic, shedding light on its rich history and current advancements.

The paper begins with an introduction to Bäcklund transformations and their significance in various mathematical fields. We provide an overview of the classical results and techniques used to study these transformations, including the work of Bäcklund himself, as well as that of other prominent mathematicians such as Lie, Engeström, and Cartan.

Next, we delve into some of the more recent developments in the field, including the relationship between Bäcklund transformations and other geometric and algebraic structures, such as integrable systems, dynamical systems, and hierarchy structures. We also discuss the role of Bäcklund transformations in modern physics, particularly in the context of quantum field theory and string theory.

One of the main focuses of the paper is the presentation of novel approaches and insights into Bäcklund transformations. These include fresh perspectives on the classical theory, as well as new applications and generalizations of the technique. We illustrate these ideas through worked examples and case studies, demonstrating their power and versatility.

Finally, we conclude by highlighting some of the open problems and future research directions in the area of Bäcklund transformations. This includes the potential application of these transformations in current topics such as mirror symmetry, the homological conjecture, and the positive Grassmannian.

In summary, our paper provides a comprehensive review of Bäcklund transformations, covering both classic results and cutting-edge developments. It offers valuable insights and tools for researchers and students interested in differential geometry, lie theory, and related areas.

We present XMM-Newton and Chandra observations of two low-metallicity
cometary blue compact dwarf (BCD) galaxies, Mrk 59 and Mrk 71. The first BCD,
Mrk 59, contains two ultraluminous X-ray (ULX) sources, IXO 72 and IXO 73, both
associated with bright massive stars and H II complexes, as well as one fainter
extended source associated with a massive H II complex at the head of the
cometary structure. The low-metallicity of Mrk 59 appears to be responsible for
the presence of the two ULXs. IXO 72 has varied little over the last 10 yr,
while IXO 73 has demonstrated a variability factor of ~4 over the same period.
The second BCD, Mrk 71, contains two faint X-ray point sources and two faint
extended sources. One point source is likely a background AGN, while the other
appears to be coincident with a very luminous star and a compact H II region at
the "head" of the cometary structure. The two faint extended sources are also
associated with massive H II complexes. Although both BCDs have the same
metallicity, the three sources in Mrk 71 have X-ray luminosities ~1-2 orders of
magnitude fainter than those in Mrk 59. The age of the starburst may play a
role.

We present for the first time a complete solution to the problem of proving
the correctness of a concurrency control algorithm for collaborative text
editors against the standard consistency model. The success of our approach
stems from the use of comprehensive stringwise operational transformations,
which appear to have escaped a formal treatment until now. Because these
transformations sometimes lead to an increase in the number of operations as
they are transformed, we cannot use inductive methods and adopt the novel idea
of decreasing diagrams instead. We also base our algorithm on a client-server
model rather than a peer-to-peer one, which leads to the correct application of
operational transformations to both newly generated and pending operations. And
lastly we solve the problem of latency, so that our algorithm works perfectly
in practice. The result of these innovations is the first ever formally correct
concurrency control algorithm for collaborative text editors together with a
fast, fault tolerant and highly scalable implementation.

The segmentation of synthetic aperture radar (SAR) images is a longstanding
yet challenging task, not only because of the presence of speckle, but also due
to the variations of surface backscattering properties in the images.
Tremendous investigations have been made to eliminate the speckle effects for
the segmentation of SAR images, while few work devotes to dealing with the
variations of backscattering coefficients in the images. In order to overcome
both the two difficulties, this paper presents a novel SAR image segmentation
method by exploiting a multi-scale active contour model based on the non-local
processing principle. More precisely, we first formulize the SAR segmentation
problem with an active contour model by integrating the non-local interactions
between pairs of patches inside and outside the segmented regions. Secondly, a
multi-scale strategy is proposed to speed up the non-local active contour
segmentation procedure and to avoid falling into local minimum for achieving
more accurate segmentation results. Experimental results on simulated and real
SAR images demonstrate the efficiency and feasibility of the proposed method:
it can not only achieve precise segmentations for images with heavy speckles
and non-local intensity variations, but also can be used for SAR images from
different types of sensors.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to semantic image segmentation called Auto-DeepLab, which leverages hierarchical neural architecture search (HNAS) to optimize the design of deep neural networks (DNNs) for this task. Unlike traditional methods that rely on hand-crafted architectures or brute-force search, Auto-DeepLab uses a hierarchical search strategy to efficiently explore the space of possible architectures and identify the most effective ones for semantic image segmentation.

Our approach consists of three main components: (1) a hierarchical search algorithm that iteratively refines the architecture of a DNN, (2) a set of evaluation metrics that guide the search process, and (3) a robust optimization method that enables efficient training of the identified architectures. We evaluate Auto-DeepLab on several benchmark datasets, including Cityscapes, PASCAL VOC, and COCO, and compare its performance to state-of-the-art methods.

The results show that Auto-DeepLab significantly outperforms existing methods, achieving an average IoU of 81.7% on Cityscapes and 85.1% on PASCAL VOC. Moreover, we perform ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of the hierarchical search strategy and demonstrate that it is crucial for achieving better performance.

Our work has important implications for the field of computer vision and deep learning. First, it demonstrates the potential of HNAS for solving complex tasks like semantic image segmentation. Second, it provides a new way to design high-performance DNNs that do not rely on manual design or brute-force search. Finally, it highlights the importance of considering the hierarchical structure of images when designing DNNs for semantic segmentation.

In summary, Auto-DeepLab represents a significant step forward in the field of semantic image segmentation, and we believe that its hierarchical search strategy and evaluation metrics can be applied to other computer vision tasks, leading to further advances in the field.

The application of deep learning to medical image segmentation has been
hampered due to the lack of abundant pixel-level annotated data. Few-shot
Semantic Segmentation (FSS) is a promising strategy for breaking the deadlock.
However, a high-performing FSS model still requires sufficient pixel-level
annotated classes for training to avoid overfitting, which leads to its
performance bottleneck in medical image segmentation due to the unmet need for
annotations. Thus, semi-supervised FSS for medical images is accordingly
proposed to utilize unlabeled data for further performance improvement.
Nevertheless, existing semi-supervised FSS methods has two obvious defects: (1)
neglecting the relationship between the labeled and unlabeled data; (2) using
unlabeled data directly for end-to-end training leads to degenerated
representation learning. To address these problems, we propose a novel
semi-supervised FSS framework for medical image segmentation. The proposed
framework employs Poisson learning for modeling data relationship and
propagating supervision signals, and Spatial Consistency Calibration for
encouraging the model to learn more coherent representations. In this process,
unlabeled samples do not involve in end-to-end training, but provide
supervisory information for query image segmentation through graph-based
learning. We conduct extensive experiments on three medical image segmentation
datasets (i.e. ISIC skin lesion segmentation, abdominal organs segmentation for
MRI and abdominal organs segmentation for CT) to demonstrate the
state-of-the-art performance and broad applicability of the proposed framework.

Ultrathin nanopore membranes based on 2D materials have demonstrated ultimate
resolution toward DNA sequencing. Among them, molybdenum disulphide (MoS2)
shows long-term stability as well as superior sensitivity enabling high
throughput performance. The traditional method of fabricating nanopores with
nanometer precision is based on the use of focused electron beams in
transmission electron microscope (TEM). This nanopore fabrication process is
time-consuming, expensive, not scalable and hard to control below 1 nm. Here,
we exploited the electrochemical activity of MoS2 and developed a convenient
and scalable method to controllably make nanopores in single-layer MoS2 with
sub-nanometer precision using electrochemical reaction (ECR). The
electrochemical reaction on the surface of single-layer MoS2 is initiated at
the location of defects or single atom vacancy, followed by the successive
removals of individual atoms or unit cells from single-layer MoS2 lattice and
finally formation of a nanopore. Step-like features in the ionic current
through the growing nanopore provide direct feedback on the nanopore size
inferred from a widely used conductance vs. pore size model. Furthermore, DNA
translocations can be detected in-situ when as-fabricated MoS2 nanopores are
used. The atomic resolution and accessibility of this approach paves the way
for mass production of nanopores in 2D membranes for potential solid-state
nanopore sequencing.

In this paper, we investigate the consistency of matter models with asymptotically safe quantum gravity, a theoretical framework that seeks to merge quantum mechanics and general relativity. We focus on the paradigmatic example of scalar matter and explore the implications of the asymptotic safety conjecture on the behavior of matter at high energies.

Using a combination of analytical and numerical techniques, we demonstrate that the matter models considered are consistent with the principles of asymptotically safe quantum gravity, provided certain conditions are met. In particular, we show that the matter couplings exhibit a non-trivial dependence on the energy scale, which is a characteristic feature of asymptotic safety.

Our results provide support for the idea that matter and gravity can be described within a single, consistent theoretical framework, and offer a promising avenue for understanding the behavior of matter at the highest energies. Furthermore, our findings have important implications for the search for a complete theory of quantum gravity, and highlight the potential of asymptotic safety as a guiding principle in this quest.

Overall, our work represents a significant step forward in our understanding of the interplay between matter and gravity at the smallest distances and highest energies, and paves the way for further exploration of the theoretical landscape of quantum gravity.

Spectral properties of the Hamiltonian function which characterizes a trapped
ion are investigated. In order to study semiclassical dynamics of trapped ions,
coherent state orbits are introduced as sub-manifolds of the quantum state
space, with the K\"ahler structure induced by the transition probability. The
time dependent variational principle (TDVP) is applied on coherent states'
orbits. The Hamilton equations of motion on K\"ahler manifolds of the type of
classical phase spaces naturally arise. The associated classical Hamiltonian is
obtained from the expected values on symplectic coherent states of the quantum
Hamiltonian. Spectral information is thus coded within the phase portrait. We
deal with the bosonic realization of the Lie algebra of the SU(1,1) group,
which we particularize for the case of an ion confined in a combined, Paul and
Penning trap. This formalism can be applied to Hamiltonians which are nonlinear
in the infinitesimal generators of a dynamical symmetry group, such as the case
of ions confined in electrodynamic traps. Discrete quasienergy spectra are
obtained and the corresponding quasienergy states are explicitly realized as
coherent states parameterized by the stable solutions of the corresponding
classical equations of motion. A correspondence between quantum and classical
stability domains is thus established, using the Husimi representation.

The most recent fast and accurate image segmentation methods are built upon
fully convolutional deep neural networks. In this paper, we propose new deep
learning strategies for DenseNets to improve segmenting images with subtle
differences in intensity values and features. We aim to segment brain tissue on
infant brain MRI at about 6 months of age where white matter and gray matter of
the developing brain show similar T1 and T2 relaxation times, thus appear to
have similar intensity values on both T1- and T2-weighted MRI scans. Brain
tissue segmentation at this age is, therefore, very challenging. To this end,
we propose an exclusive multi-label training strategy to segment the mutually
exclusive brain tissues with similarity loss functions that automatically
balance the training based on class prevalence. Using our proposed training
strategy based on similarity loss functions and patch prediction fusion we
decrease the number of parameters in the network, reduce the complexity of the
training process focusing the attention on less number of tasks, while
mitigating the effects of data imbalance between labels and inaccuracies near
patch borders. By taking advantage of these strategies we were able to perform
fast image segmentation (90 seconds per 3D volume), using a network with less
parameters than many state-of-the-art networks, overcoming issues such as
3Dvs2D training and large vs small patch size selection, while achieving the
top performance in segmenting brain tissue among all methods tested in first
and second round submissions of the isointense infant brain MRI segmentation
(iSeg) challenge according to the official challenge test results. Our proposed
strategy improves the training process through balanced training and by
reducing its complexity while providing a trained model that works for any size
input image and is fast and more accurate than many state-of-the-art methods.

This paper presents a robust regression approach for image binarization under
significant background variations and observation noises. The work is motivated
by the need of identifying foreground regions in noisy microscopic image or
degraded document images, where significant background variation and severe
noise make an image binarization challenging. The proposed method first
estimates the background of an input image, subtracts the estimated background
from the input image, and apply a global thresholding to the subtracted outcome
for achieving a binary image of foregrounds. A robust regression approach was
proposed to estimate the background intensity surface with minimal effects of
foreground intensities and noises, and a global threshold selector was proposed
on the basis of a model selection criterion in a sparse regression. The
proposed approach was validated using 26 test images and the corresponding
ground truths, and the outcomes of the proposed work were compared with those
from nine existing image binarization methods. The approach was also combined
with three state-of-the-art morphological segmentation methods to show how the
proposed approach can improve their image segmentation outcomes.

We propose nonstochastic, fast nonparametric clustering based on local regression method as a data-driven approach to segmenting images into distinct clusters according to individual characteristics like color and contrast. We leverage the fact that features that are more similar in different segments (e.g., nearby areas) tend to remain stable across the entire analysis window, whereas features less similar in different segments show lower stability. We use our technique to perform efficient segmentation and to explore how well it performs with highly varied inputs including real time video and other naturalistic visualizations. Our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods on a diverse range of benchmarked datasets involving both human and machine perception tasks such as face recognition and object detection, by several orders of magnitude between simple 2 × 2 designs versus 10 × 9 structures; we provide an evaluation at four levels of sophistication with two categories representing simple 3D scene vs scene analysis, object vs geometry and object vs geometric analysis. Moreover, we test our tool by using it to classify subjects as male or female and also demonstrate classification accuracy above 90% in all these cases. In line with many existing approaches, our technique employs global linear models which incorporate both continuous, local random covariates and a large spatial extent. Unlike a priori fixed prediction weights, we do not train the initial models before starting the training, nor evaluate model performance during training itself. Thus by making only small amounts of changes to the source code, one can tune different aspects of nonparametric clustering so that it will fit the model well under any circumstance. Finally, our system should be able to converge to robust conclusions from incomplete input sets in practice, as demonstrated from 20 out of 21 runs when used on the same dataset compared by comparison with three published techniques; therefore is a promising candidate to serve the next generations of nonparametric image inference models even if the learning algorithms themselves undergo substantial optimization challenges.

We study integrated characteristics of ~14000 low-redshift (0<z<1) compact
star-forming galaxies (SFGs) selected from the Data Release 12 of the Sloan
Digital Sky Survey. It is found that emission of these galaxies is dominated by
strong young bursts of star formation, implying that their luminosities
experience rapid variations on a time scale of a few Myr. Reducing integrated
characteristics of these galaxies to zero burst age would result in a
considerably tighter and almost linear relation between stellar mass and star
formation rate (SFR). The same correction implies that the specific star
formation rate (the ratio of SFR and stellar mass) is not dependent on the
galaxy stellar mass. We conclude that the correction for rapid luminosity
evolution must be taken into account in a similar way when comparing different
samples of low- and high-redshift SFGs. If the bursting nature of star
formation and young burst ages are characteristics of the galaxies selected at
high redshifts, the age correction of observed SFRs derived from the Hbeta
emission line or UV continua would modify the derived SFR densities in the
early universe.

In this paper, we present a novel approach for generating image collages that combines the strengths of guided and unguided methods. Our proposed method, called Transform the Set (TTS), leverages memory attention to create visually coherent and diverse collages that can be used in various applications such as art, design, and data visualization.

Existing methods for image collage generation can be broadly classified into two categories: guided and unguided. Guided methods use explicit instructions or templates to generate collages, resulting in predictable outcomes but limited creativity. On the other hand, unguided methods rely solely on algorithmic combinations of images, often leading to visually appealing but lacking contextual relevance.

Our TTS method addresses these limitations by introducing a memory attentive module that learns to attend to the input images and their relationships during the generative process. This allows the model to create collages that are both visually pleasing and semantically meaningful. We evaluate our method through several experiments, demonstrating its ability to generate high-quality collages that can be further fine-tuned using user feedback.

The key contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows:

1. Introduction of a memory attentive module for image collage generation, enabling the creation of visually coherent and contextually relevant collages.
2. Development of an end-to-end trainable framework that integrates the memory attentive module with a generative adversarial network (GAN).
3. Thorough evaluation of TTS through various experiments, showcasing its effectiveness in generating diverse and high-quality collages.
4. Demonstration of the versatility of TTS in different application scenarios, including artistic collages, fashion design, and data visualization.

Overall, our proposed Transform the Set method offers a significant improvement over existing image collage generation techniques, providing a powerful tool for artists, designers, and researchers alike.

In this paper, we numerically investigate thetailoring of magnetic dipole radiation using substrates. Magnetic dipoles are important elements in various applications, including wireless power transfer, magnetic resonance imaging, and sensing. The radiation pattern of magnetic dipoles can be controlled by manipulating their geometry or surrounding materials. Here,we explore the effectiveness of different substrate materials on the radiation characteristics of magnetic dipoles.

Using a numerical simulation approach, we model a magnetic dipole placed above different substrate materials with varying dielectric constants and conductivity properties. We analyze the resulting radiation patterns and illustrate how they are influenced by the substrate's parameters. Our results show that the substrate material significantly affects the directionality and strength of themagnetic field, permitting tailoring of the radiation pattern. By selecting anappropriate substrate material, we demonstrate the possibility to control the direction of maximum radiation, alter theradial distance of the radiation lobe,and manipulate the polarization state of the emitted waves. Our findings have significant implications for optimizing magnetic dipole-based devices and open up new possibilitiesfor novel applications such as reconfigurable antennas, waveguides, andmetamaterials.

Many deep learning architectures for semantic segmentation involve a Fully
Convolutional Neural Network (FCN) followed by a Conditional Random Field (CRF)
to carry out inference over an image. These models typically involve unary
potentials based on local appearance features computed by FCNs, and binary
potentials based on the displacement between pixels. We show that while current
methods succeed in segmenting whole objects, they perform poorly in situations
involving a large number of object parts. We therefore suggest incorporating
into the inference algorithm additional higher-order potentials inspired by the
way humans identify and localize parts. We incorporate two relations that were
shown to be useful to human object identification - containment and attachment
- into the energy term of the CRF and evaluate their performance on the Pascal
VOC Parts dataset. Our experimental results show that the segmentation of fine
parts is positively affected by the addition of these two relations, and that
the segmentation of fine parts can be further influenced by complex structural
features.
