Standard segmentation of medical images based on full-supervised
convolutional networks demands accurate dense annotations. Such learning
framework is built on laborious manual annotation with restrict demands for
expertise, leading to insufficient high-quality labels. To overcome such
limitation and exploit massive weakly labeled data, we relaxed the rigid
labeling requirement and developed a semi-supervised learning framework based
on a teacher-student fashion for organ and lesion segmentation with partial
dense-labeled supervision and supplementary loose bounding-box supervision
which are easier to acquire. Observing the geometrical relation of an organ and
its inner lesions in most cases, we propose a hierarchical organ-to-lesion
(O2L) attention module in a teacher segmentor to produce pseudo-labels. Then a
student segmentor is trained with combinations of manual-labeled and
pseudo-labeled annotations. We further proposed a localization branch realized
via an aggregation of high-level features in a deep decoder to predict
locations of organ and lesion, which enriches student segmentor with precise
localization information. We validated each design in our model on LiTS
challenge datasets by ablation study and showed its state-of-the-art
performance compared with recent methods. We show our model is robust to the
quality of bounding box and achieves comparable performance compared with
full-supervised learning methods.

Solving crystal structures from kinematical X-ray or electron diffraction
patterns of single crystals requires many more diffracted beams to be recorded
than there are atoms in the structure, since the phases of the structure
factors can only be retrieved from such data if the atoms can be resolved as
sharply peaked objects. Here a method is presented by which the fact that
multiple scattering encodes structure factor phases in the diffracted
intensities is being used for solving the crystallographic phase problem. The
retrieval of both amplitudes and phases of electron structure factors from
diffraction patterns recorded with varying angle of incidence will be
demonstrated. No assumption about the scattering potential itself is being
made. In particular, the resolution in the diffraction data does not need to be
sufficient to resolve atoms, making this method potentially interesting for
electron crystallography of 2-dimensional protein crystals and other
beam-sensitive complex structures.

Biomedical image segmentation is a critical task in medical imaging analysis, with applications in disease diagnosis, treatment planning, and monitoring. Deep learning-based methods have shown promising results in segmenting biomedical images, but they often suffer from limited accuracy and robustness, particularly when dealing with complex and varied images. In this paper, we propose a novel deep learning architecture called ACE-Net, which stands for Augmented Contracting and Expansive Paths, to improve the accuracy and robustness of biomedical image segmentation.

To address these limitations, ACE-Net introduces three key components: (1) augmented contracting paths, (2) expansive paths, and (3) feature pyramid networks.

Augmented contracting paths are designed to enhance feature extraction and representation by incorporating multi-scale and multi-orientation information into the network. The classical problem of foam film rupture dynamics has been investigated
when surfaces exhibit very high rigidity due to the presence of specific
surfactants. Two new features are reported. First a strong deviation to the
well-known Taylor-Culick law is observed. Then, crack-like patterns can be
visualized in the film; these patterns are shown to appear at a well defined
deformation. The key role of surface active material on these features is
quantitatively investigated, pointing the importance of surface elasticity to
describe these fast dynamical processes, and thus providing an alternative tool
to characterize surface elasticity in conditions extremely far from
equilibrium. The origin of the cracks and their consequences on film rupturing
dynamics are also discussed.

We analyze the data complexity of ontology-mediated querying where the
ontologies are formulated in a description logic (DL) of the ALC family and
queries are conjunctive queries, positive existential queries, or acyclic
conjunctive queries. Our approach is non-uniform in the sense that we aim to
understand the complexity of each single ontology instead of for all ontologies
formulated in a certain language. While doing so, we quantify over the queries
and are interested, for example, in the question whether all queries can be
evaluated in polynomial time w.r.t. a given ontology. Our results include a
PTime/coNP-dichotomy for ontologies of depth one in the description logic
ALCFI, the same dichotomy for ALC- and ALCI-ontologies of unrestricted depth,
and the non-existence of such a dichotomy for ALCF-ontologies. For the latter
DL, we additionally show that it is undecidable whether a given ontology admits
PTime query evaluation. We also consider the connection between PTime query
evaluation and rewritability into (monadic) Datalog.

The extended Bondi-Metzner-Sachs (BMS) algebra is a symmetry algebra that describes the asymptotic symmetries of gravitational waves. In this paper, we investigate the conserved charges of the extended BMS algebra. We find that the conserved charges are related to the supertranslations and superrotations of the spacetime. We also show that the conserved charges are related to the Brown-Henneaux central charge, which is a key ingredient in the AdS/CFT correspondence. Our results provide a deeper understanding of the structure of the extended BMS algebra and its role in the study of gravitational waves and holography.

Let $G$ be the interior domain of a piecewise analytic Jordan curve without
cusps. Let $\{p_n\}_{n=0}^\infty$ be the sequence of polynomials that are
orthonormal over $G$ with respect to the area measure, with each $p_n$ having
leading coefficient $\lambda_n>0$. N. Stylianopoulos has recently proven that
the asymptotic behavior of $\lambda_n$ as $n\to\infty$ is given by \[
\frac{n+1}{\pi}\frac{\gamma^{2n+2}}{ \lambda_n^{2}}=1-\alpha_n, \] where
$\alpha_n=O(1/n)$ as $n\to\infty$ and $\gamma$ is the reciprocal of the
logarithmic capacity of the boundary $\partial G$. In this paper, we prove that
the $O(1/n)$ estimate for the error term $\alpha_n$ is, in general, best
possible, by exhibiting an example for which \[
\liminf_{n\to\infty}\,n\alpha_n>0. \] The proof makes use of the Faber
polynomials, about which a conjecture is formulated.

In this paper, we explore the relationship between quantum circuits and spin(3n) groups. We show that certain families of quantum circuits can be used to implement generating sets for spin(3n) groups, which are a class of Lie groups that include the rotation group SO(3n) as a subclass.

We begin by introducing a general framework for constructing quantum circuits from elements of the spin(3n) group. We then specialize our construction to several important subfamilies of quantum circuits, including the Clifford gates, the quaternion gates, and the universal quantum gates. For each of these subfamilies, we demonstrate how to use them to generate spin(3n) groups and discuss their properties and applications.

Our results provide new insights into the connections between quantum computing and representation theory, and have potential implications for fault-tolerant quantum computation, topological quantum computing, and other areas where the symmetries of quantum systems play an essential role. Along the way, we also develop novel techniques for analyzing quantum circuits using tools from group theory and algebraic geometry, which may be useful in future research.

Overall, our work deepens our understanding of the interplay between quantum information science and geometric algebra, and opens up new directions for exploring the mathematical foundations of quantum computing.

In this paper, we investigate the properties of 3D convolutional neural networks (CNNs) when applied to the task of brain parcellation. Specifically, we explore the compactness, efficiency, and representation capabilities of 3D CNNs, and examine the extent to which they can be improved through the use of a pretext task.

Brain parcellation is the process of dividing the brain into distinct regions, each with its own unique characteristics and functions. This task is of great importance in neuroscience, as it can help researchers to better understand the structure and function of the brain, and to identify biomarkers for various neurological and psychiatric conditions.

3D CNNs have shown great promise in addressing this task, due to their ability to learn rich and hierarchical representations of 3D data. However, their computational requirements can be prohibitively expensive, and their performance can suffer from overfitting.

To address these limitations, we propose a pretext task that leverages the spatial structure of the brain to learn a compact and efficient representation of the data. Specifically, we use a self-supervised loss function that encourages the network to predict the location of a given brain region within a 3D volume.

Our results show that this pretext task leads to significant improvements in the compactness and efficiency of the 3D CNN, without sacrificing performance on the main parcellation task. In addition, we find that the pretext task helps the network to learn more meaningful and robust representations of the brain data, as evidenced by improved performance on a variety of downstream tasks.

Overall, our findings demonstrate the potential of 3D CNNs for brain parcellation, and highlight the importance of carefully designing pretext tasks to improve their performance and efficiency. This work has important implications for the development of machine learning algorithms for neuroscience applications, and may lead to new insights into the structure and function of the brain.

This research explores quantitative automata, a model of computation that combines aspects of formal language theory and probability. Recent advances in appearance-based models have shown improved eye tracking
performance in difficult scenarios like occlusion due to eyelashes, eyelids or
camera placement, and environmental reflections on the cornea and glasses. The
key reason for the improvement is the accurate and robust identification of eye
parts (pupil, iris, and sclera regions). The improved accuracy often comes at
the cost of labeling an enormous dataset, which is complex and time-consuming.
This work presents two semi-supervised learning frameworks to identify
eye-parts by taking advantage of unlabeled images where labeled datasets are
scarce. With these frameworks, leveraging the domain-specific augmentation and
novel spatially varying transformations for image segmentation, we show
improved performance on various test cases. For instance, for a model trained
on just 48 labeled images, these frameworks achieved an improvement of 0.38%
and 0.65% in segmentation performance over the baseline model, which is trained
only with the labeled dataset.

In this paper, we present SwipeCut, an interactive segmentation method that leverages diversified seed proposals to improve the accuracy and efficiency of image segmentation. Existing interactive segmentation methods rely on a single initial guess or user input, which can be time-consuming and may not capture the desired details. SwipeCut addresses these limitations by generating multiple diverse seed proposals that cover various regions of interest in an image.

We propose a novel algorithm that combines region proposal networks (RPNs) and density-based clustering to generate high-quality seed proposals. The RPN generates a set of regions of interest, which are then used as seeds for density-based clustering. By iteratively adding clusters and refining their boundaries, our method produces a diverse set of seed proposals that cover different parts of the image. We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets and show that it outperforms state-of-the-art interactive segmentation techniques in terms of both accuracy and efficiency.

Furthermore, we introduce a new post-processing technique called boundary smoothness optimization, which enhances the quality of the final segmentation masks produced by SwipeCut. This technique enables us to further improve the segmentation results while maintaining the same level of interactivity. Our experiments demonstrate that SwipeCut achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks while providing a more intuitive and efficient interaction experience for users.

Color and intensity are two important components in an image. Usually, groups
of image pixels, which are similar in color or intensity, are an informative
representation for an object. They are therefore particularly suitable for
computer vision tasks, such as saliency detection and object proposal
generation. However, image pixels, which share a similar real-world color, may
be quite different since colors are often distorted by intensity. In this
paper, we reinvestigate the affinity matrices originally used in image
segmentation methods based on spectral clustering. A new affinity matrix, which
is robust to color distortions, is formulated for object discovery. Moreover, a
Cohesion Measurement (CM) for object regions is also derived based on the
formulated affinity matrix. Based on the new Cohesion Measurement, a novel
object discovery method is proposed to discover objects latent in an image by
utilizing the eigenvectors of the affinity matrix. Then we apply the proposed
method to both saliency detection and object proposal generation. Experimental
results on several evaluation benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed CM based
method has achieved promising performance for these two tasks.

segmentation problems. Many modifications have been proposed for U-Net, such as
attention U-Net, recurrent residual convolutional U-Net (R2-UNet), and U-Net
with residual blocks or blocks with dense connections. However, all these
modifications have an encoder-decoder structure with skip connections, and the
number of paths for information flow is limited. We propose LadderNet in this
paper, which can be viewed as a chain of multiple U-Nets. Instead of only one
pair of encoder branch and decoder branch in U-Net, a LadderNet has multiple
pairs of encoder-decoder branches, and has skip connections between every pair
of adjacent decoder and decoder branches in each level. Inspired by the success
of ResNet and R2-UNet, we use modified residual blocks where two convolutional
layers in one block share the same weights. A LadderNet has more paths for
information flow because of skip connections and residual blocks, and can be
viewed as an ensemble of Fully Convolutional Networks (FCN). The equivalence to
an ensemble of FCNs improves segmentation accuracy, while the shared weights
within each residual block reduce parameter number. Semantic segmentation is
essential for retinal disease detection. We tested LadderNet on two benchmark
datasets for blood vessel segmentation in retinal images, and achieved superior
performance over methods in the literature. The implementation is provided

The generalised colouring numbers $\mathrm{col}_r(G)$ and
$\mathrm{wcol}_r(G)$ were introduced by Kierstead and Yang as a generalisation
of the usual colouring number, and have since then found important theoretical
and algorithmic applications. In this paper, we dramatically improve upon the
known upper bounds for generalised colouring numbers for graphs excluding a
fixed minor, from the exponential bounds of Grohe et al. to a linear bound for

excludes $K_t$ as a minor, for some fixed $t\ge4$, then
$\mathrm{col}_r(G)\le\binom{t-1}{2}\,(2r+1)$ and
$\mathrm{wcol}_r(G)\le\binom{r+t-2}{t-2}\cdot(t-3)(2r+1)\in\mathcal{O}(r^{\,t-1})$.
In the case of graphs $G$ of bounded genus $g$, we improve the bounds to
$\mathrm{col}_r(G)\le(2g+3)(2r+1)$ (and even $\mathrm{col}_r(G)\le5r+1$ if
$g=0$, i.e. if $G$ is planar) and
$\mathrm{wcol}_r(G)\le\Bigl(2g+\binom{r+2}{2}\Bigr)\,(2r+1)$.

In this paper, we propose an unsupervised method for pathology image segmentation using representation learning with spherical k-means. Traditional methods rely on hand-crafted features and manual annotation of large datasets, which can be time-consuming and costly to obtain. We then use these features to train a spherical k-means model, which is capable of capturing non-linear relationships between the data points. The resulting clusters are used to segregate the image into its constituent parts, such as tumor regions, healthy tissue, and background.

Our proposed method was evaluated on several publicly available datasets, including colon cancer, breast cancer, and lung cancer slides. Specifically, we achieved an average DICE score of 0.87 across all datasets, compared to 0.75 for traditional methods. Additionally, our method has the advantage of not requiring any prior knowledge about the number of classes or their labels, making it truly unsupervised.

The main contribution of this work is the introduction of spherical k-means to the field of pathology image segmentation, which allows for more accurate and efficient clustering. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of using representation learning with spherical k-means for unsupervised image segmentation tasks, highlighting its potential to significantly reduce the amount of manual effort required for annotating medical images. This work paves the way for future research in developing more sophisticated and robust models for pathology image analysis using self-supervised learning techniques.

We introduce a high-level graphical framework for designing and analysing
quantum error correcting codes, centred on what we term the coherent parity
check (CPC). The graphical formulation is based on the diagrammatic tools of
the zx-calculus of quantum observables. The resulting framework leads to a
construction for stabilizer codes that allows us to design and verify a broad
range of quantum codes based on classical ones, and that gives a means of
discovering large classes of codes using both analytical and numerical methods.
We focus in particular on the smaller codes that will be the first used by
near-term devices. We show how CSS codes form a subset of CPC codes and, more
generally, how to compute stabilizers for a CPC code. As an explicit example of
this framework, we give a method for turning almost any pair of classical
[n,k,3] codes into a [[2n - k + 2, k, 3]] CPC code. Further, we give a simple
technique for machine search which yields thousands of potential codes, and
demonstrate its operation for distance 3 and 5 codes. Finally, we use the
graphical tools to demonstrate how Clifford computation can be performed within
CPC codes. As our framework gives a new tool for constructing small- to
medium-sized codes with relatively high code rates, it provides a new source
for codes that could be suitable for emerging devices, while its zx-calculus
foundations enable natural integration of error correction with graphical
compiler toolchains. It also provides a powerful framework for reasoning about
all stabilizer quantum error correction codes of any size.

on the same rays, and if one unit ball is a polyhedron so is the other.
  Among norms arising from inner products, two norms are angularly equivalent
if and only if they are topological equivalent. But, unlike topological
equivalence, angular equivalence is able to distinguish between different norms
on a finite-dimensional space. In particular, no two $\ell^p$ norms on $\mathbb
R^n$ are angularly equivalent.

This paper proposes a novel active contour segmentation model that utilizes multiple features to address the issue of intensity inhomogeneity in infrared images. The intensity feature is used to capture the overall brightness of the image, while the texture feature captures the spatial information and patterns in the image. The edge feature, on the other hand, provides information about the boundaries between different objects in the scene.

The proposed model also incorporates a novel optimization algorithm that utilizes a combination of gradient descent and level set methods to optimize the segmentation results. The algorithm iteratively updates the contour curve to minimize an energy functional that incorporates the multi-feature representation and a regularization term.

Experiments conducted on a dataset of infrared images demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed model in segmenting objects in scenes with intensity inhomogeneity. The results show that the proposed model outperforms traditional active contour models and other state-of-the-art segmentation methods in terms of both accuracy and efficiency.

The main contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows:

* A novel active contour segmentation model that combines multiple features to address intensity inhomogeneity in infrared images.
* A novel optimization algorithm that utilizes a combination of gradient descent and level set methods to optimize the segmentation results.
* Experimental results that demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed model in segmenting objects in scenes with intensity inhomogeneity.

Overall, this paper provides a valuable contribution to the field of image segmentation, particularly in the context of infrared imaging, and demonstrates the potential of the proposed model for applications such as object detection, tracking, and recognition.

We introduce mixings and dualities between finite event spaces, i.e. mixed events that occur not only inside their respective generators but also in a random number generator to which they are added one after another, to explore issues related to event mixing in general and about duality-based modeling. Here we present an example based on our own analysis for a randomized lottery using the probability group of two distinct dice tossed with equal likelihoods. We show how to construct mixed probabilities and how to create pairwise triplets (and triples), where each member is one of its members separated by one or more triplets which result from the mixing process. This can be a powerful tool for analyzing interactions among elements because it allows us to look at relationships between objects which otherwise appear disconnected or discontinuous. Furthermore, as shown, in an arbitrary bounded state space one may design mixed probability-generator states. Finally, we discuss the mathematical characterization and application of this method, and conclude by considering how other applications might arise.

We give an a posteriori analysis of a semi-discrete discontinuous Galerkin
scheme approximating solutions to a model of multiphase elastodynamics, which
involves an energy density depending not only on the strain but also the strain
gradient. A key component in the analysis is the reduced relative entropy
stability framework developed in [Giesselmann 2014]. This framework allows
energy type arguments to be applied to continuous functions. Since we advocate
the use of discontinuous Galerkin methods we make use of two families of
reconstructions, one set of discrete reconstructions [Makridakis and Nochetto
2006] and a set of elliptic reconstructions [Makridakis and Nochetto 2003] to
apply the reduced relative entropy framework in this setting.

This paper compares the accuracy of a data-fitted generalized Aw-Rascle-Zhang (ARZ) model with other state-of-the-art models in predicting turbulent flow over a flat plate. The ARZ model is a widely used model for wall-bounded turbulent flows, but its accuracy has not been thoroughly evaluated against experimental data. In this study, we use a machine learning algorithm to optimize the parameters of the ARZ model and compare its performance with that of other models, including the Reynolds number decomposition (RND) model, the wall-attached eddy-viscosity (WALE) model, and the realizable k-ε model. Our results show that the data-fitted ARZ model outperforms the other models in predicting the mean velocity profile and the root mean square (RMS) fluctuations of the velocity components. Specifically, the ARZ model accurately captures the log-law behavior of the mean velocity profile and the scaling behavior of the RMS fluctuations, which are not well-predicted by the other models. Our findings suggest that the ARZ model can be a useful tool for predicting turbulent flow over flat plates and other wall-bounded surfaces, and that data-fitting can significantly improve its accuracy.

support the importance of these attention modules in the proposed architecture.

In this paper, we present a novel approach for splenomegaly segmentation in medical images using global convolutional kernels and conditional generative adversarial networks (cGANs). Splenomegaly is a condition where the spleen becomes enlarged, which can be caused by various diseases such as liver cirrhosis, malaria, and sickle cell anemia. Accurate segmentation of the spleen is important for diagnosis and treatment planning, but it remains a challenging task due to the organ's complex shape and variable size.

Our proposed method combines the strengths of global convolutional kernels and cGANs to effectively segment the spleen from CT scans. Global convolutional kernels are used to extract features from the entire image, while cGANs are utilized to generate high-quality images that are similar to the original input data. The generated images are then used to augment the training dataset, increasing its diversity and improving the accuracy of the subsequent segmentation model.

We evaluate our method on a publicly available dataset of abdominal CT scans and demonstrate superior performance compared to traditional U-Net and U-Net++ models. Our results show that the inclusion of cGAN-generated images into the training set leads to improved segmentation accuracy, with Dice similarity coefficients increasing by up to 10%. We also perform experiments to analyze the effectiveness of different components of our approach, providing insights into the contributions of each module.

The main contributions of this work are:

* A novel approach for splenomegaly segmentation combining global convolutional kernels and cGANs
* Improved segmentation accuracy through the use of cGAN-generated images for data augmentation
* Analysis of the significance of individual components of the proposed method

This research has potential applications in computer-aided diagnosis systems and could serve as a foundation for further advancements in automated organ segmentation techniques.

In this paper, we present a Van der Waals (vdW) density-functional theory (DFT) study of bulk solids with body-centered cubic (BCC), face-centered cubic (FCC), and diamond crystal structures. The vdW DFT method is used to investigate the structural, electronic, and thermodynamic properties of these materials, which are relevant to a wide range of technological applications.

Using a set of state-of-the-art functionals, including the local density approximation (LDA), the generalized gradient approximation (GGA), and hybrid functional, we compute the electron density, lattice parameters, cohesive energy, and other structural properties of the three systems. We also analyze the electronic band structure and optical properties, such as dielectric constants, refractive indices, and absorption spectra, using the GGA+GW approximation.

Our calculations reveal that the chosen functionals can accurately predict the experimental lattice parameters but typically underestimate the cohesive energies of all three solids. This trend is more pronounced in the case of BCC and diamond, which have stronger inter atom bonding compared to FCC. When comparing the performance of the different functionals, we find that the hybrid functional leads to a better description of the cohesive properties than the LDA or GGA. Additionally, our results show fair agreement between the calculated and expected behavior of the electronic band gaps for each crystal structure.

The optical properties exhibit varying degrees of disagreement among the considered functionals, suggesting further investigation into their ability to capture complex excitations and screening effects. Overall, our study provides valuable information and insights about Van der Waals density-functional theory studies of bulk solids with differing crystal structures; our conclusions should prove useful in guiding future developments and applications involving solid-state materials design relying on theoretical modeling techniques.

attempts have been made in quantifying the uncertainty in image segmentation
architectures, e.g. to learn a density segmentation model conditioned on the
input image. Typical work in this field restricts these learnt densities to be
strictly Gaussian. In this paper, we propose to use a more flexible approach by
introducing Normalizing Flows (NFs), which enables the learnt densities to be
more complex and facilitate more accurate modeling for uncertainty. We prove
this hypothesis by adopting the Probabilistic U-Net and augmenting the
posterior density with an NF, allowing it to be more expressive. Our
qualitative as well as quantitative (GED and IoU) evaluations on the
multi-annotated and single-annotated LIDC-IDRI and Kvasir-SEG segmentation
datasets, respectively, show a clear improvement. This is mostly apparent in
the quantification of aleatoric uncertainty and the increased predictive
performance of up to 14 percent. This result strongly indicates that a more
flexible density model should be seriously considered in architectures that
attempt to capture segmentation ambiguity through density modeling. The benefit
of this improved modeling will increase human confidence in annotation and
segmentation, and enable eager adoption of the technology in practice.

In this paper, we present a novel approach for improving the accuracy of pancreas segmentation in medical images using a technique called Attention U-Net. The pancreas is a vital organ that plays an essential role in digestion and glucose regulation, and its accurate segmentation is crucial for diagnosis and treatment of various pancreatic diseases. However, manual segmentation of the pancreas can be time-consuming and challenging due to its complex shape and location near other organs.

To address this challenge, we propose an attention mechanism that learns to focus on the most relevant regions when segmenting the pancreas. Our proposed method uses a U-Net architecture with an additional attention branch that learns to predict a weight map indicating the importance of each pixel in the input image. This attention map is then used to guide the feature extraction process, allowing the network to selectively focus on pixels that are most informative for pancreas segmentation.

We evaluate our Attention U-Net on a dataset of contrast-enhanced CT scans and compare it to traditional U-Net architectures without attention. Our results show that Attention U-Net achieves significantly higher segmentation accuracy than existing methods (mean Dice score = 0.87 vs. 0.83), while also reducing computational cost by approximately 25%. We further analyze the attention maps generated by our model and find that they accurately identify key features such as the pancreatic duct and blood vessels, which are important for successful segmentation.

Our work demonstrates the potential of incorporating attention mechanisms into deep learning models for medical image segmentation tasks, particularly for organs with complex shapes and locations like the pancreas. By selectively focusing on relevant regions, Attention U-Net offers a promising solution for improving segmentation accuracy and efficiency in clinical settings.

PC-U Net: Learning to Jointly Reconstruct and Segment the Cardiac Walls in 3D from CT Data

Abstract:

Accurate segmentation and reconstruction of the cardiac walls from computed tomography (CT) data is crucial for various cardiovascular applications, such as diagnosis, treatment planning, and monitoring of cardiac diseases. However, the complexity and variability of the cardiac anatomy, as well as the limited resolution and quality of CT images, make this task challenging. In this paper, we propose a novel deep learning approach, called PC-U Net, which jointly reconstructs and segments the cardiac walls in 3D from CT data.

PC-U Net is built upon a U-Net architecture and incorporates a novel partitioned convolutional branch (PCB) to simultaneously learn the cardiac wall segmentation and 3D reconstruction. The PCB divides the input image into four sub-images, each of which is processed by a separate convolutional neural network (CNN) to predict the corresponding cardiac wall. This allows the network to focus on the unique features and spatial relationships of each wall, leading to improved segmentation and reconstruction accuracy.

We evaluated PC-U Net on a dataset of 320 CT scans and compared its performance to state-of-the-art methods. Our results show that PC-U Net achieves superior segmentation and reconstruction accuracy, with a mean Dice similarity coefficient of 0.86 and a mean absolute error of 1.23 mm. In addition, we demonstrate the efficacy of PC-U Net in handling various challenges, such as low contrast, noise, and artifacts, and its potential for real-time application.

Our work has significant implications for the diagnosis and treatment of cardiac diseases, as well as the development of personalized medicine. The accurate segmentation and reconstruction of the cardiac walls provided by PC-U Net can be used for quantitative assessment of cardiac function, detection of subtle cardiac abnormalities, and planning of minimally invasive procedures.

reliable results in adverse weather conditions is to use video-segmentation
approaches instead of commonly used single-image segmentation methods.
Video-segmentation approaches capture temporal information of the previous
video-frames in addition to current image information, and hence, they are more
robust against disturbances, especially if they occur in only a few frames of
the video-sequence. However, video-segmentation approaches, which are often
based on recurrent neural networks, cannot be applied in real-time applications
anymore, since their recurrent structures in the network are computational
expensive. For instance, the inference time of the LSTM-ICNet, in which
recurrent units are placed at proper positions in the single-segmentation
approach ICNet, increases up to 61 percent compared to the basic ICNet. Hence,
in this work, the LSTM-ICNet is sped up by modifying the recurrent units of the
network so that it becomes real-time capable again. Experiments on different
datasets and various weather conditions show that the inference time can be
decreased by about 23 percent by these modifications, while they achieve
similar performance than the LSTM-ICNet and outperform the single-segmentation
approach enormously in adverse weather conditions.

Our results have important implications for the study of normal numbers and their applications in various fields, including number theory, probability theory, and computational complexity theory. Global Formulation of Generalized Einfeel-Rabi Maxwell (GESM) The global formulation of Generalized Einfeel-Rabi Maxwell (GESM) describes and analyzes two new forms of particle creation using nonlinear differential equations, using general relativity to generate a quantum field in which light can be carried without being absorbed or emitted by particles. For each of these objects, it also solves its own complex Hamiltonian in order to make accurate measurements from different places around the globe. A special feature of GESM is that it makes use of the fact that the nonlinear differential equations at the end of the first limit only describe the initial state of particles, but the laws of gravity determine how they propagate. So far no experimentally tested theory has been able to do this, yet it's one of the most direct ways possible of understanding why things behave as they do, since all of the above can take place without any feedback whatsoever. Theoretically it predicts such nonlocality that if it is verified, nonlocal communication using electromagnetic waves would not be very slow given high enough energies (though it might increase by orders of magnitude). It was an obvious assumption even then that light travel would depend strongly on momentum transfer and nothing else was specified. However, we have no idea what speed energy spreads out in the gravitational fields, so now we are trying to derive a theory of energy distributions in space – even though there is something more fundamental here than simply conservation of energy (unless you count the lack of conservation of energy). GESM may thus provide a way of investigating exotic behavior in extreme circumstances. There are some interesting possibilities, notably that the mass in unstable quantum systems grows exponentially with time, rather than linearly according to classical physics, which is what your everyday Newtonian system suggests. But it will still remain highly speculative until it has some actual experimental demonstration or theoretical justification.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to image-to-image translation for semantic segmentation tasks, which we term "extremely weak supervision." This method leverages a small number of labeled images, typically in the order of tens or hundreds, to train a deep neural network to translate between two different imaging modalities. The translated images are then used to obtain dense and accurate semantic segmentations without requiring any additional annotation efforts.

Our proposed approach is based on a combination of adversarial training and self-supervised learning techniques. Specifically, we use a CycleGAN architecture to perform image-to-image translations, while incorporating an additional discriminator branch that enforces the generated images to follow the statistical properties of the target modality. Moreover, we introduce a new regularization term that encourages the preservation of semantic information during the translation process.

We evaluate our method on several publicly available datasets including Cityscapes, PASCAL VOC, and Mapillary Vistas, where it significantly outperforms state-of-the-art weakly supervised segmentation methods. Our experiments demonstrate that with only a few dozen labeled images, our approach can produce high-quality segmentations that accurately capture the desired semantics. Furthermore, by gradually increasing the amount of annotated data, we show that our method adapts well to improved supervision conditions and consistently achieves better performance.

The main contributions of this work include: (1) introducing extremely weak supervision for image-to-image translation-based semantic segmentation, (2) developing a robust and effective training strategy combining adversarial and self-supervised learning, and (3) demonstrating superior performance compared to existing weakly supervised segmentation approaches.

This research has broad implications for applications where labeled data is scarce or difficult to acquire, such as medical imaging, autonomous driving, and robotics. With its ability to generate highly accurate semantic segmentations from minuscule annotation effort, our technique paves the way for more efficient and scalable deployments of machine vision systems in real-world scenarios.

We develop a system for measurements of power spectra of transmitted light
intensity fluctuations, in which the extraneous noise, including shot noise, is
reduced. In essence, we just apply light, measure the power of the transmitted
light and derive its power spectrum. We use this to observe the spontaneous
noise spectra of photon atom interactions. Applying light with frequency
modulation, we can also observe the spontaneous noise reflecting the coherence
between the hyperfine levels in the excited state. There are two in novel
components in the measurement system, the noise reduction scheme and the
stabilization of the laser system. The noise reduction mechanism can be used to
reduce the shot noise contribution to arbitrarily low levels through averaging,
in principle. This is combined with differential detection to keep unwanted
noise at low levels. The laser system is stabilized to obtain spectral width
below 1\,kHz without high frequency ($\gtrsim10\,$MHz) noise. These methods are
described systematically and the performance of the asurement system is
examined through experimental results.

Image segmentation is a fundamental task in computer vision that involves partitioning an image into its constituent parts or objects. Despite decades of research, existing segmentation methods still suffer from several limitations, including poor performance on complex images, reliance on domain-specific heuristics, and lack of generalizability across different datasets. In this paper, we propose K-Net, a novel deep learning architecture designed to address these challenges and move towards unified image segmentation.

K-Net is built upon a simple yet powerful idea: leveraging knowledge from diverse segmentation modalities to improve overall performance. By modality, we refer to the specific approach or technique used to obtain the image data, such as color, depth, or texture. Traditional segmentation methods typically rely on a single modality, which can lead to suboptimal results when the chosen modality is not well-suited for a particular image. K-Net addresses this limitation by jointly incorporating multiple modalities within a single network, allowing it to adapt to various image types and capture a richer representation of the visual data.

The proposed architecture consists of three primary components: (1) a shared encoder that extracts high-level features from all modalities, (2) a set of modality-specific decoders that refine the feature maps according to their corresponding modalities, and (3) a novel fusion module that combines the outputs from each decoder to produce the final segmentation mask. anabelian properties proved by Mochizuki for hyperbolic curves over

In this paper, we propose a novel approach for semantic image segmentation called Double Similarity Distillation (DSD). Semantic image segmentation is a fundamental task in computer vision that involves assigning a class label to each pixel in an image, where the classes represent meaningful objects or regions. We present Spectrogram of a fundamental mode in which all harmonics are equal to 1. The harmonic magnitude can be reconstructed using this level signal and no additional information, provided that harmonics above or below one octave are not considered when reconstructing the mode. We also present a more sophisticated reconstruction based on two independent spectrograms that uses all harmonics rather than just 1. Our spectral analysis shows that spectra could well have been available during the first century B.C., if one assumes that the modes were obtained by spectrospheroidic methods (see also refs. 32⇓–35). This implies that spectracophers at

such a time would use the spectral mode as a basis for their measurement techniques because such measurements were possible with high probability. In particular, our results support the view that some of the earliest

quantitative descriptions of basic frequency representations should be dated to around 100 B.C.. Such an age implies that other sources of the spectrum used in early frequency analyses, both digital and analog (e.g., sound waves), may never have existed! Spectroscopic recordings made long before 100 B.C do appear to show several features common to this class; however, their spectral signatures are substantially less consistent from region to region and may differ significantly in the degree of overlap between neighboring signatures. Thus much remains to study and investigate further the origin and structure of this important acoustic source (the so called Ptolemaic paradigm) and perhaps discover even more complex harmonic representation underlying it.

Image segmentation is the problem of partitioning an image into different
subsets, where each subset may have a different characterization in terms of
color, intensity, texture, and/or other features. Segmentation is a fundamental
component of image processing, and plays a significant role in computer vision,
object recognition, and object tracking. Active Contour Models (ACMs)
constitute a powerful energy-based minimization framework for image
segmentation, which relies on the concept of contour evolution. Starting from
an initial guess, the contour is evolved with the aim of approximating better
and better the actual object boundary. Handling complex images in an efficient,
effective, and robust way is a real challenge, especially in the presence of
intensity inhomogeneity, overlap between the foreground/background intensity
distributions, objects characterized by many different intensities, and/or
additive noise. In this thesis, to deal with these challenges, we propose a
number of image segmentation models relying on variational level set methods
and specific kinds of neural networks, to handle complex images in both
supervised and unsupervised ways. Experimental results demonstrate the high
accuracy of the segmentation results, obtained by the proposed models on
various benchmark synthetic and real images compared with state-of-the-art
active contour models.

When evaluating computer vision systems, we are often concerned with
performance on a task-specific evaluation measure such as the
Intersection-Over-Union score used in the PASCAL VOC image segmentation
challenge. Ideally, our systems would be tuned specifically to these evaluation
measures. However, despite much work on loss-aware structured prediction, top
performing systems do not use these techniques. In this work, we seek to
address this problem, incorporating loss-aware prediction in a manner that is
amenable to the approaches taken by top performing systems. Our main idea is to
simultaneously leverage two systems: a highly tuned pipeline system as is found
on top of leaderboards, and a traditional CRF. We show how to combine high
quality candidate solutions from the pipeline with the probabilistic approach
of the CRF that is amenable to loss-aware prediction. The result is that we can
use loss-aware prediction methodology to improve performance of the highly
tuned pipeline system.

"A Novel Semantic Data Processing Approach For Deep Discriminator Learning using Polarimetry Sensitivity as an Independent Dependent Variable."


Abstract: We propose a novel approach to the estimation of deep discriminator learning models based on polarimetric radar images data to study polarimetal structure/location at low bandwidths (e.g., 1μm). Our model architecture exploits signal inversion techniques through decomposition, which allows us to generate both unstructured and structured representations that can be used as semantic datasets. Specifically we demonstrate two algorithms in which these structures are generated by differential modulation. In the first algorithm, our reconstruction step modulates spectral features between the sparse representation in the middle-right quadrant of each image and a highly sensitive (i.e., polarimi-sensitive) structure consisting of a complex multichannel signal component over all other possible directions (in this case including horizontal directions) of polarization along the xy plane. To achieve such spatial coverage, each feature undergoes directional attenuation decay during its propagation path due to linear combination with polarimeters, allowing an important part of the signal to penetrate into the more sensitive detector. The resulting reconstructed shape and direction are then detected as vectors by the discriminator and normalized according to their value at the time of detection. Using both methodologies with different weights it was proven by means of cross validation studies that both approaches produce relatively robust results, i.e., a good proportion of the reconstructed features belong to the desired class while a minimum of half of them did not contribute towards the predicted classification. All spectral signatures are correctly classified using simple multilevel regression. Thus, using high resolution radio spectrases as neural data sets greatly eases development of artificial brain architectures and enables new applications.

This paper presents an extended technical report on the development of an Extended LTLvis Motion Planning interface. The LTLvis Motion Planning algorithm is a widely used tool for generating collision-free paths for robots and other kinematic systems. However, its limitations in terms of workspace constraints and motion smoothness have hindered its applicability in certain domains.

The proposed Extended LTLvis Motion Planning interface aims to address these limitations by incorporating additional features and enhancements to the original algorithm. Firstly, the interface includes a new workspace constraint handling mechanism that enables the algorithm to consider complex workspace constraints, such as non-convex obstacles and dynamic environments. Secondly, the algorithm is modified to generate smoother and more natural motions, reducing the jerk and oscillations in the robot's trajectory.

The extended interface also includes a novel optimization technique that improves the computational efficiency of the algorithm, making it capable of handling larger and more complex problems. The proposed technique leverages the concept of lazy evaluation and incremental search to significantly reduce the computational cost of the algorithm.

The effectiveness of the proposed Extended LTLvis Motion Planning interface is demonstrated through simulations and experiments using a real-world robotic platform. The results show that the algorithm is able to generate collision-free paths that satisfy complex workspace constraints while maintaining smooth and natural motions. The computational efficiency of the algorithm is also shown to be significantly improved compared to the original LTLvis Motion Planning algorithm.

The Extended LTLvis Motion Planning interface has the potential to significantly enhance the capabilities of robotic systems in various domains, including manufacturing, healthcare, and logistics. The algorithm's ability to handle complex workspace constraints and generate smooth motions makes it particularly useful in applications where safety and precision are paramount.

This paper presents a systematic approach to identifying the frequency modulation raman (FMR) parameters for spin reorientation transitions in (Ga,Mn)As. The FMR technique is used to study the magnetic properties of this material, which exhibits a complex magnetic behavior due to its diluted magnetic semiconductor nature. By analyzing the interval of the magnetic field sweep rate and temperature, we are able to extract the important parameters that govern the spin reorientation transition in (Ga,Mn)As. Our results show that the critical field, Hc, and the coefficient of the quadratic term in the magnetic free energy, A, can be accurately determined using this method. We also observe a strong dependence of these parameters on temperature, indicating significant changes in the magnetic interactions near the Curie temperature. The findings of this study provide valuable insights into the magnetic behavior of (Ga,Mn)As and demonstrate the potential of the FMR technique for investigating the spin dynamics in such materials.

In this paper, we develop a model theory for compact cardinals, a class of topological spaces that have garnered significant attention in recent years due to their unique properties and applications in various fields. Our approach is based on the idea of a "compact cardinal" - a topological space that is both compact and has the cardinality of the continuum.

We begin by introducing the basic definitions and properties of compact cardinals, including their characterization in terms of the Cantor-Bendixson theorem and their relationship to other classes of topological spaces, such as metric spaces and Stone-Čech compacta. We then develop a model theory for compact cardinals, which allows us to study their properties and behavior using tools from mathematical logic and model theory.

Our model theory for compact cardinals is based on a certain class of "nice" models, which are defined in terms of their ability to satisfy certain axioms related to compactness and cardinality. We show that these models are consistent with the usual axioms of set theory, and that they provide a useful framework for studying the properties of compact cardinals.

One of the key results of our paper is the development of a decidable theory of compact cardinals, which allows us to determine whether a given statement about compact cardinals is true or false. This result has important implications for the study of compact cardinals, as it provides a way to resolve questions about their properties and behavior that were previously open.

In addition to our work on the model theory of compact cardinals, we also explore the relationship between compact cardinals and other areas of mathematics, such as topology, analysis, and set theory. We show that compact cardinals have connections to a variety of interesting mathematical objects and phenomena, such as the Cantor set, the Baire space, and the continuum hypothesis.

Overall, our paper provides a comprehensive introduction to the model theory of compact cardinals, and demonstrates the power and flexibility of this approach for studying the properties and behavior of these fascinating topological spaces.

Segmentation is a fundamental task in medical image analysis. However, most
existing methods focus on primary region extraction and ignore edge
information, which is useful for obtaining accurate segmentation. In this
paper, we propose a generic medical segmentation method, called Edge-aTtention
guidance Network (ET-Net), which embeds edge-attention representations to guide
the segmentation network. Specifically, an edge guidance module is utilized to
learn the edge-attention representations in the early encoding layers, which
are then transferred to the multi-scale decoding layers, fused using a weighted
aggregation module. The experimental results on four segmentation tasks (i.e.,
optic disc/cup and vessel segmentation in retinal images, and lung segmentation
in chest X-Ray and CT images) demonstrate that preserving edge-attention
representations contributes to the final segmentation accuracy, and our
proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art segmentation methods. The
source code of our method is available at https://github.com/ZzzJzzZ/ETNet.

We propose a novel framework for structured prediction via adversarial
learning. Existing adversarial learning methods involve two separate networks,
i.e., the structured prediction models and the discriminative models, in the
training. The information captured by discriminative models complements that in
the structured prediction models, but few existing researches have studied on
utilizing such information to improve structured prediction models at the
inference stage. In this work, we propose to refine the predictions of
structured prediction models by effectively integrating discriminative models
into the prediction. Discriminative models are treated as energy-based models.
Similar to the adversarial learning, discriminative models are trained to
estimate scores which measure the quality of predicted outputs, while
structured prediction models are trained to predict contrastive outputs with
maximal energy scores. In this way, the gradient vanishing problem is
ameliorated, and thus we are able to perform inference by following the ascent
gradient directions of discriminative models to refine structured prediction
models. The proposed method is able to handle a range of tasks, e.g.,
multi-label classification and image segmentation. Empirical results on these
two tasks validate the effectiveness of our learning method.

Simultaneous segmentation of multiple organs from different medical imaging
modalities is a crucial task as it can be utilized for computer-aided
diagnosis, computer-assisted surgery, and therapy planning. Thanks to the
recent advances in deep learning, several deep neural networks for medical
image segmentation have been introduced successfully for this purpose. In this
paper, we focus on learning a deep multi-organ segmentation network that labels
voxels. In particular, we examine the critical choice of a loss function in
order to handle the notorious imbalance problem that plagues both the input and
output of a learning model. The input imbalance refers to the class-imbalance
in the input training samples (i.e., small foreground objects embedded in an
abundance of background voxels, as well as organs of varying sizes). The output
imbalance refers to the imbalance between the false positives and false
negatives of the inference model. In order to tackle both types of imbalance
during training and inference, we introduce a new curriculum learning based
loss function. Specifically, we leverage Dice similarity coefficient to deter
model parameters from being held at bad local minima and at the same time
gradually learn better model parameters by penalizing for false
positives/negatives using a cross entropy term. We evaluated the proposed loss
function on three datasets: whole body positron emission tomography (PET) scans
with 5 target organs, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) prostate scans, and
ultrasound echocardigraphy images with a single target organ i.e., left
ventricular. We show that a simple network architecture with the proposed
integrative loss function can outperform state-of-the-art methods and results
of the competing methods can be improved when our proposed loss is used.

It proposes an importance-driven approach to address the challenge of adapting to new domains while preserving the performance on previously seen domains. The proposed method focuses on identifying and prioritizing important features for each domain, allowing the model to adapt more effectively while minimizing the impact on previous knowledge. The paper presents experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed method in various segmentation tasks across different domains.

This paper presents a variational based approach to fusing hyperspectral and
multispectral images. The fusion process is formulated as an inverse problem
whose solution is the target image assumed to live in a much lower dimensional
subspace. A sparse regularization term is carefully designed, relying on a
decomposition of the scene on a set of dictionaries. The dictionary atoms and
the corresponding supports of active coding coefficients are learned from the
observed images. Then, conditionally on these dictionaries and supports, the
fusion problem is solved via alternating optimization with respect to the
target image (using the alternating direction method of multipliers) and the
coding coefficients. Simulation results demonstrate the efficiency of the

patches and requires contextual information to reach label consensus. In this
paper we introduce Segmenter, a transformer model for semantic segmentation. In
contrast to convolution-based methods, our approach allows to model global
context already at the first layer and throughout the network. We build on the
recent Vision Transformer (ViT) and extend it to semantic segmentation. To do
so, we rely on the output embeddings corresponding to image patches and obtain
class labels from these embeddings with a point-wise linear decoder or a mask
transformer decoder. We leverage models pre-trained for image classification
and show that we can fine-tune them on moderate sized datasets available for
semantic segmentation. The linear decoder allows to obtain excellent results
already, but the performance can be further improved by a mask transformer
generating class masks. We conduct an extensive ablation study to show the
impact of the different parameters, in particular the performance is better for
large models and small patch sizes. Segmenter attains excellent results for
semantic segmentation. It outperforms the state of the art on both ADE20K and
Pascal Context datasets and is competitive on Cityscapes.

Algorithms can be used to prove and to discover new theorems. This paper
shows how algorithmic skills in general, and the notion of invariance in
particular, can be used to derive many results from Euclid's algorithm. We
illustrate how to use the algorithm as a verification interface (i.e., how to
verify theorems) and as a construction interface (i.e., how to investigate and
derive new theorems).
  The theorems that we verify are well-known and most of them are included in
standard number theory books. The new results concern distributivity properties
of the greatest common divisor and a new algorithm for efficiently enumerating
the positive rationals in two different ways. One way is known and is due to
Moshe Newman. The second is new and corresponds to a deforestation of the
Stern-Brocot tree of rationals. We show that both enumerations stem from the
same simple algorithm. In this way, we construct a Stern-Brocot enumeration
algorithm with the same time and space complexity as Newman's algorithm. A
short review of the original papers by Stern and Brocot is also included.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to image segmentation using 3D Fully Convolutional Deep Networks (FCNs) equipped with the Tversky loss function. Image segmentation is a fundamental task in computer vision that involves dividing an image into its constituent parts or objects, which can be helpful in various applications such as object recognition, tracking, and scene understanding.

Traditionally, FCNs have been widely used for image segmentation tasks due to their ability to learn rich feature representations from raw image data. However, their performance can be limited by the choice of loss function used during training. The most commonly used loss functions for image segmentation are Intersection over Union (IoU) and Cross-Entropy (CE), but they have some limitations. IoU is sensitive to class imbalance issues, whereas CE treats all classes equally, ignoring their relative importance.

To address these limitations, we propose the use of the Tversky loss function, which was originally designed for anomaly detection and segmentation tasks. The Tversky loss function modifies the standard CE loss function by introducing a parameter that controls the balance between precision and recall, allowing the model to focus on either precise segmentation of smaller regions or loose segmentation of larger regions.

Our results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art segmentation models trained with traditional loss functions, achieving better segmentation accuracy while also showing improved robustness to class imbalance issues. We evaluate our approach using different values of the Tversky parameter and provide ablation studies to analyze the contribution of each component in our framework.

Our findings suggest that the Tversky loss function can be an effective alternative to traditional loss functions for image segmentation tasks, providing a new tool for improving segmentation accuracy in complex scenes. This work paves the way for exploring other non-traditional loss functions that could potentially benefit image segmentation tasks, and highlights the need for further investigation into the design and analysis of specialized loss functions tailored to specific application domains.

Our results show that the multi-contrast approach significantly improves the accuracy and robustness of thalamus segmentation, particularly in regions where the thalamus is complex or distorted. We also demonstrate the potential of our approach for identifying abnormalities in the thalamus, such as volume loss or structural changes, which can be indicative of various neurological conditions.

Overall, our study demonstrates the benefits of a multi-contrast MRI approach to thalamus segmentation, and highlights its potential for improving the accuracy and robustness of thalamus segmentation in various clinical and research applications.

In this paper, we explore the relationship between the Quantum Zeno effect and the well-known literary character Hamlet. We propose that the Quantum Zeno effect, which is a phenomenon where the continuous measurement of a quantum system can prevent it from evolving into its ultimate state, can be analogously applied to the protagonist of Shakespeare's famous play. By frequently detecting the polarization oflight in a quantum system, we can draw parallels with the way in which Hamlet's repeated introspection and self-doubt prevent him from taking decisive action. Through this analogy, we gain new insights into the nature of indecision and the role of observation in both quantum mechanics and human behavior. Our findings have implications for our understanding of how frequent monitoring and feedback loops can influence the evolution of complex systems, both in the quantum realm and in the realms of human psychology and decision making.

This paper proposes a novel approach for incorporating near-infrared (NIR) information into semantic image segmentation. Semantic segmentation is a fundamental task in computer vision that aims to assign a semantic label to each pixel in an image, such as road, building, or vegetation. Most existing semantic segmentation methods rely solely on visible light images, which can be limited in certain scenarios, such as low-light conditions or when the image is captured through a hazy atmosphere. In contrast, NIR images can provide valuable information about the scene, even in these challenging conditions.

The proposed approach leverages a deep learning framework to fuse visible and NIR images and improve the accuracy of semantic segmentation. The authors introduce a novel convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture that jointly processes the visible and NIR images, exploiting the complementary information between the two modalities. The network is trained on a large dataset of paired visible and NIR images, and the authors evaluate its performance on several benchmarks.

The results show that the proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods that rely solely on visible light images, especially in low-light conditions. The authors also demonstrate the effectiveness of their approach in applications such as nighttime road detection and vegetation mapping.

The main contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows:

* The authors propose a novel deep learning approach for incorporating NIR information into semantic image segmentation.
* They introduce a CNN architecture that jointly processes visible and NIR images, leveraging the complementary information between the two modalities.
* The proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods that rely solely on visible light images, especially in low-light conditions.
* The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of their approach in various applications, such as nighttime road detection and vegetation mapping.

Overall, this paper provides a significant contribution to the field of semantic image segmentation, and its findings have important implications for a wide range of applications, including autonomous driving, environmental monitoring, and agricultural management.

We present highly efficient algorithms for performing forward and backward
propagation of Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for pixelwise classification
on images. For pixelwise classification tasks, such as image segmentation and
object detection, surrounding image patches are fed into CNN for predicting the
classes of centered pixels via forward propagation and for updating CNN
parameters via backward propagation. However, forward and backward propagation
was originally designed for whole-image classification. Directly applying it to
pixelwise classification in a patch-by-patch scanning manner is extremely
inefficient, because surrounding patches of pixels have large overlaps, which
lead to a lot of redundant computation.
  The proposed algorithms eliminate all the redundant computation in
convolution and pooling on images by introducing novel d-regularly sparse
kernels. It generates exactly the same results as those by patch-by-patch
scanning. Convolution and pooling operations with such kernels are able to
continuously access memory and can run efficiently on GPUs. A fraction of
patches of interest can be chosen from each training image for backward
propagation by applying a mask to the error map at the last CNN layer. Its
computation complexity is constant with respect to the number of patches
sampled from the image. Experiments have shown that our proposed algorithms
speed up commonly used patch-by-patch scanning over 1500 times in both forward
and backward propagation. The speedup increases with the sizes of images and
patches.

The need for labour intensive pixel-wise annotation is a major limitation of
many fully supervised learning methods for segmenting bioimages that can
contain numerous object instances with thin separations. In this paper, we
introduce a deep convolutional neural network for microscopy image
segmentation. Annotation issues are circumvented by letting the network being
trainable on coarse labels combined with only a very small number of images
with pixel-wise annotations. We call this new labelling strategy `lazy' labels.
Image segmentation is stratified into three connected tasks: rough inner region
detection, object separation and pixel-wise segmentation. These tasks are
learned in an end-to-end multi-task learning framework. The method is
demonstrated on two microscopy datasets, where we show that the model gives
accurate segmentation results even if exact boundary labels are missing for a
majority of annotated data. It brings more flexibility and efficiency for
training deep neural networks that are data hungry and is applicable to
biomedical images with poor contrast at the object boundaries or with diverse
textures and repeated patterns.

including semantic segmentation becomes an increasingly popular task in
computer vision today. Convolutional neural networks are powerful visual models
that yield hierarchies of features and practitioners widely use them to process
remote sensing data. When performing remote sensing image segmentation,
multiple instances of one class with precisely defined boundaries are often the
case, and it is crucial to extract those boundaries accurately. The accuracy of
segments boundaries delineation influences the quality of the whole segmented
areas explicitly. However, widely-used segmentation loss functions such as BCE,
IoU loss or Dice loss do not penalize misalignment of boundaries sufficiently.
In this paper, we propose a novel loss function, namely a differentiable
surrogate of a metric accounting accuracy of boundary detection. We can use the
loss function with any neural network for binary segmentation. We performed
validation of our loss function with various modifications of UNet on a
synthetic dataset, as well as using real-world data (ISPRS Potsdam, INRIA AIL).
Trained with the proposed loss function, models outperform baseline methods in
terms of IoU score.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to ensemble learning for polyp localization in colonoscopy images. Our method combines classifier prediction confidence and comprehensive learning particle swarm optimization (PSO) to improve the accuracy of polyp detection.

First, we train multiple deep learning models as base classifiers to predict the presence or absence of polyps in colonoscopy images. We then calculate the prediction confidence of each classifier and use it as a weighting factor to combine their outputs. This ensures that the final prediction is made by combining the predictions from all classifiers while giving more weightage to the ones with higher prediction confidences.

Next, we employ PSO to optimize the hyperparameters of the ensemble model. PSO is a population-based optimization algorithm that simulates the social behavior of bird flocking and fish schooling. It searchs for optimal solutions by iteratively updating the positions of particles in a population, which correspond to the hyperparameters of our model. By using comprehensive learning PSO, we are able to simultaneously optimize both the weights and the biases of the ensemble model.

We evaluate our approach on a benchmark dataset consisting of 1000 high-resolution color images of colonoscopies. The results show that our proposed ensemble learning strategy significantly outperforms any single classifier, achieving an improvement in detection accuracy of up to 23%. Additionally, the visualization of the learned features reveals meaningful patterns in the data that can help doctors and researchers better understand the characteristics of polyps and their precursors.

Our findings have important implications for improving the efficiency and accuracy of computer-aided diagnosis systems in gastroenterology. The proposed method has the potential to support clinical decision-making and reduce the risk of missing polyps during colonoscopic examinations.

This academic paper presents a highly efficient method for forward and backward propagation of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for pixelwise classification. The proposed method utilizes a combination of optimized algorithms and parallel processing techniques to significantly improve the speed and accuracy of CNNs. The paper provides a detailed analysis of the performance of the proposed method and compares it to existing approaches. The results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves significant improvements in both speed and accuracy, making it an effective solution for pixelwise classification tasks.

In this paper, we introduce a novel method for coherently averaging multiple representations of a signal, which we term "coherent averaging." This approach leverages the concept of coherence, which measures the similarity between two signals in terms of their phase relationship, to combine multiple versions of a signal into a single, more accurate representation.

We demonstrate that coherent averaging outperforms traditional methods of averaging, such as linear or median filtering, in various applications including noise reduction and image processing. Additionally, we show that our method can be used to improve the quality of signals corrupted by various types of distortions, such as multiplicative noise or blurring.

The key advantage of coherent averaging lies in its ability to preserve the underlying structure of the signal being processed. By exploiting the coherence between different versions of the signal, our technique is able to extract meaningful information from each version and combine it in a way that enhances the overall quality of the output. This makes it particularly suitable for applications where the input signals are noisy or contain errors, but still contain valuable information.

Our results confirm that coherent averaging offers a substantial improvement over existing approaches, and has significant potential for use in a wide range of fields, including signal processing, machine learning, and data analysis.

This special essay explores the relationship between extreme intensities and extremality among several game-theoretic forms including 'flooding'. Extreme conditions and extreme intensities represent fundamental constraints imposed on the emergence, complexity, and behavior within such contexts, an aspect that has received little attention in the current literature. However, we argue above all of their importance as they offer a powerful framework into which theoretical debates can be brought back to reality while at the same time highlighting some important areas where theoretical considerations should not stop here and can actually serve to advance the discussion further. The first part focuses on the case of flooding, exploring certain basic characteristics relating it to different types of extreme environments. In particular, we focus on four factors underlying this phenomenon. First, extreme conditions in the real world are often limited by physical limits arising solely from those associated directly with our own bodies; e.g., floodwaters are typically bounded by oceans or other terrain features. Second, extreme situations require that actors have specific cognitive capabilities beyond those required under most realistic scenarios (e.g., understanding that flooding may occur and acting accordingly). Third, extreme situations provide distinct problems of scale – often leading people to ask what level of impact one's actions will cause given available resources. Finally, the extreme situation needs to allow sufficient scope for large external changes with consequences beyond the immediate interests of affected parties. These dimensions lead us not only to consider flooding within nonhuman context but also to take account of alternative perspectives – especially on external change theory. It thus stands out that even though we approach these studies through similar methodological lens, many conclusions can arise differently based on whether one begins with the perspective from inside or outside the body itself. Our main goal then remains threefold: to clarify how extremes emerge, how extreme conditions depend on players' cognitive powers, and how players navigate against the background of these effects that can affect all aspects of decision-making.
