In this paper, we propose a novel teacher-student framework for semi-supervised medical image segmentation from mixed supervision. The proposed method leverages both labeled and unlabeled data to train a deep neural network for segmenting medical images, which can help alleviate the scarcity of annotated data in medical imaging.

The proposed framework consists of two main components: a teacher model and a student model. The teacher model is trained on a small set of labeled data and serves as a guide to provide high-quality pseudo labels for the remaining unlabeled data. The student model is then trained on the combined dataset of labeled and pseudolabeled data, and learns to segment medical images under the guidance of the teacher model.

We evaluate our framework on several publicly available datasets and show that it outperforms existing semi-supervised learning methods for medical image segmentation. Our experiments also demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework when dealing with different types of label noise and limited annotation rates.

Our main contributions are threefold: (1) We introduce a novel teacher-student framework for semi-supervised medical image segmentation; (2) We demonstrate the efficacy of using a teacher model to provide high-quality pseudo labels for unlabeled data; (3) We show that our proposed framework outperforms existing methods in various experimental settings.

This work has the potential to significantly impact the field of medical image analysis by providing an effective solution to the problem of scarce annotations, which is a major bottleneck in many medical image segmentation tasks.

Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) for cross-modality medical image
segmentation has shown great progress by domain-invariant feature learning or
image appearance translation. Adapted feature learning usually cannot detect
domain shifts at the pixel level and is not able to achieve good results in
dense semantic segmentation tasks. Image appearance translation, e.g. CycleGAN,
translates images into different styles with good appearance, despite its
population, its semantic consistency is hardly to maintain and results in poor
cross-modality segmentation. In this paper, we propose intra- and
cross-modality semantic consistency (ICMSC) for UDA and our key insight is that
the segmentation of synthesised images in different styles should be
consistent. Specifically, our model consists of an image translation module and
a domain-specific segmentation module. The image translation module is a
standard CycleGAN, while the segmentation module contains two domain-specific
segmentation networks. The intra-modality semantic consistency (IMSC) forces
the reconstructed image after a cycle to be segmented in the same way as the
original input image, while the cross-modality semantic consistency (CMSC)
encourages the synthesized images after translation to be segmented exactly the
same as before translation. Comprehensive experimental results on
cross-modality hip joint bone segmentation show the effectiveness of our
proposed method, which achieves an average DICE of 81.61% on the acetabulum and
88.16% on the proximal femur, outperforming other state-of-the-art methods. It
is worth to note that without UDA, a model trained on CT for hip joint bone
segmentation is non-transferable to MRI and has almost zero-DICE segmentation.

Weakly-supervised instance segmentation, which could greatly save labor and
time cost of pixel mask annotation, has attracted increasing attention in
recent years. The commonly used pipeline firstly utilizes conventional image
segmentation methods to automatically generate initial masks and then use them
to train an off-the-shelf segmentation network in an iterative way. However,
the initial generated masks usually contains a notable proportion of invalid
masks which are mainly caused by small object instances. Directly using these
initial masks to train segmentation model is harmful for the performance. To
address this problem, we propose a hybrid network in this paper. In our
architecture, there is a principle segmentation network which is used to handle
the normal samples with valid generated masks. In addition, a complementary
branch is added to handle the small and dim objects without valid masks.
Experimental results indicate that our method can achieve significantly
performance improvement both on the small object instances and large ones, and
outperforms all state-of-the-art methods.

The EXO-200 experiment is a search for neutrino-less double beta decay ($0\nu\beta\beta$) in $^{136}$Xe using a tonne-scale xenon detector. The experiment is designed to detect the tiny energy signal of $0\nu\beta\beta$ decay, which requires a high level of background suppression. However, radioactivity in the detector and surrounding materials can produce backgrounds that mimic the signal, posing a significant challenge to the experiment's sensitivity.

In this paper, we present the results of a detailed investigation into radioactivity-induced backgrounds in the EXO-200 detector. We use a combination of simulations and data-driven techniques to identify and characterize the sources of radioactivity and their impact on the experiment's background.

Our results show that the dominant background source in the EXO-200 detector is due to radon ($^{222}$Rn) contamination in the xenon gas. We measure the radon concentration in the detector and find that it is consistent with atmospheric levels. We also identify other radioactive isotopes, such as $^{210}$Pb and $^{210}$Po, which contribute to the background.

To mitigate the impact of these backgrounds, we implement a series of measures, including radon purging, surface decontamination, and material selection. We demonstrate that these measures effectively reduce the background rate in the detector, improving the sensitivity of the $0\nu\beta\beta$ decay search.

Our findings have important implications for the design and operation of future xenon-based experiments, particularly those searching for rare events such as $0\nu\beta\beta$ decay. By understanding and controlling radioactivity-induced backgrounds, these experiments can achieve higher sensitivities and push the boundaries of our understanding of fundamental physics.

The paper "A Thorough View of Exact Inference in Graphs from the Degree-4 Sum-of-Squares Hierarchy" presents a comprehensive analysis of exact inference in graphs using the degree-4 sum-of-squares (SOS) hierarchy. This work builds upon previous research that established the SOS hierarchy as a powerful tool for solving graphical models, and provides a thorough understanding of its capabilities and limitations.

The authors demonstrate that the degree-4 SOS hierarchy can be used to perform exact inference in various classes of graphs, including bounded-degree graphs, planar graphs, andgraphs with excluded minors. They provide explicit bounds on the computational complexity of exact inference using the SOS hierarchy for these classes of graphs, and show that it can be performed in polynomial time for many interesting cases.

The paper also explores the connections between the SOS hierarchy and other approaches to exact inference, such as belief propagation and linear programming relaxations. The authors show that the SOS hierarchy can be seen as an alternate formulation of these methods, providing new insights into their strengths and weaknesses.

Finally, the authors investigate the relationship between the SOS hierarchy and the statistical properties of graphs. They prove lower bounds on the size of the smallest witnesses required by the SOS hierarchy to refute independence claims in certain families of graphs, and provide evidence for the conjecture that the SOS hierarchy is optimal for testing independence in some regimes.

Overall, this work provides a thorough view of the power and limitations of the degree-4 SOS hierarchy for exact inference in graphs, and establishes it as a fundamental tool for future research in this area.

This study investigates whether deep learning is truly a viable and effective technique for image segmentation, as it has been widely touted in recent years. Through an examination of various research studies utilizing diverse datasets and evaluation metrics, we aim to provide insights into both the strengths and limitations of using deep learning methods within this domain. Our findings suggest that while there are certainly promising aspects associated with employing these approaches, they should not necessarily be considered as universally superior to traditional computer vision techniques without carefully considering particular application contexts. Ultimately, our goal is to contribute towards fostering critical discourse surrounding contemporary machine learning trends so that researchers can better navigate through the hype cycle when selecting appropriate tools for their specific applications.

In this paper, we investigate the complexity of improving all-switches strategies in various games. All-switches strategies are strategies that involve switching between different options or actions in a game, with the goal of maximizing payoffs or utilities. We examine the computational complexity of improving all-switches strategies in a variety of games, including finite and infinite horizon games, and games with perfect and imperfect information.

Our results show that improving all-switches strategies can be a computationally complex task, even for relatively simple games. In particular, we prove that computing an optimal all-switches strategy for a class of games known as "mean-payoff games" is PPAD-complete, which implies that it is unlikely that a polynomial-time algorithm for computing optimal all-switches strategies exists.

We also study the complexity of improving all-switches strategies in games with multiple players, where players can coordinate their actions to achieve higher payoffs. Our results show that computing a Nash equilibrium for a class of games with multiple players and all-switches strategies is also PPAD-complete.

Our findings have important implications for the design and analysis of algorithms for improving all-switches strategies in games. In particular, they suggest that computing optimal all-switches strategies may be intractable for many games, and that approximations or heuristics may be necessary to achieve good performance in practice.

Overall, our paper provides new insights into the complexity of all-switches strategies and their computational limitations, and highlights the need for further research in this area to develop efficient and effective algorithms for improving all-switches strategies in games.

This paper proposes a novel approach for iris recognition using image segmentation and retraining off-the-shelf deep neural networks. Existing iris recognition systems rely heavily on hand-crafted features and domain-specific algorithms, which can be time-consuming and costly to develop. In contrast, our approach leverages pre-trained deep neural networks to learn discriminative features from the iris images, resulting in improved recognition performance and reduced computational complexity.

We begin by segmenting the iris images using a fully convolutional network (FCN), which produces a binary mask that isolates the iris region from the rest of the eye. We then apply data augmentation techniques to increase the size of the segmented iris images and retrain a pre-trained ResNet-50 network to learn iris-specific features.

Our experimental results on the CASIA-IrisV4 dataset show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance in iris recognition, with an accuracy of 98.52%. Additionally, we perform a series of ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of our approach, demonstrating that both image segmentation and feature learning contribute significantly to the improved recognition performance.

Our work has important implications for the development of efficient and accurate iris recognition systems. By leveraging pre-trained deep neural networks and image segmentation techniques, we can reduce the computational complexity and development time of iris recognition systems, making them more accessible and cost-effective for a wider range of applications.

In this paper, we present a novel approach to machine vision-guided 3D medical image compression for efficient transmission and accurate segmentation in the clouds. utilizing cutting-edge techniques in machine learning and computer vision, our proposed method enables the reduction of data transfer rates and enhances the accuracy of segmentation in medical imaging applications.

Existing methods for medical image compression often suffer from high computational complexity or compromised image quality. Our proposed method addresses these limitations by exploiting the capabilities of cloud computing and recent advancements in convolutional neural networks (CNN). Specifically, we develop a two-stage framework that first employs a lightweight CNN model to rapidly preview and compress the input data followed by a deeper CNN model refinement stage to accurately segment the compressed image volumes.

Our approach enables real-time performance while maintaining high-quality segmentation standards, as demonstrated through extensive evaluation using various publicly available datasets. We also perform a thorough analysis of the trade-off between compression ratio and segmentation accuracy, providing insights into the optimal selection of hyperparameters for diverse application scenarios.

The key contributions of this study are:
1. A novel, effective solution for machine vision-guided 3D medical image compression and segmentation in the clouds;
2. An innovative two-stage framework combining lightweight and deep CNN models for efficient and precise processing;
3. Extensive experimentation and analysis, yielding valuable insights into compression ratio, segmentation performance, and associated trade-offs.
4. Demonstrated efficacy and potential for enabling remote collaboration and AI-assisted diagnosis in healthcare settings.

This research has significant implications for improving the efficiency and reliability of medical imaging workflows, facilitating expert interpretation remotely, and ultimately contributing towards superior patient outcomes.

Brain tumors are complex and aggressive cancers that pose significant challenges for clinicians and researchers. Accurate segmentation of brain tumors is essential for surgical planning, radiation therapy, and monitoring treatment response. Similarly, predicting overall survival is crucial for clinical decision-making and personalized patient care. In this paper, we propose an ensemble of 3D U-Nets for brain tumor segmentation and overall survival prediction using radiomic features.

Our proposed method utilizes a combination of three 3D U-Nets, each with a different architecture, to segment brain tumors from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans. The ensemble approach allows for improved accuracy and robustness compared to a single model. We evaluate the performance of our method using a dataset of 100 brain tumor patients and demonstrate superior segmentation accuracy compared to existing methods.

In addition to tumor segmentation, we extract radiomic features from the segmented tumors and use them to predict overall survival. Radiomic features are quantitative imaging biomarkers that capture the spatial and intensity patterns of the tumor. We use a machine learning algorithm to identify the most relevant radiomic features that are associated with overall survival. Our results show that the combination of radiomic features and clinical variables can significantly improve the prediction of overall survival compared to clinical variables alone.

Our findings have important implications for the diagnosis and treatment of brain tumors. Accurate segmentation of brain tumors can help clinicians identify the most effective treatment strategies and monitor treatment response. Predicting overall survival can help clinicians make informed decisions about patient care and tailor treatment plans to individual patients. Our ensemble of 3D U-Nets and radiomic feature analysis provides a promising approach for improving brain tumor diagnosis and treatment.

An alternative procedure calls for distributing population so it does not influence election results or elective representation, but it entails higher costs. In this article we examine whether voting populations should be used as a proxy to model whether competitive districts result in less redistributive outcomes. We exploit unique characteristics of Wisconsin's legislative system, which results in competitive districts with larger areas of influence compared to all American districts. We find two main effects on redistrictings. First, we discover that Democratic districts decrease, whereas Republican majority-minority seats increase when voters are counted uniformly across states. Second, we also show evidence supporting concerns about an 'unfair' effect—that there was more redistricting going into 2010 based on factors like geography, and partisanship increased, therefore making minority voting influence even greater.

In this paper, we present a novel approach to aerial image segmentation using online maps. Traditional methods of aerial image segmentation rely on manually labeled data, which can be time-consuming and expensive to obtain. In contrast, our approach leverages the vast amount of unlabeled data available in online maps to train a deep neural network for aerial image segmentation.

We propose a two-stage framework that first extracts features from online maps using a combination of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and spatial pyramid pooling. These features are then used to train a fully connected Conditional Random Field (CRF) model for pixel-level classification of aerial images. We evaluate our approach using several datasets of aerial images with different resolutions and diverse land cover types.

Our experimental results show that our proposed method outperforms traditional CNN-based approaches that rely solely on labeled data. Additionally, we demonstrate that incorporating spatial information from online maps improves segmentation accuracy compared to using only visual features. Our findings have important implications for real-world applications such as crop type mapping, disaster response, and urban planning, where accurate and efficient aerial image segmentation is critical.

Automated segmentation in medical image analysis is a challenging task that
requires a large amount of manually labeled data. However, manually annotating
medical data is often laborious, and most existing learning-based approaches
fail to accurately delineate object boundaries without effective geometric
constraints. Contrastive learning, a sub-area of self-supervised learning, has
recently been noted as a promising direction in multiple application fields. In
this work, we present a novel Contrastive Voxel-wise Representation Learning
(CVRL) method with geometric constraints to learn global-local visual
representations for volumetric medical image segmentation with limited
annotations. Our framework can effectively learn global and local features by
capturing 3D spatial context and rich anatomical information. Specifically, we
introduce a voxel-to-volume contrastive algorithm to learn global information
from 3D images, and propose to perform local voxel-to-voxel contrast to
explicitly make use of local cues in the embedding space. Moreover, we
integrate an elastic interaction-based active contour model as a geometric
regularization term to enable fast and reliable object delineations in an
end-to-end learning manner. Results on the Atrial Segmentation Challenge
dataset demonstrate superiority of our proposed scheme, especially in a setting
with a very limited number of annotated data.

We propose a novel framework for multimodal and semi-supervised image segmentation. Our method is based on a disentanglement-alignment-fusion strategy. First, we disentangle the input image into a set of latent representations, each of which is associated with a specific modality. Then, we align the latent representations across modalities by minimizing a modality-invariant loss. Finally, we fuse the aligned latent representations to generate the segmentation mask. Our method is able to leverage the complementary information from multiple modalities and can be easily extended to semi-supervised learning by incorporating unlabeled data. Extensive experiments on three multimodal datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.

Deep convolutional networks for semantic image segmentation typically require
large-scale labeled data, e.g. ImageNet and MS COCO, for network pre-training.
To reduce annotation efforts, self-supervised semantic segmentation is recently
proposed to pre-train a network without any human-provided labels. The key of
this new form of learning is to design a proxy task (e.g. image colorization),
from which a discriminative loss can be formulated on unlabeled data. Many
proxy tasks, however, lack the critical supervision signals that could induce
discriminative representation for the target image segmentation task. Thus
self-supervision's performance is still far from that of supervised
pre-training. In this study, we overcome this limitation by incorporating a
"mix-and-match" (M&M) tuning stage in the self-supervision pipeline. The
proposed approach is readily pluggable to many self-supervision methods and
does not use more annotated samples than the original process. Yet, it is
capable of boosting the performance of target image segmentation task to
surpass fully-supervised pre-trained counterpart. The improvement is made
possible by better harnessing the limited pixel-wise annotations in the target
dataset. Specifically, we first introduce the "mix" stage, which sparsely
samples and mixes patches from the target set to reflect rich and diverse local
patch statistics of target images. A "match" stage then forms a class-wise
connected graph, which can be used to derive a strong triplet-based
discriminative loss for fine-tuning the network. Our paradigm follows the
standard practice in existing self-supervised studies and no extra data or
label is required. With the proposed M&M approach, for the first time, a
self-supervision method can achieve comparable or even better performance
compared to its ImageNet pre-trained counterpart on both PASCAL VOC2012 dataset
and CityScapes dataset.

We present a simple and robust construction of a real-time quantum random
number generator (QRNG). Our minimalist approach ensures stable operation of
the device as well as its simple and straightforward hardware implementation as
a stand-alone module. As a source of randomness the device uses measurements of
time intervals between clicks of a single-photon detector. The obtained raw
sequence is then filtered and processed by a deterministic randomness
extractor, which is realized as a look-up table. This enables high speed
on-the-fly processing without the need of extensive computations. The overall
performance of the device is around 1 random bit per detector click, resulting
in 1.2 Mbit/s generation rate in our implementation.

In this paper, we present a novel approach to performing boolean operations on triangulated surfaces. Our method is based on a simple and robust algorithm that allows for efficient computation of union, intersection, and difference operations between surface meshes.

Unlike traditional methods that rely on mesh fusion or iterative refinement techniques, our approach uses a single pass algorithm that directly computes the resultant surface mesh by traversing the input surfaces in a particular order. This simplifies the process and reduces computational complexity, making it well-suited for large and complex data sets.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through experimental results on several benchmark datasets and compare its performance with existing state-of-the-art algorithms. The results show that our method produces high-quality results with improved efficiency and scalability compared to previous approaches. Additionally, we discuss various optimization techniques and tradeoffs that can be used to further improve performance depending on the specific application requirements.

The contributions of this paper include:

1. A new boolean operation algorithm for triangulated surfaces that combines simplicity and robustness
2. An efficient single-pass approach that eliminates the need for iterative refinement or mesh fusion
3. Improved performance and scalability compared to existing methods, demonstrated through experiments on realistic datasets
4. Discussion of practical optimizations and tradeoffs for different use cases.

This work has significant implications for applications where boolean operations are essential, such as computer-aided design (CAD), additive manufacturing, scientific computing, and virtual reality. It also provides a solid foundation for developing more advanced manipulation tools and algorithms for working with triangle meshes.

What is aging? Mechanistic answers to this question remain elusive despite
decades of research. Here, we propose a mathematical model of cellular aging
based on a model gene interaction network. Our network model is made of only
non-aging components - the biological functions of gene interactions decrease
with a constant mortality rate. Death of a cell occurs in the model when an
essential gene loses all of its interactions to other genes, equivalent to the
deletion of an essential gene. Gene interactions are stochastic based on a
binomial distribution. We show that the defining characteristic of biological
aging, the exponential increase of mortality rate over time, can arise from
this gene network model during the early stage of aging. Hence, we demonstrate
that cellular aging is an emergent property of this model network. Our model
predicts that the rate of aging, defined by the Gompertz coefficient, is
approximately proportional to the average number of active interactions per
gene and that the stochastic heterogeneity of gene interactions is an important
factor in the dynamics of the aging process. This theoretic framework offers a
mechanistic foundation for the pleiotropic nature of aging and can provide
insights on cellular aging.

We explore several generalizations of Whitney's theorem -- a classical
formula for the chromatic polynomial of a graph. Following Stanley, we replace
the chromatic polynomial by the chromatic symmetric function. Following Dohmen
and Trinks, we exclude not all but only an (arbitrarily selected) set of broken
circuits, or even weigh these broken circuits with weight monomials instead of
excluding them. Following Crew and Spirkl, we put weights on the vertices of
the graph. Following Gebhard and Sagan, we lift the chromatic symmetric
function to noncommuting variables. In addition, we replace the graph by an
"ambigraph", an apparently new concept that includes both hypergraphs and
multigraphs as particular cases.
  We show that Whitney's formula endures all these generalizations, and a
fairly simple sign-reversing involution can be used to prove it in each
setting. Furthermore, if we restrict ourselves to the chromatic polynomial,
then the graph can be replaced by a matroid.
  We discuss an application to transitive digraphs (i.e., posets), and reprove
an alternating-sum identity by Dahlberg and van Willigenburg.

In this paper, we investigate the problem of determining who can win a single-elimination tournament, in which each player is randomly paired with an opponent and the winner advances to the next round. We show that the probability of winning the tournament depends on the distribution of skills among players, and that there exists a threshold skill level below which no player has a positive chance of winning. We also derive expressions for the expected number of rounds until the tournament champion is determined, and for the probability that a given player will reach a particular round. Our results have implications for the design of tournaments and the prediction of their outcomes, and provide insights into the role of luck and skill in competition.

In this paper, we propose a new approach to modeling complex data distributions using dynamic adaptive mixture models (DAMMs). DAMMs are a generalization of traditional mixture models, which are widely used in machine learning and statistics to model data that can be represented as a mixture of underlying distributions. However, traditional mixture models have limitations when it comes to modeling data that is non-stationary, has varying densities, or contains anomalies.

DAMMs address these limitations by introducing dynamics and adaptivity into the mixture modeling framework. Specifically, DAMMs allow the mixture weights to change over time, enabling the model to adapt to changes in the data distribution. Additionally, DAMMs incorporate a novel clustering algorithm that can identify and separate anomalous data points from the rest of the data.

We evaluate the performance of DAMMs on several real-world datasets, including a dataset of sensor readings from a mechanical system, a dataset of user behavior on a social media platform, and a dataset of financial transactions. Our results show that DAMMs outperform traditional mixture models in terms of modeling accuracy and anomaly detection.

Furthermore, we analyze the effects of different parameters on the performance of DAMMs and provide guidance on how to choose these parameters in practice. We also discuss the limitations of DAMMs and suggest directions for future research.

Overall, DAMMs provide a powerful tool for modeling complex data distributions and have a wide range of applications in areas such as anomaly detection, clustering, and time-series analysis.

Recently, dense connections have attracted substantial attention in computer
vision because they facilitate gradient flow and implicit deep supervision
during training. Particularly, DenseNet, which connects each layer to every
other layer in a feed-forward fashion, has shown impressive performances in
natural image classification tasks. We propose HyperDenseNet, a 3D fully
convolutional neural network that extends the definition of dense connectivity
to multi-modal segmentation problems. Each imaging modality has a path, and
dense connections occur not only between the pairs of layers within the same
path, but also between those across different paths. This contrasts with the
existing multi-modal CNN approaches, in which modeling several modalities
relies entirely on a single joint layer (or level of abstraction) for fusion,
typically either at the input or at the output of the network. Therefore, the
proposed network has total freedom to learn more complex combinations between
the modalities, within and in-between all the levels of abstraction, which
increases significantly the learning representation. We report extensive
evaluations over two different and highly competitive multi-modal brain tissue
segmentation challenges, iSEG 2017 and MRBrainS 2013, with the former focusing
on 6-month infant data and the latter on adult images. HyperDenseNet yielded
significant improvements over many state-of-the-art segmentation networks,
ranking at the top on both benchmarks. We further provide a comprehensive
experimental analysis of features re-use, which confirms the importance of
hyper-dense connections in multi-modal representation learning. Our code is
publicly available at https://www.github.com/josedolz/HyperDenseNet.

Overall, this paper demonstrates the potential of deep learning techniques for automatic tracking of the tongue surface in real-time ultrasound videos, and highlights the advantages of using landmarks instead of contours for this task. The priority map is generated using a novel combination of image features and class probabilities, which are computed using a pre-trained deep neural network. The features capture the spatial and spectral information of the image, while the class probabilities provide a measure of the model's confidence in its predictions. By combining these two types of information, the priority map can effectively identify regions of the image that are most likely to contain class boundaries, even in the presence of occlusions, clutter, or other challenges.

Our results show that MetaBox+ significantly outperforms these methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency, achieving higher accuracy with fewer labeled samples. We also perform a series of ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of different components of the MetaBox+ method, providing insights into the role of each component in improving performance.

Overall, MetaBox+ offers a promising approach to active learning for semantic segmentation, with potential applications in a wide range of fields, including robotics, autonomous driving, and medical imaging. Deep neural networks (DNN) have rapidly been implemented to perform tasks ranging from image recognition through natural language understanding to robotic control that are significantly more complex than those used by earlier machine learning methods, which typically rely on highly structured representations without explicit regularization or prior knowledge about their structure. Recently DNNs exhibit extreme features such as local minima and extraordinary training performance owing to strong stochasticity effects. While these characteristics enable large-scale learning in this domain, previous models suffer from an absence of normalizing laws that allow different features of similar domains to be learned using different models. We investigate two main aspects related to distribution that underlie DNN learning—namely its behavior when data are sparsely sampled and its behavior with respect to a linear regression model—using deep convolutional networks with four hidden layers at both ends of the dimensionality spectrum. As predicted, the trained network exhibits an incredibly diverse range of features due to stochastic gradients in the network's internal parameters associated with the many degrees of freedom of the training set. In contrast, we find no clear evidence for small or discontinuous gradients even with an appropriate linear filter on each training dataset, and no significant effects even in the presence of negative cross-validation loss functions. This finding suggests two distinct mechanisms that allow DNN architectures, where gradient descent is applied over multiple inputs, to exploit very general structure-preserving optimization actions available within deep learning frameworks that may not require explicit, local information preservation across the entire parameter space.

By combining these two types of contrastive learning, our model can learn both generalizable and task-specific knowledge, leading to improved performance on few-shot segmentation tasks.

We consider a set of vertices that are arranged in a regular grid and are connected by edges to form a tiling of the space. We define the radial projection of a vertex as the set of all points on the rays emanating from the vertex and intersecting the boundary of a small disk centered at the vertex.

Using a combination of analytical and numerical methods, we study the spacing distribution of the radial projections of the tiling vertices. We show that the spacing distribution is related to the packing density of the tiling and can be described using a simple mathematical function. We also demonstrate that the spacing distribution exhibits a universal behavior that is independent of the specific tiling pattern.

Our results have important implications for the study of two-dimensional tilings and their properties. In particular, they provide a new way to analyze the packing density and spatial arrangement of tiling vertices, which can be useful in various fields such as materials science, physics, and computer science. Additionally, our findings shed light on the intrinsic structure of two-dimensional spaces and the way that they can be tiled with regular polygons.

Overall, this paper contributes to the understanding of the properties of two-dimensional tilings and their relationship to the spatial arrangement of their vertices. The results presented here can be used to guide the design and analysis of two-dimensional structures and patterns, and they provide a new perspective on the study of tiling theory and its applications.

Several, recently proposed methods of surface manufacturing based on ion beam
sputtering, which involve dual beam setups, sequential application of ion beams
from different directions, or sample rotation, are studied with the method of
kinetic Monte Carlo simulation of ion beam erosion and surface diffusion. In
this work, we only consider erosion dominated situations. The results are
discussed by comparing them to a number of theoretical propositions and to
experimental findings. Two ion-beams aligned opposite to each other produce
stationary, symmetric ripples. Two ion beams crossing at right angle will
produce square patterns only, if they are exactly balanced. In all other cases
of crossed beams, ripple patterns are created, and their orientations are shown
to be predictable from linear continuum theory. In sequential ion beam
sputtering we find a very rapid destruction of structures created from the
previous beam direction after a rotation step, which leads to a transient
decrease of overall roughness. Superpositions of patterns from several rotation
steps are difficult to obtain, as they exist only in very short time windows.
In setups with a single beam directed towards a rotating sample, we find a
non-monotonic dependence of roughness on rotation frequency, with a very
pronounced minimum appearing at the frequency scale set by the relaxation of
prestructures observed in sequential ion beam setups. Furthermore we find that
the logarithm of the height of structures decreases proportional to the inverse
frequency.

Accurate delineation of pathological lungs from computed tomography (CT)
images remains mostly unsolved because available methods fail to provide a
reliable generic solution due to high variability of abnormality appearance.
Local descriptor-based classification methods have shown to work well in
annotating pathologies; however, these methods are usually computationally
intensive which restricts their widespread use in real-time or near-real-time
clinical applications. In this paper, we present a novel approach for fast,
accurate, reliable segmentation of pathological lungs from CT scans by
combining region-based segmentation method with local descriptor classification
that is performed on an optimized sampling grid. Our method works in two
stages; during stage one, we adapted the fuzzy connectedness (FC) image
segmentation algorithm to perform initial lung parenchyma extraction. In the
second stage, texture-based local descriptors are utilized to segment abnormal
imaging patterns using a near optimal keypoint analysis by employing centroid
of supervoxel as grid points. The quantitative results show that our
pathological lung segmentation method is fast, robust, and improves on current
standards and has potential to enhance the performance of routine clinical
tasks.

For a sound field observed on a sensor array, compressive sensing (CS)
reconstructs the direction-of-arrival (DOA) of multiple sources using a
sparsity constraint. The DOA estimation is posed as an underdetermined problem
by expressing the acoustic pressure at each sensor as a phase-lagged
superposition of source amplitudes at all hypothetical DOAs. Regularizing with
an $\ell_1$-norm constraint renders the problem solvable with convex
optimization, and promoting sparsity gives high-resolution DOA maps. Here, the
sparse source distribution is derived using maximum a posteriori (MAP)
estimates for both single and multiple snapshots. CS does not require inversion
of the data covariance matrix and thus works well even for a single snapshot
where it gives higher resolution than conventional beamforming. For multiple
snapshots, CS outperforms conventional high-resolution methods, even with
coherent arrivals and at low signal-to-noise ratio. The superior resolution of
CS is demonstrated with vertical array data from the SWellEx96 experiment for
coherent multi-paths.

This paper proposes a novel approach to edge detection using deep neural networks, inspired by traditional methods in image processing. The proposed method leverages the strengths of both worlds to improve the accuracy and efficiency of edge detection at low computational cost.

Firstly, we review and analyze traditional methods for edge detection, such as Canny edge detection and Sobel operators, and identify their key components and limitations. We then employ these components to design a novel architecture for deep neural networks that can learn and adapt to various types of edges in images. Specifically, we propose a convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture with custom-designed filters and activation functions that mimic the behavior of traditional edge detectors.

The resulting model is able to effectively detect edges with high precision while reducing computational complexity compared to state-of-the-art CNN models. Furthermore, our experiments demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms traditional edge detection methods in terms of accuracy and robustness across different datasets and scenarios.

This work provides new insights into the convergence between traditional signal processing techniques and modern machine learning approaches, highlighting their complementary nature and potential synergies. It contributes to the development of efficient and accurate edge detection algorithms, crucial for a wide range of applications including object recognition, segmentation, and autonomous driving.

In this paper we present our system for human-in-the-loop video object
segmentation. The backbone of our system is a method for one-shot video object
segmentation. While fast, this method requires an accurate pixel-level
segmentation of one (or several) frames as input. As manually annotating such a
segmentation is impractical, we propose a deep interactive image segmentation
method, that can accurately segment objects with only a handful of clicks. On
the GrabCut dataset, our method obtains 90% IOU with just 3.8 clicks on
average, setting the new state of the art. Furthermore, as our method
iteratively refines an initial segmentation, it can effectively correct frames
where the video object segmentation fails, thus allowing users to quickly
obtain high quality results even on challenging sequences. Finally, we
investigate usage patterns and give insights in how many steps users take to
annotate frames, what kind of corrections they provide, etc., thus giving
important insights for further improving interactive video segmentation.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to few-shot segmentation that combines self-guided and cross-guided learning. Few-shot segmentation is a challenging task due to the limited number of training examples available for each class, which can lead to overfitting and poor generalization to unseen data. To address this challenge, we introduce a framework that leverages both self-guided and cross-guided information to improve the segmentation performance.

The proposed method consists of two main components: (1) a self-guided module that uses intra-modal similarity to learn a robust representation of each class, and (2) a cross-guided module that utilizes inter-modal correspondence to refine the segmentation results. The self-guided module encourages the model to learn a compact and discriminative feature space where samples from the same class are close together, while the cross-guided module aligns the features across different modalities to enhance the segmentation accuracy.

We evaluate our framework on several benchmark datasets, including PASCAL VOC and Cityscapes, and demonstrate its superiority compared to state-of-the-art few-shot segmentation methods. Our experiments show that the combination of self-guided and cross-guided learning leads to improved performance in terms of segmentation accuracy and robustness to variations in the input data. We also conduct an ablation study to analyze the contribution of each component and provide insights into the working mechanism of our framework.

Our work has important implications for real-world applications where labeled data is scarce or difficult to obtain. By enabling accurate segmentation with fewer annotations, our approach has the potential to reduce the cost and increase the efficiency of segmentation tasks in various domains such as medical imaging, autonomous driving, and robotics.

Random fields have remained a topic of great interest over past decades for
the purpose of structured inference, especially for problems such as image
segmentation. The local nodal interactions commonly used in such models often
suffer the short-boundary bias problem, which are tackled primarily through the
incorporation of long-range nodal interactions. However, the issue of
computational tractability becomes a significant issue when incorporating such
long-range nodal interactions, particularly when a large number of long-range
nodal interactions (e.g., fully-connected random fields) are modeled.
  In this work, we introduce a generalized random field framework based around
the concept of stochastic cliques, which addresses the issue of computational
tractability when using fully-connected random fields by stochastically forming
a sparse representation of the random field. The proposed framework allows for
efficient structured inference using fully-connected random fields without any
restrictions on the potential functions that can be utilized. Several
realizations of the proposed framework using graph cuts are presented and
evaluated, and experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework can
provide competitive performance for the purpose of image segmentation when
compared to existing fully-connected and principled deep random field
frameworks.

The Seiberg-Witten geometry of four-dimensional $\mathcal N=2$ quiver gauge theories is studied in this paper. The proposed method was evaluated on a dataset of stereo images captured during minimally invasive surgical procedures. The results demonstrate that the Bayesian dense inverse searching algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art stereo matching methods in terms of accuracy, robustness, and computational efficiency.

The proposed method has the potential to significantly improve the quality and accuracy of 3D reconstruction and visualization in minimally invasive surgery, which can enhance the safety and effectiveness of surgical procedures. In this paper, we investigate the generalized colouring numbers of graphs that exclude a fixed minor, which is a graph that can be obtained from a given graph by edge deletions, vertex deletions, and edge contractions. We prove that the generalized colouring number of such graphs can be bounded in terms of the minimum degree of the graph and the size of the minor. Specifically, we show that the generalized colouring number is at most $O(n\sqrt{\log n})$ for graphs with minimum degree at least $n/2$ and excluding a fixed minor with at most $n/2$ vertices. This bound is tight up to the logarithmic factor, as we demonstrate by constructing a family of graphs that achieves the bound. Our results have implications for the study of graph colouring and the structure of graphs that exclude a fixed minor.

Quantum dots are tiny particles made of semiconductor material that exhibit unique optical properties due to their small size and confinement of electrons and holes within their structure. When excited by an external source, quantum dots can emit light through a process known as spontaneous emission.

In a system of multiple quantum dots, the interaction between the dots can lead to a collective behavior of the emitted light, known as collective spontaneous emission. This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, including coupled quantum wells, quantum wires, and quantum dots.

In this work, we study the collective spontaneous emission from a system of quantum dots using a theoretical model that takes into account the interactions between the dots and the external environment. We show that the collective emission exhibits a number of interesting features, including enhancement of the emission rate, spectral narrowing, and the emergence of new emission peaks.

We also explore the dependence of the collective spontaneous emission on various parameters, such as the size and spacing of the dots, the intensity of the external field, and the temperature of the system. Our results provide a deeper understanding of the mechanisms behind collective spontaneous emission and its potential applications in fields such as optoelectronics and quantum information.

We study the applicability of a set of texture descriptors introduced in
recent work by the author to texture-based segmentation of images. The texture
descriptors under investigation result from applying graph indices from
quantitative graph theory to graphs encoding the local structure of images. The
underlying graphs arise from the computation of morphological amoebas as
structuring elements for adaptive morphology, either as weighted or unweighted
Dijkstra search trees or as edge-weighted pixel graphs within structuring
elements. In the present paper we focus on texture descriptors in which the
graph indices are entropy-based, and use them in a geodesic active contour
framework for image segmentation. Experiments on several synthetic and one
real-world image are shown to demonstrate texture segmentation by this
approach. Forthermore, we undertake an attempt to analyse selected
entropy-based texture descriptors with regard to what information about texture
they actually encode. Whereas this analysis uses some heuristic assumptions, it
indicates that the graph-based texture descriptors are related to fractal
dimension measures that have been proven useful in texture analysis.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to referring image segmentation using a dual convolutional LSTM network. Referring image segmentation is the task of identifying and segments objects in an image based on a natural language description provided by a user. Our proposed model combines the strengths of both CNNs and LSTMs to accurately segment objects in images.

The proposed model consists of two main components: a convolutional neural network (CNN) and a long short-term memory (LSTM) network. The CNN is used to extract features from the input image, while the LSTM is used to process the natural language description and generate a segmentation mask. The CNN and LSTM are connected through a dual-stream fusion module that fuses the visual and linguistic information together. This allows the model to learn a joint representation of both modalities and improve the accuracy of object segmentation.

We evaluate our model on several benchmark datasets, including PASCAL VOC and COCO, and achieve state-of-the-art performance compared to other referring image segmentation models. We also perform ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of each component of our proposal model.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

* We propose a novel approach to referring image segmentation using a dual convolutional LSTM network that combines the strengths of both CNNs and LSTMs.
* Our model achieves state-of-the-art performance on several benchmark datasets, demonstrating its superiority over other existing approaches.
* We provide detailed analysis and experimental results to demonstrate the effectiveness of each key component of our proposed model.

We present a computer-checked generic implementation for solving
finite-horizon sequential decision problems. This is a wide class of problems,
including inter-temporal optimizations, knapsack, optimal bracketing,
scheduling, etc. The implementation can handle time-step dependent control and
state spaces, and monadic representations of uncertainty (such as stochastic,
non-deterministic, fuzzy, or combinations thereof). This level of genericity is
achievable in a programming language with dependent types (we have used both
Idris and Agda). Dependent types are also the means that allow us to obtain a
formalization and computer-checked proof of the central component of our
implementation: Bellman's principle of optimality and the associated backwards
induction algorithm. The formalization clarifies certain aspects of backwards
induction and, by making explicit notions such as viability and reachability,
can serve as a starting point for a theory of controllability of monadic
dynamical systems, commonly encountered in, e.g., climate impact research.

Numerical studies illustrate the properties of the measures.

We consider several examples of statistics that are asymptotically chi-square distributed, including the sample variance, the sample variance of a normalized sample, and the sample variance of a sample from a non-central chi-square distribution. For each of these statistics, we use Stein's method to derive bounds on the rate of convergence to the chi-square distribution. Our results provide insight into the rate at which these statistics converge to their limiting distributions, and can be used to assess the accuracy of statistical methods that rely on these statistics.

Our findings have important implications for statistical inference and hypothesis testing. In particular, we show that the sample variance and related statistics converge at a rate that is optimal in the sense that it cannot be improved by any other method. This has important implications for the design of statistical experiments and the choice of statistical tests.

Overall, our paper provides new insights into the rate of convergence of some commonly used statistics in statistical inference and hypothesis testing. Our results demonstrate the power and flexibility of Stein's method for studying the rate of convergence of asymptotically distributed statistics, and provide a valuable contribution to the field of statistical theory.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach for generating multimode maximally entangled states of photons using weak nonlinearities. Our method utilizes an entangler component that combines multiple photons in a way that creates strong entanglement between them, followed by an analyzer component that projects the output onto a particular Bell state. We demonstrate that our scheme can efficiently generate high-quality entangled states even when the nonlinearity is quite small, which makes it feasible to implement with current technology. This work paves the way for studies of quantum information processing and other applications where high-quality multimode entanglement is required.

In this paper, we propose and experimentally demonstrate a broadband and energy-concentrating terahertz coherent perfect absorber (CPA) based on a self-complementary metasurface. The designed CPAs exhibit high absorption efficiency over a wide range of frequencies, with a peak absorbance exceeding 90%, and concentrate the incident energy into a small area, leading to enhanced thermal radiation and potential applications in thermophotovoltaic devices, thermal imaging, and non-destructive testing.

The proposed CPA is based on a self-complementary metasurface, which consists of an array of asymmetric unit cells that are symmetrically arranged to form a periodic structure. By carefully designing the geometry and arrangement of the unit cells, we achieve strong resonant absorption in the THz frequency range. The self-complementarity of the metasurface enables the formation of a high-quality factor resonator, which enhances the absorption efficiency and concentration of energy.

We fabricate the CPA using standard photolithography techniques and measure its performance using Fourier transform spectroscopy and finite-difference time-domain simulations. Our experiments show good agreement with theoretical predictions, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed design.

Our work presents a significant advance in the development of broadband and high-efficiency terahertz CPAs, which have important implications for various applications. Furthermore, the demonstrated self-complementary metasurface design offers a new degree of freedom for tailoring electromagnetic waves and has the potential to be adapted for operation at other frequencies and functionalities.

factor $uvu$ (respectively, $u^Rvu$) of $w$. In such a repeat (palindrome) $u$
is called the arm of the repeat (respectively, palindrome), while $v$ is called
the gap. We show how to compute efficiently, for every position $i$ of the word
$w$, the longest gapped repeat and palindrome occurring at that position,
provided that the length of the gap is subject to various types of
restrictions. That is, that for each position $i$ we compute the longest prefix
$u$ of $w[i..n]$ such that $uv$ (respectively, $u^Rv$) is a suffix of
$w[1..i-1]$ (defining thus a gapped repeat $uvu$ -- respectively, palindrome
$u^Rvu$), and the length of $v$ is subject to the aforementioned restrictions.

Radial anisotropy, where the particle's optical properties vary with angle from its center, provides an additional degree of freedom to manipulate the scattered light. By studying the interplay between these two effects, we show that it is possible to achieve high levels of scattering efficiency and control over the scattered energy density.

We present both theoretical and experimental results demonstrating the existence of UDSS in radially anisotropic spheres. Our computational model uses the T-matrix method, while experiments are performed using custom-made spherical particles fabricated through direct laser writing. We observe that the presence of radial anisotropy significantly enhances the scattering strength and alters the character of the scattered radiation. Specifically, we find that the directionality of the scattered light can be controlled by adjusting the orientation of the anisotropy axis relative to the incident direction. Moreover, we demonstrate that by tailoring the particle size and anisotropy parameters, the scattered energy can be focused into narrow lobes or directed towards particular locations.

Our work has important implications for applications such as sensing, imaging, and communication systems that rely on controlling and manipulating electromagnetic waves at the nanoscale. The ability to engineer and optimize the scattering behavior of individual particles offers new prospects for materials design and device performance optimization. Additionally, we obtain a new understanding of the relationship between motivic integration and the intersection theory of algebraic cycles.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to medical image segmentation that leverages knowledge transfer from pre-trained deep neural networks, without requiring explicit network architecture modifications or task-specific fine-tuning. Our method, called Network-Agnostic Knowledge Transfer (NAKT), exploits the shared underlying structure present in various medical imaging modalities and applications, to transfer knowledge across different segmentation tasks. This is achieved by using a domain adaptation technique that aligns feature representations from source and target domains, allowing the sharing of knowledge between them.

We evaluate NAKT on three distinct medical image segmentation tasks: brain tumor segmentation from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), lung nodule detection from computed tomography (CT) scans, and retinal vessel segmentation from fundus images. Our results show that NAKT outperforms traditional fine-tuning methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance on all three tasks while using significantly fewer annotations. Additionally, we demonstrate the generalizability of NAKT by applying it to unseen datasets and comparing its performance to task-specific architectures.

The key contributions of this paper are:

1. The introduction of Network-Agnostic Knowledge Transfer (NAKT), a novel approach to medical image segmentation that enables knowledge transfer across different segmentation tasks and imaging modalities.
2. The development of a domain adaptation technique that aligns feature representations from source and target domains, enabling the sharing of knowledge between them.
3. An extensive evaluation of NAKT on three diverse medical image segmentation tasks, demonstrating its superiority over traditional fine-tuning methods and highlighting its potential as a versatile solution for segmentation tasks in medical imaging.
4. The demonstration of NAKT's generalizability by applying it to unseen datasets and comparing its performance to task-specific architectures.

Overall, our work has important implications for the efficient utilization of annotated data in medical image segmentation tasks, paving the way for more robust and adaptable AI models that can be applied to a wide range of medical imaging applications.

This paper presents a new approach for relatively accurate brain region of
interest (ROI) detection from dynamic susceptibility contrast (DSC) perfusion
magnetic resonance (MR) images of a human head with abnormal brain anatomy.
Such images produce problems for automatic brain segmentation algorithms, and
as a result, poor perfusion ROI detection affects both quantitative
measurements and visual assessment of perfusion data. In the proposed approach
image segmentation is based on CUSUM filter usage that was adapted to be
applicable to process DSC perfusion MR images. The result of segmentation is a
binary mask of brain ROI that is generated via usage of brain boundary
location. Each point of the boundary between the brain and surrounding tissues
is detected as a change-point by CUSUM filter. Proposed adopted CUSUM filter
operates by accumulating the deviations between the observed and expected
intensities of image points at the time of moving on a trajectory. Motion
trajectory is created by the iterative change of movement direction inside the
background region in order to reach brain region, and vice versa after boundary
crossing. Proposed segmentation approach was evaluated with Dice index
comparing obtained results to the reference standard. Manually marked brain
region pixels (reference standard), as well as visual inspection of detected
with CUSUM filter usage brain ROI, were provided by experienced radiologists.
The results showed that proposed approach is suitable to be used for brain ROI
detection from DSC perfusion MR images of a human head with abnormal brain
anatomy and can, therefore, be applied in the DSC perfusion data analysis.

Publication bias, the fact that studies identified for inclusion in a meta
analysis do not represent all studies on the topic of interest, is commonly
recognized as a threat to the validity of the results of a meta analysis. One
way to explicitly model publication bias is via selection models or weighted
probability distributions. We adopt the nonparametric approach initially
introduced by Dear (1992) but impose that the weight function $w$ is monotonely
non-increasing as a function of the $p$-value. Since in meta analysis one
typically only has few studies or "observations", regularization of the
estimation problem seems sensible. In addition, virtually all parametric weight
functions proposed so far in the literature are in fact decreasing. We discuss
how to estimate a decreasing weight function in the above model and illustrate
the new methodology on two well-known examples. The new approach potentially
offers more insight in the selection process than other methods and is more
flexible than parametric approaches. Some basic properties of the
log-likelihood function and computation of a $p$-value quantifying the evidence
against the null hypothesis of a constant weight function are indicated. In
addition, we provide an approximate selection bias adjusted profile likelihood
confidence interval for the treatment effect. The corresponding software and
the datasets used to illustrate it are provided as the R package selectMeta.
This enables full reproducibility of the results in this paper.

A unified formulation that obtains solitary waves for various background
densities in the Bose-Einstein condensate of a system of hard-core bosons with
nearest neighbor attractive interactions is presented.
  In general, two species of solitons appear: A nonpersistent (NP) type that
fully delocalizes at its maximum speed, and a persistent (P) type that survives
even at its maximum speed, and transforms into a periodic train of solitons
above this speed. When the background condensate density is nonzero, both
species coexist, the soliton is associated with a constant intrinsic frequency,
and its maximum speed is the speed of sound. In contrast, when the background
condensate density is zero, the system has neither a fixed frequency, nor a
speed of sound. Here, the maximum soliton speed depends on the frequency, which
can be tuned to lead to a cross-over between the NP-type and the P-type at a
certain critical frequency, determined by the energy parameters of the system.
We provide a single functional form for the soliton profile, from which diverse
characteristics for various background densities can be obtained. Using the
mapping to spin systems enables us to characterize the corresponding class of
magnetic solitons in

fashion.

A multi-scale greedy-based object proposal generation approach is presented.
Based on the multi-scale nature of objects in images, our approach is built on
top of a hierarchical segmentation. We first identify the representative and
diverse exemplar clusters within each scale by using a diversity ranking
algorithm. Object proposals are obtained by selecting a subset from the
multi-scale segment pool via maximizing a submodular objective function, which
consists of a weighted coverage term, a single-scale diversity term and a
multi-scale reward term. The weighted coverage term forces the selected set of
object proposals to be representative and compact; the single-scale diversity
term encourages choosing segments from different exemplar clusters so that they
will cover as many object patterns as possible; the multi-scale reward term
encourages the selected proposals to be discriminative and selected from
multiple layers generated by the hierarchical image segmentation. The
experimental results on the Berkeley Segmentation Dataset and PASCAL VOC2012
segmentation dataset demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of our object
proposal model. Additionally, we validate our object proposals in simultaneous
segmentation and detection and outperform the state-of-art performance.

Traditional image registration methods rely on hand-crafted features and optimization techniques, which can be time-consuming and limited in their ability to handle complex deformations. In this paper, we propose a deep learning-based approach called NeurReg, which leverages neural networks to learn a mapping between images and their corresponding transformations.

NeurReg consists of two main components: a registration network and a segmentation network. The registration network takes two images as input and outputs a transformation matrix that aligns the images. The segmentation network takes the aligned images as input and outputs a segmentation mask that separates the objects of interest from the background. We train NeurReg using a large dataset of images with manual segmentation masks, and evaluate its performance on several benchmark datasets.

Our experiments show that NeurReg outperforms traditional image registration methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency. It also demonstrates superior performance in handling complex deformations and occlusions, which are challenging for traditional methods. Additionally, NeurReg can be used for a variety of applications, including image-guided surgery, object tracking, and 3D reconstruction.

We also perform a series of ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of different components of NeurReg. The results show that the use of a segmentation network and the integration of multi-scale features are crucial for its performance. Furthermore, we demonstrate the generalization ability of NeurReg by applying it to unseen data, including images with different modalities and resolutions.

In conclusion, NeurReg presents a novel deep learning-based approach to image registration and segmentation, which has the potential to significantly improve the accuracy and efficiency of image registration tasks in various applications.

Title: Octahedral Conversion of a-SiO2-Host Matrix by Pulsed Ion Implantation

Abstract:
In this study, we investigate the octahedral conversion of amorphous silica (a-SiO2) host matrices through pulsed ion implantation. By using a combination of high-dose ion implantation and rapid thermal annealing, we demonstrate the ability to convert the amorphous structure into a crystalline octahedral phase. X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy were used to characterize the structural evolution of the samples during the process. Our results show that the as-implanted samples exhibit a significant increase in crystallinity with increasing ion dose, followed by the formation of well-defined octahedral crystal structures upon annealing. The observed transformations are attributed to the creation of point defects and their subsequent aggregation under the influence of ionic species and thermal energy. These findings have important implications for the development of advanced materials and devices based on silicon oxide, and highlight the potential of pulsed ion implantation as a versatile tool for tailoring material properties at the nanoscale.

Deep learning-based segmentation methods are vulnerable to unforeseen data
distribution shifts during deployment, e.g. change of image appearances or
contrasts caused by different scanners, unexpected imaging artifacts etc. In
this paper, we present a cooperative framework for training image segmentation
models and a latent space augmentation method for generating hard examples.
Both contributions improve model generalization and robustness with limited
data. The cooperative training framework consists of a fast-thinking network
(FTN) and a slow-thinking network (STN). The FTN learns decoupled image
features and shape features for image reconstruction and segmentation tasks.
The STN learns shape priors for segmentation correction and refinement. The two
networks are trained in a cooperative manner. The latent space augmentation
generates challenging examples for training by masking the decoupled latent
space in both channel-wise and spatial-wise manners. We performed extensive
experiments on public cardiac imaging datasets. Using only 10 subjects from a
single site for training, we demonstrated improved cross-site segmentation
performance and increased robustness against various unforeseen imaging
artifacts compared to strong baseline methods. Particularly, cooperative
training with latent space data augmentation yields 15% improvement in terms of
average Dice score when compared to a standard training method.

The technique allows to compress 3D data into 4d space with low computational cost compared to traditional methods. Further, by using nonlinear superposition in which multiple small scale samples can be processed simultaneously, no memory bandwidth usage is introduced and noise is eliminated by creating multiple pseudo-3D maps where each corresponds to an independent sample on one axis. Transformers have shown impressive performance in various natural language
processing and computer vision tasks, due to the capability of modeling
long-range dependencies. Recent progress has demonstrated to combine such
transformers with CNN-based semantic image segmentation models is very
promising. However, it is not well studied yet on how well a pure transformer
based approach can achieve for image segmentation. In this work, we explore a
novel framework for semantic image segmentation, which is encoder-decoder based
Fully Transformer Networks (FTN). Specifically, we first propose a Pyramid
Group Transformer (PGT) as the encoder for progressively learning hierarchical
features, while reducing the computation complexity of the standard visual
transformer(ViT). Then, we propose a Feature Pyramid Transformer (FPT) to fuse
semantic-level and spatial-level information from multiple levels of the PGT
encoder for semantic image segmentation. Surprisingly, this simple baseline can
achieve new state-of-the-art results on multiple challenging semantic
segmentation benchmarks, including PASCAL Context, ADE20K and COCO-Stuff. The
source code will be released upon the publication of this work.

This paper presents an analysis of Fisher information and the Cramér-Rao bound for nonlinear parameter estimation after compressed sensing. The study focuses on the performance of compressed sensing in estimating nonlinear parameters from incomplete and noisy data. The Fisher information matrix is used to quantify the information content of the data, and the Cramér-Rao bound is derived to establish the lower limit on the variance of the estimated parameters. The results show that compressed sensing can significantly improve the accuracy of nonlinear parameter estimation, and the performance depends on the signal-to-noise ratio, the sparsity level, and the nonlinearity of the model. The paper provides insights into the design of efficient compressed sensing algorithms for nonlinear parameter estimation in various applications.

In this paper, we present our pure-algebraic approach of implementing generalizations of the the first two generalizations of the generalized Jacobian conjecture. An example of such an application has been found in connection with nonabelian fields that exhibit very high dimensionality for the number of nodes, including a 2D geometry based on the Hölder space [1]. By extending our approach to nonabelian manifolds as well as to other domains of natural mathematics, and taking advantage of both local geometric structure as well as the generalized Jacobi theorem, we are able to produce extremely different proofs of many types of conjectures associated with 3-manifold structures (for instance, by way of a new type of groupoid) using classical proof techniques. This is the only theory whose purely algebraic formulation allows one to derive much more than merely weak conjectures. In some cases, it may even lead to proofs which are stronger or equal to those obtained with standard algebraic formulations (that is, through the "extended K-theory"). Thereby, the resulting system of equations gives rise to unique, nontrivial, nontransitive proofs, providing a great opportunity for proving conjectures relevant at the scale of particle physics. We also show how this novel idea is capable of producing solutions for all known problems in high dimensions where there are unknown lattices. Image segmentation is a fundamental task in computer vision that involves dividing an image into its constituent parts or objects. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to image segmentation based on iterative inference from conditional score estimation. Our method leverages the strengths of probabilistic graphical models and Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) inference to produce accurate and efficient segmentations.

We begin by modeling the image as a random field, where each pixel is associated with a set of labels representing the possible classes it could belong to. We then define a conditional score function that captures the relationships between neighboring pixels and their labels. The score function is designed to encourage spatial coherence and consistency with the image data.

To perform segmentation, we use an iterative inference algorithm that alternates between estimating the conditional scores and updating the label assignments of the pixels. At each iteration, we compute the conditional scores for all pixels given their current label assignments and the scores of their neighbors. We then update the label assignments of the pixels based on the scores, repeating the process until convergence.

We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets and compare it to state-of-the-art segmentation algorithms. Our results show that our method produces high-quality segmentations that are competitive with the best performing methods in the literature. Additionally, we demonstrate the versatility of our approach by applying it to a variety of tasks, including image denoising and object recognition.

Our main contribution is the introduction of a novel iterative inference algorithm for image segmentation based on conditional score estimation. Our method is efficient, scalable, and can handle complex images with varying sizes and structures. We also provide a thorough analysis of the algorithm's convergence properties and computational complexity, making it a valuable contribution to the field of computer vision.

The Margulis cusp is a fascinating feature of hyperbolic 3-manifolds, which has been extensively studied in recent years. However, its counterpart in higher dimensions, specifically in hyperbolic 4-manifolds, remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we investigate Margulis cusps of hyperbolic 4-manifolds and their properties.

Firstly, we establish the existence of Margulis cusps in compact, orientable, hyperbolic 4-manifolds with finite volume, building on previous work by Hodgson and Kerckhoff. We demonstrate that these cusps are necessarily discrete and have a rich geometric structure, including a natural orientation and a well-defined notion of horospheres.

Next, we focus on the behavior of Margulis cusps under covering maps between hyperbolic 4-manifolds. Using a combination of geometric and topological techniques, we show that Margulis cusps are stable under such maps, meaning that they persist even when the rest of the manifold may change dramatically under the covering map. This result has significant implications for our understanding of the topology and geometry of hyperbolic 4-manifolds, and provides a new lens through which to view known results about their structure.

Finally, we explore the relationship between Margulis cusps and other important concepts in manifold theory, such as geometrization and h-cobordism. This deep connection further solidifies the relevance of Margulis cusps to broad areas of mathematics and geometry.
