In this paper, we propose a novel framework called HCDG (Hierarchical Consistency Framework for Domain Generalization) to address the problem of domain shift in medical image segmentation. Our approach leverages a hierarchical structure of consistency regularizations to improve the generalization ability of deep learning models across different domains.

Existing methods for domain adaptation mainly focus on aligning feature distributions between source and target domains, but they often overlook the hierarchical relationships between features at multiple scales. HCDG fills this gap by introducing a hierarchy of consistency terms that enforce the model to produce consistent predictions from top-level labels down to low-level features. This hierarchical regularization framework enables the model to learn more robust and transferable representations across diverse domains.

We evaluate HCDG on several challenging medical image segmentation tasks, including brain tumor segmentation, retinal fundus disease detection, and lung nodule segmentation. The results demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art domain adaptation approaches, achieving superior performance on unseen target data. Additionally, we conduct comprehensive ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of each component in HCDG, providing insights into the working mechanisms of our framework.

The main contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows:

* We introduce HCDG, a hierarchical consistency framework for domain generalization on medical image segmentation, which enforces multi-scale consistency regularizations to improve the generalization ability of deep learning models.
* Our approach is evaluated on various medical image segmentation tasks and shows better performance than existing domain adaptation methods.
* Ablation studies provide insightful findings on the contribution of each component in HCDG, shedding light on the design of future domain adaptation frameworks.

Overall, HCDG presents a promising solution for improving the generalization ability of deep learning models in medical image analysis, paving the way towards more reliable and robust AI systems for healthcare applications.

In this paper, we present a formal study of the behavioral complexity of the π-calculus, a theoretical framework for concurrency. We prove that the π-calculus is both behaviorially complete and orbit-finitely executable.

Behavioral completeness refers to the ability of a system to simulate any possible sequence of interactions between processes, while preserving the observable behavior of the system. In other words, it means that any process can be written in terms of the basic constructions of the language, up to bisimulation equivalence.

Orbit-finite executability, on the other hand, requires that every process in the language can be executed by a finite number of steps, where each step consists of a single action or synchronization event. This property ensures that processes in the π-calculus are locally computable and do not involve infinite sequences of actions.

Our results demonstrate that the π-calculus provides an expressive and well-behaved foundation for modeling concurrent systems. The π-calculus has been widely used in practice, but these results provide the first rigorous justification of its behavioral properties. They also establish a new connection between the theory of concurrent programming and the theory of programming languages, deepening our understanding of the fundamental principles underlying computation.

In conclusion, while deep learning techniques have undoubtedly revolutionized image segmentation, it is crucial to recognize both their merits and drawbacks. Volumetric image segmentation with convolutional neural networks (CNNs)
encounters several challenges, which are specific to medical images. Among
these challenges are large volumes of interest, high class imbalances, and
difficulties in learning shape representations. To tackle these challenges, we
propose to improve over traditional CNN-based volumetric image segmentation
through point-wise classification of point clouds. The sparsity of point clouds
allows processing of entire image volumes, balancing highly imbalanced
segmentation problems, and explicitly learning an anatomical shape. We build
upon PointCNN, a neural network proposed to process point clouds, and propose
here to jointly encode shape and volumetric information within the point cloud
in a compact and computationally effective manner. We demonstrate how this
approach can then be used to refine CNN-based segmentation, which yields
significantly improved results in our experiments on the difficult task of
peripheral nerve segmentation from magnetic resonance neurography images. By
synthetic experiments, we further show the capability of our approach in
learning an explicit anatomical shape representation.

For the task of medical image segmentation, fully convolutional network (FCN)
based architectures have been extensively used with various modifications. A
rising trend in these architectures is to employ joint-learning of the target
region with an auxiliary task, a method commonly known as multi-task learning.
These approaches help impose smoothness and shape priors, which vanilla FCN
approaches do not necessarily incorporate. In this paper, we propose a novel
plug-and-play module, which we term as Conv-MCD, which exploits structural
information in two ways - i) using the contour map and ii) using the distance
map, both of which can be obtained from ground truth segmentation maps with no
additional annotation costs. The key benefit of our module is the ease of its
addition to any state-of-the-art architecture, resulting in a significant
improvement in performance with a minimal increase in parameters. To
substantiate the above claim, we conduct extensive experiments using 4
state-of-the-art architectures across various evaluation metrics, and report a
significant increase in performance in relation to the base networks. In
addition to the aforementioned experiments, we also perform ablative studies
and visualization of feature maps to further elucidate our approach.

We define a class of groups equipped with an invariant probability measure,
which includes all compact groups and is closed under taking ultraproducts with
the induced Loeb measure; in fact, this class also contains the ultraproducts
all locally compact unimodular amenable groups. We call the members of this
class probability groups and develop the basics of the theory of their
measure-preserving actions on probability spaces, including a natural notion of
mixing. A short proof reveals that for probability groups mixing implies double
recurrence, which generalizes a theorem of Bergelson and Tao proved for
ultraproducts of finite groups. Moreover, a quantitative version of our proof
gives that $\varepsilon$-approximate mixing implies
$3\sqrt{\varepsilon}$-approximate double recurrence. Examples of approximately
mixing probability groups are quasirandom groups introduced by Gowers, so the
last theorem generalizes and sharpens the corresponding results for quasirandom
groups of Bergelson and Tao, as well as of Austin. Lastly, we point out that
the fact that the ultraproduct of locally compact unimodular amenable groups is
a probability group provides a general alternative to Furstenberg
correspondence principle.

Charlier polynomials to Hermite polynomials. This transition, which is still
presented in its classical form in modern reference works, is valid if and only
if a certain parameter is integer. In this light, it is surprising that a much
more powerful transition exists from Charlier polynomials to the Hermite
function, valid for any real value of the parameter. This greatly strengthens
the asymptotic connections between Charlier polynomials and special functions,
with applications for instance in queueing theory.
  It is shown in this paper that the convergence is uniform in bounded
intervals, and a sharp rate bound is proved. It is also shown that there is a
transition of derivatives of Charlier polynomials to the derivative of the
Hermite function, again with a sharp rate bound. Finally, it is proved that
zeros of Charlier polynomials converge to zeros of the Hermite function. While
rigorous, the proofs use only elementary techniques.

The anomalously robust valley polarization and valley coherence in bilayer WS2 make it an attractive material for valleytronics applications, as it could provide improved performance and stability compared to other materials. This is achieved by introducing an additional inference network that learns to predict the neural factors, which are the inputs to the SVM, from the input features. The inference network is trained simultaneously with the SVM, and the two networks are regularized using a shared penalty term that encourages the inference network to produce accurate predictions of the neural factors.

A path in an edge-colored graph $G$ is rainbow if no two edges of it are
colored the same. The graph $G$ is rainbow-connected if there is a rainbow path
between every pair of vertices. If there is a rainbow shortest path between
every pair of vertices, the graph $G$ is strongly rainbow-connected. The
minimum number of colors needed to make $G$ rainbow-connected is known as the
rainbow connection number of $G$, and is denoted by $\text{rc}(G)$. Similarly,
the minimum number of colors needed to make $G$ strongly rainbow-connected is
known as the strong rainbow connection number of $G$, and is denoted by
$\text{src}(G)$. We prove that for every $k \geq 3$, deciding whether
$\text{src}(G) \leq k$ is NP-complete for split graphs, which form a subclass
of chordal graphs. Furthermore, there exists no polynomial-time algorithm for
approximating the strong rainbow connection number of an $n$-vertex split graph
with a factor of $n^{1/2-\epsilon}$ for any $\epsilon > 0$ unless P = NP. We
then turn our attention to block graphs, which also form a subclass of chordal
graphs. We determine the strong rainbow connection number of block graphs, and
show it can be computed in linear time. Finally, we provide a polynomial-time
characterization of bridgeless block graphs with rainbow connection number at
most 4.

We demonstrate that a 2-generator free Kleinian group is purely loxodromic if and only if it satisfies Jorgensen's inequality, which states that the product of the coefficients of the generators' axes must be less than or equal to 1.

We first show that if a 2-generator free Kleinian group is purely loxodromic, then it must satisfy Jorgensen's inequality. This is done by considering the action of the group on hyperbolic space and using the fact that the set of points in hyperbolic space with arbitrarily small neighborhoods has measure zero.

The converse direction is also proved by showing that if a 2-generator free Kleinian group satisfies Jorgensen's inequality, then it must be purely loxodromic. To do this, we exhibit an algorithm that computes a bound for the size of the systoles of the group's limit set that decreases exponentially fast as the number of iterations increases. From this, we deduce that the group cannot have any parabolic elements and must therefore be purely loxodromic.

As corollaries of our main result, we obtain a characterization of purely loxodromic 2-generator free Kleinian groups and show that every such group contains at least one axis of translation. Additionally, we prove that there exists a finite boundary crossed punctured sphere surface bundle over the Cantor set whose fundamental group is a purely loxodromic 2-generator free Kleinian group satisfying Jorgensen's inequality. We use these results to solve problems related to automatic groups and provide examples of non-elementary Gromov-hyperbolic groups that are not lattice-ordered. Overall, our work deepens the understanding of the connection between Jorgensen's inequality and pure loxodromicy in free group theory and provides new insights into the structure and properties of 2-generator free Kleinian groups.

Abstract Non-automated image segmentation for facial reference identification is extremely challenging even with large data sets, especially when there are multiple eyes and/or nose pointing to a given face in an array representation. In this work we present such a scalable automatic system for automated multi-modality image segmentations based both on the similarity between two images taken at high resolution and their relative orientation similarity at all pixel resolutions (e.g., depth). The resulting classification results are compared at various reference types for human or robot recognition tasks: facial, occlusion and hair matching. Compared to previous state-of-the-art approaches, our approach uses more sparse feature representations from higher resolutions while maintaining good performance for different training images at the same spatial resolution (i.e., ~400×500). Our algorithm has excellent localization accuracy with very low error rate under similar test conditions using a variety of object attributes including depth, face shape parameters, orientation and texture data. We demonstrate our method's robustness by applying it to five widely used object data formats that make up a wide range of real world applications, yielding successful model learning for facial match, occlusion detection and partial occlusion classifying as well as hair type matches. Furthermore, the overall improvement over previously published methods on several categories is considerable. Overall, these results suggest that our methodology is effective enough during general task requirements and that it could be further developed through tuning its framework for faster iteration times. Additionally, our method may also have application in robotics where human-robot interactions involve pose sensing since many activities might require accurate recognition of the subject's facial appearance. In conclusion, we apply our comprehensive multi-modality inference technique for image segmentation towards building robust automatic reference object segmentation systems using a diverse set of diverse domain attires and thereby improve the quality of personal assistant application input features. This condition has been found empirically on a variety of datasets including real-world medical image segmentations, but also on relatively simple object labels presented on many different images. On these tasks it can often take longer than usual time to infer whether a given image belongs to our training datasets or not thanks to random data biases introduced by classifiers or by human interpretations made while judging the label of an image. In this context, this problem appears as one where there may be unanticipated information at the first sample, especially after introducing several new features into a neural net during training that are completely uncorrelated with each other, thus potentially adding noise to their resulting estimates (i.e., a model averaging). The basic idea with one single objective follows naturally from previous work related to SG: we generate training examples consisting entirely of 0's and 1's and then train a classifier which will assign an example belonging to a specific subset based on its current weights.

In this paper, we investigate the relationship between Jorgensen's inequality and purely loxodromic 2-generator free Kleinian groups. We show that any purely loxodromic 2-generator free Kleinian group satisfies Jorgensen's inequality, and conversely, any group that satisfies Jorgensen's inequality is virtually a purely loxodromic 2-generator free Kleinian group. We also provide examples of groups that satisfy Jorgensen's inequality but are not purely loxodromic 2-generator free Kleinian, demonstrating that the two conditions are not equivalent. Our results provide new insights into the structure and properties of Kleinian groups and have implications for the study of geometric and topological problems in group theory.

Deep learning methods have achieved promising performance in many areas, but
they are still struggling with noisy-labeled images during the training
process. Considering that the annotation quality indispensably relies on great
expertise, the problem is even more crucial in the medical image domain. How to
eliminate the disturbance from noisy labels for segmentation tasks without
further annotations is still a significant challenge. In this paper, we
introduce our label quality evaluation strategy for deep neural networks
automatically assessing the quality of each label, which is not explicitly
provided, and training on clean-annotated ones. We propose a solution for
network automatically evaluating the relative quality of the labels in the
training set and using good ones to tune the network parameters. We also design
an overfitting control module to let the network maximally learn from the
precise annotations during the training process. Experiments on the public
biomedical image segmentation dataset have proved the method outperforms
baseline methods and retains both high accuracy and good generalization at
different noise levels.

This paper presents a Spatially Adaptive Stochastic Multigrid Method for solving Fluid-Structure Systems with Thermal Fluctuations. The paper concludes by discussing potential applications of the method in engineering and scientific simulations involving fluid-structure interactions with thermal fluctuations.

We prove a number of results related to a problem of Po-Shen Loh, which is
equivalent to a problem in Ramsey theory. Let $a=(a_1,a_2,a_3)$ and
$b=(b_1,b_2,b_3)$ be two triples of integers. Define $a$ to be 2-less than $b$
if $a_i<b_i$ for at least two values of $i$, and define a sequence
$a^1,\dots,a^m$ of triples to be 2-increasing if $a^r$ is 2-less than $a^s$
whenever $r<s$. Loh asks how long a 2-increasing sequence can be if all the
triples take values in $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$, and gives a $\log_*$ improvement over
the trivial upper bound of $n^2$ by using the triangle removal lemma. In the
other direction, a simple construction gives a lower bound of $n^{3/2}$. We
look at this problem and a collection of generalizations, improving some of the
known bounds, pointing out connections to other well known problems in extremal
combinatorics, and asking a number of further questions.

In this paper, an stereo-based traversability analysis approach for all
terrains in off-road mobile robotics, e.g. Unmanned Ground Vehicles (UGVs) is
proposed. This approach reformulates the problem of terrain traversability
analysis into two main problems: (1) 3D terrain reconstruction and (2) terrain
all surfaces detection and analysis. The proposed approach is using stereo
camera for perception and 3D reconstruction of the terrain. In order to detect
all the existing surfaces in the 3D reconstructed terrain as superpixel
surfaces (i.e. segments), an image segmentation technique is applied using
geometry-based features (pixel-based surface normals). Having detected all the
surfaces, Superpixel Surface Traversability Analysis approach (SSTA) is applied
on all of the detected surfaces (superpixel segments) in order to classify them
based on their traversability index. The proposed SSTA approach is based on:
(1) Superpixel surface normal and plane estimation, (2) Traversability analysis
using superpixel surface planes. Having analyzed all the superpixel surfaces
based on their traversability, these surfaces are finally classified into five
main categories as following: traversable, semi-traversable, non-traversable,
unknown and undecided.

This academic paper explores the concept of the Quantum Zeno Effect, which states that frequent measurements of a quantum system can effectively "freeze" its evolution. The paper examines the similarities between this effect and the literary character of Hamlet, who is often described as being stuck in a state of indecision. The paper also discusses the implications of these effects on the field of quantum mechanics and the potential for future research.

Preparation of high-quality datasets for the urban scene understanding is a
labor-intensive task, especially, for datasets designed for the autonomous
driving applications. The application of the coarse ground truth (GT)
annotations of these datasets without detriment to the accuracy of semantic
image segmentation (by the mean intersection over union - mIoU) could simplify
and speedup the dataset preparation and model fine tuning before its practical
application. Here the results of the comparative analysis for semantic
segmentation accuracy obtained by PSPNet deep learning architecture are
presented for fine and coarse annotated images from Cityscapes dataset. Two
scenarios were investigated: scenario 1 - the fine GT images for training and
prediction, and scenario 2 - the fine GT images for training and the coarse GT
images for prediction. The obtained results demonstrated that for the most
important classes the mean accuracy values of semantic image segmentation for
coarse GT annotations are higher than for the fine GT ones, and the standard
deviation values are vice versa. It means that for some applications some
unimportant classes can be excluded and the model can be tuned further for some
classes and specific regions on the coarse GT dataset without loss of the
accuracy even. Moreover, this opens the perspectives to use deep neural
networks for the preparation of such coarse GT datasets.

This paper presents a novel approach to forward and backward propagation in convolutional neural networks (CNNs) used for pixel-level classification. The proposed method significantly improves efficiency by optimizing mathematical operations, resulting in faster processing times without sacrificing accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate that our technique outperforms existing methods while reducing computational complexity, making it an invaluable tool for researchers and practitioners working with CNNs in computer vision applications.

This academic paper proposes a novel approach to semantic segmentation using a highly fused convolutional network with multiple soft cost functions. The proposed method combines the advantages of multiple cost functions to improve the accuracy and robustness of semantic segmentation. The highly fused convolutional network is designed to effectively fuse multi-scale features and capture contextual information. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art methods on several benchmark datasets, confirming its effectiveness and potential for practical applications.

This academic paper examines the current state of deep learning for image segmentation, exploring whether it is a viable and reliable technology or if it has been overhyped. Through a comprehensive analysis of recent research and applications, the paper provides insights into the strengths and limitations of deep learning in image segmentation, ultimately offering a nuanced perspective on the potential of this powerful machine learning technique.

Contrastive Learning (CL) is a recent representation learning approach, which
encourages inter-class separability and intra-class compactness in learned
image representations. Since medical images often contain multiple semantic
classes in an image, using CL to learn representations of local features (as
opposed to global) is important. In this work, we present a novel
semi-supervised 2D medical segmentation solution that applies CL on image
patches, instead of full images. These patches are meaningfully constructed
using the semantic information of different classes obtained via pseudo
labeling. We also propose a novel consistency regularization (CR) scheme, which
works in synergy with CL. It addresses the problem of confirmation bias, and
encourages better clustering in the feature space. We evaluate our method on
four public medical segmentation datasets and a novel histopathology dataset
that we introduce. Our method obtains consistent improvements over
state-of-the-art semi-supervised segmentation approaches for all datasets.

An important statistical task in disease mapping problems is to identify
divergent regions with unusually high or low risk of disease. Leave-one-out
cross-validatory (LOOCV) model assessment is the gold standard for estimating
predictive p-values that can flag such divergent regions. However, actual LOOCV
is time-consuming because one needs to rerun a Markov chain Monte Carlo
analysis for each posterior distribution in which an observation is held out as
a test case. This paper introduces a new method, called integrated importance
sampling (iIS), for estimating LOOCV predictive p-values with only Markov chain
samples drawn from the posterior based on a full data set. The key step in iIS
is that we integrate away the latent variables associated the test observation
with respect to their conditional distribution \textit{without} reference to
the actual observation. By following the general theory for importance
sampling, the formula used by iIS can be proved to be equivalent to the LOOCV
predictive p-value. We compare iIS and other three existing methods in the
literature with two disease mapping datasets. Our empirical results show that
the predictive p-values estimated with iIS are almost identical to the
predictive p-values estimated with actual LOOCV, and outperform those given by
the existing three methods, namely, the posterior predictive checking, the
ordinary importance sampling, and the ghosting method by Marshall and
Spiegelhalter (2003).

Detection faults in seismic data is a crucial step for seismic structural
interpretation, reservoir characterization and well placement. Some recent
works regard it as an image segmentation task. The task of image segmentation
requires huge labels, especially 3D seismic data, which has a complex structure
and lots of noise. Therefore, its annotation requires expert experience and a
huge workload. In this study, we present lambda-BCE and lambda-smooth L1loss to
effectively train 3D-CNN by some slices from 3D seismic data, so that the model
can learn the segmentation of 3D seismic data from a few 2D slices. In order to
fully extract information from limited data and suppress seismic noise, we
propose an attention module that can be used for active supervision training
and embedded in the network. The attention heatmap label is generated by the
original label, and letting it supervise the attention module using the
lambda-smooth L1loss. The experiment demonstrates the effectiveness of our loss
function, the method can extract 3D seismic features from a few 2D slice
labels. And it also shows the advanced performance of the attention module,
which can significantly suppress the noise in the seismic data while increasing
the model's sensitivity to the foreground. Finally, on the public test set, we
only use the 2D slice labels training that accounts for 3.3% of the 3D volume
label, and achieve similar performance to the 3D volume label training.

This paper presents an improved MUSIC (MUltiple SIgnal Classification) Direction of Arrival (DoA) estimator and evaluates its performance through simulations and experimental results. The proposed estimator enhances the conventional MUSIC algorithm by incorporating a novel spatial smoothing technique and an improved parameter selection method. The smoothing technique utilizes a Gaussian filter to mitigate the effects of noise and multipath, resulting in improved resolution and accuracy. The parameter selection method optimizes the choice of parameters based on the characteristics of the received signals, leading to improved robustness and adaptability.

The performance of the proposed estimator is evaluated using simulations and experiments conducted in a controlled environment. The results show that the improved MUSIC DoA estimator outperforms conventional MUSIC and other state-of-the-art DoA estimation techniques in terms of accuracy, resolution, and robustness. Specifically, the proposed estimator achieves a higher accuracy and resolution in the presence of noise and multipath, and demonstrates improved robustness against various types of interference.

The paper also provides a comprehensive analysis of the effects of various parameters on the performance of the proposed estimator, including the filter bandwidth, smoothing parameter, and number of snapshots. The results of this analysis provide valuable insights into the optimal choice of parameters for the proposed estimator and can be used to guide the design of practical DoA estimation systems.

Overall, the paper demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed improved MUSIC DoA estimator and its potential for use in a variety of applications, including radar, sonar, and wireless communication systems. The results provide a valuable contribution to the field of DoA estimation and highlight the importance of incorporating advanced signal processing techniques to improve the accuracy and robustness of DoA estimation systems.

This paper proposes a novel method for region-based image segmentation and inpainting that incorporates curvature penalization into a linear framework. The proposed method seeks to overcome the limitations of traditional boundary-following algorithms by using a regions-growing approach that is guided by the minimization of a energy functional. This energy functional includes terms that promote smoothness of the segmentation boundaries, enforceregion consistency, and impose constraints on the Curvature of the boundaries.
The proposed method is tested on several images with varying levels of complexity, noise, and missing data, and the results demonstrate its superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. Specifically , the authors show that their method produces more accurate segmentations and inpaintings, while also reducing computational time and memory usage . Furthermore, they provide theoretical analysis guaranteeing the existence and uniqueness of the solution to the proposed optimization problem. Contributions to the field include introduction of new iterative scheme that combines gradient descent wit hahomotopy--type convergence guarantees, as well as  novel way of incorporating curvature informationintoth segmenation process.. 
Overall, this work has important implications for medical imaging applications where both accuracy and efficiency are crucial, such as tumor detection and treatment planning.

Nominal Logic is a version of first-order logic with equality, name-binding,
renaming via name-swapping and freshness of names. Contrarily to higher-order
logic, bindable names, called atoms, and instantiable variables are considered
as distinct entities. Moreover, atoms are capturable by instantiations,
breaking a fundamental principle of lambda-calculus. Despite these differences,
nominal unification can be seen from a higher-order perspective. From this
view, we show that nominal unification can be reduced to a particular fragment
of higher-order unification problems: Higher-Order Pattern Unification. This
reduction proves that nominal unification can be decided in quadratic
deterministic time, using the linear algorithm for Higher-Order Pattern
Unification. We also prove that the translation preserves most generality of
unifiers.

Cooperating cellular networks are characterized by high levels of competition among small and large cells using downstream signaling channels, causing both to exhibit differential signaling efficiencies as well as different behaviors towards neighboring cells with similar characteristics. We show that coexistence will not be an invariant property. Our theory shows that cooperative balancing can take place even between cells based on identical functional properties such as rate-of-fire, firing rate variability, temporal dynamics and information transmission efficiency. The resulting equilibrium between two systems which do not compete or cooperate will evolve faster than was expected until now. We use this principle to study how cooperation between cells within a network evolves under imperfect sampling conditions which leads to the formation of stable networks where neighboring cells are allowed to evolve their behavior toward each other but never directly at a defectively selected state. Our results suggest some interesting new mathematical frameworks for studying these kinds of processes in living biological systems. For example, our method provides a simple description to explain the observation of cooperatively balanced states arising in nature at the fundamental limit of selection under the assumption of non-zero additive fitness.

We propose a novel approach for selecting the best jammer from a set of potential jammers, with the goal of maximizing the secrecy degree of freedom (DoF) and minimizing the number of jammers required. Our approach is based on a combination of random jamming and network coding, and we demonstrate its effectiveness through theoretical analysis and simulations.

Our results show that the proposed approach achieves a higher secrecy DoF than existing methods, and that the number of jammers required scales logarithmically with the number of users. We also show that the proposed approach is robust to various types of attacks, including jamming and eavesdropping.

The main contributions of this paper are:

* A novel approach for opportunistic jammer selection for secrecy communications
* A theoretical analysis of the secrecy DoF and jammer scaling law for the proposed approach

Finally, we conclude the paper in Section VI with a discussion of the results and future work.

We present and analyze a pollution-free Petrov-Galerkin multiscale finite
element method for the Helmholtz problem with large wave number $\kappa$ as a
variant of [Peterseim, ArXiv:1411.1944, 2014]. We use standard continuous $Q_1$
finite elements at a coarse discretization scale $H$ as trial functions,
whereas the test functions are computed as the solutions of local problems at a
finer scale $h$. The diameter of the support of the test functions behaves like
$mH$ for some oversampling parameter $m$. Provided $m$ is of the order of
$\log(\kappa)$ and $h$ is sufficiently small, the resulting method is stable
and quasi-optimal in the regime where $H$ is proportional to $\kappa^{-1}$. In
homogeneous (or more general periodic) media, the fine scale test functions
depend only on local mesh-configurations. Therefore, the seemingly high cost
for the computation of the test functions can be drastically reduced on
structured meshes. We present numerical experiments in two and three space
dimensions.

Articular cartilage lesions are a common occurrence in orthopedic diseases such as osteoarthritis, and their formation is influenced by both cellular and mechanical processes. However, the interplay between these processes remains poorly understood, and there lacks a comprehensive model that can capture their interactions. This study aimed to develop a mathematical model that links cellular and mechanical processes in articular cartilage lesion formation, providing new insights into the mechanisms of disease progression.

The proposed model integrates elements from cellular biology, tissue mechanics, and numerical analysis to simulate the dynamics of articular cartilage degeneration. It considers the effects of various factors, including cells' metabolic activities, membrane transport, and mechanical forces, on the evolution of cartilage lesions. The model was validated using experimental data obtained from an in vitro scratch assay and compared with clinical data from patients with osteoarthritis.

Our results demonstrate that the integrated model accurately predicts the temporal and spatial patterns of cartilage degradation, which are consistent with experimental and clinical observations. We found that cellular processes, such as proteoglycan synthesis and matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) expression, play a crucial role in initiating and propagating lesions. Moreover, mechanical factors, such as compressive loading and fluid flow, significantly influence lesion growth and shape.

Our findings have important implications for understanding the pathophysiology of articular cartilage lesions and may help identify potential therapeutic targets. By simulating the interplay between cellular and mechanical processes, this computational approach enables the optimization of treatment strategies through virtual testing of different scenarios. Ultimately, this study contributes to a better comprehension of the complex mechanisms underlying articular cartilage lesion formation and paves the way for personalized medicine approaches in joint healthcare.

Overall, this paper provides a detailed description of the point-centered quarter method and demonstrates its effectiveness in quantitative analysis. The method has the potential to be a valuable tool for researchers and practitioners in a wide range of fields.

Although deep models have greatly improved the accuracy and robustness of
image segmentation, obtaining segmentation results with highly accurate
boundaries and fine structures is still a challenging problem. In this paper,
we propose a simple yet powerful Boundary-Aware Segmentation Network (BASNet),
which comprises a predict-refine architecture and a hybrid loss, for highly
accurate image segmentation. The predict-refine architecture consists of a
densely supervised encoder-decoder network and a residual refinement module,
which are respectively used to predict and refine a segmentation probability
map. The hybrid loss is a combination of the binary cross entropy, structural
similarity and intersection-over-union losses, which guide the network to learn
three-level (ie, pixel-, patch- and map- level) hierarchy representations. We
evaluate our BASNet on two reverse tasks including salient object segmentation,
camouflaged object segmentation, showing that it achieves very competitive
performance with sharp segmentation boundaries. Importantly, BASNet runs at
over 70 fps on a single GPU which benefits many potential real applications.
Based on BASNet, we further developed two (close to) commercial applications:
AR COPY & PASTE, in which BASNet is integrated with augmented reality for
"COPYING" and "PASTING" real-world objects, and OBJECT CUT, which is a
web-based tool for automatic object background removal. Both applications have
already drawn huge amount of attention and have important real-world impacts.
The code and two applications will be publicly available at:
https://github.com/NathanUA/BASNet.

Deep learning techniques have gained significant attention in recent years for medical image segmentation tasks, due to their ability to automatically learn features and generalize well to unseen data. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive overview of deep learning methods applied to medical image segmentation, highlighting their strengths, weaknesses, and future research directions.

We begin by discussing the fundamentals of deep learning and its application to image segmentation, including the different architectures and loss functions commonly used in this field. We then survey various deep learning algorithms that have been employed for medical image segmentation, such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs), recurrent neural networks (RNNs), and generative adversarial networks (GANs).

Next, we focus on specific applications of deep learning in medical image segmentation, including brain tumor segmentation, lung nodule detection, and cardiac imaging. For each application, we discuss the dataset used, the deep learning models developed, and the performance achieved. We also highlight the challenges faced in these applications, such as limited annotated datasets, variability in image quality, and the need for expert domain knowledge.

Finally, we discuss some of the open challenges in deep learning for medical image segmentation, including the need for better interpretability and explainability of deep learning models, the lack of standardization in dataset annotation, and the high computational requirements for training large-scale deep learning models. We conclude with recommendations for future research directions, emphasizing the importance of multidisciplinary collaboration between experts in deep learning, medical imaging, and clinical sciences to address these challenges and fully realize the potential of deep learning for medical image segmentation.

technique based on diffuse interface methods to multilayer graphs. Besides the
treatment of various applications with an inherent multilayer structure, we
present a very flexible approach that interprets high-dimensional data in a
low-dimensional multilayer graph representation. Highly efficient numerical

The proposed method is based on a spatially adaptive stochastic multigrid algorithm, which uses a hierarchy of grids with different spatial resolutions to solve the fluid-structure system. The algorithm adapts the grid resolution and the number of iterations based on the spatial variation of the solution and the thermal fluctuations. This allows for a more accurate representation of the solution while reducing the computational cost.

The results show that the proposed method accurately captures the effects of thermal fluctuations and provides a significant reduction in computational cost compared to traditional deterministic methods.

* A novel spatially adaptive stochastic multigrid method for solving fluid-structure systems with thermal fluctuations
* An efficient algorithm that adapts the grid resolution and the number of iterations based on the spatial variation of the solution and the thermal fluctuations

In this paper, we investigate the relationship between fisher information and the Cramér-Rao bound in the context of nonlinear parameter estimation with compressed sensing. We consider a scenario where a signal is observed through a nonlinear measurement model, and the goal is to estimate the parameters of the signal using compressive measurements. We derive an expression for the fisher information matrix (FIM) for this setup, which takes into account the nonlinear measurement model and the compression process. We then use the FIM to evaluate the Cramér-Rao bound, which provides a lower bound on the variance of any unbiased estimator of the parameters. Our analysis reveals that the Cramér-Rao bound can be significantly affected by the compression ratio and the nonlinearity of the measurement model. Specifically, we show that as the compression ratio increases, the Cramér-Rao bound decreases, indicating that more informative measurements are required to achieve accurate parameter estimation. In this paper, we explore the relationship between Hirzebruch-type inequalities and plane curve configurations. Quantum correlations are a fundamental aspect of quantum mechanics and have been found to play a crucial role in various quantum information processing tasks such as quantum communication, computation, and cryptography. In order to quantify and characterize these correlations, several measures have been proposed in recent years. However, a clear understanding of the criteria that a measure of quantum correlation should satisfy is still lacking.

In this paper, we aim to provide a systematic approach towards identifying the necessary criteria that a measure of quantum correlation must fulfill. We first discuss the different types of quantum correlations, including entanglement, non-locality, and steering, and their relationship with each other. We then identify five essential criteria that any measure of quantum correlation should satisfy: (i) positivity, (ii) normativity, (iii) faithfulness, (iv) locality, and (v) monotonicity under restrictions.

We demonstrate the importance of each criterion by considering various examples of quantum systems and comparing the performance of different correlation measures. We show that some commonly used measures fail to satisfy one or more of these criteria, which can lead to inconsistent or incorrect results when analyzing quantum correlations.

Our work provides a deeper understanding of the requirements for a valid measure of quantum correlation, and we hope it will guide future research in developing better measures that can accurately capture the complexity of quantum correlations. Ultimately, our findings would be valuable for advancing the field of quantum information science and its applications in quantum computing, quantum communication, and beyond.

Deep neural networks have achieved satisfactory performance in piles of
medical image analysis tasks. However the training of deep neural network
requires a large amount of samples with high-quality annotations. In medical
image segmentation, it is very laborious and expensive to acquire precise
pixel-level annotations. Aiming at training deep segmentation models on
datasets with probably corrupted annotations, we propose a novel Meta Corrupted
Pixels Mining (MCPM) method based on a simple meta mask network. Our method is
targeted at automatically estimate a weighting map to evaluate the importance
of every pixel in the learning of segmentation network. The meta mask network
which regards the loss value map of the predicted segmentation results as
input, is capable of identifying out corrupted layers and allocating small
weights to them. An alternative algorithm is adopted to train the segmentation
network and the meta mask network, simultaneously. Extensive experimental
results on LIDC-IDRI and LiTS datasets show that our method outperforms
state-of-the-art approaches which are devised for coping with corrupted
annotations.

In this paper, we propose a novel deep learning model, called RA-UNet, which combines the strengths of both attention-based and fully convolutional network (FCN) architectures to improve the accuracy and efficiency of liver and tumor segmentation in computed tomography (CT) scans.

Existing methods for liver and tumor segmentation in CT scans often suffer from limited accuracy and efficiency, particularly in cases where the liver and tumor have complex shapes or are in close proximity. To address these challenges, we designed RA-UNet to incorporate both attention mechanisms and FCNs to effectively capture spatial and contextual information.

The proposed RA-UNet model consists of three main components: a backbone network, a spatial attention module, and a segmentation head. The backbone network is used to extract high-level features from the input CT scan, while the spatial attention module is employed to focus on the most relevant regions of the feature maps and learn contextual information. The segmentation head is then applied to generate the final segmentation masks for the liver and tumor.

We evaluated the performance of RA-UNet on a publicly available dataset of CT scans and compared it with several state-of-the-art segmentation methods. Our results show that RA-UNet achieves superior performance in terms of both accuracy and efficiency, with an average Dice similarity coefficient of 0.93 for liver segmentation and 0.88 for tumor segmentation. Additionally, we conducted a series of ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of the attention mechanism and the hybrid architecture, demonstrating the improvements in performance achieved by combining these two components.

Our findings suggest that the proposed RA-UNet model has the potential to improve the accuracy and efficiency of liver and tumor segmentation in CT scans, and may have important implications for clinical applications such as radiation therapy planning and image-guided surgery.

Efficient and real time segmentation of color images has a variety of
importance in many fields of computer vision such as image compression, medical
imaging, mapping and autonomous navigation. Being one of the most
computationally expensive operation, it is usually done through software imple-
mentation using high-performance processors. In robotic systems, however, with
the constrained platform dimensions and the need for portability, low power
consumption and simultaneously the need for real time image segmentation, we
envision hardware parallelism as the way forward to achieve higher
acceleration. Field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) are among the best suited
for this task as they provide high computing power in a small physical area.
They exceed the computing speed of software based implementations by breaking
the paradigm of sequential execution and accomplishing more per clock cycle
operations by enabling hardware level parallelization at an architectural
level. In this paper, we propose three novel architectures of a well known
Efficient Graph based Image Segmentation algorithm. These proposed
implementations optimizes time and power consumption when compared to software
implementations. The hybrid design proposed, has notable furtherance of
acceleration capabilities delivering atleast 2X speed gain over other implemen-
tations, which henceforth allows real time image segmentation that can be
deployed on Mobile Robotic systems.

Here we introduce image processing systems based on cellular automata, an artificial computational device which computes discrete elements of images by iterating over and transforming simple cellular automaton cells in accordance with a specified set of rules. Image processing problems can be solved using either sequential or probabilistic approaches. Our algorithms, while similar to traditional convolutional neural networks, do not rely on pre-trained feature maps, meaning they are able to address all kinds of image segmentation tasks such as detection of faces in pictures, object classification, etc., without the need for any knowledge about the semantic content of the data. These results pave the way to build a new generation of machine learning applications that require less information, are faster and generally more effective than traditional models to solve difficult image task like face and object recognition. We also propose an easy proof-of-concept system in C# to demonstrate the power of our methods over classic convnets (cf. [5]). In future work, we aim specifically at reducing the amount of memory used when training visual systems. It has been argued before that increasing the computation complexity may reduce performance due to increased memory traffic [16]. This could have serious consequences in image segmenting where the data must be kept up to date, even when it's still being processed. The current approach requires the user upload large datasets or generate very many features in order for the algorithm to produce good results compared to simpler variants. Our work is motivated by this idea since we believe that our approach should allow building visual and speech-based applications out of the box without the use of external libraries/languages and without having to write complex programs.

State-of-the-art image segmentation algorithms generally consist of at least
two successive and distinct computations: a boundary detection process that
uses local image information to classify image locations as boundaries between
objects, followed by a pixel grouping step such as watershed or connected
components that clusters pixels into segments. Prior work has varied the
complexity and approach employed in these two steps, including the
incorporation of multi-layer neural networks to perform boundary prediction,
and the use of global optimizations during pixel clustering. We propose a
unified and end-to-end trainable machine learning approach, flood-filling
networks, in which a recurrent 3d convolutional network directly produces
individual segments from a raw image. The proposed approach robustly segments
images with an unknown and variable number of objects as well as highly
variable object sizes. We demonstrate the approach on a challenging 3d image
segmentation task, connectomic reconstruction from volume electron microscopy
data, on which flood-filling neural networks substantially improve accuracy
over other state-of-the-art methods. The proposed approach can replace complex
multi-step segmentation pipelines with a single neural network that is learned
end-to-end.

Image segmentation is a primary task in many medical applications. Recently,
many deep networks derived from U-Net have been extensively used in various
medical image segmentation tasks. However, in most of the cases, networks
similar to U-net produce coarse and non-smooth segmentations with lots of
discontinuities. To improve and refine the performance of U-Net like networks,
we propose the use of parallel decoders which along with performing the mask
predictions also perform contour prediction and distance map estimation. The
contour and distance map aid in ensuring smoothness in the segmentation
predictions. To facilitate joint training of three tasks, we propose a novel
architecture called Psi-Net with a single encoder and three parallel decoders
(thus having a shape of $\Psi$), one decoder to learns the segmentation mask
prediction and other two decoders to learn the auxiliary tasks of contour
detection and distance map estimation. The learning of these auxiliary tasks
helps in capturing the shape and the boundary information. We also propose a
new joint loss function for the proposed architecture. The loss function
consists of a weighted combination of Negative Log likelihood and Mean Square
Error loss. We have used two publicly available datasets: 1) Origa dataset for
the task of optic cup and disc segmentation and 2) Endovis segment dataset for
the task of polyp segmentation to evaluate our model. We have conducted
extensive experiments using our network to show our model gives better results
in terms of segmentation, boundary and shape metrics.

Efficient transport of cold atoms or ions is a subject of increasing concern
in many experimental applications reaching from quantum information processing
to frequency metrology. For the scalable quantum computer architectures based
on the shuttling of individual ions, different transport schemes have been
developed, which allow to move single atoms minimizing their energy gain. In
this article we discuss the experimental implementation of the transport of a
three-dimensional ion cloud in a macroscopic linear radiofrequency (RF) trap.
The present work is based on numerical simulations done by molecular dynamics
taking into account a realistic experimental environment. The deformation of
the trapping potential and the spatial extension of the cloud during transport
appears to be the major source of the ion energy gain. The efficiency of
transport in terms of transfer probability and ion number is also discussed.

training. However, most of existing methods underestimate the importance of
challenging regions (e.g. small branches or blurred edges) during training. We
believe that these unlabeled regions may contain more crucial information to
minimize the uncertainty prediction for the model and should be emphasized in
the training process. Therefore, in this paper, we propose a novel Mutual
Consistency Network (MC-Net) for semi-supervised left atrium segmentation from
3D MR images. Particularly, our MC-Net consists of one encoder and two slightly
different decoders, and the prediction discrepancies of two decoders are
transformed as an unsupervised loss by our designed cycled pseudo label scheme
to encourage mutual consistency. Such mutual consistency encourages the two
decoders to have consistent and low-entropy predictions and enables the model
to gradually capture generalized features from these unlabeled challenging
regions. We evaluate our MC-Net on the public Left Atrium (LA) database and it
obtains impressive performance gains by exploiting the unlabeled data
effectively. Our MC-Net outperforms six recent semi-supervised methods for left
atrium segmentation, and sets the new state-of-the-art performance on the LA
database.

recalibrating the deep networks on a few unlabeled images from the target

This paper addresses the issue of accounting for model error in ensemble Kalman filtering (EnKF) due to unresolved scales. The EnKF is a widely used data assimilation technique that combines observations with a numerical model to estimate the state of a system. However, in many cases, the model used in EnKF does not capture all of the relevant physical processes and thus leads to biases in the estimated state. One way to mitigate this problem is by using ensemble methods, which rely on multiple realizations of the forecast and analysis cycles to represent the uncertainty in the solution. Nonetheless, even with ensembles, the model errors caused by unresolved scales can still have a significant impact on the accuracy of the results.

In this study, we propose an approach to quantify and correct for the effects of unresolved scales on the ensemble spread in EnKF, thereby improving the accuracy of the predictions. Our method involves introducing a stochastic parameterization scheme that captures the effects of the neglected scales on the ensemble mean and covariance. By incorporating this scheme into the ensemble Kalman filter, we are able to properly account for the unknown effects of the small-scale fluctuations and obtain more reliable estimates of the state variables. We demonstrate our approach using several experiments with a simple ocean model, where the unresolved scales correspond to subgrid-scale eddies. The results show that our strategy reduces significantly the bias in the ensemble mean and increases the precision of the predictions compared to the standard EnKF configuration without explicitly resolving the unresolved scales.

Existing works on semantic segmentation typically consider a small number of
labels, ranging from tens to a few hundreds. With a large number of labels,
training and evaluation of such task become extremely challenging due to
correlation between labels and lack of datasets with complete annotations. We
formulate semantic segmentation as a problem of image segmentation given a
semantic concept, and propose a novel system which can potentially handle an
unlimited number of concepts, including objects, parts, stuff, and attributes.
We achieve this using a weakly and semi-supervised framework leveraging
multiple datasets with different levels of supervision. We first train a deep
neural network on a 6M stock image dataset with only image-level labels to
learn visual-semantic embedding on 18K concepts. Then, we refine and extend the
embedding network to predict an attention map, using a curated dataset with
bounding box annotations on 750 concepts. Finally, we train an attention-driven
class agnostic segmentation network using an 80-category fully annotated
dataset. We perform extensive experiments to validate that the proposed system
performs competitively to the state of the art on fully supervised concepts,
and is capable of producing accurate segmentations for weakly learned and
unseen concepts.

> We propose a generic edge-attention guidance network (ET-Net) for medical image segmentation. The proposed ET-Net is a fully convolutional network that can be applied to various medical image segmentation tasks. The ET-Net consists of a feature extraction module, an edge-attention module, and a segmentation module. The feature extraction module extracts features from the input image. The edge-attention module generates edge-attention maps by using the features extracted by the feature extraction module. The segmentation module generates the segmentation results by using the features extracted by the feature extraction module and the edge-attention maps generated by the edge-attention module. The edge-attention maps generated by the edge-attention module can guide the segmentation module to focus on the edges of the target objects, thus improving the segmentation performance. The proposed ET-Net has been evaluated on three medical image segmentation tasks, including brain tumor segmentation, liver segmentation, and kidney segmentation. The experimental results show that the proposed ET-Net outperforms the state-of-the-art methods on these three tasks.

In this paper, we continue our investigation of foliated backgrounds for M-theory compactifications. We introduce a new type of foliation, which we term "M-folioations," that are particularly well-suited to studying the low-energy effective actions of M-theory compactified on manifolds with boundaries.
We demonstrate how M-folioations can be used to construct solutions of the low-energy effective action of M-theory that are not possible using traditional Kaluza-Klein compactifications. These solutions have novel properties and singularities that are forbidden in traditional compactifications.
We also explore the relationship between M-folioations and other approaches to M-theory compactification, such as calibrated geometries and exceptional generalized geometry. We show that M-folioations provide a natural framework for understanding the structure of these other approaches, and offer a means of connecting them in a consistent way.
Our work opens up new possibilities for understanding the structure of M-theory spacetimes and their behavior under various duality symmetries. It offers a rich landscape of new physics beyond the familiar realms of string theory, including novel types of charged black holes, gravitational waves, and cosmologies. The results of this paper establish foliated backgrounds as an essential tool for exploring the vast universe of M-theory vacua.

In this paper, we address the problem of computing valid p-values for image segmentation, a fundamental task in computer vision. Existing methods for computing p-values for image segmentation often rely on simplistic models and assumptions, which can lead to invalid p-values and incorrect conclusions.

We propose a new method called Selective Inference for computing valid p-values for image segmentation. Our method is based on a careful consideration of the inference process and the selection of relevant features for each image. We demonstrate that Selective Inference can significantly improve the accuracy of p-values compared to existing methods.

We evaluate the performance of Selective Inference on several benchmark datasets and compare it to state-of-the-art methods. Our results show that Selective Inference achieves higher accuracy and robustness in computing p-values, leading to more reliable and accurate segmentation results.

Our work has important implications for a wide range of applications, including object recognition, tracking, and scene understanding. We demonstrate the practicality and effectiveness of Selective Inference through experiments on real-world images.

Overall, this paper makes a significant contribution to the field of image segmentation by providing a reliable and accurate method for computing p-values, which can be used to evaluate and validate segmentation results.

Image segmentation and classification are the two main fundamental steps in
pattern recognition. To perform medical image segmentation or classification
with deep learning models, it requires training on large image dataset with
annotation. The dermoscopy images (ISIC archive) considered for this work does
not have ground truth information for lesion segmentation. Performing manual
labelling on this dataset is time-consuming. To overcome this issue,
self-learning annotation scheme was proposed in the two-stage deep learning
algorithm. The two-stage deep learning algorithm consists of U-Net segmentation
model with the annotation scheme and CNN classifier model. The annotation
scheme uses a K-means clustering algorithm along with merging conditions to
achieve initial labelling information for training the U-Net model. The
classifier models namely ResNet-50 and LeNet-5 were trained and tested on the
image dataset without segmentation for comparison and with the U-Net
segmentation for implementing the proposed self-learning Artificial
Intelligence (AI) framework. The classification results of the proposed AI
framework achieved training accuracy of 93.8% and testing accuracy of 82.42%
when compared with the two classifier models directly trained on the input
images.

Intelligent architecture for neural networks is needed to address problems that are currently very hard, involving large numbers of neural factors, complex functions, or dense stochastic environments. However until now there has been no general framework which systematically treats these issues with respect to their underlying computational difficulty. Here we present a method by which many neural network architectures can be evaluated using a set of criteria for how well they have learned representations of non-linear constraints (i.e. information about data structure) through experience. The evaluation methodology takes advantage of existing research on structured neural factor models (SMFs), with an emphasis given to SMFs which employ multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) as input/network layers; this review focuses specifically on neural architecture with these MLP as the layer function. Our approach also applies generically to neural networks on other types of supervised training data where the number of variables varies greatly across the problem domain (e.g. multi-layer fully connected nets versus small-scale sparse subspace clustering). We discuss several key findings, including a systematic comparison between several commonly used evaluation metrics including variational inference, dimensionality reduction, robustness, and memory complexity, along with a classification analysis based on the most common approaches for computing optimal parameters from the available values. We conclude with recommendations for future work.

Zipf's Law holds strong implications for our long-run forecasting results, which rely heavily on data driven predictions of future prices given information about past prices. The Zipf law suggests that short-term strategies cannot improve past performance by more than 10 percent relative to risk management and forecast error. While this result has been interpreted as suggesting we may not be able to make useful observations over time about price momentum using historical short-term data sets (or even trends) or even to forecast trend changes well enough to meet our own long run investment requirements, Zipf's law suggests instead that it does not matter how good forecasts are if investors pursue inefficient asset allocation choices—such as high exposure to the most volatile assets in the broad market index. In addition, Zipf's Law supports other hypotheses for explaining past performance variability that don't depend on imperfect correlations between markets or on measurement errors. More generally, although there have also been proposals that suggest it may take longer for a stock or investment to experience a loss compared with its price gain once it becomes widely regarded as an underperformer1, this conjecture appears to require either unobserved shifts in short-term trading activity or unobservable shifts in expectations about long-term return. This paper presents a novel approach for high-resolution segmentation of tooth root fuzzy edges based on polynomial curve fitting with landmark detection. The proposed method aims to accurately separate the tooth roots from the surrounding dental tissues in digital dental images.

Existing methods for tooth root segmentation are often limited by their reliance on hand-crafted features, low accuracy, and high computational complexity. In contrast, our approach leverages the power of polynomial curve fitting to accurately model the fuzzy edges of tooth roots and detect landmarks that define the boundary between the tooth roots and the surrounding tissues.

The proposed method consists of three stages: 1) preprocessing, 2) polynomial curve fitting, and 3) landmark detection. In the preprocessing stage, the input image is filtered to enhance the contrast and remove noise. In the polynomial curve fitting stage, a cubic polynomial curve is fitted to the fuzzy edge of the tooth root using a non-linear least squares optimization algorithm. The curve is then used to separate the tooth root from the surrounding tissues. Finally, landmarks are detected by identifying the points on the curve that correspond to the maximum gradient values.

The proposed method was evaluated on a dataset of 20 digital dental images using a leave-one-out cross-validation scheme. The results show that our method outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy, efficiency, and robustness. The mean absolute error was found to be 0.15 mm, and the processing time was less than 30 seconds per image.

The proposed method has important implications for dental image analysis and related applications such as orthodontic treatment planning, dental implant planning, and oral disease diagnosis. With its high accuracy, efficiency, and robustness, the method has the potential to improve the accuracy and efficiency of dental procedures and contribute to better patient outcomes.

In the context of linear coasting nucleosynthesis, Coulomb screening plays a crucial role in determining the abundances of elements produced during the nucleosynthesis process. In this paper, we investigate the effects of Coulomb screening on the nucleosynthesis process and its impact on the abundances of elements produced.

We use a combination of analytical and numerical methods to study the effect of Coulomb screening on the nuclear reaction rates and the resulting element abundances. Our results show that Coulomb screening significantly affects the reaction rates, leading to a suppression of the abundances of elements with high atomic numbers.

We find that the suppression of element abundances due to Coulomb screening is most pronounced in the region of the nuclear chart where the nucleon separation energy is low. In this region, the Coulomb repulsion between nucleons is strong, leading to a significant reduction in the reaction rates and a decrease in the abundances of heavy elements.

Our results have important implications for the understanding of nucleosynthesis processes in various astrophysical environments, such as supernovae and neutron star mergers. We find that the inclusion of Coulomb screening in nucleosynthesis models can significantly affect the predicted abundances of elements, and that it is essential to include this effect in order to obtain a more accurate understanding of the nucleosynthesis process.

Overall, our study highlights the importance of Coulomb screening in linear coasting nucleosynthesis and demonstrates the need for its inclusion in nucleosynthesis models in order to obtain a more accurate understanding of the abundances of elements produced in astrophysical environments.

A standard method in statistical calibration assumes that both the raw and residual values are deterministic, independent events. In this paper we present a novel approach to account for model error arising when residuals are not linear in their coefficients. This method ensures that residual values are correctly predicted using only estimates by unmeasured units (UMUs). Our data set consisted of 483,085 individual UU's that were used in a regression analysis performed on a series of 10 year rolling windows called the "Kalman distribution," whose standard deviation was 5×10-3. The UMU predictions of the logarithmically scaled residuals can be analyzed using a new class of estimational techniques that explicitly take into account the time variance and variability intrinsic to UMU's rather than simply fitting an equation to a discrete set of parameters and relying strictly on the results generated by the system as derived from theory or fit tests. We show that these methods can accurately separate true errors from residual noise, a result which supports the notion that models with nonzero mean will have high residual variance without causing overfitting in models that rely solely on the linear relation between residual variances and correlation probabilities.[*]

The study of solitons, localized wave packets that maintain their shape over long distances, has garnered significant interest in various fields of physics. In the context of Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs), solitons have been extensively investigated using mean-field theory via the Gross-Pitaevskii equation (GPE). However, recent advancements in experimental techniques have enabled the exploration of few-body dynamics in ultracold atomic systems, prompting a need to extend our understanding of solitons beyond the mean-field regime.

In this work, we examine solitons in a hard-core bosonic system, leveraging both analytical and numerical approaches. Our analysis reveals a rich landscape of soliton solutions, which include not only GPE-type solitons but also novel configurations that are inaccessible within the mean-field framework. We showcase that these non-mean-field solitons exhibit distinct properties and dynamical behaviors compared to their GPE counterparts. Specifically, they display increased stability against perturbations and demonstrate self-trapping capabilities even under conditions where GPE solitons would dissipate.

Furthermore, our investigation unveils an intriguing connection between the emergence of non-mean-field solitons and the interplay between effective interactions and confinement. This relationship can be controlled by tuning parameters such as density and temperature, offering potential avenues for manipulating soliton properties experimentally.

Our findings expand upon the current understanding of solitons in many-body quantum systems and offer fresh insights into the complex phenomena arising from interparticle correlations. These results carry implications for both theoretical models and experimental investigations in the dynamically developing field of ultracold atom research, with potential applications in the realization of novel quasiparticles and the engineering of synthetic gauge fields.

The graph Laplacian is a standard tool in data science, machine learning, and
image processing. The corresponding matrix inherits the complex structure of
the underlying network and is in certain applications densely populated. This
makes computations, in particular matrix-vector products, with the graph
Laplacian a hard task. A typical application is the computation of a number of
its eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Standard methods become infeasible as the
number of nodes in the graph is too large. We propose the use of the fast
summation based on the nonequispaced fast Fourier transform (NFFT) to perform
the dense matrix-vector product with the graph Laplacian fast without ever
forming the whole matrix. The enormous flexibility of the NFFT algorithm allows
us to embed the accelerated multiplication into Lanczos-based eigenvalues
routines or iterative linear system solvers and even consider other than the
standard Gaussian kernels. We illustrate the feasibility of our approach on a
number of test problems from image segmentation to semi-supervised learning
based on graph-based PDEs. In particular, we compare our approach with the
Nystr\"om method. Moreover, we present and test an enhanced, hybrid version of
the Nystr\"om method, which internally uses the NFFT.

We propose an automated method to enforce mutual consistency between semi-supervised segmentation rules in medical images, and evaluate its robustness compared with existing methods via several validation experiments on MNIST. In the framework of medical image sequence classification our method leverages common statistical properties of neural networks (nonlinearity) and gradient descent algorithms. We then show that semi-supervised segmentation does not suffer from high-dimensional, low-variance or weak alignment, which makes it more flexible than other proposed methods of medical segmentation. Moreover, we present a novel method for ensuring compliance with rule consistency: cross-validation using multiple samples of an unknown subset yields nonparametric tests. We show that this approach can be used as an efficient proof-of-concept system for implementation in medical image recognition systems where automatic segmentation relies heavily on supervised features as well as machine learning. This work demonstrates the versatility and utility of adversarial techniques that leverage information theoretic methods while making them accessible through standard computer science concepts. The robustness of our new testbed for enforcing mutual consistency between different semiautomated segmentations also provides insights into how some classifiers with complex architectures can be formulated robustly and efficiently.

In this work, we address two fundamental problems in Machine Vision research and propose an evolutionary approach to solving both them : (1) The problem of object recognition in image data with low temporal resolution; and (2) The need to classify new images into previously unseen classes using knowledge about the classification accuracy of earlier training images. We provide such an evolved method by employing a machine learning process based on Markov Decision Processes. Our model is capable of generating high-quality class labels from highly noisy feature vectors. It allows us to efficiently learn and extract large data sets that are not easily tractable through supervised methods, e.g., feature extraction or feature selection.
