In this paper, we introduce a new framework for understanding the second law of thermodynamics in the context of quantum systems. Building on recent work that has established connections between the quantum relative entropy and various thermodynamic quantities, we derive novel inequality relations that share similarities with the classical second law of thermodynamics. These inequalities provide bounds on the rates at which certain thermodynamic observables can change over time, and have important implications for our understanding of non-equilibrium quantum dynamics. We demonstrate the applicability of these inequalities by considering several example systems and processes, including heat transport in quantum circuits and the driven-dissipative dynamics of many-body systems. Our results open up new possibilities for studying non-equilibrium quantum phenomena through the lens of information-theoretic tools, and pave the way for further investigations into the interplay between quantum mechanics and thermodynamics.

Hourglass networks such as the U-Net and V-Net are popular neural
architectures for medical image segmentation and counting problems. Typical
instances of hourglass networks contain shortcut connections between mirroring
layers. These shortcut connections improve the performance and it is
hypothesized that this is due to mitigating effects on the vanishing gradient
problem and the ability of the model to combine feature maps from earlier and
later layers. We propose a method for not only combining feature maps of
mirroring layers but also feature maps of layers with different spatial
dimensions. For instance, the method enables the integration of the bottleneck
feature map with those of the reconstruction layers. The proposed approach is
applicable to any hourglass architecture. We evaluated the contextual hourglass
networks on image segmentation and object counting problems in the medical
domain. We achieve competitive results outperforming popular hourglass networks
by up to 17 percentage points.

This paper introduces a new method for measuring dependence between random variables, called copula correlation. The proposed measure is based on the concept of copulas, which are multidimensional distributions that capture the dependencies between random variables in a way that is independent of their marginal distributions. Copula correlation is shown to have several desirable properties, such as being non-negative, symmetric, and satisfying the triangle inequality. Moreover, it can be used to quantify both linear and nonlinear dependencies, and is robust to outliers and influential observations. As an extension of Pearson's correlation coefficient, copula correlation provides a more comprehensive picture of dependence between random variables than traditional methods, particularly in cases where the relationship is not linear or Gaussian. The paper also discusses various applications of copula correlation, including hypothesis testing, regression analysis, and risk management. Overall, this work offers a valuable tool for researchers and practitioners who seek to better understand complex dependencies in data.

We propose a novel deep learning framework for left atrium (LA) segmentation in cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) images. The proposed framework consists of two components: a global shape prior and an autoencoder for local intensity prior. The global shape prior is modeled by a mixture of Gaussian distributions, which is learned from a large number of LA shapes. The local intensity prior is modeled by an autoencoder, which is trained to reconstruct the local intensity distribution of LA. The proposed framework is evaluated on a large dataset of CMR images. The results show that the proposed framework outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in terms of segmentation accuracy.

Most progress in semantic segmentation reports on daytime images taken under
favorable illumination conditions. We instead address the problem of semantic
segmentation of nighttime images and improve the state-of-the-art, by adapting
daytime models to nighttime without using nighttime annotations. Moreover, we
design a new evaluation framework to address the substantial uncertainty of
semantics in nighttime images. Our central contributions are: 1) a curriculum
framework to gradually adapt semantic segmentation models from day to night via
labeled synthetic images and unlabeled real images, both for progressively
darker times of day, which exploits cross-time-of-day correspondences for the
real images to guide the inference of their labels; 2) a novel
uncertainty-aware annotation and evaluation framework and metric for semantic
segmentation, designed for adverse conditions and including image regions
beyond human recognition capability in the evaluation in a principled fashion;
3) the Dark Zurich dataset, which comprises 2416 unlabeled nighttime and 2920
unlabeled twilight images with correspondences to their daytime counterparts
plus a set of 151 nighttime images with fine pixel-level annotations created
with our protocol, which serves as a first benchmark to perform our novel
evaluation. Experiments show that our guided curriculum adaptation
significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods on real nighttime sets both
for standard metrics and our uncertainty-aware metric. Furthermore, our
uncertainty-aware evaluation reveals that selective invalidation of predictions
can lead to better results on data with ambiguous content such as our nighttime
benchmark and profit safety-oriented applications which involve invalid inputs.

On a fundamental level, most approaches to neural network modeling are based on classical algorithms that have been well-known (or believed to be) for a long time but were never seen as suitable solutions when running complex models under heavy learning loads or simulation and inference tasks. To our knowledge we show here how to easily improve these current methods by refining them using modern machine-learning techniques, leading to a simple yet general solution with up-to two orders of magnitude speedups. At first sight it seems straightforward; however, the challenge is really about scaling this approach beyond today's technology limitations. The main innovation of such refined algorithms lies not only in being able to more efficiently encode labels across their gradients via sparse set transformations but also in the implementation of those transformations into gradient codes in parallel across several CPUs in batch mode without explicit precomputation, which was not previously known possible. Our work will provide practical guidance on a variety of theoretical issues regarding optimal dimensionality reduction. On a conceptual basis, more general principles also need to be introduced and the relevant literature reviewed so that efficient implementations can then be devised in different applications beyond deep learning. We believe this could lead to new insights for future problems like real-time perception and cognition where similar performance requirements exist even at large amounts of data input. -Raphael Schöberle

Deep convolutional neural networks are powerful tools for learning visual
representations from images. However, designing efficient deep architectures to
analyse volumetric medical images remains challenging. This work investigates
efficient and flexible elements of modern convolutional networks such as
dilated convolution and residual connection. With these essential building
blocks, we propose a high-resolution, compact convolutional network for
volumetric image segmentation. To illustrate its efficiency of learning 3D
representation from large-scale image data, the proposed network is validated
with the challenging task of parcellating 155 neuroanatomical structures from
brain MR images. Our experiments show that the proposed network architecture
compares favourably with state-of-the-art volumetric segmentation networks
while being an order of magnitude more compact. We consider the brain
parcellation task as a pretext task for volumetric image segmentation; our
trained network potentially provides a good starting point for transfer
learning. Additionally, we show the feasibility of voxel-level uncertainty
estimation using a sampling approximation through dropout.

This paper introduces a novel technique called trace refinement, which improves the accuracy of approximations used in the analysis and optimization of labelled Markov decision processes (LMDPs). LMDPs are widely used mathematical models that capture the behavior of systems with both discrete and continuous states. They have applications in various fields such as finance, biology, robotics, and communication networks. In many cases, exact solutions to LMDPs are intractable due to their computational complexity. Therefore, solving approximate solvers that return near-optimal policies while providing guarantees on the suboptimality gap is essential.

The proposed method leverages ideas from deductive verification and model checking to effectively prune the state space of irrelevant states while preserving temporal logic properties encoded using Linear Temporal Logic formulae (LTL) or Computational Tree Logic (CTL) specifications. UNet++, a nested U-Net architecture, is presented in this paper as a novel approach to medical image segmentation. The U-Net architecture has been widely used for segmenting medical images, but its limitations, such as poor performance on small objects and lack of contextual information, have been well-documented.

The proposed UNet++ addresses these limitations by incorporating a nested U-Net structure that utilizes multi-scale features to improve segmentation accuracy. The nested U-Net consists of an outer network that captures high-level contextual information and an inner network that focuses on low-level detailed information. The two networks are connected through skip connections, allowing them to share information and work collaboratively.

Experiments were conducted using several publicly available datasets, including segmenting tumors from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans, detecting diabetic retinopathy in fundus images, and identifying cells in microscopy images. The results demonstrated that UNet++ outperformed state-of-the-art methods, achieving an improvement in mean intersection over union (MIOU) of up to 10% compared to the original U-Net.

Furthermore, we analyzed the effect of different components of the U-Net++ architecture and found that both the outer and inner networks contributed significantly to the improved performance. Ablation studies also showed that theskip connections between the two networks were crucial for combining local and global information effectively.

Our findings suggest that the nested U-Net architecture offers a promising direction for improving medical image segmentation models. The use of multiple scales and shared information can lead to better feature representation, resulting in more accurate and robust segmentation. UNet++ has important implications for various medical applications where precise segmentation is critical, such as disease diagnosis and treatment planning.

The proposed system significantly reduces labor costs while improving accuracy compared to traditional manual methods. Our experimental results demonstrate that the generated datasets achieve high levels of performance when trained using deep neural networks. Overall, our innovation offers a promising solution with broad applications across agriculture industries.

Quantum cryptography is the art and science of exploiting quantum mechanical
effects in order to perform cryptographic tasks. While the most well-known
example of this discipline is quantum key distribution (QKD), there exist many
other applications such as quantum money, randomness generation, secure two-
and multi-party computation and delegated quantum computation. Quantum
cryptography also studies the limitations and challenges resulting from quantum
adversaries---including the impossibility of quantum bit commitment, the
difficulty of quantum rewinding and the definition of quantum security models
for classical primitives. In this review article, aimed primarily at
cryptographers unfamiliar with the quantum world, we survey the area of
theoretical quantum cryptography, with an emphasis on the constructions and
limitations beyond the realm of QKD.

In this work, we present a Monte Carlo simulation study of surface sputtering by dual and rotated ion beams. Surface sputtering is a widely used technique in various fields such as semiconductor manufacturing, data storage, and thin film deposition. The use of dual and rotated ion beams offers improved performance and versatility compared to traditional single-beam systems. Our simulations aim to investigate the effects of beam parameters, such as ion energy, angle of incidence, and beam spacing, on sputtering yields and surface roughness.

We employ a Monte Carlo method to simulate the interactions between ion beams and a target surface, taking into account the scattering and diffusion of ions and atoms during the sputtering process. Our results show that increasing the ion energy and narrowing the beam spacing lead to higher sputtering yields, while larger angles of incidence result in increased surface roughness. We also find that there exists an optimal beam spacing at which the sputtering yield is maximized, which depends on the specific beam conditions.

Furthermore, we explore the effectiveness of rotating one or both beams and observe that this leads to uniformity improvements in some cases, particularly when the beams are highly inclined. By systematically varying the rotation angles and speeds, we identify regimes where enhanced surface smoothing can be achieved without sacrificing sputtering efficiency.

Our findings provide valuable insights into how the choice of ion beam configuration influences the outcome of surface sputtering processes, and may serve as guidance for optimizing experimental settings in future studies.

The rapid advancements in deep learning have led to significant progress in medical image segmentation. This review focuses on recent advances in using limited supervision techniques that leverage readily available data such as images or videos without explicit labels via active learning strategies. In this paper, we present a novel approach for 3D medical image segmentation using elastic boundary projection. Our method leverages the concept of elasticity in image processing to accurately segment objects in 3D medical images. We propose a new algorithm that projects the image intensity values onto an elastic boundary, which is a surface that deforms to match the object boundary in the image. The resulting boundary is then used to segment the object from the rest of the image.

We evaluate our method on several 3D medical image datasets, including MRI and CT scans, and compare it to traditional segmentation techniques. Our results show that elastic boundary projection outperforms traditional methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency. We also demonstrate the versatility of our method by applying it to various medical applications, such as tumor segmentation, organ segmentation, and vessel segmentation.

Our main contribution is the introduction of elastic boundary projection as a novel approach to 3D medical image segmentation. Our method has the advantage of being robust to noise and irregularities in the image data, and it can handle complex object boundaries with ease. Additionally, it is computationally efficient and can be used in real-time applications.

Overall, our paper provides a significant contribution to the field of medical image segmentation, and it has the potential to improve the accuracy and efficiency of various medical applications that rely on image segmentation.

In this paper, we present Fully Transformer Networks (FTN) for semantic image segmentation, a novel approach that leverages the transformer architecture to improve segmentation accuracy and efficiency. Unlike traditional CNN-based methods that rely on hand-crafted features and fixed-size receptive fields, FTN employs self-attention mechanisms to learn flexible and hierarchical representations of images. Our framework is designed to handle input images of arbitrary size and produces instance-level segmentation masks without requiring anchor boxes or predefined templates.

Experiments conducted on several benchmark datasets show that FTN achieves state-of-the-art performance in various settings, outperforming contemporary segmentation methods such as U-Net, DeepLab, and Swin Transformer. Notably, our method demonstrates superiority in scenarios with low-resolution images, instances with varied sizes, and cluttered scenes. We also perform ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of different components within FTN, providing insights into the design choices that contribute to its success.

Our key contributions can be summarized as follows:

1. We introduce Fully Transformer Networks (FTN), a paradigm shift in semantic image segmentation that fully embraces the transformer architecture and abolishes the need for convolutional layers.
2. FTN learns rich and adaptable feature representations using self-attention, enabling the network to capture intricate contextual relationships between image elements.
3. Our method operates effectively on inputs of varying dimensions, eliminating the requirement for fixed-size inputs and grid-like output structures.
4. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FTN surpasses previous state-of-the-art methods in terms of segmentation accuracy, computational efficiency, and generalization capability across multiple datasets.
5. We provide comprehensive analysis and visualizations to understand the strengths and limitations of FTN, shedding light on future research directions in this field.

The proposed Fully Transformer Networks mark a significant milestone in the evolution of neural networks for image understanding tasks, offering a promising path towards more accurate, efficient, and scalable segmentation models.

Using a novel algorithm for generating complex morphological patterns in natural images, we present Backlund transformations that transform a morphology to an image. We show they can generate very large sets of very different shapes using an image containing only standard geometric features. In particular, when applying the feature representation of arbitrary features with known parameters to random samples derived from a single underlying structure (a back-projection of a circle), such as circles or ellipses, we observe morphologies whose geometry closely resembles standard geometrical patterns. This suggests that Backlund transforms may represent well defined geometries with more than one unique element that could be obtained by chance if sampled independently without regard to any given feature. These results suggest new avenues on which computer vision applications can leverage the power provided through advanced computation, and give further support to their application to human perception and behavior, where our perceptual capabilities are still limited in number.

In this paper, we investigate the phenomenon of itinerant magnetism in spin-orbit coupled Bose gases. Spin-orbit coupling is a fundamental interaction that arises from the coupling of the spin and orbital degrees of freedom of particles. In Bose gases, this interaction can lead to novel magnetic phenomena due to the exchange of virtual bosons between atoms.

By using a combination of theoretical and numerical approaches, we demonstrate the emergence of itinerant magnetism in these systems. We show that the spin-orbit coupling induces a magnetic response in the gas, characterized by a non-zero average magnetization. This magnetization arises from the collective oscillations of the spins, which are driven by the spatially varying exchange field generated by the spin-orbit coupling.

Our results reveal a rich phase diagram, with three distinct regimes of itinerant magnetism: a ferromagnetic regime, a canted antiferromagnetic regime, and a paramagnetic regime. These regimes arise due to the interplay between the strength of the spin-orbit coupling, the temperature, and the density of the gas.

We also study the effects of an external magnetic field on the system and find that it can substantially modify the magnetic properties of the gas. By tuning the strength and direction of the external field, we observe a variety of interesting phenomena, including the suppression of magnetization at certain angles and the emergence of spin vortices.

Overall, our work provides new insights into the behavior of spin-orbit coupled Bose gases and highlights their potential for studying novel magentic phases and phenomena that cannot be observed in traditional condensed matter systems.

To address these challenges, we developed a novel on-chip kinesin substrate design that takes into account the kinetic parameters of kinesin and the requirements of molecular communication systems. The design consists of a combination of microgrooves and nanopillars that provide a geometrically confined environment for kinesin motion. We used finite element simulations to optimize the dimensions of the microgrooves and nanopillars in order to maximize the binding affinity between kinesin and the substrate, while minimizing the energetic barrier for kinesin movement.

We fabricated the optimized on-chip kinesin substrate using standard semiconductor manufacturing processes and characterized its performance using fluorescence microscopy and other biochemical assays. Our results show that the designed substrate enhances the processivity and speed of kinesin moving along the microtubule track, resulting in improved communication performance compared to traditional bulk substrates. Moreover, we demonstrate the versatility of our design by integrating different functional groups onto the substrate surface, enabling the manipulation of kinesin's directionality and spatial organization.

Our work presents a significant advancement in the development of on-chip kinesin substrates for molecular communication, offering new possibilities for the implementation of kinesin-based logic and memory devices. Furthermore, the insights gained from this study can be generally applied to the design of other motor protein-based biomolecular systems, opening up new opportunities for developing complex nanoscale biological circuits and networks.

Medical image segmentation is inherently an ambiguous task due to factors
such as partial volumes and variations in anatomical definitions. While in most
cases the segmentation uncertainty is around the border of structures of
interest, there can also be considerable inter-rater differences. The class of
conditional variational autoencoders (cVAE) offers a principled approach to
inferring distributions over plausible segmentations that are conditioned on
input images. Segmentation uncertainty estimated from samples of such
distributions can be more informative than using pixel level probability
scores. In this work, we propose a novel conditional generative model that is
based on conditional Normalizing Flow (cFlow). The basic idea is to increase
the expressivity of the cVAE by introducing a cFlow transformation step after
the encoder. This yields improved approximations of the latent posterior
distribution, allowing the model to capture richer segmentation variations.
With this we show that the quality and diversity of samples obtained from our
conditional generative model is enhanced. Performance of our model, which we
call cFlow Net, is evaluated on two medical imaging datasets demonstrating
substantial improvements in both qualitative and quantitative measures when
compared to a recent cVAE based model.

Sparse decomposition has been widely used for different applications, such as
source separation, image classification and image denoising. This paper
presents a new algorithm for segmentation of an image into background and
foreground text and graphics using sparse decomposition. First, the background
is represented using a suitable smooth model, which is a linear combination of
a few smoothly varying basis functions, and the foreground text and graphics
are modeled as a sparse component overlaid on the smooth background. Then the
background and foreground are separated using a sparse decomposition framework
and imposing some prior information, which promote the smoothness of
background, and the sparsity and connectivity of foreground pixels. This
algorithm has been tested on a dataset of images extracted from HEVC standard
test sequences for screen content coding, and is shown to outperform prior
methods, including least absolute deviation fitting, k-means clustering based
segmentation in DjVu, and shape primitive extraction and coding algorithm.

Recent advances in brain clearing and imaging have made it possible to image
entire mammalian brains at sub-micron resolution. These images offer the
potential to assemble brain-wide atlases of projection neuron morphology, but
manual neuron reconstruction remains a bottleneck. In this paper we present a
probabilistic method which combines a hidden Markov state process that encodes
neuron geometric properties with a random field appearance model of the
flourescence process. Our method utilizes dynamic programming to efficiently
compute the global maximizers of what we call the "most probable" neuron path.
We applied our algorithm to the output of image segmentation models where false
negatives severed neuronal processes, and showed that it can follow axons in
the presence of noise or nearby neurons. Our method has the potential to be
integrated into a semi or fully automated reconstruction pipeline.
Additionally, it creates a framework for conditioning the probability to fixed
start and endpoints through which users can intervene with hard constraints to,
for example, rule out certain reconstructions, or assign axons to particular
cell bodies.

In this paper, we investigate the behavior of the average singular value of a complex random matrix as a function of the matrix dimension. Specifically, we show that the average singular value of a complex random matrix decayes monotonically with increasing matrix dimension. This result has important implications for the study of complex systems, where large matrices are often used to model interactions between numerous components. Our findings suggest that the growth of the matrix dimension leads to a decrease in the average importance of individual elements, which may have significant consequences for the overall behavior and stability of the system.

We prove our result using a combination of analytical and numerical methods. First, we derive an expression for the expected value of the singular values of a complex random matrix, and then use this expression to establish the monotonicity of the average singular value as a function of the matrix dimension. We also perform extensive numerical simulations to validate our results and explore the convergence properties of the average singular value.

Our work builds on previous research in the field of random matrix theory, which has focused primarily on real random matrices. By extending these results to complex random matrices, we provide new insights into the behavior of complex systems, and highlight the unique challenges and opportunities presented by working with complex data. The decline of the average singular value with growing matrix dimension observed in this work has far-reaching consequences for the analysis and understanding of large-scale complex systems, and will inform the development of novel techniques for modeling and analyzing such systems.

In this paper, we present a theoretical analysis of the photoelectric effect induced by blackbody radiation as a potential heat energy harvesting mechanism. The photoelectric effect is a phenomenon where light incident on a material can eject electrons from its surface, and has been widely studied in the context of solar cells and other photovoltaic devices. However, most previous studies have focused on the use of visible or ultraviolet light, which are not readily available in many industrial settings.

In contrast, blackbody radiation is a ubiquitous source of thermal radiation that is present in any environment at a temperature above absolute zero. By analyzing the spectral properties of blackbody radiation, we show that it can also be used to induce the photoelectric effect and potentially harness waste heat energy. We develop a theoretical model based on the Einstein-Smoluchowski equation and the Drude-Lorentz model, which allows us to calculate the photoelectric current generated by blackbody radiation. Our results indicate that the photoelectric effect induced by blackbody radiation can produce significant power output, especially at high temperatures.

We also discuss the feasibility of implementing this concept in practical applications, such as heat exchangers and thermophotovoltaic systems. Our analysis suggests that the efficiency of these systems could be significantly improved by incorporating a blackbody radiator, leading to enhanced heat energy conversion and reduced energy loss. This work provides new insights into the potential of using blackbody radiation for heat energy harvesting, and may open up novel avenues for sustainable energy capture and utilization.

In this paper, we present a unified solution to three longstanding open problems in number theory, namely the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer Conjecture, the Hodge Conjecture, and the Taniyama-Shimura Conjecture. Our approach leverages recent advances in algebraic geometry and representation theory to establish a deep connection between these seemingly disparate problems.

We first introduce a novel framework that enables us to study the arithmetic of elliptic curves and their associated moduli spaces in a new light. This allows us to establish a precise relationship between the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer Conjecture and the Hodge Conjecture, which has eluded mathematicians for decades.

Next, we exploit this connection to prove the Taniyama-Shimura Conjecture, thereby resolving a century-old problem in number theory. Our proof relies on a combination of advanced geometric techniques and delicate arithmetic computations, and it provides strong evidence for the truth of the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer Conjecture in a broad range of cases.

Finally, we demonstrate that our method can be further generalized to attack other important problems in number theory, such as the Riemann Hypothesis and the Hodge-Atiyah theorem. Our work not only furnishes a powerful toolkit for tackling these challenges but also underscores the profound interconnectedness of different areas of mathematics.

The main results of this paper have far-reaching implications for our understanding of the arithmetic of elliptic curves, the geometry of moduli spaces, and the structure of Galois representations in number theory. In this paper, we present a novel approach to semantic image segmentation called Double Similarity Distillation (DSD). This method leverages the power of similarity learning to improve the accuracy and efficiency of semantic segmentation models.

Existing methods for semantic segmentation often rely on complex neural network architectures that require large amounts of annotated data and computational resources to train. In contrast, our proposed method uses a simple and efficient framework that exploits the concept of similarity between images. We demonstrate that by distilling the similarity information from two different levels of abstraction, we can significantly improve the performance of a semantic segmentation model.

The key insight behind DSD is that similarities between images can be used to transfer knowledge across different domains and tasks. Specifically, we use a pre-trained convolutional neural network (CNN) to extract features from pairs of images that are semantically similar but visually distinct. These feature representations are then distilled into a lower-dimensional space using a contrastive loss function, which encourages the model to focus on the most discriminative aspects of the input data.

We evaluate the effectiveness of DSD on several benchmark datasets, including PASCAL VOC and Cityscapes. Our results show that with minimal annotation effort and computation cost, DSD achieves competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art segmentation methods. Furthermore, we perform ablation studies to analyze the contribution of each component in our framework, providing insights into the role of similarity learning in this task.

Our work has important implications for real-world applications where labeled data is scarce or difficult to obtain. By harnessing the power of similarity learning, we can develop more efficient and effective segmentation models that can adapt to new environments and objects. The simplicity and generalizability of DSD make it an attractive solution for various computer vision tasks beyond segmentation, such as object detection and tracking.

This breakthrough has significant implications for the study of biological structures and materials, and paves the way for new discoveries in fields such as drug discovery, materials science, and nanotechnology.

This paper addresses the problems of relabeling and summarizing posterior
distributions that typically arise, in a Bayesian framework, when dealing with
signal decomposition problems with an unknown number of components. Such
posterior distributions are defined over union of subspaces of differing
dimensionality and can be sampled from using modern Monte Carlo techniques, for
instance the increasingly popular RJ-MCMC method. No generic approach is
available, however, to summarize the resulting variable-dimensional samples and
extract from them component-specific parameters. We propose a novel approach,
named Variable-dimensional Approximate Posterior for Relabeling and Summarizing
(VAPoRS), to this problem, which consists in approximating the posterior
distribution of interest by a "simple"---but still
variable-dimensional---parametric distribution. The distance between the two
distributions is measured using the Kullback-Leibler divergence, and a
Stochastic EM-type algorithm, driven by the RJ-MCMC sampler, is proposed to
estimate the parameters. Two signal decomposition problems are considered, to
show the capability of VAPoRS both for relabeling and for summarizing variable
dimensional posterior distributions: the classical problem of detecting and
estimating sinusoids in white Gaussian noise on the one hand, and a particle
counting problem motivated by the Pierre Auger project in astrophysics on the
other hand.

Deep learning techniques for 3D brain vessel image segmentation have not been
as successful as in the segmentation of other organs and tissues. This can be
explained by two factors. First, deep learning techniques tend to show poor
performances at the segmentation of relatively small objects compared to the
size of the full image. Second, due to the complexity of vascular trees and the
small size of vessels, it is challenging to obtain the amount of annotated
training data typically needed by deep learning methods. To address these
problems, we propose a novel annotation-efficient deep learning vessel
segmentation framework. The framework avoids pixel-wise annotations, only
requiring weak patch-level labels to discriminate between vessel and non-vessel
2D patches in the training set, in a setup similar to the CAPTCHAs used to
differentiate humans from bots in web applications. The user-provided weak
annotations are used for two tasks: 1) to synthesize pixel-wise pseudo-labels
for vessels and background in each patch, which are used to train a
segmentation network, and 2) to train a classifier network. The classifier
network allows to generate additional weak patch labels, further reducing the
annotation burden, and it acts as a noise filter for poor quality images. We
use this framework for the segmentation of the cerebrovascular tree in
Time-of-Flight angiography (TOF) and Susceptibility-Weighted Images (SWI). The
results show that the framework achieves state-of-the-art accuracy, while
reducing the annotation time by ~77% w.r.t. learning-based segmentation methods
using pixel-wise labels for training.

We employed an ensemble of three dimensional U-Net models, which are widely used in medical image analysis due to their robust performance on segmenting complex structures. This work demonstrates that combining state-of-the art deep learning techniques with advanced feature extraction methods can lead to improved diagnosis and prognosis capabilities in neuro-oncology.

In this study, we investigate the superconducting properties of niobium (Nb) thin films in the BiOCl/Nb heterostructure. The heterostructures were fabricated using a combination of molecular beam epitaxy and pulsed laser deposition techniques. The structural and compositional characteristics of the samples were analyzed using X-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy, and energy-dispersive spectroscopy. The superconducting properties were evaluated using transport measurements, including direct current (DC) critical current density and magnetoresistance.

Specifically, we observed a higher critical temperature (Tc = 18 K) and lower critical field (Hc2 = 50 mT) for the BiOCl/Nb heterostructure compared to pure Nb films under identical conditions. We attribute these improvements to the presence of an electron gas at the interface between the BiOCl and Nb layers, which increases the carriers' concentration and mobility. Additionally, defects introduced by the low lattice mismatch between the two materials improve the vortex pinning centers, leading to increased Jc. Our findings demonstrate the potential of combining complex oxides with traditional superconductors to create high-performance hybrid structures with enhanced superconducting properties. This approach could lead to novel applications in various fields such as power transmission, medical imaging, and quantum computing.

BiSeNet has been proved to be a popular two-stream network for real-time
segmentation. However, its principle of adding an extra path to encode spatial
information is time-consuming, and the backbones borrowed from pretrained
tasks, e.g., image classification, may be inefficient for image segmentation
due to the deficiency of task-specific design. To handle these problems, we
propose a novel and efficient structure named Short-Term Dense Concatenate
network (STDC network) by removing structure redundancy. Specifically, we
gradually reduce the dimension of feature maps and use the aggregation of them
for image representation, which forms the basic module of STDC network. In the
decoder, we propose a Detail Aggregation module by integrating the learning of
spatial information into low-level layers in single-stream manner. Finally, the
low-level features and deep features are fused to predict the final
segmentation results. Extensive experiments on Cityscapes and CamVid dataset
demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by achieving promising trade-off
between segmentation accuracy and inference speed. On Cityscapes, we achieve
71.9% mIoU on the test set with a speed of 250.4 FPS on NVIDIA GTX 1080Ti,
which is 45.2% faster than the latest methods, and achieve 76.8% mIoU with 97.0
FPS while inferring on higher resolution images.

Trainsenvornet : A network composed of both trees and regular grids; this network can be fed images which are segmented into pixels through standard training or supervised classification procedures (it consists only of image segments). It trains faster than the other type because it has more weights attached towards higher dimensionality of data and thus allows the weight calculations to be optimized without sacrificing performance (e.g., by finding better connections between sparse elements). In this study, we investigate the superconductivity of niobium (Nb) thin films in the context of BiOCl/Nb heterostructures. By depositing Nb thin films on top of a BiOCl substrate, we observe a significant enhancement in the superconducting properties of the Nb film. We report a critical temperature (Tc) of 18 K for the Nb film in the BiOCl/Nb heterostructure, which is significantly higher than the Tc of 10 K observed for a pure Nb film.

We attribute this enhancement in superconductivity to the presence of the BiOCl substrate, which introduces a strong electron-phonon coupling in the Nb film. This is supported by our theoretical calculations, which show a strong electron-phonon coupling constant in the BiOCl/Nb heterostructure. We also observe a reduction in the film's resistivity and an increase in its Hall coefficient, indicating a higher electron density and improved carrier mobility.

Our results demonstrate the potential of using BiOCl/Nb heterostructures for high-temperature superconducting applications. The observed enhancement in superconductivity is promising for the development of new materials and devices that can operate at higher temperatures and with improved performance. Further studies are needed to fully understand the underlying mechanisms and to optimize the properties of these heterostructures for practical applications.

We find that this relationship has been stable over time, with no evidence of a decline in the influence of individualism on smoking prevalence. Our results suggest that policies aimed at reducing smoking rates may be more effective if they take into account the cultural and societal factors that influence smoking behaviors, rather than solely focusing on individual-level interventions. In this paper, we propose ComBiNet, a compact convolutional Bayesian neural network designed specifically for image segmentation tasks. ComBiNet combines the strengths of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and Bayesian neural networks (BNNs), allowing for efficient and accurate segmentation while minimizing memory requirements. Our novel approach leverages a compact architecture that significantly reduces the number of parameters and computations required for training and inference, making it particularly suitable for resource-constrained devices.

We evaluated ComBiNet on several benchmark datasets, including Cityscapes, PASCAL VOC, and CamVid, and compared its performance to state-of-the-art models. The results demonstrate that ComBiNet achieves competitive segmentation accuracy with a significant reduction in computational cost. Specifically, our model shows an average of 45% fewer parameters and 30% less computation per pixel than existing CNN and BNN models. Furthermore, we show that ComBiNet can be easily integrated into real-world applications such as object detection and autonomous driving systems.

Our key contributions include:

* A novel compact convolutional Bayesian neural network architecture that efficiently integrates Bayesian and convolutional layers
* An effective training methodology using a combination of stochastic gradient descent and dropout regularization
* State-of-the-art segmentation accuracy on multiple benchmark datasets while maintaining low computational complexity

In summary, ComBiNet presents a significant step forward in the field of image segmentation by providing a computationally efficient, memory-friendly, and highly accurate solution for resource-constrained environments.

This report describes the design, implementation, evaluation and original
enhancements to the Live-Wire method for 2D and 3D image segmentation.
Live-Wire 2D employs a semi-automatic paradigm; the user is asked to select a
few boundary points of the object to segment, to steer the process in the right
direction, while the result is displayed in real time. In our implementation
segmentation is extended to three dimensions by performing this process on a
slice-by-slice basis. User's time and involvement is further reduced by
allowing him to specify object contours in planes orthogonal to the slices. If
these planes are chosen strategically, Live-Wire 3D can perform 2D segmentation
in the plane of each slice automatically. This report also proposes two
improvements to the original method, path heating and a new graph edge feature
function based on variance of path properties along the boundary. We show that
these improvements lead up to a 33% reduction in interaction with the user, and
improved delineation in presence of strong interfering edges.

In this paper, we present a novel approach to referring segmentation that leverages cross-modal progressive comprehension to improve object segmentation in images. Referring segmentation is the task of segregating objects in an image based on their mentions in natural language descriptions. Existing approaches have relied heavily on visual features and suffer from limitations in handling complex scenes with multiple objects or non-descriptive language. Our proposed method addresses these challenges by incorporating cognitive theories of human language understanding and vision, which posits that humans use language to guide attention and eye movements when describing visual stimuli.

We propose a two-stage framework that first generates region proposals using a DeepLabv3+ model and then refines them using a Cross-Modal Attention Module (CMAM). The CMAM integrates information from both modalities through multi-layer perceptron networks, allowing it to learn how to weigh the importance of different words in relation to the visual context. We evaluate our model on three benchmark datasets and show significant improvements over existing methods, especially in cases where the language description contains incomplete or ambiguous information.

Our experiments also provide insights into the role of each modality in referring segmentation, revealing that both visual and linguistic cues play crucial roles in achieving optimal performance. Furthermore, we analyze the effectiveness of our attention mechanism and demonstrate its ability to focus on relevant regions and dismiss irrelevant ones, even in presence of distractors. Overall, this work represents an important step towards developing more accurate and robust real-time referring segmentation systems that can enable improved scene understanding capabilities for various applications such as robotics, autonomous vehicles, and virtual assistants.

We evaluate the performance of TernausNet on several benchmark datasets, including Cityscapes, PASCAL VOC, and CIFAR-10. Our experiments show that our proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art segmentation models, achieving an average IoU score of 95% on Cityscapes and 87% on PASCAL VOC. We also perform ablation studies to analyze the contributions of different components of our model, demonstrating the effectiveness of the pre-trained VGG11 encoder and the U-Net decoder.

Our work has important implications for real-world applications such as autonomous driving, robotics, and medical imaging, where accurate image segmentation is critical. histopathological gland segmentation adapting from one stain domain to another.

considers the differences of image color and style; 2) the feature-level
addresses the spatial inconsistency between two domains. The two components are
implemented as domain classifiers with adversarial training. We evaluate our
new approach using two gland segmentation datasets with H&E and DAB-H stains
respectively. The extensive experiments and ablation study demonstrate the
effectiveness of our approach on the domain adaptive segmentation task. We show
that the proposed approach performs favorably against other state-of-the-art
methods.

In this paper, we explore the problem of semantic image segmentation, which involves assigning a class label to each pixel in an image. While category-level semantic segmentation focuses on predicting the class label of each object instance, instance-level segmentation aims to identify individual instances within a class. We propose a novel approach that bridges these two levels of segmentation by introducing a new granularity level: the instance prototype.

We introduce a probabilistic framework that models the relationship between objects, their categories, and theirinstance prototypes. This allows us to propagate information across different granularity levels and perform joint optimization of category-level and instance-level segmentation tasks. Our method improves upon state-of-the-art approaches by better capturing object boundaries and reducing confusion between similar instances.

Our experiments show that our proposed method outperforms previous work on several benchmark datasets including PASCAL VOC and COCO. Additionally, we analyze the benefits of our approach through ablation studies, demonstrating its robustness to various design choices.

This research has important implications for applications such as autonomous driving, robotics, and computer vision. By providing more accurate segmentations at multiple levels of granularity, we enable machines to better understand and interpret visual data, leading to improved performance in complex tasks.

layer-wise weight initialization using Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA).

values, greedy layer-wise pre-training (usually as Deep Belief Network or as

We compute the relative-order-v^4 contribution to gluon fragmentation into
quarkonium in the 3S1 color-singlet channel, using the nonrelativistic QCD
(NRQCD) factorization approach. The QCD fragmentation process contains infrared
divergences that produce single and double poles in epsilon in 4-2epsilon
dimensions. We devise subtractions that isolate the pole contributions, which
ultimately are absorbed into long-distance NRQCD matrix elements in the NRQCD
matching procedure. The matching procedure involves two-loop renormalizations
of the NRQCD operators. The subtractions are integrated over the phase space
analytically in 4-2epsilon dimensions, and the remainder is integrated over the
phase-space numerically. We find that the order-v^4 contribution is enhanced
relative to the order-v^0 contribution. However, the order-v^4 contribution is
not important numerically at the current level of precision of
quarkonium-hadroproduction phenomenology. We also estimate the contribution to
hadroproduction from gluon fragmentation into quarkonium in the 3PJ color-octet
channel and find that it is significant in comparison to the complete
next-to-leading-order-in-alpha_s contribution in that channel.

Quantum key distribution (QKD) is a method of secure communication that uses quantum mechanics to encode and decode messages. In a standard QKD system, two parties, traditionally referred to as Alice and Bob, share a secret key that is used to encrypt and decrypt messages. The security of the key relies on the principles of quantum mechanics, specifically the no-cloning theorem, which states that it is impossible to create a perfect copy of an arbitrary quantum state.

However, in practice, the implementation of QKD systems can be vulnerable to various types of attacks, such as side-channel attacks, which can compromise the security of the shared key. To overcome these vulnerabilities, researchers have proposed various countermeasures, including the use of entangled states, the implementation of quantum key distribution networks, and the development of measurement-device-independent (MDI) QKD protocols.

MDI QKD protocols eliminate the vulnerability of side-channel attacks by removing the measurement device from the quantum communication process. In these protocols, the measurement is performed by a trusted third party, known as Charlie, who publicly announces the measurement outcome. Alice and Bob can then use the announced outcome to extract their shared secret key.

In this paper, we propose a novel MDI QKD protocol that uses modified coherent states (MCSs) to encode the quantum information. MCSs are a generalization of the traditional coherent states, which are widely used in quantum optics. Our protocol exploits the properties of MCSs to enhance the security of the shared key and improve the performance of the QKD system.

We analyze the security of our protocol against various types of attacks, including intercept-and-resend attacks, entanglement attacks, and side-channel attacks. Our results show that our protocol provides a high level of security against these attacks and can be implemented with current technology.

We also perform a detailed analysis of the performance of our protocol in terms of the secret key rate, the quantum bit error rate (QBER), and the distance over which the key can be securely distributed. Our results show that our protocol outperforms existing MDI QKD

Deep learning methods have shown promising results in addressing this task, but they require significant computational resources and large amounts of labeled data.

To overcome these challenges, we introduce a piecewise training method that enables efficient training of deep structured models for semantic segmentation. Our approach partitions the input data into smaller regions and trains separate model parts for each region. This allows us to reduce the computational complexity and memory requirements of the training process without sacrificing accuracy.

We evaluate our method on several popular datasets and compare it with state-of-the-art techniques. The experimental results demonstrate that our proposed approach achieves better performance than existing methods while requiring significantly less training time and memory usage. We also conduct a series of ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of different components of our method and provide insights into their contributions.

Our main contributions are:

* A novel piecewise training method for efficient training of deep structured models for semantic segmentation
* Significant reduction of computational complexity and memory requirements compared to traditional training approaches
* Improved performance compared to state-of-the-art techniques while maintaining competitive accuracy
* Comprehensive analysis of the effects of various components of our method through ablation studies

The significance of our work lies in its ability to improve the efficiency of deep structured models for semantic segmentation, making them more accessible to researchers and practitioners who lack extensive computing resources. This breakthrough can accelerate advancements in computer vision and enable broader applications in areas such as autonomous driving, robotics, and medical imaging.

Cloud based medical image analysis has become popular recently due to the
high computation complexities of various deep neural network (DNN) based
frameworks and the increasingly large volume of medical images that need to be
processed. It has been demonstrated that for medical images the transmission
from local to clouds is much more expensive than the computation in the clouds
itself. Towards this, 3D image compression techniques have been widely applied
to reduce the data traffic. However, most of the existing image compression
techniques are developed around human vision, i.e., they are designed to
minimize distortions that can be perceived by human eyes. In this paper we will
use deep learning based medical image segmentation as a vehicle and demonstrate
that interestingly, machine and human view the compression quality differently.
Medical images compressed with good quality w.r.t. human vision may result in
inferior segmentation accuracy. We then design a machine vision oriented 3D
image compression framework tailored for segmentation using DNNs. Our method
automatically extracts and retains image features that are most important to
the segmentation. Comprehensive experiments on widely adopted segmentation
frameworks with HVSMR 2016 challenge dataset show that our method can achieve
significantly higher segmentation accuracy at the same compression rate, or
much better compression rate under the same segmentation accuracy, when
compared with the existing JPEG 2000 method. To the best of the authors'
knowledge, this is the first machine vision guided medical image compression
framework for segmentation in the clouds.

In this paper, we investigate Morse boundaries of proper geodesic metric spaces. We establish a characterization of Morse boundaries in terms of convexity and curvature bounds, showing that they can be described as a quotient space of a geodesic hyperbolic space by a certain finite group action.We also demonstrate that Morse boundaries are always Alexandrov spaces with curvature bounded below, generalizing results from Riemannian geometry to the setting of geodesic metric spaces with curvature bounds.

Our main result provides a new insight into the structure of Morse boundaries: they are necessarily `rimable', meaning they admit a local isometric embedding into Euclidean space combined with a notion of a` horizon' which is intrinsically defined in termsof the metric space. This property allows us to classify Morse boundaries up to quasi-isometry using tools from geometric measure theory and representation theory. Furthermore, we introduce and study the concept of `generalized notion of souls' of Morse boundary components, providing another way to understand their structural properties. Our work builds on earlier studies in the field while introducing several innovative techniques that significantly advances our understanding of Morse boundaries in geodesic metric spaces .It is intended for researchers and advanced students interested in the interplay between geometry, topology and analysis in non-Riemannian settings

manifold; when "looking at it from infinity" (following Gromov), we obtain the
tangent cone at infinity, which is parametrized by equivalence classes of
complete geodesics. In the present paper, we study the associated limit for the
family of metrics on the toric variety, its quantization, and degeneration of
generic divisors.
  The limits of the corresponding K\"ahler polarizations become degenerate
along the Lagrangian fibration defined by the moment map. This allows us to
interpolate continuously between geometric quantizations in the holomorphic and
real polarizations and show that the monomial holomorphic sections of the
prequantum bundle converge to Dirac delta distributions supported on
Bohr-Sommerfeld fibers.

study the limit of compact hypersurface amoebas and show that in Legendre

our approach gives a different, complementary, perspective on the relation
